In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.
The earth was then formless and desolate, darkness brooded over the abyss, and the Spirit of God hovered upon the face of the waters.
And God said, “Let there be light,” and light came into being.
God perceived that the light was good, and He sundered the light from the darkness.
God designated the light Day, and the darkness He designated Night; and evening came, and morning came—the first day.
And God said, “Let an expanse be established amid the waters, separating water from water.”
So God fashioned the expanse and separated the waters beneath the expanse from the waters above it, and it was so.
God named the expanse Heaven; and evening came, and morning came—the second day.
And God said, “Let the waters beneath the heavens be gathered into a single place, that the dry land may emerge,” and it was so.
God named the dry land Earth, and the gathered waters He named Seas; and God saw that it was good.
Then God said, “Let the earth produce vegetation—herbs bearing seed and fruit-bearing trees, each according to its kind, with seed within them—upon the earth,” and it was so.
The earth produced vegetation—herbs bearing seed according to their kinds and trees bearing fruit with seed in them according to their kinds—and God saw that it was good.
And evening came, and morning came—the third day.
And God said, “Let luminaries appear in the expanse of the heavens to distinguish day from night, and let them serve as signs, and for appointed seasons, and for days and years.
Let them be luminaries in the expanse of the heavens to illuminate the earth,” and it was so.
God made the two great luminaries—the greater to govern the day and the lesser to govern the night—and the stars.
God placed them in the expanse of the heavens to illuminate the earth,
to govern day and night, and to separate light from darkness; and God saw that it was good.
And evening came, and morning came—the fourth day.
And God said, “Let the waters swarm with living creatures, and let birds fly above the earth across the face of the expanse of the heavens.”

So God created the great sea monsters and every living creature that moves, with which the waters swarmed, according to their kinds, and every winged bird according to its kind; and God saw that it was good.
God blessed them, saying, “Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the waters in the seas, and let birds multiply on the earth.”
And evening came, and morning came—the fifth day.
And God said, “Let the earth bring forth living creatures according to their kinds—livestock, creeping things, and beasts of the earth according to their kinds,” and it was so.
God made the beasts of the earth according to their kinds, the livestock according to their kinds, and all that creeps on the ground according to its kind; and God saw that it was good.

Then God said, “Let Us make man in Our image, according to Our likeness, and let them exercise dominion over the fish of the sea, the birds of the heavens, the livestock, all the earth, and every creeping thing that creeps upon the earth.”
So God created man in His own image; in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them.

God blessed them and said to them, “Be fruitful and multiply, fill the earth and subdue it, and exercise dominion over the fish of the sea, the birds of the heavens, and every living thing that moves upon the earth.”
God said, “Behold, I have given to you every plant yielding seed that is upon the face of all the earth, and every tree whose fruit contains seed; to you it shall be for food.
And to every beast of the earth, every bird of the heavens, and everything that creeps on the earth, which possesses the breath of life, I have given every green plant for food,” and it was so.
And God saw all that He had made, and behold, it was exceedingly good. And evening came, and morning came—the sixth day.
Thus were the heavens and the earth brought to their consummation, together with the totality of their celestial and terrestrial hosts.
By the seventh day God had brought to completion the labor that He had undertaken; and on that seventh day He desisted from every species of work that He had performed.
God then blessed the seventh day and consecrated it, for on it He rested from all the creative labor that He had undertaken to perform.
Such is the genealogy of the heavens and the earth at the time of their creation: when the LORD God fashioned the earth and the heavens,

no shrub of the field had yet manifested itself upon the earth, nor had any herb of the field yet burgeoned, because the LORD God had not caused rain to fall upon the earth, and there was no human being to cultivate the soil;
yet a mist ascended from the earth and irrigated the entire face of the ground.
Then the LORD God fashioned the human being from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, so that the human being became a living being.
Moreover, the LORD God had planted a garden in Eden, toward the east, and there He placed the human being whom He had formed.

Out of the ground the LORD God caused to spring every tree that is delightful to behold and salutary for nourishment; and in the midst of the garden were the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.
A river issued forth from Eden to irrigate the garden, and from thence it divided and became four headstreams.
The first is called Pishon; it circumnavigates the whole land of Havilah, where gold is found.
The gold of that land is excellent; bdellium and onyx stone are also there.
The second river is called Gihon; it circumnavigates the whole land of Cush.
The third river is called Tigris; it flows eastward of Assyria. And the fourth river is the Euphrates.
The LORD God took the man and settled him in the garden of Eden, to cultivate it and to keep it.
And the LORD God issued a command to the man, saying, “You may freely eat from every tree of the garden;
but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat, for in the day that you eat from it you shall surely die.”
Then the LORD God said, “It is not good for the man to be alone; I will make for him a helper commensurate with him.”

Now the LORD God had formed out of the ground every beast of the field and every bird of the heavens, and He brought them to the man to see what he would call them; and whatever the man called each living creature, that became its name.
The man therefore bestowed names upon all the cattle, upon the birds of the heavens, and upon every beast of the field; yet for the man no helper was found who was commensurate with him.
So the LORD God caused a deep sleep to fall upon the man, and while he slept He took one of his ribs and closed up the flesh in its place.
And from the rib that the LORD God had taken from the man He fashioned a woman, and He brought her to the man.
Then the man said, “This is now bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called Woman, because she was taken out of Man.”
Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and cleave to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.
And the man and his wife were both naked, yet they were not ashamed.
Now the serpent was more crafty than any beast of the field that the the LORD God had made, and he said to the woman, “Did God indeed say, ‘You shall not eat from any tree of the garden’?”
The woman said to the serpent, “We may eat of the fruit of the trees of the garden,
but God said, ‘You shall not eat of the fruit of the tree that is in the midst of the garden, nor shall you touch it, lest you die.’”
The serpent said to the woman, “You will not surely die.
For God knows that in the day you eat of it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.”

So when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was desirable to make one wise, she took of its fruit and ate; and she also gave some to her husband, who was with her, and he ate.
Then the eyes of both were opened, and they knew that they were naked; and they sewed fig leaves together and made themselves loincloths.

And they heard the sound of the the LORD God walking in the garden in the breeze of the day, and the man and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the the LORD God among the trees of the garden.
The LORD God called to the man and said to him, “Where are you?”
He said, “I heard your voice in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked; and I hid myself.”
He said, “Who told you that you were naked? Have you eaten of the tree of which I commanded you not to eat?”
The man said, “The woman whom You gave to be with me—she gave me fruit of the tree, and I ate.”
Then the the LORD God said to the woman, “What is this that you have done?” The woman said, “The serpent deceived me, and I ate.”

The LORD God said to the serpent, “Because you have done this, cursed are you above all livestock and above every beast of the field; on your belly you shall go, and dust you shall eat all the days of your life.
I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring; he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel.”
To the woman He said, “I will surely multiply your pain in childbearing; in pain you shall bring forth children. Your desire shall be for your husband, and he shall rule over you.”

And to Adam He said, “Because you have listened to the voice of your wife and have eaten of the tree of which I commanded you, ‘You shall not eat of it,’ cursed is the ground because of you; in pain you shall eat of it all the days of your life.
Thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you, and you shall eat the plants of the field.
By the sweat of your face you shall eat bread, till you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken; for you are dust, and to dust you shall return.”
The man called his wife’s name Eve, because she was the mother of all living.
And the the LORD God made for Adam and for his wife garments of skins and clothed them.
Then the the LORD God said, “Behold, the man has become like one of Us, knowing good and evil. Now, lest he reach out his hand and take also of the tree of life and eat, and live forever—”
Therefore the the LORD God sent him out from the garden of Eden to work the ground from which he was taken.
He drove out the man, and at the east of the garden of Eden He placed the cherubim and a flaming sword that turned every way to guard the way to the tree of life.
Adam knew his wife Eve; she conceived and bore Cain, declaring, “With the help of the LORD I have acquired a man.”
She bore again, this time his brother Abel. Abel became a shepherd, whereas Cain tilled the soil.
After some time had elapsed, Cain brought an offering to the LORD from the fruit of the ground.
Abel, for his part, brought some of the firstlings of his flock, along with their fat portions. The LORD regarded Abel and his offering with favor,
but He did not regard Cain and his offering. Cain therefore grew intensely wrathful, and his countenance fell.
The LORD said to Cain, “Why are you incensed, and why has your countenance fallen?
If you act rightly, will you not be accepted? Yet if you do not act rightly, sin is crouching at the door; its desire is directed toward you, but you must master it.”
Cain spoke to his brother Abel. And when they were in the field, Cain rose up against his brother Abel and slew him.
The LORD said to Cain, “Where is your brother Abel?” Cain replied, “I do not know. Am I my brother’s keeper?”
The LORD said, “What have you done? The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to Me from the ground.”
The LORD continued, “Now you are cursed and banished from the ground, which opened its mouth to receive your brother’s blood from your hand.
When you cultivate the ground, it will no longer yield its vigor to you; you will become a restless fugitive upon the earth.”
Cain said to the LORD, “My punishment exceeds what I can endure.
Behold, You have driven me this day from the land, and from Your presence I shall be concealed. I will be a restless fugitive upon the earth, and anyone who encounters me will kill me.”
The LORD said to him, “No; if anyone slays Cain, vengeance shall be exacted upon him sevenfold.” And the LORD placed a mark upon Cain, so that whoever encountered him might not strike him down.
So Cain departed from the LORD’s presence and settled in the land of Nod, east of Eden.
Cain was intimate with his wife; she conceived and bore Enoch. Cain built a city and named it after his son Enoch.
To Enoch was born Irad; Irad fathered Mehujael; Mehujael fathered Methushael; and Methushael fathered Lamech.
Lamech took two wives: one named Adah and the other Zillah.
Adah bore Jabal, the progenitor of those who dwell in tents and tend livestock.
His brother was named Jubal, the progenitor of all who play the lyre and the pipe.
Zillah likewise bore Tubal-cain, a forger of every implement of bronze and iron; the sister of Tubal-cain was Naamah.
Lamech said to his wives, “Adah and Zillah, hear my voice; wives of Lamech, attend to my words: I have slain a man for wounding me, and a young man for bruising me.
If Cain is avenged sevenfold, then Lamech shall be avenged seventy-sevenfold.”
Adam was intimate with his wife once more; she bore a son and named him Seth, saying, “God has granted me another offspring in place of Abel, because Cain killed him.”
To Seth also a son was born, and he named him Enosh. At that time people began to invoke the name of the LORD.
This is the book of the generations of Adam: on the day when God created humankind, He fashioned him in the likeness of God;
male and female He created them, He blessed them, and He called their name Adam in the day of their creation.
Adam lived one hundred and thirty years, and he begot a son in his own likeness, after his image, and he called his name Seth.
After he begot Seth, the days of Adam were eight hundred years, and he begot sons and daughters.
Thus all the days of Adam amounted to nine hundred and thirty years, and he died.
Seth lived one hundred and five years, and he begot Enosh.
After he begot Enosh, Seth lived eight hundred and seven years, and he begot sons and daughters.
Thus all the days of Seth amounted to nine hundred and twelve years, and he died.
Enosh lived ninety years, and he begot Kenan.
After he begot Kenan, Enosh lived eight hundred and fifteen years, and he begot sons and daughters.
Thus all the days of Enosh amounted to nine hundred and five years, and he died.
Kenan lived seventy years, and he begot Mahalalel.
After he begot Mahalalel, Kenan lived eight hundred and forty years, and he begot sons and daughters.
Thus all the days of Kenan amounted to nine hundred and ten years, and he died.
Mahalalel lived sixty-five years, and he begot Jared.
After he begot Jared, Mahalalel lived eight hundred and thirty years, and he begot sons and daughters.
Thus all the days of Mahalalel amounted to eight hundred and ninety-five years, and he died.
Jared lived one hundred and sixty-two years, and he begot Enoch.
After he begot Enoch, Jared lived eight hundred years, and he begot sons and daughters.
Thus all the days of Jared amounted to nine hundred and sixty-two years, and he died.
Enoch lived sixty-five years, and he begot Methuselah.
After he begot Methuselah, Enoch walked with God three hundred years, and he begot sons and daughters.
Thus all the days of Enoch amounted to three hundred and sixty-five years.
Enoch walked with God, and he was no more, for God took him.
Methuselah lived one hundred and eighty-seven years, and he begot Lamech.
After he begot Lamech, Methuselah lived seven hundred and eighty-two years, and he begot sons and daughters.
Thus all the days of Methuselah amounted to nine hundred and sixty-nine years, and he died.
Lamech lived one hundred and eighty-two years, and he begot a son.
He called his name Noah, saying, “This one shall comfort us concerning our work and the toil of our hands, because of the ground which the LORD has cursed.”
After he begot Noah, Lamech lived five hundred and ninety-five years, and he begot sons and daughters.
Thus all the days of Lamech amounted to seven hundred and seventy-seven years, and he died.
Noah was five hundred years old, and Noah begot Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
When the human race began to proliferate across the face of the earth, and daughters were born unto them,
the sons of God beheld that the daughters of men were beautiful, and they took wives for themselves from among all whom they selected.
The LORD said, “My Spirit shall not contend with humankind in perpetuity, for he is but flesh; nevertheless, his days shall be limited to one hundred and twenty years.”

The Nephilim were upon the earth in those days—and also afterward—when the sons of God consorted with the daughters of men, who bore children unto them. These were the mighty men of antiquity, men of renown.
The LORD saw that the wickedness of humankind was great upon the earth, and that every inclination of the thoughts of his heart was solely evil all the day long.
And the LORD regretted that He had made humankind upon the earth, and He was grieved in His heart.
The LORD said, “I will blot out humankind, whom I have created, from the face of the ground—both man and beast, creeping thing and bird of the heavens—for I regret that I have made them.”
But Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD.
These are the generations of Noah. Noah was a righteous man, blameless among his contemporaries; Noah walked with God.
And Noah fathered three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
Now the earth was corrupted before God, and the earth was filled with violence.
And God saw the earth, and behold, it was corrupted, for all flesh had corrupted its conduct upon the earth.
God said to Noah, “The end of all flesh has come before Me, for the earth is filled with violence by their doing; and behold, I am about to destroy them together with the earth.
Construct for yourself an ark of gopher wood; make compartments within the ark, and seal it inside and out with pitch.
And this is how you shall make it: the length of the ark shall be three hundred cubits, its breadth fifty cubits, and its height thirty cubits.
You shall make a roof for the ark, finishing it to a cubit above; and you shall set the door of the ark in its side; with lower, second, and third decks you shall make it.
“And I, behold, I am bringing a deluge of waters upon the earth, to destroy all flesh in which is the breath of life from under heaven; everything that is on the earth shall perish.
But I will establish My covenant with you; and you shall enter the ark—you, your sons, your wife, and your sons’ wives with you.
And of every living thing of all flesh, two of every sort you shall bring into the ark, to keep them alive with you; they shall be male and female.
Of the birds after their kind, and of the beasts after their kind, of every creeping thing of the ground after its kind, two of every sort shall come to you, to keep them alive.
And you shall take for yourself of every food that is eaten, and you shall gather it, and it shall be food for you and for them.”
And Noah did according to all that God had commanded him; thus he acted.
The LORD said to Noah, "Come into the ark—you and your entire household—for I have found you righteous before Me in this generation.
You are to take with you seven pairs of every clean animal, a male with its mate, and one pair of every unclean animal, a male with its mate,
as well as seven pairs of the birds of the sky, male and female, so that their offspring may be preserved upon the face of the whole earth.
For in seven days I will cause rain to fall upon the earth for forty days and forty nights, and I will eradicate from the face of the earth every living thing that I have made."
Noah executed all that the LORD had commanded him.
Noah was six hundred years old when the deluge came upon the earth.
Noah entered the ark with his sons, his wife, and his sons' wives, to find refuge from the waters of the flood.
Clean and unclean animals, birds, and every creature that crawls upon the ground
came to Noah and entered the ark, two by two, male and female, as God had commanded Noah.
After seven days, the floodwaters came upon the earth.
In the six hundredth year of Noah's life, on the seventeenth day of the second month—on that very day—all the fountains of the great deep burst forth, and the floodgates of heaven were opened.
Rain fell upon the earth for forty days and forty nights.
On that very day Noah and his sons—Shem, Ham, and Japheth—together with Noah's wife and the three wives of his sons entered the ark.

They were joined by every beast according to its kind, all livestock according to their kinds, every creature that moves along the ground according to its kind, and every bird according to its kind, every winged creature.
They came to Noah and entered the ark, two by two, of all flesh in which there was the breath of life.
Those that entered, male and female of every living creature, came as God had commanded Noah; then the LORD shut him in.
The deluge remained upon the earth for forty days, and the waters increased and lifted the ark high above the earth.
The waters prevailed and increased greatly upon the earth, and the ark drifted upon the surface of the waters.
The waters prevailed so overwhelmingly upon the earth that all the high mountains beneath the whole heaven were covered.
The waters rose fifteen cubits above the mountains.
Every living thing that moved on the earth perished—birds, livestock, beasts, every creature that swarms upon the earth, and all humanity.
Everything that had the breath of life in its nostrils and lived on dry land died.

Thus He obliterated every living thing upon the face of the earth—humanity and livestock, creeping things and birds of the air—and they were blotted out from the earth. Only Noah and those with him in the ark survived.
The waters prevailed upon the earth for one hundred fifty days.
When God remembered Noah, and every living creature, and all the livestock that were with him in the ark, He caused a wind to pass over the earth, and the waters abated.
The fountains of the deep and the windows of heaven were closed, and the rain from heaven was withheld.
The waters steadily retreated from the earth in a continual ebb and flow, and at the end of one hundred fifty days they had markedly diminished.
The ark came to rest upon the mountains of Ararat on the seventeenth day of the seventh month.
The waters continued to abate until the tenth month, and on the first day of that month the summits of the mountains became visible.
At the end of forty days Noah opened the window he had made in the ark.
He sent forth the raven, and it went out and returned repeatedly until the waters had dried from the earth.
Then he sent out the dove to ascertain whether the waters had abated from the face of the ground.

But the dove found no resting place for the sole of its foot, and it returned to him at the ark, because the waters still covered the whole earth; so he extended his hand, took it, and brought it back into the ark beside him.
He waited yet another seven days and again sent the dove out of the ark.
In the evening it returned to him, and there in its beak was a freshly plucked olive leaf; then Noah knew that the waters had receded from the earth.
He waited another seven days and sent out the dove, but it did not return to him again.

In the six hundred and first year, on the first day of the first month, the waters had dried from the earth. Noah removed the covering of the ark and looked, and behold, the surface of the ground was dry.
In the second month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, the earth was dry.
Then God spoke to Noah, saying,
"Come out of the ark—you and your wife, your sons and your sons' wives with you.

Bring out with you every living creature of all flesh that is with you—birds, beasts, and every creeping thing that creeps on the earth—so that they may swarm upon the earth and be fruitful and multiply upon it."
So Noah came out, together with his sons, his wife, and his sons' wives.
Every animal, every creeping thing, and every bird—everything that moves on the earth—went out of the ark according to their families.
Then Noah built an altar to the LORD and took from every clean animal and every clean bird, and offered burnt offerings on the altar.

The LORD smelled the soothing aroma, and the LORD said in His heart, "I will not again curse the ground on account of man, for the inclination of man's heart is evil from his youth; nor will I again strike down every living thing, as I have done.
As long as the earth endures, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night shall never cease."
God blessed Noah and his sons, and He addressed them thus: “Procreate and proliferate, and replenish the earth.

A reverential terror and dread of you shall fall upon every terrestrial beast, upon every avian creature of the heavens, upon every creeping thing of the ground, and upon all the fish of the sea; they are consigned to your dominion.
Every living creature that moves shall constitute sustenance for you; even as I conferred upon you the verdure of vegetation, so now I bestow upon you all things.
Nevertheless, you shall not consume flesh together with its life—that is, its blood.
Moreover, for your lifeblood I shall demand an accounting: from every beast I shall require it, and from humanity; from each man's fellow I shall exact retribution for the life of a man.
Whoever sheds the blood of a human being, by a human being shall his blood be shed, for God fashioned humanity in His own image.
And you, procreate and multiply; teem abundantly upon the earth and proliferate therein.”
Then God spoke to Noah and to his sons who were with him, saying,
“Behold, I am establishing My covenant with you and with your descendants after you,
and with every living creature that is with you—the birds, the cattle, and every beast of the earth with you, as many as emerged from the ark; it is ordained for every beast of the earth.
I establish My covenant with you: never again shall all flesh be extirpated by the waters of the deluge, nor shall there ever again be a flood to devastate the earth.”
And God said, “This is the token of the covenant that I am ratifying between Me and you and every living creature that is with you, for all successive generations:
I have set My bow in the cloud, and it shall serve as a sign of the covenant between Me and the earth.
When I bring clouds over the earth and the bow becomes visible in the clouds,
I will remember My covenant, which is between Me and you and every living creature of all flesh; and the waters shall never again swell into a flood to annihilate all flesh.
When the bow appears in the clouds, I shall behold it and remember the everlasting covenant between God and every living creature of all flesh that is upon the earth.”
God said to Noah, “This is the token of the covenant that I have established between Me and all flesh that is upon the earth.”
The sons of Noah who disembarked from the ark were Shem, Ham, and Japheth; Ham was the progenitor of Canaan.
These three were Noah's sons, and from them the entirety of the earth was peopled.
Noah, now a cultivator of the soil, planted a vineyard.
He imbibed of the wine, became inebriated, and lay exposed within his tent.
Ham, the father of Canaan, beheld his father's nakedness and reported it to his two brothers outside.
Then Shem and Japheth took a garment, draped it across their shoulders, walked backward, and covered their father's nakedness; with their faces averted, they did not behold their father's nakedness.
When Noah awakened from his wine and discerned what his youngest son had perpetrated against him,
he declared, “Cursed be Canaan; the lowliest of servants shall he become to his brothers.
Blessed be the LORD, the God of Shem; and let Canaan be his servant.
May God enlarge Japheth, and may he dwell in the tents of Shem, and let Canaan be his servant.”
After the deluge, Noah lived 350 years.
All the days of Noah amounted to 950 years, and then he died.
These, then, constitute the genealogical record of Noah—namely, Shem, Ham, and Japheth—and sons were born to them after the deluge.
The sons of Japheth were Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras.
The sons of Gomer were Ashkenaz, Riphath, and Togarmah.
The sons of Javan were Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim, and Dodanim.
From these the maritime peoples dispersed into their territories, each according to its language, by their clans, within their nations.
The sons of Ham were Cush, Mizraim, Put, and Canaan.
The sons of Cush were Seba, Havilah, Sabtah, Raamah, and Sabteca; the sons of Raamah were Sheba and Dedan.
Cush fathered Nimrod, who first became a mighty man upon the earth.
He was a mighty hunter before the LORD; therefore the proverb arose, "Like Nimrod—a mighty hunter before the LORD."
The inception of his dominion comprised Babel, Erech, Accad, and Calneh, situated in the land of Shinar.
From that land he went forth into Assyria and built Nineveh, Rehoboth-Ir, and Calah,
and Resen, which lies between Nineveh and the great city of Calah.
Mizraim fathered the Ludim, the Anamim, the Lehabim, and the Naphtuhim,
the Pathrusim, the Casluhim—from whom the Philistines emerged—and the Caphtorim.
Canaan fathered Sidon, his firstborn, and Heth,
and the Jebusites, the Amorites, and the Girgashites,
the Hivites, the Arkites, and the Sinites,
the Arvadites, the Zemarites, and the Hamathites; and afterward the clans of the Canaanites were dispersed.
The Canaanite border extended from Sidon toward Gerar, as far as Gaza, and toward Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim, as far as Lasha.
These are the sons of Ham, according to their clans, by their languages, within their lands and nations.
Sons were likewise born to Shem, the brother of Japheth the elder; Shem was the father of all the descendants of Eber.
The sons of Shem were Elam, Asshur, Arpachshad, Lud, and Aram.
The sons of Aram were Uz, Hul, Gether, and Mash.
Arpachshad fathered Shelah, and Shelah fathered Eber.
To Eber were born two sons: one was named Peleg, because in his days the earth was divided; and his brother was named Joktan.
Joktan fathered Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, and Jerah,
Ophir, Havilah, and Jobab; all these were the sons of Joktan.
Their settlement extended from Mesha toward Sephar, into the eastern hill country.
These are the sons of Shem, according to their clans, by their languages, within their lands and nations.
These are the clans of the sons of Noah, according to their generations, in their nations; and from these the nations were dispersed over the earth after the flood.
Initially, the entire earth possessed a single language and a unified lexicon.
As humanity migrated eastward, its members discovered a plain in the land of Shinar and established residence there.
They exhorted one another: "Come now, let us fabricate bricks and fire them thoroughly." Thus brick served them as stone, and bitumen as mortar.

Then they declared, "Come now, let us erect for ourselves a city and a tower whose summit reaches the heavens, and let us secure an enduring renown, lest we be dispersed across the face of the entire earth."
But the LORD descended to inspect the city and the tower that humankind had constructed.

The LORD said, "Observe, they constitute one people with one language, and this enterprise is merely the prelude to all they intend; henceforth nothing they scheme to accomplish will be unattainable for them.
Come, let us descend and there confound their speech, so that no one may comprehend his neighbor's tongue."
So the LORD scattered them from that place across the face of the whole earth, and they abandoned the construction of the city.
Therefore it was named Babel, because there the LORD confounded the speech of the whole earth, and from there the LORD dispersed them across the face of the whole earth.
These are the generations of Shem. When Shem had lived one hundred years, he fathered Arpachshad two years after the Flood.
After fathering Arpachshad, Shem lived five hundred years and fathered sons and daughters.
Arpachshad lived thirty-five years and fathered Shelah.
After fathering Shelah, Arpachshad lived four hundred and three years and fathered sons and daughters.
Shelah lived thirty years and fathered Eber.
After fathering Eber, Shelah lived four hundred and three years and fathered sons and daughters.
Eber lived thirty-four years and fathered Peleg.
After fathering Peleg, Eber lived four hundred and thirty years and fathered sons and daughters.
Peleg lived thirty years and fathered Reu.
After fathering Reu, Peleg lived two hundred and nine years and fathered sons and daughters.
Reu lived thirty-two years and fathered Serug.
After fathering Serug, Reu lived two hundred and seven years and fathered sons and daughters.
Serug lived thirty years and fathered Nahor.
After fathering Nahor, Serug lived two hundred years and fathered sons and daughters.
Nahor lived twenty-nine years and fathered Terah.
After fathering Terah, Nahor lived one hundred and nineteen years and fathered sons and daughters.
Terah lived seventy years and fathered Abram, Nahor, and Haran.
These are the generations of Terah. Terah fathered Abram, Nahor, and Haran; and Haran fathered Lot.
Haran died before his father Terah in his native land, in Ur of the Chaldeans.
Abram and Nahor took wives: Abram's wife was Sarai, and Nahor's wife was Milcah, daughter of Haran, who was the father of Milcah and Iscah.
Sarai was barren and bore no child.

Terah took Abram his son, Lot the son of Haran, his grandson, and Sarai his daughter-in-law, the wife of Abram his son, and they set out together from Ur of the Chaldeans to travel to the land of Canaan; but when they reached Haran, they settled there.
The days of Terah totaled two hundred and five years, and Terah died in Haran.
Now the LORD said to Abram, “Go forth from your country, from your kindred, and from your father’s house, to the land that I will show you.
I will make of you a great nation, I will bless you, I will make your name great, and you shall be a blessing.
I will bless those who bless you, and whoever dishonors you I will curse; and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.”
So Abram departed, precisely as the LORD had spoken to him, and Lot went with him; Abram was seventy-five years old when he left Haran.

Abram took Sarai his wife, Lot his nephew, all the wealth they had accumulated, and the people they had acquired in Haran, and they set out for the land of Canaan; thus they entered the land of Canaan.
Abram traversed the land as far as the place at Shechem, to the oak of Moreh, while the Canaanites were then dwelling in the land.
Then the LORD appeared to Abram and said, “To your offspring I will give this land.” Thereupon Abram built an altar there to the LORD, who had appeared to him.
From there he moved to the hill country east of Bethel and pitched his tent, with Bethel to the west and Ai to the east; there he built an altar to the LORD and invoked the name of the LORD.
Then Abram continued his journey, pressing steadily southward toward the Negev.
Now a severe famine afflicted the land, so Abram descended into Egypt to sojourn there, for the famine was grievous in the land.
As he was about to enter Egypt, he said to Sarai his wife, “Behold, I know that you are a woman of striking beauty;
when the Egyptians see you, they will say, ‘This is his wife,’ and they will kill me, but they will spare you.
Say that you are my sister, so that it may be well with me on your account and my life may be preserved for your sake.”
When Abram entered Egypt, the Egyptians saw that the woman was exceedingly beautiful.
The princes of Pharaoh saw her and extolled her to Pharaoh, and the woman was taken into Pharaoh’s house.
For her sake he treated Abram well: he received sheep, cattle, male and female donkeys, male and female servants, and camels.
But the LORD afflicted Pharaoh and his household with severe plagues because of Sarai, Abram’s wife.
So Pharaoh summoned Abram and said, “What is this you have done to me? Why did you not tell me that she was your wife?
Why did you say, ‘She is my sister,’ so that I took her as my wife? Now, behold, here is your wife; take her and depart.”
Pharaoh then commanded his men concerning him, and they sent him away, together with his wife and all that he possessed.
Abram ascended from Egypt toward the Negev—he together with his wife, all that belonged to him, and Lot in his company.
Abram was exceedingly wealthy in livestock, silver, and gold.
Proceeding by stages from the south, he came to Bethel, to the place between Bethel and Ai where his tent had first been pitched.
It was the site of the altar he had originally erected; there Abram invoked the name of the LORD.
Lot, who traveled with Abram, likewise possessed flocks, herds, and tents.
The land could not sustain both men dwelling together, for their holdings had become too vast; they could not remain in the same territory.
Strife arose between Abram’s herdsmen and Lot’s, while the Canaanites and Perizzites were still dwelling in the land.
Abram said to Lot, “Let there be no strife between me and you, nor between my herdsmen and your herdsmen, for we are brothers.
Is not the whole land before you? Separate, I pray, from me: if you go to the left, I will go to the right; and if you go to the right, I will go to the left.”

Lot lifted his eyes and beheld the whole plain of the Jordan, that it was well watered throughout—before the LORD destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah—like the garden of the LORD, like the land of Egypt as you approach Zoar.
Lot chose for himself the entire plain of the Jordan, and he journeyed eastward; thus the two men separated from each other.
Abram settled in the land of Canaan, while Lot settled in the cities of the plain and pitched his tent as far as Sodom.
Now the men of Sodom were exceedingly wicked and sinful against the LORD.
After Lot had separated from him, the LORD said to Abram, “Lift your eyes from the place where you are, and look northward, southward, eastward, and westward.
For all the land that you see, I will give to you and to your offspring forever.
I will make your offspring like the dust of the earth, so that if anyone can count the dust of the earth, your offspring also shall be counted.
Arise, walk through the land in its length and breadth, for I will give it to you.”
Abram moved his tent and came to dwell by the oaks of Mamre, which are at Hebron, and there he built an altar to the LORD.
In the days of Amraphel king of Shinar, Arioch king of Ellasar, Chedorlaomer king of Elam, and Tidal king of nations,
these kings made war with Bera king of Sodom, Birsha king of Gomorrah, Shinab king of Admah, Shemeber king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela, that is, Zoar.
All these latter kings joined forces in the Valley of Siddim, which is the Salt Sea.
For twelve years they had served Chedorlaomer, but in the thirteenth year they rebelled.
In the fourteenth year Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him came and struck the Rephaim in Ashteroth-karnaim, the Zuzim in Ham, the Emim in Shaveh-kiriathaim,
and the Horites in their hill country of Seir as far as El-paran, which is by the wilderness.
Then they turned back and came to En-mishpat, that is, Kadesh, and struck all the country of the Amalekites, and also the Amorites who were dwelling in Hazazon-tamar.
Then the king of Sodom, the king of Gomorrah, the king of Admah, the king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela, that is, Zoar, went out and drew up for battle against them in the Valley of Siddim—
with Chedorlaomer king of Elam, Tidal king of nations, Amraphel king of Shinar, and Arioch king of Ellasar, four kings against five.
Now the Valley of Siddim was full of tar pits; and as the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fled, they fell into them, while the rest fled to the hill country.
The victors took all the goods of Sodom and Gomorrah, and all their food, and went away.
They also took Lot, the son of Abram's brother, who was dwelling in Sodom, and his goods, and departed.
Then one who had escaped came and told Abram the Hebrew, who was dwelling by the oaks of Mamre the Amorite, brother of Eshcol and brother of Aner; these were allies of Abram.
When Abram heard that his brother had been taken captive, he led out his three hundred and eighteen trained men, born in his house, and pursued them as far as Dan.
He divided his forces against them by night, he and his servants, and struck them and pursued them to Hobah, north of Damascus.
He brought back all the goods, and also brought back his brother Lot with his goods, and the women and the people.
After his return from the defeat of Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him, the king of Sodom went out to meet him at the Valley of Shaveh, that is, the King's Valley.
Then Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine; he was priest of God Most High.
And he blessed him and said, "Blessed be Abram by God Most High, Possessor of heaven and earth;
and blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your enemies into your hand." And Abram gave him a tenth of everything.
The king of Sodom said to Abram, "Give me the persons, but take the goods for yourself."
But Abram said to the king of Sodom, "I have lifted my hand to the LORD, God Most High, Possessor of heaven and earth,
that I will not take a thread or a sandal strap or anything that is yours, lest you say, 'I have made Abram rich.'
I will take nothing but what the young men have eaten, and the share of the men who went with me—Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre; let them take their share."
After these things, the word of the LORD came to Abram in a vision, saying, “Do not fear, Abram; I am your shield; your recompense shall be exceedingly great.”
Abram said, “O Lord GOD, what will You give me, since I continue childless, and the heir of my house is Eliezer of Damascus?
Behold, You have given me no offspring, and behold, one born in my house is my heir.”
Then the word of the LORD came to him, saying, “This man shall not be your heir; rather, one who proceeds from your own body shall be your heir.”
He brought him outside and said, “Look toward heaven and count the stars, if you are able to count them.” He said to him, “So shall your offspring be.”
Abram believed in the LORD, and He reckoned it to him as righteousness.
He said to him, “I am the LORD, who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans, to give you this land as your possession.”
He said, “O Lord GOD, how shall I know that I shall possess it?”
He said to him, “Take for Me a three-year-old heifer, a three-year-old female goat, a three-year-old ram, a turtledove, and a young pigeon.”
Abram brought all these to Him, split each down the middle, and laid the halves opposite one another; but he did not cut the birds in half.
Then birds of prey descended upon the carcasses, and Abram drove them away.
As the sun was setting, a deep sleep fell upon Abram; and behold, a great and fearsome darkness overwhelmed him.
He said to Abram, “Know with certainty that your descendants shall be sojourners in a land not their own, and that they shall be enslaved and oppressed for four hundred years.
Yet I shall judge the nation whom they serve, and afterward they shall depart with great wealth.
As for you, you shall join your fathers in peace; you shall be buried at a good old age.
In the fourth generation they shall return hither, for the iniquity of the Amorites has not yet reached its full measure.”
When the sun had set and darkness had fallen, behold, a smoking firepot and a blazing torch passed between those pieces.
On that day the LORD made a covenant with Abram, saying, “To your descendants I have given this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river, the Euphrates—
the land of the Kenites, the Kenizzites, the Kadmonites,
the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Rephaim,
and the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Girgashites, and the Jebusites.”
Now Sarai, Abram’s wife, had borne him no children, but she had an Egyptian maidservant whose name was Hagar.
Sarai said to Abram, “Behold, the LORD has restrained me from bearing; please go in to my servant, that perhaps I may have children through her.” And Abram listened to the voice of Sarai.
After Abram had dwelt ten years in the land of Canaan, Sarai, Abram’s wife, took Hagar the Egyptian, her maidservant, and gave her to Abram her husband as a wife.
He went in to Hagar, and she conceived. When she saw that she had conceived, her mistress became contemptible in her eyes.

Sarai said to Abram, “The wrong done to me is upon you. I gave my maidservant into your bosom, and when she saw that she had conceived, I was despised in her eyes. May the LORD judge between me and you.”
Abram said to Sarai, “Behold, your maidservant is in your hand; do to her what is good in your eyes.” Then Sarai dealt harshly with her, and she fled from her presence.
The angel of the LORD found her by a spring of water in the wilderness, by the spring on the road to Shur.
He said, “Hagar, maidservant of Sarai, where have you come from, and where are you going?” She said, “I am fleeing from my mistress Sarai.”
The angel of the LORD said to her, “Return to your mistress, and humble yourself under her authority.
I will greatly multiply your offspring, so that they cannot be counted for multitude.
Behold, you are with child and shall bear a son, and you shall name him Ishmael, because the LORD has heard your affliction.
He shall be a wild donkey of a man: his hand against everyone, and everyone’s hand against him; and he shall live in hostility toward all his brothers.”
She called the name of the LORD who spoke to her, “You are the God who sees me,” for she said, “Truly, here I have seen the One who sees me.”
Therefore the well was called Beer-lahai-roi; it lies between Kadesh and Bered.
Hagar bore Abram a son, and Abram named his son, whom Hagar bore, Ishmael.
Abram was eighty-six years old when Hagar bore Ishmael to Abram.
When Abram had attained the age of ninety-nine years, the LORD appeared to him and said, "I am God Almighty; live in My presence and be blameless.
I will establish My covenant between Me and you, and I will multiply you exceedingly."
Then Abram fell upon his face, and God spoke to him:
"As for Me, behold, My covenant is with you, and you shall be the father of a multitude of nations.
No longer shall you be called Abram; your name shall be Abraham, for I have appointed you the father of a multitude of nations.
I will render you exceedingly fruitful, and I will make nations of you, and kings shall issue from you.
I will establish My covenant as an everlasting covenant between Me and you and your descendants after you, throughout their generations, to be God to you and to your descendants after you.
To you and to your descendants after you I will give the land of your sojournings, all the land of Canaan, as an everlasting possession; and I will be their God."
God further said to Abraham, "As for you, you shall keep My covenant, you and your descendants after you, throughout their generations.
This is My covenant, which you shall keep, between Me and you and your descendants: every male among you shall be circumcised.
You shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between Me and you.

Throughout your generations, every male among you who is eight days old shall be circumcised, including those born in your household or acquired with your money from any foreigner who is not of your offspring.
Both the one born in your household and the one purchased with your money must be circumcised; thus My covenant shall be in your flesh as an everlasting covenant.
Any uncircumcised male who is not circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin shall be excluded from his people; he has broken My covenant."
God also said to Abraham, "As for your wife Sarai, you shall not call her Sarai, for Sarah is her name.
I will bless her, and I will indeed give you a son by her. I will bless her, and she shall become the mother of nations; kings of peoples shall descend from her."
Then Abraham fell upon his face and laughed, saying in his heart, "Shall a child be born to a man of a hundred years? Shall Sarah, who is ninety years old, bear a child?"
And Abraham said to God, "If only Ishmael might live in Your presence!"
God said, "No, but your wife Sarah shall bear you a son, and you shall name him Isaac. I will establish My covenant with him as an everlasting covenant for his descendants after him.
As for Ishmael, I have heard you. I will surely bless him, and I will make him fruitful and multiply him exceedingly. He shall become the father of twelve rulers, and I will make him a great nation.
But My covenant I will establish with Isaac, whom Sarah shall bear to you at this appointed time next year."
When He had finished speaking with Abraham, God withdrew from him.

On that very day Abraham took his son Ishmael and all who were born in his household or purchased with his money—every male among the men of Abraham's household—and circumcised them, just as God had spoken to him.
Abraham was ninety-nine years old when he was circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin,
and his son Ishmael was thirteen years old when he was circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin.
On that very day Abraham and his son Ishmael were circumcised.
All the men of his household, both those born in the house and those purchased from a foreigner, were circumcised along with him.
The LORD appeared to Abraham by the oaks of Mamre while he was sitting at the entrance of his tent in the heat of the day.
He lifted his eyes and saw three men standing near him. When he saw them, he ran from the tent door to meet them and bowed to the ground.
He said, "My Lord, if I have found favor in Your eyes, please do not pass by Your servant.
Let a little water be brought, that you may wash your feet and rest under the tree.
I will bring a morsel of bread, that you may refresh your hearts—for you have come to your servant." They said, "Do as you have said."
So Abraham hurried into the tent to Sarah and said, "Hurry! Take three seahs of fine flour, knead it, and make cakes."
Then Abraham ran to the herd, took a tender and choice calf, and gave it to a servant, who hurried to prepare it.
He took curds and milk and the calf that had been prepared, set them before them, and stood by them under the tree while they ate.
They said to him, "Where is Sarah your wife?" He said, "She is in the tent."
And the LORD said, "I will surely return to you at this time next year, and behold, Sarah your wife shall have a son." Now Sarah was listening at the tent door behind him.
Now Abraham and Sarah were old, advanced in years; the way of women had ceased for Sarah.
So Sarah laughed within herself, saying, "After I am worn out and my lord is old, shall I have such pleasure?"
The LORD said to Abraham, "Why did Sarah laugh, saying, 'Shall I indeed bear a child, now that I am old?'"
"Is anything too hard for the LORD? At the appointed time I will return to you, about this time next year, and Sarah shall have a son."
But Sarah denied it, saying, "I did not laugh," for she was afraid. He said, "No, but you did laugh."
Then the men rose up from there and looked toward Sodom, and Abraham went with them to send them on their way.
And the LORD said, "Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do,
seeing that Abraham shall surely become a great and mighty nation, and all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in him?

For I have known him, that he may command his children and his household after him to keep the way of the LORD, to do righteousness and justice, so that the LORD may bring to Abraham what He has promised him."
Then the LORD said, "Because the outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah is great and their sin is exceedingly grave,
I will go down and see whether they have done altogether according to the outcry that has come to Me; and if not, I will know."
So the men turned from there and went toward Sodom, but Abraham remained standing before the LORD.
Then Abraham drew near and said, "Will You indeed sweep away the righteous with the wicked?
Suppose there are fifty righteous within the city: will You then sweep away the place and not spare it for the sake of the fifty righteous who are in it?
Far be it from You to do such a thing, to put the righteous to death with the wicked so that the righteous fare as the wicked! Far be it from You! Shall not the Judge of all the earth do justice?"
The LORD said, "If I find at Sodom fifty righteous within the city, I will spare the whole place for their sake."
Abraham said, "Behold, I have undertaken to speak to the Lord, though I am but dust and ashes.
Suppose five of the fifty righteous are lacking: will You destroy the whole city for lack of five?" The LORD said, "I will not destroy it if I find forty-five there."
Abraham said, "Suppose forty are found there." The LORD said, "For the sake of forty I will not do it."
Abraham said, "Oh, let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak. Suppose thirty are found there." The LORD said, "I will not do it if I find thirty there."
Abraham said, "Behold, I have undertaken to speak to the Lord. Suppose twenty are found there." The LORD said, "For the sake of twenty I will not destroy it."
Abraham said, "Oh, let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak once more. Suppose ten are found there." The LORD said, "For the sake of ten I will not destroy it."
When the LORD had finished speaking with Abraham, He went on His way, and Abraham returned to his place.
In the evening, two angels arrived at Sodom while Lot was sitting in the city gate; upon seeing them, Lot rose to meet them and bowed with his face to the ground.

He said, “Please, my lords, turn aside into your servant’s house, wash your feet, spend the night, and rise early to continue your journey.” They replied, “No; we shall spend the night in the square.”
Yet he urged them so insistently that they turned toward him and entered his house; there he prepared a feast, baking unleavened bread, and they ate.
Before they retired, the men of the city—the men of Sodom, from the youngest to the oldest, every last one of them—surrounded the house.
They called to Lot and demanded, “Where are the men who came to you tonight? Bring them out to us, that we may have sexual relations with them.”
Lot went out to them at the entrance and closed the door behind him.
He pleaded, “Please, my brothers, do not act so wickedly.”

“Look, I have two daughters who have never known a man; let me bring them out to you, and you may do with them as seems good to you. Only do nothing to these men, for they have come under the shelter of my roof.”

They retorted, “Stand back!” and added, “This fellow came as an alien, and now he presumes to judge us? We shall treat you worse than them.” They pressed Lot so violently that they nearly broke down the door.
The men reached out, drew Lot back into the house, and shut the door.
Then they struck the men at the doorway, from the least to the greatest, with blindness, so that they exhausted themselves trying to find the entrance.
The men said to Lot, “Whom else do you have here? Bring out your sons-in-law, your sons, your daughters, and anyone else belonging to you in the city; take them out of this place.
For we are about to destroy it, because the outcry against its people has grown so great before the LORD that the LORD has sent us to annihilate it.”
Lot went out and spoke to his sons-in-law, the men betrothed to his daughters: “Get up and leave this place, for the LORD is about to destroy the city.” But his sons-in-law thought he was jesting.
At dawn the angels urged Lot, “Arise, take your wife and your two daughters who are here, lest you be swept away in the city’s punishment.”
When he hesitated, the men seized him, his wife, and his two daughters by the hand and brought them outside the city, for the LORD had compassion on him.
As soon as they had brought them out, one said, “Flee for your life! Do not look behind you, and do not stop anywhere in the plain; flee to the mountains, lest you be swept away.”
Lot answered them, “No, my lords, please!
Behold, your servant has found favor with you, and you have shown your abundant mercy to me by preserving my life; yet I cannot flee to the mountains, lest disaster overtake me and I perish.
Look, that city is near enough to flee to, and it is small. Please let me escape there—is it not a small place?—so that my life may be spared.”
He said to him, “Very well, I grant you this request as well: I will not overthrow the city of which you have spoken.
Hurry and escape there, for I cannot do anything until you arrive.” Therefore the city was called Zoar.
The sun had risen over the land when Lot entered Zoar.
Then the LORD rained sulfur and fire upon Sodom and Gomorrah from the LORD out of heaven.
He overthrew those cities, the entire plain, all the inhabitants of the cities, and the vegetation of the ground.
But Lot’s wife looked back, and she became a pillar of salt.
Early in the morning, Abraham went to the place where he had stood before the LORD.
He looked down upon Sodom and Gomorrah and upon the whole plain, and he saw smoke rising from the land like the smoke of a furnace.
So when God destroyed the cities of the plain, God remembered Abraham and brought Lot out from the midst of the overthrow, when He overthrew the cities in which Lot had lived.
Lot went up from Zoar and settled in the mountains with his two daughters, for he was afraid to remain in Zoar; so he and his daughters lived in a cave.
The older daughter said to the younger, “Our father is old, and there is no man in the land to marry us according to the custom of all humankind.
Come, let us make our father drink wine, and we will lie with him, so that we may preserve offspring through our father.”
That night they made their father drink wine, and the older daughter went in and lay with her father; he did not know when she lay down or when she rose.

The next day the older daughter said to the younger, “I lay with my father last night. Let us make him drink wine tonight as well; then you go in and lie with him, so that we may preserve offspring through our father.”
So they made their father drink wine that night too, and the younger daughter arose and lay with him; but he did not know when she lay down or when she rose.
Thus both of Lot’s daughters conceived by their father.
The older bore a son and named him Moab; he is the ancestor of the Moabites to this day.
The younger also bore a son and named him Ben-ammi; he is the ancestor of the Ammonites to this day.
Abraham departed thence and journeyed into the Negev, establishing his residence between Kadesh and Shur, and he sojourned in Gerar.
Abraham represented his wife Sarah as his sister; whereupon Abimelech, king of Gerar, dispatched for Sarah and brought her into his household.
But God appeared to Abimelech in a nocturnal dream and said, “You are a dead man because of the woman you have taken, for she is bound to another husband.”
Now Abimelech had not approached her, so he said, “Lord, will You slay even an innocent nation?
Did he not say to me, ‘She is my sister’? And did she not herself say, ‘He is my brother’? I have acted with integrity of heart and innocence of hands.”
Then God said to him in the dream, “I know indeed that you acted with integrity of your heart, and I Myself withheld you from sinning against Me; hence I did not allow you to touch her.

Now therefore restore the man’s wife, for he is a prophet, and he shall intercede for you, that you may live. But if you do not restore her, be assured that you and all who belong to you shall perish.”
At dawn Abimelech arose, summoned all his servants, and disclosed these matters in their hearing; and the men were seized with great fear.

Then Abimelech summoned Abraham and said to him, “What have you done to us? How have I offended you, that you have brought upon me and upon my kingdom so grave a sin? You have perpetrated against me deeds that ought never to be done.”
And Abimelech said to Abraham, “What design prompted you to commit this deed?”
Abraham replied, “I reasoned within myself, ‘There is surely no fear of God in this place, and they will slay me on account of my wife.’
Besides, she is indeed my sister—my father’s daughter, though not my mother’s—and she became my wife.
And when God caused me to wander from my father’s household, I said to her, ‘This is the kindness you must show me: at every place to which we come, say of me, “He is my brother.”’”
Then Abimelech took sheep, cattle, male and female servants, and gave them to Abraham, and restored his wife Sarah to him.
And Abimelech said, “Behold, my land lies before you; dwell wherever it pleases you.”
And to Sarah he said, “Look, I have given your brother a thousand pieces of silver; it is your vindication before all who are with you, and you are entirely cleared.”
Then Abraham prayed to God, and God healed Abimelech, his wife, and his female servants, so that they resumed bearing children,
for the LORD had closed every womb in Abimelech’s household on account of Sarah, Abraham’s wife.
The LORD attended to Sarah, precisely as He had declared, and the LORD accomplished for Sarah that which He had spoken.
Sarah conceived and bore a son to Abraham in his advanced age, at the designated season of which God had spoken.
Abraham bestowed upon the son born to him by Sarah the name Isaac.
Abraham circumcised his son Isaac when he had reached eight days of age, in accordance with the divine command.
Abraham was one hundred years old when his son Isaac was born to him.
Sarah said, “God has made me to laugh; everyone who hears of this will laugh with me.”
And she said, “Who would have declared to Abraham that Sarah would nurse children? Yet I have borne him a son in his old age.”
The child grew and was weaned, and Abraham prepared a great feast on the day Isaac was weaned.
Sarah observed that the son whom Hagar the Egyptian had borne to Abraham was mocking.
So she said to Abraham, “Expel this slave woman and her son, for the son of this slave woman shall not inherit alongside my son Isaac.”
The matter proved exceedingly grievous to Abraham on account of his son.
God said to Abraham, “Let it not be grievous in your sight because of the boy and your slave woman. Heed Sarah’s voice in all that she says to you, for through Isaac your offspring shall be named.”
“I shall also constitute the son of the slave woman a nation, because he is your offspring.”

Abraham rose early in the morning, took bread and a skin of water, gave them to Hagar, placing them upon her shoulder, and gave her the boy, and sent her away. She departed and strayed in the wilderness of Beersheba.
When the water in the skin was spent, she placed the child beneath one of the bushes.
She went and sat down opposite him at a distance, about a bowshot away, for she said, “Let me not behold the death of the child.” She sat opposite him and raised her voice and wept.
God heard the voice of the boy, and the angel of God called to Hagar from heaven and said to her, “What ails you, Hagar? Do not fear, for God has heard the voice of the boy in the place where he is.”
“Arise, lift up the boy, and sustain him by the hand, for I will make of him a great nation.”
Then God opened her eyes, and she beheld a well of water. She went and filled the skin with water and gave the boy a drink.
God was with the boy, and he grew up. He dwelt in the wilderness and became an archer.
He dwelt in the wilderness of Paran, and his mother took for him a wife from the land of Egypt.
At that time Abimelech and Phicol, commander of his army, said to Abraham, “God is with you in all that you do.”

“Now therefore swear to me here by God that you will not deal deceitfully with me, or with my offspring, or with my descendants; according to the kindness I have shown to you, you shall do to me and to the land in which you have sojourned.”
Then Abraham reproved Abimelech concerning a well of water that Abimelech’s servants had seized.
Abimelech said, “I did not know who perpetrated this deed; you did not inform me, nor did I hear of it until today.”
Abraham took sheep and oxen and gave them to Abimelech, and the two of them ratified a covenant.
Abraham set apart seven ewe lambs from the flock.
Abimelech said to Abraham, “What is the significance of these seven ewe lambs that you have set apart?”
He said, “You shall take these seven ewe lambs from my hand, that they may serve as witness for me that I dug this well.”
Therefore that place was called Beersheba, because there the two of them swore an oath.
Thus they ratified a covenant at Beersheba. Then Abimelech and Phicol, commander of his army, arose and returned to the land of the Philistines.
Abraham planted a tamarisk in Beersheba and invoked there the name of the LORD, the Everlasting God.
Abraham sojourned in the land of the Philistines for many days.
After these events, God subjected Abraham to a trial. He called out to him, "Abraham!" Abraham replied, "Here I am."
Then He declared, "Take now your son, your only son, whom you love—Isaac—and go to the land of Moriah; offer him there as a burnt offering upon one of the mountains that I will tell you."
Abraham rose at dawn, saddled his donkey, and took with him two of his young men and Isaac his son. Having split wood for the burnt offering, he set out for the place God had indicated.
On the third day, Abraham raised his eyes and perceived the appointed place from afar.
Abraham said to his young men, "Remain here with the donkey; the boy and I will go yonder to worship, and we shall return to you."
Abraham took the wood for the burnt offering and laid it upon Isaac his son; bearing the fire and the knife in his hand, the two advanced together.
Isaac addressed his father Abraham, saying, "My father!" Abraham answered, "Here I am, my son." Isaac continued, "Here are the fire and the wood, but where is the lamb for the burnt offering?"
Abraham replied, "God Himself will provide the lamb for the burnt offering, my son." Thus the two continued on together.
Upon arriving at the place God had designated, Abraham erected an altar there, arranged the wood, bound his son Isaac, and placed him upon the altar, above the wood.
Abraham extended his hand and seized the knife to slay his son.
The angel of the LORD called to him from heaven, "Abraham, Abraham!" Abraham answered, "Here I am."
The angel declared, "Do not raise your hand against the boy, nor do him any harm; for now I know that you fear God, seeing that you have not withheld your son, your only son, from Me."
Abraham lifted his eyes and beheld a ram behind him, caught by its horns in a thicket. He went and took the ram and offered it up as a burnt offering in lieu of his son.
Abraham named that place the LORD Will Provide; hence it is said to this day, "On the mountain of the LORD it will be provided."
The angel of the LORD called to Abraham from heaven a second time.
He said, "By Myself I have sworn, declares the LORD, that because you have done this and have not withheld your son, your only son,
I will surely bless you and multiply your offspring like the stars of heaven and like the sand upon the seashore; your offspring shall possess the gates of their enemies.
Through your offspring all the nations of the earth shall be blessed, because you have obeyed My voice."
Abraham returned to his young men, and they journeyed together to Beersheba; Abraham took up residence in Beersheba.
After these things, Abraham was informed, "Milcah also has borne sons to your brother Nahor:
Uz his firstborn, Buz his brother, Kemuel the father of Aram,
Chesed, Hazo, Pildash, Jidlaph, and Bethuel."
Bethuel fathered Rebekah. These eight Milcah bore to Nahor, Abraham's brother.
His concubine, Reumah by name, likewise bore Tebah, Gaham, Tahash, and Maacah.
Sarah’s years numbered one hundred twenty-seven; such were the days of Sarah’s life.
Sarah died in Kiriath-arba—that is, Hebron—in the land of Canaan, and Abraham came to mourn for Sarah and to weep over her.
Abraham arose from before his dead and spoke to the Hittites, saying,
“I am a stranger and sojourner among you; grant me a burial holding among you, that I may bury my dead out of my sight.”
The Hittites answered Abraham, saying to him,
“Hear us, my lord; you are a prince of God among us. Bury your dead in the choicest of our tombs; none of us will withhold from you a tomb for burying your dead.”
Abraham rose and bowed to the people of the land, to the Hittites.
He spoke with them, saying, “If it is your will that I bury my dead out of my sight, hear me and entreat Ephron son of Zohar on my behalf,
that he may give me the cave of Machpelah, which is his, at the end of his field; for the full price let him give it to me in your presence as a burial holding.”
Now Ephron was sitting among the Hittites, and Ephron the Hittite answered Abraham in the hearing of all the Hittites, of all who entered the gate of his city, saying,
“No, my lord, hear me: I give you the field, and I give you the cave that is in it; in the sight of the sons of my people I give it to you. Bury your dead.”
Abraham bowed before the people of the land.
He spoke to Ephron in the hearing of the people of the land, saying, “No, but if you are willing, hear me: I will give the price of the field; take it from me, that I may bury my dead there.”
Ephron answered Abraham, saying to him,
“My lord, listen to me: a piece of land worth four hundred shekels of silver—what is that between me and you? Bury your dead.”
Abraham listened to Ephron, and Abraham weighed out for Ephron the silver he had named in the hearing of the Hittites—four hundred shekels of silver, current among the merchants.
Thus the field of Ephron in Machpelah, which lay before Mamre—the field, the cave in it, and all the trees in the field throughout its surrounding boundary—was transferred to Abraham as a possession,
in the presence of the Hittites, of all who entered the gate of his city.
Afterward Abraham buried Sarah his wife in the cave of the field of Machpelah before Mamre—that is, Hebron—in the land of Canaan.
The field and the cave in it were made over to Abraham as a burial holding by the Hittites.
Now Abraham had grown venerable and advanced in years, and the LORD had blessed him in every respect.
Abraham said to the eldest servant of his household, the steward who governed all that he possessed, “Place your hand beneath my thigh,
and I will make you swear by the LORD, the God of heaven and the God of the earth, that you will not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites among whom I dwell;
but you shall go to my country and my kindred, and take a wife for my son Isaac.”
The servant said to him, “What if the woman is unwilling to follow me to this land? Should I then take your son back to the land from which you came?”
Abraham said to him, “Take heed that you do not take my son back there.

The LORD, the God of heaven, who took me from my father’s house and from the land of my birth, and who spoke to me and swore to me, saying, ‘To your seed I will give this land’—He will send His angel before you, and you shall take a wife for my son from there.
If the woman is unwilling to follow you, then you shall be released from this oath; only do not take my son back there.”
So the servant placed his hand under the thigh of Abraham his master, and swore to him concerning this matter.
Then the servant took ten camels from his master’s camels and departed, carrying all manner of his master’s goods in his hand; he arose and journeyed to Aram-naharaim, to the city of Nahor.
At evening, the time when the women go out to draw water, he made the camels kneel outside the city by the well.
He said, “O the LORD, God of my master Abraham, please grant me success this day, and show steadfast love to my master Abraham.”
“Behold, I stand by the spring of water, and the daughters of the men of the city are coming out to draw water.

Let it be that the young woman to whom I say, ‘Please tip your jar that I may drink,’ and who says, ‘Drink, and I will water your camels also’—let her be the one You have appointed for Your servant Isaac. By this I shall know that You have shown steadfast love to my master.”
Before he had finished speaking, behold, Rebekah came out—the daughter of Bethuel, son of Milcah, the wife of Abraham’s brother Nahor—with her jar upon her shoulder.
She was exceedingly beautiful in appearance, a virgin whom no man had known; she went down to the spring, filled her jar, and came up.
The servant ran to meet her and said, “Please give me a little water from your jar.”
She said, “Drink, my lord,” and she hurried and lowered her jar upon her hand and gave him a drink.
When she had finished giving him a drink, she said, “I will draw water for your camels also, until they have finished drinking.”
She hurried, emptied her jar into the trough, ran again to the well to draw, and drew for all his camels.
Meanwhile the man gazed upon her in silence, seeking to discern whether the LORD had prospered his journey or not.
When the camels had finished drinking, the man took a gold nose ring weighing a beka, and two gold bracelets weighing ten shekels, and affixed them to her.
He said, “Whose daughter are you? Tell me, please. Is there room in your father’s house for us to lodge?”
She said to him, “I am the daughter of Bethuel, son of Milcah, whom she bore to Nahor.”
She also said to him, “We have both straw and fodder in abundance, and room to lodge.”
Then the man bowed and worshiped the LORD.

He said, “Blessed be the LORD, the God of my master Abraham, who has not withdrawn His steadfast love and His faithfulness from my master. As for me, the LORD has led me in the way to the house of my master’s kinsmen.”
The young woman ran and told her mother’s household these things.
Now Rebekah had a brother named Laban, and Laban ran outside to the man at the spring.

When he saw the ring and the bracelets on his sister’s hands, and heard the words of Rebekah his sister, saying, “Thus spoke the man to me,” he came to the man; and behold, he was standing by the camels at the spring.
He said, “Come in, you who are blessed of the LORD. Why do you stand outside? I have prepared the house, and there is a place for the camels.”
So the man came into the house; he unloaded the camels and gave straw and fodder to the camels, and water to wash the feet of him and the men who were with him.
Food was set before him, but he said, “I will not eat until I have spoken my words.” They said, “Speak.”
The LORD has greatly blessed my master, and he has become great; He has given him flocks and herds, silver and gold, servants and maidservants, camels and donkeys.
Sarah my master’s wife bore a son to my master in her old age, and he has given him all that he has.
My master made me swear, saying, ‘You shall not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites in whose land I dwell;
but you shall go to my father’s house and to my kindred, and take a wife for my son.’
“I said to my master, ‘What if the woman will not follow me?’
He said to me, ‘The LORD, before whom I have walked, will send His angel with you and prosper your way; you shall take a wife for my son from my kindred, from my father’s house.
Then you will be free from my oath: if, when you come to my kindred, they do not give her to you, you will be free from my oath.’
“So I came today to the spring, and I said, ‘O the LORD, God of my master Abraham, if now You are prospering my way on which I am going—
behold, I stand by the spring of water—let it be that the young woman who comes out to draw, to whom I say, “Please give me a little water from your jar,”
and who says to me, “Drink, and I will draw for your camels also”—let her be the woman whom the LORD has appointed for my master’s son.’
Before I had finished speaking in my heart, behold, Rebekah came out with her jar upon her shoulder; she went down to the spring and drew. I said to her, ‘Please give me a drink.’
She hurried and lowered her jar from her shoulder and said, ‘Drink, and I will water your camels also.’ So I drank, and she watered the camels also.
Then I asked her, ‘Whose daughter are you?’ She said, ‘The daughter of Bethuel, son of Nahor, whom Milcah bore to him.’ So I put the ring on her nose and the bracelets on her arms.
Then I bowed and worshiped the LORD, and blessed the LORD, the God of my master Abraham, who led me in the way of truth to take the daughter of my master’s brother for his son.
Now if you will deal kindly and truly with my master, tell me; and if not, tell me, that I may turn to the right hand or to the left.”
Laban and Bethuel answered, “The thing has come from the LORD; we cannot speak to you either evil or good.
Behold, Rebekah is before you; take her and go, and let her be the wife of your master’s son, as the LORD has spoken.”
When Abraham’s servant heard their words, he bowed to the ground before the LORD.
The servant brought out silver and gold jewelry, and garments, and gave them to Rebekah; he also gave precious things to her brother and to her mother.
He and the men who were with him ate and drank, and lodged there. They rose in the morning, and he said, “Send me away to my master.”
Her brother and her mother said, “Let the young woman stay with us a few days, at least ten; after that she may go.”
He said to them, “Do not delay me, since the LORD has prospered my way; send me away, that I may go to my master.”
They said, “We will call the young woman and ask her.”
They called Rebekah and said to her, “Will you go with this man?” She said, “I will go.”
So they sent away Rebekah their sister, and her nurse, together with Abraham’s servant and his men.
They blessed Rebekah and said to her, “Our sister, may you become thousands of ten thousands, and may your seed possess the gate of those who hate them.”
Then Rebekah and her young women arose, mounted the camels, and followed the man. The servant took Rebekah and departed.
Now Isaac had come from the way to Beer-lahai-roi, and he was dwelling in the land of the Negev.
Isaac went out to meditate in the field toward evening; he lifted up his eyes and saw, and behold, camels were coming.
Rebekah lifted up her eyes, and when she saw Isaac, she dismounted from the camel.
She said to the servant, “Who is that man walking in the field to meet us?” The servant said, “He is my master.” So she took her veil and covered herself.
The servant told Isaac all the things that he had done.
Then Isaac brought her into the tent of Sarah his mother; he took Rebekah, and she became his wife, and he loved her. Thus Isaac was comforted after his mother’s death.
Abraham took another wife, whose name was Keturah;
she bore him Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah.
Jokshan begat Sheba and Dedan, and the sons of Dedan were the Asshurim, the Letushim, and the Leummim.
The sons of Midian were Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abida, and Eldaah; all these were the sons of Keturah.
Abraham gave everything he possessed to Isaac,
but while he still lived he gave gifts to the sons of his concubines and sent them away eastward, away from Isaac his son, into the eastern country.
These are the days of the years of Abraham's life: one hundred seventy-five years.
Abraham breathed his last and died in a good old age, an old man and full of years, and was gathered to his people.
His sons Isaac and Ishmael buried him in the cave of Machpelah, in the field of Ephron the son of Zohar the Hittite, which lies near Mamre.
