That is the field Abraham purchased from the Hittites; there Abraham and Sarah his wife were buried.
After Abraham's death, God blessed Isaac his son, and Isaac dwelt at Beer-lahai-roi.
These are the generations of Ishmael, Abraham's son, whom Hagar the Egyptian, Sarah's maidservant, bore to Abraham.
These are the names of the sons of Ishmael, by their generations: Nebaioth the firstborn of Ishmael, then Kedar, Adbeel, Mibsam,
Hadad, Tema, Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah.
These are the sons of Ishmael, and these are their names, by their villages and by their encampments—twelve princes according to their nations.
The years of Ishmael's life were one hundred thirty-seven years; he breathed his last and died, and was gathered to his people.
His descendants settled from Havilah to Shur, which is opposite Egypt as you go toward Assyria, and they lived in hostility toward all their brothers.
These are the generations of Isaac, Abraham's son: Abraham begat Isaac.
Isaac was forty years old when he took Rebekah, the daughter of Bethuel the Aramean of Paddan-aram, the sister of Laban the Aramean, to be his wife.
Isaac prayed to the LORD for his wife, because she was barren; and the LORD granted his plea, and Rebekah his wife conceived.
The children struggled together within her, and she said, "If it is so, why am I thus?" So she went to inquire of the LORD.
And the LORD said to her, "Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall be divided from within your body; the one shall be stronger than the other, and the elder shall serve the younger."
When her days to be delivered were fulfilled, behold, there were twins in her womb.
The first came out red, all over like a hairy garment, and they called his name Esau.
Afterward his brother came out, his hand taking hold of Esau's heel, and his name was called Jacob. Isaac was sixty years old when she bore them.
When the boys grew up, Esau became a skillful hunter, a man of the field, while Jacob was a quiet man, dwelling in tents.
Isaac loved Esau, because he ate of his game, but Rebekah loved Jacob.
Jacob had cooked a stew when Esau came in from the field, famished.
Esau said to Jacob, "Feed me, I pray, some of that red stew, for I am famished." Therefore he was called Edom.
Jacob said, "Sell me your birthright this day."
Esau said, "Behold, I am going to die; what good is the birthright to me?"
Jacob said, "Swear to me this day." So he swore to him, and sold his birthright to Jacob.
Then Jacob gave Esau bread and lentil stew; he ate and drank, rose up, and went his way. Thus Esau despised his birthright.
Now a famine afflicted the land, distinct from the earlier famine that had occurred in Abraham’s days. And Isaac went to Abimelech, king of the Philistines, at Gerar.
And the LORD appeared to him and said, “Do not descend to Egypt; abide in the land that I will show you.
Sojourn in this land, and I will be with you and will bless you, for to you and to your posterity I will give all these lands, and I will establish the oath that I swore to Abraham, your father.
I will multiply your posterity as the stars of heaven and will give to your posterity all these lands, and in your posterity all the nations of the earth shall be blessed,
because Abraham hearkened to My voice and kept My charge, My commandments, My statutes, and My laws.”

When the men of the place inquired concerning his wife, he said, “She is my sister,” for he feared to say, “My wife,” lest the men of the place should slay him, since Rebekah was exceedingly beautiful.
After he had resided there for a protracted interval, Abimelech, king of the Philistines, gazed through a window and beheld Isaac caressing Rebekah, his wife.
Abimelech summoned Isaac and said, “Behold, she is your wife! How then did you say, ‘She is my sister’?” Isaac replied, “Because I said, ‘Lest I perish on account of her.’”
Abimelech said, “What have you done to us? One of the people might easily have lain with your wife, and you would have incurred guilt upon us.”
Abimelech charged all the people, saying, “Whoever touches this man or his wife shall surely be put to death.”
Isaac sowed in that land and reaped in that same year a hundredfold, because the LORD blessed him.
The man prospered and continued to increase in wealth until he became exceedingly affluent.
He acquired flocks, herds, and a substantial household, so that the Philistines envied him.
Now all the wells that his father’s servants had excavated in Abraham’s days, the Philistines had stopped up and filled with earth.
Abimelech said to Isaac, “Depart from us, for you have become far mightier than we.”
So Isaac departed thence and encamped in the Valley of Gerar and dwelt there.

Isaac reopened the wells of water that had been excavated in the days of Abraham his father, which the Philistines had stopped up after Abraham’s death, and he restored to them the names his father had bestowed.
When Isaac’s servants dug in the valley, they discovered a well of living water.
But the herdsmen of Gerar contended with Isaac’s herdsmen, saying, “The water belongs to us.” Therefore he named the well Esek, because they had quarreled with him.
Then they excavated another well, and they quarreled over it as well; so he named it Sitnah.
He moved from there and dug yet another well, over which they did not quarrel. He named it Rehoboth, saying, “For now the LORD has made ample space for us, and we shall flourish in the land.”
From there he ascended to Beersheba.

The LORD appeared to him that very night and said, “I am the God of Abraham, your father. Fear not, for I am with you and will bless you and multiply your posterity for the sake of My servant Abraham.”
So he erected an altar there and invoked the name of the LORD; he pitched his tent there, and Isaac’s servants excavated a well.
Abimelech came to him from Gerar, accompanied by Ahuzzath, his counselor, and Phicol, commander of his army.
Isaac said to them, “Why have you come to me, seeing that you hate me and have expelled me from your presence?”
They said, “We have clearly perceived that the LORD has been with you. Therefore we said, ‘Let there be an oath between us, between us and you, and let us establish a covenant with you,
that you will do us no harm, just as we have not molested you but have dealt with you only in kindness and have sent you away in peace. You are now blessed by the LORD.’”
So he prepared a feast for them, and they ate and drank.
They rose early the next morning and swore an oath to one another. Then Isaac dismissed them, and they departed from him in peace.
That same day, Isaac’s servants came and reported to him concerning the well they had dug, saying, “We have found water.”
He named it Shibah; hence the city is called Beersheba to this day.
When Esau was forty years old, he married Judith, daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and Basemath, daughter of Elon the Hittite.
And they proved a source of bitterness to Isaac and Rebekah.
When Isaac had grown old and his eyes had become so dim that he could no longer see, he summoned Esau, his elder son, and said to him, “My son.” Esau answered, “Here am I.”
Isaac said, “Behold, I am old; I do not know the day of my death.
Now, then, take your gear—your quiver and your bow—and go out into the field and hunt game for me.
Prepare for me savory delicacies, such as I love, and bring them to me, that I may eat, so that my soul may bless you before I die.”
Now Rebekah was listening while Isaac spoke to his son Esau; and when Esau went into the field to hunt game and bring it,
Rebekah said to Jacob her son, “I have heard your father speaking to Esau your brother, saying,
‘Bring me game and prepare savory delicacies for me, that I may eat and bless you before the LORD before I die.’”
“Now therefore, my son, obey my voice in what I command you.
Go to the flock and bring me two choice young goats, that I may prepare from them savory delicacies for your father, such as he loves.
Then bring them to your father to eat, so that he may bless you before he dies.”
Jacob said to Rebekah his mother, “Behold, Esau my brother is a hirsute man, whereas I am a smooth man.
Perhaps my father will palpate me, and I shall seem to him a deceiver, and I shall bring a curse upon myself instead of a blessing.”
His mother said to him, “Let your curse be upon me, my son; only obey my voice, and go fetch them for me.”
So he went and took them and brought them to his mother, and his mother prepared savory delicacies, such as his father loved.
Then Rebekah took the best garments of Esau her elder son, which she had in the house, and put them on Jacob her younger son.
She put the skins of the young goats upon his hands and upon the smooth part of his neck.
She placed the savory delicacies and the bread that she had prepared into the hand of Jacob her son.
He came to his father and said, “My father.” Isaac said, “Here am I; who are you, my son?”
Jacob said to his father, “I am Esau your firstborn. I have done as you bade me. Arise, please, sit and eat of my game, that your soul may bless me.”
Isaac said to his son, “How is it that you have found it so quickly, my son?” Jacob said, “Because the LORD your God granted me success.”
Then Isaac said to Jacob, “Please come near, that I may feel you, my son, to know whether you are indeed my son Esau or not.”
So Jacob went near to Isaac his father, and he felt him and said, “The voice is Jacob’s voice, but the hands are Esau’s hands.”
He did not recognize him, because his hands were hairy like his brother Esau’s hands; so he blessed him.
Isaac said, “Are you really my son Esau?” Jacob said, “I am.”
Isaac said, “Bring it near to me, that I may eat of my son’s game and bless you.” So he brought it near, and he ate, and he brought wine, and he drank.
Then Isaac his father said to him, “Come near and kiss me, my son.”
He came near and kissed him; and when Isaac smelled the smell of his garments, he blessed him and said, “See, the smell of my son is like the smell of a field that the LORD has blessed.”
“May God give you of the dew of heaven and of the fatness of the earth, and abundance of grain and wine.

Let peoples serve you, and nations bow down to you. Be lord over your brothers, and let your mother’s sons bow down to you. Cursed be everyone who curses you, and blessed be everyone who blesses you.”
As soon as Isaac had finished blessing Jacob, and Jacob had scarcely gone out from the presence of Isaac his father, Esau his brother came in from his hunting.
He too prepared savory delicacies and brought them to his father, and said to his father, “Let my father arise and eat of his son’s game, that you may bless me.”
Isaac his father said to him, “Who are you?” He said, “I am your son, your firstborn, Esau.”
Then Isaac trembled exceedingly violently and said, “Who then is he who hunted game and brought it to me, and I ate of all before you came, and I have blessed him? Indeed, he shall be blessed.”
When Esau heard the words of his father, he cried out with an exceedingly great and bitter cry and said to his father, “Bless me, even me also, O my father!”
Isaac said, “Your brother came deceitfully and took away your blessing.”

Esau said, “Is he not rightly named Jacob? For he has supplanted me these two times: he took away my birthright, and behold, now he has taken away my blessing.” Then he said, “Have you not reserved a blessing for me?”
Isaac answered Esau, “Behold, I have made him lord over you, and all his brothers I have given to him for servants, and with grain and wine I have sustained him. What then can I do for you, my son?”
Esau said to his father, “Have you but one blessing, my father? Bless me, even me also, O my father!” And Esau lifted up his voice and wept.
Isaac his father answered and said to him, “Behold, away from the fatness of the earth shall be your dwelling, and away from the dew of heaven from above.
By your sword you shall live, and you shall serve your brother; but when you grow restless, you shall break his yoke from your neck.”

Now Esau hated Jacob because of the blessing with which his father had blessed him, and Esau said in his heart, “The days of mourning for my father are approaching; then I will kill my brother Jacob.”

And the words of Esau, the elder son, were told to Rebekah, and she sent and called Jacob her younger son and said to him, “Behold, Esau your brother comforts himself concerning you by planning to kill you.”
“Now therefore, my son, obey my voice: arise, flee to Laban my brother in Haran.”
“Stay with him a few days, until your brother’s fury turns away—
until your brother’s anger turns away from you and he forgets what you have done to him. Then I will send and bring you from there. Why should I be bereaved of you both in one day?”

Rebekah said to Isaac, “I am weary of my life because of the daughters of Heth. If Jacob takes a wife from the daughters of Heth, such as these, from the daughters of the land, what good will my life be to me?”
Isaac summoned Jacob, blessed him, and charged him, saying, “You shall not take a wife from the daughters of Canaan.”
“Arise, go to Paddan-aram, to the house of Bethuel, your mother's father, and take for yourself a wife from there—from the daughters of Laban, your mother's brother.”
May God Almighty bless you and make you fruitful and multiply you, so that you become a company of peoples.
May He give you the blessing of Abraham—to you and to your offspring with you—so that you may possess the land of your sojournings, which God gave to Abraham.
So Isaac sent Jacob away, and he traveled to Paddan-aram, to Laban son of Bethuel the Aramean, the brother of Rebekah, mother of Jacob and Esau.

Esau saw that Isaac had blessed Jacob and sent him to Paddan-aram to take a wife from there, and that while blessing him he had commanded him, “You shall not take a wife from the daughters of Canaan,”
and that Jacob had obeyed his father and mother and had gone to Paddan-aram.
Esau also perceived that the daughters of Canaan were displeasing to Isaac his father.
Therefore Esau went to Ishmael and, in addition to his wives, took Mahalath, daughter of Ishmael son of Abraham and sister of Nebaioth, as a wife.
Jacob departed from Beersheba and journeyed toward Haran.
He reached a certain place and lodged there because the sun had set; and taking one of the stones of the place, he placed it under his head and lay down there.
He dreamed, and there appeared a ladder set upon the earth with its top reaching to heaven, and there the angels of God were ascending and descending upon it.
And the the LORD stood above it and said, “I am the the LORD, the God of Abraham, your father, and the God of Isaac. The land on which you lie I will give to you and to your offspring.”

“Your offspring shall be like the dust of the earth, and you shall spread out to the west and to the east and to the north and to the south; and in you and in your offspring shall all the families of the earth be blessed.”
“Behold, I am with you, and I will guard you wherever you go and bring you back to this land; for I will not abandon you until I have fulfilled what I have spoken to you.”
Then Jacob awoke from his sleep and said, “Surely the the LORD is in this place, and I did not know it.”
He was afraid and said, “How awe-inspiring is this place! This is none other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven.”
Jacob rose early in the morning, took the stone he had put under his head, set it up as a pillar, and poured oil on its top.
He named that place Bethel, although the city had formerly been called Luz.
And Jacob made a vow, saying, “If God will be with me and will keep me in the way I am traveling, and will give me bread to eat and clothing to wear,
so that I may return in peace to my father's house, then the the LORD shall be my God,
and this stone, which I have set up as a pillar, shall be God's house; and of all that You give me I will surely give a tenth to You.”
Jacob resumed his journey and traveled toward the land of the eastern peoples.
There he saw a well in the field, beside which three flocks of sheep were reclining, for the flocks drew their water from that well; the stone covering the mouth of the well was massive.
Whenever all the flocks were gathered there, the shepherds would roll the stone from the mouth of the well, water the sheep, and then restore the stone to its place atop the well's mouth.
Jacob said to them, "My brothers, where are you from?" They answered, "We are from Haran."
He asked, "Do you know Laban son of Nahor?" They said, "We know him."
He said, "Is he well?" They said, "He is well; and here comes his daughter Rachel with the sheep."
He said, "See, the day is still long; it is not yet time to gather the livestock. Water the sheep and go, pasture them."
They said, "We cannot until all the flocks are gathered and the stone is rolled from the mouth of the well; then we water the sheep."
While he was still conversing with them, Rachel arrived with her father's sheep, for she tended them.

When Jacob saw Rachel, daughter of his mother's brother Laban, together with Laban's sheep, he approached, rolled the stone from the mouth of the well, and watered the flock belonging to his mother's brother Laban.
Jacob kissed Rachel and wept aloud.
Jacob informed Rachel that he was her father's kinsman and Rebekah's son; whereupon she ran and reported it to her father.
Upon hearing the tidings concerning Jacob, his sister's son, Laban ran to meet him, embraced him, kissed him, and conducted him to his house. Jacob then recounted all these matters to Laban.
Laban said to him, "Surely you are my own flesh and blood." And he remained with him for a month.
Laban said to Jacob, "Because you are my kinsman, should you serve me gratuitously? Tell me, what shall your wages be?"
Now Laban had two daughters: the elder was named Leah, and the younger Rachel.
Leah's eyes were delicate, whereas Rachel was beautiful in form and beautiful in countenance.
Jacob loved Rachel and said, "I will serve you seven years for Rachel your younger daughter."
Laban replied, "It is better that I give her to you than to another man; stay with me."
Jacob served seven years for Rachel, and they seemed to him but a few days because of his love for her.
Jacob said to Laban, "Give me my wife, for my days are completed, that I may go in to her."
Laban gathered all the men of the place and prepared a feast.
In the evening he took his daughter Leah and brought her to him, and he went in to her.
Laban gave his daughter Leah his maidservant Zilpah as her attendant.
In the morning, he discovered that it was Leah. He said to Laban, "What is this you have done to me? Did I not serve you for Rachel? Why then have you deceived me?"
Laban said, "Such is not done in our place, to give the younger before the elder.
Fulfill the bridal week of this one, and we will give you that one also, for the service that you shall render me yet seven other years."
Jacob did so and fulfilled her week; then he gave him Rachel his daughter as a wife.
Laban gave Rachel his daughter his maidservant Bilhah as her attendant.
He went in also to Rachel, and he loved Rachel more than Leah; and he served with him yet seven other years.
When the the LORD saw that Leah was unloved, He opened her womb, but Rachel was barren.
Leah conceived and bore a son, and she named him Reuben, for she said, "Because the the LORD has looked upon my affliction; surely now my husband will love me."
She conceived again and bore a son, and said, "Because the the LORD has heard that I am unloved, He has given me this son also." And she named him Simeon.
She conceived again and bore a son, and said, "Now this time my husband will be joined to me, because I have borne him three sons." Therefore she named him Levi.
She conceived again and bore a son, and said, "This time I will praise the the LORD." Therefore she named him Judah; then she ceased bearing.
When Rachel perceived that she bore Jacob no offspring, she grew envious of her sister and entreated Jacob, "Grant me children, or I shall perish."
Jacob's anger was kindled against Rachel, and he said, "Am I in the place of God, who has withheld from you the fruit of the womb?"
She replied, "Behold my maidservant Bilhah; go in to her, that she may bear upon my knees, so that I too may be built up through her."
So she gave him her maidservant Bilhah as a wife, and Jacob went in to her.
Bilhah conceived and bore Jacob a son.
Rachel said, "God has vindicated me, and has indeed heard my voice, and has given me a son"; therefore she called his name Dan.
Bilhah, Rachel's maidservant, conceived again and bore Jacob a second son.
Rachel said, "With mighty wrestlings have I wrestled with my sister, and I have prevailed"; and she called his name Naphtali.
When Leah saw that she had ceased bearing, she took her maidservant Zilpah and gave her to Jacob as a wife.
Zilpah, Leah's maidservant, bore Jacob a son.
Leah said, "What good fortune!" and she called his name Gad.
Zilpah, Leah's maidservant, bore Jacob a second son.
Leah said, "How happy I am, for the daughters will call me blessed"; and she called his name Asher.
In the days of the wheat harvest, Reuben went out and found mandrakes in the field and brought them to his mother Leah. Then Rachel said to Leah, "Please give me some of your son's mandrakes."

Leah said, "Is it a small thing that you have taken my husband? Would you take away my son's mandrakes as well?" Rachel said, "Then he shall lie with you tonight in exchange for your son's mandrakes."
When Jacob came in from the field that evening, Leah went out to meet him and said, "You must come in to me, for I have hired you with my son's mandrakes." So he lay with her that night.
God listened to Leah, and she conceived and bore Jacob a fifth son.
Leah said, "God has given me my hire, because I gave my maidservant to my husband"; and she called his name Issachar.
Leah conceived again and bore Jacob a sixth son.
Leah said, "God has endowed me with a good dowry; now my husband will dwell with me, because I have borne him six sons"; and she called his name Zebulun.
Afterward she bore a daughter and called her name Dinah.
God remembered Rachel, and God listened to her and opened her womb.
She conceived and bore a son and said, "God has taken away my reproach."
She called his name Joseph, saying, "May the LORD add to me another son."
When Rachel had borne Joseph, Jacob said to Laban, "Send me away, that I may go to my own place and to my country.
Give me my wives and my children for whom I have served you, and let me go, for you know the service I have rendered to you."
Laban said to him, "If now I have found favor in your eyes, stay, for I have learned by divination that the LORD has blessed me on your account."
He said, "Appoint your wages, and I will give it."
Jacob said to him, "You know how I have served you and how your livestock has fared with me.
For you had little before I came, and it has increased abundantly, and the LORD has blessed you since my coming; but now when shall I provide for my own household as well?"
Laban said, "What shall I give you?" Jacob said, "You shall not give me anything; if you will do this for me, I will again pasture and keep your flock:"

"I will pass through all your flock today, removing from there every speckled and spotted sheep, every dark-colored sheep among the flock, and every spotted and speckled goat; and such shall be my wages.
So my honesty will answer for me hereafter, when you come to inspect my wages: every goat that is not speckled or spotted and every sheep that is not dark-colored shall be accounted stolen by me."
Laban said, "Behold, let it be according to your word."

That day he removed the male goats that were streaked and spotted and all the female goats that were speckled and spotted—every one marked with white—and all the dark-colored among the sheep, and gave them into the hand of his sons.
He set a distance of three days' journey between himself and Jacob, while Jacob pastured the rest of Laban's flock.
Jacob took fresh rods of poplar, hazel, and chestnut, and peeled white streaks in them, exposing the white beneath the bark.
He set the peeled rods in the troughs before the flocks, in the watering places where the flocks came to drink; and they conceived when they came to drink.
The flocks conceived before the rods and brought forth streaked, speckled, and spotted young.
Jacob separated the lambs and set the faces of the flock toward the streaked and all the dark-colored in Laban's flock, and he kept his own flocks separate, not mixing them with Laban's.
Whenever the stronger of the flock were breeding, Jacob would place the rods in the troughs before the eyes of the flock, that they might conceive among the rods.
But when the flock were feeble, he did not put them in; so the feebler were Laban's and the stronger Jacob's.
Thus the man increased exceedingly and had large flocks, and maidservants and menservants, and camels and donkeys.
Now Jacob heard the words of Laban's sons, who said, "Jacob has taken everything that belonged to our father, and from what was our father's he has acquired all this wealth."
Jacob also saw that Laban's demeanor toward him was not as it had been in former days.
Then the LORD said to Jacob, "Return to the land of your fathers and to your kindred, and I will be with you."
So Jacob sent word and summoned Rachel and Leah to the field, to his flock,
and said to them, "I see that your father's face is not toward me as it was yesterday and the day before, but the God of my father has been with me.
You yourselves know that I have served your father with all my strength.
"Yet your father has deceived me and changed my wages ten times, but God did not permit him to harm me.
If he said, 'The speckled shall be your wages,' then all the flock bore speckled; and if he said, 'The striped shall be your wages,' then all the flock bore striped.
Thus God has taken away your father's livestock and given them to me.
"And it came to pass at the time the flock were mating, that I lifted up my eyes and saw in a dream, and behold, the rams that leaped upon the flock were streaked, speckled, and spotted.
Then the angel of God said to me in the dream, 'Jacob,' and I said, 'Here I am.'
And he said, 'Lift up your eyes and see: all the rams that leap upon the flock are streaked, speckled, and spotted; for I have seen all that Laban is doing to you.
I am the God of Bethel, where you anointed a pillar and where you vowed a vow to Me. Now arise, leave this land, and return to the land of your birth.'"
Then Rachel and Leah answered and said to him, "Is there still any portion or inheritance for us in our father's house?
Are we not regarded by him as foreigners? For he has sold us, and he has indeed consumed our money.
For all the wealth that God has rescued from our father is ours and our children's. Now then, do all that God has said to you."
Then Jacob arose and set his sons and his wives on camels,
and he drove away all his livestock and all his property that he had acquired, the livestock of his acquiring that he had acquired in Paddan-aram, to go to Isaac his father in the land of Canaan.
Now Laban had gone to shear his sheep, and Rachel stole her father's household gods.
And Jacob deceived Laban the Aramean by not telling him that he was fleeing.
So he fled with all that he had; he arose and crossed the River, and set his face toward the hill country of Gilead.
On the third day it was told Laban that Jacob had fled.
So he took his relatives with him and pursued him for seven days, and overtook him in the hill country of Gilead.
But God came to Laban the Aramean in a dream by night and said to him, "Beware that you do not speak to Jacob either good or bad."
And Laban overtook Jacob. Now Jacob had pitched his tent in the hill country, and Laban with his relatives pitched in the hill country of Gilead.
And Laban said to Jacob, "What have you done, that you have stolen my heart and carried away my daughters like captives of the sword?
Why did you flee secretly and steal away from me, and not tell me, so that I might have sent you away with mirth and songs, with tambourine and lyre?
And why did you not permit me to kiss my grandchildren and my daughters? Now you have done foolishly.
"It is in my power to do you harm, but the God of your father spoke to me last night, saying, 'Beware that you do not speak to Jacob either good or bad.'
And now you have gone away because you longed greatly for your father's house; but why have you stolen my gods?"
Jacob answered and said to Laban, "Because I was afraid, for I said, 'Perhaps you will take your daughters from me by force.'
With whomever you find your gods, let him not live. In the presence of our relatives, point out what I have that is yours, and take it." Now Jacob did not know that Rachel had stolen them.
So Laban went into Jacob's tent and into Leah's tent and into the tent of the two maidservants, but he did not find them. Then he went out of Leah's tent and entered Rachel's tent.
Now Rachel had taken the household gods and put them in the camel's saddle and sat on them. Laban searched the whole tent but did not find them.
And she said to her father, "Let not my lord be angry that I cannot rise before you, for the way of women is upon me." So he searched but did not find the household gods.
Then Jacob became angry and argued with Laban, and Jacob said to Laban, "What is my offense? What is my sin, that you have hotly pursued me?
Although you have searched all my goods, what have you found of all your household goods? Set it here before my relatives and your relatives, that they may judge between the two of us.
"These twenty years I have been with you; your ewes and your female goats have not miscarried, and I have not eaten the rams of your flock.
What was torn by beasts I did not bring to you; I bore the loss of it. From my hand you required it, whether stolen by day or stolen by night.
Thus I was: by day the heat consumed me, and the frost by night, and my sleep fled from my eyes.
These twenty years I have served in your house: fourteen years for your two daughters, and six years for your flock, and you have changed my wages ten times.

If the God of my father, the God of Abraham and the Fear of Isaac, had not been with me, surely now you would have sent me away empty. God has seen my affliction and the labor of my hands, and rebuked you last night."

Laban answered and said to Jacob, "The daughters are my daughters, and the children are my children, and the flock is my flock, and all that you see is mine. But what can I do this day to these daughters of mine, or to their children whom they have borne?
Come now, let us make a covenant, you and I, and let it be a witness between me and you."
So Jacob took a stone and set it up as a pillar.
And Jacob said to his relatives, "Gather stones." So they gathered stones and made a heap, and they ate there by the heap.
Laban called it Jegar-sahadutha, but Jacob called it Galeed.
Laban said, "This heap is a witness between me and you today." Therefore its name was called Galeed.
And Mizpah, for he said, "The LORD watch between me and you, when we are absent one from another.
If you afflict my daughters, or if you take wives besides my daughters, although no man is with us, see, God is witness between me and you."
Then Laban said to Jacob, "Behold this heap and behold the pillar, which I have set between me and you.
This heap be a witness, and the pillar be a witness, that I will not pass over this heap to you, and that you will not pass over this heap and this pillar to me, for harm.
The God of Abraham and the God of Nahor, the God of their father, judge between us." So Jacob swore by the Fear of his father Isaac.
Then Jacob offered a sacrifice on the mountain and called his relatives to eat bread, and they ate bread and spent the night on the mountain.
Early in the morning Laban arose and kissed his grandchildren and his daughters and blessed them. Then Laban departed and returned to his place.
Jacob went on his way, and the angels of God met him.
When Jacob saw them, he said, “This is God’s camp,” and he called that place Mahanaim.
Jacob sent messengers ahead to his brother Esau in the land of Seir, the territory of Edom,
and instructed them, “Thus you shall say to my lord Esau: ‘Thus says your servant Jacob, “I have sojourned with Laban and have remained until now.
I have oxen, donkeys, sheep, male and female servants, and I have sent to tell my lord, that I may find favor in your sight.”’”
The messengers returned to Jacob and said, “We came to your brother Esau, and indeed he is coming to meet you, and four hundred men are with him.”
Jacob was greatly afraid and distressed, so he divided the people who were with him, along with the flocks, the herds, and the camels, into two camps.
He thought, “If Esau comes to the one camp and attacks it, then the other camp will escape.”
Then Jacob said, “O God of my father Abraham and God of my father Isaac, the LORD who told me to return to my country and my kindred and promised to deal well with me,
I am unworthy of all the steadfast love and all the faithfulness that You have shown to Your servant; for with only my staff I crossed this Jordan, and now I have become two camps. “
Deliver me, please, from the hand of my brother, from the hand of Esau, for I am afraid of him, lest he come and strike me down, mothers and children alike.
But You said, ‘I will surely deal well with you and make your offspring as the sand of the sea, which cannot be counted for multitude.’”
So he spent the night there. Then, from what he had at hand, he took a gift for his brother Esau:
two hundred female goats and twenty male goats, two hundred ewes and twenty rams,
thirty nursing camels with their young, forty cows and ten bulls, twenty female donkeys and ten young donkeys.
He put them into the hands of his servants, each herd by itself, and said to his servants, “Pass on ahead of me, and leave a space between herd and herd.”
He commanded the first that, when his brother Esau met him and asked who he was, where he was going, and whose animals these were before him,
he should answer that they belonged to his servant Jacob, that they were a gift sent to his lord Esau, and that Jacob himself was following behind.
He gave the same order to the second and the third and to all who followed the herds, that when they met Esau they should speak to him in this way and add that his servant Jacob was behind them.
For he said, “I will appease his face with the gift that goes before me, and afterward I will see his face; perhaps he will receive me.”
So the gift passed on ahead of him, and he himself spent that night in the camp.
He arose that night and took his two wives, his two female servants, and his eleven children, and crossed the ford of the Jabbok.
He took them and brought them across the stream, and sent over everything he had.
Jacob was left alone, and a man wrestled with him until the dawn came up.
When He saw that He could not prevail against Jacob, He touched the socket of his hip, and the socket of Jacob’s hip was dislocated as they wrestled.
Then He said, “Let Me go, for the dawn is breaking.” But Jacob said, “I will not let You go unless You bless me.”
He said to him, “What is your name?” Jacob answered, “Jacob.”
And He said, “Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel, for you have striven with God and with men, and have prevailed.”
Then Jacob asked Him, “Please tell me Your name.” But He said, “Why is it that you ask My name?” And He blessed him there.
So Jacob called the name of the place Peniel, for he said, “I have seen God face to face, and yet my life has been delivered.”
The sun rose upon him as he passed Penuel, limping because of his hip.
Therefore to this day the children of Israel do not eat the sinew of the thigh that is on the hip socket, because He touched the socket of Jacob’s hip on the sinew of the thigh.
Jacob lifted his gaze and saw Esau approaching with four hundred men; thereupon he apportioned the children among Leah, Rachel, and the two maidservants.
He set the maidservants and their children first, Leah and her children after them, and Rachel with Joseph last.
He himself passed on before them, prostrating himself to the ground seven times until he drew near his brother.
Esau ran to meet him, embraced him, fell upon his neck, kissed him, and they wept.
Esau lifted his eyes, saw the women and the children, and said, "Who are these with you?" Jacob replied, "The children whom God has graciously bestowed upon your servant."
The maidservants drew near with their children and bowed down.
Leah and her children likewise drew near and bowed; afterward Joseph and Rachel drew near and bowed.
Esau asked, "What do you mean by all this company that I met?" Jacob answered, "To find favor in the eyes of my lord."
Esau said, "I have abundance, my brother; keep what is yours."
Jacob said, "Please, no; if I have found favor in your eyes, accept my gift from my hand, for I have seen your face as though it were the face of God, and you have been gracious to me.
Please take my blessing, which has been brought to you, because God has dealt graciously with me, and I have everything." He urged him, and he accepted it.
Esau said, "Let us set out and travel; I will go before you."
Jacob said to him, "My lord knows that the children are tender and that the flocks and herds are nursing; if they are driven hard for one day, all the flock will die.
Let my lord go on ahead of his servant, while I move along slowly at the pace of the livestock before me and at the pace of the children, until I come to my lord at Seir."
Esau said, "Let me leave with you some of the people who are with me." Jacob said, "Why that? Let me find favor in my lord's eyes."
So Esau returned that day to Seir.
Jacob journeyed to Succoth and built a house for himself; for his livestock he made shelters; therefore the place was called Succoth.
Jacob came safely to the city of Shechem in the land of Canaan, on his return from Paddan-aram, and he encamped before the city.
From the sons of Hamor, Shechem's father, he bought the parcel of ground where he had pitched his tent, for a hundred pieces of money.
There he erected an altar and named it El Elohe Israel.
Now Dinah, the daughter of Leah, whom she had borne to Jacob, went out to observe the young women of the land.
Shechem, son of Hamor the Hivite and a prince of that country, beheld her; seizing her, he lay with her and violated her.
Yet his soul clung to Dinah, Jacob's daughter; he loved the maiden and spoke tenderly to her.
Shechem said to his father Hamor, "Obtain this maiden for me as a wife."
When Jacob learned that his daughter Dinah had been defiled, his sons were in the field with his livestock; Jacob remained silent until their return.
Hamor, Shechem's father, went out to Jacob to confer with him.

When Jacob's sons returned from the field and heard of the matter, the men were grieved and exceedingly incensed, because Shechem had committed an outrage in Israel by lying with Jacob's daughter—a deed that should never be done.
Hamor spoke with them: "My son Shechem's soul longs for your daughter; I entreat you to give her to him as a wife.
Intermarry with us: give your daughters to us, and take our daughters for yourselves.
Dwell with us; the land shall be before you; dwell and trade in it, and acquire property there."
Shechem said to her father and her brothers, "Let me find favor in your eyes; whatever you say to me I will give.
Name an exorbitant bride-price and gift, and I will pay as you specify; only give me the maiden as a wife."
Jacob's sons answered Shechem and his father Hamor deceitfully, because he had defiled their sister Dinah.
They said to them, "We cannot do this thing—giving our sister to an uncircumcised man—for it would be a disgrace to us.
But on this condition we will consent to you: if you will be circumcised like us, every male among you.
Then we will give our daughters to you, take your daughters for ourselves, dwell with you, and become one people.
But if you will not listen to us and be circumcised, we will take our daughter and depart."
Their proposal pleased Hamor and his son Shechem.
The young man did not delay in carrying out the matter, for he delighted in Jacob's daughter; indeed, he was the most honored in his father's household.
Hamor and his son Shechem went to the gate of their city and spoke to its men:
"These men are at peace with us; therefore let them dwell in the land and trade in it, for the land is spacious enough for them. Let us take their daughters as wives and give them our daughters.
Only on this condition will these men consent to dwell with us and become one people: every male among us must be circumcised, as they are circumcised.
Will not their livestock, their property, and all their animals become ours? Let us only agree to this, and they will dwell with us."
All who went out at the city gate listened to Hamor and his son Shechem, and every male was circumcised.
On the third day, when they were still in pain, two of Jacob's sons—Simeon and Levi, Dinah's brothers—each took his sword, came upon the city unawares, and killed every male.
They killed Hamor and his son Shechem with the sword, took Dinah from Shechem's house, and departed.
Jacob's sons came upon the slain and plundered the city, because its men had defiled their sister.
They seized their flocks, herds, donkeys, and everything in the city and in the field.
They took captive all their wealth, their children, and their wives, plundering everything in the houses.

Jacob said to Simeon and Levi, "You have brought trouble upon me, making me odious among the inhabitants of the land, among the Canaanites and the Perizzites. Since I am few in number, they will gather against me and strike me down, and I and my household will be destroyed."
They replied, "Should he have treated our sister as though she were a prostitute?"
God said to Jacob, “Arise, ascend to Bethel and abide there, and erect an altar there to the God who manifested Himself to you when you fled from your brother Esau.”
Jacob said to his household and to all who accompanied him, “Expunge the foreign deities that dwell in your midst, purify yourselves, and exchange your garments.
Let us arise and go up to Bethel, that I may make there an altar to the God who answered me in the day of my distress and has been with me in the way that I have gone.”
Accordingly, they surrendered to Jacob all the foreign deities in their possession, together with the rings in their ears; and Jacob interred them beneath the oak near Shechem.
As they departed, a divinely instilled terror descended upon the surrounding cities, so that none pursued the sons of Jacob.
Jacob, together with all the people accompanying him, arrived at Luz—that is, Bethel—in the land of Canaan.
There he erected an altar and designated the place El-bethel, for it was there that God had disclosed Himself to him as he fled from his brother.
Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, died and was interred beneath the oak below Bethel; hence the place was called Allon-bacuth.
God appeared to Jacob again when he came from Paddan-aram, and He blessed him.
God said to him, “Your name is Jacob; Jacob shall no longer be your appellation, but Israel shall be your name.
I am God Almighty: be fruitful and multiply. A nation, indeed a confederacy of nations, shall spring from you, and kings shall issue from your loins.
The land that I bestowed upon Abraham and Isaac I shall bestow upon you, and to your posterity after you I shall give the land.”
Then God withdrew from him in the place where He had spoken with him.
Jacob erected a pillar of stone in the place where He had spoken with him; he poured a libation upon it and anointed it with oil.
Jacob called the name of the place where God had spoken with him Bethel.
They departed from Bethel; and while they were yet some distance from Ephrath, Rachel went into labor and endured a grievous travail.
As her travail intensified, the midwife said to her, “Fear not; you have another son as well.”
As her life ebbed away—for she was dying—she named him Ben-oni; but his father called him Benjamin.
Rachel died and was buried on the way to Ephrath—that is, Bethlehem.
Jacob erected a pillar above her grave; that pillar marks Rachel's tomb to this day.
Israel journeyed onward and pitched his tent beyond the Tower of Eder.
While Israel sojourned in that region, Reuben went in and lay with Bilhah, his father's concubine, and Israel learned of it. Now the sons of Jacob numbered twelve.
The sons of Leah were Reuben, Jacob's firstborn, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun.
The sons of Rachel were Joseph and Benjamin.
The sons of Bilhah, Rachel's maidservant, were Dan and Naphtali.
The sons of Zilpah, Leah's maidservant, were Gad and Asher. These are the sons of Jacob who were born to him in Paddan-aram.
Jacob came to his father Isaac at Mamre—that is, Kiriath-arba, or Hebron—where Abraham and Isaac had sojourned.
The days of Isaac were one hundred and eighty years.
Isaac breathed his last and died, being gathered to his people, old and full of days; and his sons Esau and Jacob interred him.
The following constitutes the genealogical register of Esau, whose identity is inextricably bound to Edom.
Esau contracted matrimonial alliances among the Canaanite population, taking Adah, daughter of Elon the Hittite; Oholibamah, daughter of Anah and granddaughter of Zibeon the Hivite;
and Basemath, daughter of Ishmael and sister of Nebaioth.
Through Adah he begot Eliphaz; through Basemath, Reuel;
and through Oholibamah, Jeush, Jalam, and Korah—all of whom were born to him within Canaan.

Esau thereafter assembled his wives, sons, daughters, every constituent of his household, his livestock and beasts, together with all property he had amassed in Canaan, and he migrated to a region removed from his brother Jacob.
Their aggregated possessions had become too prodigious for communal habitation; the land of their sojourn could not sustain them because of their herds.
Consequently, Esau established himself in the hill country of Seir, and Esau is Edom.
Such, then, are the generations of Esau, father of Edom, in the hill country of Seir.
These are the names of Esau's sons: Eliphaz, son of Esau by Adah, and Reuel, son of Esau by Basemath.
Eliphaz's sons were Teman, Omar, Zepho, Gatam, and Kenaz.
Timna, who functioned as concubine to Eliphaz, son of Esau, bore Amalek to him; these are the sons associated with Adah, Esau's wife.
Reuel's sons were Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah—the sons associated with Basemath, Esau's wife.
The sons of Oholibamah, daughter of Anah and granddaughter of Zibeon, Esau's wife, were Jeush, Jalam, and Korah.
These are the chiefs among the sons of Esau: from the line of Eliphaz, Esau's firstborn, emerged Chief Teman, Chief Omar, Chief Zepho, and Chief Kenaz;
Chief Korah, Chief Gatam, and Chief Amalek likewise belonged to this lineage. These were the chiefs of Eliphaz in the land of Edom, descending from Adah.
The sons of Reuel, Esau's son, produced Chief Nahath, Chief Zerah, Chief Shammah, and Chief Mizzah; these were the chiefs of Reuel in Edom, descending from Basemath, Esau's wife.
The sons of Oholibamah, Esau's wife, produced Chief Jeush, Chief Jalam, and Chief Korah; these were the chiefs of Oholibamah, daughter of Anah and wife of Esau.
These are the sons of Esau, and these are their chiefs; he is Edom.
These are the sons of Seir the Horite, the autochthonous inhabitants of the land: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah,
Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan. These are the chiefs of the Horites, the sons of Seir in the land of Edom.
The sons of Lotan were Hori and Hemam, and Lotan's sister was Timna.
The sons of Shobal were Alvan, Manahath, Ebal, Shepho, and Onam.
The sons of Zibeon were Aiah and Anah; this is the Anah who discovered the hot springs in the wilderness while pasturing the donkeys of his father Zibeon.
The sons of Anah were Dishon and Oholibamah, daughter of Anah.
The sons of Dishon were Hemdan, Eshban, Ithran, and Cheran.
The sons of Ezer were Bilhan, Zaavan, and Akan.
The sons of Dishan were Uz and Aran.
These are the chiefs of the Horites: Chief Lotan, Chief Shobal, Chief Zibeon, Chief Anah,
Chief Dishon, Chief Ezer, and Chief Dishan. These are the chiefs of the Horites, enumerated according to their chiefs in the land of Seir.
These are the kings who reigned in the land of Edom before any king reigned over the Israelites:
Bela, son of Beor, reigned in Edom, and the name of his city was Dinhabah.
Upon Bela's death, Jobab, son of Zerah of Bozrah, succeeded him.
Upon Jobab's death, Husham from the land of the Temanites succeeded him.
Upon Husham's death, Hadad, son of Bedad, who defeated Midian in the field of Moab, succeeded him, and the name of his city was Avith.
Upon Hadad's death, Samlah from Masrekah succeeded him.
Upon Samlah's death, Saul from Rehoboth on the River succeeded him.
Upon Saul's death, Baal-hanan, son of Achbor, succeeded him.
Upon the death of Baal-hanan, son of Achbor, Hadar succeeded him; the name of his city was Pau, and his wife was Mehetabel, daughter of Matred, daughter of Mezahab.
These are the names of the chiefs of Esau, according to their families and localities, by their names: Chief Timna, Chief Alvah, Chief Jetheth,
Chief Oholibamah, Chief Elah, Chief Pinon,
Chief Kenaz, Chief Teman, Chief Mibzar,
Chief Magdiel, and Chief Iram. These are the chiefs of Edom, according to their settlements in the land of their possession. He is Esau, the father of Edom.
Jacob took up residence in the land of his father's sojournings, within Canaan.

These are the generations of Jacob: Joseph, at seventeen years of age, was tending the flock alongside his brothers; while still an adolescent, he was in the company of the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah, his father's wives; and Joseph conveyed an unfavorable report concerning them to their father.
Now Israel loved Joseph above all his sons, for he was the son of his old age, and he fashioned for him a robe of many colors.
When his brothers perceived that their father loved him more than any of them, they conceived a hatred for him and could not address him with civility.
Joseph dreamed a dream and recounted it to his brothers, whereupon they hated him still more.

He said, “Hear, I pray you, this dream that I have dreamed: behold, we were binding sheaves in the field, and, lo, my sheaf arose and stood upright; and, behold, your sheaves gathered round about and bowed down to my sheaf.”
His brothers said to him, “Shall you indeed reign over us? Or shall you indeed exercise dominion over us?” And they hated him yet more on account of his dreams and his words.
He dreamed yet another dream and told it to his brothers, saying, “Behold, I have dreamed a further dream: behold, the sun and the moon and eleven stars bowed down to me.”

He told it to his father and to his brothers; and his father rebuked him and said to him, “What is this dream that you have dreamed? Shall I and your mother and your brothers indeed come to bow ourselves down to you to the earth?”
His brothers envied him, but his father kept the saying in mind.
His brothers went to pasture their father's flock in Shechem.
Israel said to Joseph, “Are not your brothers pasturing in Shechem? Come now, and I will send you to them.” And he said, “Here I am.”
He said to him, “Go now, see whether it is well with your brothers and with the flock, and bring me back word.” So he sent him out of the valley of Hebron, and he came to Shechem.
A man found him, and, behold, he was wandering in the field; and the man asked him, “What are you seeking?”
He said, “I am seeking my brothers. Please tell me where they are pasturing.”
The man said, “They have departed from here, for I heard them say, ‘Let us go to Dothan.’” So Joseph went after his brothers and found them at Dothan.
They saw him from afar, and before he drew near to them they conspired against him to put him to death.
They said to one another, “Behold, this dreamer is coming.
Come now, let us kill him and cast him into one of the pits, and say, ‘A wild beast has devoured him’; then we shall see what becomes of his dreams.”
Reuben heard it and rescued him from their hand, saying, “Let us not take his life.”
Reuben said to them, “Shed no blood; cast him into this pit in the wilderness, but lay no hand on him”—intending to rescue him from their hand and restore him to his father.
When Joseph came to his brothers, they stripped him of his robe, the robe of many colors that was upon him.
They seized him and cast him into the pit; the pit was empty, and there was no water in it.

They sat down to eat bread; and they lifted up their eyes and looked, and, behold, a caravan of Ishmaelites was coming from Gilead, with their camels bearing spices, balm, and myrrh, on their way to carry them down to Egypt.
Judah said to his brothers, “What profit is there if we slay our brother and conceal his blood?
Come, let us sell him to the Ishmaelites, and let not our hand be upon him; for he is our brother, our own flesh.” And his brothers listened.
Midianite traders passed by; they drew Joseph up out of the pit and sold him for twenty shekels of silver to the Ishmaelites, and they brought Joseph into Egypt.
Reuben returned to the pit, and, behold, Joseph was not in the pit; and he tore his garments.
He returned to his brothers and said, “The boy is gone; and I—where shall I go?”
They took Joseph's robe and slaughtered a young goat and dipped the robe in the blood.
They sent the robe of many colors and brought it to their father, and said, “We have found this; know now whether it is your son's robe or not.”
He recognized it and said, “It is my son's robe; an evil beast has devoured him; Joseph is without doubt torn in pieces.”
Jacob tore his garments and put sackcloth upon his loins and mourned for his son many days.
All his sons and all his daughters rose up to comfort him, but he refused to be comforted, and said, “I will go down to Sheol mourning for my son.” And his father wept for him.
The Midianites sold him in Egypt to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, the captain of the guard.
At that juncture, Judah withdrew from his brothers and descended to reside with an Adullamite named Hirah.
There Judah beheld the daughter of a Canaanite called Shua; he took her in marriage and cohabited with her.
She conceived and bore a son, whom he named Er.
She conceived once more and bore a son, naming him Onan.
She bore yet another son and named him Shelah; his birth occurred at Kezib.
Judah procured a wife for Er, his firstborn, and her name was Tamar.
But Er, Judah’s firstborn, proved wicked in the sight of the LORD, and the LORD slew him.
Then Judah said to Onan, “Go in to your brother’s wife, fulfill the levirate obligation for her, and raise up offspring for your brother.”
Yet Onan knew that the offspring would not be his own; consequently, whenever he lay with his brother’s wife, he spilled his semen upon the ground, lest he provide offspring for his brother.
What he did displeased the LORD, so the LORD put him to death as well.

Thereupon Judah said to Tamar, his daughter-in-law, “Remain a widow in your father’s house until my son Shelah matures.” For he reasoned, “Perhaps he too will die, like his brothers.” So Tamar departed and dwelt in her father’s house.
After many days, Judah’s wife—the daughter of Shua—died. Once Judah was consoled, he ascended to Timnah with his friend Hirah the Adullamite, to the shearers of his flock.
Tamar was informed, “Your father-in-law is going up to Timnah to shear his sheep.”

She therefore removed her widow’s garments, veiled herself, and sat at the entrance of Enaim, which lies on the road to Timnah; for she perceived that Shelah had grown up, yet she had not been given to him as wife.
When Judah saw her, he took her for a prostitute, because she had covered her face.
Unaware that she was his daughter-in-law, he turned aside to her by the roadside and said, “Come, pray, let me lie with you.” She replied, “What will you give me, that you may lie with me?”
“I will send you a young goat from the flock,” he said. “Will you give me a pledge until you send it?” she asked.
“What pledge shall I give you?” he asked. “Your seal and its cord, and the staff in your hand,” she answered. So he gave them to her, lay with her, and she conceived by him.
Then she arose and departed, removed her veil, and resumed her widow’s garments.
Judah sent the young goat by his Adullamite friend to retrieve the pledge from the woman, but he could not find her.
He inquired of the men of that place, “Where is the shrine prostitute who was beside the road at Enaim?” They replied, “No shrine prostitute has been here.”
So he returned to Judah and said, “I did not find her; moreover, the men of the place declared, ‘No shrine prostitute has been here.’”
Judah responded, “Let her keep them, lest we become a byword; after all, I sent this goat, yet you did not find her.”
About three months later, Judah was told, “Your daughter-in-law Tamar has engaged in prostitution, and behold, she is pregnant by her harlotry.” Judah said, “Bring her out and let her be burned.”
As she was being brought out, she sent word to her father-in-law: “I am pregnant by the man to whom these belong,” she said; “pray see whether you recognize whose seal, cords, and staff these are.”
Judah recognized them and said, “She is more righteous than I, for I did not give her to my son Shelah.” And he never again lay with her.
When the time of her delivery arrived, behold, twins were in her womb.
As she was giving birth, one child put forth his hand, and the midwife took a scarlet thread and bound it upon his wrist, saying, “This one came out first.”
But as he drew back his hand, his brother emerged, and she said, “How you have burst forth!” So he was named Perez.
Afterward his brother came out, the one with the scarlet thread upon his wrist, and he was named Zerah.
Joseph had been conveyed down to Egypt, where an Egyptian named Potiphar—an officer of Pharaoh and captain of the guard—purchased him from the Ishmaelites who had brought him thither.
The LORD was with Joseph, so that he prospered; he resided in the house of his Egyptian master.
His master perceived that the LORD was with him and that the LORD granted success to all his undertakings.
Joseph thus found favor in his sight and attended him; Potiphar appointed him over his household and entrusted all his possessions into his hands.

From the moment Potiphar placed him in charge of his household and of all that he possessed, the LORD blessed the Egyptian’s house on account of Joseph; the blessing of the LORD rested upon everything Potiphar had, both in the house and in the field.
So Potiphar relinquished all his affairs into Joseph’s care; apart from the food he ate, he concerned himself with nothing. Now Joseph was strikingly handsome in form and countenance.
After these events, his master’s wife cast her eyes upon Joseph and said, “Lie with me.”
But he refused, saying to his master’s wife, “Behold, with me in charge, my master does not concern himself with anything in the house, and everything he owns he has entrusted to my care.
No one in this house is greater than I, and he has withheld nothing from me except you, because you are his wife. How then could I perpetrate this great wickedness and sin against God?”
Although she importuned Joseph day after day, he would not lie with her, nor even remain in her presence.
One day, when he entered the house to perform his duties, and no one of the household servants was within,
she seized him by his garment, saying, “Lie with me,” but he left his garment in her hand and fled, escaping outside.
When she saw that he had left his garment in her hand and had fled outside,
she summoned the men of her household and said to them, “Look! This Hebrew has been brought to us to toy with us. He came to me to lie with me, but I cried out with a loud voice.
When he heard me cry aloud, he left his garment beside me and fled outside.”
She kept his garment beside her until his master came home.
Then she addressed him, saying, “That Hebrew slave whom you brought to us came to me to toy with me.
But as soon as I cried out with a loud voice, he left his garment beside me and fled outside.”
When his master heard the words his wife spoke to him—namely, “This is how your slave treated me”—his anger burned.
Joseph’s master took him and put him into the prison, the place where the king’s prisoners were confined; and he remained there in prison.
But the LORD was with Joseph and extended kindness to him; He granted him favor in the eyes of the prison warden.
The warden committed to Joseph’s charge all the prisoners in the prison, and he became responsible for all that was done there.
The warden did not supervise anything that was in Joseph’s hand, because the LORD was with him, and the LORD made all that he did prosper.
After these events, the cupbearer and the baker of the king of Egypt incurred the wrath of their lord, Pharaoh, by offending him.
Pharaoh's anger was kindled against his two courtiers, the chief cupbearer and the chief baker.
Consequently, he remanded them to custody in the house of the captain of the guard, within the very prison where Joseph was confined.
The captain of the guard entrusted them to Joseph's supervision; Joseph attended to their needs, and they remained in custody.

After a considerable interval had elapsed, both the cupbearer and the baker of the king of Egypt—those imprisoned there—dreamed during the same night, each dream bearing its own distinctive significance.
When Joseph came to them in the morning and observed their demeanor, he found them disconsolate.
He therefore inquired of Pharaoh's officers who were confined with him in his master's house, "Why do your countenances appear so dejected this day?"
They answered, "We have both dreamed dreams, yet no interpreter is at hand." Joseph then said to them, "Do not interpretations belong to God? Please recount your dreams to me."
The chief cupbearer thereupon related his dream to Joseph, saying, "In my dream, behold, a vine stood before me.
Upon the vine were three branches; and as it budded, its blossoms unfolded, and its clusters ripened into grapes.
Now Pharaoh's cup was in my hand, and I took the grapes, pressed them into Pharaoh's cup, and placed the cup into Pharaoh's hand."
Joseph said to them, "This is the interpretation: the three branches are three days.

Within three days, Pharaoh will restore you to favor and reinstate you in your office, and you shall once again place Pharaoh's cup into his hand, according to the former custom when you served as his cupbearer.
Yet when prosperity attends you, remember me and deal graciously with me; speak of me to Pharaoh, and secure my deliverance from this dungeon.
For I was stolen away from the land of the Hebrews, and here also I have committed no offense warranting my consignment to this pit."
When the chief baker perceived that the interpretation was auspicious, he said to Joseph, "I too dreamed a dream: three baskets of white bread were upon my head.
In the uppermost basket were all manner of baked goods for Pharaoh, but the birds were devouring them from the basket atop my head."
Joseph answered, "This is the interpretation: the three baskets are three days.
Within three days, Pharaoh will remove you from life and hang you upon a tree, where the birds will consume your flesh."
On the third day, which was Pharaoh's birthday, he prepared a banquet for all his servants and, in their midst, rendered judgment upon the chief cupbearer and the chief baker.
He restored the chief cupbearer to his office, so that he once more placed the cup in Pharaoh's hand.
But the chief baker he hanged, precisely as Joseph had interpreted for them.
Yet the chief cupbearer did not remember Joseph; he forgot him.
After two full years had elapsed, Pharaoh dreamed that he was standing beside the Nile.
And behold, seven cows, comely in form and corpulent in flesh, ascended from the river and grazed in the marshland.
After them, seven other cows—repulsive in appearance and emaciated in flesh—came up from the Nile and stood beside the first cows on the riverbank.
The cows that were repulsive and lean devoured the seven comely, well-fattened cows; then Pharaoh awoke.
He fell asleep again and dreamed a second time: behold, seven ears of grain, plump and excellent, sprouted on a single stalk.
After them, seven ears, thin and scorched by the east wind, sprang up.
The thin ears swallowed the seven plump, full ears; then Pharaoh awoke and realized it had been a dream.
In the morning his spirit was agitated, so he summoned all the magicians of Egypt and all its sages; Pharaoh recounted his dreams to them, yet no one could interpret them for Pharaoh.
Then the chief cupbearer addressed Pharaoh: “I am reminded today of my offenses.
When Pharaoh was incensed against his servants and consigned me and the chief baker to the custody of the captain of the guard,
we both dreamed in the same night, each of us a dream with its own interpretation.
A Hebrew youth, a servant of the captain of the guard, was with us there; we related our dreams to him, and he interpreted them for us, assigning to each a meaning according to his dream.
And it transpired exactly as he had interpreted: I was restored to my post, and the other was hanged.”
Pharaoh then sent for Joseph, and they brought him swiftly from the dungeon; he shaved, changed his garments, and entered Pharaoh’s presence.
Pharaoh said to Joseph, “I have dreamed a dream, and no one can interpret it; but I have heard of you that, upon hearing a dream, you can interpret it.”
Joseph answered Pharaoh, “It is not in me; God will give Pharaoh a favorable answer.”
Pharaoh said to Joseph, “In my dream I was standing on the bank of the Nile.
And behold, seven cows, fat in flesh and beautiful in form, came up from the Nile and grazed in the marshland.
After them came seven other cows—scrawny, exceedingly ugly, and lean in flesh; I have never seen such hideous cattle anywhere in Egypt.
The lean and ugly cows devoured the first seven fat cows.
Yet when they had consumed them, one could not tell that they had done so, for their appearance remained as wretched as before. Then I awoke.
I also saw in my dream seven ears, full and good, growing on one stalk.
After them sprang up seven ears, withered, thin, and scorched by the east wind.
The thin ears swallowed the seven good ears. I related this to the magicians, but no one could explain it to me.”
Joseph said to Pharaoh, “The dreams of Pharaoh are one: God has revealed to Pharaoh what He is about to do.
The seven good cows are seven years, and the seven good ears are seven years; the dreams are one.
The seven lean and ugly cows that came up after them are seven years of famine, as are the seven empty ears scorched by the east wind; they shall be seven years of famine.
It is just as I told Pharaoh: God has shown Pharaoh what He is about to do.
Behold, seven years of great abundance are coming throughout the whole land of Egypt.
After them seven years of famine will arise, and all the abundance will be forgotten in Egypt, and famine will consume the land.
The abundance will not be remembered in the land because of the famine that follows, for it will be exceedingly severe.
And because the dream was given to Pharaoh twice, the matter is firmly established by God, and God will bring it to pass soon.”
“Now therefore, let Pharaoh seek out a discerning and wise man and set him over the land of Egypt.
Let Pharaoh act thus: appoint overseers over the land and take a fifth of the produce of Egypt during the seven years of plenty.
Let them gather all the food of the good years that are coming and store up grain under Pharaoh’s authority, keeping it in the cities for food.
That food shall be a reserve for the land against the seven years of famine that will befall Egypt, so that the land may not be cut off by famine.”
The proposal pleased Pharaoh and all his servants.
Pharaoh said to his servants, “Can we find anyone like this, a man in whom is the Spirit of God?”
Pharaoh said to Joseph, “Since God has shown you all this, there is no one so discerning and wise as you.
You shall be over my house, and all my people shall obey your orders; only in regard to the throne will I be greater than you.”
Pharaoh said to Joseph, “See, I have set you over all the land of Egypt.”
Pharaoh removed his signet ring from his hand and put it on Joseph’s hand; he clothed him in garments of fine linen and placed a gold chain around his neck.
He made him ride in the second chariot, and they cried before him, “Bow the knee!” Thus he set him over all the land of Egypt.
Pharaoh said to Joseph, “I am Pharaoh, and without your consent no one shall lift hand or foot in all the land of Egypt.”
Pharaoh called Joseph’s name Zaphenath-paneah and gave him Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera, priest of On, as his wife. Joseph went out over the land of Egypt.
Joseph was thirty years old when he stood before Pharaoh, king of Egypt. Joseph went out from Pharaoh’s presence and passed through all the land of Egypt.
During the seven years of plenty the land produced abundantly.
Joseph gathered all the food of those seven years in Egypt and stored the food in the cities; the food from the fields surrounding each city he stored within it.
Joseph amassed grain in great abundance, like the sand of the sea, until he ceased to measure it, for it was beyond numbering.
Before the year of famine came, two sons were born to Joseph by Asenath, daughter of Potiphera, priest of On.
Joseph named his firstborn Manasseh, saying, “God has made me forget all my hardship and all my father’s house.”
He named the second Ephraim, saying, “God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction.”
The seven years of plenty in Egypt came to an end,
and the seven years of famine began to come, just as Joseph had said. There was famine in all lands, but throughout Egypt there was bread.
When all Egypt was famished, the people cried out to Pharaoh for bread; Pharaoh said to all Egypt, “Go to Joseph; do whatever he tells you.”
The famine was over all the face of the earth. Joseph opened all the storehouses and sold grain to the Egyptians, and the famine grew severe in Egypt.
All the earth came to Egypt, to Joseph, to buy grain, because the famine was severe over all the earth.
Jacob perceived that grain was available in Egypt, and he said to his sons, “Why do you gaze at one another?
Behold, I have heard that there is grain in Egypt; go down there and procure grain for us, that we may live and not perish.”
So ten of Joseph’s brothers descended to purchase grain from Egypt.
Yet Jacob did not send Benjamin, Joseph’s brother, with his brothers, for he said, “Lest some calamity befall him.”
Thus the sons of Israel came to buy among the throng of arrivals, for the famine prevailed in the land of Canaan.
Joseph, who served as viceroy over the land and purveyor of grain to all its inhabitants, received his brothers, and they prostrated themselves before him with their faces to the ground.
Joseph recognized his brothers and, concealing his identity, addressed them with severity: “Whence have you come?” They answered, “From the land of Canaan, to purchase food.”
Although Joseph recognized his brothers, they did not recognize him.
Joseph remembered the dreams he had dreamed concerning them and said, “You are spies; you have come to discern the land’s vulnerability.”
They replied, “No, my lord; your servants have come to buy food.”
“We are all sons of one man; we are honest men, not spies.”
He said, “No, you have come to discern the land’s vulnerability.”
They said, “Your servants are twelve brothers, sons of one man in Canaan; the youngest is with our father today, and one is no more.”
Joseph said, “It is just as I told you: you are spies.”
“By this you shall be tested: as Pharaoh lives, you shall not depart from here unless your youngest brother comes here.
Send one of you to fetch your brother, while the rest of you remain imprisoned, so that your words may be tested and truth found in you; otherwise, as Pharaoh lives, you are spies.”
So he confined them in custody for three days.
On the third day Joseph said to them, “Do this and live, for I fear God.
If you are honest men, let one of your brothers be confined in prison, while the rest of you go and carry grain for the famine of your households.
Bring your youngest brother to me, so that your words may be verified and you may not die.” And they did so.
They said to one another, “Truly we are guilty concerning our brother, for we saw the anguish of his soul when he pleaded with us, and we did not listen; therefore this distress has come upon us.”
Reuben answered them, “Did I not say to you, ‘Do not sin against the boy’? But you would not listen. Now his blood is required of us.”
They did not know that Joseph understood them, for an interpreter stood between them.
He turned away from them and wept; then he returned and spoke to them. He took Simeon from among them and bound him before their eyes.
Joseph then commanded that their sacks be filled with grain, that each man’s silver be restored to his sack, and that provisions be given them for the journey; and so it was done.
They loaded their grain upon their donkeys and departed from there.
At the lodging place, one of them opened his sack to give fodder to his donkey and saw his silver in the mouth of the sack.
He said to his brothers, “My silver has been returned; here it is in my sack!” Their hearts sank, and they trembled, saying to one another, “What is this that God has done to us?”
They came to Jacob their father in the land of Canaan and recounted to him all that had happened to them.
“The man who is lord of the land addressed us harshly and treated us as spies of the land.
We replied, ‘We are honest men; we are not spies.’
‘We are twelve brothers, sons of our father; one is no more, and the youngest remains with our father in Canaan.’
But the man, lord of the land, said that by this he would know whether we were honest: we were to leave one brother with him, take grain for the famine of our households, and go.
He further said that we must bring our youngest brother to him, so that he might know we were not spies but honest men; then he would return our brother to us and permit us to trade in the land.”
As they emptied their sacks, behold, each man’s bundle of silver was in his sack; and when they and their father saw the bundles of silver, they were afraid.
Their father Jacob said to them, “You have bereaved me: Joseph is no more, Simeon is no more, and now you would take Benjamin. All these things are against me.”
Reuben said to his father, “You may put my two sons to death if I do not bring him back to you. Entrust him to my care, and I will return him to you.”

But Jacob said, “My son shall not go down with you, for his brother is dead and he alone is left. If harm should befall him on the journey you are to take, then you would bring down my gray hair with sorrow to Sheol.”
Now the famine bore heavily upon the land.
And when they had consumed the grain that they had brought from Egypt, their father said to them, "Return; procure for us a modest quantity of provisions."
But Judah said to him, "The man solemnly warned us, saying, 'You shall not see my face unless your brother is with you.'
If you send our brother with us, we will descend and buy food for you.
Yet if you will not send him, we will not descend, for the man said to us, 'You shall not see my face unless your brother is with you.'"
Then Israel said, "Why have you dealt so grievously with me by telling the man that you had yet another brother?"

They answered, "The man questioned us closely concerning ourselves and our kindred, saying, 'Is your father still alive? Have you a brother?' Thus we answered him according to these words. How could we have known that he would say, 'Bring your brother down'?"
Then Judah said to Israel his father, "Send the boy with me, and we will arise and go, that we may live and not die—both we and you and our little ones.
I myself will be surety for him; from my hand you shall require him. If I do not bring him back to you and set him before you, then let me bear the blame before you all my days.
For had we not delayed, we would surely have returned by now a second time."

Then Israel their father said to them, "If it must be so, then do this: take some of the best produce of the land in your bags and carry down a present to the man—a little balm, a little honey, gum, myrrh, pistachio nuts, and almonds.
Take double money with you, and take back in your hand the money that was returned in the mouths of your sacks; perhaps it was an oversight.
Take also your brother and arise; go again to the man.
May God Almighty grant you mercy before the man, that he may send back your other brother and Benjamin. As for me, if I am bereaved, I am bereaved."
So the men took this present, and they took double money with them, and Benjamin. They arose and went down to Egypt and stood before Joseph.
When Joseph saw Benjamin with them, he said to the steward of his house, "Bring the men into the house, and slaughter an animal and make ready, for the men shall dine with me at noon."
The man did as Joseph had commanded and brought the men into Joseph's house.

Now the men were afraid because they had been brought into Joseph's house, and they said, "It is because of the money that was returned in our sacks the first time that we are brought in, so that he may assault us and fall upon us and take us for slaves, together with our donkeys."
So they drew near to the steward of Joseph's house and spoke to him at the door of the house,
saying, "Oh, my lord, we came down the first time to buy food.
And when we came to the lodging place and opened our sacks, behold, each man's money was in the mouth of his sack—our money in full weight—so we have brought it back in our hand.
We have also brought down other money with us to buy food. We do not know who put our money in our sacks."
He replied, "Peace be to you; do not fear. Your God and the God of your father has put treasure in your sacks for you. I have received your money." Then he brought Simeon out to them.
And the man brought the men into Joseph's house and gave them water; they washed their feet, and he gave their donkeys fodder.
They prepared the present for Joseph's arrival at noon, for they had heard that they were to eat bread there.
When Joseph came into the house, they brought into the house to him the present that was in their hand, and bowed down to him to the ground.
He inquired after their welfare and said, "Is your father well, the old man of whom you spoke? Is he still alive?"
They said, "Your servant our father is well; he is still alive." And they bowed down and prostrated themselves.
He lifted up his eyes and saw his brother Benjamin, his mother's son, and said, "Is this your younger brother, of whom you spoke to me?" And he said, "God be gracious to you, my son."
Then Joseph hurried out, for his compassion was stirred for his brother, and he sought a place to weep. He went into his chamber and wept there.
Then he washed his face, came out, restrained himself, and said, "Serve the food."

They served him by himself, and them by themselves, and the Egyptians who ate with him by themselves, because the Egyptians could not eat bread with the Hebrews, for that is an abomination to the Egyptians.
They sat before him, the firstborn according to his birthright and the youngest according to his youth; and the men looked at one another in astonishment.
