Then the three companies blew the trumpets and broke the jars; they held the torches in their left hands and the trumpets in their right hands to blow them, and they cried out, "A sword for the LORD and for Gideon!"
And each man stood in his place around the camp; and the whole camp ran, cried out, and fled.

When the three hundred blew the trumpets, the LORD set every man's sword against his fellow throughout the camp, and the host fled as far as Beth-shittah toward Zererah, as far as the border of Abel-meholah, by Tabbath.
And the men of Israel were called out from Naphtali, Asher, and Manasseh, and they pursued after Midian.

Then Gideon sent messengers throughout all the hill country of Ephraim, saying, "Go down against Midian and seize the waters of the Jordan before them, as far as Beth-barah." So all the men of Ephraim were called out and seized the waters as far as Beth-barah.

And they captured Oreb and Zeeb, the two princes of Midian; they killed Oreb at the rock of Oreb, and Zeeb they killed at the winepress of Zeeb; and they pursued Midian, and brought the heads of Oreb and Zeeb to Gideon beyond the Jordan.
The men of Ephraim then said to him, “What is this deed that you have done to us, that you did not summon us when you went forth to wage war against Midian?” And they contended with him vehemently.
He replied to them, “What have I now accomplished in comparison with you? Are not the gleanings of Ephraim superior to the vintage of Abiezer?
God has delivered into your hands the princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb; what, then, could I have done to rival you?” When he spoke thus, their wrath subsided toward him.
Gideon, together with the three hundred men who accompanied him, came to the Jordan and crossed it, though they were weary, yet still in pursuit.
He said to the men of Succoth, “Please give loaves of bread to the people who are following me, for they are exhausted, and I am pursuing Zebah and Zalmunna, the kings of Midian.”
But the officials of Succoth answered, “Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your possession, that we should give bread to your army?”
Gideon replied, “Very well; when the LORD has given Zebah and Zalmunna into my hand, I will thresh your flesh with the thorns of the wilderness and with briers.”
From there he ascended to Penuel and spoke to them in the same manner; the men of Penuel answered him just as the men of Succoth had answered.
So he said to the men of Penuel, “When I return in peace, I will demolish this tower.”

Now Zebah and Zalmunna were in Karkor with their camp—about fifteen thousand men, all that remained of the entire host of the people of the East, for a hundred and twenty thousand men who drew the sword had already fallen.
Gideon went up by the route of the tent-dwellers east of Nobah and Jogbehah, and struck the camp, for the camp was unsuspecting.
Zebah and Zalmunna fled, and he pursued them and captured the two kings of Midian, Zebah and Zalmunna, and threw the whole camp into consternation.
Gideon, the son of Joash, then returned from the battle by the ascent of Heres.
He captured a young man of Succoth and interrogated him; and the youth wrote down for him the officials and elders of Succoth—seventy-seven men.

Then he came to the men of Succoth and said, “Behold Zebah and Zalmunna, concerning whom you taunted me, saying, ‘Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna now in your hand, that we should give bread to your men?’”
He then took the elders of the city, together with thorns of the wilderness and briers, and with them he chastised the men of Succoth.
He also demolished the tower of Penuel and slew the men of the city.
He said to Zebah and Zalmunna, “Where are the men whom you killed at Tabor?” They answered, “As you are, so were they—each one resembling the son of a king.”
He said, “They were my brothers, the sons of my mother. As the LORD lives, if you had spared them alive, I would not have killed you.”
Then he said to Jether, his firstborn, “Arise and kill them.” But the youth did not draw his sword, for he was afraid, because he was still a youth.

Then Zebah and Zalmunna said, “Arise yourself and fall upon us; for as the man is, so is his strength.” Gideon arose and killed Zebah and Zalmunna, and took the crescent ornaments that were on the necks of their camels.
Then the men of Israel said to Gideon, “Rule over us—you and your son and your grandson as well—for you have delivered us from the hand of Midian.”
Gideon said to them, “I will not rule over you, nor will my son rule over you; the LORD will rule over you.”
Gideon also said to them, “Let me make one request of you: each of you give me the earrings from his spoil.” (For they had golden earrings, because they were Ishmaelites.)
They answered, “We will willingly give them.” And they spread out a cloak, and each man cast into it the earrings of his spoil.

The weight of the gold earrings that he requested came to seventeen hundred shekels, besides the crescent ornaments, the pendants, the purple garments worn by the kings of Midian, and the chains that were on their camels’ necks.
Gideon fashioned an ephod from it and set it up in his city, Ophrah; and all Israel gave themselves to idolatry in following it, so that it became a snare to Gideon and to his household.
Thus Midian was subdued before the people of Israel, and they did not again lift up their heads; and the land enjoyed rest for forty years in the days of Gideon.
Then Jerubbaal, the son of Joash, went and dwelt in his own house.
Now Gideon had seventy sons of his own issue, for he had many wives.
His concubine, who was in Shechem, also bore him a son, and he named him Abimelech.
Gideon, the son of Joash, died at a good old age and was buried in the tomb of Joash his father, at Ophrah of the Abiezrites.
As soon as Gideon was dead, the people of Israel turned back and gave themselves to the Baals in idolatrous devotion, and made Baal-berith their god.
The people of Israel did not remember the LORD their God, who had delivered them from the hand of all their enemies round about.
Neither did they show steadfast love to the house of Jerubbaal—that is, Gideon—in proportion to all the good that he had done for Israel.
Abimelech the son of Jerubbaal went unto Shechem, unto his mother’s brethren, and communed with them and with all the family of his mother’s father, saying,

“Pray, speak in the ears of all the lords of Shechem, ‘Which is better for you: that seventy men, all the sons of Jerubbaal, should rule over you, or that one man should rule over you? Remember also that I am your own flesh and blood.’”
And his mother’s brethren spake of him all these words in the ears of all the lords of Shechem; and their heart inclined to follow Abimelech, for they said, “He is our brother.”
And they gave him seventy pieces of silver out of the house of Baal-berith, wherewith Abimelech hired worthless and reckless men, who followed him.

And he went unto his father’s house at Ophrah, and slew his brethren, the sons of Jerubbaal, being seventy persons, upon one stone; but Jotham the youngest son of Jerubbaal was left, for he hid himself.
And all the lords of Shechem assembled, and all the house of Millo, and went and made Abimelech king by the oak of the pillar that was in Shechem.

And when they told Jotham, he went and stood in the top of mount Gerizim, and lifted up his voice, and cried, and said unto them, “Hearken unto me, you lords of Shechem, that God may hearken unto you.
The trees went forth to anoint a king over them; and they said unto the olive tree, ‘Reign over us.’
But the olive tree said unto them, ‘Shall I forsake my fatness, wherewith by me God and man are honoured, and go to sway over the trees?’
And the trees said to the fig tree, ‘Come, and reign over us.’
But the fig tree said unto them, ‘Shall I forsake my sweetness and my good fruit, and go to sway over the trees?’
And the trees said unto the vine, ‘Come, and reign over us.’
And the vine said unto them, ‘Shall I leave my wine, which cheereth God and man, and go to sway over the trees?’
Then said all the trees unto the bramble, ‘Come, and reign over us.’

And the bramble said unto the trees, ‘If in truth you anoint me king over you, then come and take refuge under my shadow; and if not, let fire come out of the bramble and devour the cedars of Lebanon.’

“Now therefore, if you have dealt truly and uprightly, in that you have made Abimelech king, and if you have dealt well with Jerubbaal and with his house, and have done unto him according to the deserving of his hands—
for my father fought for you, and adventured his life far, and delivered you out of the hand of Midian;

and you are risen up against my father’s house this day, and have slain his sons, seventy men, upon one stone, and have made Abimelech, the son of his maidservant, king over the lords of Shechem, because he is your brother—
if you then have dealt truly and uprightly with Jerubbaal and with his house this day, then rejoice in Abimelech, and let him also rejoice in you;

but if not, let fire come out from Abimelech, and devour the lords of Shechem and the house of Millo; and let fire come out from the lords of Shechem and from the house of Millo, and devour Abimelech.”
And Jotham ran away, and fled, and went to Beer, and dwelt there, for fear of Abimelech his brother.
And Abimelech reigned over Israel three years.
And God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the lords of Shechem; and the lords of Shechem dealt treacherously with Abimelech,

that the violence done to the seventy sons of Jerubbaal might come, and their blood be laid upon Abimelech their brother, who slew them, and upon the lords of Shechem, who strengthened his hands to slay his brethren.
And the lords of Shechem set liers in wait for him upon the tops of the mountains, and they robbed all that came along that way by them; and it was told Abimelech.
And Gaal the son of Ebed came with his brethren, and went over to Shechem; and the lords of Shechem put their trust in him.
And they went out into the field, and gathered their vineyards, and trod the grapes, and held festival, and went into the house of their god, and did eat and drink, and cursed Abimelech.

And Gaal the son of Ebed said, “Who is Abimelech, and who is Shechem, that we should serve him? Is not he the son of Jerubbaal, and Zebul his officer? Serve the men of Hamor, the father of Shechem; and why should we serve him?”
“Would that this people were given into my hand! then would I remove Abimelech. And he said unto Abimelech, ‘Increase your host, and come out.’”
And when Zebul the ruler of the city heard the words of Gaal the son of Ebed, his anger was kindled.
And he sent messengers unto Abimelech secretly, saying, “Behold, Gaal the son of Ebed and his brethren are come to Shechem; and, behold, they fortify the city against you.
Now therefore, up by night, you and the people that are with you, and lie in wait in the field.

And it shall be, that in the morning, as soon as the sun is up, you shall rise early and rush upon the city; and, behold, when he and the people that are with him come out against you, then may you do to them as your hand shall find occasion.”
And Abimelech rose up, and all the people that were with him, by night, and they laid wait against Shechem in four companies.
And Gaal the son of Ebed went out, and stood in the entering of the gate of the city; and Abimelech rose up, and the people that were with him, from the ambush.
And when Gaal saw the people, he said unto Zebul, “Behold, people come down from the tops of the mountains.” And Zebul said unto him, “You see the shadow of the mountains as if they were men.”
And Gaal spake again, and said, “See, there come people down by the middle of the land, and one company cometh by the way of the oak of Meonenim.”

Then said Zebul unto him, “Where is now your mouth, wherewith you said, ‘Who is Abimelech, that we should serve him?’ Is not this the people that you have despised? Go out, I pray you, and fight with them.”
And Gaal went out before the lords of Shechem, and fought with Abimelech.
And Abimelech chased him, and he fled before him; and many were overthrown and slain, even unto the entrance of the gate.
And Abimelech dwelt at Arumah; and Zebul thrust out Gaal and his brethren, that they should not dwell in Shechem.
And it came to pass on the morrow, that the people went out into the field; and they told Abimelech.

And he took the people, and divided them into three companies, and laid wait in the field; and he looked, and, behold, the people came forth out of the city; and he rose up against them, and smote them.
And Abimelech, and the companies that were with him, rushed forward and stood in the entrance of the gate of the city; and the two companies rushed upon all that were in the field, and smote them.
And Abimelech fought against the city all that day; and he took the city, and slew the people that were therein; and he beat down the city, and sowed it with salt.
And when all the lords of the tower of Shechem heard thereof, they entered into the hold of the house of El-berith.
And it was told Abimelech that all the lords of the tower of Shechem were gathered together.

And Abimelech gat him up to mount Zalmon, he and all the people that were with him; and Abimelech took an axe in his hand, and cut down a bough from the trees, and took it, and laid it on his shoulder, and said unto the people that were with him, “Make haste, and do as you have seen me do.”

And all the people likewise cut down every man his bough, and followed Abimelech, and put them to the hold, and set the hold on fire upon them; so that all the men of the tower of Shechem died also, about a thousand men and women.
Then went Abimelech to Thebez, and encamped against Thebez, and took it.
But there was a strong tower within the city, and thither fled all the men and the women, and all the lords of the city, and shut themselves in, and gat them up to the roof of the tower.
And Abimelech came unto the tower, and fought against it, and drew near unto the door of the tower to burn it with fire.
And a certain woman cast a piece of a millstone upon Abimelech’s head, and brake his skull.

Then he called hastily unto the young man his armour-bearer, and said unto him, “Draw your sword, and slay me, that men say not of me, ‘A woman slew him.’” And his young man thrust him through, and he died.
And when the men of Israel saw that Abimelech was dead, they departed every man unto his place.
Thus God repaid the wickedness of Abimelech, which he had done unto his father, in slaying his seventy brethren;
and all the wickedness of the men of Shechem did God bring upon their heads; and upon them came the curse of Jotham the son of Jerubbaal.
Following the demise of Abimelech, Tola—son of Puah, son of Dodo, and a man of Issachar—arose to effect Israel's deliverance; he took up residence in Shamir, within the hill country of Ephraim.
He adjudicated Israel for twenty-three years; upon his death, he was interred in Shamir.
After him, Jair the Gileadite arose and judged Israel for twenty-two years.
He had thirty sons who rode upon thirty donkeys, and they held thirty towns in the land of Gilead, still designated Havvoth-jair to this day.
Jair died and was buried in Kamon.

The Israelites once more perpetrated evil in the sight of the LORD: they venerated the Baals and the Ashtoreths, together with the deities of Aram, Sidon, Moab, the Ammonites, and the Philistines; they abandoned the LORD and rendered Him no service.
The LORD's wrath was kindled against Israel, and He consigned them into the power of the Philistines and the Ammonites.
In that year they shattered and crushed the Israelites; for eighteen years they oppressed all the Israelites beyond the Jordan in Gilead, in the land of the Amorites.
The Ammonites likewise crossed the Jordan to wage war against Judah, Benjamin, and the house of Ephraim, and Israel was exceedingly distressed.
The Israelites cried out to the LORD, saying, "We have sinned against you, for we have forsaken our God and served the Baals."
The LORD said to the Israelites, "Did I not deliver you from the Egyptians, the Amorites, the Ammonites, and the Philistines?
The Sidonians, Amalek, and Maon oppressed you; you cried out to Me, and I delivered you from their hand.
Yet you have forsaken Me and served other gods; consequently I shall no longer deliver you.
Go and cry out to the gods you have chosen; let them deliver you in your time of distress."
The Israelites said to the LORD, "We have sinned; do unto us whatever seems good in Your sight; only deliver us this day."
So they removed the foreign gods from their midst and served the LORD, and His soul was grieved by Israel's affliction.
The Ammonites assembled and encamped in Gilead, while the Israelites gathered and encamped at Mizpah.
The people and the leaders of Gilead said to one another, "Who is the man who will take the lead in fighting the Ammonites? He shall be head over all the inhabitants of Gilead."
Now Jephthah the Gileadite was a mighty warrior, and he was the son of a prostitute; Gilead had fathered Jephthah.
Gilead’s wife bore him sons, and when the sons of the wife grew up, they drove Jephthah out and said to him, “You shall not inherit in our father’s house, for you are the son of another woman.”
Then Jephthah fled from his brothers and dwelt in the land of Tob, and worthless men gathered to Jephthah and went out with him.
After some time, the Ammonites fought against Israel.
When the Ammonites fought against Israel, the elders of Gilead went to bring Jephthah from the land of Tob.
They said to Jephthah, “Come and be our leader, that we may fight against the Ammonites.”
Jephthah said to the elders of Gilead, “Did you not hate me and drive me out of my father’s house? Why have you come to me now when you are in distress?”
The elders of Gilead said to Jephthah, “Therefore we have now returned to you, that you may go with us and fight against the Ammonites, and you shall be head over all the inhabitants of Gilead.”
Jephthah said to the elders of Gilead, “If you are bringing me back to fight against the Ammonites, and the LORD gives them before me, I will be your head.”
The elders of Gilead said to Jephthah, “The LORD be witness between us, if we do not do according to your words.”
Then Jephthah went with the elders of Gilead, and the people made him head and leader over them; and Jephthah spoke all his words before the LORD at Mizpah.
Jephthah sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites, saying, “What have you to do with me, that you have come against me in my land?”
The king of the Ammonites said to Jephthah, “Because Israel took my land when he came up from Egypt, from the Arnon to the Jabbok and to the Jordan; now therefore restore those to me peacefully.”
Jephthah again sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites.
He said to him, “Thus says Jephthah: Israel did not take the land of Moab, nor the land of the Ammonites.
For when they came up from Egypt, Israel went through the wilderness to the Red Sea and came to Kadesh.

Israel sent messengers to the king of Edom, saying, ‘Please let me pass through your land,’ but the king of Edom would not listen; Israel also sent to the king of Moab, but he would not consent, so Israel remained at Kadesh.

Then he went through the wilderness and went around the land of Edom and the land of Moab, and came from the east, toward the sun, to the land of Moab, and camped beyond the Arnon; yet they did not enter the territory of Moab, for the Arnon was the border of Moab. “
Israel sent messengers to Sihon, king of the Amorites, king of Heshbon, and Israel said to him, ‘Please let us pass through your land to my place.’
But Sihon did not trust Israel to pass through his territory; so Sihon gathered all his people and camped at Jahaz and fought against Israel.
The LORD, the God of Israel, gave Sihon and all his people into the hand of Israel, and they struck them; so Israel possessed all the land of the Amorites, the inhabitants of that country.
They possessed all the territory of the Amorites from the Arnon to the Jabbok, and from the wilderness to the Jordan. “
So now the LORD, the God of Israel, has dispossessed the Amorites from before His people Israel, and should you possess it?
Will you not possess what Chemosh your god gives you to possess? So whatever the LORD our God has dispossessed from before us, that we will possess.
Are you any better than Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab? Did he ever strive against Israel, or did he ever fight against them?
While Israel dwelt in Heshbon and its villages, and in Aroer and its villages, and in all the cities along the Arnon, three hundred years, why did you not recover them within that time?
I therefore have not sinned against you, but you do me wrong by waging war against me. The LORD, the Judge, judge this day between the sons of Israel and the sons of Ammon.”
But the king of the Ammonites did not heed the words of Jephthah which he sent to him.
Then the Spirit of the LORD came upon Jephthah, and he passed over Gilead and Manasseh, and passed over Mizpah of Gilead, and from Mizpah of Gilead he passed over to the Ammonites.
Jephthah made a vow to the LORD and said, “If You will indeed give the Ammonites into my hand,
then whatever comes out of the doors of my house to meet me when I return in peace from the Ammonites shall be the LORD’s, and I will offer it up as a burnt offering.”
So Jephthah crossed over to the Ammonites to fight against them, and the LORD gave them into his hand.
He struck them from Aroer to the entrance of Minnith, twenty cities, and as far as Abel-keramim, with a very great slaughter; so the Ammonites were subdued before Israel.
When Jephthah came to his house at Mizpah, behold, his daughter came out to meet him with tambourines and dancing; and she was his only child; besides her he had neither son nor daughter.
When he saw her, he tore his clothes and said, “Alas, my daughter! You have brought me very low, and you are among those who trouble me; for I have opened my mouth to the LORD, and I cannot go back.”
She said to him, “My father, you have opened your mouth to the LORD; do to me according to what has gone out of your mouth, since the LORD has avenged you of your enemies, the Ammonites.”
She said to her father, “Let this thing be done for me: leave me alone two months, that I may go up and down on the mountains and bewail my virginity, I and my companions.”
He said, “Go.” And he sent her away for two months; and she went, she and her companions, and bewailed her virginity on the mountains.
At the end of two months she returned to her father, who did to her according to his vow which he had vowed; and she had not known a man. And it became a statute in Israel
that the daughters of Israel went four days in the year to lament the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite.

The Ephraimites mustered their forces, crossed northward, and said to Jephthah, “Why did you cross over to wage war against the Ammonites without summoning us to accompany you? We shall burn your house down upon you.”
Jephthah answered them, “My people and I were embroiled in a grave conflict with the Ammonites, and I did summon you, yet you did not deliver me from their power.

When I perceived that no deliverance would be forthcoming from you, I staked my life and crossed over against the Ammonites, and the LORD delivered them into my hand. Why, then, have you ascended against me this day to wage war upon me?”

Then Jephthah gathered all the men of Gilead and fought against Ephraim; the Gileadites struck them down because the Ephraimites had said, “You Gileadites are fugitives of Ephraim—scattered among Ephraim and among Manasseh.”

The Gileadites seized the fords of the Jordan to intercept the Ephraimites. Whenever an Ephraimite fugitive pleaded, “Let me cross over,” the Gileadites would question him. They would ask, “Are you an Ephraimite?” If he answered, “No,” they would proceed to the phonetic test.

They would say, “Pronounce ‘Shibboleth.’” He would answer, “Sibboleth,” because he could not articulate the word correctly. Then they seized him and slaughtered him at the fords of the Jordan; at that time forty-two thousand Ephraimites fell.
Jephthah judged Israel six years. Then Jephthah the Gileadite died and was interred among the cities of Gilead.
After him, Ibzan of Bethlehem judged Israel.
He had thirty sons and thirty daughters; he gave his thirty daughters in marriage outside his household and brought in thirty young women from outside for his sons. He judged Israel seven years.
Then Ibzan died and was buried at Bethlehem.
After him, Elon the Zebulunite judged Israel; he judged Israel ten years.
Then Elon the Zebulunite died and was buried at Aijalon in the land of Zebulun.
After him, Abdon son of Hillel the Pirathonite judged Israel.
He had forty sons and thirty grandsons, who rode upon seventy donkeys; he judged Israel eight years.
Then Abdon son of Hillel the Pirathonite died and was buried at Pirathon in the land of Ephraim, in the hill country of the Amalekites.
The Israelites once more perpetrated evil in the sight of the the LORD, so the the LORD delivered them into the Philistines' power for forty years.
A certain man of Zorah, belonging to the Danite clan and named Manoah, had a wife who was barren and had borne no children.
The angel of the the LORD appeared to the woman and said to her, “Behold, you are barren and have borne no children; yet you shall conceive and bear a son.
Therefore, please guard yourself: do not drink wine or strong drink, and do not eat anything unclean.

For behold, you shall conceive and bear a son, and no razor shall come upon his head, for the boy shall be a Nazirite to God from the womb; and he shall begin to deliver Israel from the hand of the Philistines.”

The woman went and told her husband, “A man of God came to me; his appearance was like the appearance of an angel of God—remarkably awe-inspiring. I did not ask where he came from, and he did not tell me his name.

He said to me, ‘Behold, you shall conceive and bear a son. Now drink no wine or strong drink, and eat nothing unclean, for the boy shall be a Nazirite to God from the womb until the day of his death.’”
Then Manoah prayed to the the LORD and said, “O Lord, please let the man of God whom You sent come to us again and teach us what we are to do for the child who is to be born.”
And God listened to Manoah's voice, and the angel of God came again to the woman while she sat in the field; but her husband Manoah was not with her.
The woman hurried and ran and told her husband, “Behold, the man who came to me the other day has appeared to me.”
Manoah rose and followed his wife, came to the man, and said to him, “Are you the man who spoke to the woman?” He answered, “I am.”
Manoah said, “Now may your words be fulfilled. How shall the boy be reared, and what shall be his vocation?”
The angel of the the LORD said to Manoah, “Of all that I said to the woman, let her heed it.
She must not eat anything that comes from the vine, neither drink wine or strong drink, nor eat anything unclean; she must observe all that I commanded her.”
Manoah said to the angel of the the LORD, “Please let us detain you, and we will prepare a young goat for you.”

The angel of the the LORD said to Manoah, “Even if you detain me, I will not eat your bread; but if you prepare a burnt offering, offer it to the the LORD.” For Manoah did not know that he was the angel of the the LORD.
Manoah said to the angel of the the LORD, “What is your name, so that when your word is fulfilled we may honor you?”
The angel of the the LORD said to him, “Why do you ask my name, seeing that it is wonderful?”
So Manoah took a young goat with a grain offering and offered it on the rock to the the LORD, and the angel acted wondrously while Manoah and his wife looked on.
As the flame rose heavenward from the altar, the angel of the the LORD ascended in the altar's flame. Manoah and his wife looked on and fell prostrate upon the ground.
The angel of the the LORD did not appear again to Manoah or his wife. Then Manoah knew that he had been the angel of the the LORD.
Manoah said to his wife, “We shall surely die, for we have seen God.”

His wife said to him, “If the the LORD had desired to kill us, He would not have accepted a burnt offering and a grain offering from our hands, nor would He have shown us all these things, nor would He have told us such things at this time.”
The woman bore a son and named him Samson; and the child grew, and the the LORD blessed him.
The Spirit of the the LORD began to stir him in the camp of Dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol.
Samson descended to Timnah, where he espied a woman among the daughters of Timnah who was of Philistine extraction.
He ascended and disclosed to his father and mother, saying, "I have seen a woman among the daughters of the Philistines in Timnah; therefore procure her for me as my wife."

His father and mother said to him, "Is there no woman among the daughters of your brothers, or among all my people, that you must go to take a wife from the uncircumcised Philistines?" Samson said to his father, "Take her for me, for she is pleasing to me."
His father and mother did not apprehend that this matter derived from the LORD, since He was seeking a pretext against the Philistines at a time when the Philistines exercised dominion over Israel.
Samson descended to Timnah with his father and mother, and they came as far as the vineyards of Timnah, where a young lion roared to confront him.
Then the Spirit of the LORD surged upon him, and he tore the lion as one tears a young goat, although nothing was in his hand; yet he did not disclose to his father or mother what he had done.
He descended and spoke to the woman, and she proved pleasing to Samson.
After some days he returned to take her, and he turned aside to inspect the carcass of the lion, only to discover a swarm of bees and honey within the carcass.
He scooped it into his palms and ate while proceeding; he also gave some to his father and mother, and they ate, yet he did not disclose that he had scooped the honey from the lion's carcass.
His father descended to the woman, and Samson prepared a banquet there, as was customary among the young men.
When they saw him, they brought thirty companions to be with him.

Samson said to them, "Let me now propound a riddle to you: if you can fully declare it to me within the seven days of the feast and solve it, I will give you thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothing."
"But if you cannot tell me, then you shall give me thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothing." They said, "Propound your riddle, and we will hear it."
He said to them, "Out of the devourer proceeded nourishment, and out of the mighty proceeded sweetness." For three days they were unable to explicate the riddle.
On the seventh day they said to Samson's wife, "Coerce your husband into divulging the riddle, lest we incinerate you and your father's household; have you summoned us merely to despoil us?"

Samson's wife wept before him and said, "You merely hate me and do not love me; you have posed a riddle to the sons of my people and have not told it to me." He said, "Behold, I have not told it to my father or my mother; shall I tell you?"

She wept in his presence throughout the seven days of their feast; and on the seventh day he disclosed it to her, because she importuned him; whereupon she revealed the riddle to the sons of her people.

Before sunset on the seventh day, the men of the city said to him, "What is sweeter than honey? What is stronger than a lion?" He said, "Had you not exploited my wife, you would never have unraveled my riddle."

Then the Spirit of the LORD came powerfully upon him, and he descended to Ashkelon, struck down thirty of their men, took their plunder, and gave the changes of clothing to those who had explained the riddle. Burning with anger, he returned to his father's house.
Meanwhile, Samson's wife was consigned to his companion, the one who had attended him.

After an interval of days, in the season of the wheat harvest, Samson took a kid of the goats and went to visit his wife; he declared, "I shall enter the chamber to my wife." Yet her father refused to grant him admittance.

Her father rejoined, "I was persuaded that you had come to abhor her beyond measure, and therefore I bestowed her upon your companion. Is not her younger sister more comely than she? I entreat you, let her be yours instead."
Samson said to them, "On this occasion I shall be held guiltless when I bring calamity upon the Philistines."
Samson went forth and captured three hundred foxes; he procured torches, turned the animals tail to tail, and placed a single torch between each pair of tails.

He ignited the torches and released the foxes into the standing grain of the Philistines, consuming the shocks and the standing crop, and extending the conflagration to the vineyards and olive orchards.

The Philistines demanded, "Who perpetrated this outrage?" They were informed, "Samson, the son-in-law of the Timnite, because his wife was transferred to his companion." Thereupon the Philistines ascended and burned both the woman and her father with fire.
Samson said to them, "If you act in this manner, I shall not desist until I have exacted vengeance upon you."
He fell upon them with ferocious violence and slew them in great numbers; thereafter he descended and took refuge in the cleft of the rock of Etam.
The Philistines marched up and encamped in Judah, deploying their forces in Lehi.
The men of Judah asked, "Why have you ascended against us?" They replied, "We have come to bind Samson, that we may repay him in kind for what he has done to us."

Three thousand men of Judah descended to the cleft of the rock of Etam and said to Samson, "Do you not perceive that the Philistines rule over us? What, then, is this that you have wrought against us?" He answered them, "I have merely rendered to them what they first rendered to me."
They said to him, "We have come to bind you and deliver you into the hands of the Philistines." Samson said to them, "Swear to me that you yourselves will not attack me."
They assured him, "No, we shall only bind you securely and hand you over to them; we will not put you to death." Accordingly, they bound him with two new cords and led him up from the rock.

As he approached Lehi, the Philistines raised a shout to meet him. Then the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him with power, and the ropes upon his arms became like flax consumed by fire, so that the bonds melted from his hands.
Finding a fresh jawbone of a donkey, he reached out his hand, seized it, and with it struck down a thousand men.
Samson said, "With the jawbone of a donkey I have heaped them in piles; with the jawbone of a donkey I have slain a thousand men."
When he had finished speaking, he cast the jawbone from his hand and named that place Ramath-lehi.

Being exceedingly thirsty, he cried out to the LORD, saying, "You have granted this great deliverance by the hand of Your servant; must I now die of thirst and fall into the hands of the uncircumcised?"

Then God split open the hollow place that is in Lehi, and water issued forth; when Samson drank, his spirit returned, and he was revived. Therefore he named it En-hakkore, which remains in Lehi to this day.
Samson judged Israel for twenty years during the days of the Philistines.
Samson repaired to Gaza, where, upon esping a prostitute, he entered her abode.

The Gazites were apprised of his arrival and therefore encompassed the city, lying in ambush for him throughout the night at the gate; they kept silent the while, determining, "We shall put him to death at daybreak."

Samson, however, lay only until midnight, then arose in the dead of night, gripped the doors of the city gate together with its two posts, wrenched them free, bar and all, laid them upon his shoulders, and carried them to the crest of the hill facing Hebron.
Thereafter he became enamored of a woman in the Valley of Sorek, whose name was Delilah.

The Philistine lords approached her and said, "Entice him, and ascertain the source of his prodigious strength and by what means we may subdue him, so that we may bind him in order to torment him; each of us will bestow upon you eleven hundred pieces of silver."
Delilah therefore said to Samson, "Please reveal to me whence your great strength derives, and how you may be restrained so as to be tormented."
Samson replied, "If they bind me with seven fresh bowstrings that have not been dried, I shall be rendered powerless and become like any other man."
The Philistine lords accordingly brought her seven fresh bowstrings that had not been dried, and she bound him with them.

Now an ambush was concealed in an inner chamber; she exclaimed, "Samson, the Philistines are attacking you!" Yet he broke the bowstrings as a thread of tow snaps at the scent of flame, so his strength remained a mystery.
Delilah then said to him, "Behold, you have deceived me and lied to me. Now, I pray, tell me how you may be bound."
He answered, "If they bind me fast with new ropes that have never been employed for any task, I shall be rendered powerless and become like any other man."

Delilah therefore took new ropes and bound him with them; then she cried, "Samson, the Philistines are attacking you!" while the ambush waited in the chamber. Yet he snapped them from his arms as if they were thread.

Delilah said to Samson, "You have hitherto deceived me and lied to me. Now, I beseech you, tell me how you may be bound." He said, "If you weave the seven locks of my hair into the fabric on the loom."
So she secured them with a pin and said, "Samson, the Philistines are attacking you!" He awoke from his sleep and tore away the pin together with the web.
She said to him, "How can you say that you love me, when your heart is not with me? This is the third time you have deceived me and have not told me wherein your great strength lies."
And because she harassed him daily with her importunities and pressed him, his very soul was worn down to the point of death.

He therefore revealed to her his inmost heart and said, "No razor has ever touched my head, for from my mother's womb I have been consecrated to God as a Nazirite. If I am shaven, my strength will depart from me, and I shall be rendered powerless and become like any other man."

When Delilah discerned that he had told her his whole heart, she dispatched a messenger to summon the Philistine lords, saying, "Come up once more, for he has told me all his heart." The Philistine lords therefore came up to her, bringing the silver with them.
She lulled him to sleep upon her knees, called for a man, and sheared the seven locks of his head; thereby she began to subdue him, and his strength left him.
She cried, "Samson, the Philistines are attacking you!" He awoke from his sleep and said, "I will go forth as before and shake myself free." But he did not know that the LORD had departed from him.
The Philistines seized him, put out his eyes, brought him down to Gaza, fettered him with bronze chains, and compelled him to grind grain in the prison house.
Yet the hair of his head began to grow again once it had been shorn.
The Philistine lords assembled to present a great sacrifice to Dagon, their god, and to make merry, saying, "Our god has delivered Samson, our foe, into our power."
When the populace beheld him, they extolled their god, saying, "Our god has delivered into our hands our enemy, the devastator of our land, who slew so many of us."
When their hearts were gladdened, they said, "Summon Samson, that he may amuse us." They therefore brought Samson out of the prison, and he performed for them; then they set him between the pillars.
Samson said to the youth who supported his hand, "Let me feel the pillars on which the house rests, that I may lean upon them."
The house was thronged with men and women, and all the Philistine lords were present, while upon the roof stood some three thousand men and women who were watching Samson's performance.
Samson called to the LORD and said, "O Lord the LORD, remember me, I pray, and strengthen me, O God, only this once, that I may be avenged upon the Philistines for my two eyes."
Then Samson grasped the two middle pillars upon which the house rested, and leaned his weight upon them, one with his right hand and the other with his left.

Samson said, "Let me die together with the Philistines." Then he thrust with all his strength, and the house fell upon the lords and upon all the people who were in it. Thus the dead he slew in his dying exceeded those he had slain in his lifetime.
Then his brothers and all his father's house came down, carried him up, and buried him between Zorah and Eshtaol in the tomb of Manoah his father. He had judged Israel for twenty years.
In those days there was a man in the hill country of Ephraim whose name was Micah.

He said to his mother, “The eleven hundred shekels of silver that were stolen from you, and over which you pronounced a curse in my hearing—look, the silver is with me; I took it.” His mother answered, “Blessed be my son by the LORD.”

He restored the eleven hundred shekels of silver to his mother, and his mother declared, “I have fully consecrated the silver to the LORD from my hand for my son, to fashion a carved image and a molded image; and now I give it back to you.”

So he returned the silver to his mother. His mother took two hundred shekels of silver and gave them to a silversmith, who fashioned them into a carved image and a molded image, and these were placed in the house of Micah.
The man Micah had a shrine, and he made an ephod and household idols, and he consecrated one of his sons to serve as his priest.
In those days there was no king in Israel; every man did what was right in his own eyes.
Now there was a young man from Bethlehem in Judah, of the clan of Judah, who was a Levite residing there as an alien.
This man left the city, Bethlehem in Judah, to sojourn wherever he might find a place, and on his journey he came to the hill country of Ephraim, to the house of Micah.
Micah asked him, “Where do you come from?” He replied, “I am a Levite from Bethlehem in Judah, and I am traveling to sojourn wherever I may find a place.”
Micah said to him, “Stay with me and be to me a father and a priest, and I will give you ten shekels of silver per year, a set of garments, and your sustenance.” So the Levite went in.
The Levite consented to dwell with the man, and the young man became to him like one of his sons.
Micah consecrated the Levite, and the young man became his priest and remained in the house of Micah.
Then Micah said, “Now I know that the LORD will prosper me, because I have a Levite as my priest.”
In those days Israel had no king, and the tribe of Dan was seeking an inheritance in which to settle, because no allotment had yet fallen to it among the tribes of Israel.

The Danites sent five men from their clans, from the outlying districts—valiant men—from Zorah and Eshtaol, to spy out the land and reconnoiter it. They said to them, "Go and reconnoiter the land." So they went up into the hill country of Ephraim, to Micah's house, and lodged there.
While they were with Micah, they recognized the young Levite's voice and turned aside there, asking, "Who brought you here? What are you doing in this place? What do you have here?"
He answered, "Micah has done such and such for me: he hired me, and I became his priest."
They said to him, "Please inquire of God, that we may know whether the way on which we are going will prosper."
The priest said to them, "Go in peace; the LORD looks with favor on your path, the one in which you are going."

The five men departed and came to Laish, where they saw a people dwelling securely, in the manner of the Sidonians—quiet and secure—with no authority in the land to humiliate them in any way. They were far from the Sidonians and had no dealings with anyone.
They returned to their brothers at Zorah and Eshtaol, and their brothers asked them, "What do you report?"
They answered, "Arise and let us go up against them, for we have seen the land, and behold, it is very good. And will you remain idle? Do not be remiss in going to take possession of the land."
When you go, you will come upon a secure people, and the land is broad, for God has given it into your hand—a place lacking nothing that is in the earth.
Six hundred men of the Danites set out from there, from Zorah and Eshtaol, girded with weapons of war.
They went up and encamped at Kiriath-jearim in Judah; therefore they called that place Mahaneh-dan to this day—it lies west of Kiriath-jearim.
From there they passed on into the hill country of Ephraim and came to Micah's house.

The five men who had gone to spy out the land of Laish said to their brothers, "Do you know that in these houses there are an ephod, teraphim, a carved image, and a cast image? Now therefore consider what you will do."
They turned aside there and came to the house of the young Levite at Micah's house, and greeted him.
The six hundred Danites, armed with their weapons of war, were stationed at the entrance of the gate.

The five men who had gone to spy out the land went in and took the carved image, the ephod, the teraphim, and the cast image, while the priest stood at the entrance of the gate with the six hundred men armed for war.
These men entered Micah's house and took the carved image, the ephod, the teraphim, and the cast image. Then the priest said to them, "What are you doing?"
They said to him, "Hush. Come with us and be a father and priest to us. Is it better for you to be priest to one man's house, or to a tribe and clan in Israel?"
The priest's heart was glad; he took the ephod, the teraphim, and the carved image, and went in the midst of the people.
They turned and departed, putting the little ones, the livestock, and the baggage ahead of them.
When they had gone far from Micah's house, the men who were in the houses near Micah's house were called together and overtook the Danites.
They called to the Danites, who turned their faces and said to Micah, "What troubles you, that you have raised such a cry?"
He said, "You have taken my gods that I made, and the priest, and gone away; and what do I have left? How then do you say to me, 'What troubles you?'"
The Danites said to him, "Do not let your voice be heard among us, lest fierce men fall upon you and you lose your life and the lives of your household."
The Danites went on their way; and when Micah saw that they were too strong for him, he turned and went back to his house.
They took what Micah had made, and the priest who had belonged to him, and came to Laish, to a people quiet and secure, and put them to the sword and burned the city with fire.
There was no deliverer, because it was far from Sidon and they had no dealings with anyone; it lay in the valley that belongs to Beth-rehob. They rebuilt the city and dwelt in it.
They called the name of the city Dan, after the name of Dan their father, who was born to Israel; however, the name of the city formerly was Laish.

The Danites set up for themselves the carved image; and Jonathan, the son of Gershom, the son of Manasseh, he and his sons were priests to the tribe of the Danites until the day the land was carried into exile.
They kept Micah's carved image, which he had made, all the days that the house of God was in Shiloh.
In those days, when there was no king in Israel, a Levite was sojourning in the remote quarters of the hill country of Ephraim, and he took to himself a concubine from Bethlehem in Judah.
His concubine was sexually unfaithful to him, so she departed from him to her father’s house in Bethlehem of Judah, where she remained for four months.

Then her husband arose and went after her, to appeal to her affections and bring her back; he brought with him his young servant and a pair of donkeys. When she ushered him into her father’s house, the young woman’s father saw him and rejoiced to meet him.
Her father—her husband’s father-in-law—detained him, and he stayed with him three days; they ate and drank and lodged there.
On the fourth day they rose early, and as he prepared to depart, the young woman’s father said to his son-in-law, “Refresh yourself with a morsel of bread, and afterward you may go.”
So the two of them sat down and ate and drank together, and the young woman’s father said to the man, “Please be willing to stay the night, and let your heart be glad.”
The man rose to go, but his father-in-law pressed him, so he lodged there again.
On the fifth day he rose early to depart, and the young woman’s father said, “Refresh yourself, and tarry until the day declines.” So they ate together.

When the man rose to go with his concubine and his servant, his father-in-law, the young woman’s father, said to him, “Behold, the day is waning toward evening; please stay the night. The day is drawing to a close; lodge here, and let your heart be glad. Tomorrow you shall rise early for your journey and go to your home.”
But the man would not consent to lodge; he arose and departed, and came as far as opposite Jebus—that is, Jerusalem. He had with him two saddled donkeys, and his concubine accompanied him.
When they were near Jebus, the day was far spent, and the servant said to his master, “Come, please, let us turn aside into this city of the Jebusites and lodge there.”
But his master said to him, “We will not turn aside into a city of foreigners that does not belong to the Israelites; we will pass on to Gibeah.”
He said to his young servant, “Come, let us draw near to one of these places and lodge in Gibeah or in Ramah.”
So they passed on, and the sun set upon them beside Gibeah, which belongs to Benjamin.
They turned aside there to lodge in Gibeah, and he went in and sat down in the open square of the city, for no one took them into a house to spend the night.
And behold, an old man was coming from his field work in the evening; he was from the hill country of Ephraim and was sojourning in Gibeah, while the men of the place were Benjaminites.
He lifted his eyes and saw the traveler in the open square, and the old man said, “Where are you going, and from where have you come?”

He replied, “We are passing from Bethlehem in Judah to the remote parts of the hill country of Ephraim; from there I am, and I went to Bethlehem in Judah. Now I am going to the house of the LORD, and no one has taken me into his house.
We have both straw and fodder for our donkeys, and bread and wine for me, your maidservant, and the young man with us; we lack nothing.”
The old man said, “Peace be with you; let all your need rest upon me; only do not spend the night in the street.”
So he brought him into his house and provided fodder for the donkeys; they washed their feet and ate and drank.

While they were making merry, behold, the men of the city—worthless scoundrels—surrounded the house and beat upon the door. They said to the old man, the master of the house, “Bring out the man who came into your house, that we may have sexual relations with him.”
The master of the house went out to them and said, “No, my brothers, do not act so wickedly; since this man has come into my house, do not commit this outrage.
Behold, I will bring out my virgin daughter and his concubine; you may violate them and do with them as seems best to you, but do not commit this outrage against this man.”

But the men would not heed him; so he seized his concubine and brought her out to them, and they had sexual relations with her and abused her all night until morning, when, at the break of dawn, they released her.
As morning approached, the woman came and fell at the door of the man’s house where her master was, and she lay there until daylight.
In the morning her master rose, opened the doors of the house, and went out to go his way; and behold, the woman, his concubine, was lying at the door of the house with her hands upon the threshold.
He said to her, “Rise, and let us be going,” but she did not answer. So he took her upon the donkey, and the man went to his home.
When he reached his house, he took a knife, seized his concubine, and cut her into twelve pieces, limb by limb, and sent them throughout all the territory of Israel.
Everyone who saw it said, “Such a thing has never occurred nor been seen since Israel came up from the land of Egypt until this day. Consider it, take counsel, and speak.”
From Dan to Beersheba, together with the land of Gilead, all the Israelites came forth; the congregation assembled as one man before the LORD at Mizpah.
The chiefs of all the people, every tribe of Israel, took their stand in the assembly of God—four hundred thousand foot soldiers who drew the sword.
The Benjaminites heard that the Israelites had gone up to Mizpah. The Israelites said, "Tell us, how did this wickedness come to pass?"
The Levite, the husband of the woman who was slain, answered, "I came to Gibeah in Benjamin, I and my concubine, to lodge for the night.
The men of Gibeah rose against me and surrounded the house by night, intending to kill me; they violated my concubine, and she died.
So I seized my concubine, dismembered her, and sent her through all the territory of Israel, because they had committed a shameful outrage in Israel.
Behold, all you Israelites, give here your counsel and advice."
All the people arose as one man, saying, "None of us will go to his tent, and none of us will turn aside to his house."
"Now this is what we shall do to Gibeah: we shall go up against it by lot.

We will take ten men of every hundred throughout all the tribes of Israel, a hundred of every thousand, and a thousand of every ten thousand, to fetch provisions for the people, so that when they come to Geba of Benjamin they may requite all the folly that has been wrought in Israel."
So all the men of Israel gathered against the city, knit together as one man.
The tribes of Israel sent men throughout the tribe of Benjamin, saying, "What is this evil that has happened among you?"

"Now therefore deliver up the worthless men who are in Gibeah, that we may put them to death and purge the evil from Israel." But the Benjaminites would not listen to the voice of their brothers, the Israelites.
The Benjaminites gathered from their cities to Gibeah to go out to battle against the Israelites.
On that day the Benjaminites mustered from their cities twenty-six thousand swordsmen, besides the inhabitants of Gibeah, who mustered seven hundred select men.
Among all this people were seven hundred chosen men who were left-handed; every one could sling a stone at a hair and not miss.
The Israelites, apart from Benjamin, mustered four hundred thousand swordsmen, all men of war.
The Israelites arose and went up to Bethel and inquired of God, saying, "Who shall go up first for us to battle against the Benjaminites?" The LORD said, "Judah shall go up first."
The Israelites rose in the morning and encamped against Gibeah.
The men of Israel went out to battle against Benjamin, and they drew up in battle array against them at Gibeah.
The Benjaminites came out of Gibeah and struck down to the ground twenty-two thousand men of Israel on that day.
But the people, the men of Israel, took courage and again set the battle in array in the place where they had arrayed themselves the first day.
The Israelites went up and wept before the LORD until evening, and they inquired of the LORD, saying, "Shall I go up again to battle against my brother Benjamin?" The LORD said, "Go up against him."
The Israelites drew near to the Benjaminites on the second day.
Benjamin went out from Gibeah to meet them on the second day and struck down to the ground eighteen thousand men of the Israelites; all these were men who drew the sword.

Then all the Israelites, the whole people, went up and came to Bethel and wept, and sat there before the LORD, and fasted that day until evening, and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before the LORD.
The Israelites inquired of the LORD—for the ark of the covenant of God was there in those days,

and Phinehas the son of Eleazar, son of Aaron, stood before it in those days—saying, "Shall I go up yet again to battle against my brother Benjamin, or shall I cease?" The LORD said, "Go up, for tomorrow I will give them into your hand."
So Israel set ambushes around Gibeah.
The Israelites went up against the Benjaminites on the third day and drew up against Gibeah as before.

The Benjaminites went out to meet the people and were drawn away from the city; then they began to strike down the people and kill them, as on previous occasions, along the highways—one ascending to Bethel and the other to Gibeah in the open country—about thirty men of Israel.
The Benjaminites said, "They are struck down before us, as at first." But the Israelites said, "Let us flee and draw them away from the city to the highways."
All the men of Israel rose from their place and drew up at Baal-tamar, and the ambush of Israel burst forth from its place at Maareh-geba.
Ten thousand chosen men from all Israel came against Gibeah, and the battle was fierce, but the Benjaminites did not know that disaster was close upon them.
The LORD defeated Benjamin before Israel, and the Israelites destroyed on that day twenty-five thousand one hundred men of Benjamin, all of them swordsmen.
The Benjaminites saw that they were defeated. The men of Israel gave ground to Benjamin, because they trusted in the ambush that they had set against Gibeah.
The ambush hurried and rushed against Gibeah; the ambush drew itself out and struck all the city with the edge of the sword.
The appointed signal between the men of Israel and the ambush was that they should make a great column of smoke rise up from the city.
The men of Israel turned in the battle, and Benjamin began to strike and kill about thirty men of Israel, for they said, "Surely they are struck down before us, as in the first battle."
But the column of smoke began to rise from the city in a pillar, and Benjamin looked behind him, and behold, the whole city was going up in smoke to heaven.
Then the men of Israel turned, and the Benjaminites were dismayed, for they saw that disaster had come upon them.
So they turned their backs before the men of Israel toward the way of the wilderness, but the battle overtook them, and those who came out of the cities destroyed them in their midst.
They surrounded the Benjaminites, pursued them, and trampled them down with ease as far as a point opposite Gibeah toward the sunrise.
Eighteen thousand men of Benjamin fell, all of them men of valor.

They turned and fled toward the wilderness to the rock of Rimmon, and they cut down five thousand of them along the highways, and pursued them as far as Gidom, and struck down two thousand men of them.
So all who fell that day of Benjamin were twenty-five thousand men who drew the sword, all of them men of valor.
But six hundred men turned and fled toward the wilderness to the rock of Rimmon and remained at the rock of Rimmon four months.

The men of Israel turned back against the Benjaminites and struck them with the edge of the sword—the city, the cattle, and all that they found; moreover they burned with fire all the cities that they found.
The men of Israel had sworn at Mizpah, saying, “No man among us shall give his daughter to Benjamin in marriage.”
The people went to Bethel and sat there before God until evening; then they raised their voices and wept with great sorrow.
And they said, “Why, O the LORD God of Israel, has this happened in Israel, that today one tribe is missing from Israel?”
The next day the people rose early, built an altar there, and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings.

The Israelites said, “Who among all the tribes of Israel failed to come up to the assembly before the the LORD?” For they had sworn a solemn oath that anyone who did not assemble before the the LORD at Mizpah would surely be put to death.
The Israelites grieved for their brother Benjamin and said, “Today one tribe has been cut off from Israel.”
“What shall we do for wives for those who remain, since we have sworn by the the LORD not to give them any of our daughters in marriage?”
They said, “Who among the tribes of Israel did not come up to the the LORD at Mizpah?” And indeed, no one from Jabesh-gilead had come to the camp, to the assembly.
For when the people were mustered, no inhabitant of Jabesh-gilead was found there.
So the congregation sent twelve thousand men of valor and commanded them, “Go and strike the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead with the sword, including the women and children.”
“This is what you are to do: you shall utterly destroy every male, and every woman who has known a man intimately.”
They found among the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead four hundred young women who were virgins, who had not known a man intimately; and they brought them to the camp at Shiloh, in the land of Canaan.
Then the whole congregation sent word and spoke to the Benjaminites who were at the rock of Rimmon, proclaiming peace to them.
Benjamin returned at that time, and they gave them the women whom they had kept alive from the women of Jabesh-gilead, but there were not enough for them.
The people grieved for Benjamin, because the the LORD had made a breach among the tribes of Israel.
Then the elders of the congregation said, “What shall we do for wives for those who remain, since the women of Benjamin have been destroyed?”
They added, “There must be an inheritance for the survivors of Benjamin, so that a tribe is not wiped out from Israel.”
“But we cannot give them any of our daughters as wives, for the Israelites have sworn, saying, ‘Cursed is he who gives a wife to Benjamin.’”
They observed, “There is the annual festival of the the LORD at Shiloh, which lies north of Bethel, east of the highway that goes up from Bethel to Shechem, and south of Lebonah.”
They commanded the Benjaminites, “Go and lie in wait in the vineyards,

and when you see the daughters of Shiloh coming out to dance, then you are to come out of the vineyards and seize for yourselves each a wife from the daughters of Shiloh, and go to the land of Benjamin.

And it shall be that, when their fathers or brothers come to complain to us, we will say to them, ‘Do us the favor of helping them, because we did not take a wife for each man in the battle; for you did not give them wives at this time—otherwise you would be guilty.’”
The Benjaminites did so: they carried off wives, according to their number, from the dancers whom they seized, and went and returned to their inheritance, rebuilt the cities, and dwelt in them.
The Israelites departed from there at that time, each to his tribe and family, and went out from there, each to his own inheritance.
In those days there was no king in Israel; every man did what was right in his own eyes.
In the days when Israel was governed by judges, a famine ravaged the land, and a certain man from Bethlehem in Judah—accompanied by his wife and two sons—set out to sojourn in the fields of Moab.
The man was named Elimelech; his wife was Naomi, and his sons were Mahlon and Chilion, Ephrathites from Bethlehem in Judah. Having arrived in the fields of Moab, they established residence there.
Then Elimelech, Naomi's husband, died, leaving her with her two sons.
The sons took Moabite wives—Orpah and Ruth—and the family dwelt there for roughly a decade.
In time, Mahlon and Chilion also died, so the woman was bereft of both her children and her husband.
Having heard in the fields of Moab that the LORD had visited His people by granting them bread, Naomi rose, together with her daughters-in-law, to return from the fields of Moab.
Accompanied by her two daughters-in-law, she departed from the place where she had been living, and they set out along the road to return to the land of Judah.
Naomi said to her two daughters-in-law, "Go, return each of you to her mother's house. May the LORD deal kindly with you, as you have dealt with the dead and with me.
May the LORD grant that you find repose, each in the house of her husband." Then she kissed them, and they raised their voices and wept.
They replied, "No; we will return with you to your people."
Naomi said, "Turn back, my daughters; why would you accompany me? Have I still sons in my womb who could become husbands for you?
Turn back, my daughters; go your way, for I am too old to have a husband. Even if I were to say that I still have hope, even if I were to have a husband tonight and bear sons,
would you wait for them until they grew up? Would you refrain from marrying for their sake? No, my daughters; my bitterness is far greater than yours, for the LORD has turned against me."
They lifted their voices and wept again. Orpah kissed her mother-in-law, but Ruth clung to her.
Naomi said, "Look, your sister-in-law has returned to her people and to her gods; return after your sister-in-law."
Ruth replied, "Do not press me to abandon you or to turn back from following you. Where you go, I will go; where you lodge, I will lodge. Your people shall be my people, and your God my God.
Where you die, I will die, and there I will be buried. May the LORD do so to me, and more besides, if anything but death separates me from you."
When Naomi saw that Ruth was determined to go with her, she ceased speaking to her.
So the two of them traveled on until they reached Bethlehem. When they arrived in Bethlehem, the whole city was stirred on their account, and the women asked, "Is this Naomi?"
She answered, "Do not call me Naomi; call me Mara, for the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with me.
I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty. Why then would you call me Naomi, when the LORD has testified against me and the Almighty has afflicted me?"
Thus Naomi returned, with Ruth the Moabitess, her daughter-in-law, who had accompanied her from the fields of Moab. They arrived in Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest.
Now Naomi had a kinsman of her husband, a man of eminent standing and martial valor from the clan of Elimelech, whose name was Boaz.
Ruth the Moabite said to Naomi, "Please allow me to go into the fields and glean among the ears of grain behind anyone in whose eyes I may find favor." Naomi replied, "Go, my daughter."
So she went out and entered a field, gleaning behind the reapers; and, as providence would have it, the portion of field she worked belonged to Boaz, who was of the clan of Elimelech.
And behold, Boaz came from Bethlehem and said to the reapers, "The LORD be with you!" They answered him, "The LORD bless you!"
Boaz said to his servant who was set over the reapers, "To whom does this young woman belong?"
The servant who was set over the reapers answered, "She is the Moabite woman who returned with Naomi from the country of Moab.
She requested permission to glean and gather among the sheaves behind the reapers; she arrived and has remained here from morning until now, apart from a brief respite in the shelter."
Then Boaz said to Ruth, "Listen, my daughter: do not go to glean in another field, neither pass beyond this one; instead, cleave to my young women.

Keep your eyes on the field they are reaping, and follow after them. Have I not charged the young men not to touch you? And when you are thirsty, go to the vessels and drink what the young men have drawn."
Then she fell on her face and bowed to the ground, and said to him, "Why have I found favor in your eyes, that you should take notice of me, though I am a foreigner?"

Boaz answered and said to her, "It has been fully reported to me all that you have done for your mother-in-law after the death of your husband: how you left your father and your mother and the land of your birth, and came to a people you did not know before.
May the LORD repay your work, and may your reward be complete from the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge."
Then she said, "May I find favor in your eyes, my lord, for you have comforted me and spoken kindly to your servant, though I am not like one of your servants."

At mealtime Boaz said to her, "Come here and eat some bread, and dip your piece in the vinegar." So she sat beside the reapers, and he offered her roasted grain; she ate until she was satisfied and had some left over.
When she rose to glean, Boaz commanded his young men, saying, "Let her glean even among the sheaves, and do not reproach her.
Also pull out some handfuls for her from the bundles and leave them for her to gather, and do not rebuke her."
So Ruth gleaned in the field until evening; then she beat out what she had gathered, and it was about an ephah of barley.
She carried it into the city, and her mother-in-law saw how much she had gleaned. Ruth also brought out and gave her what she had left over after she had eaten her fill.

Her mother-in-law said to her, "Where did you glean today, and where did you work? Blessed be the man who took notice of you!" Then Ruth told her mother-in-law, "The name of the man with whom I worked today is Boaz."

Naomi said to her daughter-in-law, "May he be blessed by the LORD, who has not withdrawn His kindness from the living and the dead. That man is a close relative of ours; he is one of our kinsman-redeemers."
Ruth the Moabite said that he had also told her to cling to his young men until they had finished all his harvest.
Naomi said to Ruth, "It is good, my daughter, that you go out with his young women, so that you are not molested in another field."
So Ruth stayed close to the young women of Boaz to glean until the barley harvest and the wheat harvest were completed; and she dwelt with her mother-in-law.
Naomi, her mother-in-law, addressed her: “My daughter, is it not incumbent upon me to secure for you a tranquil domestic settlement, so that your welfare may be advanced?
Moreover, is not Boaz our kinsman, alongside whose maidens you have been laboring? Observe: this very night he is winnowing barley upon the threshing floor.
Therefore bathe, anoint yourself, array yourself in your garments, and descend to the threshing floor; yet do not disclose your presence to the man until he has concluded his eating and drinking.
And when he reclines, mark precisely the place of his repose; then approach, uncover his feet, and lie down; whereupon he will apprise you of what you ought to do.”
She replied, “Everything you have enjoined, I shall perform.”
Thus she descended to the threshing floor and executed all that her mother-in-law had prescribed.
Boaz, having eaten and drunk and finding his heart gladdened, went to lie down at the extremity of the grain heap; thereupon Ruth approached with circumspection, uncovered his feet, and reclined.
At midnight the man was startled and turned; and, to his astonishment, a woman lay at his feet.
He said, “Who are you?” She said, “I am Ruth, your maidservant; take me under your marital protection, for you are my kinsman-redeemer.”
He replied, “May the LORD bless you, my daughter. Your present act of devotedness surpasses your former kindness, inasmuch as you have not pursued younger men, whether affluent or impoverished.
And now, my daughter, be not apprehensive; I will accomplish for you all that you request, for the entire populace of my city recognizes you as a woman of exemplary virtue.
It is indeed true that I am a kinsman-redeemer; nevertheless, there exists a redeemer nearer of kin than I.

Remain here this night; and in the morning, if he is willing to perform the office of redeemer for you, well and good—let him redeem you. Yet should he decline, then, as the LORD lives, I myself will redeem you. Recline here until morning.”
So she reclined at his feet until morning, then arose before anyone could discern another; and he cautioned, “Let it not be reported that a woman has visited the threshing floor.”
He said, “Bring the mantle that is upon you and hold it forth.” She held it, and he measured six measures of barley into it and laid it upon her; then he repaired to the city.
When Ruth returned to her mother-in-law, Naomi inquired, “How fares it with you, my daughter?” Ruth then recounted all that the man had done for her.
“He bestowed upon me these six measures of barley, saying, ‘You must not return to your mother-in-law empty-handed.’”
Naomi replied, “Be patient, my daughter, until you learn how the matter will eventuate; for the man will not be at rest until he has brought the affair to completion this very day.”

Boaz had ascended to the city gate and seated himself there when, behold, the kinsman-redeemer of whom Boaz had spoken passed by; whereupon Boaz called out, "Turn aside, my friend, and sit down here." The man turned aside and sat down.
Boaz then selected ten of the city's elders and said, "Sit down here," and they sat down.
He said to the redeemer, "Naomi, who has returned from the territory of Moab, is selling the parcel of land that belonged to our kinsman Elimelech."

"I determined to apprise you of this," he added, "and to say, 'Purchase it before those seated here and before the elders of my people. If you will redeem it, redeem it; but if you will not, tell me, so that I may know, for there is no one besides you to redeem it, and I come after you.'" And he replied, "I will redeem it."
Then Boaz said, "On the day you acquire the field from Naomi, you also acquire Ruth the Moabitess, the widow of the deceased, in order to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance."
The redeemer said, "I cannot redeem it for myself, lest I impair my own inheritance. Redeem it for yourself, for I cannot redeem it."
Now this had been the custom in Israel concerning redemption and exchange: to ratify any matter, a man would remove his sandal and give it to his neighbor, and this served as attestation in Israel.
So when the redeemer said to Boaz, "Buy it for yourself," he removed his sandal.
Boaz said to the elders and all the people, "You are witnesses today that I have purchased from Naomi's hand all that belonged to Elimelech, and all that belonged to Chilion and Mahlon.

I have also acquired Ruth the Moabitess, Mahlon's widow, as my wife, to raise up the name of the deceased upon his inheritance, so that the name of the deceased may not be cut off from among his brothers and from the gate of his place. You are witnesses today."

All the people at the gate and the elders said, "We are witnesses. May the LORD make the woman entering your house like Rachel and Leah, who together built up the house of Israel. May you prosper in Ephrathah and gain renown in Bethlehem,
and may your house be like the house of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah, because of the offspring the LORD will give you by this young woman."
So Boaz took Ruth, and she became his wife; and he went in to her, and the LORD granted her conception, and she bore a son.
The women said to Naomi, "Blessed be the LORD, who has not left you this day without a redeemer, and may his name be proclaimed in Israel!
He shall be to you a restorer of life and a sustainer of your old age, for your daughter-in-law, who loves you, is better to you than seven sons, and she has borne him."
Naomi took the child, laid him in her bosom, and became his nurse.
The neighboring women gave him a name, saying, "A son has been born to Naomi." They named him Obed; he was the father of Jesse, the father of David.
These are the generations of Perez: Perez fathered Hezron,
Hezron fathered Ram, Ram fathered Amminadab,
Amminadab fathered Nahshon, Nahshon fathered Salmon,
Salmon fathered Boaz, Boaz fathered Obed,
Obed fathered Jesse, and Jesse fathered David.
Now there was a certain man from Ramathaim-zophim in the hill country of Ephraim, whose name was Elkanah, son of Jeroham, son of Elihu, son of Tohu, son of Zuph, an Ephraimite.
He had two wives: one was named Hannah, and the other Peninnah. Peninnah had children, but Hannah had none.
This man went up from his city year by year to worship and to sacrifice to the LORD of Hosts in Shiloh, where Eli’s two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were priests to the LORD.
On the day when Elkanah sacrificed, he would give portions to Peninnah his wife and to all her sons and daughters;
but to Hannah he gave a double portion, because he loved Hannah, although the LORD had closed her womb.
Her rival, moreover, provoked her bitterly, seeking to vex her, because the LORD had closed her womb.
And so it was year after year: whenever Hannah went up to the house of the LORD, Peninnah provoked her, so that she wept and would not eat.
Then Elkanah her husband said to her, “Hannah, why do you weep? Why do you not eat? Why is your heart so downcast? Am I not better to you than ten sons?”
After they had eaten and drunk in Shiloh, Hannah rose up. Now Eli the priest was sitting on a seat by the doorpost of the temple of the LORD.
In bitterness of soul she prayed to the LORD and wept bitterly.

And she vowed a vow, saying, “O the LORD of Hosts, if You will indeed look upon the affliction of Your maidservant and remember me, and not forget Your maidservant, but give to Your maidservant a male offspring, then I will give him to the LORD all the days of his life, and no razor shall come upon his head.”
As she continued praying before the LORD, Eli watched her mouth.
Hannah was speaking in her heart; only her lips moved, but her voice was not heard, so Eli supposed she was drunk.
Then Eli said to her, “How long will you be drunk? Put away your wine from you.”
Hannah answered, “No, my lord; I am a woman troubled in spirit. I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink, but I have poured out my soul before the LORD.
Do not regard your maidservant as a worthless woman, for I have been speaking out of the abundance of my complaint and my vexation.”
Then Eli answered, “Go in peace, and may the God of Israel grant your petition that you have asked of Him.”
She said, “Let your maidservant find favor in your eyes.” Then the woman went her way and ate, and her countenance was no longer downcast.
They rose early in the morning and worshiped before the LORD, then returned and came to their house at Ramah. Elkanah lay with his wife Hannah, and the LORD remembered her.
In the course of time Hannah conceived and bore a son, and she called his name Samuel, saying, “Because I have asked him of the LORD.”
The man Elkanah went up with all his household to offer to the LORD the annual sacrifice and his vow.
But Hannah did not go up, for she said to her husband, “Not until the child is weaned will I bring him, that he may appear before the LORD and remain there forever.”
Elkanah her husband said to her, “Do what seems good to you; stay until you have weaned him; only may the LORD establish His word.” So the woman stayed and nursed her son until she weaned him.
When she had weaned him, she took him up with her, along with three bulls, an ephah of flour, and a skin of wine, and brought him to the house of the LORD in Shiloh. The child was young.
They slaughtered the bull and brought the child to Eli.
She said, “Oh, my lord, as surely as you live, my lord, I am the woman who stood here by you, praying to the LORD.
For this child I prayed, and the LORD has granted me my petition that I asked of Him.
Therefore I have dedicated him to the LORD; as long as he lives, he is dedicated to the LORD.” And he worshiped the LORD there.
Hannah prayed and said, “My heart exults in the LORD; my horn is exalted in the LORD; my mouth opens wide in triumph over my adversaries, for I rejoice in Your salvation.
No one is holy like the LORD, for there is none besides You, and no Rock is like our God.
