Do not persist in speaking with such lofty arrogance; let no insolence issue from your mouth, for the LORD is a God of knowledge, and by Him deeds are weighed.
The bows of the mighty are shattered, while those who stumble gird themselves with strength.
The sated hire themselves out for bread, while the hungry cease from their hunger; the barren woman has borne seven, but she who abounded in children has been left desolate.
The LORD puts to death and gives life; He brings down to Sheol and raises up.
The LORD impoverishes and enriches; He humbles and exalts.

He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap, to seat them with princes and to endow them with a throne of glory; for the pillars of the earth belong to the LORD, and upon them He has set the world.
He guards the feet of His faithful ones, but the wicked are silenced in darkness, for not by might does a man prevail.
The LORD judges the ends of the earth; He gives strength to His king and exalts the horn of His anointed.”
Then Elkanah departed to his house at Ramah, while the boy continued to minister before the LORD in the presence of Eli the priest.
Now the sons of Eli were scoundrels; they had no knowledge of the LORD.
And this was the custom of the priests with the people: whenever any man offered a sacrifice, the priest’s servant would come while the meat was boiling, holding a three-pronged fork in his hand.
He would thrust it into the basin, pot, cauldron, or kettle, and whatever the fork lifted the priest would take for himself. Thus they treated all Israel who came to Shiloh.
Moreover, before the fat was burned, the priest’s servant would come and say to the man who was sacrificing, “Give meat for the priest to roast; for he will not accept boiled meat from you, but raw.”
If the man said, “Let them burn the fat first, then take whatever you desire,” the servant would reply, “No; you must give it now, or I will seize it by force.”
So the sin of the young men was exceedingly great in the sight of the LORD, because they treated the offering of the LORD with contempt.
But Samuel, though still a boy, ministered before the LORD, wearing a linen ephod.
Each year his mother made him a small robe and brought it up when she went up with her husband to offer the annual sacrifice.
Then Eli would bless Elkanah and his wife and say, “May the LORD give you offspring from this woman in place of the one lent to the LORD.” And they would return to their home.
The LORD indeed visited Hannah; she conceived and bore three sons and two daughters. Meanwhile the boy Samuel grew up in the presence of the LORD.
Now Eli was exceedingly old; he heard of all that his sons were doing to all Israel, and that they were lying with the women who served at the entrance of the tent of meeting.
He said to them, “Why do you do such things? For I hear from all this people of your evil deeds.
No, my sons; the report I hear is not good; you cause the LORD’s people to transgress.

If a man sins against a man, God can arbitrate; but if a man sins against the LORD, who shall intercede for him?” But they would not listen to their father’s voice, for the LORD was pleased to put them to death.
Meanwhile the boy Samuel continued to grow in stature and in favor with both the LORD and with people.
A man of God came to Eli and said, “Thus says the LORD: ‘Did I not reveal Myself to your father’s house when they were in Egypt under Pharaoh?

Did I not choose him out of all the tribes of Israel to be My priest, to ascend to My altar, to burn incense, and to wear an ephod before Me? Did I not give to your father’s house all the fire offerings of the children of Israel?

Why then do you spurn My sacrifice and My offering, which I commanded for My dwelling, and honor your sons above Me by fattening yourselves on the choicest parts of every offering of My people Israel?

Therefore the LORD, the God of Israel, declares: I indeed said that your house and your father’s house should walk before Me forever; but now the LORD declares, “Far be it from Me! For those who honor Me I will honor, and those who despise Me shall be lightly esteemed.”
Behold, the days are coming when I will cut off your arm and the arm of your father’s house, so that no old man will be in your house.
You will see distress in My dwelling, in all that I do good to Israel; and there shall never be an old man in your house.
Yet I will not cut off every one of your line from My altar; rather, your eyes will fail and your soul will grieve, and all the increase of your house shall die in the flower of their manhood.
And this shall be the sign to you: both your sons, Hophni and Phinehas, shall die on the same day.
Then I will raise up for Myself a faithful priest, who shall do according to what is in My heart and My mind; I will build him a sure house, and he shall walk before My anointed forever.

And it shall come to pass that everyone who is left of your house will come and bow down to him for a piece of silver and a loaf of bread, and will say, ‘Please appoint me to one of the priestly offices, that I may eat a piece of bread.’”
Now the boy Samuel was ministering to the LORD before Eli; and in those days the word of the LORD was rare, and vision was not widespread.
On that day Eli was lying in his place, and his eyes had begun to grow dim so that he could not see.
Before the lamp of God went out, Samuel was lying in the temple of the LORD, where the ark of God was.
Then the LORD called Samuel, and he said, “Here I am.”
He ran to Eli and said, “Here I am, for you called me.” But Eli said, “I did not call; go back and lie down.” So he went and lay down.
The LORD called again, “Samuel!” Samuel rose and went to Eli and said, “Here I am, for you called me.” But Eli said, “I did not call, my son; lie down again.”
Now Samuel did not yet know the LORD, and the word of the LORD had not yet been revealed to him.
The LORD called Samuel a third time. He got up, went to Eli, and said, “Here I am, for you called me.” Then Eli understood that the LORD was calling the boy.
So Eli said to Samuel, “Go and lie down, and if He calls you, you shall say, ‘Speak, the LORD, for Your servant hears.’”
The LORD came and stood there, calling as before, “Samuel! Samuel!” Then Samuel said, “Speak, for Your servant hears.”
The LORD said to Samuel, “Behold, I am about to do a thing in Israel at which both ears of everyone who hears of it will tingle.
On that day I will carry out against Eli all that I have spoken concerning his house, from beginning to end.
For I have told him that I will judge his house forever for the iniquity that he knew, because his sons were blaspheming God, and he did not restrain them.
Therefore I have sworn to the house of Eli that the iniquity of the house of Eli shall never be atoned for by sacrifice or offering.”
Samuel lay until morning; then he opened the doors of the house of the LORD. Samuel was afraid to tell Eli the vision.
Eli called Samuel and said, “Samuel, my son.” He answered, “Here I am.”
Eli said, “What is the word that He spoke to you? Please do not hide it from me. May God punish you, and worse, if you hide from me any of the words that He spoke to you.”
So Samuel told him everything and hid nothing from him. Eli said, “It is the LORD. Let Him do what seems good to Him.”
Samuel grew, and the LORD was with him, and not one of his words failed to come to pass.
All Israel from Dan to Beersheba knew that Samuel was established as a prophet of the LORD.
The LORD continued to appear at Shiloh, for the LORD revealed Himself to Samuel at Shiloh by the word of the LORD.
The word of Samuel came to all Israel. Israel then went out to meet the Philistines in battle and encamped beside Ebenezer, while the Philistines encamped at Aphek.
The Philistines arrayed themselves for battle against Israel; when the fighting spread, Israel was defeated before the Philistines, who struck down about four thousand men upon the field.

When the people came into the camp, the elders of Israel said, “Why has the LORD defeated us today before the Philistines? Let us bring from Shiloh the ark of the covenant of the LORD, that it may come among us and deliver us from the hand of our enemies.”

So the people sent to Shiloh and brought from there the ark of the covenant of the LORD of Hosts, who is enthroned above the cherubim; and the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were there with the ark of the covenant of God.
When the ark of the covenant of the LORD entered the camp, all Israel raised a great shout, and the earth resounded.
The Philistines heard the sound of the shout and said, “What does this great shout in the camp of the Hebrews mean?” Then they learned that the ark of the LORD had come into the camp.
The Philistines were afraid, for they said, “God has come into the camp.” And they said, “Woe to us! Nothing like this has happened before.
Woe to us! Who will deliver us from the hand of these mighty gods? These are the gods who struck the Egyptians with every plague in the wilderness.”
“Be strong and conduct yourselves like men, O Philistines, lest you become enslaved to the Hebrews as they have been to you. Be men, then, and fight.”
The Philistines fought; Israel was defeated, and every man fled to his tent. The slaughter was exceedingly great: thirty thousand foot soldiers of Israel fell.
The ark of God was taken, and the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, died.
On that day a man of Benjamin ran from the battle line and came to Shiloh, with his garments torn and dust upon his head in mourning.
When he came, Eli was sitting on his seat by the roadside, watching, because his heart trembled for the ark of God. The man entered the city and told the news, and the whole city cried out.
Eli heard the sound of the outcry and said, “What does the sound of this tumult mean?” The man hurried in and told Eli.
Now Eli was ninety-eight years old, and his eyesight had failed him, so that he could not see.
The man said to Eli, “I am the one who came from the battle line, and I fled from the battle today.” And Eli said, “What happened, my son?”

The messenger answered, “Israel has fled before the Philistines, and there has been a great slaughter among the people; your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, are dead, and the ark of God has been taken.”
When he mentioned the ark of God, Eli fell backward beside the gate; his neck was broken, and he died, for the man was old and heavy. He had judged Israel forty years.

His daughter-in-law, the wife of Phinehas, was pregnant and near her time. When she heard the report that the ark of God had been taken and that her father-in-law and husband were dead, she knelt and gave birth, for her labor pangs had seized her.
About the time of her death, the women standing by said to her, “Do not be afraid, for you have borne a son.” But she did not answer or pay heed.
She named the child Ichabod, saying, “Glory has departed from Israel,” because the ark of God had been taken and because of her father-in-law and her husband.
And she said, “The glory has departed from Israel, for the ark of God has been taken.”
The Philistines seized the ark of God and conveyed it from Ebenezer to Ashdod.
Having taken the ark of God, they brought it into the temple of Dagon and installed it beside Dagon.
The next morning, the Ashdodites discovered Dagon prostrate on the ground before the ark of the LORD, so they raised Dagon and restored him to his place.
When they rose early the following morning, Dagon was again prostrate before the ark of the LORD, with his head and both hands severed at the threshold; only the torso of Dagon remained.
Therefore, to this day, the priests of Dagon and all who enter the temple of Dagon in Ashdod do not tread upon the threshold of Dagon.
The hand of the LORD grew heavy against the Ashdodites, and He devastated them, striking Ashdod and its surrounding territory with tumors.
When the men of Ashdod perceived this, they said, “The ark of the God of Israel must not dwell among us, for His hand is harsh against us and against our god Dagon.”

They sent for and assembled all the lords of the Philistines, asking, “What shall we do with the ark of the God of Israel?” The lords replied, “Let the ark of the God of Israel be taken around to Gath.” So they took the ark of the God of Israel there.

But after they had taken it there, the hand of the LORD was against the city, producing an exceedingly great panic; He struck the men of the city, from the least to the greatest, and tumors broke out among them.
They then sent the ark of God to Ekron, and as the ark of God arrived, the Ekronites cried out, “They have brought the ark of the God of Israel around to me in order to kill me and my people.”

So they sent and gathered all the lords of the Philistines and said, “Send away the ark of the God of Israel; let it return to its own place, so that it does not kill me and my people.” For a deadly panic had seized the whole city, and the hand of God was exceedingly heavy there.
The men who did not die were struck with tumors, and the outcry of the city ascended to heaven.
The ark of the LORD remained in the territory of the Philistines for seven months.
The Philistines summoned their priests and diviners and inquired, "What are we to do with the ark of the LORD? Instruct us how we might restore it to its rightful place."

They replied, "If you are sending away the ark of the God of Israel, do not send it away empty; rather, you must surely return a guilt offering to Him. Then you will be healed, and it will become clear to you why His hand has not withdrawn from you."

They asked, "What guilt offering ought we to return to Him?" They answered, "Five golden tumors and five golden mice, corresponding to the number of Philistine lords, since the same plague has afflicted you all and your lords.

You must fashion replicas of your tumors and of the mice that are ravaging the land, and thereby honor the God of Israel; perhaps He will relent and withdraw His hand from you, from your gods, and from your land.
Why do you harden your hearts as the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened theirs? When He had dealt harshly with them, did they not send the people away, so that they departed?
Therefore, prepare a new cart, take two milk cows that have never been yoked, harness them to the cart, and send their calves away from them.
Place the ark of the LORD on the cart, put the golden objects you are returning as a guilt offering in a chest beside it, and send it on its way.

Then watch: if it travels the road toward Beth-shemesh, along its own border, then He has inflicted this great calamity upon us; but if not, we shall know that His hand did not strike us and that what befell us was mere chance."
The men did as instructed: they took two milk cows, yoked them to the cart, and penned their calves at home.
They placed the ark of the LORD on the cart, along with the chest containing the golden mice and the replicas of their tumors.

The cows went straight along the road to Beth-shemesh, keeping to the highway, lowing as they went and turning neither right nor left, while the Philistine lords followed them as far as the border of Beth-shemesh.
Now the people of Beth-shemesh were harvesting wheat in the valley; when they looked up and saw the ark, they rejoiced at the sight.
The cart entered the field of Joshua of Beth-shemesh and stopped beside a large stone. They split the wood of the cart and offered the cows as a burnt offering to the LORD.

The Levites lowered the ark of the LORD and the chest beside it, which held the golden objects, and set them upon the large stone. That day the men of Beth-shemesh offered burnt offerings and presented sacrifices to the LORD.
When the five Philistine lords saw this, they returned to Ekron that same day.
These golden tumors, which the Philistines returned as a guilt offering to the LORD, were one for Ashdod, one for Gaza, one for Ashkelon, one for Gath, and one for Ekron.

The golden mice corresponded in number to all the Philistine cities under the five lords—both fortified towns and rural settlements—right up to the great stone of Abel, where they set down the ark of the LORD, a stone that remains to this day in the field of Joshua of Beth-shemesh.
Yet He struck down fifty thousand and seventy of the people because they had looked into the ark of the LORD, and the people mourned because the LORD had struck the people with a great blow.
The men of Beth-shemesh exclaimed, "Who can stand before the LORD, this holy God? And to whom can we send it away from us?"
So they sent messengers to the inhabitants of Kiriath-jearim, saying, "The Philistines have returned the ark of the LORD. Come down and take it up to yourselves."

The inhabitants of Kiriath-jearim ascended and brought up the ark of the LORD, transporting it into the house of Abinadab upon the hill; there they consecrated his son Eleazar to guard the ark of the LORD.
From the day the ark tarried at Kiriath-jearim, the days were multiplied—twenty years in all—and all the house of Israel mourned and sought after the LORD.

Samuel then addressed the entirety of Israel, declaring, “If you return to the LORD with all your heart, expunge the foreign gods and the Ashtaroth from your midst, prepare your heart toward the LORD, and serve Him alone, He will rescue you from the Philistines’ hand.”
Accordingly, the Israelites removed the Baals and the Ashtaroth and served the LORD alone.
Samuel commanded, “Assemble all Israel at Mizpah, and I will intercede with the LORD on your behalf.”
They convened at Mizpah, drew water, and poured it out before the LORD; on that day they fasted and confessed, “We have sinned against the LORD.” Samuel judged Israel at Mizpah.
When the Philistines learned that Israel had assembled at Mizpah, the Philistine lords advanced against Israel; upon hearing of it, the Israelites were seized with fear.
The Israelites entreated Samuel, “Do not desist from crying out to the LORD our God for us, that He may deliver us from the Philistines’ hand.”
Samuel took a milk-fed lamb and offered it as a whole burnt offering to the LORD; he cried out to the LORD on Israel’s behalf, and the LORD answered him.

As the Philistines approached to wage war against Israel, Samuel was presenting the burnt offering; the LORD thundered with a mighty voice over the Philistines, throwing them into disarray, and they were struck down before Israel.
The men of Israel sallied forth from Mizpah, pursued the Philistines, and struck them down as far as below Beth-car.
Samuel took a stone and placed it between Mizpah and Shen, naming it Ebenezer, and said, “Thus far has the LORD helped us.”
The Philistines were humbled and no longer entered Israel’s territory; the hand of the LORD was against the Philistines throughout all Samuel’s days.

The cities from Ekron to Gath that the Philistines had seized from Israel were restored to Israel; Israel reclaimed its territory from the Philistines’ hand, and peace obtained between Israel and the Amorites.
Samuel judged Israel throughout his life.
Annually he made a circuit to Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah, judging Israel in all these places.
His circuit returned to Ramah, for his household was there; there he judged Israel and erected an altar to the LORD.
When Samuel had grown old, he appointed his sons as judges over Israel.
The firstborn was named Joel, and his second son was named Abijah; they served as judges in Beersheba.
Yet his sons did not walk in his ways; instead, they turned aside after dishonest gain, accepted bribes, and perverted justice.
Then all the elders of Israel assembled and came to Samuel at Ramah.
They said to him, “Behold, you are old, and your sons do not walk in your ways. Now appoint for us a king to judge us, as all the nations have.”
But the matter displeased Samuel when they said, “Give us a king to judge us.” So Samuel prayed to the LORD.
And the LORD said to Samuel, “Listen to the voice of the people in all that they say to you, for they have not rejected you, but they have rejected Me from reigning over them.
According to all the deeds they have done from the day I brought them up out of Egypt until this day—forsaking Me and serving other gods—so they are also doing to you.
Now listen to their voice; yet solemnly warn them and declare to them the manner of the king who will reign over them.”
So Samuel reported all the words of the LORD to the people who were asking him for a king.
He said, “This will be the manner of the king who will reign over you: he will take your sons and appoint them for himself to his chariots and horsemen, and they will run before his chariots.
He will appoint captains of thousands and captains of fifties, and he will set some to plow his ground and reap his harvest, and to make his implements of war and the equipment of his chariots.
He will take your daughters to be perfumers, cooks, and bakers.
He will take the best of your fields, vineyards, and olive groves and give them to his servants.
He will take a tenth of your seed and of your vineyards and give it to his eunuchs and servants.
He will take your male and female servants, the best of your young men, and your donkeys, and put them to his work.
He will take a tenth of your flocks, and you will be his servants.
And on that day you will cry out because of your king whom you have chosen for yourselves, but the LORD will not answer you in that day.”
But the people refused to listen to the voice of Samuel, and they said, “No! Rather, a king shall reign over us,
so that we may be like all the nations, and our king may judge us and go out before us and fight our battles.”
And Samuel heard all the words of the people and repeated them in the ears of the LORD.
Then the LORD said to Samuel, “Listen to their voice and appoint them a king.” So Samuel said to the men of Israel, “Go, every man, to his own city.”
There was once a man of Benjamin—Kish son of Abiel, son of Zeror, son of Becorath, son of Aphiah—a Benjamite of formidable valor.
He had a son named Saul, select in bearing and strikingly comely; among the Israelites no man surpassed him in handsomeness, and from the shoulders upward he towered over all the people.
Now the donkeys belonging to Saul's father Kish had strayed away. Kish therefore said to his son Saul, "Please take one of the servants with you and go; seek out the donkeys."

So Saul traversed the hill country of Ephraim and the territory of Shalishah, yet they did not find them; they then passed through the land of Shaalim, but the animals were not there; and when they crossed into Benjamin, they still found nothing.
When they reached the land of Zuph, Saul said to the servant accompanying him, "Come, let us turn back, lest my father abandon his concern for the donkeys and grow disquieted on our account."

The servant replied, "Look, in this city there is a man of God, a person of considerable honor; every word he utters is fulfilled. Let us proceed there; perhaps he will disclose to us the route we ought to take."
Saul said to the servant, "If we go, what shall we present to the man? The bread in our sacks has been consumed, and we have no offering for the man of God. What remains at our disposal?"
The servant answered, "Look, I have in my possession a quarter shekel of silver; I will give it to the man of God, and he will tell us our route."
(In former times in Israel, when one went to consult God, one would say, "Come, let us go to the seer," for the figure now termed a prophet was then called a seer.)
Saul said to his servant, "Your words are sound; come, let us go." So they went to the city where the man of God resided.
As they ascended the hill toward the city, they encountered young women emerging to draw water, and they asked them, "Is the seer here?"
They answered, "He is; he is just ahead of you. Make haste, for he has arrived in the city today, because the people are holding a sacrifice at the high place today.

As soon as you enter the city, you will find him before he ascends to the high place to eat; for the people will not eat until he arrives, since he must bless the sacrifice, and only afterward will those invited eat. Go up now; today you will find him."
So they went up to the city, and as they were entering, Samuel came out to meet them as he was going up to the high place.
Now on the day preceding Saul's arrival, the the LORD had revealed to Samuel:

"Tomorrow at about this hour I will send you a man from the land of Benjamin, and you shall anoint him as leader over My people Israel, and he shall deliver My people from the hand of the Philistines; for I have regarded My people, because their cry has reached Me."
When Samuel saw Saul, the the LORD said to him, "Here is the man of whom I spoke to you. He shall govern My people."
Then Saul approached Samuel in the gateway and said, "Please tell me where the seer's house is."
Samuel answered, "I am the seer. Go up ahead of me to the high place, for today you are to eat with me, and in the morning I will send you on your way and tell you all that is in your heart.

As for the donkeys that were lost to you three days ago, do not set your heart on them, for they have been found. And to whom does all the desire of Israel belong? Is it not to you and to your father's house?"
Saul answered, "Am I not a Benjamite, from the smallest of the tribes of Israel, and is not my clan the least of all the clans of Benjamin? Why then have you spoken to me in this manner?"
Then Samuel took Saul and his servant and brought them into the chamber and seated them at the head of those invited, about thirty in number.
Samuel said to the cook, "Bring the portion that I gave you, the one I told you to set aside."

So the cook brought up the thigh with its attached portion and set it before Saul. And Samuel said, "Here is what was reserved for you. Eat, for it was kept for you for this appointed time, for I said, 'I have invited the people.'" So Saul ate with Samuel that day.
After they descended from the high place into the city, Samuel spoke with Saul on the roof.
They rose early in the morning, and at dawn Samuel called to Saul on the roof, "Get up, and I will send you on your way." So Saul got up, and the two of them went out together.
As they were going down to the edge of the city, Samuel said to Saul, "Tell the servant to go on ahead of us; but you remain here for a while, so that I may make known to you the word of God."
Samuel took a flask of oil, poured it upon Saul’s head, kissed him, and said, “Has not the LORD anointed you ruler over His inheritance?”

“When you leave me today, you will meet two men near Rachel’s tomb at Zelzah in the territory of Benjamin. They will say to you, ‘The donkeys you set out to find have been found. And now your father has ceased to concern himself with the donkeys and is anxious about you, asking, “What shall I do for my son?”’

Then, as you continue on from there, you will come to the oak of Tabor, where three men ascending to God at Bethel will meet you. One will bear three young goats, another three loaves of bread, and another a skin of wine.
They will greet you and give you two loaves of bread, which you are to receive from their hands.”

“Afterward you will come to Gibeah of God, where the Philistine garrison is stationed. As you enter the city, you will meet a band of prophets descending from the high place, preceded by harp, tambourine, flute, and lyre, and they will be prophesying.
Then the Spirit of the LORD will rush upon you, and you will prophesy with them and be transformed into a different man.
When these signs have come to pass, do whatever your hand finds to do, for God is with you.”
“Then go down before me to Gilgal. I will come down to you to offer burnt offerings and to sacrifice peace offerings. Wait seven days until I come to you and disclose what you are to do.”
As Saul turned to leave Samuel, God altered his heart, and all these signs came to pass that very day.
When Saul and his servant arrived at Gibeah, a band of prophets met him. The Spirit of God rushed upon him, and he prophesied among them.
Everyone who had previously known him saw him prophesying with the prophets, and they asked one another, “What has happened to the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?”
A man from there replied, “Who is their father?” Hence the saying, “Is Saul also among the prophets?”
When Saul had finished prophesying, he went to the high place.
Saul’s uncle asked him and his servant, “Where did you go?” “To look for the donkeys,” Saul replied. “When we saw that they could not be found, we went to Samuel.”
His uncle said, “Please tell me what Samuel said to you.”
Saul replied, “He told us that the donkeys had been found.” But he did not tell his uncle what Samuel had said concerning the kingship.
Samuel summoned the people to the LORD at Mizpah.

He said to the Israelites, “This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘I brought Israel up out of Egypt, and I delivered you from the hand of the Egyptians and from the hand of all the kingdoms that oppressed you.’

‘But you have rejected your God, who saves you from all your calamities and your distresses. You have said to Him, “No, appoint a king over us.” Now present yourselves before the LORD by your tribes and by your clans.’”
Samuel brought all the tribes of Israel near, and the tribe of Benjamin was selected by lot.
Then he brought the tribe of Benjamin near by its clans, and the clan of the Matrites was selected. Saul son of Kish was then selected. But when they sought him, he could not be found.
So they inquired of the LORD again, “Has the man come here yet?” And the LORD said, “Behold, he is hiding among the supplies.”
They ran and brought him out from there. When he stood among the people, he was a head taller than any of them from the shoulders upward.
Then Samuel said to all the people, “Do you see the man the LORD has chosen? There is no one like him among all the people.” And all the people shouted, “Long live the king!”
Samuel explained to the people the rights and duties of the kingship. He wrote them in a book and placed it before the LORD. Then Samuel dismissed all the people, each to his own home.
Saul went to his home in Gibeah, and valiant men whose hearts God had touched accompanied him.
But some worthless fellows said, “How can this man save us?” They despised him and brought him no gift. But Saul remained silent.
Nahash the Ammonite advanced and laid siege to Jabesh-gilead. All the men of Jabesh said to him, "Make a treaty with us, and we will serve you."
But Nahash the Ammonite replied, "I will make a treaty with you on this condition: that I gouge out the right eye of every one of you and thereby bring disgrace upon all Israel."
The elders of Jabesh said to him, "Grant us seven days so that we may send messengers throughout all Israel; and if no one comes to deliver us, we will surrender to you."
When the messengers arrived at Gibeah of Saul, they reported these words to the people, and all the people wept aloud.
Just then Saul was returning from the fields behind his oxen. "What troubles the people?" he asked. "Why are they weeping?" They told him what the men of Jabesh had said.
When Saul heard these words, the Spirit of God rushed upon him, and his anger burned fiercely.

He took a yoke of oxen, dismembered them, and sent the pieces by messengers throughout all the territory of Israel, proclaiming, "This is what will be done to the oxen of anyone who does not follow Saul and Samuel." Then the terror of the LORD fell upon the people, and they mustered as one man.
When he had mustered them at Bezek, the Israelites numbered three hundred thousand, and the men of Judah thirty thousand.

They said to the messengers who had come, "Say to the men of Jabesh-gilead, 'Tomorrow, by the time the sun is hot, deliverance will be yours.'" When the messengers reported this to the men of Jabesh, they rejoiced.
The men of Jabesh said, "Tomorrow we will come out to you, and you may deal with us as you see fit."

The next day Saul divided the people into three companies. They broke into the Ammonite camp during the morning watch and struck them down until the heat of the day. The survivors scattered, so that no two of them were left together.
The people then said to Samuel, "Who was it who said, 'Must Saul reign over us?' Hand those men over, and we will put them to death."
But Saul said, "No one will be put to death today, for today the LORD has brought deliverance to Israel."
Then Samuel said to the people, "Come, let us go to Gilgal and renew the kingship there."

So all the people went to Gilgal, and there they made Saul king in the presence of the LORD. There they sacrificed peace offerings before the LORD, and Saul and all the men of Israel rejoiced exceedingly.
Samuel declared to all Israel, “Behold, I have hearkened to your voice in all that you have said to me, and I have installed a king over you.
And now, behold, the king walks before you, while I have grown old and gray; behold, my sons are in your midst, and I have walked before you from my youth until this very day.

Here I stand; testify against me before the LORD and before His anointed: Whose ox have I taken? Whose donkey have I taken? Whom have I defrauded? Whom have I oppressed? From whose hand have I taken a bribe to blind my eyes? I will restore it to you.”
They answered, “You have defrauded no one, oppressed no one, and taken nothing from anyone's hand.”
Samuel said to them, “The LORD is witness against you, and His anointed is witness this day, that you have found nothing in my hand.” “He is witness,” they replied.
Samuel said to the people, “The LORD is He who made Moses and Aaron and who brought your fathers up from the land of Egypt.
Now therefore stand still, that I may contend with you before the LORD concerning all the righteous deeds the LORD has done for you and for your fathers.
When Jacob came into Egypt, your fathers cried out to the LORD, and the LORD sent Moses and Aaron, who brought your fathers out of Egypt and settled them in this place.

Yet they forgot the LORD their God, so He sold them into the hand of Sisera, commander of the army of Hazor, and into the hand of the Philistines, and into the hand of the king of Moab, and they fought against them.

Then they cried out to the LORD and said, ‘We have sinned, because we have forsaken the LORD and served the Baals and the Ashtoreths; now deliver us from the hand of our enemies, and we will serve You.’
And the LORD sent Jerubbaal, Bedan, Jephthah, and Samuel, and delivered you from the hand of your enemies on every side, so that you dwelt in safety.
But when you saw that Nahash, king of the Ammonites, came against you, you said to me, ‘No; a king shall reign over us,’ though the LORD your God was your king.
Now therefore behold the king whom you have chosen, whom you asked for; and behold, the LORD has set a king over you.
If you fear the LORD and serve Him and obey His voice, and do not rebel against the command of the LORD, then both you and the king who reigns over you will walk after the LORD your God.
But if you do not obey the voice of the LORD and rebel against the command of the LORD, then the hand of the LORD will be against you, as it was against your fathers.”
“Now therefore stand and see this great thing the LORD will do before your eyes.

Is it not wheat harvest today? I will call to the LORD, and He will send thunder and rain; and you will know and see that your wickedness is great, which you have done in the sight of the LORD, in asking for yourselves a king.”
So Samuel called to the LORD, and the LORD sent thunder and rain that day; and all the people greatly feared the LORD and Samuel.
And all the people said to Samuel, “Pray for your servants to the LORD your God, that we may not die; for we have added to all our sins this evil, to ask for ourselves a king.”
And Samuel said to the people, “Do not fear; you have done all this wickedness; yet do not turn aside from following the LORD, but serve the LORD with all your heart.
And do not turn aside after empty things, which cannot profit nor deliver, for they are empty.”
“For the LORD will not forsake His people for His great name's sake, because it has pleased the LORD to make you His people.
Moreover, as for me, far be it from me that I should sin against the LORD by ceasing to pray for you; and I will teach you the good and right way.
Only fear the LORD and serve Him in truth with all your heart; for consider what great things He has done for you.
But if you still do wickedly, you shall be swept away, both you and your king.”
Saul was one year old when he became king, and he reigned two years over Israel.

Saul chose three thousand men of Israel for himself; two thousand were with Saul in Michmash and in the hill country of Bethel, and one thousand were with Jonathan in Gibeah of Benjamin, while the rest of the people he sent, each to his own tent.
Jonathan struck the Philistine garrison that was in Geba, and the Philistines heard of it. Then Saul blew the trumpet throughout the land, saying, "Let the Hebrews hear."
All Israel heard the report, "Saul has struck the Philistine garrison, and Israel has become a stench to the Philistines." Then the people were summoned after Saul to Gilgal.

The Philistines gathered to fight against Israel: thirty thousand chariots, six thousand horsemen, and people as numerous as the sand on the seashore. They came up and encamped in Michmash, east of Beth Aven.
When the men of Israel saw that they were in dire straits, for the people were hard pressed, they hid themselves in caves, in thickets, among rocks, in strongholds, and in cisterns.
Some of the Hebrews crossed the Jordan into the land of Gad and Gilead, while Saul was still at Gilgal and all the people followed him trembling.
He waited seven days, to the time that Samuel had appointed, but Samuel did not come to Gilgal, and the people were scattering from him.
Saul said, "Bring the burnt offering and the peace offerings to me." And he offered the burnt offering.
As soon as he had finished offering the burnt offering, behold, Samuel came; and Saul went out to meet him and to greet him.

Samuel said, "What have you done?" Saul said, "Because I saw that the people were scattering from me, and that you did not come within the appointed days, and that the Philistines were assembling at Michmash, I said, 'Now the Philistines will come down against me at Gilgal, and I have not sought the favor of the the LORD; therefore I forced myself and offered the burnt offering.'"

Samuel said to Saul, "You have acted foolishly; you have not kept the commandment of the the LORD your God, which He commanded you. For now the the LORD would have established your kingdom over Israel forever.

But now your kingdom shall not endure; the the LORD has sought for Himself a man after His own heart, and the the LORD has commanded him to be prince over His people, because you have not kept what the the LORD commanded you."
Samuel then arose and went up from Gilgal to Gibeah of Benjamin. Saul mustered the people who remained with him, about six hundred men.
Saul and his son Jonathan, together with the people who remained with them, were dwelling in Geba of Benjamin, while the Philistines encamped at Michmash.
Then marauders issued from the Philistine camp in three companies: one company turned toward Ophrah, in the land of Shual;
another turned toward Beth-horon; and the third turned toward the border overlooking the Valley of Zeboim toward the wilderness.
No blacksmith was to be found throughout the land of Israel, for the Philistines said, "Otherwise the Hebrews will make swords or spears."
So all Israel went down to the Philistines, each to sharpen his plowshare, his mattock, his axe, and his sickle.
The charge was two-thirds of a shekel for the plowshares and mattocks, and one-third of a shekel for sharpening the axes and for setting the goads.
Thus on the day of battle neither sword nor spear was found in the hand of any of the people with Saul and Jonathan; only Saul and his son Jonathan possessed them.
And a garrison of the Philistines advanced to the pass of Michmash.

Now it happened one day that Jonathan, the son of Saul, said to the young man who bore his armor, “Come, let us cross over to the Philistine garrison on the far side,” though he did not disclose this to his father.
Saul was sitting beneath the pomegranate tree at Migron, near the edge of Gibeah, with about six hundred men.
Ahijah, who wore the ephod—Ahitub’s son, Ichabod’s brother, Phinehas’s son, Eli’s son, priest of the LORD at Shiloh—was with them, and the people did not know that Jonathan had gone.
Between the passes by which Jonathan sought to reach the Philistine encampment lay a rocky crag on one side and a rocky crag on the other; one was called Bozez, and the other Seneh.
One crag rose steeply to the north toward Michmash, and the other to the south toward Geba.

Jonathan said to the young man bearing his armor, “Come, let us cross over to the garrison of these uncircumcised men; perhaps the LORD will act on our behalf, for nothing hinders the LORD from saving, whether by many or by few.”
His armor-bearer replied, “Do all that is in your heart. Proceed; I am with you as your heart desires.”
Jonathan said, “Behold, we will cross over to the men and reveal ourselves to them.
If they say to us, ‘Wait until we come to you,’ then we will stand our ground and not go up to them.
But if they say, ‘Come up to us,’ then we will go up, for that will be our sign that the LORD has delivered them into our hands.”
So the two of them showed themselves to the Philistine garrison, and the Philistines said, “Look, the Hebrews are coming out of the holes where they have been hiding!”

The men of the garrison called to Jonathan and his armor-bearer, “Come up to us, and we will teach you a lesson.” Jonathan said to his armor-bearer, “Follow me, for the LORD has delivered them into the hand of Israel.”
Jonathan climbed up on his hands and feet, with his armor-bearer behind him. The Philistines fell before Jonathan, and his armor-bearer followed and killed them.
In that first assault Jonathan and his armor-bearer struck down about twenty men within an area of roughly half an acre.
Then terror struck the camp and the field, as well as all the people; the garrison and the raiders also trembled, and the earth quaked, so that it became a great panic from God.
Saul’s lookouts at Gibeah in Benjamin saw the multitude melting away in every direction.
Saul said to the men with him, “Muster the troops and see who has gone out from among us.” When they mustered them, behold, Jonathan and his armor-bearer were missing.
Saul said to Ahijah, “Bring the ark of God,” for at that time the ark of God was with the Israelites.
While Saul was speaking to the priest, the tumult in the Philistine camp grew greater and greater, so Saul said to the priest, “Withdraw your hand.”
Then Saul and all the people with him assembled and went to the battle, and behold, every man’s sword was against his fellow, so that there was very great confusion.
Moreover, the Hebrews who had formerly been with the Philistines and had gone up with them into the camp turned and joined the Israelites who were with Saul and Jonathan.
Likewise, all the Israelites who had hidden themselves in the hill country of Ephraim, when they heard that the Philistines were fleeing, pursued them closely in the battle.
So the LORD saved Israel that day, and the battle passed beyond Beth-aven.

The men of Israel were hard pressed that day, for Saul had bound the people by an oath, saying, “Cursed be the man who eats food before evening and before I have avenged myself on my enemies.” So none of the people tasted food.
Now all the land entered the forest, and there was honey on the ground.
When the people entered the forest, behold, the honey was oozing, yet no one put his hand to his mouth, for the people feared the oath.

But Jonathan had not heard when his father charged the people with the oath, so he put out the end of the staff that was in his hand, dipped it into the honeycomb, and put his hand to his mouth, and his eyes brightened.
Then one of the people answered and said, “Your father strictly charged the people with an oath, saying, ‘Cursed be the man who eats food today,’ and the people are faint.”
Jonathan said, “My father has brought trouble upon the land. See how my eyes have brightened because I tasted a little of this honey.
How much more if the people had freely eaten today of the spoil of their enemies! For then the slaughter of the Philistines would have been much greater.”
They struck down the Philistines that day from Michmash to Aijalon, and the people were very faint.
The people rushed upon the spoil and took sheep, oxen, and calves, slaughtered them on the ground, and ate them with the blood.
They told Saul, “Behold, the people are sinning against the LORD by eating with the blood.” He said, “You have dealt treacherously. Roll a great stone here to me today.”

Saul said, “Disperse among the people and tell them, ‘Each of you bring me his ox or his sheep, slaughter them here, and eat; do not sin against the LORD by eating with the blood.’” So all the people brought his ox that night and slaughtered it there.
Saul built an altar to the LORD; it was the first altar that he built to the LORD.

Saul said, “Let us go down after the Philistines by night, plunder them until morning, and leave not one of them.” They said, “Do whatever seems best to you.” But the priest said, “Let us draw near to God here.”
Saul inquired of God, “Shall I go down after the Philistines? Will You give them into the hand of Israel?” But He did not answer him that day.
Saul said, “Come here, all you leaders of the people, and know and see how this sin came about today.
For as the LORD lives, who saves Israel, though it be in Jonathan my son, he shall surely die.” But no one answered him from all the people.
Then he said to all Israel, “You shall be on one side, and I and Jonathan my son will be on the other side.” And the people said, “Do what seems best to you.”
Therefore Saul said to the LORD, the God of Israel, “Give a perfect answer.” Jonathan and Saul were taken, but the people went free.
Saul said, “Cast the lot between me and Jonathan my son.” And Jonathan was taken.
Saul said to Jonathan, “Tell me what you have done.” Jonathan told him, “I tasted a little honey with the end of the staff that was in my hand. Here I am; I must die.”
Saul said, “God do so to me, and more also, for you shall surely die, Jonathan.”

But the people said to Saul, “Shall Jonathan die, who has worked this great salvation in Israel? Far be it! As the LORD lives, not one hair of his head shall fall to the ground, for he has worked with God this day.” So the people rescued Jonathan, and he did not die.
Then Saul ceased pursuing the Philistines, and the Philistines withdrew to their own land.

After Saul had consolidated his kingship over Israel, he fought against all his enemies on every side—against Moab, against the Ammonites, against Edom, against the kings of Zobah, and against the Philistines—and wherever he turned, he inflicted punishment on them.
He fought valiantly and struck down Amalek, and delivered Israel from the hand of those who plundered them.
The sons of Saul were Jonathan, Ishvi, and Malchi-shua; the name of his firstborn daughter was Merab, and the name of the younger was Michal.
The name of Saul’s wife was Ahinoam, the daughter of Ahimaaz. The name of the commander of his army was Abner, the son of Ner, who was Saul’s uncle.
Kish, Saul’s father, and Ner, Abner’s father, were sons of Abiel.
There was fierce war against the Philistines all the days of Saul, and whenever Saul saw any mighty man or any valiant man, he took him into his service.
Samuel said to Saul, “The LORD sent me to anoint you king over His people, over Israel. Now therefore attend to the voice of the words of the LORD.”
“This is what the LORD of Hosts says: ‘I have taken note of what Amalek did to Israel—how he opposed them on their way up from Egypt.
Now go and strike Amalek and devote to destruction all that belongs to him; show him no mercy; put to death men and women, children and infants, oxen and sheep, camels and donkeys.’”
Saul summoned the troops and numbered them at Telaim: two hundred thousand foot soldiers and ten thousand men of Judah.
Saul came to the city of Amalek and laid an ambush in the valley.

Saul said to the Kenites, “You have shown kindness to all the Israelites when they came up from Egypt. Depart now; withdraw from among the Amalekites, lest I destroy you along with them.” So the Kenites withdrew from among the Amalekites.
Saul defeated Amalek from Havilah to Shur, which lies east of Egypt.
He captured Agag, king of Amalek, alive, but devoted all the other people to destruction with the sword.

Saul and his troops spared Agag and the best of the sheep and cattle, the fatlings and lambs, and all that was good; they were unwilling to devote them to destruction, but everything despised and worthless they devoted to destruction.
Then the word of the LORD came to Samuel, saying,
“I regret that I have made Saul king, for he has turned back from following Me and has not carried out My commands.” Samuel was angry, and he cried out to the LORD all night.
Early in the morning Samuel rose to meet Saul, but he was told, “Saul has gone to Carmel, and behold, he has erected a monument for himself; then he turned and passed on and went down to Gilgal.”
Samuel came to Saul, and Saul said to him, “Blessed are you of the LORD! I have carried out the command of the LORD.”
Samuel said, “What then is this bleating of sheep in my ears and the lowing of cattle that I hear?”
Saul said, “They have brought them from the Amalekites; for the people spared the best of the sheep and cattle to sacrifice to the LORD your God, but the rest we devoted to destruction.”
“Enough!” Samuel said to Saul. “Let me tell you what the LORD said to me last night.” “Tell me,” Saul replied.
Samuel said, “Although you were once small in your own eyes, did you not become the head of the tribes of Israel? The LORD anointed you king over Israel.
And He sent you on a mission and said, ‘Go and devote to destruction the sinners, the Amalekites; wage war against them until you have wiped them out.’
Why then did you not obey the LORD? Why did you rush upon the plunder and do evil in the sight of the LORD?”
Saul said to Samuel, “I did obey the LORD. I went on the mission the LORD assigned me. I brought back Agag king of Amalek and devoted the Amalekites to destruction.
But the troops took sheep and cattle from the plunder—the best of the things devoted to destruction—to sacrifice to the LORD your God at Gilgal.”
Samuel said, “Does the LORD delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices as much as in obedience to His voice? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to heed is better than the fat of rams.
For rebellion is as the sin of divination, and arrogance is as the evil of idolatry. Because you have rejected the word of the LORD, He has rejected you as king.”
Saul said to Samuel, “I have sinned; I have transgressed the LORD’s command and your words, because I feared the people and obeyed their voice.
Now, I beg you, pardon my sin and return with me, so that I may worship the LORD.”
Samuel said to Saul, “I will not return with you, for you have rejected the word of the LORD, and the LORD has rejected you from being king over Israel.”
As Samuel turned to go, Saul seized the hem of his robe, and it tore.
Samuel said to him, “The LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today and has given it to your neighbor who is better than you.
Moreover, the Glory of Israel will not lie or change His mind, for He is not a man, that He should change His mind.”
Saul said, “I have sinned; but please honor me now before the elders of my people and before Israel, and return with me, that I may bow in worship to the LORD your God.”
So Samuel went back with Saul, and Saul worshiped the LORD.
Samuel said, “Bring me Agag king of the Amalekites.” So Agag came to him cheerfully, for Agag thought, “Surely the bitterness of death is past.”
Samuel said, “As your sword has made women childless, so shall your mother be childless among women.” And Samuel hacked Agag to pieces before the LORD at Gilgal.
Then Samuel went to Ramah, and Saul went up to his house at Gibeah of Saul.
Samuel did not see Saul again until the day of his death, though Samuel grieved over Saul. And the LORD regretted that He had made Saul king over Israel.

The LORD said to Samuel, “How long will you mourn for Saul, seeing that I have rejected him from reigning over Israel? Fill your horn with oil and go; I am sending you to Jesse the Bethlehemite, for I have discerned among his sons a king for Myself.”
Samuel said, “How can I go? Saul will hear of it and kill me.” The the LORD said, “Take a heifer with you and say, ‘I have come to sacrifice to the the LORD.’
And you shall summon Jesse to the sacrifice, and I will disclose to you what you are to do; you shall anoint for Me whomever I designate to you.”
Samuel did what the the LORD had spoken, and he came to Bethlehem. The elders of the city came trembling to meet him and asked, “Do you come in peace?”
He replied, “Peace. I have come to sacrifice to the the LORD. Consecrate yourselves and come with me to the sacrifice.” So he consecrated Jesse and his sons and summoned them to the sacrifice.
When they arrived, he beheld Eliab and said, “Surely the the LORD’s anointed stands before Him.”

The The LORD said to Samuel, “Do not regard his appearance or his lofty stature, for I have rejected him; for the the LORD does not perceive as a mortal perceives: a mortal looks upon the outward appearance, but the the LORD looks upon the heart.”
Then Jesse summoned Abinadab and made him pass before Samuel, who said, “The the LORD has not chosen this one either.”
Next Jesse made Shammah pass by, and Samuel said, “The the LORD has not chosen this one either.”
Jesse made seven of his sons pass before Samuel, and Samuel said to Jesse, “The the LORD has not chosen any of these.”

Samuel asked Jesse, “Are these all the sons you have?” Jesse answered, “The youngest still remains; behold, he is tending the sheep.” Samuel said, “Send for him and bring him here, for we will not sit down until he arrives.”
So Jesse sent and brought him in. He was ruddy, with beautiful eyes, and handsome in appearance. The The LORD said, “Arise and anoint him, for this is he.”
Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed him in the midst of his brothers, and the Spirit of the the LORD rushed upon David from that day forward. Then Samuel rose and went to Ramah.
Now the Spirit of the the LORD had departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the the LORD tormented him.
Saul’s servants said to him, “Behold, an evil spirit from God is terrifying you.

Let our lord now command your servants before you to seek out a man skilled in playing the harp, so that when the evil spirit from God comes upon you, he may play with his hand, and you will be well.”
Saul said to his servants, “Find me a man who plays well, and bring him to me.”

One of the young men answered, “Behold, I have seen a son of Jesse the Bethlehemite who knows how to play, a mighty man of valor, a warrior, discerning in speech, handsome in form, and the the LORD is with him.”
So Saul sent messengers to Jesse, saying, “Send me David your son, who is with the sheep.”
Jesse took a donkey loaded with bread, a skin of wine, and a young goat, and sent them with his son David to Saul.
David came to Saul and entered his service; Saul loved him greatly, and David became his armor-bearer.
Saul sent word to Jesse: “Let David remain before me, for he has found favor in my eyes.”
Whenever the spirit from God came upon Saul, David would take the harp and play with his hand; Saul would be relieved and feel better, and the evil spirit would depart from him.
Now the Philistines gathered their forces for war and assembled at Socoh in Judah; they encamped between Socoh and Azekah, at Ephes-dammim.
Saul and the men of Israel gathered and encamped in the Valley of Elah, where they drew up their battle lines against the Philistines.
The Philistines occupied the hillside on one side, Israel occupied the hillside on the other, and the valley lay between them.
A champion emerged from the Philistine camp—Goliath of Gath—whose height was six cubits and a span.
He wore a bronze helmet upon his head and was clad in a coat of mail; the coat weighed five thousand shekels of bronze.
He had bronze greaves upon his legs and a bronze javelin slung between his shoulders.
The shaft of his spear resembled a weaver's beam, and the iron point of his spear weighed six hundred shekels; moreover, his shield-bearer advanced before him.

He took his stand and cried out to Israel's battle lines, "Why do you come out to array yourselves for war? Am I not a Philistine, and are you not Saul's servants? Choose a man for yourselves, and let him descend to me."
"If he can fight with me and strike me down, then we shall become your servants; but if I prevail against him and strike him down, then you shall become our servants and serve us."
The Philistine continued, "I have defied the ranks of Israel this day. Give me a man, that we may fight together."
When Saul and all Israel heard these words of the Philistine, they were dismayed and filled with great dread.
Now David was the son of an Ephrathite of Bethlehem in Judah, whose name was Jesse; he had eight sons. In Saul's days the man was old, advanced in years among men.
The three eldest sons of Jesse had followed Saul into the war: the firstborn Eliab, the second Abinadab, and the third Shammah.
David was the youngest, while the three eldest followed Saul.
David went back and forth from Saul to tend his father's sheep at Bethlehem.
For forty days the Philistine approached morning and evening and took his stand.
Jesse said to David his son, "Take for your brothers an ephah of this roasted grain and these ten loaves, and carry them quickly to the camp to your brothers."
"Take these ten cheeses to the commander of their thousand, and see how your brothers fare, and bring back their token."
Now Saul and all the men of Israel were in the Valley of Elah, fighting with the Philistines.

David rose early in the morning, left the sheep with a keeper, took the provisions, and went as Jesse had commanded him. He reached the encampment as the army was marching out to the battle line, shouting the war cry.
Israel and the Philistines drew up in battle array, army against army.
David left his baggage with the keeper of supplies, ran to the ranks, and went and greeted his brothers.
As he was speaking with them, behold, the champion—the Philistine of Gath named Goliath—came up from the Philistine ranks and uttered the same words as before; and David heard them.
All the men of Israel, upon seeing the man, fled from him and were seized with great terror.

The men of Israel said, "Have you seen this man who has come up? Surely he has come up to defy Israel. The king will enrich the man who kills him with great wealth, give him his daughter, and make his father's house free in Israel."

David said to the men standing by him, "What shall be done for the man who kills this Philistine and removes the reproach from Israel? For who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God?"
The people answered him in the same manner, "So it shall be done for the man who kills him."

His eldest brother Eliab heard him speaking to the men, and Eliab's anger burned against David. He said, "Why have you come down? With whom have you left those few sheep in the wilderness? I know your presumption and the evil of your heart, for you have come down to see the battle."
David replied, "What have I done now? Was it not merely a word?"
He turned away from him toward another and spoke in the same way, and the people answered him as before.
When the words that David had spoken were heard, they were reported to Saul, and he sent for him.
David said to Saul, "Let not my lord's heart fail on account of this Philistine; your servant will go and fight with this Philistine."
Saul said to David, "You cannot go against this Philistine to fight with him, for you are only a youth, and he has been a warrior from his youth."
David said to Saul, "Your servant was tending sheep for his father. When a lion or a bear came and carried off a lamb from the flock,
I went out after it, struck it down, and rescued the lamb from its mouth; and when it rose against me, I seized it by its beard, struck it down, and killed it.
Your servant has struck down both lion and bear; and this uncircumcised Philistine shall be like one of them, since he has defied the armies of the living God."

David added, "The LORD, who delivered me from the paw of the lion and from the paw of the bear, He will deliver me from the hand of this Philistine." Saul said to David, "Go, and the the LORD be with you."
Saul clothed David with his own armor; he placed a bronze helmet on his head and clothed him with a coat of mail.

David girded his sword over the armor and attempted to walk, but he could not, for he had not tested them. David said to Saul, "I cannot go in these, for I have not tested them." So David took them off.
He took his staff in his hand and chose five smooth stones from the brook, placing them in his shepherd's bag; his sling was in his hand. Then he drew near to the Philistine.
The Philistine advanced and drew near to David, with his shield-bearer before him.
When the Philistine looked and saw David, he disdained him, for he was but a youth—ruddy and handsome in appearance.
The Philistine said to David, "Am I a dog, that you come to me with sticks?" And the Philistine cursed David by his gods.
The Philistine said to David, "Come to me, and I will give your flesh to the birds of the air and to the beasts of the field."
David said to the Philistine, "You come to me with sword and spear and javelin, but I come to you in the name of the the LORD of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied.

This day the the LORD will deliver you into my hand, and I will strike you down and cut off your head. I will give the carcasses of the Philistine host this day to the birds of the air and to the beasts of the earth, so that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel.
And all this assembly shall know that the the LORD does not save by sword or spear; for the battle is the the LORD's, and He will give you into our hands."
When the Philistine arose and came and drew near to meet David, David ran quickly toward the battle line to meet the Philistine.
David put his hand into his bag and took out a stone and slung it; he struck the Philistine on the forehead. The stone sank into his forehead, and he fell on his face to the ground.
Thus David prevailed over the Philistine with sling and stone: he struck the Philistine and killed him, though there was no sword in David's hand.
David ran and stood over the Philistine, took his sword, drew it from its sheath, and killed him, cutting off his head with it. When the Philistines saw that their champion was dead, they fled.

The men of Israel and Judah rose and shouted and pursued the Philistines as far as the entrance of the valley and the gates of Ekron. The slain of the Philistines fell along the way from Shaaraim to Gath and Ekron.
The children of Israel returned from pursuing the Philistines and plundered their camp.
David took the head of the Philistine and brought it to Jerusalem, but he put his armor in his tent.
When Saul saw David going out against the Philistine, he said to Abner, the commander of the army, "Abner, whose son is this youth?" Abner said, "As surely as you live, O king, I do not know."
The king said, "Inquire whose son this young man is."
As David returned from striking down the Philistine, Abner took him and brought him before Saul, with the head of the Philistine in his hand.
Saul said to him, "Whose son are you, young man?" David said, "I am the son of your servant Jesse the Bethlehemite."
After David had concluded his discourse to Saul, the soul of Jonathan was knit to the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul.
From that day forward Saul retained David in his service and would not permit him to return to his father's household.
Jonathan then concluded a covenant with David, because he loved him as himself.
Jonathan stripped off the robe he was wearing and gave it to David, together with his tunic, his sword, his bow, and his belt.

Wherever Saul dispatched him, David conducted himself with such sagacity that Saul elevated him to command over the men of war; this found favor in the eyes of all the people and in the eyes of Saul's servants as well.
When the troops returned from striking down the Philistine, the women emerged from every city of Israel to meet King Saul, celebrating with tambourines, songs of joy, and stringed instruments.
And as the women danced, they sang, "Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his tens of thousands."

Saul was exceedingly incensed, for this saying was grievous in his sight; he declared, "They have ascribed to David tens of thousands, but to me they have ascribed only thousands. What more is there for him but the kingdom?"
And from that day onward Saul regarded David with a jealous and hostile eye.

On the following day an evil spirit from God rushed upon Saul, and he prophesied in the midst of the house while David played the harp, as he did day by day; Saul, meanwhile, held a spear in his hand.
Saul hurled the spear, saying, "I will pin David to the wall," but David eluded him on two occasions.
Saul feared David, because the LORD was with David but had departed from Saul.
Therefore Saul removed David from his presence and appointed him commander of a thousand; and David went out and came in before the people.
David prospered in all his undertakings, for the LORD was with him.
When Saul perceived how exceedingly prosperous he was, he grew fearful of him.
Yet all Israel and Judah loved David, because he went out and came in before them.

Then Saul said to David, "Here is my elder daughter Merab; I will give her to you in marriage. Only prove yourself valiant on my behalf and fight the battles of the LORD." For Saul thought, 'I will not raise my hand against him; let the Philistines do that.'
David answered Saul, "Who am I, and what is my family—indeed, my father's clan—in Israel, that I should become the king's son-in-law?"
Yet when the time arrived to give Saul's daughter Merab to David, she was given in marriage to Adriel the Meholathite.
Now Saul's daughter Michal loved David; when this was reported to Saul, it pleased him,

for he thought, 'I will give her to him, that she may become a snare to him, and that the hand of the Philistines may be against him.' Therefore Saul said to David, "Today you shall become my son-in-law through one of the two."
Then Saul commanded his servants, "Speak to David privately and say, 'Look, the king delights in you, and all his servants love you; now therefore become his son-in-law.'"
So Saul's servants conveyed these words to David, and David asked, "Does it seem a trivial thing in your eyes to become the son-in-law of the king, when I am a poor man and lightly esteemed?"
The servants reported to Saul exactly what David had said.

Saul replied, "Tell David, 'The king desires no dowry except a hundred Philistine foreskins, to avenge himself upon his enemies.'" Now Saul was scheming to cause David's death by the hand of the Philistines.
When the servants reported these terms to David, it pleased him to become the king's son-in-law; and before the allotted time had elapsed,

David and his men went out and struck down two hundred Philistines. David brought their foreskins and presented them in full number to the king, so as to become the king's son-in-law; whereupon Saul gave him his daughter Michal as wife.
When Saul recognized that the LORD was with David, and that his daughter Michal loved David,
Saul grew still more afraid of David; and Saul was David's enemy continually.
Whenever the Philistine commanders went out to battle, David achieved greater success than all of Saul's servants, so that his name became highly esteemed.
Saul enjoined his son Jonathan, together with all his attendants, to bring about David’s death; nevertheless, Jonathan, Saul’s son, was deeply devoted to David.
Jonathan warned David, saying, “My father Saul is intent upon killing you; therefore, exercise vigilance at daybreak, remain in a secluded place, and conceal yourself.
I shall go forth and stand beside my father in the field where you are, and I shall speak concerning you to my father; then, having ascertained his disposition, I shall report it to you.”

Jonathan interceded favorably for David before Saul his father, saying, “Let not the king transgress against his servant David, for he has committed no offense against you, and his conduct has been exceedingly beneficial to you.

He hazarded his life, struck down the Philistine, and the LORD wrought a great deliverance for all Israel; you beheld it and rejoiced. Why, then, would you incur guilt by shedding innocent blood, putting David to death without justification?”
Saul heeded Jonathan’s entreaty and swore by the LORD, “As the LORD lives, he shall not be put to death.”
Jonathan then summoned David and recounted all these things to him; he brought David before Saul, and David resumed his former station in the king’s presence.
War erupted once more; David sallied forth, engaged the Philistines, and inflicted upon them a devastating defeat, so that they fled before him.
An evil spirit from the LORD seized Saul while he sat in his house, spear in hand, as David was playing the lyre.
Saul endeavored to transfix David against the wall with the spear, but David eluded him; the spear struck the wall, and David fled and escaped during the night.

Saul dispatched messengers to David’s house to keep watch over him and to kill him at daybreak; Michal, David’s wife, warned him, “If you do not contrive to save your life this night, tomorrow you shall be slain.”
Michal lowered David through the window, whereupon he departed, fled, and made good his escape.
Michal then took the teraphim, placed it in the bed, arranged a goat-hair bolster at its head, and covered it with a garment.
When Saul sent messengers to seize David, she replied, “He is ill.”
Saul then sent the messengers back to inspect David, with the command, “Bring him up to me in the bed, so that I may put him to death.”
The messengers entered and discovered the teraphim in the bed, the goat-hair bolster at its head.
Saul said to Michal, “Why have you deceived me in this manner, sending away my enemy so that he escaped?” Michal answered Saul, “He said to me, ‘Let me go, or I shall kill you.’”
David fled and made his escape, coming to Samuel at Ramah, where he recounted all that Saul had done to him; then the two of them went and took up residence at Naioth.
Saul was informed, “David is at Naioth in Ramah.”
Saul sent messengers to seize David, but when they beheld the assembly of prophets prophesying, with Samuel presiding over them, the Spirit of God came upon the messengers, and they too prophesied.
When this was reported to Saul, he dispatched a second contingent of messengers, who likewise prophesied; then he sent a third, and they too prophesied.
He himself then set out for Ramah and arrived at the great cistern in Secu, where he inquired, “Where are Samuel and David?” He was told, “They are at Naioth in Ramah.”
He proceeded to Naioth in Ramah; there the Spirit of God came upon him as well, and he continued prophesying as he went until he reached Naioth in Ramah.
He even stripped off his garments and prophesied before Samuel, lying naked throughout that day and night. Hence the proverb, “Is Saul also among the prophets?”
David fled from Naioth in Ramah and came before Jonathan, saying, "What have I done? What is my iniquity, and what is my sin before your father, that he seeks my life?"

Jonathan said to him, "Far be it! You shall not die. Behold, my father does nothing, whether great or small, without disclosing it to me. Why then would my father conceal this matter from me? It is not so."

Yet David swore again, saying, "Your father knows well that I have found favor in your eyes, and he has said, 'Let Jonathan not learn of this, lest he be grieved.' But truly, as the LORD lives and as your soul lives, there is but a step between me and death."
Jonathan said to David, "Whatever your soul desires, I will do for you."
David said to Jonathan, "Behold, tomorrow is the new moon, and I am obliged to sit with the king at table. But let me go, that I may hide in the field until the third evening.
If your father inquires after me, then say, 'David earnestly asked leave of me to run to Bethlehem, his city, for there is a yearly sacrifice there for all the clan.'
If he says, 'Good,' it shall be well with your servant; but if he is angry, know that evil is determined by him.

Therefore deal kindly with your servant, for you have brought your servant into a covenant of the LORD with you. But if there is iniquity in me, kill me yourself; for why should you bring me to your father?"
Jonathan said, "Far be it from you! If I knew that harm was determined by my father against you, would I not tell you?"
David said to Jonathan, "Who will tell me if your father answers you harshly?"
Jonathan said to David, "Come, let us go out into the field." So they both went out into the field.

Jonathan said to David, "As the LORD, the God of Israel, is witness, when I have sounded my father about this time tomorrow, or the third day, if it is well with David, shall I not then send to you and disclose it to you?

But if it pleases my father to do you harm, may the LORD do so to Jonathan and more also, if I do not disclose it to you and send you away, that you may go in safety. May the LORD be with you, as He has been with my father.
If I am still alive, show me the steadfast love of the LORD, that I may not die;
and do not cut off your steadfast love from my house forever, when the LORD cuts off every one of the enemies of David from the face of the earth."
So Jonathan made a covenant with the house of David, saying, "May the LORD take vengeance on David's enemies."
And Jonathan made David swear again by his love for him, for he loved him as he loved his own soul.
Jonathan said to him, "Tomorrow is the new moon, and you will be missed, because your seat will be empty.
On the third day go down quickly to the place where you hid yourself when the matter was in hand, and remain beside the stone Ezel.
I will shoot three arrows to the side of it, as though I shot at a mark.

And behold, I will send the boy, saying, 'Go, find the arrows.' If I say to the boy, 'Look, the arrows are on this side of you; take them,' then you are to come, for, as the LORD lives, it is safe for you and there is no danger.
But if I say to the youth, 'Look, the arrows are beyond you,' then go, for the LORD has sent you away.
And as for the matter of which you and I have spoken, behold, the LORD is between you and me forever."
So David hid himself in the field. And when the new moon came, the king sat down to eat.
The king sat on his seat, as at other times, on the seat by the wall. Jonathan sat opposite, and Abner sat by Saul's side, but David's place was empty.
Yet Saul said nothing that day, for he thought, "Something has happened to him; he is not clean, surely he is not clean."
But the next day, the second day of the month, David's place was empty. And Saul said to Jonathan his son, "Why has not the son of Jesse come to the meal, either yesterday or today?"
Jonathan answered Saul, "David earnestly asked leave of me to go to Bethlehem.

He said, 'Let me go, for our clan holds a sacrifice in the city, and my brother has commanded me to be there. So now, if I have found favor in your eyes, let me get away and see my brothers.' For this reason he has not come to the king's table."

Then Saul's anger was kindled against Jonathan, and he said to him, "You son of a perverse, rebellious woman! Do I not know that you have chosen the son of Jesse to your own shame, and to the shame of your mother?
For as long as the son of Jesse lives on the earth, neither you nor your kingdom shall be established. Therefore send and bring him to me, for he shall surely die."
Jonathan answered Saul his father, "Why should he be put to death? What has he done?"
But Saul hurled his spear at him to strike him. So Jonathan knew that his father was determined to put David to death.
And Jonathan rose from the table in fierce anger and ate no food the second day of the month, for he was grieved for David, because his father had disgraced him.
In the morning Jonathan went out into the field to the appointment with David, and with him a little boy.
He said to his boy, "Run and find the arrows that I shoot." As the boy ran, he shot an arrow beyond him.
And when the boy came to the place of the arrow that Jonathan had shot, Jonathan called after the boy and said, "Is not the arrow beyond you?"
Jonathan called after the boy, "Hurry! Be quick! Do not stay!" So Jonathan's boy gathered up the arrows and came to his master.
But the boy knew nothing. Only Jonathan and David knew the matter.
Jonathan gave his weapons to his boy and said to him, "Go, carry them to the city."

And as soon as the boy had gone, David rose from beside the stone Ezel and fell on his face to the ground and bowed three times. And they kissed one another and wept with one another, David weeping the most.

Then Jonathan said to David, "Go in peace, because we have sworn both of us in the name of the LORD, saying, 'The LORD shall be between me and you, and between my offspring and your offspring, forever.'" And he rose and departed, and Jonathan went into the city.
David came to Nob, to Ahimelech the priest. Ahimelech came trembling to meet David and said to him, "Why are you alone, with no one accompanying you?"

David said to Ahimelech the priest, "The king has charged me with a confidential matter and said to me, 'Let no one know anything of the matter about which I am sending you, or of the command I have given you.' As for the young men, I have directed them to such-and-such a place.
Now what do you have on hand? Give me five loaves of bread, or whatever is available."
The priest answered David, "There is no ordinary bread at hand, but there is consecrated bread—provided the young men have abstained from women."

David answered the priest, "Women have indeed been kept from us, as is customary when I set out. The vessels of the young men are holy even on an ordinary journey, and how much more today will they be sanctified."

So the priest gave him the consecrated bread, for no bread was there except the bread of the Presence, which had been removed from before the LORD, to be replaced by hot bread on the day it was taken away.
Now one of Saul's servants was there that day, detained before the LORD; his name was Doeg the Edomite, the chief of Saul's herdsmen.
David said to Ahimelech, "Do you have a spear or sword here at hand? I brought neither my sword nor my weapons with me, for the king's business was urgent."

The priest said, "Here is the sword of Goliath the Philistine, whom you struck down in the Valley of Elah; it is wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod. If you wish to take it, take it, for there is no other here." David said, "There is none like it; give it to me."
