On that day David arose and fled from Saul, and he came to Achish, king of Gath.
The servants of Achish said to him, "Is this not David, the king of the land? Did they not sing of him in the dances, saying, 'Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands'?"
David took these words to heart and was greatly afraid of Achish, king of Gath.
He altered his conduct before them, feigned insanity in their presence, scrawled on the doors of the gate, and let his spittle run down his beard.
Achish said to his servants, "Behold, you see a man who is mad. Why have you brought him to me?
Do I lack madmen, that you have brought this fellow to act the madman before me? Shall this man come into my house?"
David departed from that place and escaped to the cave of Adullam; when his brothers and all his father’s household heard of it, they went down to him there.
Every man in distress, every man who was indebted, and every man who was discontented gathered to him, and he became their commander; about four hundred men were with him.
From there David went to Mizpeh of Moab and said to the king of Moab, “Please let my father and mother come out to you until I know what God will do for me.”
So he left them with the king of Moab, and they remained with him all the days David was in the stronghold.
Then the prophet Gad said to David, “Do not remain in the stronghold; depart and go into the land of Judah.” So David departed and came to the forest of Hereth.

Saul heard that David and the men with him had been discovered. Now Saul was sitting in Gibeah under the tamarisk tree on the hill, with his spear in his hand, and all his servants were standing around him.

Saul said to his servants standing around him, “Hear now, Benjamites! Will the son of Jesse give all of you fields and vineyards? Will he make all of you commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds?

For all of you have conspired against me, and no one informs me when my son makes a covenant with the son of Jesse. None of you is concerned about me or informs me that my son has stirred up my servant against me to lie in wait, as at this day.”
Then Doeg the Edomite, who was standing by Saul’s servants, answered, “I saw the son of Jesse come to Ahimelech son of Ahitub at Nob.
He inquired of the the LORD for him, gave him provisions, and gave him the sword of Goliath the Philistine.”
So the king sent to summon Ahimelech the priest, son of Ahitub, and all his father’s household, the priests in Nob; they all came to the king.
Saul said, “Listen now, son of Ahitub.” He answered, “Here I am, my lord.”

Saul said to him, “Why have you conspired against me, you and the son of Jesse, in that you gave him bread and a sword, and inquired of God for him, so that he has risen against me to lie in wait, as at this day?”
Ahimelech answered the king, “Who among all your servants is as faithful as David, the king’s son-in-law, captain of your guard, and highly esteemed in your household?

Have I today begun to inquire of God for him? May that never be! Do not charge your servant, or any of my father’s household, with anything; for your servant knew nothing of all this, small or great.”
The king said, “You shall surely die, Ahimelech, you and all your father’s house.”

The king said to the guards standing around him, “Turn and kill the priests of the the LORD, because they too have sided with David, and because they knew he was fleeing and did not disclose it to me.” But the king’s servants were unwilling to raise their hands to strike the priests of the the LORD.
The king said to Doeg, “You turn and strike the priests.” Doeg the Edomite turned and struck the priests, and that day he killed eighty-five men who wore the linen ephod.
He also struck Nob, the city of the priests, with the edge of the sword—men and women, children and infants, oxen, donkeys, and sheep—with the edge of the sword.
But one son of Ahimelech son of Ahitub, named Abiathar, escaped and fled after David.
Abiathar told David that Saul had killed the priests of the the LORD.
David said to Abiathar, “I knew that day, when Doeg the Edomite was there, that he would surely tell Saul. I have brought about the deaths of everyone in your father’s household.
Stay with me; do not be afraid, for the one who seeks your life seeks mine as well; you will be safe with me.”
David was informed: “The Philistines are fighting against Keilah and plundering the threshing floors.”
David inquired of the LORD, “Shall I go and attack these Philistines?” The LORD answered, “Go and attack the Philistines and deliver Keilah.”
David’s men said to him, “We are already afraid here in Judah; how much more, then, if we go to Keilah to face the Philistine battle lines?”
David inquired of the LORD again. The LORD answered him, “Arise, go down to Keilah, for I will deliver the Philistines into your power.”
So David and his men went to Keilah, fought the Philistines, drove off their livestock, and struck them with a great slaughter; thus David saved the inhabitants of Keilah.
When Abiathar son of Ahimelech fled to David at Keilah, he came down with an ephod in his hand.
Saul was told that David had come to Keilah, and Saul said, “God has delivered him into my power, for he has shut himself in by entering a town with gates and bars.”
Saul mobilized all the people for war, to go down to Keilah and besiege David and his men.
David perceived that Saul was contriving evil against him, and he said to Abiathar the priest, “Bring the ephod here.”
David said, “O the LORD, God of Israel, Your servant has certainly heard that Saul seeks to come to Keilah to destroy the city on my account.”
“Will the citizens of Keilah surrender me to him? Will Saul come down, as Your servant has heard? O the LORD, God of Israel, please tell Your servant.” The LORD said, “He will come down.”
David asked, “Will the citizens of Keilah surrender me and my men to Saul?” The LORD said, “They will surrender you.”
Then David and his men—about six hundred—rose and departed from Keilah, wandering wherever they could. When Saul was told that David had escaped from Keilah, he desisted from marching forth.
David stayed in the wilderness, in the strongholds, and remained in the hill country in the wilderness of Ziph. Saul sought him every day, but God did not deliver him to Saul.
David was in the wilderness of Ziph at Horesh, and he saw that Saul had come out to seek his life.
Jonathan, Saul’s son, came to David at Horesh and encouraged him in God.
He said to him, “Do not be afraid, for my father Saul will not capture you. You will be king over Israel, and I will be second to you; even my father Saul knows this.”
The two of them made a covenant before the LORD. David remained at Horesh, while Jonathan went home.
The Ziphites went up to Saul at Gibeah and said, “Is David not hiding among us in the strongholds at Horesh, on the hill of Hachilah, south of Jeshimon?
Now, O king, come down whenever you wish; our part is to surrender him to the king.”
Saul said, “May you be blessed by the LORD, for you have had compassion on me.”
“Go, please, and prepare further, and find out exactly where he is and who has seen him there, for I am told he is very shrewd.
See and know all the hiding places where he hides, and return to me with reliable information; then I will go with you. If he is in the land, I will search him out among all the thousands of Judah.”
They set out and went to Ziph ahead of Saul. David and his men were in the wilderness of Maon, in the Arabah, south of Jeshimon.
Saul and his men went to seek David. David was informed, and he went down to the rock and stayed in the wilderness of Maon. When Saul heard of it, he pursued David in the wilderness of Maon.
Saul went along one side of the mountain, and David and his men along the other. David hurried to get away from Saul, while Saul and his men were encircling David and his men in order to seize them.
A messenger came to Saul, saying, “Hurry and come, for the Philistines have raided the land.”
Saul turned back from pursuing David and went to meet the Philistines. Therefore that place was called the Rock of Escape.
David went up from there and lived in the strongholds of En-gedi.
Upon Saul’s return from pursuing the Philistines, he was informed that David was in the wilderness of En Gedi.
Saul therefore selected three thousand chosen men from all Israel and went to seek David and his men upon the Rocks of the Wild Goats.
He came to the sheepfolds beside the road, where there was a cave; Saul entered it to relieve himself, while David and his men were sitting in the innermost recesses of the cave.

David’s men said to him, “Behold, this is the day of which the LORD spoke to you: ‘Behold, I am giving your enemy into your hand, and you shall do to him whatever seems good to you.’” Then David arose and stealthily cut off the corner of Saul’s robe.
Afterward David’s conscience smote him because he had cut off the corner of Saul’s robe.
He said to his men, “The LORD forbid that I should do such a thing to my lord, the LORD’s anointed, by stretching out my hand against him; for he is the LORD’s anointed.”
So David restrained his men with these words and did not permit them to rise against Saul. Then Saul rose from the cave and went on his way.
Afterward David arose, went out of the cave, and called after Saul, “My lord the king!” When Saul looked behind him, David bowed with his face to the ground and prostrated himself.
David said to Saul, “Why do you give credence to the words of men who say, ‘David seeks your harm’?

Behold, this day your eyes have seen how the LORD gave you into my hand today in the cave, and some urged me to kill you, but I spared you; for I said, ‘I will not stretch out my hand against my lord, for he is the LORD’s anointed.’

See, my father, see the corner of your robe in my hand; for in that I cut off the corner of your robe and did not kill you, know and see that there is no evil or rebellion in my hand, and I have not sinned against you, though you hunt my life to take it.”
“May the LORD judge between me and you, and may the LORD avenge me upon you; but my hand shall not be against you.
As the ancient proverb declares, ‘Wickedness proceeds from the wicked’; but my hand shall not be against you.
After whom has the king of Israel come out? After whom do you pursue? After a dead dog? After a single flea?
Therefore may the LORD be judge and adjudicate between me and you, and may He see and contend for my cause and deliver me out of your hand.”
When David had finished speaking these words to Saul, Saul said, “Is this your voice, my son David?” And Saul lifted up his voice and wept.
“You are more righteous than I, for you have repaid me with good, whereas I have repaid you with evil.
You have declared this day how well you have dealt with me, in that when the LORD gave me into your hand, you did not kill me.”
“For if a man finds his enemy, will he let him go away unharmed? So may the LORD reward you with good for what you have done to me this day.
Now I know that you shall surely be king, and that the kingdom of Israel shall be established in your hand.
Swear to me therefore by the LORD that you will not cut off my offspring after me and that you will not destroy my name from my father’s house.”
David swore to Saul. Then Saul went to his home, but David and his men went up to the stronghold.
When Samuel died, all Israel assembled, mourned him, and interred him at his home in Ramah; thereupon David arose and descended into the wilderness of Paran.
There was a man in Maon whose enterprise was in Carmel, and he was surpassingly affluent, possessing three thousand sheep and a thousand goats; he was shearing his sheep in Carmel.
The man's name was Nabal, and his wife's name was Abigail; the woman was sagacious and comely, whereas the man was harsh and depraved in his dealings.
While David was in the wilderness, he learned that Nabal was shearing his sheep.
David therefore sent ten young men and said to them, "Go up to Carmel, present yourselves before Nabal, and greet him in my name.
Thus you shall say: 'Peace be to you, to your house, and to all that is yours.'
I have heard that you have shearers; now your shepherds have been with us, and we neither insulted them nor missed anything of theirs throughout their sojourn in Carmel.

Ask your young men, and they will tell you. Therefore let these young men find favor in your eyes, for we have come on a festive day; please bestow whatever you can afford upon your servants and upon your son David."
David's men went, delivered all these words to Nabal in David's name, and waited.
Nabal answered David's servants, "Who is David, and who is the son of Jesse? There are many servants nowadays who are breaking away from their masters.
Shall I take my bread, my water, and my meat, which I have prepared for my shearers, and give it to men whom I do not know?"
So David's men turned back and reported to him every one of these words.
David said to his men, "Gird on your swords!" So David girded on his own sword, and about four hundred men followed David, while two hundred remained with the baggage.
But one of the young men told Abigail, Nabal's wife, "David sent messengers from the wilderness to greet our master, but he reviled them.
Yet the men were very good to us; we were not insulted, and we missed nothing all the days we went about with them in the fields.
They were a wall to us both by day and by night throughout the time we were with them tending the sheep.
Now consider what you should do, for calamity is irrevocably decreed against our master and all his household; he is such a scoundrel that no one can speak to him."

Then Abigail hurried and took two hundred loaves, two skins of wine, five sheep already prepared, five seahs of roasted grain, a hundred clusters of raisins, and two hundred cakes of figs, and loaded them on donkeys.
She said to her servants, "Go on ahead of me; I am coming after you." But she did not tell her husband Nabal.
As she was riding on the donkey and descending the mountain under cover, behold, David and his men were coming down toward her, and she met them.
Now David had said, "Surely in vain I guarded all that belongs to this man in the wilderness, so that nothing of his was missing; yet he has repaid me evil for good.
May God do so to the enemies of David, and more also, if by morning I leave so much as one male of all who belong to him."
When Abigail saw David, she hurried, dismounted from the donkey, fell before David with her face to the ground, and bowed to the ground.
She fell at his feet and said, "On me, my lord, be the guilt; please let your maidservant speak in your ears and hear the words of your maidservant.
Let not my lord regard this worthless man, Nabal, for as his name is, so is he: Nabal is his name, and folly is with him; but I, your maidservant, did not see the young men whom you sent.

Now, my lord, as the LORD lives, and as your soul lives, since the LORD has restrained you from bloodguilt and from avenging yourself with your own hand, now let your enemies and those who seek harm for my lord be as Nabal.
And now let this gift, which your maidservant has brought to my lord, be given to the young men who follow my lord.

Please forgive the transgression of your maidservant, for the LORD will certainly make for my lord an enduring dynasty, because my lord fights the battles of the LORD, and evil will not be found in you throughout your days.

If a man rises to pursue you and to seek your life, the life of my lord will be bound in the bundle of life with the LORD your God, while the lives of your enemies He will sling out as from the pouch of a sling.
And when the LORD has done for my lord according to all the good that He has spoken concerning you and has appointed you ruler over Israel,

this shall not be a source of pangs to you or a snare to your conscience, namely, that my lord has shed blood without cause or that my lord has avenged himself; and when the LORD has dealt well with my lord, then remember your maidservant."
David said to Abigail, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who sent you this day to meet me.
Blessed be your discernment, and blessed be you, who this day kept me from bloodshed and from avenging myself.
Nevertheless, as the LORD, the God of Israel, lives, who restrained me from harming you, if you had not hurried to meet me, surely by morning not one male would have been left to Nabal."
Then David received from her hand what she had brought him, and he said to her, "Go up to your house in peace; see, I have heard your voice and have granted your request."

Abigail came to Nabal, and behold, he was holding a feast in his house, like the feast of a king; Nabal's heart was merry, and he was very drunk, so she told him nothing, small or great, until the morning light.
In the morning, when the wine had gone out of Nabal, his wife told him these things, and his heart died within him, and he became as a stone.
About ten days later, the LORD struck Nabal, and he died.

When David heard that Nabal was dead, he said, "Blessed be the LORD, who has pleaded the cause of my reproach from the hand of Nabal, and has kept His servant from evil; the LORD has returned the wickedness of Nabal upon his own head." Then David sent and spoke to Abigail, to take her as his wife.
When David's servants came to Abigail at Carmel, they spoke to her, saying, "David has sent us to you to take you as his wife."
She arose, bowed with her face to the ground, and said, "Behold, your maidservant is here to be a servant, to wash the feet of my lord's servants."
Then Abigail hurried and arose, rode on a donkey, with her five maidservants following her, and she went after David and became his wife.
David had also taken Ahinoam of Jezreel, and both of them became his wives.
Saul had given Michal, his daughter and David's wife, to Palti the son of Laish, who was from Gallim.
The Ziphites repaired to Saul at Gibeah, reporting, “Is not David concealed upon the height of Hakilah, opposite the wasteland?”
Saul arose, and with him three thousand select men of Israel, and descended into the wilderness of Ziph to seek David.
Saul encamped beside the road upon the hill of Hakilah, facing the wilderness, while David remained in the wilderness and perceived that Saul had come in pursuit of him there.
David dispatched scouts and ascertained with certainty that Saul had indeed arrived.

David arose and advanced to the place where Saul was encamped; he observed the site where Saul and Abner son of Ner, commander of his army, were reclining—Saul lying within the encampment's circle, with the troops bivouacked around him.
David addressed Ahimelech the Hittite and Abishai son of Zeruiah, Joab's brother, saying, “Who will descend with me into Saul's camp?” Abishai answered, “I will accompany you.”
That night David and Abishai penetrated the people's lines and found Saul sleeping within the encampment, his spear thrust into the ground at his head, while Abner and the troops lay round about him.
Abishai said to David, “Today God has surrendered your adversary into your grasp; permit me, I pray, to transfix him to the earth with one thrust of the spear, and I shall not need to strike again.”
David replied, “Do not annihilate him; for who may lay hand upon the LORD's anointed and remain innocent?”
He added, “As the LORD lives, either the LORD will smite him, or his appointed day will arrive and he will die, or he will descend into battle and be consumed.”
“Far be it from me, by the LORD, to stretch forth my hand against the LORD's anointed; but now take the spear beside his head and the water jar, and let us depart.”
David seized the spear and the water jar from beside Saul's head, and they withdrew; no one saw, knew, or awoke, for all were asleep, since a profound slumber from the LORD had fallen upon them.
David crossed to the opposite side and took his stand upon the summit of the hill at a distance, with a great interval between them.
David called out to the people and to Abner son of Ner, saying, “Will you not answer, Abner?” Abner answered, “Who are you that you call to the king?”

David said to Abner, “Are you not a man? And who is like you in Israel? Why then have you not guarded your lord the king? For one of the people came to destroy your lord the king. This thing that you have done is not good.”
“As the LORD lives, you are men doomed to die, because you have not guarded your lord, the LORD's anointed. And now behold the king's spear and the water jar that was at his head.”
Saul recognized David's voice and said, “Is this your voice, my son David?” David answered, “It is my voice, my lord the king.”
“Why does my lord pursue his servant? For what have I done, and what evil is in my hand?

Now therefore, please, my lord the king, hear the words of his servant. If the LORD has incited you against me, let Him accept an offering; but if it be the sons of men, cursed are they before the LORD, for they have driven me out this day from sharing in the inheritance of the LORD, saying, ‘Go, serve other gods.’
Now therefore, let not my blood fall to the earth away from the presence of the LORD; for the king of Israel has come out to seek a flea, as one hunts a partridge in the mountains.”
Saul said, “I have sinned; return, my son David, for I will no more do you harm, because my life was precious in your eyes this day. Behold, I have played the fool and erred exceedingly.”
David answered, “Here is the king's spear; let one of the young men come over and take it.”
“The LORD will render to every man his righteousness and his faithfulness; for the LORD delivered you into my hand today, but I would not put forth my hand against the LORD's anointed.”
“And behold, as your life was precious this day in my eyes, so may my life be precious in the eyes of the LORD, and may He deliver me out of all tribulation.”
Saul said to David, “Blessed are you, my son David; you will surely accomplish great things and indeed prevail.” Then David went his way, and Saul returned to his place.

David said within himself, "Sooner or later I shall be consumed by Saul's hand; no prospect is more advantageous to me than to escape into the land of the Philistines. Then Saul will cease searching for me throughout all the territory of Israel, and I shall slip from his grasp."
Accordingly, David arose and crossed over with the six hundred men who accompanied him to Achish son of Maoch, king of Gath.
David and his men settled in Gath with Achish, each with his household, and David with his two wives—Ahinoam the Jezreelite and Abigail, Nabal's widow from Carmel.
When Saul was informed that David had fled to Gath, he ceased searching for him.

Then David said to Achish, "If I have found favor in your sight, let them assign me a residence in one of the country towns, that I may dwell there. Why should your servant reside in the royal city with you?"
So on that day Achish gave him Ziklag; therefore Ziklag has belonged to the kings of Judah to this day.
The number of days David lived in the Philistine countryside was a year and four months.
Now David and his men went up and raided the Geshurites, the Girzites, and the Amalekites—for from ancient times these peoples had inhabited the land extending to Shur and Egypt.
Whenever David attacked a region, he left neither man nor woman alive, but took sheep, cattle, donkeys, camels, and garments; then he returned to Achish.
When Achish asked, "Where did you raid today?" David replied, "Against the Negev of Judah," or "Against the Negev of the Jerahmeelites," or "Against the Negev of the Kenites."

David left no man or woman alive to be brought to Gath, for he thought, "They might inform against us, saying, 'This is what David did.'" And such was his custom throughout all the time he lived in the Philistine territory.
So Achish trusted David, thinking, "He has made himself utterly abhorrent to his people Israel; therefore he shall be my servant forever."

Now it came to pass in those days that the Philistines mustered their hosts for war against Israel; and Achish said to David, “You must understand assuredly that you and your men shall march out with me in the campaign.”
David replied, “Therefore you know what your servant will do.” Achish then said to David, “Therefore I will appoint you the perpetual guardian of my person.”
Now Samuel had died, and all Israel had mourned him and buried him in Ramah, his own city; and Saul had expelled from the land the mediums and the spiritists.
The Philistines assembled and advanced, encamping at Shunem; Saul likewise gathered all Israel, and they encamped at Gilboa.
When Saul beheld the Philistine encampment, he was seized with fear, and his heart trembled exceedingly.
When Saul consulted the LORD, the LORD gave him no answer—neither by dreams, nor by the Urim, nor by prophets.
Saul then said to his servants, “Seek for me a woman who is a medium, that I may go to her and inquire through her.” His servants replied, “Behold, there is such a woman at En-dor.”
Saul disguised himself, putting on other garments, and set out with two men; they came to the woman by night. He said, “Please perform divination for me, and bring up for me whomever I name to you.”
The woman said to him, “You surely know what Saul has done—how he has extirpated mediums and spiritists from the land. Why then do you imperil my life to bring about my death?”
Saul swore to her by the LORD, saying, “As the LORD lives, no guilt shall be imputed to you in this matter.”
The woman asked, “Whom shall I bring up for you?” He answered, “Bring up Samuel for me.”
When the woman saw Samuel, she cried out with a loud voice and said to Saul, “Why have you deceived me? You are Saul!”
The king said to her, “Do not be afraid; but tell me what you see.” The woman said to Saul, “I see a divine being ascending from the earth.”

He asked her, “What is his appearance?” She replied, “An old man is coming up, and he is wrapped in a robe.” Saul then recognized that it was Samuel; he bowed with his face to the ground and prostrated himself.

Samuel said to Saul, “Why have you disturbed me by bringing me up?” Saul answered, “I am in great distress: the Philistines are waging war against me, God has withdrawn from me, and He no longer answers me—neither through prophets nor through dreams. Therefore I have summoned you, that you may disclose to me what I ought to do.”
Samuel said, “Why do you inquire of me, seeing that the LORD has departed from you and has become your adversary?
The LORD has done what He foretold through me: the LORD has torn the kingdom from your hand and given it to your neighbor—to David.
Because you did not obey the LORD and did not execute His fierce wrath against Amalek, the LORD has brought this upon you today.

Moreover, the LORD will deliver Israel, together with you, into the hand of the Philistines; tomorrow you and your sons shall be with me. Indeed, the LORD will give the camp of Israel into the hand of the Philistines.”
Saul immediately fell full length to the ground, overcome with great fear at Samuel’s words; moreover, no strength remained in him, for he had eaten no bread all that day and all that night.

The woman came to Saul and, seeing that he was utterly terrified, said to him, “Behold, your maidservant has hearkened to your voice; I have risked my life and have obeyed the words that you spoke to me.
Now, therefore, please let your maidservant set a morsel of bread before you, that you may eat and recover your strength for the journey.”
He refused, saying, “I will not eat.” Yet his servants, together with the woman, pressed him; he yielded to their voice, rose from the ground, and sat upon the bed.
The woman had a fattened calf in the house; she quickly slaughtered it, took flour, kneaded it, and baked unleavened bread from it.
She brought it before Saul and his servants, and they ate. Then they arose and departed that night.
The Philistines mustered all their forces at Aphek, and Israel encamped by the spring in Jezreel.
As the Philistine rulers advanced with their companies of hundreds and thousands, David and his men marched in the rear with Achish.

The Philistine commanders asked, “What are these Hebrews doing here?” Achish answered, “Is this not David, servant of Saul king of Israel? He has been with me for a year or two, and from the day of his defection until now I have found no fault in him.”

But the Philistine commanders were incensed with Achish and said, “Send the man back! Let him return to the place you assigned him. He must not descend with us into battle, lest he become an adversary to us in the fighting; for how else might he regain his master’s favor, if not by presenting the heads of our men?
Is this not the David of whom they sing in their dances, ‘Saul has slain his thousands, and David his tens of thousands’?”

So Achish summoned David and said to him, “As the LORD lives, you are upright, and your coming and going with me in the camp is good in my sight, because I have found no fault in you from the day you came to me until now. But you are not acceptable to the rulers.
Now then, turn back and go in peace, so that you do not displease the Philistine rulers.”
“But what have I done?” David asked. “What have you found in your servant from the day I came to you until now, that I should not go and fight against the enemies of my lord the king?”
Achish replied, “I know that you are pleasing to me, like an angel of God. But the Philistine commanders have said, ‘He must not go up with us into battle.’
So get up early in the morning, along with your master’s servants who came with you, and leave at daybreak.”
So David and his men rose early in the morning to return to the land of the Philistines, and the Philistines went up to Jezreel.
On the third day, when David and his men arrived at Ziklag, the Amalekites had already raided the Negev and Ziklag, assaulting the town and burning it with fire.
They had carried off the women who were in it, from the least to the greatest; they had killed no one, but had driven them away and gone on their own way.
When David and his men came to the city and found it burned with fire, their wives, sons, and daughters having been taken captive,
David and the people with him raised their voices in lamentation until their grief had exhausted their strength.
David’s two wives, Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail, the widow of Nabal of Carmel, had been taken captive.
David was sorely distressed, for the people spoke of stoning him, each man being bitter of soul over his sons and daughters; yet David fortified himself in the LORD his God.
David said to Abiathar the priest, the son of Ahimelech, “Please bring me the ephod.” So Abiathar brought the ephod to David.
Then David inquired of the LORD, saying, “Shall I pursue this raiding party? Shall I overtake them?” He answered him, “Pursue, for you will surely overtake them and rescue them.”
So David went, he and his six hundred men, and they came to the Brook of Besor, where those left behind remained.
Two hundred men stayed behind because they were too exhausted to cross the brook; David and the four hundred men continued in pursuit.
They found an Egyptian in the field and brought him to David; they gave him water to drink and bread to eat.
They also gave him a piece of fig cake and two clusters of raisins. He ate, and his vigor returned to him, for he had not eaten bread or drunk water for three days and three nights.
David said to him, “To whom do you belong, and where are you from?” The man replied, “I am an Egyptian, the servant of an Amalekite; my master abandoned me three days ago because I became ill.
We raided the Negev of the Cherethites, the territory of Judah, and the Negev of Caleb, and we burned Ziklag with fire.”

David said to him, “Will you bring me down to this raiding party?” He replied, “Swear to me by God that you will not kill me or hand me over to my master, and I will bring you down to this raiding party.”

So he brought him down, and there they were, dispersed across the countryside, eating, drinking, and reveling because of all the great plunder they had taken from the land of the Philistines and from the land of Judah.
David struck them down from twilight until the evening of the next day; not one of them escaped, except four hundred young men who fled on camels.
David recovered everything the Amalekites had taken, and he rescued his two wives.
Nothing was missing, from the least to the greatest, sons and daughters, plunder and everything they had taken; David brought back all of it.
David took all the flocks and herds, and his men drove them ahead of the other livestock, saying, “This is David’s plunder.”

When David came to the two hundred men who had been too exhausted to follow him and had been left at the Brook of Besor, they came out to meet him and the people with him. David approached them and greeted them.

Then all the wicked and worthless men among those who had gone with David said, “Because they did not go with us, we will not share with them the plunder we recovered, except that each man may take his wife and children and lead them away.”
David replied, “My brothers, you shall not do so with what the LORD has given us, for He has preserved us and delivered into our hand the raiding party that came against us.
Who will listen to you in this matter? For as is the share of the one who goes down to the battle, so shall be the share of the one who stays with the baggage; they shall share alike.”
And so it has been from that day forward; David made this a statute and an ordinance for Israel to this very day.
When David came to Ziklag, he sent some of the plunder to the elders of Judah, his friends, saying, “Here is a gift for you from the plunder of the enemies of the LORD.”
He sent it to those in Bethel, in Ramoth of the Negev, and in Jattir;
to those in Aroer, in Siphmoth, and in Eshtemoa;
to those in Racal, in the cities of the Jerahmeelites, and in the cities of the Kenites;
to those in Hormah, in Bor-ashan, and in Athach;
and to those in Hebron, and to all the places where David and his men had roamed.
When the Philistines waged war against Israel, the Israelite host fled before them and fell slain upon Mount Gilboa.
The Philistines pressed hard after Saul and his sons, striking down Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua.
The battle pressed crushingly upon Saul; the archers found him, and he was grievously wounded.

Saul said to his armor-bearer, "Draw your sword and pierce me with it, lest these uncircumcised men come and pierce me and abuse me." But his armor-bearer would not, for he was terrified; so Saul took the sword and fell upon it.
When the armor-bearer saw that Saul was dead, he likewise fell upon his sword and died with him.
Thus Saul died, together with his three sons, his armor-bearer, and all his men, on that same day.

When the Israelites across the valley and beyond the Jordan saw that their countrymen had fled and that Saul and his sons were dead, they abandoned their cities and fled; the Philistines came and occupied them.
On the following day the Philistines came to strip the slain, and they found Saul and his three sons fallen on Mount Gilboa.
They cut off his head, stripped his armor, and sent messengers throughout the Philistine country to proclaim the tidings in the temples of their idols and among the people.
They placed his armor in the temple of Ashtaroth and fastened his body to the wall of Beth-shan.
When the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead heard what the Philistines had done to Saul,
every valiant man arose and marched through the night, took the bodies of Saul and his sons from the wall of Beth-shan, brought them to Jabesh, and burned them there.
Then they took their bones and buried them beneath the tamarisk at Jabesh, and they fasted seven days.
After Saul's death, David returned from striking down the Amalekites and remained in Ziklag for two days.
On the third day, a man came from Saul's camp with his garments torn and dust upon his head; when he reached David, he fell to the ground and prostrated himself.
David asked him, "Where have you come from?" He said, "I have escaped from the camp of Israel."
David said to him, "How did the matter turn out? Pray tell me." He answered, "The troops fled from the battle; many have fallen and perished, and Saul and his son Jonathan are dead as well."
David said to the young man who brought the report, "How do you know that Saul and his son Jonathan are dead?"
The young man replied, "I happened to be on Mount Gilboa, and there was Saul, leaning upon his spear, while the chariots and horsemen pressed hard after him.
When he turned and saw me, he called to me; I said, 'Here I am.'
He asked, 'Who are you?' and I answered, 'I am an Amalekite.'
He said to me, 'Stand over me and put me to death, for agony has seized me, though life still lingers within me.'
So I stood over him and slew him, for I knew he could not survive his fall; I took the crown from his head and the bracelet from his arm, and I have brought them to my lord."
Then David seized his garments and tore them, as did all the men with him.
They mourned, wept, and fasted until evening—for Saul, for Jonathan his son, for the people of the LORD, and for the house of Israel—because they had fallen by the sword.
David said to the young man who had brought him the tidings, "Where are you from?" He answered, "I am the son of an alien, an Amalekite."
David said to him, "How were you not afraid to stretch forth your hand to destroy the the LORD's Anointed?"
David called one of the young men and said, "Draw near and strike him down." So he struck him, and he died.
David said to him, "Your blood be upon your head, for your mouth has testified against you, saying, 'I have slain the the LORD's Anointed.'"
David chanted this lamentation over Saul and over his son Jonathan.
He also commanded that the sons of Judah be taught the use of the bow, noting that it is written in the Book of Jashar.
"The glory of Israel lies slain upon your high places! How the mighty have fallen!
Tell it not in Gath, proclaim it not in the streets of Ashkelon, lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice, lest the daughters of the uncircumcised exult.
"You mountains of Gilboa, let there be no dew or rain upon you, nor fields of offerings, for there the shield of the mighty was defiled, the shield of Saul, unanointed with oil.
From the blood of the slain, from the fat of the mighty, the bow of Jonathan did not turn back, and the sword of Saul did not return empty.
"Saul and Jonathan, beloved and pleasant in their lives, in death were not divided; swifter than eagles, stronger than lions.
Daughters of Israel, weep over Saul, who clothed you in scarlet and luxury, who put ornaments of gold upon your apparel.
"How the mighty have fallen in the midst of battle! Jonathan lies slain upon your high places.
I am distressed for you, my brother Jonathan; you were very pleasant to me; your love to me was wonderful, surpassing the love of women.
How the mighty have fallen, and the weapons of war have perished!"

Subsequent to these occurrences, David inquired of the LORD, saying, "Shall I ascend to one of the cities of Judah?" And the LORD said to him, "Ascend." David then asked, "To which city shall I ascend?" and He answered, "To Hebron."
Accordingly, David went up there, taking with him his two wives, Ahinoam the Jezreelite and Abigail, the widow of Nabal the Carmelite.
David also brought up the men who accompanied him, each with his household, and they settled in the towns of Hebron.
Then the men of Judah came, and there they anointed David king over the house of Judah. When it was reported to David, "The men of Jabesh-gilead are those who buried Saul,"
David dispatched messengers to the men of Jabesh-gilead and said to them, "May you be blessed by the LORD, because you have shown this kindness to Saul your lord and have buried him.
Now may the LORD show steadfast love and faithfulness to you; and I myself will likewise requite you with good, because you have done this deed.
Therefore let your hands be strengthened, and be valiant, for Saul your lord is dead, and the house of Judah has anointed me king over them."
Meanwhile, Abner son of Ner, commander of Saul's army, took Ish-bosheth son of Saul and conveyed him across to Mahanaim,
where he installed him as king over Gilead, the Ashurites, Jezreel, Ephraim, Benjamin, and all Israel.
Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, was forty years old when he began to reign over Israel, and he reigned two years; but the house of Judah followed David.
The period during which David reigned in Hebron over the house of Judah amounted to seven years and six months.
Abner son of Ner, together with the servants of Ish-bosheth son of Saul, set out from Mahanaim for Gibeon.
Joab son of Zeruiah, along with David's servants, likewise went forth and encountered them at the pool of Gibeon; there they sat, one party on one side of the pool and the other on the opposite side.
Abner said to Joab, "Let the young men arise and hold a martial contest before us." Joab answered, "Let them arise."
So they arose and were counted off, twelve for Benjamin and for Ish-bosheth son of Saul, and twelve of David's servants.
Each seized his opponent by the head and thrust his sword into his opponent's side, so that they fell together; therefore that place was called Helkath-hazzurim, which is at Gibeon.
The battle that day was exceedingly fierce, and Abner and the men of Israel were defeated before David's servants.
The three sons of Zeruiah were present there—Joab, Abishai, and Asahel—and Asahel was swift of foot as a gazelle in the open field.
Asahel pursued Abner without deviating to the right or to the left.
Abner turned and asked, "Are you Asahel?" He replied, "I am."
Abner said to him, "Turn aside to your right or to your left, seize one of the young men, and take his equipment." But Asahel would not turn aside from pursuing him.
Abner spoke again to Asahel: "Turn aside from pursuing me. Why should I strike you to the ground? How could I then lift my face before Joab your brother?"

Yet he refused to turn aside; therefore Abner struck him in the abdomen with the butt of his spear, so that the spear emerged from his back, and he fell and died on the spot. Everyone who came to the place where Asahel had fallen and died stood still.
Joab and Abishai pursued Abner; and as the sun was setting they reached the hill of Ammah, which lies before Giah on the way to the wilderness of Gibeon.
The Benjaminites rallied behind Abner, formed a single company, and took their stand on the top of a hill.
Abner called to Joab, "Shall the sword devour forever? Do you not know that the end will be bitter? How long before you tell the people to turn back from pursuing their brothers?"
Joab replied, "As God lives, if you had not spoken, the men would not have withdrawn from pursuing their brothers until morning."
Then Joab blew the trumpet, and all the people halted; they pursued Israel no further and fought no more.
Abner and his men marched through the Arabah all that night, crossed the Jordan, and came to Mahanaim.
Joab returned from pursuing Abner and mustered all the people; among David's servants nineteen men were missing besides Asahel.
But David's servants had struck down three hundred and sixty men among the Benjaminites and Abner's men.
They took up Asahel and buried him in his father's tomb at Bethlehem. Joab and his men marched all night and reached Hebron at daybreak.
A protracted war raged between the house of Saul and the house of David; and while David grew ever stronger, the house of Saul waned into ever greater weakness.
Sons were born to David at Hebron: his firstborn, Amnon, by Ahinoam the Jezreelite;
his second, Chileab, by Abigail, the widow of Nabal the Carmelite;
the third, Absalom, son of Maacah, daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur;
the fourth, Adonijah, son of Haggith; the fifth, Shephatiah, son of Abital; and the sixth, Ithream, by Eglah, David's wife. These six were born to David in Hebron.
While the war between the houses of Saul and David persisted, Abner was consolidating power within the house of Saul.
Now Saul had possessed a concubine named Rizpah, daughter of Aiah; and Ish-bosheth said to Abner, "Why have you gone in to my father's concubine?"

Abner was exceedingly incensed at Ish-bosheth's words and said, "Am I some contemptible cur of Judah? To this very day I have shown steadfast love to the house of Saul your father, to his brothers, and to his friends, and I have not delivered you into David's hand; yet today you charge me with an offense concerning a woman.
May God deal with Abner, and more severely still, if I do not accomplish for David what the LORD has sworn to him—
to transfer the kingdom from the house of Saul and establish David's throne over Israel and over Judah, from Dan to Beersheba."
Ish-bosheth could not answer Abner another word, for he feared him.
Abner sent messengers to David on his own behalf, saying, "To whom does the land belong? Make your covenant with me, and behold, my hand shall be with you to bring all Israel over to you."
David said, "Good; I will make a covenant with you. But I require one thing of you: you shall not see my face unless you first bring Michal, Saul's daughter, when you come to see my face."
Then David sent messengers to Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, saying, "Give me my wife Michal, for whom I paid the bridal price of a hundred Philistine foreskins."
Ish-bosheth sent and took her from her husband, Paltiel son of Laish.
Her husband went with her, weeping after her all the way to Bahurim. Then Abner said to him, "Go, return." And he returned.
Abner conferred with the elders of Israel, saying, "For some time past you have been seeking David as king over you.
Now then do it, for the LORD has promised David, saying, 'By the hand of My servant David I will save My people Israel from the hand of the Philistines and from the hand of all their enemies.'"
Abner also spoke to Benjamin; then he went to tell David at Hebron all that Israel and the whole house of Benjamin thought good to do.
When Abner came with twenty men to David at Hebron, David made a feast for Abner and the men who were with him.

Abner said to David, "I will arise and go and gather all Israel to my lord the king, that they may make a covenant with you, and that you may reign over all that your soul desires." And David sent Abner away, and he went in peace.
Just then David's servants and Joab came from a raid, bringing much spoil with them. But Abner was not with David at Hebron, for he had sent him away, and he had gone in peace.
When Joab and all the army with him came, they told Joab, "Abner son of Ner came to the king, and he has sent him away, and he has gone in peace."
Then Joab went to the king and said, "What have you done? Behold, Abner came to you. Why is it that you have sent him away, so that he is gone?"
You know that Abner son of Ner came to deceive you and to know your going out and your coming in, and to know all that you are doing."
Then Joab went out from the presence of David and sent messengers after Abner, and they brought him back from the cistern of Sirah. But David did not know it.
When Abner returned to Hebron, Joab took him aside into the midst of the gate to speak with him privately, and there he struck him in the stomach so that he died, for the blood of Asahel his brother.
Afterward, when David heard of it, he said, "I and my kingdom are guiltless before the LORD forever of the blood of Abner son of Ner.

May it fall on the head of Joab and on all his father's house, and may there not fail to be in the house of Joab one who has a discharge, or who is leprous, or who is reduced to women's work, or who falls by the sword, or who lacks bread."
So Joab and Abishai his brother killed Abner, because he had put their brother Asahel to death in the battle at Gibeon.
Then David said to Joab and to all the people who were with him, "Tear your clothes and put on sackcloth and mourn before Abner." And King David followed the bier.
They buried Abner at Hebron. And the king lifted up his voice and wept at the grave of Abner, and all the people wept.
And the king lamented for Abner, saying, "Should Abner die as a fool dies?
Your hands were not bound nor your feet put in fetters; you fell as one falls before the wicked." And all the people wept again over him.
Then all the people came to persuade David to eat bread while it was still day. But David swore, saying, "God do so to me, and more also, if I taste bread or anything else before the sun goes down!"
And all the people took notice of it, and it pleased them, as everything that the king did pleased all the people.
For all the people and all Israel understood that day that it had not been the king's will to put Abner son of Ner to death.
And the king said to his servants, "Do you not know that a prince and a great man has fallen this day in Israel?
And I am this day weak, though anointed king. And these men, the sons of Zeruiah, are too hard for me. The LORD repay the man who does evil according to his wickedness!"
When Saul’s son heard that Abner had died in Hebron, his hands grew slack, and all Israel was thrown into dismay.
Now Saul had a son, Ish-bosheth, and two men who commanded raiding bands: Baanah and Rechab, sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, of the Benjaminites—for Beeroth was reckoned among Benjamin.
The Beerothites fled to Gittaim and have sojourned there as aliens down to this very day.

Jonathan, Saul’s son, had a son who was lame in both feet; he was five years old when the report concerning Saul and Jonathan reached Jezreel. His nurse seized him and fled, and in her precipitous flight he fell and was lamed; his name was Mephibosheth.
Rechab and Baanah, sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, set out and arrived at the house of Ish-bosheth at the oppressive heat of noon, while he was taking his midday rest.
They penetrated into the interior of the house under the pretense of fetching wheat, struck him in the abdomen, and then Rechab and his brother Baanah made their escape.
They entered the house where he lay upon his bed in his sleeping chamber, struck him down and killed him, beheaded him, carried off his head, and traveled all night along the Arabah road.

They brought the head of Ish-bosheth to David at Hebron and said to the king, “Behold, the head of Ish-bosheth, son of Saul, your enemy, who sought your life; and the the LORD has this day granted vengeance to my lord the king against Saul and his offspring.”
David answered Rechab and Baanah his brother, sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, “As the the LORD lives, who has redeemed my soul from every tribulation,
when one came to tell me, ‘Behold, Saul is dead,’ supposing himself the bearer of glad tidings, I seized him and put him to death at Ziklag—that was the recompense I gave him for his news.
How much more, then, when wicked men have slain a righteous man in his own house upon his bed? Shall I not now demand his blood from your hand and eradicate you from the earth?”

David then commanded the young men, and they put them to death, cut off their hands and their feet, and hanged them beside the pool in Hebron. As for the head of Ish-bosheth, they took it and buried it in Abner’s tomb at Hebron.
Then all the tribes of Israel came to David at Hebron and said, “Behold, we are your own flesh and blood.

In times past, when Saul was king over us, you were the one who led Israel out and brought them in; and the LORD said to you, ‘You shall shepherd My people Israel, and you shall be prince over Israel.’
So all the elders of Israel came to the king at Hebron, and King David made a covenant with them before the LORD; then they anointed David king over Israel.
David was thirty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned forty years in all.
In Hebron he reigned over Judah seven years and six months, and in Jerusalem he reigned thirty-three years over all Israel and Judah.

The king and his men marched on Jerusalem against the Jebusites, the inhabitants of the land, who said to David, “You shall not come in here; rather, the blind and the lame will turn you away,” thinking, “David cannot come in here.”
Nevertheless, David captured the stronghold of Zion—that is, the City of David.

On that day David said, “Whoever strikes the Jebusites must go up by the water shaft and strike the lame and the blind, who are despised by David’s soul.” Therefore it is said, “The blind and the lame shall not enter the house.”
David dwelt in the stronghold and called it the City of David; and David built all around from the Millo inward.
David grew steadily greater, and the LORD God of Hosts was with him.
Hiram king of Tyre sent messengers to David, together with cedar timber, carpenters, and stonemasons, and they built a house for David.
Then David knew that the LORD had established him as king over Israel and had exalted his kingdom for the sake of His people Israel.
After David came from Hebron, he took still more concubines and wives in Jerusalem, and more sons and daughters were born to him.
These are the names of those born to him in Jerusalem: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, and Solomon;
When the Philistines heard that David had been anointed king over Israel, all the Philistines went up to seek David; but David heard of it and went down to the stronghold.
The Philistines had come and spread themselves in the Valley of Rephaim.

David inquired of the LORD, saying, “Shall I go up against the Philistines? Will You give them into my hand?” And the LORD said to David, “Go up, for I will surely give the Philistines into your hand.”
So David came to Baal-perazim and struck them there. Then he said, “The LORD has broken through my enemies before me like a breakthrough of waters.” Therefore he named that place Baal-perazim.
They abandoned their idols there, and David and his men carried them away.
The Philistines came up again and spread themselves in the Valley of Rephaim.
David inquired of the LORD, and He said, “You shall not go up; circle around behind them and come upon them in front of the balsam trees.
When you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees, then rouse yourself, for then the LORD has gone out before you to strike the camp of the Philistines.”
David did as the LORD commanded him, and he struck the Philistines from Geba to Gezer.
David again mustered the elect of Israel’s soldiery, thirty thousand strong.

David, together with the entire host accompanying him, departed from Baale-judah to convey thence the ark of God, which bears the Name, even the name of the LORD of Hosts, enthroned upon the cherubim.
They set the ark of God upon a newly fashioned cart and bore it from Abinadab’s hillside dwelling; Uzzah and Ahio, Abinadab’s sons, were guiding the new cart.
They conveyed it, together with the ark of God, from Abinadab’s house on the hill, Ahio proceeding before the ark.
David and the whole house of Israel were celebrating before the LORD with every instrument fashioned of cypress wood—lyres, harps, tambourines, castanets, and cymbals.
Upon arriving at the threshing floor of Nacon, Uzzah stretched forth his hand and laid hold of the ark of God, for the oxen had stumbled.
Then the LORD’s anger flared against Uzzah, and God struck him down there on account of his irreverence; he perished there beside the ark of God.
David was incensed because the LORD had broken out against Uzzah; therefore he named that place Perez-uzzah, a designation it retains to this day.
David feared the LORD that day and asked, “How shall the ark of the LORD ever come to me?”
Accordingly, David would not remove the ark of the LORD into the City of David; rather, he turned it aside to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite.
The ark of the LORD abode in the house of Obed-edom the Gittite for three months, and the LORD blessed Obed-edom and his entire household.

King David was told, “The LORD has blessed the house of Obed-edom and all that pertains to him on account of the ark of God.” Thereupon David went and brought up the ark of God from Obed-edom’s house to the City of David with great rejoicing.
After those bearing the ark of the LORD had advanced six paces, he sacrificed an ox and a fatted beast.
David, girded with a linen ephod, was dancing before the LORD with all his might.
Thus David and all the house of Israel were conveying the ark of the LORD upward amid shouting and the blast of the trumpet.

As the ark of the LORD was entering the City of David, Michal, daughter of Saul, looked down from the window and beheld King David leaping and dancing before the LORD; and she despised him in her heart.
They brought the ark of the LORD and stationed it in its appointed place within the tent David had pitched for it; and David offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before the LORD.
When David had completed the burnt offering and the peace offerings, he blessed the people in the name of the LORD of Hosts.

He apportioned to the entire assemblage of Israel, men and women alike, one loaf of bread, one portion of meat, and one raisin cake for each person; thereafter the whole people dispersed, every man to his own dwelling.

As David returned to bless his household, Michal daughter of Saul came forth to meet him and exclaimed, “How gloriously the king of Israel has distinguished himself today, exposing himself before the eyes of his servants’ handmaids, like one of the vulgar rabble who shamelessly bares himself!”

David replied to Michal, “It was before the LORD, who chose me above your father and above all his house, to appoint me ruler over the people of the LORD, over Israel; therefore I will celebrate before the LORD.
I will demean myself still further than this, and I will be lowly in my own sight; yet with the handmaids of whom you have spoken, with them I shall be held in honor.”
And Michal, daughter of Saul, remained childless until the day of her death.
Now it came to pass that, when the king was dwelling in his house and the LORD had given him rest on every side from all his enemies,
the king said to Nathan the prophet, "See now, I am dwelling in a house of cedar, but the ark of God is dwelling in the midst of a tent."
Nathan said to the king, "Go, do all that is in your heart, for the LORD is with you."
And it came to pass that same night that the word of the LORD came to Nathan, saying,
"Go and say to My servant, to David, Thus says the LORD: Are you the one who would build a house for Me to dwell in?
For I have not dwelt in a house from the day I brought up the sons of Israel out of Egypt even to this day, but I have been moving about in a tent and in a tabernacle.

In all the places where I have moved about with all the sons of Israel, did I speak a word to any of the tribes of Israel whom I commanded to shepherd My people Israel, saying, 'Why have you not built Me a house of cedar?'
Now therefore, thus shall you say to My servant David, Thus says the LORD of hosts: I took you from the pasture, from following the flock, to be ruler over My people, over Israel.
I have been with you wherever you have gone, and I have cut off all your enemies from before you; and I will make for you a name like the name of the great ones who are in the earth.

I will appoint a place for My people Israel, and I will plant them, that they may dwell in their own place and be disturbed no more; nor shall the sons of wickedness afflict them anymore, as formerly.
Moreover, from the day that I appointed judges over My people Israel, I have given you rest from all your enemies. The LORD also declares to you that the LORD will make you a house.
When your days are fulfilled and you lie down with your fathers, I will raise up your offspring after you, who shall come from your body, and I will establish his kingdom.
He shall build a house for My name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever.
I will be to him a father, and he shall be to Me a son. When he commits iniquity, I will discipline him with the rod of men and with the stripes of the sons of men.
But My steadfast love shall not depart from him, as I took it from Saul, whom I removed from before you.
And your house and your kingdom shall be made sure forever before you; your throne shall be established forever.'"
So Nathan spoke to David in accordance with all these words and all this vision.
Then King David went in and sat before the LORD, and he said, "Who am I, O Lord, the LORD, and what is my house, that You have brought me this far?
And yet this was a small thing in Your eyes, O Lord, the LORD; You have also spoken concerning the house of Your servant for the distant future, and this is the manner of humankind, O Lord, the LORD.
And what more can David say to You? For You know Your servant, O Lord, the LORD.
Because of Your word and according to Your heart You have done all this greatness, to make Your servant know it.
Therefore You are great, O Lord, the LORD; for there is none like You, and there is no God besides You, according to all that we have heard with our ears.

And who is like Your people Israel, the one nation on earth whom God went to redeem for Himself as a people, and to make a name for Himself, and to perform for them great and awesome wonders for Your land, before Your people whom You redeemed for Yourself from Egypt, from the nations and their gods?
And You have established Your people Israel for Yourself as a people forever; and You, O LORD, have become their God.
And now, O LORD God, establish forever the word that You have spoken concerning Your servant and concerning his house, and do as You have spoken.
And let Your name be magnified forever, saying, 'The LORD of hosts is God over Israel,' and let the house of Your servant David be established before You.
For You, O LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, have revealed to Your servant, saying, 'I will build you a house.' Therefore Your servant has found it in his heart to pray this prayer to You.
And now, O Lord, the LORD, You are God, and Your words are true, and You have promised this good thing to Your servant.

And now be pleased to bless the house of Your servant, that it may continue forever before You; for You, O Lord, the LORD, have spoken, and with Your blessing the house of Your servant shall be blessed forever."
After these events, David defeated the Philistines and subdued them; he also wrested Metheg-ammah from their grasp.

He likewise defeated Moab, forcing them to lie prostrate upon the ground and measuring them with a cord: two cords’ worth he consigned to death, while a full cord’s worth he spared. Thus Moab became tributary to David, rendering tribute.
David also defeated Hadadezer son of Rehob, king of Zobah, as the latter marched to reassert his dominion at the Euphrates River.
From him David captured seventeen hundred horsemen and twenty thousand foot soldiers; he hamstrung all the chariot horses, though he retained enough for a hundred chariots.
When the Arameans of Damascus came to Hadadezer’s aid, David struck down twenty-two thousand of them.
David then stationed garrisons in Aram of Damascus, and the Arameans became tributary to David, bringing tribute. Moreover, the LORD granted David victory in all his campaigns.
David seized the golden shields carried by Hadadezer’s officers and conveyed them to Jerusalem.
From Betah and Berothai, cities of Hadadezer, King David took an exceedingly great quantity of bronze.
When Toi, king of Hamath, heard that David had defeated Hadadezer’s entire host,
Toi sent his son Joram to King David to greet him and to congratulate him on his triumph over Hadadezer—for Hadadezer had been Toi’s adversary—and Joram brought vessels of silver, gold, and bronze.
King David consecrated these to the LORD, together with the silver and gold he had dedicated from all the nations he had subdued:
from Aram, Moab, the Ammonites, the Philistines, Amalek, and the plunder of Hadadezer son of Rehob, king of Zobah.
David thereby won renown when he returned from striking down eighteen thousand Arameans in the Valley of Salt.
He stationed garrisons throughout Edom—throughout all Edom—and all Edom became subject to David. The LORD also granted David victory in every campaign.
So David reigned over all Israel, administering justice and righteousness to all his people.
Joab son of Zeruiah commanded the army, and Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud served as recorder.
Zadok son of Ahitub and Ahimelech son of Abiathar were priests, and Seraiah was scribe.
Benaiah son of Jehoiada oversaw the Cherethites and the Pelethites, and David’s sons were priests.
David inquired, "Is there yet any survivor of the house of Saul to whom I might extend steadfast love for Jonathan's sake?"
There was a servant of Saul's house named Ziba, and he was summoned before David. The king said to him, "Are you Ziba?" He replied, "I am your servant."
The king asked, "Is there no one still remaining of the house of Saul to whom I may manifest the steadfast love of God?" Ziba said to the king, "There is still a son of Jonathan, lame in both feet."
The king said to him, "Where might he be?" Ziba answered, "He resides in the house of Machir son of Ammiel, in Lo Debar."
King David therefore dispatched messengers and brought him from the house of Machir son of Ammiel in Lo Debar.
When Mephibosheth, son of Jonathan, son of Saul, came into David's presence, he prostrated himself with his face to the ground. David said, "Mephibosheth?" He answered, "Here is your servant."

David said to him, "Fear not, for I shall surely show you steadfast love for the sake of your father Jonathan, and I shall restore to you the whole patrimony of your father Saul; moreover, you shall take your meals at my table in perpetuity."
He bowed and said, "What is your servant, that you should look with favor upon one so utterly inconsequential as I?"
The king then summoned Ziba, Saul's servant, and said to him, "I have consigned to your master's son everything that belonged to Saul and to his entire household.

You, therefore, together with your sons and your servants, shall cultivate the land for him, and you shall gather in the harvest, so that your master's son may have sustenance; yet Mephibosheth, your master's son, shall always dine at my table." Now Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants.
Ziba said to the king, "Your servant shall do precisely as my lord the king commands." The king said, "As for Mephibosheth, he shall dine at my table like one of the king's sons."
Mephibosheth had a young son named Mica, and everyone residing in Ziba's household was in Mephibosheth's service.
Thus Mephibosheth dwelt in Jerusalem, for he continually ate at the king's table, though he was lame in both feet.
After these events, the king of the Ammonites died, and his son Hanun succeeded to the throne.

David resolved, “I shall extend faithful kindness to Hanun son of Nahash, for his father extended such kindness to me,” and therefore dispatched his servants to console him over his father’s death. Thus David’s servants entered the land of the Ammonites.

Yet the princes of the Ammonites said to Hanun, their lord, “Do you suppose that David honors your father by sending consolers to you? Has David not sent his servants to you in order to reconnoiter the city, to spy upon it, and to subvert it?”
Consequently, Hanun seized David’s servants, shaved off half of each man’s beard, cut their garments at the hips—indeed, to the buttocks—and dismissed them.
When report reached David, he sent envoys to meet them, for the men were profoundly humiliated; and the king instructed, “Remain in Jericho until your beards have regrown, and afterward return.”

When the Ammonites perceived that they had rendered themselves abhorrent to David, they dispatched agents and hired twenty thousand Aramean infantry from Beth-rehob and Zobah, together with the king of Maacah and his thousand men, and twelve thousand men from Tob.
Upon hearing this, David sent Joab and the entire host, including the mighty men.
The Ammonites sallied forth and arrayed themselves for battle at the city gate, whereas the Arameans of Zobah and Rehob, along with the men of Tob and Maacah, remained apart in the open field.
Perceiving that the battle confronted him on both front and rear, Joab selected from all the elite troops of Israel and arrayed them against the Arameans.
He entrusted the remainder of the force to his brother Abishai, who arrayed them against the Ammonites.
He declared, “If the Arameans prove too strong for me, then you must come to my aid; but if the Ammonites prove too strong for you, then I shall hasten to deliver you.
Be strong, and let us comport ourselves courageously for our people and for the cities of our God, and may the LORD effect what is good in His sight.”
Joab and the troops accompanying him advanced to engage the Arameans, and the Arameans fled before him.
When the Ammonites observed the Arameans’ flight, they too fled before Abishai and withdrew into the city. Joab then returned from the Ammonites and went to Jerusalem.
Perceiving their defeat before Israel, the Arameans regrouped.
Hadadezer dispatched agents and brought forth the Arameans from beyond the River; they advanced to Helam, with Shobach, commander of Hadadezer’s army, leading them.
When David received report, he mustered all Israel, crossed the Jordan, and arrived at Helam. The Arameans arrayed themselves against David and engaged him in battle.
The Arameans fled before Israel; David slew seven hundred charioteers and forty thousand horsemen among the Arameans, and he struck down Shobach, their army’s commander, who died there.

When all the kings who were vassals of Hadadezer saw that they had been defeated before Israel, they made peace with Israel and became its subjects. Thus the Arameans dared no longer to succor the Ammonites.

In the spring, at the season when kings customarily took the field, David dispatched Joab with his officers and all Israel; they devastated the Ammonites and besieged Rabbah, while David himself remained in Jerusalem.
One evening David arose from his bed and walked upon the roof of the king's house, and from that vantage he beheld a woman bathing; the woman was exceedingly comely.
David sent to inquire concerning the woman, and it was reported, "She is Bathsheba, daughter of Eliam and wife of Uriah the Hittite."
David sent messengers and took her; she came to him, and he lay with her. She had been purifying herself from her uncleanness, and afterward she returned to her house.
The woman conceived, and she sent word to David, saying, "I am pregnant."
David sent word to Joab, "Send me Uriah the Hittite." Joab sent Uriah to David.
When Uriah came, David asked how Joab fared, how the people fared, and how the war progressed.
David said to Uriah, "Go down to your house and wash your feet." Uriah departed from the king's house, and a present from the king followed him.
Yet Uriah slept at the door of the king's house with all his lord's servants and did not go down to his house.
When David was told that Uriah had not gone down to his house, he said to Uriah, "Did you not come from a journey? Why did you not go down to your house?"

Uriah answered David, "The ark and Israel and Judah dwell in booths, and my lord Joab and the servants of my lord are encamped in the open field; shall I then go to my house to eat and drink and lie with my wife? As surely as you live, I will not do this thing."
David said to him, "Remain here today also, and tomorrow I will send you away." So Uriah remained in Jerusalem that day and the next.
David invited him, and he ate and drank before him, and David made him drunk; in the evening Uriah went out to lie on his bed with his lord's servants, but he did not go down to his house.
In the morning David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it by the hand of Uriah.
In the letter he wrote, "Set Uriah in the forefront of the hardest fighting, and withdraw from him, that he may be struck down and die."
As Joab besieged the city, he assigned Uriah to the place where he knew valiant men were.
The men of the city came out and fought against Joab, and some of David's servants fell; Uriah the Hittite also died.
Joab sent to tell David all the news of the war.

He instructed the messenger, "When you have finished telling the king all the news of the battle, if the king's anger rises and he asks you, 'Why did you approach so near to the city to fight? Did you not know that they shoot from the wall? Who struck down Abimelech son of Jerub-Besheth? Did not a woman cast an upper millstone upon him from the wall, so that he died at Thebez? Why did you approach so near to the wall?' then you shall say, 'Moreover, your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead.'"
The messenger went and came and told David all that Joab had sent him to say.
The messenger said to David, "The men prevailed against us and came out to us in the field, but we drove them back to the gate.
The archers shot at your servants from the wall, and some of the king's servants died; moreover, your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead."

David said to the messenger, "Say thus to Joab: 'Do not let this matter distress you, for the sword devours now one and now another; strengthen your assault against the city and overthrow it,' and encourage him."
When Uriah's wife heard that her husband was dead, she lamented for him.
When her mourning was over, David sent and brought her to his house, and she became his wife and bore him a son. But the thing David had done displeased the LORD.
The LORD sent Nathan to David. When he came to him, he said, “There were two men in a certain city—one affluent and the other impoverished.
The affluent man possessed exceedingly many sheep and cattle,

but the impoverished man had nothing at all save one diminutive ewe lamb, which he had acquired and nurtured; it grew up alongside him and his children, partaking of his bread, drinking from his cup, and resting in his bosom, and it became to him as a daughter.

Now a wayfarer came to the affluent man, yet he spared his own flock and herd, unwilling to slaughter from them for the guest who had arrived; instead, he seized the impoverished man’s ewe lamb and prepared it for the man who had come to him.”
David’s anger blazed fiercely against that man, and he said to Nathan, “As the the LORD lives, the man who has done this deserves death!
Moreover, because he perpetrated this deed and showed no compassion, he shall repay the lamb fourfold.”
Nathan said to David, “You are the man! Thus says the the LORD, the God of Israel: ‘I anointed you king over Israel, and I delivered you from the hand of Saul.
I gave you your master’s house and your master’s wives into your embrace; I gave you the house of Israel and Judah, and had that been too little, I would have added to you far more.

Why, then, have you despised the word of the the LORD by doing what is evil in His sight? You have struck down Uriah the Hittite with the sword, taken his wife as your own, and slain him by the sword of the Ammonites.
Now, therefore, the sword shall never depart from your house, because you despised Me and took Uriah’s wife as your own.’

Thus says the the LORD: ‘Behold, I will raise up calamity against you from within your own house; before your very eyes I will take your wives and give them to one near you, and he shall lie with your wives in the sight of this sun.
For you acted in secret, but I will do this thing before all Israel and before this sun.’”
David said to Nathan, “I have sinned against the the LORD.” Nathan replied, “The the LORD has taken away your sin; You shall not die.
Nevertheless, because by this deed you have utterly scorned the the LORD, the son born to you shall surely die.”
After Nathan had departed to his house, the the LORD struck the child whom Uriah’s wife had borne to David, and he became gravely ill.
David therefore sought God on behalf of the child; he fasted, went in, and lay all night upon the ground.
The elders of his household arose beside him to raise him from the ground, but he refused, and he would not eat bread with them.

On the seventh day the child died. David’s servants were afraid to inform him that the child was dead, for they said, “While the child was still alive, we spoke to him and he would not heed our voice; how then can we tell him that the child is dead? He might do himself harm.”
When David saw that his servants were whispering among themselves, he perceived that the child was dead, and he asked them, “Is the child dead?” They replied, “He is dead.”

Then David arose from the ground, washed, anointed himself, changed his garments, and entered the house of the the LORD and worshiped. He then came to his own house and, at his request, they set food before him, and he ate.
His servants said to him, “What is this thing that you have done? While the child was alive, you fasted and wept; but now that the child is dead, you arise and eat!”
He answered, “While the child was still alive, I fasted and wept, for I said, ‘Who knows? Perhaps the the LORD will be gracious to me, and the child will live.’
But now that he is dead, why should I fast? Can I bring him back again? I shall go to him, but he will not return to me.”
Then David comforted his wife Bathsheba; he went in to her and lay with her, and she bore a son, and he called his name Solomon. The the LORD loved him,
and He sent word through Nathan the prophet, and he named him Jedidiah, because of the the LORD.
Meanwhile Joab fought against Rabbah of the Ammonites and captured the royal city.
Joab sent messengers to David and said, “I have fought against Rabbah and have also captured the city’s water supply.
Now therefore gather the rest of the people, encamp against the city, and take it, lest I take the city and it be named after me.”
So David gathered all the people and went to Rabbah, fought against it, and captured it.

He took the crown from the head of their king; its weight was a talent of gold, and it was set with precious stones, and it was placed upon David’s head. He also carried off a great amount of plunder from the city.

He brought out the people who were in it and consigned them to labor with saws, iron picks, and iron axes, and made them pass through the brick kilns; and thus he did to all the cities of the Ammonites. Then David and all the people returned to Jerusalem.
After these events, David's son Amnon conceived an ardent infatuation with Tamar, the daughter of David and sister of Absalom; she was exceedingly beautiful.

Amnon became so distressed and physically debilitated on account of his sister Tamar that he fell ill, for she was a virgin, and it seemed to him an impossibility that he should have his way with her.
Now Amnon had a friend, Jonadab son of Shimeah, David's brother; Jonadab was an exceedingly astute man.
He said to him, “Why do you, the king's son, grow so gaunt morning after morning? Will you not confide in me?” Amnon replied, “I am in love with Tamar, the sister of my brother Absalom.”

Jonadab said to him, “Lie down upon your bed and feign illness. When your father comes to see you, say to him, ‘Please let my sister Tamar come and prepare food before me, that I may watch and eat from her hand.’”
So Amnon lay down and pretended to be ill. When the king came to see him, Amnon said to the king, “Please let my sister Tamar come and make two cakes in my sight, that I may eat from her hand.”
David sent to Tamar at the house, saying, “Go now to your brother Amnon's house and prepare food for him.”
Tamar went to the house of her brother Amnon, who was lying down. She took dough, kneaded it, made cakes in his sight, and cooked them.
