She took the pan and poured them out before him, but he refused to eat. Amnon said, “Send everyone away from me.” So they all went out.
Amnon said to Tamar, “Bring the food into the chamber, that I may eat from your hand.” Tamar took the cakes she had made and brought them into the chamber to Amnon.
As she brought them near for him to eat, he seized her and said, “Come, lie with me, my sister.”
She said to him, “No, my brother; do not violate me, for such a thing is not done in Israel. Do not commit this outrage.”
“Where should I carry my shame? And you would be counted among the fools in Israel. Now, I pray you, speak to the king, for he will not deny me to you.”
But he would not listen to her. He was stronger than she was, and he violated her and lay with her.
Then Amnon hated her with a very great hatred; indeed, the hatred with which he hated her was greater than the love with which he had loved her. Amnon said to her, “Get up and be gone.”
She said to him, “No, for sending me away would be a greater evil than the other you did to me.” But he would not listen to her.
He called the young man who served him and said, “Send this woman away from me and bolt the door after her.”
His servant brought her out and locked the door after her. She was wearing a robe of many colors, for such were the garments of the king's virgin daughters.
Tamar put ashes on her head, tore the robe she was wearing, laid her hand upon her head, and went away crying aloud as she went.

Her brother Absalom said to her, “Has Amnon your brother been with you? Now be silent, my sister; he is your brother. Do not take this to heart.” So Tamar remained desolate in her brother Absalom's house.
When King David heard of all these things, he was very angry.
Absalom spoke to Amnon neither good nor bad, for Absalom hated Amnon because he had violated his sister Tamar.
After two full years, Absalom had sheepshearers at Baal-hazor, which is near Ephraim, and Absalom invited all the king's sons.
Absalom came to the king and said, “See now, your servant is shearing sheep; I pray that the king and his servants may go with your servant.”

The king said to Absalom, “No, my son, let us not all go, lest we be a burden to you.” He urged him, but he would not go; instead, he blessed him. Absalom said, “If not, then please let my brother Amnon go with us.” The king said to him, “Why should he go with you?”
But Absalom pressed him, and he sent Amnon and all the king's sons with him.

Absalom commanded his servants, saying, “Watch now: when Amnon's heart is merry with wine and I say to you, ‘Strike Amnon and kill him,’ do not be afraid. Have I not commanded you? Be strong and valiant.”
The servants of Absalom did to Amnon as Absalom had commanded. Then all the king's sons arose, and each mounted his mule and fled.
While they were on the way, the report came to David, saying, “Absalom has struck down all the king's sons, and not one of them is left.”
The king arose, tore his garments, and lay on the ground; all his servants stood by with their garments torn.

Jonadab son of Shimeah, David's brother, answered and said, “Let not my lord say, ‘They have killed all the young men, the king's sons,’ for only Amnon is dead. This has been determined by Absalom from the day he violated his sister Tamar.”
“Now therefore let not my lord the king take this to heart, to say, ‘All the king's sons are dead,’ for only Amnon is dead.”
Absalom fled. The young man, the watchman, lifted his eyes and saw, and behold, many people were coming along the road behind him on the side of the hill.
Jonadab said to the king, “Behold, the king's sons are coming; as your servant said, so it is.”
As soon as he finished speaking, behold, the king's sons came and lifted up their voices and wept; the king and all his servants wept exceedingly.
Absalom fled and went to Talmai son of Ammihur, king of Geshur. David mourned for his son all his days.
Absalom fled and went to Geshur, and remained there three years.
King David longed to go to Absalom, for he had been consoled over Amnon's death.
Now Joab, the son of Zeruiah, discerned that the king's affections were inclined toward Absalom.

Accordingly, Joab dispatched a messenger to Tekoa and procured from there a sagacious woman, to whom he said, "Please feign mourning: don mourning garments, do not anoint yourself with oil, and present yourself as a woman who has lamented the dead for a protracted season. Then go to the king and speak to him in this manner."
And Joab placed the words in her mouth.
When the woman of Tekoa addressed the king, she fell upon her face to the earth, prostrated herself, and cried, "Help me, O king!"
The king asked her, "What ails you?" She replied, "Alas, I am a widow, and my husband has perished.
"Your maidservant had two sons; they contended in the field, and, with no one to interpose, one struck the other and slew him.

"And behold, the entire clan has risen against your maidservant, demanding, 'Surrender the one who struck his brother, that we may put him to death for the life of his brother whom he killed, and annihilate the heir as well.' Thus they would extinguish the last ember of my household, leaving my husband neither name nor remnant upon the earth."
The king said to the woman, "Go to your house, and I will issue a decree concerning you."
The woman of Tekoa said to the king, "My lord the king, let the guilt rest upon me and upon my father's house; but may the king and his throne be held guiltless."
The king said, "If anyone molests you, bring him to me, and he will not molest you again."

She said, "Please let the king remember the LORD your God, that the avenger of blood may not destroy, so that they will not destroy my son." The king replied, "As the LORD lives, not one hair of your son shall fall to the ground."
Then the woman said, "Please let your maidservant speak a further word to my lord the king." He said, "Speak."
The woman said, "Why then have you devised such a thing against the people of God? For by speaking this word, the king incurs guilt, inasmuch as he does not restore his banished son.

"For we must all die, and we are like water spilled upon the ground, which cannot be gathered up again; yet God does not take away life, but devises means by which the banished one may not remain estranged from Him.

"Now I have come to speak this word to my lord the king because the people have intimidated me; and your maidservant said, 'Let me speak to the king; perhaps the king will grant the request of his maidservant.'
"For the king will listen, to deliver his maidservant from the hand of the man who would destroy me and my son together from the inheritance of God.
"Your maidservant said, 'May the word of my lord the king bring repose; for my lord the king is like the angel of God in discerning good and evil; and may the the LORD your God be with you.'"
The king answered and said to the woman, "Do not conceal from me anything that I ask you." She said, "Let my lord the king speak."

The king said, "Is the hand of Joab with you in all this?" She answered, "As surely as you live, my lord the king, no one can turn to the right or to the left from all that my lord the king has spoken; for your servant Joab commanded me, and he placed all these words in the mouth of your maidservant.
Your servant Joab has done this to alter the appearance of the matter; but my lord is wise, according to the wisdom of the angel of God, to know all that is upon the earth."
The king said to Joab, "Behold, I have granted this request; go, bring back the young man Absalom."

Joab fell on his face to the ground, prostrated himself, and blessed the king. Then Joab said, "Today your servant knows that he has found favor in your sight, my lord the king, in that the king has granted the request of his servant."
Joab arose, journeyed to Geshur, and brought Absalom to Jerusalem.
The king said, "Let him withdraw to his own house, but let him not see my face." So Absalom withdrew to his own house and did not see the king's face.
Now in all Israel there was no man so handsome as Absalom; from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head there was no blemish in him.
When he sheared the hair of his head—and at the end of every year he sheared it, because it was heavy upon him—he weighed the hair of his head at two hundred shekels by the king's standard.
Three sons were born to Absalom, and one daughter named Tamar; she was a woman of beautiful appearance.
Absalom resided in Jerusalem two full years without seeing the king's face.
Absalom sent for Joab, in order to send him to the king, but he would not come; he sent again a second time, but he would not come.
Absalom said to his servants, "See, Joab's field is next to mine, and he has barley there; go and set it ablaze." So Absalom's servants burned the field.
Joab arose, came to Absalom's house, and said to him, "Why have your servants set my field on fire?"

Absalom said to Joab, "Behold, I sent to you, saying, 'Come here, that I may send you to the king, to say, "Why have I come from Geshur? It would be better for me still to be there."' Now therefore let me see the king's face; and if there is iniquity in me, let him put me to death."
Joab went to the king and reported; and the king summoned Absalom, who came to the king, bowed himself with his face to the ground before the king, and the king kissed Absalom.
After these events, Absalom procured for himself a chariot and horses, together with fifty men to run before him.

He would rise early and take his stand beside the road leading to the city gate; and whenever a man with a grievance came to the king for judgment, Absalom would call out to him, “What town are you from?” and the man would reply, “Your servant is from one of the tribes of Israel.”
Then Absalom would say to him, “See, your claims are good and right, but there is no one deputed by the king to hear you.”
He would add, “If only I were appointed judge in the land! Then everyone who has any suit or case could come to me, and I would see that he received justice.”
Moreover, whenever anyone approached him to bow down before him, Absalom would extend his hand, seize him, and kiss him.
In this manner Absalom treated all the Israelites who came to the king for judgment, and so he purloined the hearts of the people of Israel.
At the end of four years, Absalom said to the king, “Let me go to Hebron and fulfill the vow that I made to the LORD.
For while your servant was living at Geshur in Aram, I made this vow: ‘If the LORD brings me back to Jerusalem, I will worship the LORD in Hebron.’”
The king said to him, “Go in peace.” So he arose and went to Hebron.
Then Absalom sent secret messengers throughout all the tribes of Israel, saying, “As soon as you hear the sound of the trumpet, you shall say, ‘Absalom is king in Hebron.’”
Two hundred men from Jerusalem had accompanied Absalom; they had been invited as guests and went in all innocence, knowing nothing of the matter.

While Absalom was offering sacrifices, he also sent for Ahithophel the Gilonite, David’s counselor, from his city Giloh; and the conspiracy became formidable, while Absalom’s following continued to increase.
A messenger came to David and said, “The hearts of the men of Israel have gone after Absalom.”

David then said to all his servants who were with him in Jerusalem, “Arise, and let us flee, for otherwise we shall have no escape from Absalom. Let us depart in haste, lest he overtake us suddenly, bring disaster upon us, and strike the city with the edge of the sword.”
The king’s servants answered him, “Behold, Your servants are ready to do whatever our lord the king chooses.”
The king went out, and all his household followed him on foot; but the king left ten concubines to keep the house.
The king went out, and all the people followed him on foot, and they halted at the last house.
All his servants passed by him, and all the Cherethites and Pelethites, and all the six hundred Gittites who had come with him from Gath, passed before the king.
The king said to Ittai the Gittite, “Why should you go along with us? Return and remain with the king, for you are a foreigner and an exile from your own country.
You came only yesterday; should I make you wander with us when I do not know where I am going? Return and take your people with you. May the LORD show you kindness and faithfulness.”
But Ittai answered the king, “As the LORD lives, and as my lord the king lives, wherever my lord the king shall be, whether for life or for death, there shall your servant be.”
David said to Ittai, “Go then, and pass over.” So Ittai the Gittite passed over, with all his men and all the little ones who were with him.
All the land wept with a loud voice as all the people passed by; the king also crossed the brook Kidron, and all the people passed on toward the wilderness.

Zadok was there also, and all the Levites with him, bearing the ark of the covenant of God; they set down the ark of God, and Abiathar offered sacrifices until all the people had finished passing out of the city.
The king said to Zadok, “Take the ark of God back into the city. If I find favor in the eyes of the LORD, He will bring me back and let me see it and His dwelling place again.
But if He says, ‘I have no pleasure in you,’ then here I am; let Him do to me what seems good in His eyes.”
The king also said to Zadok the priest, “Are you not a seer? Return to the city in peace, taking your son Ahimaaz and Jonathan son of Abiathar. You and Abiathar shall take your two sons with you.
See, I will wait at the fords of the wilderness until word comes from you to inform me.”
So Zadok and Abiathar carried the ark of God back to Jerusalem and remained there.
But David went up the ascent of the Mount of Olives, weeping as he went, with his head covered and walking barefoot; and all the people who were with him covered their heads and went up weeping.
David had been told, “Ahithophel is among the conspirators with Absalom,” and David prayed, “O LORD, turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness.”
When David came to the summit, where God was worshipped, Hushai the Archite came to meet him with his coat torn and dust upon his head.
David said to him, “If you pass on with me, you will be a burden to me.

But if you return to the city, you can say to Absalom, ‘I will be your servant, O king; I was your father’s servant from the beginning, but now I am your servant.’ Then you can help me by frustrating Ahithophel’s advice.”
“Are not Zadok and Abiathar the priests there with you? Tell them everything you hear in the king’s house.
Behold, their two sons are there with them, Ahimaaz son of Zadok and Jonathan son of Abiathar; by them you shall send me word of everything you hear.”
So Hushai, David’s friend, came into Jerusalem just as Absalom was entering the city.

David had scarcely passed a little beyond the summit when Ziba, the servant of Mephibosheth, met him with a pair of saddled donkeys, upon which were two hundred loaves of bread, a hundred cakes of raisins, a hundred cakes of summer fruit, and a skin of wine.

The king asked, "What are these?" Ziba replied, "The donkeys are for the king's household to ride, the bread and summer fruit are for the young men to eat, and the wine is for those who grow weary in the wilderness to drink."
The king asked, "Where is your master?" Ziba answered, "He is staying in Jerusalem, for he said, 'Today the house of Israel will restore my father's kingdom to me.'"
The king said to Ziba, "Behold, all that belonged to Mephibosheth is yours." Ziba bowed and said, "May I find favor in your eyes, my lord the king."
When King David reached Bahurim, a man from the family of the house of Saul came out from there; his name was Shimei son of Gera, and as he came he kept cursing.
He pelted David and all the king's servants, all the people, and all the mighty men with stones, and the people and the mighty men were on David's right and on his left.
As he cursed, Shimei said, "Get out, get out, you bloodstained man, you worthless scoundrel!

The LORD has brought back upon you all the blood of the house of Saul, in whose place you reigned, and the LORD has given the kingdom into the hand of your son Absalom. Behold, you are caught in your own evil, for you are a man of blood!"
Then Abishai son of Zeruiah said to the king, "Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? Let me cross over and remove his head."
The king said, "What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah? If he curses, it is because the LORD has said to him, 'Curse David'; who then can say, 'Why have you done so?'"

David said to Abishai and to all his servants, "Behold, my own son, who came forth from my body, seeks my life; how much more now this Benjaminite! Leave him alone and let him curse, for the LORD has told him to.
Perhaps The LORD will look upon my affliction and the LORD will repay me with good for his cursing this day."
So David and his men went on their way, while Shimei went along the hillside opposite him, cursing as he went and throwing stones at him and flinging dust.
The king and all the people who were with him arrived weary, and there they refreshed themselves.
Absalom and all the people, the men of Israel, came to Jerusalem, and Ahithophel was with him.
When David's friend Hushai the Archite came to Absalom, Hushai said, "May the king live! May the king live!"
Absalom said to Hushai, "Is this your loyalty to your friend? Why did you not go with your friend?"
Hushai said to Absalom, "No; rather, whom the LORD has chosen, and this people, and all the men of Israel—to him I will belong, and with him I will remain.
And again, whom should I serve? Should I not serve his son? As I served your father, so I will serve you."
Absalom said to Ahithophel, "Give your advice. What shall we do?"

Ahithophel said to Absalom, "Go in to your father's concubines, whom he left to keep the house, and all Israel will hear that you have made yourself abhorrent to your father, and the hands of all who are with you will be strengthened."
So they pitched a tent for Absalom on the roof, and Absalom went in to his father's concubines in the sight of all Israel.
In those days the counsel that Ahithophel gave was as though one had consulted the word of God; such was all the counsel of Ahithophel, whether to David or to Absalom.
Ahithophel said to Absalom, “Let me choose twelve thousand men, and I will set out tonight to pursue David.
I will overtake him while he is weary and disheartened, throw him into panic, and make all the people with him flee; then I will strike down the king alone.
I will restore the entire populace to your allegiance; once the man you seek is dead, the whole nation will be at peace.
This counsel seemed sound to Absalom and to all the elders of Israel.
Absalom said, “Summon Hushai the Archite as well, so that we may hear what he has to say.”
When Hushai came before Absalom, Absalom said to him, “Ahithophel has proposed this plan. Should we adopt it? If not, speak your mind.”
Hushai replied to Absalom, “The counsel Ahithophel has offered this time is not sound.

You know your father and his men: they are formidable and desperate fighters, like a bear robbed of her cubs in the open country; and your father, a veteran of war, will not spend the night with the troops.
Even now he is hidden in some cave or stronghold; if your forces suffer an initial reverse, whoever hears of it will say, ‘There has been a slaughter among the people following Absalom.’
Then even the boldest soldier, whose heart is like a lion’s, will lose courage, for all Israel knows that your father is a mighty warrior and that those with him are valiant men.
Therefore I advise that all Israel be gathered to you—from Dan to Beersheba, as innumerable as sand on the shore—and that you yourself lead them into battle.
We will overtake him wherever he is found and fall upon him like dew upon the ground, leaving not one of his men alive.
And if he withdraws into a city, all Israel will drag that city into the valley with ropes until not even a pebble remains.”
Absalom and all the men of Israel declared Hushai’s counsel superior to Ahithophel’s, for the LORD had ordained that Ahithophel’s sound advice be frustrated, bringing disaster upon Absalom.
Hushai reported to the priests Zadok and Abiathar what Ahithophel had advised Absalom and the elders of Israel, and what he himself had advised in response.
“Send word quickly to David,” he said, “and tell him, ‘Do not spend the night in the plains of the wilderness; cross the Jordan at once, lest the king and all his people be consumed.’”

Jonathan and Ahimaaz were stationed at En-rogel, where a maidservant would come and relay messages to them; they would then go and inform King David, since they could not risk being seen entering the city.
But a young man spotted them and reported them to Absalom, so the two fled swiftly to the house of a man at Bahurim, who had a well in his courtyard, and they climbed down into it.
The man’s wife took a covering, spread it over the mouth of the well, and scattered grain over it, so that nothing was noticed.

When Absalom’s servants came to the woman at the house and asked, “Where are Ahimaaz and Jonathan?” She answered, “They crossed the brook.” The men searched but could not find them, and returned to Jerusalem.
After they had gone, the two climbed out of the well and went to inform King David. “Rise and cross the water quickly,” they told him, “for Ahithophel has counseled thus against you.”
So David and all the people with him arose and crossed the Jordan; by dawn not one of them remained on the near side.
When Ahithophel saw that his advice had not been followed, he saddled his donkey, went home to his city, set his house in order, and hanged himself. He died and was buried in his father’s tomb.
David reached Mahanaim, while Absalom and all the men of Israel crossed the Jordan.
Absalom appointed Amasa over the army in place of Joab; Amasa was the son of a man named Ithra the Israelite, who had married Abigail daughter of Nahash, sister of Zeruiah, Joab’s mother.
Israel and Absalom encamped in the land of Gilead.
When David came to Mahanaim, Shobi son of Nahash from Rabbah of the Ammonites, Machir son of Ammiel from Lo-debar, and Barzillai the Gileadite from Rogelim
brought beds, basins, and pottery, together with wheat, barley, flour, parched grain, beans, lentils, and parched legumes,

as well as honey, curds, sheep, and cheese from the cattle. They presented these provisions to David and to the people with him, for they said, “The people are hungry, weary, and thirsty in the wilderness.”
David mustered the people who were with him and appointed over them commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds.

He dispatched the troops in three divisions: a third under Joab, a third under Abishai son of Zeruiah, Joab’s brother, and a third under Ittai the Gittite. The king then said to the people, “I myself will surely go out with you.”

But the people replied, “You must not go out, for if we flee, they will be utterly indifferent to us; and even if half of us perish, they will be utterly indifferent to us. Yet you are worth ten thousand of us, so it is better that you remain in the city to succor us.”
The king answered them, “I will do whatever seems good in your eyes.” So the king stood beside the gate, while all the people marched out by hundreds and by thousands.
The king had charged Joab, Abishai, and Ittai, saying, “Deal gently, for my sake, with the young man Absalom.” All the people heard the king’s charge to all the commanders concerning Absalom.
So the army went out into the field to meet Israel, and the battle was joined in the forest of Ephraim.
There the people of Israel were defeated before David’s servants, and the slaughter was great that day—twenty thousand men.
The battle spread over the whole countryside, and on that day the forest devoured more of the people than the sword did.

Absalom happened to encounter David’s servants. He was riding on his mule, and as the mule passed beneath the thick boughs of a great oak, Absalom’s head became entangled in the tree, so that he was suspended between heaven and earth while the mule beneath him kept going.
When one of the men saw this, he told Joab, “Behold, I saw Absalom hanging in an oak.”
Joab said to the man who reported it, “What? You saw him? Why did you not strike him to the ground there? I would have given you ten shekels of silver and a belt.”

But the man replied to Joab, “Even if a thousand shekels were weighed into my hand, I would not lay my hand on the king’s son, for in our hearing the king charged you and Abishai and Ittai, saying, ‘Guard the young man Absalom.’
Otherwise, had I dealt treacherously with his life—and nothing is concealed from the king—you would have stood aloof from me.”
Joab said, “I shall not linger in this fashion before you.” He took three javelins in his hand and thrust them into Absalom’s heart while he was still alive in the oak.
Then ten young men who bore Joab’s armor surrounded Absalom, struck him, and killed him.
Joab blew the trumpet, and the people ceased pursuing Israel, for Joab restrained the people.
They took Absalom and cast him into a great pit in the forest and raised over him a very large heap of stones, while all Israel fled, each to his own tent.

Now Absalom, in his lifetime, had taken and set up for himself a pillar in the King’s Valley, for he said, “I have no son to keep my name in remembrance.” He called the pillar after his own name, and it is called Absalom’s Monument to this day.
Then Ahimaaz son of Zadok said, “Let me run and carry tidings to the king that the LORD has vindicated him against his enemies.”
Joab said to him, “You are not a man of good tidings today; you may bring tidings another day, but today you shall bring no tidings, because the king’s son is dead.”
Joab said to the Cushite, “Go, tell the king what you have seen.” The Cushite bowed to Joab and ran.
Ahimaaz son of Zadok said yet again to Joab, “Let happen what may, I will run after the Cushite.” Joab said, “Why would you run, my son, seeing that you will have no reward for your tidings?”
“Let happen what may,” he said, “I will run.” So Joab said, “Run.” Ahimaaz ran by way of the plain and passed the Cushite.
Now David was sitting between the two gates, and the watchman went up to the roof of the gate by the wall. He looked out and saw a man running alone.
So the watchman called out and told the king. The king said, “If he is alone, he has good news.” As the man drew nearer,

the watchman saw another man running. So he called to the gatekeeper and said, “Look, there is another man running alone. This one must be bringing good news as well.” “He is also a bearer of good tidings,” said the king.
The watchman said, “I think the running of the first man is like the running of Ahimaaz son of Zadok.” The king said, “He is a good man and comes with good news.”

Then Ahimaaz called out to the king, “All is well!” He bowed down before the king with his face to the ground and said, “Blessed be the LORD your God, who has delivered up the men who raised their hands against my lord the king.”
The king asked, “Is the young man Absalom safe?” Ahimaaz answered, “When Joab sent your servant, I saw a great commotion, but I did not know what it was.”
“Turn aside and stand here,” said the king. So he turned aside and stood still.
Just then the Cushite arrived and said, “May my lord the king receive good news: The LORD has vindicated you today from all who rose up against you.”
The king asked the Cushite, “Is the young man Absalom safe?” The Cushite replied, “May the enemies of my lord the king and all who rise up against you to harm you be like that young man.”

Then the king was deeply moved, and he went up to the chamber above the gate and wept. And as he went, he said, “O my son Absalom! My son, my son Absalom! If only I had died instead of you—O Absalom, my son, my son!”
It was reported to Joab that the king was weeping and mourning over Absalom.
Moreover, the triumph of that day had been transmuted into universal lamentation, for the people had heard that the king was grieving for his son.
Thus the troops entered the city stealthily, as soldiers who have been routed slink back in shame.
The king, meanwhile, veiled his face and wailed with a great cry, "O my son Absalom! O Absalom, my son, my son!"

Joab then entered the king's residence and said, "Today you have humiliated all your servants who preserved your life this day, together with the lives of your sons and your daughters, your wives and your concubines.

You cherish those who despise you and despise those who cherish you! Indeed, you have made unmistakably clear today that commanders and troops are of no account to you. I now perceive that if Absalom were alive and all of us dead today, you would be gratified.

Now, therefore, arise, go forth, and speak to the heart of your servants; for I swear by the LORD that if you do not go out, not one man will remain with you tonight, and that calamity will be worse for you than every adversity that has befallen you from your youth until now."

So the king arose and took his seat at the gate. When all the people were informed that the king was sitting at the gate, they came before the king. Meanwhile, the Israelites had fled, each man to his own home.

Throughout the tribes of Israel, the people were contending, saying, "The king rescued us from the hand of our enemies and delivered us from the Philistines; yet now he has fled the land because of Absalom.
But Absalom, whom we anointed over us, has perished in battle. Why, then, are you silent about restoring the king?"

King David sent word to Zadok and Abiathar, the priests: "Say to the elders of Judah, 'Why should you be the last to restore the king to his palace, when word of all Israel has reached the king at his house?
You are my brothers, my own flesh and blood. Why, then, should you be the last to restore the king?' And say to Amasa,
'Are you not my own flesh and blood? May God deal with me, and ever so severely, if from now on you are not the commander of my army in place of Joab.'"
Thus Amasa won the hearts of all the men of Judah as though they were one man, and they sent word to the king: "Return, you and all your servants."
So the king returned and came to the Jordan. The men of Judah, having gone to Gilgal to meet the king, were prepared to escort him across the Jordan.
Shimei son of Gera, the Benjaminite from Bahurim, hurried down with the men of Judah to meet King David.
A thousand men of Benjamin were with him, along with Ziba, the steward of Saul's house, with his fifteen sons and twenty servants; they pressed forward to the Jordan ahead of the king
and crossed the ford to bring over the king's household and to do whatever seemed good to him. As Shimei son of Gera crossed the Jordan, he fell prostrate before the king
and said, "My lord, do not impute guilt to me, and do not remember the wrong your servant committed on the day my lord the king departed from Jerusalem; let not the king take it to heart.
For your servant knows that he has sinned, and behold, I have come today, first among all the house of Joseph, to go down and meet my lord the king."
Abishai son of Zeruiah, however, said, "Should not Shimei be put to death for this, since he cursed the LORD's anointed?"

David replied, "What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah, that you should be adversaries to me today? Is any man to be put to death in Israel today? Do I not know that today I am king over Israel?"
So the king said to Shimei, "You shall not die." And the king swore an oath to him.

Mephibosheth, Saul's grandson, also went down to meet the king. He had neither dressed his feet nor trimmed his mustache nor washed his clothes from the day the king departed until the day he returned in peace.
When he came to Jerusalem to meet the king, the king said to him, "Why did you not go with me, Mephibosheth?"

"My lord the king," he replied, "because your servant is lame, I said, 'I will saddle a donkey for myself, mount it, and accompany the king.' But my servant Ziba deceived me and slandered your servant to my lord the king.
Yet my lord the king is like the angel of God; therefore do what is good in your eyes.
For all my father's house were as good as dead before my lord the king, yet you placed your servant among those who eat at your table. What further claim, then, do I have to cry out to the king?"
The king replied, "Why speak further of your affairs? I have decided that you and Ziba shall divide the field."
Mephibosheth said to the king, "Let him take it all, since my lord the king has returned to his house in peace."
Barzillai the Gileadite came down from Rogelim to escort the king across the Jordan.
Barzillai was very old, eighty years of age, and he had sustained the king during his stay at Mahanaim, for he was a man of great wealth.
The king said to Barzillai, "Cross over with me, and I will provide for you in Jerusalem."
Barzillai replied to the king, "How many years of life remain to me, that I should go up to Jerusalem with the king?"

"I am eighty years old today. Can I still distinguish good from evil? Can your servant taste what he eats or drinks? Can he hear the voices of singing men and women? Why should your servant be a burden to my lord the king?"
"Your servant will go only a little way across the Jordan with the king. Why should the king repay me with such a reward?"

"Please let your servant return, that I may die in my own city, near the tomb of my father and mother. But here is your servant Chimham; let him cross over with my lord the king, and do for him what seems good to you."
The king replied, "Chimham shall cross over with me, and I will do for him what seems good to you; whatever you desire of me, I will do for you."
So all the people crossed the Jordan, and then the king crossed. The king kissed Barzillai, blessed him, and he returned to his home.
The king then went on to Gilgal, and Chimham accompanied him. All the people of Judah, and half the people of Israel, escorted the king across.

Soon all the men of Israel came to the king and said, "Why have our brothers, the men of Judah, stolen you away and brought the king and his household across the Jordan, together with all David's men?"
The men of Judah answered the men of Israel, "Because the king is our close kinsman. Why are you angry over this? Have we eaten at the king's expense, or has he given us any gift?"

The men of Israel answered the men of Judah, "We have ten shares in the king, and we have even more claim on David than you. Why then did you despise us? Were we not the first to speak of restoring our king?" But the words of the men of Judah were harsher than those of the men of Israel.

A worthless fellow named Sheba son of Bichri, a Benjamite, happened to be there; he sounded the trumpet and proclaimed, “We have no portion in David, no patrimony in the son of Jesse. Every man to his own home, Israel!”
So all the men of Israel deserted David and followed Sheba son of Bichri, while the men of Judah remained loyal to their king from the Jordan to Jerusalem.

When David returned to his house in Jerusalem, the king took the ten concubines whom he had left to keep the house and placed them in a guarded residence; he provided for them, but he did not go in to them. They were confined as though widowed until the day of their death.
Then the king said to Amasa, “Summon the men of Judah to me within three days, and you be present here.”
Amasa went to summon Judah, but he tarried beyond the appointed time.
David said to Abishai, “Now Sheba son of Bichri will do us more harm than Absalom did. You take your lord's servants and pursue him, lest he secure fortified cities and elude us.”
So Joab's men went out after him—the Cherethites, the Pelethites, and all the mighty men—and they departed from Jerusalem to pursue Sheba son of Bichri.

When they reached the great stone in Gibeon, Amasa came to meet them. Joab was wearing his military tunic, with a sword in its sheath fastened at his waist; as he advanced, the sword slipped from its sheath.
Joab said to Amasa, “Is it well with you, my brother?” and took Amasa by the beard with his right hand to kiss him.

Amasa was not on guard against the sword in Joab's hand; Joab struck him in the abdomen, spilling his entrails to the ground, and he did not need to strike again. So Amasa died. Then Joab and his brother Abishai pursued Sheba son of Bichri.
One of Joab's young men stood beside Amasa and cried, “Whoever is for Joab and whoever is for David, follow Joab!”
Amasa lay wallowing in his blood in the middle of the highway. When the man saw that everyone who came by stopped, he dragged Amasa from the highway into the field and threw a garment over him.
Once he had been removed from the highway, all the men passed on after Joab to pursue Sheba son of Bichri.
He passed through all the tribes of Israel to Abel of Beth-maachah and to all the Berites, who mustered and followed him as well.
They came and besieged him in Abel of Beth-maachah, raising a siege ramp against the city until it reached the wall; all the people with Joab were battering the wall to bring it down.
Then a wise woman called from the city, “Listen! Listen! Please tell Joab, ‘Come here, that I may speak with you.’”
He approached her, and the woman said, “Are you Joab?” He answered, “I am.” She said, “Listen to the words of your servant.” He said, “I am listening.”
She said, “In former times people would say, ‘Let them inquire in Abel,’ and so the matter would be settled.
I am among the peaceful and faithful of Israel. You seek to destroy a city, a mother in Israel. Why would you consume the inheritance of the LORD?”
Joab answered, “Far be it from me, far be it, that I should consume or destroy!”

Joab said, “The matter is not so. A man named Sheba son of Bichri from the hill country of Ephraim has raised his hand against the king, against David. Hand over that man alone, and I will withdraw from the city.” The woman said to Joab, “Behold, his head shall be thrown to you over the wall.”

Then the woman went to all the people in her wisdom, and they cut off the head of Sheba son of Bichri and threw it to Joab. He blew the trumpet, and they dispersed from the city, each to his own home. Joab returned to the king in Jerusalem.
Joab was over all the army of Israel; Benaiah son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and the Pelethites.
Adoram was over the forced labor; Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was the recorder.
Sheva was scribe; Zadok and Abiathar were priests.
Ira the Jairite was also priest to David.

In the days of David a famine prevailed for three years, year after year; and David sought the face of the LORD. And the LORD said, “It is for Saul and for his bloodthirsty house, because he put the Gibeonites to death.”

So the king called the Gibeonites and spoke to them. Now the Gibeonites were not among the children of Israel, but were of the remnant of the Amorites; although the children of Israel had sworn an oath to them, Saul had sought to destroy them in his zeal for the children of Israel and Judah.
David said to the Gibeonites, “What shall I do for you? And with what shall I make atonement, that you may bless the inheritance of the LORD?”
The Gibeonites said to him, “We have neither silver nor gold with Saul or with his house, nor is it ours to put any man to death in Israel.” David said, “Whatever you say, I will do for you.”
They said to the king, “The man who consumed us and plotted against us, so that we should be destroyed from remaining in all the territory of Israel—
let seven men of his sons be given to us, and we will hang them before the LORD in Gibeah of Saul, the chosen of the LORD.” David said, “I will give them.”
But the king spared Mephibosheth son of Jonathan son of Saul, because of the oath of the LORD that was between them, between David and Jonathan son of Saul.

So the king took Armoni and Mephibosheth, the two sons of Rizpah daughter of Aiah whom she bore to Saul, and the five sons of Michal daughter of Saul whom she bore to Adriel son of Barzillai the Meholathite.

And he gave them into the hand of the Gibeonites, and they hanged them on the hill before the LORD; and all seven fell together. They were put to death in the first days of harvest, at the beginning of the barley harvest.

Then Rizpah daughter of Aiah took sackcloth and spread it for herself on the rock, from the beginning of harvest until rain from heaven poured down upon them; and she did not allow the birds of heaven to rest on them by day, nor the beasts of the field by night.
And it was told to David what Rizpah daughter of Aiah, the concubine of Saul, had done.

So David went and took the bones of Saul and the bones of Jonathan his son from the men of Jabesh-gilead, who had stolen them from the public square of Beth-shan, where the Philistines had hanged them, on the day the Philistines struck down Saul at Gilboa.
And he brought up from there the bones of Saul and the bones of Jonathan his son; and they gathered the bones of those who had been hanged.

And they buried the bones of Saul and of Jonathan his son in the land of Benjamin at Zela, in the tomb of Kish his father; and they did all that the king commanded. After that, God was entreated for the land.
Moreover, the Philistines had war again with Israel; and David went down, and his servants with him, and fought against the Philistines; and David grew weary.
And Ishbi-benob, who was among the descendants of the giant, whose spear weighed three hundred shekels of bronze, and who was girded with a new sword, sought to kill David.

But Abishai son of Zeruiah came to his aid, struck the Philistine, and killed him. Then David’s men swore to him, saying, “You shall go out no more with us to battle, lest your death extinguish the light of Israel.”
After this there was again war with the Philistines at Gob; then Sibbecai the Hushathite struck down Saph, who was among the descendants of the giant.
And there was again war with the Philistines at Gob; and Elhanan son of Jaare-oregim the Bethlehemite struck down Goliath the Gittite, the shaft of whose spear was like a weaver’s beam.
And there was again war at Gath; and there was a man of great stature who had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot, twenty-four in number; and he also was born to the giant.
And when he defied Israel, Jonathan son of Shimea, David’s brother, struck him down.
These four were born to the giant in Gath, and they fell by the hand of David and by the hand of his servants.
David spoke these words to the LORD in song on the day the LORD delivered him from the grasp of all his enemies and from Saul’s hand.
“The LORD is my rock, my fortress, and my deliverer.
God is my rock, in whom I take refuge; He is my shield and the horn of my salvation, my stronghold and my refuge, my Savior, who saves me from violence.
I call upon the LORD, who is worthy of praise, and I am saved from my enemies.
“For the breakers of death surrounded me; the torrents of destruction terrified me.
The cords of Sheol entangled me; the snares of death confronted me.
In my distress I called upon the LORD; I cried out to my God, and from His temple He heard my voice; my cry came into His ears.
“Then the earth shook and trembled; the foundations of the heavens quaked and were shaken, because He was angry.
Smoke ascended from His nostrils, and devouring fire came from His mouth; coals were kindled by it.
He bowed the heavens and descended, with thick darkness beneath His feet.
He rode upon a cherub and flew; He was seen upon the wings of the wind.
He made darkness His canopy around Him—dark waters and thick clouds of the skies.
From the brightness before Him coals of fire burned.
The LORD thundered from heaven; the Most High uttered His voice.
He shot forth arrows and scattered them; He flashed lightning and routed them.
Then the channels of the sea appeared, and the foundations of the world were laid bare at the rebuke of the LORD, at the blast of the breath of His nostrils.
“He sent from on high and took me; He drew me out of many waters.
He delivered me from my strong enemy, from those who hated me, for they were too mighty for me.
They confronted me in the day of my calamity, but the LORD was my support.
He brought me out into a broad place; He rescued me because He delighted in me.
“The LORD has dealt with me according to my righteousness; according to the cleanness of my hands He has repaid me.
For I have kept the ways of the LORD and have not wickedly departed from my God.
For all His ordinances are before me, and from His statutes I have not turned aside.
I have been blameless before Him, and I have kept myself from my iniquity.
Therefore the LORD has repaid me according to my righteousness, according to my cleanness in His sight.
“With the faithful You show Yourself faithful; with the blameless man You show Yourself blameless.
With the pure You show Yourself pure, and with the crooked You show Yourself shrewd.
You save an afflicted people, but Your eyes are upon the haughty to bring them down.
For You are my lamp, O the LORD; and the LORD lightens my darkness.
For by You I run against a troop; by my God I leap over a wall.
As for God, His way is perfect; the word of the LORD is proven; He is a shield to all who take refuge in Him.
“For who is God besides the LORD? And who is a rock besides our God?
God is my strength and fortress, and He makes my way perfect.
He makes my feet like the feet of a deer and sets me upon my high places.
He trains my hands for war, so that my arms can bend a bow of bronze.
You have also given me the shield of Your salvation, and Your gentleness has made me great.
You enlarge my steps beneath me, so that my feet do not slip.
“I pursued my enemies and destroyed them; I did not turn back until they were consumed.
I consumed them and shattered them, so that they could not rise; they fell beneath my feet.
For You have girded me with strength for battle; You subdued under me those who rose up against me.
You made my enemies turn their backs to me, and I silenced those who hated me.
They looked, but there was no savior; they cried to the LORD, but He did not answer them.
I beat them as fine as the dust of the earth; I crushed and trampled them like mud in the streets.
“You have delivered me from the strivings of my people; You have kept me as head of the nations; a people I did not know serves me.
Foreigners cringe before me; as soon as they hear of me, they obey me.
Foreigners fade away and come trembling from their strongholds.
“The LORD lives, and blessed be my rock; and exalted be God, the rock of my salvation—
the God who gives me vengeance and brings down peoples under me,
who brings me out from my enemies. You exalt me above those who rise against me; You deliver me from the violent man.
Therefore I will give thanks to You, O the LORD, among the nations, and I will sing praises to Your name.
He is a tower of salvation to His king, and shows steadfast love to His anointed, to David and to his offspring forever.”
These are the last words of David: the oracle of David son of Jesse, the oracle of the man raised up on high, the anointed of the God of Jacob, and the sweet psalmist of Israel.
“The Spirit of the LORD has spoken through me, and His word has been upon my tongue.
The God of Israel has said, the Rock of Israel has spoken to me: ‘He who rules over men must be just, ruling in the fear of God.
He shall be like the light of morning when the sun rises, a morning without clouds, like the tender grass springing from the earth after rain.’
Is not my house right with God? For He has made with me an everlasting covenant, ordered and secured in every part. Will He not bring to fruition all my salvation and all my desire?
But the worthless are all like thorns to be cast away, for they cannot be taken by hand;
yet the man who touches them must be armed with iron and the shaft of a spear, and they shall be utterly burned with fire where they lie.”
These are the names of David’s mighty men: Josheb-basshebeth the Tahchemonite, chief of the Three—he was called Adino the Eznite—because he slew eight hundred men at one time.
After him was Eleazar son of Dodo, son of Ahohi, one of the three mighty men with David, when they defied the Philistines who had gathered there for battle, while the men of Israel had withdrawn.
He arose and struck the Philistines until his hand grew weary and clung to his sword, and the LORD wrought a great victory that day; the people returned after him only to strip the slain.
After him was Shammah son of Agee the Hararite. The Philistines had gathered into a troop where there was a plot of ground full of lentils, and the people fled from the Philistines.
But he took his stand in the midst of the plot, defended it, and struck the Philistines; and the LORD wrought a great victory.
Three of the thirty chief went down and came to David at harvest time, to the cave of Adullam; and the troop of the Philistines was encamped in the Valley of Rephaim.
David was then in the stronghold, and the garrison of the Philistines was then in Bethlehem.
And David longed and said, “Oh, that someone would give me a drink of the water from the well of Bethlehem by the gate!”

So the three mighty men broke through the camp of the Philistines, drew water from the well of Bethlehem by the gate, carried it, and brought it to David; but he would not drink it, but poured it out to the LORD.

And he said, “Far be it from me, O the LORD, that I should do this. Is this not the blood of the men who went at the risk of their lives?” Therefore he would not drink it. These things the three mighty men did.
And Abishai, the brother of Joab, son of Zeruiah, was chief of the Three; he lifted up his spear against three hundred and slew them, and had a name among the Three.
Was he not most honored among the Three, so that he became their captain? Yet he did not attain to the Three.
And Benaiah son of Jehoiada, son of a valiant man of Kabzeel, who had done many acts, slew the two sons of Ariel of Moab; he went down also and slew a lion in the midst of a pit in time of snow.

And he slew an Egyptian, a man of great stature; the Egyptian had a spear in his hand, but he went down to him with a staff, plucked the spear out of the Egyptian’s hand, and slew him with his own spear.
These things Benaiah son of Jehoiada did, and had a name among the three mighty men.
He was more honorable than the thirty, but he did not attain to the Three; and David set him over his bodyguard.
Asahel the brother of Joab was one of the thirty; Elhanan son of Dodo of Bethlehem;
Shammah the Harodite; Elika the Harodite;
Helez the Paltite; Ira son of Ikkesh the Tekoite;
Abiezer the Anathothite; Mebunnai the Hushathite;
Zalmon the Ahohite; Maharai the Netophathite;
Heleb son of Baanah the Netophathite; Ittai son of Ribai of Gibeah of the children of Benjamin;
Benaiah the Pirathonite; Hiddai of the brooks of Gaash;
Abi-albon the Arbathite; Azmaveth the Barhumite;
Eliahba the Shaalbonite; the sons of Jashen; Jonathan;
Shammah the Hararite; Ahiam son of Sharar the Hararite;
Eliphelet son of Ahasbai, son of the Maacathite; Eliam son of Ahithophel the Gilonite;
Hezro the Carmelite; Paarai the Arbite;
Igal son of Nathan of Zobah; Bani the Gadite;
Zelek the Ammonite; Naharai the Beerothite, armor-bearers of Joab son of Zeruiah;
Ira the Ithrite; Gareb the Ithrite;
and Uriah the Hittite—thirty-seven in all.
Again the anger of the LORD burned against Israel, and He incited David against them, saying, "Go, number Israel and Judah."

So the king said to Joab, the commander of the army who was with him, "Go now throughout all the tribes of Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, and count the people, so that I may know the number of the people."
But Joab said to the king, "May the LORD your God add to the people a hundred times as many as they are, while the eyes of my lord the king see; yet why does my lord the king delight in this thing?"
Nevertheless, the king's word prevailed over Joab and over the commanders of the army. So Joab and the commanders of the army went out from the presence of the king to count the people of Israel.
They crossed the Jordan and camped in Aroer, on the right side of the city that is in the middle of the valley of Gad, and toward Jazer.
Then they came to Gilead and to the land of Tahtim-hodshi; they came to Dan-jaan and around toward Sidon.
They came to the fortress of Tyre and to all the cities of the Hivites and the Canaanites, and they went out to the Negev of Judah at Beersheba.
After nine months and twenty days they had gone through all the land, and they came to Jerusalem.
Joab gave the king the number of the counted people: there were in Israel eight hundred thousand valiant men who drew the sword, and the men of Judah were five hundred thousand.

Afterward David's heart struck him, because he had numbered the people. David said to the LORD, "I have sinned greatly in what I have done. Now, O LORD, please take away the iniquity of Your servant, for I have acted very foolishly."
When David rose in the morning, the word of the LORD came to Gad the prophet, David's seer, saying,
"Go and speak to David: 'Thus says the LORD: I am bringing three things upon you; choose one of them, and I will do it to you.'"

So Gad came to David and told him, and said to him, "Shall seven years of famine come upon your land? Or shall you flee three months before your enemies while they pursue you? Or shall there be three days of pestilence in your land? Now consider and see what answer I should bring back to Him who sent me."
David said to Gad, "I am in great distress. Let us fall into the hand of the LORD, for His mercies are great; but let me not fall into the hand of man."
So the LORD sent a pestilence upon Israel from the morning until the appointed time, and seventy thousand men died, from Dan to Beersheba.

When the angel stretched out his hand toward Jerusalem to destroy it, the LORD relented from the calamity and said to the angel who was destroying the people, "It is enough; now withdraw your hand." And the angel of the LORD was then at the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.

When David saw the angel who was striking the people, he said to the LORD, "Behold, I have sinned, and I have done wrong; but these sheep, what have they done? Let Your hand be against me and against my father's house."
Gad came to David that day and said to him, "Go up and erect an altar to the LORD on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite."
So David went up, according to the word of Gad, as the LORD had commanded.
Araunah looked out and saw the king and his servants crossing over to him. Araunah went out and bowed his face to the ground before the king.

Araunah said, "Why has my lord the king come to his servant?" David said, "To buy the threshing floor from you, in order to build an altar to the LORD, so that the plague may be restrained from the people."

Araunah said to David, "Let my lord the king take and offer up what seems good to him. Look, the oxen are here for the burnt offering, and the threshing sledges and the yokes of the oxen for the wood."
Araunah gave all this to the king. Araunah said, "May the LORD your God accept you."

But the king said to Araunah, "No, I will surely buy it from you for a price; I will not offer to the LORD my God burnt offerings that cost me nothing." So David bought the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver.
David built an altar to the LORD there and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings. The LORD answered the prayer for the land, and the plague was withdrawn from Israel.
Now King David had grown old and advanced in years; though they covered him with garments, he could not be warmed.
His servants therefore said to him, “Let them seek a young virgin for my lord the king, and let her stand before the king, attend him, and lie in your bosom, that my lord the king may be warmed.”
So they sought a beautiful young woman throughout all the territory of Israel, and they found Abishag the Shunammite and brought her to the king.
The young woman was exceedingly beautiful; she became an attendant to the king and served him, but the king did not know her.
Now Adonijah the son of Haggith exalted himself, saying, “I will be king,” and he prepared for himself chariots and horsemen, together with fifty men to run before him.
His father had never displeased him by asking, “Why have you done this?” and he was also very handsome; his mother had borne him after Absalom.
He conferred with Joab the son of Zeruiah and with Abiathar the priest, and they supported Adonijah.
But Zadok the priest, Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, Nathan the prophet, Shimei, Rei, and the mighty men who belonged to David were not with Adonijah.

Adonijah sacrificed sheep, oxen, and fattened cattle by the stone of Zoheleth, which is beside En-rogel, and he invited all his brothers, the king's sons, and all the men of Judah, the king's servants.
But he did not invite Nathan the prophet, Benaiah, the mighty men, or Solomon his brother.
Then Nathan said to Bathsheba the mother of Solomon, “Have you not heard that Adonijah the son of Haggith has become king, while our lord David does not know it?
Now therefore, come, let me give you counsel, that you may save your life and the life of your son Solomon.
Go in to King David and say to him, ‘My lord the king, did you not swear to your maidservant, saying, “Solomon your son shall reign after me and sit on my throne”? Why then has Adonijah become king?’
Then, while you are still speaking with the king, I will come in after you and confirm your words.”
So Bathsheba went in to the king in the chamber. The king was very old, and Abishag the Shunammite was serving the king.
Bathsheba bowed and paid homage to the king, and the king said, “What do you wish?”
She said to him, “My lord, you swore to your maidservant by the the LORD your God that Solomon your son shall reign after me and sit on my throne.
And now, behold, Adonijah has become king, and you, my lord the king, do not know it.

He has sacrificed oxen, fattened cattle, and sheep in abundance, and has invited all the king's sons, Abiathar the priest, and Joab the commander of the army; but Solomon your servant he has not invited.
And you, my lord the king—the eyes of all Israel are upon you, to declare to them who shall sit on the throne of my lord the king after him.
Otherwise, when my lord the king sleeps with his fathers, I and my son Solomon will be reckoned offenders.”
While she was still speaking with the king, Nathan the prophet came in.
They told the king, “Nathan the prophet is here,” and he came in before the king and bowed with his face to the ground.
Nathan said, “My lord the king, have you said, ‘Adonijah shall reign after me and sit on my throne’?

For today he has gone down and sacrificed oxen, fattened cattle, and sheep, and has invited all the king's sons, the commanders of the army, and Abiathar the priest; and behold, they are eating and drinking before him, and saying, ‘Long live King Adonijah!’
But me, your servant, and Zadok the priest, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and Solomon your servant, he has not invited.
Has this affair come from my lord the king, and you have not made known to your servants who should sit on the throne of my lord the king after him?”
Then King David answered and said, “Call Bathsheba to me.” So she came into the king's presence and stood before the king.
The king swore, saying, “As the the LORD lives, who has redeemed my soul from all distress,
as I swore to you by the the LORD the God of Israel, saying, ‘Solomon your son shall reign after me and sit on my throne in my place,’ so will I do this day.”
Then Bathsheba bowed with her face to the ground and paid homage to the king, and said, “May my lord King David live forever!”
Then King David said, “Call to me Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada.” So they came before the king.
The king said to them, “Take with you the servants of your lord, have Solomon my son ride on my own mule, and bring him down to Gihon.
There Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet shall anoint him king over Israel; then blow the trumpet and say, ‘Long live King Solomon!’
Then come up after him, and he shall come and sit on my throne, for he shall be king in my place; I have appointed him ruler over Israel and Judah.”
Benaiah the son of Jehoiada answered the king and said, “Amen! May the the LORD, the God of my lord the king, say so.
As the the LORD has been with my lord the king, so may He be with Solomon, and make his throne greater than the throne of my lord the king David.”
So Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and the Cherethites and the Pelethites went down and had Solomon ride on King David's mule, and brought him to Gihon.
Zadok the priest took the horn of oil from the tent and anointed Solomon. Then they blew the trumpet, and all the people said, “Long live King Solomon!”
All the people went up after him, playing flutes and rejoicing with great joy, so that the earth split with their sound.
Adonijah and all the guests who were with him heard it as they finished eating. When they heard the sound of the trumpet, Joab said, “Why does the city make such an uproar?”
While he was still speaking, behold, Jonathan the son of Abiathar the priest came. Adonijah said, “Come in, for you are a man of valor and bring good news.”
Jonathan answered Adonijah, “No! Our lord King David has made Solomon king.
The king has sent with him Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and the Cherethites and the Pelethites, and they have had him ride on the king's mule.
Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet have anointed him king at Gihon, and they have come up from there rejoicing, so that the city is in an uproar. That is the noise that you have heard.
Solomon has also sat on the royal throne.

Moreover, the king's servants have come to bless our lord King David, saying, ‘May your God make the name of Solomon better than your name, and may He make his throne greater than your throne,’ and the king has bowed himself on the bed.”
The king also said, “Blessed be the the LORD, the God of Israel, who has granted one to sit on my throne this day, my eyes seeing it.”
Then all the guests of Adonijah were terrified and rose and went away, each to his own path.
Adonijah feared Solomon, and he arose and went and took hold of the horns of the altar.

It was told to Solomon, “Behold, Adonijah fears King Solomon, and behold, he has taken hold of the horns of the altar, saying, ‘Let King Solomon swear to me today that he will not put his servant to death with the sword.’”
Solomon said, “If he proves himself a worthy man, not one hair of his head shall fall to the earth; but if wickedness is found in him, he shall die.”
So King Solomon sent, and they brought him down from the altar. He came and bowed before King Solomon, and Solomon said to him, “Go to your house.”
As David's days drew toward their end, he summoned his son Solomon and enjoined him, saying,
"I am about to die, as every mortal must; therefore be strong, and comport yourself as a man.

Moreover, keep the charge of the the LORD your God, walking in His ways and observing His statutes, His commandments, His judgments, and His testimonies, as it is inscribed in the Law of Moses, so that you may act wisely in all your endeavors and prosper wherever you turn,

so that the the LORD may establish His word that He spoke concerning me, saying, 'If your sons attend to their way, to walk before Me in truth with all their heart and all their soul, then you shall not lack a man on the throne of Israel.'"

"Furthermore, you yourself know what Joab son of Zeruiah did to me—how he dealt with the two commanders of Israel's armies, Abner son of Ner and Amasa son of Jether—how he murdered them in a season of peace, staining with the blood of war the belt upon his loins and the sandals upon his feet.
Therefore deal with him according to your discernment, and do not allow his hoary head to descend to Sheol in peace."
"But requite with lovingkindness the sons of Barzillai the Gileadite, and let them eat at your table, for they came to my aid when I fled from your brother Absalom.

Moreover, Shimei son of Gera, the Benjaminite from Bahurim, remains with you; he uttered a bitter curse against me on the day I fled to Mahanaim, yet he came down to meet me at the Jordan, and I swore to him by the the LORD, saying, 'I will not slay you with the sword.'
Now do not acquit him, for you are a discerning man and will know what is fitting for him; bring his gray head down to Sheol in blood."
Then David rested with his ancestors and was buried in the City of David.
The days that David reigned over Israel were forty years: he reigned seven years in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem.
Solomon sat upon the throne of his father David, and his kingdom was firmly established.
Now Adonijah son of Haggith approached Bathsheba, Solomon's mother, and she asked, "Do you come peaceably?" He replied, "Peaceably."
Then he said, "I have a matter to set before you." She said, "Speak."
He said, "You know that the kingship was mine and that all Israel had set their hopes upon me to reign; yet the kingship has turned and passed to my brother, for it was his by the the LORD's decree."
"Now I ask one request of you; do not refuse me." She said, "Speak."
He said, "Please speak to King Solomon—for he will not refuse you—that he give me Abishag the Shunammite as wife."
She said, "Very well; I will intercede with the king for you."

So Bathsheba went to King Solomon to speak to him on Adonijah's behalf. The king rose to meet her, bowed before her, resumed his throne, and caused a throne to be set for the king's mother; and she sat at his right hand.
Then she said, "I have one small petition to ask of you; do not refuse me." The king said to her, "Ask, my mother, for I will not refuse you."
She said, "Let Abishag the Shunammite be given to Adonijah your brother as wife."

King Solomon answered his mother, "Why do you ask Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah? You might as well ask the kingdom for him—for he is my elder brother—and for Abiathar the priest and for Joab son of Zeruiah."
Then King Solomon swore by the the LORD, saying, "May God do so to me, and still more, if Adonijah has not forfeited his life by this very request.
Now therefore, as the the LORD lives, who has established me and set me upon my father David's throne, and who has built me a house, as He promised, Adonijah shall surely be put to death today."
So King Solomon dispatched Benaiah son of Jehoiada, who struck him down, and he died.

To Abiathar the priest the king said, "Withdraw to your fields at Anathoth, for you deserve death; yet I will not put you to death this day, because you bore the ark of the Lord, the the LORD, before David my father, and because you shared in all my father's afflictions."
So Solomon removed Abiathar from the priesthood of the the LORD, thereby fulfilling the word of the the LORD that He had spoken concerning the house of Eli in Shiloh.
When the report reached Joab—for Joab had sided with Adonijah, though he had not sided with Absalom—Joab fled to the tent of the the LORD and seized the horns of the altar.
King Solomon was told that Joab had fled to the tent of the the LORD and was beside the altar. Solomon sent Benaiah son of Jehoiada, saying, "Go, strike him down."
Benaiah came to the tent of the the LORD and said to him, "Thus says the king: 'Come out.'" But he replied, "No; I will die here."

Benaiah reported to the king, "Thus Joab spoke, and thus he answered me." The king said, "Do as he has said; strike him down and bury him, and remove from me and from my father's house the innocent blood that Joab shed.

The the LORD will bring his blood back upon his own head, because he fell upon two men more righteous and better than himself and slew them with the sword—Abner son of Ner, commander of Israel's army, and Amasa son of Jether, commander of Judah's army—without my father David's knowledge.
So their blood shall return upon Joab's head and upon his descendants' heads forever; but upon David, his descendants, his house, and his throne, there shall be peace forever from the the LORD."
Then Benaiah son of Jehoiada went up, struck him down, and killed him; and he was buried at his own house in the wilderness.
The king appointed Benaiah son of Jehoiada over the army in his stead, and Zadok the priest in Abiathar's stead.
The king sent and summoned Shimei, and said to him, "Build a house for yourself in Jerusalem and dwell there; do not leave for any other place.
For on the day you leave and cross the Brook Kidron, know with certainty that you shall surely die; your blood will be on your own head."
Shimei said to the king, "What you say is good; as my lord the king has spoken, so your servant will do." So Shimei dwelt in Jerusalem for many days.
After three years, however, two of Shimei's servants fled to Achish son of Maacah, king of Gath; and Shimei was told, "Behold, your servants are in Gath."
Shimei arose, saddled his donkey, and went to Gath, to Achish, to seek his servants; and Shimei went and brought his servants back from Gath.
It was told to Solomon that Shimei had gone from Jerusalem to Gath and had returned.

The king sent and summoned Shimei, and said to him, "Did I not make you swear by the the LORD and warn you, saying, 'On the day you leave and go anywhere, know for certain that you shall surely die'? And you said to me, 'The word I have heard is good.'
Why then have you not kept the oath of the the LORD and the commandment that I gave you?
You know in your own heart all the evil that you did to David my father; the the LORD will return your wickedness upon your own head.
But King Solomon shall be blessed, and David's throne shall be established before the the LORD forever."
The king commanded Benaiah son of Jehoiada, who went out and struck him down, and he died. Thus the kingdom was secured in Solomon's hand.

Solomon contracted a marital alliance with Pharaoh, king of Egypt; he took Pharaoh’s daughter and brought her into the City of David, where she remained until he had completed his own residence, the house of the LORD, and the wall surrounding Jerusalem.
Meanwhile, the people continued to sacrifice at the high places, for no house had yet been built for the name of the LORD.
Solomon loved the LORD, walking in the statutes of David his father; nevertheless, he himself sacrificed and burned incense at the high places.
The king went to Gibeon to sacrifice there, for it was the preeminent high place; upon that altar Solomon offered a thousand burnt offerings.
At Gibeon the LORD appeared to Solomon in a dream by night, and God said, “Ask what I shall give you.”

Solomon replied, “You have shown great and steadfast love to Your servant David my father, because he walked before You in truth, in righteousness, and in uprightness of heart toward You; and You have kept for him this great steadfast love, and have given him a son to sit on his throne, as it is this day.
And now, O the LORD my God, You have made Your servant king in place of David my father, though I am but a little child and do not know how to go out or come in.
And Your servant is in the midst of Your people whom You have chosen, a great people, too many to be numbered or counted.
Give therefore Your servant an understanding heart to govern Your people, that I may discern between good and evil; for who is able to govern this great people of Yours?”
The request pleased the Lord, because Solomon had asked for this.

And God said to him, “Because you have asked this thing, and have not asked for yourself long life, or riches, or the life of your enemies, but have asked for yourself discernment to understand justice,
behold, I have done according to your words: behold, I have given you a wise and discerning heart, so that there has been no one like you before you, and no one like you shall arise after you.
I give you also what you have not asked—both riches and honor—so that no king shall be your equal all your days.
And if you will walk in My ways, keeping My statutes and My commandments, as David your father walked, then I will lengthen your days.”

Then Solomon awoke, and behold, it had been a dream. He came to Jerusalem and stood before the ark of the covenant of the LORD, and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, and made a feast for all his servants.
Then two women who were prostitutes came to the king and stood before him.
The one woman said, “O my lord, this woman and I live in the same house, and I gave birth while she was in the house.
On the third day after I gave birth, this woman also gave birth. We were alone together; no stranger was with us in the house, only we two.
And this woman’s son died in the night, because she lay on him.
She arose at midnight and took my son from beside me, while I, your maidservant, slept, and laid him at her breast, and laid her dead son at my breast.
When I rose in the morning to nurse my son, behold, he was dead. But when I examined him carefully in the morning, behold, he was not the son I had borne.”
The other woman said, “No; the living child is mine, and the dead child is yours.” But the first said, “No; the dead child is yours, and the living child is mine.” Thus they argued before the king.
The king said, “The one says, ‘This is my living son, and your son is dead’; and the other says, ‘No, your son is dead, and my son is the living one.’”
The king said, “Bring me a sword.” So they brought a sword before the king.
The king said, “Divide the living child in two, and give half to the one and half to the other.”

Then the woman whose son was alive—because her compassion yearned for her son—said to the king, “O my lord, give her the living child, and by no means put him to death.” But the other said, “Let him be neither mine nor yours; divide him.”
The king answered, “Give the living child to the first woman, and do not kill him; she is his mother.”
When all Israel heard the judgment that the king had rendered, they stood in awe of the king, because they perceived that the wisdom of God was in him to execute justice.
King Solomon reigned over all Israel.
These were the officials he had: Azariah son of Zadok the priest;
Elihoreph and Ahijah, sons of Shisha, scribes; Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud, the recorder;
Benaiah son of Jehoiada over the army; and Zadok and Abiathar, priests.
Azariah son of Nathan was over the deputies; Zabud son of Nathan, a priest, was the king's friend.
Ahishar was over the household, and Adoniram son of Abda was over the forced labor.
Solomon had twelve governors over all Israel, who provided food for the king and his household; each was responsible for one month of the year.
Their names were these: Ben-Hur in the hill country of Ephraim;
Ben-Deker in Makaz, Shaalbim, Beth-shemesh, and Elon-beth-hanan;
Ben-Hesed in Arubboth, to whom were assigned Socoh and all the land of Hepher;
Ben-Abinadab in all Naphath-dor, who had Taphath, Solomon's daughter, as his wife;
Baana son of Ahilud in Taanach, Megiddo, and all Beth-shean beside Zarethan below Jezreel, from Beth-shean to Abel-meholah as far as Jokneam;
Ben-Geber in Ramoth-gilead, to whom belonged the villages of Jair son of Manasseh in Gilead and the region of Argob in Bashan—sixty great cities with walls and bronze bars;
Ahinadab son of Iddo in Mahanaim;
Ahimaaz in Naphtali, who had taken Basemath, Solomon's daughter, as his wife;
Baana son of Hushai in Asher and Bealoth;
Jehoshaphat son of Paruah in Issachar;
Shimei son of Ela in Benjamin;
and Geber son of Uri in the land of Gilead—the country of Sihon king of the Amorites and of Og king of Bashan. There was also one governor in that land.
Judah and Israel were as numerous as the sand on the seashore; they ate, drank, and rejoiced.
Solomon ruled over all the kingdoms from the Euphrates to the land of the Philistines and to the border of Egypt; they brought tribute and served Solomon all the days of his life.
Solomon's provision for one day was thirty kors of fine flour and sixty kors of meal.
It also included ten fat oxen, twenty pasture-fed oxen, and a hundred sheep, besides deer, gazelles, roebucks, and fattened fowl.
For he ruled over all the lands beyond the Euphrates, from Tiphsah to Gaza, over all the kings beyond the Euphrates; and he had peace on all sides.
Throughout Solomon's days, Judah and Israel dwelt securely, from Dan to Beersheba, each man under his vine and under his fig tree.
Solomon had forty thousand stalls of horses for his chariots and twelve thousand horsemen.
Those officers provided food for King Solomon and for all who came to the king's table, each in his month; they ensured that nothing was lacking.
They also brought barley and straw for the horses and chariot horses to the place where it was required, each according to his charge.
God gave Solomon wisdom and very great discernment, and breadth of mind like the sand on the seashore.
Solomon's wisdom surpassed the wisdom of all the sons of the east and all the wisdom of Egypt.
He was wiser than all men—than Ethan the Ezrahite, Heman, Calcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol—and his fame spread throughout all the surrounding nations.
He spoke three thousand proverbs, and his songs numbered a thousand and five.
He spoke about trees, from the cedar in Lebanon to the hyssop that grows out of the wall; he spoke also about beasts, birds, creeping things, and fish.
People came from all nations to hear Solomon's wisdom, sent by all the kings of the earth who had heard of his wisdom.
Now Hiram, king of Tyre, dispatched his servants to Solomon upon learning that Solomon had been anointed king in his father’s stead, for Hiram had ever been a friend to David.
Solomon, in turn, sent word to Hiram:
“You know that my father David was unable to erect a house for the Name of the LORD his God, because of the wars that encircled him, until the LORD subdued his foes beneath the soles of his feet.
But now the LORD my God has granted me tranquility on every side; there is neither adversary nor calamity.

Therefore I am resolved to build a house for the Name of the LORD my God, in accordance with what the LORD declared to my father David, saying, ‘Your son, whom I shall set upon your throne in your stead, shall build the house for My Name.’

Consequently, command that cedars be hewn for me from Lebanon; my servants shall labor alongside your servants, and I shall remunerate your servants according to whatever wage you stipulate, for you know that none among us possesses the timber-cutting expertise of the Sidonians.”
When Hiram heard Solomon’s words, he rejoiced exceedingly and said, “Blessed be the LORD this day, who has granted David a wise son to preside over this great people.”
Then Hiram sent a response to Solomon: “I have heard the message you sent me; I shall fulfill all your desire concerning cedar and cypress timber.

My servants shall convey the timber from Lebanon seaward, and I shall bind it into rafts upon the sea, directing it to whatever place you designate; there I shall have it dismantled, and you may remove it. In exchange, you shall attend to my needs by supplying provisions for my household.”
Thus Hiram supplied Solomon with all the cedar and cypress timber he desired,
while Solomon gave Hiram twenty thousand cors of wheat as provisions for his household, together with twenty cors of beaten olive oil; Solomon rendered this to Hiram on a yearly basis.
