Moreover, the LORD endowed Solomon with wisdom, as He had promised, and there was peace between Hiram and Solomon; the two of them concluded a treaty.
Then King Solomon levied a forced-labor contingent of thirty thousand men from all Israel.
He sent them to Lebanon in monthly rotations of ten thousand, whereby each cohort labored one month in Lebanon and then enjoyed two months at home; and Adoniram superintended the levy.
Solomon had seventy thousand porters and eighty thousand stonecutters in the mountains,
in addition to three thousand three hundred overseers who directed the laborers.
The king also commanded that they quarry massive, costly stones, wherewith to lay the foundation of the temple.
Consequently, the builders of Solomon and Hiram, along with the Gebalites, quarried the stone and prepared timber and stone for the erection of the temple.

In the four hundred and eightieth year after the Israelites had departed from Egypt—in the fourth year of Solomon's reign over Israel, in the month of Ziv, which is the second month—Solomon began to build the house of the LORD.
The house that King Solomon built for the LORD measured sixty cubits in length, twenty cubits in width, and thirty cubits in height.
The vestibule before the nave of the house was twenty cubits long, corresponding to the breadth of the house, and ten cubits wide in front of the house.
He also made for the house windows with beveled frames.
Against the wall of the house he built an annex encircling the walls of the house on every side, both about the nave and the inner sanctuary, and he made side chambers all around.

The lowest story was five cubits wide, the middle six cubits, and the third seven cubits, for he had provided offsets in the wall of the house all around the outside, so that the beams would not be fastened into the walls of the house.
While the house was being built, it was constructed of finished stone quarried at the site, so that no hammer, axe, or iron tool was heard in the house during its construction.
The entrance to the middle story was on the right side of the house; and by winding stairs they went up to the middle story, and from the middle to the third.
He built the house and finished it, and covered the house with beams and planks of cedar.
He built the annex against the whole house, five cubits high, and fastened the house with cedar timbers.
And the word of the LORD came to Solomon, saying,

“Concerning this house that you are building, if you walk in My statutes and observe My ordinances and keep all My commandments by walking in them, then I will establish My word with you, which I spoke to your father David.
And I will dwell among the children of Israel and will not forsake My people Israel.”
So Solomon built the house and completed it.
He lined the interior walls of the house with cedar boards, paneling from the floor of the house to the ceiling, and he overlaid the floor of the house with cypress boards.
He built twenty cubits of the rear of the house with cedar boards, from the floor to the walls, and he constructed it within as an inner sanctuary, the Most Holy Place.
The house—that is, the nave in front of it—was forty cubits long.
The cedar within the house was carved with gourds and open flowers; all was cedar, and no stone was visible.
He prepared the inner sanctuary within the house to set there the ark of the covenant of the LORD.
The inner sanctuary was twenty cubits in length, twenty cubits in width, and twenty cubits in height; he overlaid it with pure gold, and he overlaid the altar, which was of cedar.
Solomon overlaid the interior of the house with pure gold; he passed chains of gold across the front of the inner sanctuary, and he overlaid it with gold.
He overlaid the whole house with gold until the whole house was finished; he also overlaid with gold the whole altar that was before the inner sanctuary.
In the inner sanctuary he made two cherubim of olive wood, each ten cubits high.
One wing of the first cherub was five cubits, and the other wing of the first cherub was five cubits; the span from the tip of one wing to the tip of the other was ten cubits.
The second cherub was also ten cubits; the two cherubim were of one measure and one form.
The height of the one cherub was ten cubits, and so was the height of the other cherub.

He placed the cherubim in the innermost room; their wings were spread, so that the wing of one touched one wall and the wing of the other touched the opposite wall, while their wings touched one another in the middle of the room.
He overlaid the cherubim with gold.
He carved all the walls of the house around, both inner and outer chambers, with carved figures of cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers.
He overlaid the floor of the house with gold, both in the inner and outer chambers.
For the entrance to the inner sanctuary he made doors of olive wood; the lintel and doorposts occupied one-fifth of the wall.
The two doors were of olive wood; he carved on them cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers, and overlaid them with gold, spreading the gold over the cherubim and palm trees.
So also he made for the entrance to the nave doorposts of olive wood, occupying one-fourth of the wall.
He made two doors of cypress wood; each door had two leaves that folded.
He carved on them cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers, and overlaid them with gold, evenly applied over the carved work.
He built the inner court with three courses of hewn stone and a course of cedar beams.
The foundation of the house of the LORD was laid in the fourth year, in the month of Ziv.
In the eleventh year, in the month of Bul, the eighth month, the house was completed in all its details and according to all its plans; thus he built it in seven years.
Solomon devoted thirteen years to the construction of his palace, and he brought the whole of that domestic edifice to completion.

He built the Palace of the Forest of Lebanon—one hundred cubits in length, fifty in breadth, and thirty in height—resting upon four rows of cedar pillars, with trimmed cedar beams laid upon the pillars.
It was roofed in cedar above the side chambers that rested upon the pillars: forty-five beams, fifteen to each row.
The windows were elevated in three tiers, with aperture confronting aperture in threefold array.
Every doorway and doorpost was square in its framing, and opening faced opening in threefold order.
He fashioned a colonnade fifty cubits long and thirty wide, preceded by a porch, with pillars and an overhanging roof set before them.
He erected the throne hall—the hall of judgment—where he would adjudicate, and he sheathed it in cedar from pavement to soffit.

His own residence, situated in another court behind the hall, was of comparable workmanship; likewise, Solomon made a corresponding dwelling for Pharaoh’s daughter, whom he had married, matching that hall.
All these were of precious hewn stone, cut to measure with the saw, both within and without, from foundation to eaves, and outward to the great court.
The foundation was of costly great stones—some ten cubits, some eight.
Above them were costly stones cut to measure, together with cedar.
The great court was encircled by three courses of hewn stone and one course of trimmed cedar, both for the inner court of the house of the the LORD and for the porch of the house.
King Solomon dispatched envoys to Tyre and brought Hiram from there.

He was the son of a widow of the tribe of Naphtali, and his father was a Tyrian bronze-worker, endowed with wisdom, discernment, and knowledge for every kind of bronze craftsmanship; he came to King Solomon and executed all the work entrusted to him.
He cast two bronze pillars, each eighteen cubits high and twelve cubits in circumference.
He also made two capitals of cast bronze to set upon the heads of the pillars; each capital was five cubits high.
He fashioned networks of interwoven chains for the capitals upon the pillars, seven for each capital.
He made pomegranates in two rows encircling each network to adorn the capitals atop the pillars, and he did the same for the other capital.
The capitals atop the pillars in the portico were lily-shaped, four cubits high.
On the capitals at the top of both pillars, above the bulge beside the network, there were two hundred pomegranates in rows all around.
He raised the pillars at the temple portico, naming the right-hand pillar Jachin and the left-hand pillar Boaz.
The capitals on top were lily-shaped, and thus the work of the pillars was completed.
He made the Sea of cast metal, circular in shape, ten cubits from brim to brim and five cubits high; a line of thirty cubits measured around it.
Below its rim, gourds encircled it—ten to a cubit—and the gourds were cast in two rows as one piece with the Sea.
It stood upon twelve oxen: three facing north, three west, three south, and three east; the Sea rested upon them above, and their hindquarters were turned inward.
Its thickness was a handbreadth, and its rim was like the rim of a cup, like a lily blossom; it held two thousand baths.
He made ten bronze stands, each four cubits long, four wide, and three high.
The design of the stands was thus: they had side panels set between the crossbars.
On the panels between the crossbars were lions, bulls, and cherubim, and likewise upon the crossbars; above and below the lions and bulls were wreaths of hammered work.
Each stand had four bronze wheels with bronze axles, and it was supported by four foot projections; beneath the basin were cast projections on each side, embellished with wreaths.

Within the stand was an opening with a circular frame one cubit deep; the opening was round, and its design was a cubit and a half, with carvings around it, and the panels were square rather than round.
The four wheels were beneath the panels, and the axles of the wheels were attached to the stand; each wheel was a cubit and a half high.
The wheels were made like chariot wheels, their axles, rims, spokes, and hubs all cast.
Each stand had four handles, one at each corner, projecting from the stand.
At the top of the stand was a circular band half a cubit deep, and the supports and panels were attached to the top of the stand.
He engraved cherubim, lions, and palm trees on the surfaces of the supports and on the panels, in every available space, with wreaths all around.
Thus he made the ten stands: one casting, one measure, one form for all.
He made ten bronze basins, each holding forty baths and measuring four cubits across; one basin rested on each of the ten stands.
He set five stands on the south side of the temple and five on the north; he placed the Sea on the south side, at the southeast corner of the temple.
Hiram also made the pots, shovels, and sprinkling bowls; so Hiram completed all the work he had undertaken for King Solomon in the temple of the the LORD:
the two pillars; the two bowl-shaped capitals on top of the pillars; the two sets of network decorating the two bowl-shaped capitals on top of the pillars;
the four hundred pomegranates for the two networks—two rows of pomegranates for each network, adorning the bowl-shaped capitals atop the pillars;
the ten stands with their ten basins;
the Sea and the twelve oxen beneath it;
the pots, shovels, and sprinkling bowls. All these objects that Hiram made for Solomon for the temple of the the LORD were of burnished bronze.
The king had them cast in clay molds in the plain of the Jordan between Succoth and Zarethan.
Solomon left all these things unweighed, because they were so numerous; the weight of the bronze was not determined.
Solomon also made all the furnishings in the house of the the LORD: the golden altar; the golden table upon which was the bread of the Presence;
the lampstands of pure gold—five on the right and five on the left, before the inner sanctuary—and the gold flowers, lamps, and tongs;

the basins, wick trimmers, sprinkling bowls, dishes, and ladles of pure gold; and the hinges for the doors of the innermost room, the Most Holy Place, and for the doors of the main hall of the temple, were of gold.

When all the work Solomon had done for the temple of the the LORD was finished, he brought in the things his father David had dedicated—the silver, the gold, and the furnishings—and he placed them in the treasuries of the the LORD’s temple.

Then Solomon convoked the elders of Israel, together with all the heads of the tribes and the leaders of the ancestral houses of the Israelites, so that they might bring up the ark of the covenant of the LORD from the City of David, that is, Zion.
All the men of Israel assembled to King Solomon at the festival in the month Ethanim—that is, the seventh month.
When all the elders of Israel had arrived, the priests lifted the ark.
They carried up the ark of the LORD, along with the tent of meeting and all the sacred utensils that were in the tent; the priests and the Levites brought them up.

King Solomon and the entire congregation of Israel that had assembled before him stood with him before the ark, sacrificing sheep and oxen in such prodigious numbers that they could neither be counted nor enumerated.
Then the priests brought the ark of the covenant of the LORD to its appointed place, into the inner sanctuary of the house—to the Most Holy Place—beneath the wings of the cherubim.
For the cherubim spread their wings over the place of the ark, so that the cherubim overshadowed the ark and its poles from above.
The poles were of such length that their ends could be seen from the holy place before the inner sanctuary, though they were not visible from outside; and there they remain to this day.
There was nothing in the ark save the two tablets of stone that Moses had placed there at Horeb, where the LORD covenanted with the Israelites when they departed from the land of Egypt.
When the priests emerged from the holy place, the cloud filled the house of the LORD,
so that the priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud; for the glory of the LORD filled the house of the LORD.
Then Solomon said, “The LORD has declared that He would dwell in thick darkness.
I have indeed built You an exalted house, a fixed abode for Your habitation forever.”
Then the king turned about and blessed the whole assembly of Israel, while the whole assembly of Israel stood.
He said, “Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who spoke with His mouth to David my father and has fulfilled it with His hand, saying,

‘Since the day that I brought My people Israel out of Egypt, I have not chosen any city among all the tribes of Israel in which to build a house for My name to be there; rather, I have chosen David to be over My people Israel.’
“Now it was in the heart of David my father to build a house for the name of the LORD, the God of Israel.
But the LORD said to David my father, ‘Because it was in your heart to build a house for My name, you did well that it was in your heart.
“Nevertheless, you shall not build the house; but your son, who shall come forth from your loins, he shall build the house for My name.’

Now the LORD has established His word that He spoke; for I have risen in place of David my father and sit on the throne of Israel, as the LORD promised, and I have built the house for the name of the LORD, the God of Israel.
And there I have set a place for the ark, in which is the covenant of the LORD that He made with our fathers when He brought them out of the land of Egypt.”
Then Solomon stood before the altar of the LORD in the sight of all the assembly of Israel, and spread out his hands toward heaven.
He said, “O LORD, God of Israel, there is no God like You in heaven above or on earth beneath, keeping covenant and steadfast love with Your servants who walk before You with all their heart,
who have kept with Your servant David my father what You promised him; You spoke with Your mouth and fulfilled it with Your hand, as it is this day,

“And now, O LORD, God of Israel, keep for Your servant David my father what You promised him, saying, ‘You shall not lack a man to sit before Me on the throne of Israel, if only your sons take heed to their way, to walk before Me as you have walked before Me.’
And now, O God of Israel, let Your word be confirmed that You spoke to Your servant David my father.
But will God indeed dwell on the earth? Behold, heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain You; how much less this house that I have built!
“Yet have regard to the prayer of Your servant and to his plea, O LORD my God, listening to the cry and to the prayer that Your servant prays before You this day,
that Your eyes may be open night and day toward this house, the place of which You have said, ‘My name shall be there,’ that You may hear the prayer that Your servant shall pray toward this place.
And listen to the supplication of Your servant and of Your people Israel, when they pray toward this place; and listen in heaven Your dwelling place; and when You hear, forgive.
“If a man sins against his neighbor and is made to take an oath, and comes and swears before Your altar in this house,
then hear in heaven and act and judge Your servants, condemning the wicked by bringing his way upon his own head and justifying the righteous by giving to him according to his righteousness.
“When Your people Israel are defeated before an enemy because they have sinned against You, and they turn again to You and confess Your name and pray and make supplication to You in this house,
then hear in heaven and forgive the sin of Your people Israel, and bring them again to the land that You gave to their fathers.
“When heaven is shut up and there is no rain because they have sinned against You, and they pray toward this place and confess Your name and turn from their sin because You afflict them,

then hear in heaven and forgive the sin of Your servants and of Your people Israel, teaching them the good way in which they should walk, and give rain upon Your land, which You have given to Your people for an inheritance.

“If there is famine in the land, if there is pestilence or blight or mildew, locust or caterpillar, if their enemy besieges them in the land of their cities—whatever plague, whatever sickness there is—
whatever prayer, whatever plea is made by any man or by all Your people Israel, each knowing the affliction of his own heart and spreading out his hands toward this house,
then hear in heaven, Your dwelling place, and forgive and act and render to each man according to all his ways, whose heart You know—for You alone know the hearts of all the children of men—
that they may fear You all the days that they live in the land that You gave to our fathers.
“Moreover, concerning the foreigner, who is not of Your people Israel, but comes from a far country for Your name's sake
(for they shall hear of Your great name and Your mighty hand and Your outstretched arm), when he comes and prays toward this house,

hear in heaven, Your dwelling place, and do according to all that the foreigner calls to You, that all the peoples of the earth may know Your name and fear You, as do Your people Israel, and that they may know that this house which I have built is called by Your name.

“If Your people go out to battle against their enemy, by whatever way You shall send them, and they pray to the LORD toward the city that You have chosen and the house that I have built for Your name,
then hear in heaven their prayer and their supplication, and maintain their cause.
If they sin against You—for there is no man who does not sin—and You are angry with them and deliver them to the enemy, so that their captors carry them away to the land of the enemy, far or near,

yet if they turn to their heart in the land where they have been carried captive, and repent and make supplication to You in the land of their captors, saying, ‘We have sinned and have committed iniquity and have done wickedly,’

and if they return to You with all their heart and with all their soul in the land of their enemies who carried them captive, and pray to You toward their land, which You gave to their fathers, the city that You have chosen, and the house that I have built for Your name,
“then hear in heaven, Your dwelling place, their prayer and their supplication, and maintain their cause,

and forgive Your people who have sinned against You, and all their transgressions that they have committed against You, and grant them compassion before those who carried them captive, that they may have compassion on them
(for they are Your people and Your inheritance, which You brought out of Egypt, from the midst of the iron furnace),
that Your eyes may be open to the supplication of Your servant and to the supplication of Your people Israel, to listen to them whenever they call to You.

For You separated them to Yourself from among all the peoples of the earth to be Your inheritance, as You spoke through Moses Your servant, when You brought our fathers out of Egypt, O Lord, the LORD.”
Now when Solomon had finished offering all this prayer and supplication to the LORD, he arose from before the altar of the LORD, from kneeling on his knees with his hands spread out toward heaven.
He stood and blessed the whole assembly of Israel with a loud voice, saying,
“Blessed be the LORD, who has given rest to His people Israel according to all that He promised; not one word has failed of all His good promise, which He spoke by the hand of Moses His servant.
“The LORD our God be with us, as He was with our fathers; let Him not leave us nor forsake us,
that He may incline our hearts to Him, to walk in all His ways and keep His commandments, His statutes, and His judgments, which He commanded our fathers.

“And may these words of mine, which I have made supplication before the LORD, be near to the LORD our God day and night, that He may maintain the cause of His servant and the cause of His people Israel, as each day requires,
that all the peoples of the earth may know that the LORD, He is God; there is no other.
Let your hearts therefore be wholly devoted to the LORD our God, to walk in His statutes and keep His commandments, as at this day.”
Then the king and all Israel with him offered sacrifice before the LORD.
Solomon offered as peace offerings to the LORD twenty-two thousand cattle and a hundred and twenty thousand sheep. So the king and all the children of Israel dedicated the house of the LORD.

On that day the king consecrated the middle of the court that was before the house of the LORD, because there the bronze altar before the LORD was too small to contain the burnt offering and the grain offering and the fat portions of the peace offerings.
At that time Solomon held the feast, and all Israel with him—a great assembly from Lebo-hamath to the Brook of Egypt—before the LORD our God, seven days and seven days, fourteen days in all.

On the eighth day he sent the people away; and they blessed the king and went to their tents, joyful and glad of heart for all the goodness that the LORD had shown to His servant David and to His people Israel.
When Solomon had completed the construction of the house of the the LORD, the royal palace, and every undertaking that had captured his ambition,
the the LORD appeared to Solomon a second time, just as He had appeared to him at Gibeon.

The the LORD said to him, "I have heard your prayer and your supplication, which you have offered before Me; I have consecrated this house that you have built, to place My name there forever, and My eyes and My heart shall remain there for all time.
"As for you, if you walk before Me as David your father walked, with integrity of heart and uprightness, doing all that I have commanded you, and keeping My statutes and My ordinances,
then I will establish the throne of your kingdom over Israel forever, as I promised concerning David your father, saying, 'There shall never fail you a man upon the throne of Israel.'
"But if you or your sons turn away from following Me and do not keep My commandments and My statutes that I have set before you, but go and serve other gods and worship them,

then I will cut off Israel from the land that I have given them, and the house that I have consecrated for My name I will cast out of My sight; Israel shall become a proverb and a byword among all peoples.
"And this house, though exalted, shall become a spectacle; everyone who passes by it shall be appalled and hiss, and they shall say, 'Why has the the LORD done this to this land and to this house?'

And they shall answer, 'Because they forsook the the LORD their God, who brought their fathers out of the land of Egypt, and embraced other gods, worshiping and serving them; therefore the the LORD has brought all this calamity upon them.'"
At the end of twenty years, after Solomon had built the two houses—the house of the the LORD and the royal palace—
King Hiram of Tyre having supplied Solomon with cedar, cypress, and gold according to all his desire, King Solomon gave Hiram twenty cities in the land of Galilee.
Hiram came out from Tyre to inspect the cities Solomon had given him, but they did not please him.
He said, "What are these cities you have given me, my friend?" And he called them the land of Cabul to this day.
Hiram also sent the king one hundred and twenty talents of gold.
This is the account of the forced labor that King Solomon conscripted to build the house of the the LORD, his own palace, the Millo, the wall of Jerusalem, Hazor, Megiddo, and Gezer.
Pharaoh king of Egypt had marched up and captured Gezer, burning it with fire and slaying the Canaanites who inhabited the city; he then gave it as a dowry to his daughter, Solomon's wife.
Solomon rebuilt Gezer and Lower Beth-horon,
as well as Baalath and Tamar in the wilderness of the land,
together with all the store cities that belonged to Solomon, the cities for his chariots and horsemen, and everything he desired to build in Jerusalem, in Lebanon, and throughout his entire realm.
All the people who remained of the Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites—those not belonging to the Israelites—
namely, their descendants left in the land after them, whom the Israelites could not devote to destruction—Solomon drafted into forced labor, and so they remain to this day.
But Solomon did not enslave any Israelite, for they were men of war, his servants, his officials, his captains, and commanders of his chariots and horsemen.
These were the chief officers over Solomon's work: five hundred and fifty, who supervised the people performing the labor.
Pharaoh's daughter came up from the City of David to the house Solomon had built for her; then he built the Millo.
Three times a year Solomon offered burnt offerings and peace offerings on the altar he had built to the the LORD, burning incense before the the LORD; thus he completed the temple.
King Solomon also built a fleet at Ezion-geber, near Eloth on the shore of the Red Sea, in the land of Edom.
Hiram sent with the fleet his own servants—seamen acquainted with the sea—along with Solomon's servants.
They sailed to Ophir and brought back four hundred and twenty talents of gold, which they delivered to King Solomon.
When the Queen of Sheba heard of Solomon’s renown, which was inextricably bound up with the name of the LORD, she journeyed to Jerusalem to interrogate him with recondite riddles.

She arrived accompanied by a prodigiously large retinue, with camels laden with spices, an extraordinary abundance of gold, and precious stones; and upon her admission to Solomon’s presence, she laid before him every matter that occupied her heart.
Solomon resolved each of her inquiries, and no question remained so abstruse that the king could not elucidate it for her.
Having surveyed the entirety of Solomon’s wisdom, together with the palace he had erected,

the viands of his table, the disposition of his courtiers, the attendance and attire of his servants, his cupbearers, and the burnt offerings he presented in the house of the LORD, she was left utterly breathless—there was no spirit left within her.
She said to the king, “The report that I heard in my own land concerning your words and your wisdom has proved veracious.

I could not credit those tidings until I came and beheld them with my own eyes; indeed, not even half of your wisdom and prosperity had been reported to me, for your attainments transcend the rumor I had heard.
How blessed are your people, and how blessed are those servants of yours who stand perpetually before you and hearken to your wisdom!

Blessed be the LORD your God, who has delighted in you and enthroned you over Israel. Because the LORD has loved Israel forever, He has constituted you king, that you might administer justice and righteousness.”

Then she presented the king with one hundred and twenty talents of gold, together with an exceedingly great quantity of spices and precious stones; never again did spices arrive in such profusion as those the Queen of Sheba bestowed upon King Solomon.
Moreover, Hiram’s fleet, which had conveyed gold from Ophir, imported from Ophir an exceedingly great quantity of almug wood and precious stones.

From this almug wood the king fashioned supports for the house of the LORD and for the royal residence, together with lyres and harps for the singers; such almug wood had never before been seen, nor has it appeared to this day.

King Solomon granted the Queen of Sheba every desire she articulated, in addition to what he conferred upon her out of his own royal munificence. Thereupon she departed with her servants and returned to her native land.
The weight of gold that accrued to Solomon in a single year amounted to six hundred and sixty-six talents,
apart from the revenue derived from the explorers and from the merchants, together with all the kings of Arabia and the governors of the land.
King Solomon fashioned two hundred great shields of beaten gold, each consuming six hundred shekels of gold,
and three hundred smaller shields of beaten gold, three minas of gold apiece; the king deposited them in the House of the Forest of Lebanon.
The king likewise fashioned a great throne of ivory and overlaid it with the finest gold.
The throne possessed six steps; its back was rounded at the top, and armrests projected from either side of the seat, with two lions standing beside the armrests.
Twelve lions stood upon the six steps, one at each end of a step. Nothing comparable had ever been fashioned for any kingdom.
All of King Solomon’s drinking vessels were of gold, and every vessel in the House of the Forest of Lebanon was of pure gold; silver was reckoned as nothing in the days of Solomon.
For the king possessed a fleet of Tarshish ships at sea, in company with Hiram’s fleet; once every three years the Tarshish fleet arrived, bringing gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks.
Thus King Solomon surpassed all the kings of the earth in riches and in wisdom.
The whole earth sought an audience with Solomon to hear the wisdom that God had implanted in his heart,
and each visitor brought his tribute—articles of silver and gold, garments, weapons, spices, horses, and mules—year after year.
Solomon amassed chariots and horsemen: he had fourteen hundred chariots and twelve thousand horsemen, whom he stationed in the chariot cities and with the king in Jerusalem.
The king made silver as abundant in Jerusalem as stones, and cedar as plentiful as the sycamores of the Shephelah.
Solomon’s horses were imported from Egypt and from Kue; the king’s merchants procured them from Kue at a fixed price.

A chariot could be imported from Egypt for six hundred shekels of silver, and a horse for one hundred and fifty; and through the same channels they supplied all the kings of the Hittites and the kings of Aram.
King Solomon, for his part, loved many foreign women in addition to Pharaoh’s daughter—Moabite, Ammonite, Edomite, Sidonian, and Hittite women—

drawn from the nations concerning which the LORD had declared to the Israelites, “You must not intermarry with them, nor they with you, for they will assuredly incline your hearts after their gods.” Nevertheless, Solomon clung to them in love.
He had seven hundred wives of royal birth and three hundred concubines, and these women led his heart astray.
When Solomon grew old, his wives turned his heart toward other gods, so that his heart was no longer wholly devoted to the LORD his God, as the heart of his father David had been.
Solomon pursued Ashtoreth, the goddess of the Sidonians, and Milcom, the abomination of the Ammonites.
Thus Solomon perpetrated evil in the eyes of the LORD, and, unlike David his father, he did not remain wholly faithful to the LORD.
At that time, on the hill east of Jerusalem, Solomon erected a high place for Chemosh, the abomination of Moab, and for Milcom, the abomination of the Ammonites.
He did the same for all his foreign wives, who burned incense and sacrificed to their gods.
The LORD was therefore incensed with Solomon, because his heart had turned away from the LORD, the God of Israel, who had appeared to him twice.
Although He had expressly commanded him not to follow other gods, Solomon did not observe what the LORD had commanded.

The LORD said to Solomon, “Because this has befallen you, and because you have not kept My covenant and My statutes, which I enjoined upon you, I will surely tear the kingdom from you and give it to your servant.
Yet, for the sake of your father David, I will not do so in your days; I will tear it from the hand of your son.
Nevertheless, I will not tear away the entire kingdom; I will give one tribe to your son, for the sake of My servant David and for the sake of Jerusalem, which I have chosen.”
Then the LORD raised up an adversary against Solomon: Hadad the Edomite, of the royal line of Edom.
For when David was in Edom, and Joab, commander of the army, went up to bury the slain, he struck down every male in Edom.
Joab and all Israel remained there six months, until he had exterminated every male in Edom.
Hadad, however, was still a young boy when he fled to Egypt with certain Edomites who were his father’s servants.
They set out from Midian and came to Paran; then, taking men from Paran with them, they entered Egypt, to Pharaoh king of Egypt, who gave Hadad a house, allotted him land, and furnished him food.
Pharaoh looked with great favor upon Hadad, so he gave him in marriage the sister of his own wife, Queen Tahpenes.
The sister of Tahpenes bore him a son, Genubath, whom Tahpenes weaned in Pharaoh’s palace; Genubath lived in Pharaoh’s palace among the sons of Pharaoh.
When Hadad heard in Egypt that David had died and that Joab, commander of the army, was dead, he said to Pharaoh, “Let me depart, that I may return to my own country.”
But Pharaoh said to him, “What are you lacking here with me, that you seek to go to your own country?” “Nothing,” Hadad replied, “only grant me leave to depart.”
God also raised up another adversary against Solomon: Rezon son of Eliada, who had fled from his master, Hadadezer king of Zobah.
He gathered men about him and became leader of a marauding band after David’s slaughter of them; then he went to Damascus, settled there, and reigned over Damascus.
Rezon was an adversary to Israel throughout all the days of Solomon, adding to the distress caused by Hadad; he abhorred Israel and reigned over Aram.
Jeroboam son of Nebat, an Ephraimite from Zeredah, whose mother was Zeruah, a widow, rebelled against the king; he was Solomon’s servant.
This was the occasion of his rebellion against the king: Solomon built the Millo and closed the breach in the wall of the city of his father David.
Jeroboam was a man of great strength and valor; when Solomon saw that the young man was industrious, he appointed him over all the forced labor of the house of Joseph.
At that time, when Jeroboam went out from Jerusalem, the prophet Ahijah the Shilonite met him on the road; Ahijah was wrapped in a new cloak, and the two of them were alone in the field.
Ahijah seized the new cloak upon him and tore it into twelve pieces.
He said to Jeroboam, “Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: ‘See, I am about to tear the kingdom from the hand of Solomon, and I will give you ten tribes.
But I will leave him one tribe for the sake of My servant David and for the sake of Jerusalem, the city I have chosen from all the tribes of Israel.

For they have forsaken Me and have bowed down to Ashtoreth, goddess of the Sidonians, to Chemosh, god of Moab, and to Milcom, god of the Ammonites; they have not walked in My ways, nor done what is right in My eyes, nor kept My statutes and My ordinances, as David his father did.

Nevertheless, I will not take the whole kingdom from his hand; I will make him ruler all the days of his life for the sake of My servant David, whom I chose, because he kept My commandments and My statutes.
But I will take the kingdom from his son and give it to you—ten tribes.
To his son I will give one tribe, so that My servant David will always have a descendant before Me in Jerusalem, the city I have chosen to put My Name.
I will take you, and you shall rule over all that your soul desires; you shall be king over Israel.

If you listen to all that I command you, walk in My ways, and do what is right in My eyes, keeping My statutes and My commandments, as My servant David did, then I will be with you. I will build you an enduring house, as I built for David, and I will give Israel to you.
I will afflict the house of David because of this, but not forever.’”
Solomon sought therefore to put Jeroboam to death; but Jeroboam arose and fled to Egypt, to Shishak king of Egypt, and he remained in Egypt until Solomon’s death.
Now the rest of the acts of Solomon, and all that he did, and his wisdom—are they not written in the Book of the Acts of Solomon?
The time that Solomon reigned over Israel in Jerusalem was forty years.
Solomon died and was buried in the city of his father David; his son Rehoboam reigned in his place.
Rehoboam traveled to Shechem, for all Israel had assembled at Shechem to install him as king.
Jeroboam son of Nebat heard of it while he was still in Egypt, where he had fled from King Solomon, and he remained there.
So they sent for him; Jeroboam and the whole congregation of Israel came and addressed Rehoboam, saying:
“Your father imposed a grievous yoke upon us; now lighten your father’s oppressive service and the heavy yoke he laid upon us, and we will serve you.”
He said to them, “Go for three days, then return to me.” So the people departed.
Then King Rehoboam consulted the elders who had stood before his father Solomon while he was alive, asking, “How do you advise me to answer this people?”
They replied, “If today you will be a servant to this people and serve them, and answer them and speak good words to them, they will be your servants forever.”
But he rejected the counsel the elders had given him and consulted the young men who had grown up with him and stood before him.
He asked them, “What do you advise that we answer this people, who have said to me, ‘Lighten the yoke that your father put upon us’?”

The young men who had grown up with him said to him, “Thus you shall say to this people who spoke to you, saying, ‘Your father made our yoke heavy, but you must lighten it for us’—thus you shall say to them, ‘I am far more formidable than my father ever was.’
Now, whereas my father burdened you with a heavy yoke, I will add to your yoke; my father disciplined you with whips, but I will discipline you with scorpions.”
On the third day Jeroboam and all the people came to Rehoboam, as the king had said, “Return to me on the third day.”
The king answered the people harshly, rejecting the counsel of the elders that they had given him.

He spoke to them according to the counsel of the young men: “My father made your yoke heavy, but I will add to your yoke; my father disciplined you with whips, but I will discipline you with scorpions.”
So the king did not listen to the people, for this turn of affairs was from the LORD, so that He might establish His word, which He had spoken by Ahijah the Shilonite to Jeroboam son of Nebat.

When all Israel saw that the king would not listen to them, they answered the king, “What share have we in David? We have no inheritance in the son of Jesse. To your tents, O Israel! Now look to your own house, David.” Then Israel went to their tents.
But Rehoboam reigned over the Israelites who lived in the cities of Judah.
King Rehoboam sent Adoram, who was in charge of the forced labor, and all Israel stoned him to death. King Rehoboam then made haste to mount his chariot and flee to Jerusalem.
So Israel has been in rebellion against the house of David to this day.

When all Israel heard that Jeroboam had returned, they sent for him and called him to the assembly, and they made him king over all Israel. None followed the house of David except the tribe of Judah alone.

Rehoboam came to Jerusalem and assembled all the house of Judah and the tribe of Benjamin—one hundred eighty thousand chosen warriors—to fight against the house of Israel and restore the kingdom to Rehoboam son of Solomon.
But the word of God came to Shemaiah the man of God, saying,
“Say to Rehoboam son of Solomon, king of Judah, and to all the house of Judah and Benjamin, and to the rest of the people,

‘Thus says the LORD: “You shall not go up or fight against your brothers, the sons of Israel. Every man shall return to his house, for this thing is from Me.”’” They listened to the word of the LORD and returned to go their way according to the word of the LORD.
Jeroboam built Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim and settled there; he went out from there and built Penuel.
Jeroboam said in his heart, “Now the kingdom will return to the house of David.

If this people go up to offer sacrifices in the house of the LORD at Jerusalem, the heart of this people will turn again to their lord, to Rehoboam king of Judah, and they will kill me and return to Rehoboam king of Judah.”
So the king took counsel and made two calves of gold, and he said to them, “It is too much for you to go up to Jerusalem. Behold your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt.”
He set one in Bethel, and the other he put in Dan.
This thing became a sin, for the people went to worship before the one even as far as Dan.
He also made houses on high places and appointed priests from all the people, who were not of the sons of Levi.

Jeroboam ordained a feast in the eighth month on the fifteenth day of the month, like the feast that is in Judah, and he offered on the altar. So he did in Bethel, sacrificing to the calves that he had made, and he stationed in Bethel the priests of the high places that he had made.

On the fifteenth day of the eighth month—a month he had devised from his own heart—he offered on the altar that he had made in Bethel. He made a feast for the sons of Israel and offered on the altar, burning incense.
Now behold, Jeroboam was standing beside the altar to offer incense when a man of God came from Judah to Bethel by the word of the LORD.

He cried out against the altar by the word of the LORD and said, "Altar, altar, thus says the LORD: 'Behold, a son shall be born to the house of David, Josiah by name; upon you he shall sacrifice the priests of the high places who burn incense upon you, and men's bones shall be burned upon you.'"
And he gave a sign that same day, saying, "This is the sign that the LORD has spoken: Behold, the altar shall be torn apart, and the ashes that are on it shall be poured out."

When the king heard the word of the man of God, which he had cried against the altar at Bethel, Jeroboam stretched out his hand from the altar and said, "Seize him!" But the hand that he stretched out against him withered, so that he could not draw it back to himself.
The altar was also torn apart, and the ashes were poured out from the altar, according to the sign that the man of God had given by the word of the LORD.

The king said to the man of God, "Entreat now the favor of the LORD your God, and pray for me, that my hand may be restored to me." So the man of God entreated the LORD, and the king's hand was restored to him as it had been before.
Then the king said to him, "Come home with me and refresh yourself, and I will give you a present."
But the man of God said to the king, "If you were to give me half of your house, I would not go with you, nor would I eat bread or drink water in this place.
For so I was commanded by the word of the LORD, saying, 'You shall not eat bread, nor shall you drink water, nor shall you return by the way that you came.'
So he went another way and did not return by the way by which he had come to Bethel."

Now an old prophet was dwelling in Bethel, and his sons came and told him all that the man of God had done that day in Bethel, and the words that he had spoken to the king; and they reported them to their father.
Their father said to them, "Which way did he go?" For his sons had seen the way that the man of God from Judah had taken.
He said to his sons, "Saddle the donkey for me." So they saddled the donkey for him, and he mounted it.
He went after the man of God and found him sitting under an oak, and said to him, "Are you the man of God who came from Judah?" He said, "I am."
He said to him, "Come home with me and eat bread."
He said, "I cannot return with you or go with you, nor will I eat bread or drink water with you in this place.
For a word came to me by the word of the LORD, saying, 'You shall not eat bread, nor shall you drink water there, nor shall you return by the way by which you came.'"

He said to him, "I also am a prophet like you, and an angel spoke to me by the word of the LORD, saying, 'Bring him back with you to your house, that he may eat bread and drink water.'" But he lied to him.
So he went back with him and ate bread in his house and drank water.
And while they were sitting at the table, the word of the LORD came to the prophet who had brought him back.

He cried out to the man of God who had come from Judah, saying, "Thus says the LORD: 'Because you have rebelled against the mouth of the LORD and have not kept the commandment that the LORD your God commanded you,

but have returned and have eaten bread and drunk water in the place of which He said to you, "You shall not eat bread and you shall not drink water," your corpse shall not come to the grave of your fathers.'
And after he had eaten bread and after he had drunk, he saddled the donkey for him—that is, for the prophet whom he had brought back.
And as he went, a lion met him on the road and killed him. His corpse was thrown in the road, and the donkey stood beside it, and the lion stood beside the corpse.
And behold, men were passing by and saw the corpse thrown in the road, and the lion standing beside the corpse. They came and spoke in the city where the old prophet dwelt.

When the prophet who had brought him back from the road heard of it, he said, "He is the man of God who rebelled against the mouth of the LORD; therefore the LORD has given him to the lion, which has torn him and killed him, according to the word of the LORD that He spoke to him."
He said to his sons, "Saddle the donkey for me." So they saddled it.
He went and found his corpse thrown in the road, with the donkey and the lion standing beside the corpse. The lion had not eaten the corpse nor torn the donkey.
The prophet took up the corpse of the man of God, laid it on the donkey, and brought it back; and the old prophet came to the city to mourn and to bury him.
He laid his corpse in his own grave, and they mourned over him, saying, "Alas, my brother!"
After he had buried him, he said to his sons, "When I die, bury me in the grave in which the man of God is buried; lay my bones beside his bones.
For the saying that he cried by the word of the LORD against the altar in Bethel and against all the houses of the high places that are in the cities of Samaria shall surely come to pass."

After this, Jeroboam did not turn from his evil way, but again made priests for the high places from among all the people. Whoever desired it, he consecrated, and they became priests of the high places.
And this thing became sin to the house of Jeroboam, even to cut it off and to destroy it from the face of the earth.
At that time Abijah, the son of Jeroboam, fell ill.

Jeroboam said to his wife, “Please rise and disguise yourself, so that you will not be recognized as Jeroboam’s wife, and go to Shiloh. Ahijah the prophet is there; he spoke concerning me that I should be king over this people.
Take with you ten loaves, some cakes, and a jar of honey, and go to him; he will tell you what will become of the boy.”
Jeroboam’s wife did so: she arose and went to Shiloh and came to Ahijah’s house. Now Ahijah could not see, for his eyes had grown dim with age.

Then the LORD said to Ahijah, “Behold, Jeroboam’s wife is coming to inquire a word from you concerning her son, for he is sick. Address her in such terms as these, and when she arrives she will be in disguise.”
When Ahijah heard the sound of her feet as she came in at the door, he said, “Come in, wife of Jeroboam. Why are you disguising yourself? I have been sent to you with a harsh message.
Go, tell Jeroboam: ‘Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Because I exalted you from among the people and made you leader over My people Israel,

and tore the kingdom away from the house of David and gave it to you—yet you have not been like My servant David, who kept My commandments and followed Me with all his heart, doing only what was right in My eyes—
but you have done evil more than all who were before you, and have gone and made for yourself other gods and molten images to provoke Me to anger, and have cast Me behind your back—

therefore behold, I am bringing calamity upon the house of Jeroboam. I will cut off from Jeroboam every male in Israel, slave or free, and I will sweep away the house of Jeroboam as one sweeps away dung until it is gone.
The one belonging to Jeroboam who dies in the city, the dogs will eat; and the one who dies in the field, the birds of the heavens will eat; for the LORD has spoken.’
‘And as for you, arise and go to your house; when your feet enter the city, the child will die.
All Israel will mourn for him and bury him, for he alone of Jeroboam will come to the grave, because in him was found something good toward the LORD, the God of Israel, in the house of Jeroboam.
Moreover, the LORD will raise up for Himself a king over Israel who will cut off the house of Jeroboam. This is the day; yes, even now.

The LORD will strike Israel as a reed is shaken in the water, and He will uproot Israel from this good land that He gave to their fathers, and scatter them beyond the River, because they made their Asherah poles, provoking the LORD.
He will give Israel up because of the sins of Jeroboam, which he sinned and by which he caused Israel to sin.’”
Then Jeroboam’s wife arose and went, and she came to Tirzah. As she came to the threshold of the house, the child died.
All Israel buried him and mourned for him, according to the word of the LORD that He spoke by the hand of His servant Ahijah the prophet.
Now the rest of the acts of Jeroboam—how he waged war and how he reigned—are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?
The time that Jeroboam reigned was twenty-two years; then he died and was gathered to his ancestors, and Nadab his son reigned in his place.

Rehoboam son of Solomon reigned in Judah. Rehoboam was forty-one years old when he became king, and he reigned seventeen years in Jerusalem, the city that the LORD had chosen out of all the tribes of Israel, to put His name there. His mother’s name was Naamah the Ammonitess.
Judah did evil in the sight of the LORD; they provoked Him to jealousy with their sins, more than all that their fathers had done.
For they also built for themselves high places, pillars, and Asherah poles on every high hill and under every green tree.
Moreover, there were male cult prostitutes in the land; they did according to all the abominations of the nations that the LORD had driven out before the sons of Israel.
In the fifth year of King Rehoboam, Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem.
He took away the treasures of the house of the LORD and the treasures of the king’s house; he took everything, including all the gold shields that Solomon had made.
King Rehoboam made bronze shields in their place and committed them to the hands of the commanders of the guard who kept the door of the king’s house.
Whenever the king went into the house of the LORD, the guard would carry them and then bring them back to the guardroom.
Now the rest of the acts of Rehoboam, and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?
There was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam all their days.
Rehoboam died and was buried with his fathers in the City of David. His mother’s name was Naamah the Ammonitess. Abijam his son reigned in his place.
In the eighteenth year of King Jeroboam son of Nebat, Abijam ascended the throne over Judah.
He reigned in Jerusalem for three years; his mother was Maacah, the daughter of Abishalom.
Abijam walked in all the sins of his father that had preceded him, and his heart was not wholly devoted to the LORD his God, as the heart of David his father had been.
Yet for David’s sake the LORD his God granted him a continuing dynasty in Jerusalem, raising up his son after him and establishing Jerusalem.
For David had done what was right in the eyes of the LORD and had not turned aside from anything the LORD commanded him throughout the days of his life, except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite.
Throughout Abijam’s life, hostilities persisted between Rehoboam and Jeroboam.
The remaining acts of Abijam, and all that he did, are they not recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? Moreover, war continued between Abijam and Jeroboam.
Abijam rested with his fathers and was buried in the City of David; his son Asa succeeded him as king.
In the twentieth year of Jeroboam, king of Israel, Asa became king over Judah.
He reigned in Jerusalem forty-one years, and his mother was Maacah, the daughter of Abishalom.
Asa did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, as David his father had done.
He expelled the cultic male prostitutes from the land and eradicated all the idols his ancestors had fashioned.
He even removed his grandmother Maacah from her office as queen mother, because she had fashioned a detestable idol for Asherah; Asa cut down her image and burned it in the Kidron Valley.
Yet the high places were not removed; nevertheless, Asa’s heart was wholly devoted to the LORD throughout all his days.
He brought into the house of the LORD the silver, gold, and vessels that he and his father had consecrated.
War persisted between Asa and Baasha, king of Israel, throughout their days.
Baasha, king of Israel, advanced against Judah and fortified Ramah, so that no one could leave or enter the domain of Asa, king of Judah.

Asa then took all the remaining silver and gold from the treasuries of the house of the LORD and the royal palace, entrusted it to his servants, and sent them to Ben-Hadad son of Tabrimmon, son of Hezion, king of Aram, who resided in Damascus, with this message:

“Let there be a covenant between me and you, as there was between my father and your father. Behold, I have sent you a gift of silver and gold; go and break your covenant with Baasha, king of Israel, so that he may withdraw from me.”

Ben-Hadad heeded King Asa and dispatched the commanders of his forces against the cities of Israel; he conquered Ijon, Dan, Abel-beth-maacah, and all the region of Chinneroth, together with the entire land of Naphtali.
When Baasha heard of this, he ceased fortifying Ramah and withdrew to Tirzah.

Then King Asa summoned all Judah—none were exempted—and they carried away the stones and timber of Ramah that Baasha had been building; with these materials King Asa fortified Geba of Benjamin and Mizpah.

The rest of Asa’s acts, all his might, everything he accomplished, and the cities he built—are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? In his old age, however, he became afflicted in his feet.
Asa rested with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the City of David his father; his son Jehoshaphat reigned in his place.
In the second year of Asa, king of Judah, Nadab son of Jeroboam became king over Israel and reigned over Israel for two years.
He did evil in the sight of the LORD and walked in the way of his father and in the sin by which he had caused Israel to sin.

Then Baasha son of Ahijah, of the house of Issachar, conspired against him; Baasha struck him down at Gibbethon, which belonged to the Philistines, while Nadab and all Israel were besieging Gibbethon.
In the third year of Asa, king of Judah, Baasha killed Nadab and succeeded him as king.

As soon as he assumed the throne, he struck down the entire house of Jeroboam; he left Jeroboam not a single survivor, but destroyed them all, in accordance with the word of the LORD spoken through His servant Ahijah the Shilonite.
This occurred because of the sins Jeroboam had committed and had caused Israel to commit, and because he had provoked the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger.
The rest of Nadab’s acts, and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?
War persisted between Asa and Baasha, king of Israel, throughout their days.
In the third year of Asa, king of Judah, Baasha son of Ahijah became king over all Israel in Tirzah, and he reigned twenty-four years.
He did evil in the sight of the LORD and walked in the way of Jeroboam and in the sin by which he had caused Israel to sin.
The word of the LORD came to Jehu son of Hanani against Baasha, saying,

“Because I exalted you from the dust and made you leader over My people Israel, yet you have walked in the way of Jeroboam and have caused My people Israel to sin, provoking Me to anger with their sins,
behold, I will burn up Baasha and his house, and I will make your house like the house of Jeroboam son of Nebat.
Whoever of Baasha dies in the city, the dogs will eat; and whoever of him dies in the field, the birds of heaven will eat.”
Now the rest of the acts of Baasha, what he did, and his might—are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?
Baasha slept with his fathers and was buried in Tirzah, and his son Elah reigned in his place.

Moreover, the word of the LORD came by the hand of the prophet Jehu son of Hanani against Baasha and his house, both because of all the evil he did in the sight of the LORD, provoking Him to anger by the work of his hands, so that he became like the house of Jeroboam, and because he struck it down.
In the twenty-sixth year of Asa king of Judah, Elah son of Baasha became king over Israel in Tirzah, and he reigned two years.
While he was in Tirzah, drinking himself drunk in the house of Arza, who was in charge of the palace at Tirzah, his servant Zimri, commander of half the chariots, conspired against him.
In the twenty-seventh year of Asa king of Judah, Zimri went in, struck him down, and killed him, and reigned in his place.
As soon as he began to reign, as soon as he sat on his throne, he struck down all the house of Baasha; he left him not one male, neither his kinsmen nor his friends.
Thus Zimri destroyed all the house of Baasha, according to the word of the LORD which He spoke against Baasha by Jehu the prophet,
for all the sins of Baasha and the sins of Elah his son, which they sinned and by which they made Israel sin, provoking the LORD God of Israel to anger with their worthless idols.
Now the rest of the acts of Elah, and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?
In the twenty-seventh year of Asa king of Judah, Zimri reigned in Tirzah seven days; and the people were encamped against Gibbethon, which belonged to the Philistines.
The people in the camp heard that Zimri had conspired and had also struck down the king; therefore all Israel made Omri, the commander of the army, king over Israel that day in the camp.
Then Omri went up from Gibbethon, and all Israel with him, and they besieged Tirzah.
When Zimri saw that the city was taken, he went into the citadel of the king's house and burned the king's house over himself with fire, and died,
because of his sins which he sinned in doing evil in the sight of the LORD, in walking in the way of Jeroboam, and in his sin which he did, making Israel sin.
Now the rest of the acts of Zimri, and his conspiracy which he made, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?
Then the people of Israel were divided into two parts: half the people followed Tibni son of Ginath, to make him king, and half followed Omri.
But the people who followed Omri prevailed over the people who followed Tibni son of Ginath; so Tibni died, and Omri reigned.
In the thirty-first year of Asa king of Judah, Omri began to reign over Israel, and he reigned twelve years; he reigned six years in Tirzah.
He bought the hill of Samaria from Shemer for two talents of silver, and he built on the hill, and called the name of the city which he built Samaria, after the name of Shemer, owner of the hill.
Omri did evil in the sight of the LORD, and did worse than all who were before him.
For he walked in all the way of Jeroboam son of Nebat, and in his sin by which he made Israel sin, provoking the LORD God of Israel to anger with their worthless idols.
Now the rest of the acts of Omri that he did, and his might that he showed, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?
Omri slept with his fathers and was buried in Samaria, and his son Ahab reigned in his place.
In the thirty-eighth year of Asa king of Judah, Ahab son of Omri began to reign over Israel, and Ahab son of Omri reigned over Israel in Samaria twenty-two years.
Ahab son of Omri did evil in the sight of the LORD more than all who were before him.

As though it were a trivial matter for him to walk in the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, he took as wife Jezebel the daughter of Ethbaal king of the Sidonians, and went and served Baal and worshiped him.
He erected an altar for Baal in the house of Baal, which he built in Samaria.
Ahab also made the Asherah; and Ahab did more to provoke the LORD God of Israel to anger than all the kings of Israel who were before him.

In his days Hiel the Bethelite built Jericho; he laid its foundation at the cost of Abiram his firstborn, and set up its gates at the cost of Segub his youngest, according to the word of the LORD, which He spoke by Joshua son of Nun.
Elijah the Tishbite, an inhabitant of Gilead, said to Ahab, “As the LORD, the God of Israel, lives, before whom I stand, neither dew nor rain shall fall in these years except at my word.”
Then the word of the LORD came to him, saying,
“Go from here and turn eastward, and hide yourself by the brook Cherith, which is east of the Jordan.
You shall drink from the brook, and I have commanded the ravens to feed you there.”
So he went and did according to the word of the LORD; he went and lived by the brook Cherith, which is east of the Jordan.
The ravens brought him bread and meat in the morning and bread and meat in the evening, and he drank from the brook.
After some days the brook dried up, because there was no rain in the land.
Then the word of the LORD came to him, saying,
“Arise, go to Zarephath, which belongs to Sidon, and dwell there. Behold, I have commanded a widow there to sustain you.”

So he arose and went to Zarephath. When he came to the gate of the city, behold, a widow was there gathering sticks. He called to her and said, “Please bring me a little water in a vessel, that I may drink.”
As she was going to bring it, he called to her and said, “Please bring me a morsel of bread in your hand.”

But she said, “As the LORD your God lives, I have no baked cake, but only a handful of flour in the jar and a little oil in the jug. And behold, I am gathering two sticks, that I may go in and prepare it for myself and my son, that we may eat it and die.”
Elijah said to her, “Do not fear; go and do as you have said. But first make me a little cake from it and bring it to me, and afterward make one for yourself and your son.
For thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: ‘The jar of flour shall not be exhausted, and the jug of oil shall not fail, until the day the LORD sends rain upon the face of the earth.’”
She went and did according to the word of Elijah; and she and her household ate for many days.
The jar of flour was not spent, neither did the jug of oil fail, according to the word of the LORD which He had spoken by Elijah.
After these things the son of the woman, the mistress of the house, became sick; and his sickness was so severe that there was no breath left in him.
She said to Elijah, “What do you have against me, O man of God? Have you come to me to bring my sin to remembrance and to kill my son?”
He said, “Give me your son.” And he took him from her bosom and carried him up to the upper room where he was staying, and laid him on his own bed.
Then he cried to the LORD and said, “O the LORD, my God, have You brought calamity upon the widow with whom I sojourn, by killing her son?”
He stretched himself upon the child three times, and cried to the LORD and said, “O the LORD, my God, let this child’s soul return to him.”
The LORD heard the voice of Elijah, and the soul of the child returned to him, and he revived.
Elijah took the child and brought him down from the upper room into the house, and delivered him to his mother. And Elijah said, “See, your son lives.”
Then the woman said to Elijah, “Now I know that you are a man of God, and that the word of the LORD in your mouth is truth.”
After the lapse of many days—indeed, in the third year—the word of the the LORD came to Elijah, saying, "Go, present yourself to Ahab, and I shall grant rain upon the face of the earth."
So Elijah went to present himself to Ahab. Now the famine bore down with severity upon Samaria.
Meanwhile Ahab summoned Obadiah, who was in charge of the palace. (Now Obadiah feared the the LORD exceedingly.)
For when Jezebel was exterminating the prophets of the the LORD, Obadiah had taken a hundred prophets and concealed them, fifty in a cave, and had sustained them with bread and water.

Then Ahab said to Obadiah, "Go through the land to all the springs of water and to all the wadis; perhaps we may find forage and keep alive the horses and mules, so that we do not have to slaughter some of the livestock."
So they divided the land between themselves to traverse it: Ahab went one route alone, and Obadiah went another route alone.
As Obadiah was on the road, behold, Elijah encountered him; and he recognized him and fell upon his face and said, "Are you indeed my lord Elijah?"
He replied, "I am. Go, say to your lord, 'Behold, Elijah is here.'"
He said, "What sin have I committed, that you should deliver your servant into the hand of Ahab to be put to death?

As the the LORD your God lives, there is no nation or kingdom to which my lord has not sent to seek you; and when they said, 'He is not here,' he made the kingdom and the nation swear that they had not found you.
And now you say, 'Go, tell your lord, "Behold, Elijah is here."'"

"And it shall come to pass, as soon as I depart from you, that the Spirit of the the LORD will carry you off—I know not whither—and when I come and tell Ahab, and he cannot find you, he will kill me, although I, your servant, have feared the the LORD from my youth.

Has it not been told to my lord what I did when Jezebel slew the prophets of the the LORD, how I hid a hundred men of the the LORD's prophets, fifty in a cave, and sustained them with bread and water?
And now you say, 'Go, tell your lord, "Behold, Elijah is here,"' and he will kill me."
Elijah said, "As the the LORD of hosts lives, before whom I stand, I will certainly show myself to him today."
So Obadiah went to meet Ahab and reported to him; and Ahab went to meet Elijah.
When Ahab saw Elijah, Ahab said to him, "Are you he who troubles Israel?"
He answered, "I have not troubled Israel, but you and your father's house have, in that you have forsaken the commandments of the the LORD and have followed the Baals."
"Now therefore send and gather all Israel to me at Mount Carmel, and the prophets of Baal four hundred and fifty, and the prophets of Asherah four hundred, who eat at Jezebel's table."
So Ahab sent to all the Israelites and gathered the prophets together at Mount Carmel.
Elijah drew near to all the people and said, "How long will you limp between two opinions? If the the LORD is God, follow Him; but if Baal, follow him." And the people gave him no answer.
Then Elijah said to the people, "I alone am left a prophet of the the LORD, but Baal's prophets are four hundred and fifty men.

Let them therefore give us two bulls; and let them choose one bull for themselves and cut it in pieces and lay it on the wood, but put no fire to it; and I will prepare the other bull and lay it on the wood, and put no fire to it.
Then you shall call on the name of your god, and I will call on the name of the the LORD; and the God who answers by fire, He is God." And all the people answered and said, "The proposal is sound."
Elijah said to the prophets of Baal, "Choose for yourselves one bull and prepare it first, for you are many; and call on the name of your god, but put no fire to it."

So they took the bull that was given them and prepared it, and called on the name of Baal from morning until noon, saying, "O Baal, answer us!" But there was no voice, and no one answered. And they cavorted about the altar they had made.
At noon Elijah mocked them and said, "Cry aloud, for he is a god; perhaps he is meditating, or he is attending to his needs, or he is on a journey, or perhaps he is asleep and must be awakened."
So they cried with a loud voice and gashed themselves according to their custom with swords and lances, until the blood gushed out upon them.
When midday had passed, they prophesied until the time of the offering of the evening sacrifice, but there was no voice, no one answered, and no one paid attention.
Then Elijah said to all the people, "Come near to me." So all the people came near to him. And he repaired the altar of the the LORD that had been thrown down.
Elijah took twelve stones, according to the number of the tribes of the sons of Jacob, to whom the word of the the LORD had come, saying, "Israel shall be your name."
And with the stones he built an altar in the name of the the LORD; and he made a trench around the altar, large enough to hold two seahs of seed.
And he arranged the wood and cut the bull in pieces and laid it on the wood.

He said, "Fill four jars with water and pour it on the burnt offering and on the wood." Then he said, "Do it a second time." And they did it a second time. Then he said, "Do it a third time." And they did it a third time.
The water ran around the altar, and he also filled the trench with water.

At the time of the offering of the evening sacrifice, Elijah the prophet came near and said, "O the LORD, God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, let it be known this day that You are God in Israel, and that I am Your servant, and that I have done all these things at Your word.
Answer me, O the LORD, answer me, that this people may know that You are the the LORD God, and that You have turned their heart back again."
Then the fire of the the LORD fell and consumed the burnt offering and the wood and the stones and the dust, and licked up the water that was in the trench.
When all the people saw it, they fell on their faces and said, "The the LORD, He is God! The the LORD, He is God!"
Elijah said to them, "Seize the prophets of Baal; let not one of them escape." And they seized them; and Elijah brought them down to the brook Kishon and slaughtered them there.
Elijah said to Ahab, "Go up, eat and drink, for there is a sound of abundance of rain."
So Ahab went up to eat and to drink. And Elijah went up to the top of Carmel; and he bowed himself down upon the earth and put his face between his knees.
He said to his servant, "Go up now, look toward the sea." And he went up and looked and said, "There is nothing." And he said, "Go again seven times."
At the seventh time he said, "Behold, a little cloud like a man's hand is rising out of the sea." And he said, "Go up, say to Ahab, 'Prepare your chariot and go down, lest the rain stop you.'"
In a little while the heavens grew black with clouds and wind, and there was a great rain. And Ahab rode and went to Jezreel.
The hand of the the LORD was on Elijah; and he girded up his loins and ran before Ahab to the entrance of Jezreel.
Ahab told Jezebel everything Elijah had done and how he had slain all the prophets with the sword.
Jezebel sent a messenger to Elijah, saying, "I swear by the gods that by this time tomorrow I will have made your life like the life of one of them."
When Elijah saw this, he arose and fled for his life and came to Beersheba, which belongs to Judah, and left his servant there.

He himself went a day's journey into the wilderness and came and sat down under a broom tree; and he asked that he might die, saying, "I have had enough; now, O the LORD, take my life, for I am no better than my fathers."
Then he lay down and slept under the broom tree; and behold, an angel touched him and said to him, "Arise and eat."
And he looked, and behold, there was at his head a cake baked on hot stones and a jar of water. And he ate and drank and lay down again.
The angel of the LORD came again a second time and touched him and said, "Arise and eat, for the journey is too great for you."
And he arose and ate and drank, and went in the strength of that food forty days and forty nights to Horeb, the mountain of God.
There he came to a cave and lodged there; and behold, the word of the LORD came to him, saying, "What are you doing here, Elijah?"

He said, "I have been very jealous for the LORD, the God of Hosts; for the children of Israel have forsaken Your covenant, torn down Your altars, and slain Your prophets with the sword. I alone am left, and they seek my life, to take it away."

He said, "Go out and stand on the mountain before the LORD." And behold, the LORD passed by, and a great and strong wind tore the mountains and shattered the rocks before the LORD, but the LORD was not in the wind.
After the wind came an earthquake, but the LORD was not in the earthquake. After the earthquake came a fire, but the LORD was not in the fire. After the fire came a gentle whisper.
When Elijah heard it, he wrapped his face in his mantle and went out and stood at the entrance of the cave. And behold, a voice came to him and said, "What are you doing here, Elijah?"

He said, "I have been very jealous for the LORD, the God of Hosts; for the children of Israel have forsaken Your covenant, torn down Your altars, and slain Your prophets with the sword. I alone am left, and they seek my life, to take it away."
The LORD said to him, "Go, return on your way to the wilderness of Damascus; and when you arrive, anoint Hazael king over Aram.
And you shall anoint Jehu son of Nimshi king over Israel, and Elisha son of Shaphat of Abel-meholah you shall anoint as prophet in your place.
And whoever escapes from the sword of Hazael, Jehu shall put to death; and whoever escapes from the sword of Jehu, Elisha shall put to death.
Yet I will preserve seven thousand in Israel, all who have not bowed the knee to Baal, and every mouth that has not kissed him."

Elijah departed from there and found Elisha son of Shaphat, who was plowing with twelve yoke of oxen before him, and he himself was with the twelfth. Elijah passed by him and cast his mantle upon him.
He left the oxen and ran after Elijah and said, "Let me, I pray, kiss my father and my mother, and then I will follow you." Elijah said to him, "Go back again, for what have I done to you?"

He turned back from following him and took the yoke of oxen and slaughtered them and boiled their flesh with the implements of the oxen and gave it to the people, and they ate. Then he arose and went after Elijah and ministered to him.
Ben-Hadad, king of Aram, mustered his entire host and, accompanied by thirty-two kings together with cavalry and chariots, ascended and besieged Samaria, waging war against it.
He dispatched messengers into the city to Ahab, king of Israel,
and they declared, “Thus says Ben-Hadad: ‘Your silver and gold are mine; the finest of your wives and children are mine as well.’”
The king of Israel answered, “As you have said, my lord the king, I am yours, and all that I have is yours.”
The messengers returned and said, “Thus says Ben-Hadad: ‘I did send to you, saying, “Give me your silver and gold, your wives and your children.”’

Yet about this time tomorrow I will send my servants to you, and they shall search your house and the houses of your servants; they shall lay hands on whatever is precious in your eyes and carry it away.’”

Then the king of Israel summoned all the elders of the land and said, “Consider and see how this man seeks mischief, for he sent to me for my wives, my children, my silver, and my gold, and I did not refuse him.”
All the elders and the people said to him, “Do not listen to him, and do not consent.”
So he said to Ben-Hadad’s messengers, “Tell my lord the king, ‘All that you first sent for I will do, but this I cannot do.’” The messengers departed and brought back his answer.
Ben-Hadad sent to him and said, “May the gods do so to me, and more also, if the dust of Samaria suffice for handfuls for all the people who follow me.”
The king of Israel answered, “Tell him, ‘Let not the one who girds on his armor boast as though he were taking it off.’”
When Ben-Hadad heard this message, while he and the kings were drinking in the booths, he said to his servants, “Take your positions.” So they took their positions against the city.

Then a prophet drew near to Ahab, king of Israel, and said, “Thus says the the LORD: ‘Have you seen all this great multitude? Behold, I will give it into your hand today, and you shall know that I am the the LORD.’”
Ahab said, “By whom?” He said, “Thus says the the LORD: ‘By the young men of the provincial commanders.’” Ahab said, “Who shall open the battle?” He said, “You.”
So he mustered the young men of the provincial commanders, and they numbered two hundred and thirty-two; after them he mustered all the people of Israel, seven thousand.
They went out at noon, while Ben-Hadad was drinking himself drunk in the booths, he and the thirty-two kings who were helping him.
The young men of the provincial commanders went out first. Ben-Hadad sent out scouts, and they reported to him, “Men have come out from Samaria.”
He said, “Whether they have come out for peace or for war, seize them alive.”
So these went out from the city—the commanders at the head and the army behind them.
Each struck down his man, and Aram fled while Israel pursued them; Ben-Hadad, king of Aram, escaped on horseback with the horsemen.
The king of Israel went out and struck the horses and chariots, inflicting a great slaughter upon Aram.

Then the prophet drew near to the king of Israel and said to him, “Go, strengthen yourself; consider and see what you must do, for at the return of the year the king of Aram will come up against you.”
