He fashioned a bronze altar twenty cubits in length, twenty cubits in breadth, and ten cubits in height.
He also cast the Sea, a circular vessel whose rim extended ten cubits from one edge to the opposite edge and whose height was five cubits; a line of thirty cubits encompassed its circumference.
Beneath its rim, bovine figures encircled it, ten in each cubit, running continuously around the whole perimeter; these bulls were cast in two rows as an integral part of the same molten piece.
The Sea rested upon twelve oxen, three facing north, three west, three south, and three east, so that the vessel stood above them while their hindquarters were turned inward.
Its wall was a handbreadth thick, and its rim was fashioned like the rim of a cup, resembling a lily blossom; the vessel held three thousand baths.

He likewise made ten basins for washing, placing five on the right and five on the left; in them were rinsed the implements used for the burnt offering, whereas the Sea served the priests for their ablutions.
He made ten lampstands of gold according to their prescribed pattern and set them in the temple, five on the right and five on the left.
He also made ten tables and positioned them in the temple, five on the right and five on the left, together with a hundred gold sprinkling bowls.
He constructed the priests' courtyard, the great court, and the doors of the court, overlaying those doors with bronze.
He set the Sea on the south side, at the southeast corner.
Huram made the pots, the shovels, and the sprinkling bowls; thus Huram brought to completion the work he had undertaken for King Solomon in the house of God:
the two pillars; the two bowl-shaped capitals atop the pillars; the two networks intended to cover the two bowl-shaped capitals atop the pillars;
the four hundred pomegranates for the two networks, arranged in two rows on each network to cover the two bowl-shaped capitals on the faces of the pillars;
the stands and the basins resting upon the stands;
the Sea and the twelve oxen beneath it.
The pots, the shovels, the forks, and all their utensils Huram-abi fashioned for King Solomon for the house of the LORD out of polished bronze.
The king had them cast in clay molds in the plain of the Jordan, between Succoth and Zeredah.
Solomon produced all these articles in such prodigious abundance that the weight of the bronze was never determined.
Solomon also made all the furnishings for the house of God: the golden altar; the tables upon which the Bread of the Presence was laid;
the lampstands of pure gold, with their lamps, to be kindled before the inner sanctuary in accordance with the ordinance;
the floral ornaments, the lamps, and the tongs, all of pure gold;
the snuffers, the sprinkling bowls, the dishes, and the censers of pure gold; and the gold doors of the innermost chamber, the Most Holy Place, together with the doors of the main hall.

Thus all the work that Solomon had accomplished for the house of the LORD was finished; and Solomon brought in the things that his father David had consecrated—silver, gold, and all the vessels—and he deposited them in the treasuries of the house of God.

Then Solomon assembled the elders of Israel and all the heads of the tribes, the chief fathers of the sons of Israel, in Jerusalem, to bring up the ark of the covenant of the LORD from the City of David, which is Zion.
And all the men of Israel assembled themselves to the king at the feast in the seventh month.
So all the elders of Israel came, and the Levites took up the ark.
And they brought up the ark, the Tent of Meeting, and all the holy vessels that were in the Tent; the priests and the Levites brought them up.

And King Solomon, together with all the congregation of Israel that had assembled before him at the ark, was sacrificing sheep and oxen in such abundance that they could neither be counted nor numbered.
Then the priests brought the ark of the covenant of the LORD to its place, into the inner sanctuary of the house, to the Most Holy Place, beneath the wings of the cherubim.
For the cherubim spread out their wings over the place of the ark, and the cherubim covered the ark and its poles from above.
And the poles were so long that the ends of the poles were seen from the Holy Place before the inner sanctuary, but they could not be seen from outside; and there they remain to this day.
There was nothing in the ark except the two tablets that Moses had put there at Horeb, when the LORD made a covenant with the sons of Israel when they came out of the land of Egypt.
And it came to pass, when the priests came out of the Holy Place—for all the priests who were present had sanctified themselves, without regard to their divisions—

and the Levites who were the singers, all of them of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun, with their sons and their brethren, stood at the east side of the altar, clothed in fine linen, with cymbals, harps, and lyres, and with them one hundred and twenty priests sounding trumpets—

and it came to pass that, as the trumpeters and the singers were as one voice, making one sound to be heard in praising and thanking the LORD, and as they lifted up their voice with the trumpets, cymbals, and instruments of music, and praised the LORD, saying, “For He is good, for His mercy endures forever,” the house of the LORD was filled with a cloud.
So the priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud, for the glory of the LORD filled the house of God.
Then Solomon said, “The LORD has said that He would dwell in the thick darkness.
But I have built You an exalted house, a place for You to dwell forever.”
Meanwhile, the whole assembly of Israel stood, and the king turned about and blessed the whole assembly of Israel.
He said, “Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who has fulfilled with His hands what He spoke with His mouth to my father David, saying,

‘Since the day I brought My people out of the land of Egypt, I have not chosen a city among all the tribes of Israel in which to build a house for My Name to dwell, nor have I chosen any man to be ruler over My people Israel.
But I have chosen Jerusalem for My Name to be there, and I have chosen David to be over My people Israel.’
Now it was in the heart of my father David to build a house for the Name of the LORD, the God of Israel.”
“But the LORD said to my father David, ‘Because it was in your heart to build a house for My Name, you did well that it was in your heart.
Nevertheless, you shall not build the house, but your son, your own offspring, shall build the house for My Name.’”

“And the LORD has established His word that He spoke; I have succeeded my father David and sit on the throne of Israel, as the LORD promised, and I have built the house for the Name of the LORD, the God of Israel.
There I have placed the ark, in which is the covenant of the LORD that He made with the sons of Israel.”
Then Solomon stood before the altar of the LORD in the presence of the whole assembly of Israel and spread out his hands.

Now Solomon had made a bronze platform five cubits long, five cubits wide, and three cubits high, and had set it in the middle of the court; he stood upon it, then knelt on his knees before the whole assembly of Israel and spread out his hands toward heaven.
And he said, “O the LORD, God of Israel, there is no God like You in heaven or on earth, keeping covenant and steadfast love with Your servants who walk before You with all their heart.
You have kept what You promised Your servant David my father; You spoke with Your mouth and fulfilled with Your hand this very day.

And now, O the LORD, God of Israel, keep for Your servant David my father what You promised him, saying, ‘You shall never fail to have a man to sit before Me on the throne of Israel, if only your sons keep their way, to walk in My law as you have walked before Me.’
And now, O the LORD, God of Israel, let Your word be confirmed that You spoke to Your servant David.” “
But will God indeed dwell with mortals on earth? Behold, heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain You, how much less this house that I have built!
Yet have regard to the prayer of Your servant and to his plea, O the LORD my God, to hear the cry and the prayer that Your servant is praying before You.
May Your eyes be open toward this house day and night, toward the place of which You said You would put Your Name, to hear the prayer that Your servant prays toward this place.
Hear the supplications of Your servant and of Your people Israel when they pray toward this place. Hear from heaven, Your dwelling place, and when You hear, forgive.” “
If a man sins against his neighbor and is required to take an oath, and he comes to take the oath before Your altar in this house,

then may You hear from heaven and act. May You judge Your servants, condemning the wicked by bringing his way upon his own head, and vindicating the righteous by rewarding him according to his righteousness.” “
If Your people Israel are defeated before an enemy because they have sinned against You, and they return to You and confess Your Name, praying and pleading before You in this house,
then may You hear from heaven and forgive the sin of Your people Israel, and bring them back to the land You gave to them and to their fathers.” “
When the heavens are shut up and there is no rain because they have sinned against You, and they pray toward this place and confess Your Name and turn from their sin because You afflict them,

then may You hear from heaven and forgive the sin of Your servants and of Your people Israel, teaching them the good way in which they should walk, and send rain upon Your land, which You have given to Your people as an inheritance.” “
If there is famine in the land, if there is pestilence, blight, or mildew, locust or caterpillar; if their enemies besiege them in any of their cities; whatever plague or whatever sickness there is—
then whatever prayer or plea is made by any individual or by all Your people Israel, each knowing his own affliction and his own sorrow, when he spreads out his hands toward this house,
may You hear from heaven, Your dwelling place, and forgive, and render to each one according to all his ways, as You know his heart—for You alone know the hearts of the sons of men—
so that they may fear You and walk in Your ways all the days they live on the face of the land that You gave to our fathers.” “

Moreover, concerning the foreigner who is not of Your people Israel but has come from a distant land because of Your great Name and Your mighty hand and Your outstretched arm—when he comes and prays toward this house—

may You hear from heaven, Your dwelling place, and do according to all for which the foreigner calls to You, so that all the peoples of the earth may know Your Name and fear You, as do Your people Israel, and may know that this house which I have built is called by Your Name.” “
When Your people go out to war against their enemies by the way that You send them, and they pray to You toward this city that You have chosen and toward the house that I have built for Your Name,
then may You hear from heaven their prayer and their plea, and maintain their cause.” “
If they sin against You—for there is no one who does not sin—and You are angry with them and give them over to an enemy, so that they are carried away captive to a land far or near,

and they come to their senses in the land where they are carried captive, and repent and make supplication to You in the land of their captivity, saying, ‘We have sinned, we have committed iniquity, and we have done wickedly,’

and they return to You with all their heart and with all their soul in the land of their captivity, where their captors carried them, and they pray toward their land that You gave to their fathers, and toward the city that You have chosen, and toward the house that I have built for Your Name,
then may You hear from heaven, Your dwelling place, their prayer and their supplications, and maintain their cause, and forgive Your people who have sinned against You.” “
Now, my God, may Your eyes be open and Your ears attentive to the prayer made in this place.
Now arise, O the LORD God, to Your resting place, You and the ark of Your strength. May Your priests, O the LORD God, be clothed with salvation, and may Your godly ones rejoice in goodness.
O the LORD God, do not turn away the face of Your anointed; remember the steadfast love You have shown Your servant David.”
When Solomon had finished praying, fire descended from heaven and consumed the burnt offering and the sacrifices, and the glory of the the LORD filled the house.
The priests could not enter the house of the the LORD, because the glory of the the LORD had filled it.

All the Israelites saw the fire descend and the glory of the the LORD upon the house, and they bowed with their faces to the ground upon the pavement, worshipped, and gave thanks to the the LORD, saying, “For He is good, for His steadfast love endures forever.”
Then the king and all the people offered sacrifice before the the LORD.
King Solomon sacrificed twenty-two thousand cattle and one hundred twenty thousand sheep; thus the king and all the people dedicated the house of God.

The priests stood at their posts, and the Levites with the instruments of music of the the LORD, which King David had made to give thanks to the the LORD—for His steadfast love endures forever—whenever David offered praise by their hand; the priests sounded trumpets before them, and all Israel stood.

Solomon also consecrated the middle of the court that was before the house of the the LORD, for there he offered the burnt offerings and the fat of the peace offerings, because the bronze altar that Solomon had made could not contain the burnt offering, the grain offering, and the fats.
At that time Solomon and all Israel with him kept the feast seven days, a very great assembly from the entrance of Hamath to the Brook of Egypt.
On the eighth day they held a solemn assembly, for they had kept the dedication of the altar seven days and the feast seven days.

On the twenty-third day of the seventh month he sent the people away to their tents, joyful and glad of heart because of the goodness that the the LORD had shown to David, to Solomon, and to Israel His people.

Thus Solomon finished the house of the the LORD and the king’s house; everything that had come into Solomon’s heart to accomplish in the house of the the LORD and in his own house, he successfully brought to completion.
The the LORD appeared to Solomon by night and said to him, “I have heard your prayer, and I have chosen this place for Myself as a house of sacrifice.
If I shut up the heavens so that there is no rain, or if I command the locust to devour the land, or if I send pestilence among My people,
and if My people who are called by My Name humble themselves, pray, seek My face, and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven, forgive their sin, and heal their land.
“Now My eyes will be open and My ears attentive to the prayer offered in this place.
For now I have chosen and consecrated this house, that My Name may be there forever; My eyes and My heart will be there all the days.
“And as for you, if you walk before Me as David your father walked, doing all that I have commanded you, and if you keep My statutes and My judgments,
then I will establish the throne of your kingdom, as I covenanted with David your father, saying, ‘No man shall be cut off from you to rule over Israel.’
“But if you turn away and forsake My statutes and My commandments that I have set before you, and go and serve other gods and worship them,
then I will uproot them from My land that I gave them; I will cast this house, which I consecrated for My Name, out of My sight, and I will make it a proverb and a byword among all the peoples.
And this house, which was exalted, everyone who passes by it will be appalled and say, ‘Why has the the LORD done thus to this land and to this house?’

And they will answer, ‘Because they forsook the the LORD, the God of their fathers, who brought them out of the land of Egypt, and laid hold of other gods, worshipped them, and served them; therefore He has brought all this calamity upon them.’”
At the conclusion of the twenty years during which Solomon had erected the house of the LORD and his own palace,
he rebuilt the cities that Huram had given him and settled the Israelites in them.
Solomon then marched against Hamath-zobah and subjugated it.
He built Tadmor in the wilderness, together with all the store-cities he had constructed in Hamath.
He also fortified Upper Beth-horon and Lower Beth-horon, transforming them into walled cities with gates and bars.

Moreover, he built Baalath and all the store-cities belonging to Solomon, along with the chariot cities, the cavalry cities, and every other project that Solomon desired to undertake in Jerusalem, in Lebanon, and throughout the whole domain of his sovereignty.
All the people who remained from the Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites—those not belonging to Israel—
namely, their descendants who had survived in the land after them, whom the Israelites had not annihilated, Solomon conscripted into forced labor, and they remain subject to it to this day.
Yet Solomon did not consign any Israelite to servitude for his labor, because they were warriors, chief officers, commanders of his chariots, and cavalrymen.
These were the two hundred fifty chief officers who supervised the people on the king's behalf.

Solomon brought Pharaoh's daughter up from the City of David to the house he had built for her, for he reasoned, "My wife shall not dwell in the palace of David, king of Israel, because the places to which the ark of the LORD has come are holy."
Then Solomon offered burnt offerings to the LORD upon the altar of the LORD that he had erected before the portico.

He did so day by day, in accordance with the commandment of Moses, for the Sabbaths, the new moons, and the three annual festivals—the Feast of Unleavened Bread, the Feast of Weeks, and the Feast of Tabernacles.

In accordance with the ordinance of David his father, he established the divisions of the priests for their service and the Levites for their duties: to praise and to minister before the priests, as each day required, and the gatekeepers in their divisions at every gate, for such was the command of David, the man of God.
Nor did they deviate from the king's injunction to the priests and Levites in any matter, including the treasuries.
Thus all of Solomon's work was brought to completion, from the day the foundation of the house of the LORD was laid until the house of the LORD was finished.
Then Solomon traveled to Ezion-geber and Eloth on the seashore of Edom.

Huram dispatched ships to him through his servants—mariners who knew the sea—and they sailed with Solomon's servants to Ophir, whence they brought back four hundred fifty talents of gold and delivered them to King Solomon.

And the queen of Sheba, having heard the report of Solomon, came to Jerusalem to test him with enigmas, accompanied by a retinue of surpassing magnitude, with camels laden with spices, gold in prodigious abundance, and precious stones; and when she came to Solomon, she communed with him concerning every matter that occupied her heart.
Solomon expounded to her every one of her inquiries, and there was no matter so recondite that he did not elucidate it for her.
When the queen of Sheba beheld Solomon’s wisdom and the palace he had erected,

together with the fare of his table, the seating of his servants, the attendance and apparel of his ministers, his cupbearers and their raiment, and the ascent by which he went up to the house of the LORD, she was left utterly breathless.
“The report that I heard in my own land concerning your words and your wisdom was true.

Yet I gave no credence to those reports until I came and my own eyes had seen; and behold, not even half of the greatness of your wisdom had been recounted to me. You have surpassed the report that I heard.”
“Blessed are your men, and blessed are these your servants, who stand continually before you and hear your wisdom.

Blessed be the LORD your God, who has delighted in you and set you on His throne as king for the LORD your God, because your God, in His love for Israel, has established them forever and has made you king over them, to execute judgment and righteousness.”

And she presented to the king 120 talents of gold, an exceedingly great quantity, together with precious spices and stones; nor had there ever been spice like that which the queen of Sheba gave to King Solomon.
The servants of Huram and the servants of Solomon, who had brought gold from Ophir, likewise brought algum wood of great value.

From this algum wood the king fashioned steps for the house of the LORD and for the royal palace, as well as lyres and harps for the singers; and nothing of the kind had before been seen in the land of Judah.
King Solomon granted the queen of Sheba every desire she expressed, beyond what she had brought to the king; whereupon she turned and departed to her own land, she and her servants.
The weight of gold that came to Solomon in a single year was 666 talents,
besides that brought by the traders and merchants and by all the kings of Arabia and the governors of the land, who brought gold and silver to Solomon.
King Solomon made 200 large shields of beaten gold, each overlaid with 600 shekels of gold,
and 300 smaller shields of beaten gold, each overlaid with 300 shekels of gold; and the king placed them in the House of the Forest of Lebanon.
The king also made a great throne of ivory and overlaid it with pure gold.
The throne had six steps, and a footstool of gold was attached to it; armrests stood on either side of the seat, and two lions stood beside the armrests.
Twelve lions stood there upon the six steps, one on either side of each step; and no kingdom had ever fashioned the like.
All of King Solomon’s drinking vessels were of gold, and all the vessels of the House of the Forest of Lebanon were of pure gold; in the days of Solomon, silver was accounted as nothing.
For the king had ships of Tarshish sailing with the servants of Huram; once every three years the ships of Tarshish arrived, bearing gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks.
Thus King Solomon surpassed all the kings of the earth in riches and wisdom.
And all the kings of the earth sought the presence of Solomon, to hear the wisdom that God had put in his heart.
Year by year each brought his tribute: vessels of silver and gold, garments, weapons, spices, horses, and mules.
Solomon had 4,000 stalls for horses and chariots, and 12,000 horsemen; he stationed them in the chariot cities and with the king in Jerusalem.
He ruled over all the kings from the River to the land of the Philistines and to the border of Egypt.
The king made silver as common in Jerusalem as stones, and cedar as abundant as the sycamores of the Shephelah.
Horses were brought for Solomon from Egypt and from all lands.

As for the rest of the acts of Solomon, from first to last, are they not written in the records of Nathan the prophet, in the prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite, and in the visions of Iddo the seer concerning Jeroboam son of Nebat?
Solomon reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel forty years.
Then Solomon slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David his father; and Rehoboam his son reigned in his stead.
Rehoboam traveled to Shechem, since all Israel had gathered there to install him as king.
When Jeroboam son of Nebat learned of these events, he returned from Egypt, where he had fled from King Solomon.
They sent word and summoned him; Jeroboam and all Israel came to Rehoboam and spoke, saying,
“Your father imposed a severe yoke upon us; now lighten the harsh servitude and the heavy yoke that your father laid upon us, and we shall serve you.”
He said to them, “Return to me after three days.” So the people departed.
King Rehoboam consulted the elders who had attended his father Solomon while he lived, asking, “How do you advise me to answer this people?”
They replied, “If you will deal kindly with this people and gratify them, speaking gracious words to them, then they will be your servants forever.”
Yet he disregarded the elders’ counsel and consulted the young men who had grown up with him and stood in his service.
He asked them, “What counsel do you offer, that we may answer this people who said to me, ‘Lighten the yoke your father placed upon us’?”

The young men who had grown up with him replied, “Thus you shall say to the people who have spoken to you, ‘Your father made our yoke heavy, but you make it lighter for us’—thus you shall tell them, ‘I am far more formidable than my father.’
And now my father loaded you with a heavy yoke, yet I will add to your yoke; my father disciplined you with whips, but I will discipline you with stinging lashes.”
On the third day, Jeroboam and all the people came to Rehoboam, as the king had directed, saying, “Return to me on the third day.”
The king answered them harshly; King Rehoboam abandoned the elders’ counsel.
He spoke to them according to the young men’s counsel: “I will make your yoke heavier; I will add to it. My father disciplined you with whips, but I will discipline you with stinging lashes.”
The king did not heed the people, for this turn of events came from God, so that the LORD might fulfill the word He had spoken through Ahijah the Shilonite to Jeroboam son of Nebat.

When all Israel saw that the king did not listen to them, the people answered the king: “What share have we in David? We have no inheritance in the son of Jesse. To your tents, O Israel! Now look to your own house, David.” So all Israel went to their tents.
Yet Rehoboam reigned over the Israelites who dwelt in the cities of Judah.
King Rehoboam sent Hadoram, who was in charge of the forced labor; but Israel stoned him to death. King Rehoboam then made haste to mount his chariot and flee to Jerusalem.
Thus Israel has remained in rebellion against the house of David to this day.

Upon arriving in Jerusalem, Rehoboam assembled one hundred eighty thousand chosen warriors from the houses of Judah and Benjamin, intending to wage war against Israel and restore the kingdom to Rehoboam.
But the word of the LORD came to Shemaiah the man of God, saying,
“Say to Rehoboam son of Solomon, king of Judah, and to all Israel in Judah and Benjamin:

‘Thus says the LORD: You shall not go up or fight against your brothers. Each of you return to his own house, for this thing is from Me.’” And they heeded the words of the LORD and turned back from marching against Jeroboam.
Rehoboam dwelt in Jerusalem and built cities for defense in Judah.
Zorah, Aijalon, and Hebron—fortified cities in Judah and Benjamin.
He strengthened the fortifications, appointed commanders in them, and stored provisions of food, oil, and wine.
He placed shields and spears in every city and strengthened them exceedingly, so that Judah and Benjamin were his.
The priests and Levites throughout Israel aligned themselves with him.
For the Levites abandoned their pasturelands and holdings and came to Judah and Jerusalem, because Jeroboam and his sons had rejected them from serving as priests to the LORD.
Jeroboam appointed priests of his own for the high places, for the goat demons, and for the calves he had made.
And from every tribe of Israel, those who set their hearts to seek the LORD, the God of Israel, followed them to Jerusalem to sacrifice to the LORD, the God of their fathers.
Thus they strengthened the kingdom of Judah and sustained Rehoboam son of Solomon for three years, because for three years they walked in the way of David and Solomon.
Rehoboam took as wife Mahalath, daughter of Jerimoth son of David and of Abihail daughter of Eliab son of Jesse.
She bore him sons: Jeush, Shemariah, and Zaham.
After her he took Maacah daughter of Absalom, who bore him Abijah, Attai, Ziza, and Shelomith.
Rehoboam loved Maacah daughter of Absalom more than all his wives and concubines—he had taken eighteen wives and sixty concubines, and he fathered twenty-eight sons and sixty daughters.
Rehoboam appointed Abijah son of Maacah as chief, to be king after him.

He acted wisely, distributing some of his sons throughout all the territories of Judah and Benjamin, to every fortified city; he supplied them abundantly with provisions and sought many wives for them.
When Rehoboam had established his reign and grown strong, with all Israel standing beside him, he abandoned the law of the LORD.
In the fifth year of King Rehoboam—because they had acted treacherously toward the LORD—Shishak, king of Egypt, advanced against Jerusalem.
He came with twelve hundred chariots and sixty thousand horsemen, and the people who accompanied him from Egypt—Libyans, Sukkites, and Cushites—were beyond numbering.
He seized the fortified cities of Judah and pushed on to Jerusalem.

Then Shemaiah the prophet came to Rehoboam and to the leaders of Judah who had assembled in Jerusalem because of Shishak, and he said to them, “Thus says the LORD: ‘You have forsaken Me, so I have forsaken you into Shishak’s hand.’”
The leaders of Israel and the king humbled themselves and said, “The LORD is righteous.”

When the LORD saw that they had humbled themselves, the word of the LORD came to Shemaiah: “Because they have humbled themselves, I will not destroy them; I will grant them some deliverance, and My wrath will not be poured out on Jerusalem by the hand of Shishak.
Yet they shall become his servants, so that they may learn to distinguish service to Me from service to the kingdoms of the lands.”

Then Shishak, king of Egypt, advanced against Jerusalem and carried off the treasures of the LORD’s house and the treasures of the royal palace; he took everything, including the gold shields that Solomon had fashioned.
King Rehoboam fashioned bronze shields to replace them and entrusted them to the commanders of the guard who watched the entrance to the royal palace.
Whenever the king entered the LORD’s house, the guards would bring them out and then return them to the guardroom.
When he humbled himself, the LORD’s anger turned away from him, so that He would not destroy him utterly; and, indeed, good things could still be found in Judah.

King Rehoboam consolidated his position in Jerusalem and continued to reign; he was forty-one years old when he became king, and he reigned seventeen years in Jerusalem, the city the LORD had chosen from all the tribes of Israel to set His name there. His mother was Naamah the Ammonite.
He did what was evil, because he had not fixed his heart on seeking the LORD.

The earlier and later deeds of Rehoboam—are they not recorded in the annals of Shemaiah the prophet and of Iddo the seer, together with the genealogical records? Rehoboam and Jeroboam were at war throughout their days.
Rehoboam rested with his fathers and was buried in the City of David; his son Abijah succeeded him as king.
In the eighteenth year of King Jeroboam, Abijah became king over Judah.
He reigned in Jerusalem for three years; his mother was Micaiah, daughter of Uriel, from Gibeah, and war persisted between Abijah and Jeroboam.
Abijah marshaled for battle four hundred thousand chosen men, valiant warriors, whereas Jeroboam arrayed against him eight hundred thousand selected men, mighty warriors of valor.
Then Abijah ascended Mount Zemaraim in the hill country of Ephraim and declared, "Hear me, Jeroboam and all Israel!
Do you not know that the LORD, the God of Israel, conferred the kingdom upon David and his sons forever by an enduring covenant?
Yet Jeroboam son of Nebat, a servant of Solomon son of David, rose up and rebelled against his master.
Worthless and wicked men gathered about him, strengthening themselves against Rehoboam son of Solomon, who was then young and tender-hearted and could not withstand them.

And now you imagine that you can withstand the kingdom of the LORD, which rests in the hands of David's sons; indeed, you are a vast multitude, and you have with you the golden calves that Jeroboam fashioned for you as gods.

Have you not driven out the priests of the LORD, the sons of Aaron, and the Levites, and made priests for yourselves after the manner of the peoples of other lands? Anyone who comes to consecrate himself with a young bull and seven rams becomes a priest of things that are not gods.
But as for us, the LORD is our God, and we have not forsaken Him; the priests who minister to the LORD are the sons of Aaron, and the Levites attend to their duties.

Morning by morning and evening by evening they offer burnt offerings and fragrant incense to the LORD, arrange the rows of bread upon the ceremonially clean table, and light the lamps of the golden lampstand in the evening; for we are keeping the charge of the LORD our God, while you have forsaken Him.

See, God is with us at our head, and His priests with the trumpets are to sound the alarm against you. O children of Israel, do not wage war against the LORD, the God of your fathers, for you will not prosper."
Meanwhile, Jeroboam had sent an ambush around behind them, so that while his forces were before Judah, the ambush lay in their rear.
When Judah turned and beheld battle on both front and rear, they cried out to the LORD, and the priests sounded the trumpets.
Then the men of Judah raised the battle cry, and as they shouted, God struck down Jeroboam and all Israel before Abijah and Judah.
The Israelites fled before Judah, and God delivered them into Judah's hand.
Abijah and his people inflicted a devastating slaughter upon them, and five hundred thousand chosen men of Israel fell slain.
Thus were the Israelites humbled at that time, while the men of Judah prevailed, because they relied upon the LORD, the God of their fathers.
Abijah pursued Jeroboam and captured cities from him—Bethel, Jeshanah, and Ephron, together with their villages.
Jeroboam never recovered his strength during Abijah's days; the LORD struck him, and he died.
Abijah, however, grew mighty: he took fourteen wives and begot twenty-two sons and sixteen daughters.
The remainder of Abijah's acts, his ways and his words, are recorded in the Treatise of the Prophet Iddo.
Abijah slept with his fathers and was buried in the City of David, and his son Asa reigned in his place. In his days the land was quiet for ten years.
Asa did what was good and right in the eyes of the LORD his God.
He removed the foreign altars and the high places, broke the sacred pillars, and cut down the Asherah poles.
He urged Judah to seek the LORD, the God of their fathers, and to observe the law and the commandment.
He also removed the high places and the incense altars from all the cities of Judah, and the kingdom was at peace before him.
Because the land was quiet, he built fortified cities in Judah; for there was no war with him in those years, because the LORD gave him rest.

Asa said to Judah, “Let us build these cities and surround them with wall, towers, gates, and bars. The land still lies open before us, because we have sought the LORD our God; we have sought Him, and He has given us rest on every side.” So they built and prospered.

Asa had an army of three hundred thousand men from Judah, bearing shield and spear, and two hundred eighty thousand from Benjamin, bearing shield and drawing the bow; all these were mighty men of valor.
Zerah the Cushite came out against them with an army of a million men and three hundred chariots, and he came as far as Mareshah.
Asa went out to meet him, and they drew up their battle lines in the Valley of Zephathah at Mareshah.

Asa cried out to the LORD his God, “The LORD, there is no one besides You to help in the battle between the mighty and the powerless. Help us, the LORD our God, for we rely on You, and in Your name we have come against this multitude. the LORD, You are our God; do not let mere mortals prevail against You.”
The LORD struck down the Cushites before Asa and before Judah, and the Cushites fled.

Asa and the people with him pursued them as far as Gerar, and the Cushites fell until none survived, for they were shattered before the LORD and before His army; and they carried away very much spoil.
They struck all the cities around Gerar, for the terror of the LORD had fallen upon them; they plundered all the cities, because there was much spoil in them.
They also struck the tents of the herdsmen and carried away sheep and camels in abundance, and returned to Jerusalem.
The Spirit of God came upon Azariah son of Oded.

He went out to meet Asa and said, “Hear me, Asa, and all Judah and Benjamin: the LORD is with you while you are with Him. If you seek Him, He will be found by you; but if you forsake Him, He will forsake you.
“For a long time Israel has been without the true God, without a priest to instruct, and without law.
Yet in their distress they turned to the LORD God of Israel, sought Him, and He was found by them.
“In those days there was no peace for him who went out or for him who came in, for great disturbances afflicted all the inhabitants of the lands.
Nation was crushed by nation, and city by city, for God confounded them with every kind of distress.
But as for you, be strong and do not let your hands be weak, for there is reward for your labor.”

When Asa heard these words and the prophecy of Oded the prophet, he took courage and removed the abominations from all the land of Judah and Benjamin, and from the cities he had captured in the hill country of Ephraim; he also renewed the altar of the LORD that stood before the portico of the LORD.

He gathered all Judah and Benjamin, together with those from Ephraim, Manasseh, and Simeon who sojourned among them, for a multitude from Israel had defected to him when they saw that the LORD his God was with him.
They assembled at Jerusalem in the third month of the fifteenth year of Asa’s reign.
On that day they sacrificed to the LORD seven hundred oxen and seven thousand sheep from the spoil.
They entered into a covenant to seek the LORD God of their fathers with all their heart and with all their soul.
Whoever would not seek the LORD God of Israel was to be put to death, whether small or great, man or woman.
They swore to the LORD with a loud voice, with shouting, with trumpets, and with horns.
All Judah rejoiced over the oath, for they had sworn with all their heart and sought Him with their whole desire, and He was found by them; and the LORD gave them rest on every side.
Asa also removed Maacah his mother from being queen mother, because she had made an abomination for Asherah; Asa cut down her abomination, crushed it, and burned it in the Kidron Valley.
The high places, however, were not removed from Israel; nevertheless, Asa’s heart was wholly devoted to the LORD all his days.
He brought into the house of God the dedicated things of his father and his own dedicated things—silver, gold, and vessels.
There was no war until the thirty-fifth year of Asa’s reign.
In the thirty-sixth year of Asa’s reign, Baasha, king of Israel, advanced against Judah and fortified Ramah, intending to prevent anyone from going out or coming in to Asa, king of Judah.

Asa then brought out silver and gold from the treasuries of the house of the the LORD and from the royal palace, and sent them to Ben-hadad, king of Aram, who was residing in Damascus, with this message:

“Let there be a covenant between me and you, as there was between my father and your father. See, I have sent you silver and gold; go, break your covenant with Baasha, king of Israel, so that he may withdraw from me.”
Ben-hadad heeded King Asa and dispatched the commanders of his armies against the cities of Israel; they struck Ijon, Dan, Abel-maim, and all the store cities of Naphtali.
When Baasha heard of it, he ceased fortifying Ramah and abandoned his work.
Then King Asa took all Judah, and they carried away the stones and timber of Ramah that Baasha had been using; with them Asa built Geba and Mizpah.

At that time Hanani the seer came to Asa, king of Judah, and said to him, “Because you relied on the king of Aram and did not rely on the the LORD your God, the army of the king of Aram has escaped your hand.
Were not the Cushites and Libyans a vast army with very many chariots and horsemen? Yet when you relied on the the LORD, He delivered them into your hand.

For the eyes of the the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to strengthen those whose heart is fully devoted to Him. You have acted foolishly in this; therefore, from now on you will have wars.”
Asa was enraged at the seer and imprisoned him, for he was furious with him over this matter; at that time Asa also oppressed some of the people.
Now the acts of Asa, from first to last, are written in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel.
In the thirty-ninth year of his reign, Asa developed a severe disease in his feet; yet even in his illness he did not seek the the LORD, but consulted physicians.
Asa then rested with his fathers and died in the forty-first year of his reign.

They buried him in the tomb he had hewn for himself in the City of David, and laid him on a bier filled with spices and various kinds of incense—a blend prepared by the perfumers. They also burned a very great fire for him.
Jehoshaphat, his son, succeeded him and consolidated his authority over Israel.
He stationed troops in every fortified city of Judah, and appointed garrisons throughout the land of Judah and in the cities of Ephraim that Asa his father had seized.
The LORD was with Jehoshaphat, because he walked in the earlier ways of David his father and did not resort to the Baals.
Rather, he sought the God of his father and walked in His commandments, not emulating the conduct of Israel.
Therefore the LORD established the kingdom firmly in his hand, and all Judah rendered tribute to Jehoshaphat, so that he amassed wealth and honor in abundance.
His heart took courage in the ways of the LORD; moreover, he removed the high places and the Asherim from Judah.
In the third year of his reign he dispatched his officials—Ben-hail, Obadiah, Zechariah, Nethanel, and Micaiah—to teach in the cities of Judah.
With them went the Levites Shemaiah, Nethaniah, Zebadiah, Asahel, Shemiramoth, Jehonathan, Adonijah, Tobijah, and Tob-adonijah, together with the priests Elishama and Jehoram.
They instructed Judah, carrying with them the Book of the Law of the LORD; they traversed every city of Judah and taught the people.
The fear of the LORD fell upon all the kingdoms of the lands surrounding Judah, so that none waged war against Jehoshaphat.
Some Philistines brought gifts and silver as tribute to Jehoshaphat, and the Arabs brought him 7,700 rams and 7,700 goats.
Jehoshaphat continued to grow in greatness; he built fortresses and store cities in Judah.
He maintained extensive administrative and military business in the cities of Judah, and mighty men of valor were stationed in Jerusalem.
Their enrollment by ancestral houses was as follows for Judah: Adnah the commander, with 300,000 mighty men of valor;
next to him Jehohanan the commander, with 280,000;
next Amasiah son of Zichri, who had volunteered for the LORD, with 200,000 mighty men;
from Benjamin, Eliada the mighty man, with 200,000 armed with bow and shield;
and next Jehozabad, with 180,000 equipped for battle.
These served the king, in addition to those whom the king had posted in the fortified cities throughout Judah.
Now Jehoshaphat possessed wealth and honor in extraordinary abundance, and he cemented a marriage alliance with Ahab.

After several years had elapsed, he descended to Ahab in Samaria; Ahab slaughtered sheep and oxen in prodigious numbers for him and for the retinue accompanying him, and he induced Jehoshaphat to ascend against Ramoth-gilead.
Ahab, king of Israel, said to Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, "Will you go with me to Ramoth-gilead?" Jehoshaphat replied, "I am as you are, my people as your people; I shall be with you in the war."
Jehoshaphat said to the king of Israel, "Please inquire today for the word of the LORD."

Then the king of Israel assembled the prophets, four hundred men, and asked them, "Shall we go to war against Ramoth-gilead, or shall I forbear?" They answered, "Go up, for God will give it into the hand of the king."
Jehoshaphat said, "Is there not yet a prophet of the LORD here, that we may inquire of Him?"

The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "There is yet one man by whom we may inquire of the LORD—Micaiah son of Imlah—but I hate him, for he never prophesies good concerning me, but evil." Jehoshaphat said, "Let not the king say so."
Then the king of Israel summoned an officer and said, "Bring Micaiah son of Imlah quickly."

Now the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, were sitting each upon his throne, arrayed in robes, at the threshing floor by the entrance of the gate of Samaria, while all the prophets prophesied before them.
Zedekiah son of Chenaanah made for himself horns of iron and said, "Thus says the LORD: 'With these you shall gore Aram until they are consumed.'"
All the prophets prophesied likewise, saying, "Go up to Ramoth-gilead and prosper, for the LORD will give it into the hand of the king."

The messenger who had gone to summon Micaiah spoke to him, saying, "Behold, the words of the prophets are with one accord favorable to the king; let your word, I pray you, be like one of theirs, and speak favorably."
Micaiah said, "As the LORD lives, what my God says, that I will speak."
When he came to the king, the king said to him, "Micaiah, shall we go to Ramoth-gilead to battle, or shall I forbear?" Micaiah said, "Go up and prosper; they shall be given into your hand."
The king said to him, "How many times shall I adjure you to speak to me nothing but the truth in the name of the LORD?"
Micaiah said, "I saw all Israel scattered upon the mountains, like sheep that have no shepherd; and the LORD said, 'These have no master; let each return to his house in peace.'"
The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "Did I not tell you that he would not prophesy good concerning me, but evil?"
Micaiah said, "Therefore hear the word of the LORD: I saw the LORD sitting on His throne, and all the host of heaven standing on His right hand and on His left.
And the LORD said, 'Who will entice Ahab, king of Israel, that he may go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?' One spoke saying this, and another saying that.
Then a spirit came forward and stood before the LORD and said, 'I will entice him.' And the LORD said to him, 'By what means?'
He said, 'I will go out and be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.' And the LORD said, 'You shall entice him and shall succeed; go out and do so.'
Now therefore, behold, the LORD has put a lying spirit in the mouth of these prophets of yours, and the LORD has spoken evil concerning you.'"
Then Zedekiah son of Chenaanah came near and struck Micaiah on the cheek and said, "Which way did the Spirit of the LORD go from me to speak to you?"
Micaiah said, "Behold, you shall see on the day when you go into an inner chamber to hide yourself."
The king of Israel said, "Take Micaiah and return him to Amon, governor of the city, and to Joash, the king's son,
and say, 'Thus says the king: Put this fellow in prison and feed him with bread of affliction and water of affliction until I return in peace.'"
Micaiah said, "If you return in peace, the LORD has not spoken by me." And he said, "Hear, all you peoples."
So the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, went up to Ramoth-gilead.
The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "I will disguise myself and go into battle; but you put on your robes." So the king of Israel disguised himself, and they went into battle.
Now the king of Aram had commanded the captains of his chariots, "Fight neither with the small nor with the great, but only with the king of Israel."
When the captains saw Jehoshaphat, they said, "It is the king of Israel." They turned to fight against him; Jehoshaphat cried out, and the LORD helped him; God moved them away from him.
When the captains saw that it was not the king of Israel, they turned back from pursuing him.

A certain man drew his bow at random and struck the king of Israel between the joints of the armor and the breastplate. He said to the charioteer, "Turn your hand and carry me out of the camp, for I am wounded."
The battle increased that day; the king of Israel was propped up in the chariot facing the Arameans until evening; and at sunset he died.
Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, returned in peace to his house in Jerusalem.
Jehu son of Hanani, the seer, went out to meet him and said to King Jehoshaphat, “Should you help the wicked and love those who hate the LORD? Because of this, the LORD’s wrath is upon you.
Nevertheless, good things are found in you, for you have removed the Asherah poles from the land and have set your heart to seek God.”
Jehoshaphat dwelt in Jerusalem; then he went out again among the people from Beersheba to Mount Ephraim and brought them back to the LORD, the God of their fathers.
He appointed judges in the land, in all the fortified cities of Judah.
He said to the judges, “Consider what you are doing, for you do not judge for man but for the LORD, and He is with you in the matter of judgment.
Now let the fear of the LORD be upon you; be careful and do it, for with the LORD our God there is no injustice, no partiality, and no taking of bribes.”
In Jerusalem Jehoshaphat also appointed some of the Levites, priests, and heads of Israelite families to render the LORD’s judgment and to decide disputes, and they returned to Jerusalem.
He commanded them, “You shall do this in faithfulness and with a whole heart, in the fear of the LORD.

In every case that comes to you from your brothers who dwell in their cities—whether it concerns bloodshed, law and commandment, statutes and judgments—you shall warn them, so that they do not become guilty before the LORD and wrath come upon you and your brothers. Do this, and you will not be guilty.

Behold, Amariah the chief priest is over you in every matter of the LORD, and Zebadiah son of Ishmael, the ruler of the house of Judah, in every matter of the king; and the Levites are officers before you. Act with courage, and may the LORD be with those who do good.”
Following these events, the Moabites, the Ammonites, and a contingent of Meunites came to wage war against Jehoshaphat.
Some men came and told Jehoshaphat, “A vast army is coming against you from Aram, from beyond the sea; and, indeed, they are already at Hazazon-tamar” (that is, En-gedi).
Jehoshaphat was afraid and resolved to seek the LORD, and he proclaimed a fast throughout all Judah.
Judah assembled to seek help from the LORD; indeed, people came from all the cities of Judah to seek the LORD.
Jehoshaphat stood in the assembly of Judah and Jerusalem in the house of the LORD, before the new court,
and said, “O the LORD, God of our fathers, are You not God in heaven? You rule over all the kingdoms of the nations. In Your hand are power and might, so that no one can withstand You.
Did You not, our God, drive out the inhabitants of this land before Your people Israel and give it forever to the descendants of Abraham Your friend?
They have lived in it and have built for You a sanctuary for Your name in it, saying, ‘

If disaster comes upon us—sword, judgment, pestilence, or famine—we will stand before this house and before You, for Your name is in this house, and cry to You in our distress, and You will hear and save.’
And now behold, the sons of Ammon, Moab, and Mount Seir—whom You did not let Israel invade when they came from the land of Egypt, but they turned aside from them and did not destroy them—
behold, they repay us by coming to drive us out of Your possession, which You have given us to inherit.
O our God, will You not judge them? For we have no power against this great multitude that is coming against us; nor do we know what to do, but we look to You alone.”
All Judah stood before the LORD, together with their wives, their children, and their little ones.
Then the Spirit of the LORD came upon Jahaziel son of Zechariah, son of Benaiah, son of Jeiel, son of Mattaniah, a Levite of the sons of Asaph, in the midst of the assembly.

And he said, “Listen, all Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem and King Jehoshaphat: Thus says the LORD to you, ‘Do not be afraid or dismayed because of this great multitude, for the battle is not yours but God’s.
Tomorrow go down against them; behold, they are coming up by the ascent of Ziz, and you will find them at the end of the valley before the wilderness of Jeruel.

You will not need to fight in this battle. Stand firm, hold your position, and see the salvation of the LORD on your behalf, O Judah and Jerusalem. Do not be afraid or dismayed. Tomorrow go out against them, and the LORD will be with you.’”
Jehoshaphat bowed his face to the ground, and all Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem fell before the LORD, worshiping the LORD.
The Levites of the Kohathites and Korahites stood up to praise the LORD, the God of Israel, with a very loud voice.

They rose early in the morning and went out to the wilderness of Tekoa. As they went out, Jehoshaphat stood and said, “Hear me, Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem! Trust in the LORD your God, and you will be made secure; believe His prophets, and you will prosper.”

After consulting with the people, he appointed singers to the LORD, praising the splendor of His holiness, as they went out before the army, saying, “Give thanks to the LORD, for His steadfast love endures forever.”
As they began to sing and praise, the LORD set ambushes against the Ammonites, Moabites, and men of Mount Seir who had come against Judah, and they were routed.

For the Ammonites and Moabites rose up against the inhabitants of Mount Seir, devoting them to destruction and annihilating them; and when they had finished with the inhabitants of Seir, they helped destroy one another.
When Judah came to the watchtower in the wilderness, they looked toward the multitude, and behold, they were corpses fallen to the ground; none had escaped.

When Jehoshaphat and his people came to take the spoil, they found among them an abundance of goods, garments, and precious articles, which they took for themselves—more than they could carry. They spent three days collecting the spoil, because it was abundant.
On the fourth day they assembled in the Valley of Beracah, for there they blessed the LORD; therefore the name of that place has been called the Valley of Beracah to this day.
Then every man of Judah and Jerusalem returned, with Jehoshaphat at their head, to Jerusalem with joy, for the LORD had made them rejoice over their enemies.
They came to Jerusalem, to the house of the LORD, with harps, lyres, and trumpets.
The fear of God came upon all the kingdoms of the lands when they heard that the LORD had fought against the enemies of Israel.
So the realm of Jehoshaphat was quiet, and his God gave him rest on every side.
Jehoshaphat was thirty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-five years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Azubah the daughter of Shilhi.
He followed the example of his father Asa and did not turn aside from it, doing what was right in the sight of the LORD.
Nevertheless, the high places were not taken away, and the people had not yet set their hearts upon the God of their fathers.
Now the rest of the acts of Jehoshaphat, from first to last, are written in the annals of Jehu the son of Hanani, which are included in the Book of the Kings of Israel.
After this, Jehoshaphat king of Judah allied himself with Ahaziah king of Israel, who acted wickedly.
He joined with him to build ships to go to Tarshish, and they built the ships in Ezion-geber.

Then Eliezer son of Dodavahu of Mareshah prophesied against Jehoshaphat, saying, “Because you have allied yourself with Ahaziah, the LORD has destroyed your works.” The ships were wrecked and were not able to go to Tarshish.
When Jehoshaphat slept with his fathers and was buried with them in the City of David, his son Jehoram succeeded him as king.
He had brothers, the sons of Jehoshaphat—Azariah, Jehiel, Zechariah, Azariah, Michael, and Shephatiah—all sons of Jehoshaphat, king of Israel.
Their father had given them lavish gifts of silver, gold, and precious things, together with fortified cities in Judah, but he gave the kingdom to Jehoram, because he was the firstborn.
When Jehoram had established himself over his father's kingdom and strengthened his position, he put all his brothers to the sword, together with some of the princes of Israel.
Jehoram was thirty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned eight years in Jerusalem.
He walked in the way of the kings of Israel, just as the house of Ahab had done, for Ahab's daughter was his wife; and he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD.
Yet the LORD was unwilling to destroy the house of David, because of the covenant He had made with David, and because He had promised to give a lamp to him and to his sons for all time.
In his days Edom revolted from under the hand of Judah and set up a king over themselves.
Then Jehoram crossed over with his commanders and all his chariots; he rose by night and struck the Edomites who had surrounded him, along with the commanders of their chariots.
So Edom has remained in revolt against Judah to this day. At that same time Libnah also revolted, because Jehoram had forsaken the LORD, the God of his fathers.
Moreover, he made high places in the hill country of Judah; he caused the inhabitants of Jerusalem to play the harlot, and he led Judah astray.

Then a letter came to him from Elijah the prophet, saying, "Thus says the LORD, the God of your father David: Because you have not walked in the ways of your father Jehoshaphat or in the ways of Asa, king of Judah,

but have walked in the way of the kings of Israel and have caused Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem to play the harlot, as the house of Ahab played the harlot, and have also killed your brothers—your father's own household—who were better than you,
behold, the LORD will bring a great plague upon your people, your sons, your wives, and all your possessions.
And you will suffer many illnesses—a disease of your bowels—until your bowels come out day after day because of the sickness."
Moreover, the LORD stirred up against Jehoram the spirit of the Philistines and of the Arabs who are near the Cushites.
They came up into Judah, broke into it, and carried away all the possessions found in the king's house, together with his sons and his wives; no son was left to him except Jehoahaz, the youngest.
After all this, the LORD afflicted him in his bowels with an incurable disease.
In the course of time, at the end of two years, his bowels came out because of his illness, and he died in great agony. His people made no funeral pyre for him, as they had for his fathers.

He was thirty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned eight years in Jerusalem. He departed without being desired, and they buried him in the City of David, but not in the tombs of the kings.

The inhabitants of Jerusalem enthroned Ahaziah, Jehoram’s youngest son, in his stead, because the marauding contingent that had accompanied the Arabians into the encampment had slain all the elder heirs; thus Ahaziah, son of Jehoram, king of Judah, assumed the throne.
Ahaziah was forty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned one year in Jerusalem; his mother was Athaliah, the daughter of Omri.
He too pursued the ways of the house of Ahab, for his mother counseled him toward wickedness.
He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, as the house of Ahab had done, for after his father’s death they became his counselors unto his ruin.
He likewise followed their counsel and marched with Joram, son of Ahab, king of Israel, against Hazael, king of Aram, at Ramoth-gilead; and the Arameans wounded Joram.

Therefore he returned to Jezreel to recuperate from the wounds inflicted upon him at Ramah during his campaign against Hazael, king of Aram. Meanwhile, Ahaziah, son of Jehoram, king of Judah, descended to Jezreel to visit Joram, son of Ahab, because the latter was ill.
Ahaziah’s downfall was ordained by God when he went to Joram; for upon his arrival he went out with Joram to meet Jehu, son of Nimshi, whom the LORD had anointed to exterminate the house of Ahab.
While Jehu was executing judgment upon the house of Ahab, he discovered the princes of Judah and the sons of Ahaziah’s brothers who were serving Ahaziah, and he put them to death.

He sought Ahaziah, and his men captured him while he was hiding in Samaria; they brought him to Jehu and slew him. They buried him, because they said, “He is the grandson of Jehoshaphat, who sought the LORD with all his heart.” Thus the house of Ahaziah had no one possessing sufficient strength to retain the kingdom.
When Athaliah, the mother of Ahaziah, perceived that her son was dead, she arose and extirpated all the royal progeny of the house of Judah.

But Jehoshabeath, the king’s daughter, took Joash, son of Ahaziah, and stole him away from among the king’s sons who were being slain, placing him and his nurse in a bedchamber. Jehoshabeath, daughter of King Jehoram and wife of Jehoiada the priest—for she was Ahaziah’s sister—hid him from Athaliah, so that she did not kill him.
He remained concealed with them in the house of God for six years, while Athaliah reigned over the land.

In the seventh year, Jehoiada strengthened himself and entered into covenant with the commanders of hundreds—Azariah son of Jeroham, Ishmael son of Jehohanan, Azariah son of Obed, Maaseiah son of Adaiah, and Elishaphat son of Zichri.
They traversed Judah, assembling the Levites from every city of Judah together with the patriarchal heads of Israel, and they converged upon Jerusalem.

The whole assembly then covenanted with the king in the house of God. Jehoiada declared to them, “Indeed, the king’s son shall reign, precisely as the LORD has spoken concerning the descendants of David.
This is what you are to do: one-third of you who enter on the Sabbath—namely the priests and Levites serving as gatekeepers at the thresholds—shall guard the thresholds.
Another third shall be at the king’s house, and another third at the Foundation Gate, while all the people remain in the courts of the house of the LORD.
No one may enter the house of the LORD except the priests and those Levites who minister, for they are consecrated; yet all the people shall keep the watch of the LORD.
The Levites must encircle the king, each man bearing his weapon in hand; anyone entering the house shall be put to death. They are to remain with the king in his coming and going.”

The Levites and all Judah executed everything that Jehoiada the priest had commanded: each man took his contingent, both those coming on duty and those departing on the Sabbath, for Jehoiada had not dismissed the divisions.
Jehoiada the priest distributed to the commanders of hundreds the spears, shields, and bucklers that had belonged to King David and were kept in the house of God.
He stationed all the people, every man with his weapon in hand, around the king—from the right side of the house to the left side of the house, by the altar and the house.
Then they brought out the king’s son, placed the crown upon him, gave him the Testimony, and proclaimed him king. Jehoiada and his sons anointed him, and they cried, “Long live the king!”
When Athaliah heard the clamor of the people running and acclaiming the king, she came to the people in the house of the LORD.

She beheld the king standing by his pillar at the entrance, with the officers and trumpeters beside the king; all the people of the land rejoiced and sounded trumpets, while the singers, accompanied by musical instruments, led the praise. Then Athaliah tore her garments and cried, “Treason! Treason!”

Jehoiada the priest brought forth the commanders of hundreds who were over the army and said to them, “Bring her out between the ranks, and put to the sword anyone who follows her.” For the priest had said, “She must not be put to death in the house of the LORD.”
So they seized her, and she went by way of the entrance of the Horse Gate to the king’s house, where they put her to death.
Jehoiada then covenanted between himself, all the people, and the king, that they should be the people of the LORD.
All the people went to the temple of Baal, tore it down, smashed its altars and images, and slew Mattan, priest of Baal, before the altars.

Jehoiada appointed the priests and Levites over the house of the LORD, according to the divisions David had established for the house of the LORD, to offer burnt offerings to the LORD, as written in the Law of Moses, with rejoicing and singing, according to David’s ordinance.
He stationed gatekeepers at the gates of the house of the LORD, so that no one unclean in any respect might enter.

He took the captains of hundreds, the nobles, the governors of the people, and all the people of the land, and brought the king down from the house of the LORD. They passed through the Upper Gate into the king’s house and seated the king upon the throne of the kingdom.
All the people of the land rejoiced, and the city was quiet, for Athaliah had been put to the sword.
Joash was seven years old when he ascended the throne, and he reigned forty years in Jerusalem; his mother was Zibiah of Beersheba.
Throughout all the days of Jehoiada the priest, Joash executed what was righteous in the sight of the LORD.
Jehoiada secured two wives for him, and he begot sons and daughters.
Afterward, Joash resolved in his heart to restore the house of the LORD.

He assembled the priests and the Levites and charged them, “Proceed into the cities of Judah and collect, year by year, the monetary offering from all Israel for the repair of the house of your God; and you must expedite this affair.” Yet the Levites did not hasten.

The king summoned Jehoiada the chief priest and demanded, “Why have you not required the Levites to bring from Judah and Jerusalem the tax imposed by Moses, the servant of the LORD, and by the congregation of Israel, for the tent of testimony?”
For the sons of the wicked Athaliah had breached the house of God and had even devoted all the consecrated things of the house of the LORD to the Baals.
At the king’s command, they fashioned a chest and placed it outside, at the gate of the house of the LORD.
Then a proclamation was issued throughout Judah and Jerusalem, calling upon the people to bring to the LORD the tax that Moses, the servant of God, had levied upon Israel in the wilderness.
All the officials and all the people rejoiced; they brought their contributions and cast them into the chest until it was full.

Whenever the chest was brought by the Levites to the king’s overseers, and whenever they perceived that the silver was abundant, the king’s scribe and the chief priest’s officer would come, empty the chest, and carry it back to its place. Thus they proceeded day by day, amassing silver in profusion.

The king and Jehoiada entrusted it to those executing the work of the service of the house of the LORD; they hired masons and carpenters to restore the house of the LORD, and likewise smiths of iron and bronze to reinforce the house of the LORD.
The artisans labored, and the restoration progressed; they reestablished the house of God according to its original plan and strengthened it.

When they had completed the work, they brought the remaining silver before the king and Jehoiada, and from it they fashioned vessels for the house of the LORD—vessels for service, for burnt offerings, and spoons, as well as vessels of gold and silver. Throughout all the days of Jehoiada, burnt offerings were continually presented in the house of the LORD.
Jehoiada grew aged and full of days; he died at one hundred thirty years of age.
He was interred among the kings in the city of David, because he had wrought good in Israel, and toward God, and toward His house.
After Jehoiada’s death, the princes of Judah came and paid homage to the king; then the king heeded them.
They abandoned the house of the LORD, the God of their fathers, and served the Asherim and the idols; consequently, wrath descended upon Judah and Jerusalem for this guilt.
He sent prophets to them to turn them back to the LORD, and they bore witness against them, yet they would not listen.

Then the Spirit of God clothed Zechariah, the son of Jehoiada the priest, and he stood above the people and proclaimed, “Thus says God: Why do you transgress the commandments of the LORD, so that you cannot prosper? Because you have forsaken the LORD, He has forsaken you.”
They conspired against him at the king’s behest and stoned him with stones in the court of the house of the LORD.
King Joash did not remember the kindness that Jehoiada his father had shown him, but slew his son. As he was dying, he cried, “May the LORD see and require it.”
At the turn of the year, the army of Aram marched against him; they invaded Judah and Jerusalem and destroyed all the princes of the people, and they sent all their spoil to the king of Damascus.

Although the Aramean force came with few men, the LORD delivered a very great army into their hand, because they had forsaken the LORD, the God of their fathers; thus judgment was executed upon Joash.

When they withdrew, they left him in severe afflictions; his servants conspired against him on account of the blood of the sons of Jehoiada the priest, and they assassinated him upon his bed, and he died. He was buried in the city of David, but not in the tombs of the kings.
These were the conspirators against him: Zabad, the son of Shimeath the Ammonitess, and Jehozabad, the son of Shimrith the Moabitess.

As for his sons, and the magnitude of the burdens imposed upon him, and the founding of the house of God, behold, they are recorded in the commentary on the book of the kings. His son Amaziah reigned in his stead.
Amaziah was twenty-five years old at his accession to the throne in Jerusalem, and his reign extended over twenty-nine years; his mother was Jehoaddan of Jerusalem.
He executed what was right in the sight of the LORD, albeit not with a whole heart.
Once the kingdom had been firmly established under his authority, he put to death the servants who had assassinated his father the king.

Yet he did not execute their children, inasmuch as it is written in the Law—in the Book of Moses—that the LORD commanded, "Fathers shall not be put to death for their children, nor shall children be put to death for their fathers; each shall die for his own sin."

Amaziah mustered Judah, appointing officers over thousands and hundreds; he enrolled those from twenty years of age upward throughout Judah and Benjamin, and discovered three hundred thousand select warriors, proficient in spear and shield.
He also retained one hundred thousand mighty men of valor from Israel at the cost of one hundred talents of silver.
A man of God then approached him, saying, "O king, do not let the army of Israel accompany you, for the LORD is not with Israel—not with any descendant of Ephraim.
Yet if you persist in going, then go and be strong for battle; nevertheless, God will cause you to falter before the enemy, for God has power both to help and to overthrow."

Amaziah inquired of the man of God, "But what is to be done concerning the hundred talents I have already disbursed to the Israelite troop?" The man of God replied, "The LORD is able to give you far more than this."

Accordingly, Amaziah separated out the contingent that had come to him from Ephraim, dismissing them to their homes; they departed in furious anger against Judah, returning to their own places in a rage.
Amaziah, however, took courage and led his people into the Valley of Salt, where he defeated ten thousand of the sons of Seir.
The men of Judah also captured ten thousand alive, conveyed them to the summit of the rock, and cast them down from its height, so that all were dashed to pieces.
As for the troops whom Amaziah had dismissed from the campaign, they made raids upon the cities of Judah from Samaria to Beth-horon, struck down three thousand, and carried off a great spoil.
After Amaziah returned from smiting the Edomites, he brought back the gods of the sons of Seir, erected them as his own gods, bowed down before them, and burned incense to them.
Therefore the anger of the LORD was kindled against Amaziah, and He sent a prophet to him, who said, "Why have you sought the gods of a people who could not deliver their own people from your hand?"

While the prophet was still speaking, the king said to him, "Have we appointed you counselor to the king? Desist; why should you be struck down?" So the prophet refrained, but said, "I know that God has determined to destroy you, because you have done this and have not heeded my counsel."
Then Amaziah king of Judah, having taken counsel, sent to Joash son of Jehoahaz son of Jehu, king of Israel, saying, "Come, let us confront one another in battle."

Joash king of Israel sent back to Amaziah king of Judah: "A thistle in Lebanon sent to a cedar in Lebanon, saying, 'Give your daughter to my son for a wife'; but a wild beast of Lebanon passed by and trampled the thistle."
"You say, 'Behold, I have struck Edom,' and your heart has lifted you up to boast. Now stay at home; why provoke disaster, that you should fall—you and Judah with you?"
Amaziah, however, would not listen, for this was from God, that He might deliver them into the hand of Joash, because they had sought the gods of Edom.
So Joash king of Israel went up, and he and Amaziah king of Judah faced one another at Beth-shemesh in Judah.
Judah was defeated before Israel, and the men fled, each to his tent.

Joash king of Israel captured Amaziah king of Judah, son of Joash son of Jehoahaz, at Beth-shemesh; he brought him to Jerusalem and broke down the wall of Jerusalem from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate, for a distance of four hundred cubits.

He took all the gold and silver, all the vessels found in the house of God together with those in the keeping of Obed-edom, the treasures of the king's house, and the hostages, and returned to Samaria.
Amaziah son of Joash king of Judah lived fifteen years after the death of Joash son of Jehoahaz king of Israel.
The rest of the acts of Amaziah, from first to last, are they not written in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel?
From the time Amaziah turned away from following the LORD, a conspiracy arose against him in Jerusalem; he fled to Lachish, but they sent after him to Lachish and killed him there.
They carried him upon horses and buried him with his fathers in the city of Judah.
All the people of Judah took Uzziah, though he was only sixteen years of age, and enthroned him in place of his father Amaziah.
He rebuilt Elath and restored it to Judah after the king had gone to rest with his fathers.
Uzziah was sixteen years old when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty-two years in Jerusalem; his mother was Jecoliah, from Jerusalem.
He did what was right in the sight of the LORD, following in every respect the example of his father Amaziah.
In the days of Zechariah, a man conversant with divine visions, he devoted himself to seeking God; and throughout the entire period in which he sought the LORD, God caused him to prosper.
He marched out against the Philistines, dismantled the walls of Gath, Jabneh, and Ashdod, and founded settlements in Ashdod and throughout Philistia.
God sustained him against the Philistines, against the Arabs who dwelt in Gur-baal, and against the Meunites.
The Ammonites paid tribute to Uzziah, whose renown extended to the frontier of Egypt, so greatly had his power increased.
Uzziah erected towers in Jerusalem at the Corner Gate, the Valley Gate, and the Angle, and he strengthened them.

He also built towers in the wilderness and hewed many cisterns, for he possessed abundant livestock in the Shephelah and on the plain; he maintained farmers and vinedressers in the hill country and in the fertile tracts, for he cherished the soil.

Furthermore, Uzziah kept a standing force prepared for battle, organized into divisions according to the muster rolls compiled by Jeiel the scribe and Maaseiah the officer, under the command of Hananiah, one of the king's principal officers.
The total number of patriarchal chiefs among the mighty warriors amounted to two thousand six hundred.
Under their command stood an army of three hundred seven thousand five hundred, capable of waging war with formidable strength, to assist the king against his adversaries.
Uzziah furnished the entire host with shields, spears, helmets, coats of mail, bows, and slingstones.

In Jerusalem he devised ingenious machines, the handiwork of skilled artisans, to be mounted upon the towers and battlements for shooting arrows and hurling massive stones; his fame spread far and wide, for he received extraordinary divine assistance until he had grown mighty.
Yet when he had become mighty, his heart was lifted up to his ruin; he dealt treacherously with the LORD his God by entering the temple of the LORD to burn incense upon the altar of incense.
Azariah the priest followed him in, together with eighty priests of the LORD, valiant men.

They confronted King Uzziah and said, "It is not your prerogative, Uzziah, to burn incense to the LORD, but the office of the priests, the sons of Aaron, who have been consecrated to offer it. Leave the sanctuary, for you have trespassed; nor will this bring you honor from the LORD God."

Uzziah, who held a censer in his hand to burn incense, became incensed; and while his wrath raged against the priests in the house of the LORD beside the altar of incense, leprosy broke out upon his forehead.

Azariah the chief priest and all the priests turned toward him, and behold, he was leprous on his forehead; they hurried him out, and he himself hastened to depart, because the LORD had afflicted him.

King Uzziah remained a leper until the day of his death; he dwelt in a secluded residence, being leprous, for he had been cut off from the house of the LORD. Jotham his son oversaw the royal household and judged the people of the land.
The rest of Uzziah's acts, from first to last, were written by Isaiah the son of Amoz, the prophet.
Uzziah slept with his fathers and was buried with them in the burial field belonging to the kings, because they said, "He is a leper." Jotham his son reigned in his stead.
Jotham was twenty-five years old when he ascended the throne, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem; his mother was Jerushah, the daughter of Zadok.

He acted uprightly in the sight of the LORD, following in every respect the example of his father Uzziah, though, unlike him, he did not enter the temple of the LORD; nevertheless, the people persisted in their corrupt practices.
He rebuilt the Upper Gate of the house of the LORD and carried out extensive construction on the wall of Ophel.
He also built cities throughout the hill country of Judah, together with fortresses and towers in the wooded regions.

He waged war against the king of the Ammonites and subdued them; in that year the Ammonites gave him a hundred talents of silver, ten thousand cors of wheat, and ten thousand cors of barley, and they rendered him the same tribute in the second and third years.
Thus Jotham grew powerful, for he ordered his ways before the LORD His God.
The remainder of Jotham's acts, including all his military campaigns and his conduct, are recorded in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah.
