but if you return to Me and keep My commandments and do them, though your outcasts are at the farthest horizon, I will gather them from there and bring them to the place I have chosen to make My Name dwell.’
They are Your servants and Your people, whom You redeemed by Your great power and Your strong hand.

O Lord, I pray, let Your ear be attentive to the prayer of Your servant and to the prayer of Your servants who delight to fear Your Name; grant success to Your servant today, and give him mercy in the sight of this man.” Now I was cupbearer to the king.
In the month of Nisan, in the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes, wine was set before him; I took up the wine and presented it to the king, for I had never before appeared sorrowful in his presence.
The king said to me, “Why does your face look so distressed, when you are not ill? This can be nothing other than sorrow of spirit.” I was seized with very great fear.
I replied to the king, “May the king live forever! Why should not my countenance be downcast, when the city of my fathers’ sepulchers lies in ruins and its gates have been consumed by fire?”
The king said to me, “What is it you are requesting?” Then I prayed to the God of heaven.
I said to the king, “If it please the king, and if your servant has found favor in your sight, send me to Judah, to the city of my fathers’ sepulchers, that I may rebuild it.”
The king said to me—the queen being seated beside him—“How long will your journey be, and when will you return?” It pleased the king to send me, and I appointed a time for my return.
I said to the king, “If it please the king, let letters be given to me for the governors beyond the River, that they may grant me passage until I reach Judah,

and a letter to Asaph, keeper of the king’s forest, that he may give me timber to make beams for the gates of the citadel by the temple, for the wall of the city, and for the house in which I shall dwell.” The king granted these requests, for the gracious favor of my God was upon me.
I came to the governors beyond the River and presented them with the king’s letters. The king had also sent with me officers of the army and cavalry.
When Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite, the servant, heard of it, they were deeply vexed that a man had come to seek the welfare of the Israelites.
I came to Jerusalem and remained there three days.
I arose during the night, I and a few men with me. I had told no one what my God had put into my heart to do for Jerusalem, and no animal was with me except the one on which I rode.
I went out by night through the Valley Gate toward the Dragon Spring and the Dung Gate, surveying the walls of Jerusalem, which were broken down, and its gates, which had been consumed by fire.
Then I passed on to the Fountain Gate and to the King’s Pool, but there was not room enough for the animal under me to pass.
So I went up by night through the valley and inspected the wall; then I turned back and reentered by the Valley Gate, and so returned.
The officials did not know where I had gone or what I was doing, for I had not yet disclosed anything to the Jews, the priests, the nobles, the officials, or the rest of those who did the work.

Then I said to them, “You see the distress in which we find ourselves, how Jerusalem lies in ruins and its gates have been burned. Come, let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem, so that we may no longer be an object of reproach.”

I recounted to them how the favor of my God had been upon me, and also what the king had said to me. They replied, “Let us rise up and build.” So they strengthened their resolve to undertake the good work.

But when Sanballat the Horonite, Tobiah the Ammonite, the servant, and Geshem the Arab heard of it, they mocked us and held us in contempt, saying, “What is this thing that you are doing? Are you rebelling against the king?”
I answered them, “The God of heaven will prosper us, and we, His servants, will arise and build; but you have no share, right, or memorial in Jerusalem.”

Eliashib the high priest, together with his priestly brethren, undertook the reconstruction of the Sheep Gate; they consecrated it, erected its doors, and extended their labors as far as the Tower of the Hundred and the Tower of Hananel, which they likewise consecrated.
The men of Jericho built adjacent to it, and Zaccur son of Imri built adjacent to them.
The sons of Hassenaah rebuilt the Fish Gate, setting its beams and installing its doors, bolts, and bars.
Next to them, Meremoth son of Uriah son of Hakkoz made repairs; next to him, Meshullam son of Berechiah son of Meshezabel made repairs; and next to him, Zadok son of Baana made repairs.
Next to them, the Tekoites made repairs, though their nobles declined to put their shoulders to the work under their supervisors.
Joiada son of Paseah and Meshullam son of Besodeiah repaired the Old Gate, setting its beams and installing its doors, bolts, and bars.
Next to them, Melatiah the Gibeonite, Jadon the Meronothite, and the men of Gibeon and Mizpah—subject to the authority of the governor of the province Beyond the River—made repairs.
Next to them, Uzziel son of Harhaiah, one of the goldsmiths, made repairs; and next to him, Hananiah, one of the perfumers, made repairs. They restored Jerusalem as far as the Broad Wall.
Next to them, Rephaiah son of Hur, ruler of half the district of Jerusalem, made repairs.
Next to them, Jedaiah son of Harumaph made repairs opposite his house; and next to him, Hattush son of Hashabneiah made repairs.
Malchijah son of Harim and Hasshub son of Pahath-moab repaired another section, together with the Tower of the Ovens.
Next to them, Shallum son of Hallohesh, ruler of the other half of the district of Jerusalem, made repairs—he and his daughters.
Hanun and the inhabitants of Zanoah repaired the Valley Gate; they rebuilt it and installed its doors, bolts, and bars, and they repaired a thousand cubits of the wall as far as the Dung Gate.
Malchijah son of Rechab, ruler of the district of Beth-haccerem, repaired the Dung Gate; he rebuilt it and installed its doors, bolts, and bars.

Shallun son of Col-hozeh, ruler of the district of Mizpah, repaired the Fountain Gate; he rebuilt it, roofed it, and installed its doors, bolts, and bars. He also repaired the wall of the Pool of Siloam by the King's Garden, as far as the stairs descending from the City of David.
After him, Nehemiah son of Azbuk, ruler of half the district of Beth-zur, made repairs up to a point opposite the tombs of David, as far as the artificial pool and the House of the Mighty.
After him, the Levites made repairs: Rehum son of Bani; and next to him, Hashabiah, ruler of half the district of Keilah, made repairs for his district.
After him, their brothers made repairs: Binnui son of Henadad, ruler of the other half of the district of Keilah.
Next to him, Ezer son of Jeshua, ruler of Mizpah, repaired another section opposite the ascent to the armory at the angle.
After him, Baruch son of Zabbai diligently repaired another section, from the angle to the doorway of the house of Eliashib the high priest.
After him, Meremoth son of Uriah son of Hakkoz repaired another section, from the doorway of Eliashib's house to the end of it.
After him, the priests—the men of the surrounding area—made repairs.
After them, Benjamin and Hasshub made repairs opposite their house; and after them, Azariah son of Maaseiah son of Ananiah made repairs beside his house.
After him, Binnui son of Henadad repaired another section, from the house of Azariah to the angle and the corner.

Palal son of Uzai made repairs opposite the angle and the tower projecting from the upper house of the king, which is by the court of the guard. After him, Pedaiah son of Parosh and the temple servants living on the Ophel made repairs up to a point opposite the Water Gate toward the east and the projecting tower.
After them, the Tekoites repaired another section, from the great projecting tower to the wall of Ophel.
Above the Horse Gate, the priests made repairs, each opposite his own house.
After them, Zadok son of Immer made repairs opposite his house; and after him, Shemaiah son of Shecaniah, the keeper of the East Gate, made repairs.
After him, Hananiah son of Shelemiah, and Hanun the sixth son of Zalaph, repaired another section. After them, Meshullam son of Berechiah made repairs opposite his chamber.
After him, Malchijah, one of the goldsmiths, made repairs as far as the house of the temple servants and the merchants, opposite the Inspection Gate, and as far as the upper chamber of the corner.
Between the upper chamber of the corner and the Sheep Gate, the goldsmiths and merchants made repairs.
Now when Sanballat heard that we were rebuilding the wall, he became furious and was filled with indignation, and he ridiculed the Jews.

In the presence of his brothers and the army of Samaria, he said, “What are these feeble Jews doing? Will they restore the wall for themselves? Will they offer sacrifices? Will they finish in a day? Can they revive the burnt stones from the heaps of rubble?”
Tobiah the Ammonite, who stood beside him, said, “Even if a fox should climb upon it, it would break down their stone wall.”
Hear, O our God, for we are despised; turn back their taunt upon their own heads, and hand them over as plunder in a land of captivity.
Do not cover their guilt, and do not let their sin be blotted out from before You, for they have provoked You to anger in the sight of the builders.
So we rebuilt the wall, and all of it was joined together up to half its height, for the people had a mind to work.

But when Sanballat, Tobiah, the Arabs, the Ammonites, and the Ashdodites heard that the repair of Jerusalem’s walls had advanced and that the breaches were beginning to be closed, they were exceedingly angry.
They all conspired together to come and fight against Jerusalem and to create confusion.
So we prayed to our God and posted a guard against them day and night.
Then Judah said, “The strength of the burden bearers is failing, and there is much rubble; we are not able to build the wall.”
Our enemies said, “Before they know or see anything, we will come among them and kill them and stop the work.”
The Jews who lived near them came and told us ten times over, “Wherever you turn, they will attack us.”
So I stationed people behind the wall at its lowest sections, at the vulnerable points, and I stationed them by families with their swords, spears, and bows.

Then I looked, rose up, and said to the nobles, the officials, and the rest of the people, “Do not be afraid of them; remember the Lord, great and awesome, and fight for your brothers, your sons and daughters, your wives and homes.”
When our enemies heard that their plan was known to us and that God had frustrated it, we all returned to the wall, each to his own work.
From that day on, half of my servants worked on the construction while the other half held spears, shields, bows, and coats of mail; and the leaders stood behind all the house of Judah.
The builders and the carriers of burdens loaded themselves, so that with one hand each performed the work while with the other he held a weapon.
Each builder had his sword strapped at his side as he built, and the trumpeter stood beside me.
Then I said to the nobles, the officials, and the rest of the people, “The work is great and extensive, and we are spread out along the wall, far from one another.
In whatever place you hear the sound of the trumpet, assemble to us there; our God will fight for us.”
So we continued the work, with half holding spears, from the break of dawn until the stars came out.
At that time I also said to the people, “Let each man and his servant spend the night within Jerusalem, so that they may be a guard for us by night and labor by day.”
Neither I, nor my brothers, nor my servants, nor the guards with me took off our clothes; each carried his weapon, even when washing.
A vociferous outcry arose among the people and their wives against their Jewish kinsmen.
Some declared, “We, together with our sons and daughters, are numerous; therefore we must procure grain in order to eat and survive.”
Others declared, “We are mortgaging our fields, vineyards, and houses merely to obtain grain amid the famine.”
Still others declared, “We have borrowed silver to satisfy the king’s levy upon our fields and vineyards.”

“And now,” they said, “our very flesh is as the flesh of our brothers, and our children are as their children; yet we are compelling our sons and daughters into servitude, and some of our daughters have already been enslaved. We are powerless, while our fields and vineyards have passed into the hands of others.”
When I heard their outcry and these particulars, I was exceedingly incensed.
After deliberating within myself, I contended with the nobles and officials, saying, “Each of you is exacting usury from his brother.” Then I convened a great assembly against them.

I said to them, “We, insofar as we were able, have redeemed our Jewish brothers who had been sold to the nations; but you are selling your brothers, and they are being sold to us!” They were silenced and could offer no reply.
Then I said, “What you are doing is not good. Should you not walk in the fear of our God, so as not to furnish the nations—our enemies—with cause for reproach?
I and my brothers and my servants are likewise lending them silver and grain. Let us, I pray, desist from this usury.
Restore to them, this very day, their fields, vineyards, olive orchards, and houses, together with the hundredth of the silver, grain, new wine, and oil that you are exacting from them.”
They replied, “We will restore these things and demand nothing from them; we will do exactly as you say.” Then I summoned the priests and bound them by oath to fulfill this promise.

I likewise shook out the fold of my robe and declared, “So may God shake out from his house and his labor every man who fails to fulfill this promise; so may he be shaken out and left empty.” And the entire assembly said, “Amen,” and praised the LORD. And the people acted in accordance with this word.

Moreover, from the day King Artaxerxes appointed me governor over Judah—from the twentieth year to the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes, that is, twelve years—neither I nor my brothers consumed the governor’s provisions.

The governors who preceded me had burdened the people heavily, taking from them bread and wine in addition to forty shekels of silver; their servants, moreover, domineered over the people. But I did not act thus, out of reverence for God.
I also devoted myself steadfastly to the work on this wall, and all my servants were assembled there for the labor; we purchased no land.
At my table sat one hundred fifty Jews and officials, in addition to those who came to us from the surrounding nations.

Each day one ox, six choice sheep, and fowl were prepared for me, and every ten days an abundant supply of wine of every kind. Nevertheless, in view of all this, I did not claim the governor’s food allowance, for the burden of labor lay heavily upon this people.
Remember me, my God, for good, for all that I have done on behalf of this people.

Now when Sanballat and Tobiah and Geshem the Arab and the rest of our enemies heard that I had built the wall and that no breach remained in it—though up to that time I had not set doors in the gates—
Sanballat and Geshem sent to me, saying, "Come, let us meet together in one of the villages in the plain of Ono." But they intended to do me harm.
I sent messengers to them, saying, "I am doing a great work and cannot come down. Why should the work cease while I leave it and come down to you?"
Four times they sent to me in this manner, and I answered them in the same manner.
The fifth time Sanballat sent his servant to me with an open letter in his hand.
In it was written: "It is reported among the nations—and Gashmu says—that you and the Jews intend to rebel; therefore you are building the wall, and you will be their king according to these words."

"Moreover, you have appointed prophets to proclaim concerning you in Jerusalem, 'There is a king in Judah.' Now this will be reported to the king according to these words. Come now, let us take counsel together."
I sent to him, saying, "No such things as you say have been done, but you are fabricating them out of your own imagination."
For they all were trying to frighten us, thinking, "Their hands will drop from the work, and it will not be done." But now strengthen my hands.

I went to the house of Shemaiah son of Delaiah son of Mehetabel, who was confined, and he said, "Let us meet together in the house of God, within the temple, and let us close the doors of the temple, for they are coming to kill you; by night they are coming to kill you."
I said, "Should a man of my station flee? Or should one such as I enter the temple merely to preserve his life? I will not enter."
I perceived that God had not sent him, but that he had prophesied against me because Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him.
For this purpose he was hired: that I should be afraid and act and sin, and so they might have an evil report with which to reproach me.
Remember, O my God, Tobiah and Sanballat in accordance with these deeds, and also Noadiah the prophetess and the rest of the prophets who were seeking to intimidate me.
The wall was completed on the twenty-fifth day of the month Elul, in fifty-two days.
When all our enemies heard of it and all the surrounding nations saw it, their self-assurance collapsed, for they perceived that this work had been accomplished by our God.
Moreover, in those days the nobles of Judah sent many letters to Tobiah, and letters from Tobiah came to them.
For many in Judah were under oath to him, because he was the son-in-law of Shecaniah son of Arah, and his son Johanan had married the daughter of Meshullam son of Berechiah.
Moreover, they kept reporting his good deeds to me and relaying my words to him. And Tobiah sent letters to intimidate me.
After the wall had been rebuilt and I had set the doors in place, the gatekeepers, the singers, and the Levites were appointed.
Then I put my brother Hanani in charge of Jerusalem, along with Hananiah, the commander of the fortress, because he was a faithful man who feared God more than most.

I said to them, “Do not open the gates of Jerusalem until the sun is hot, and while the gatekeepers are on duty, have them shut and secure the doors. Also appoint the residents of Jerusalem as guards, some at their posts and some near their own homes.”
Now the city was large and spacious, but there were few people in it, and the houses had not yet been rebuilt.

Then my God put it into my heart to assemble the nobles, the officials, and the people to be enrolled by genealogy. I found the genealogical record of those who had first returned, and I found the following written in it:
These are the people of the province who came up from the captivity of the exiles carried away to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar its king. They returned to Jerusalem and Judah, each to his own town,
accompanied by Zerubbabel, Jeshua, Nehemiah, Azariah, Raamiah, Nahamani, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispereth, Bigvai, Nehum, and Baanah. This is the count of the men of Israel:
the descendants of Pahath-moab, of the descendants of Jeshua and Joab, 2,818;
the descendants of Ater, of Hezekiah, 98;
the men of Bethlehem and Netophah, 188;
the men of Kiriath-jearim, Chephirah, and Beeroth, 743;
the men of Ramah and Geba, 621;
the men of Bethel and Ai, 123;
the men of the other Nebo, 52;
the descendants of the other Elam, 1,254;
the descendants of Lod, Hadid, and Ono, 721;
The priests: the descendants of Jedaiah, of the house of Jeshua, 973;
The Levites: the descendants of Jeshua, of Kadmiel, of the descendants of Hodevah, 74.
The singers: the descendants of Asaph, 148.
The gatekeepers: the descendants of Shallum, Ater, Talmon, Akkub, Hatita, and Shobai, 138.
The temple servants: the descendants of Ziha, Hasupha, and Tabbaoth;
the descendants of Keros, Sia, and Padon;
the descendants of Lebanah, Hagabah, and Shalmai;
the descendants of Hanan, Giddel, and Gahar;
the descendants of Reaiah, Rezin, and Nekoda;
the descendants of Gazzam, Uzza, and Paseah;
the descendants of Besai, Meunim, and Nephushesim;
the descendants of Bakbuk, Hakupha, and Harhur;
the descendants of Bazluth, Mehida, and Harsha;
the descendants of Barkos, Sisera, and Temah;
the descendants of Neziah and Hatipha.
The descendants of Solomon’s servants: the descendants of Sotai, Sophereth, and Perida;
the descendants of Jaala, Darkon, and Giddel;
the descendants of Shephatiah, Hattil, Pochereth-hazzebaim, and Amon.
The total of the temple servants and the descendants of Solomon’s servants was 392.
Those who came up from Tel-melah, Tel-harsha, Cherub, Addon, and Immer—but could not prove their ancestral houses or their descent, whether they belonged to Israel—
the descendants of Delaiah, Tobiah, and Nekoda, 642.
And of the priests: the descendants of Hobaiah, Hakkoz, and Barzillai, who had taken a wife from the daughters of Barzillai the Gileadite and was called by their name.
These sought their register among those enrolled by genealogy, but it was not found, so they were excluded from the priesthood as unclean.
The governor told them not to eat of the most holy things until a priest should stand with Urim and Thummim.
besides their 7,337 male and female servants; and they had 245 male and female singers.
Some of the heads of the fathers’ houses contributed to the work. The governor gave to the treasury 1,000 darics of gold, 50 bowls, and 530 garments for the priests.
The heads of the fathers’ houses gave to the treasury of the work 20,000 darics of gold and 2,200 minas of silver.
The rest of the people gave 20,000 darics of gold, 2,000 minas of silver, and 67 garments for the priests.

So the priests, the Levites, the gatekeepers, the singers, the temple servants, some of the people, and the rest of Israel dwelt in their cities. When the seventh month came, the people of Israel were in their cities.

All the people coalesced into a single body in the open plaza before the Water Gate, and they urged Ezra the scribe to bring forth the Book of the Law of Moses, which the LORD had commanded for Israel.
On the first day of the seventh month, Ezra the priest brought the Law before the congregation—men and women alike, together with everyone possessing the discernment to comprehend what was heard.

He read from it in the plaza before the Water Gate from daybreak until midday, in the presence of men, women, and those capable of understanding; and the ears of all the people were attentively fixed upon the Book of the Law.

Ezra the scribe stood upon a raised wooden rostrum erected for the occasion, with Mattithiah, Shema, Anaiah, Uriah, Hilkiah, and Maaseiah at his right hand, and Pedaiah, Mishael, Malchijah, Hashum, Hashbaddanah, Zechariah, and Meshullam at his left.
Ezra opened the book before the eyes of all the people, for he was positioned above them all, and when he opened it, all the people stood.
Ezra blessed the LORD, the great God, and all the people responded, “Amen, Amen,” raising their hands; then they bowed their heads and worshiped the LORD with their faces to the ground.

Jeshua, Bani, Sherebiah, Jamin, Akkub, Shabbethai, Hodiah, Maaseiah, Kelita, Azariah, Jozabad, Hanan, Pelaiah, and the other Levites explicated the Law for the people while they remained in their places.
They read from the book, from the Law of God, with clarity, rendering its meaning so that the people understood the reading.

Nehemiah the governor, Ezra the priest and scribe, and the Levites who instructed the people said to all the people, “This day is holy to the LORD your God; do not mourn or weep.” For all the people wept when they heard the words of the Law.

Then he said to them, “Go on your way; eat rich fare and drink sweet wine, and send portions to those for whom nothing has been prepared, for this day is holy to our Lord. Do not be grieved, for the joy of the LORD is your strength.”
So the Levites quieted all the people, saying, “Be still, for this day is holy; do not be grieved.”
All the people then went to eat and drink, to send portions, and to celebrate with great joy, because they had understood the words declared to them.
On the second day, the heads of the ancestral houses of all the people, together with the priests and Levites, gathered to Ezra the scribe to gain insight into the words of the Law.
They found written in the Law that the LORD had commanded through Moses that the Israelites should dwell in booths during the feast of the seventh month.

They also proclaimed throughout all their cities and in Jerusalem, saying, “Go out to the hills and bring branches of olive, wild olive, myrtle, palm, and other leafy trees to make booths, as it is written.”

So the people went out and brought the branches and made booths for themselves—each on his own roof, and in their courts, and in the courts of the house of God, and in the plaza at the Water Gate, and in the plaza at the Gate of Ephraim.

All the assembly of those who had returned from exile made booths and dwelt in them; for from the days of Jeshua son of Nun until that day the Israelites had not done so. And there was very great rejoicing.

Day by day, from the first day to the last, he read from the Book of the Law of God. They observed the feast for seven days, and on the eighth day there was a solemn assembly, according to the ordinance.
On the twenty-fourth day of this month, the Israelites assembled in fasting, clad in sackcloth, with dust upon them.
The seed of Israel separated themselves from all foreigners and stood, confessing their own sins and the iniquities of their fathers.
They stood in their place and read from the Book of the Law of the LORD their God for a quarter of the day, and for another quarter they confessed and worshiped the LORD their God.
Upon the stairs stood the Levites—Jeshua, Bani, Kadmiel, Shebaniah, Bunni, Sherebiah, Bani, and Chenani—and they cried out with a loud voice to the LORD their God.
"Stand up and bless the LORD your God from everlasting to everlasting, and let Your glorious name be blessed, exalted above every blessing and praise.

You alone are the LORD: You made the heavens, the heaven of heavens, and all their host; the earth and everything upon it; the seas and all that is in them; and You preserve them all, while the host of heaven worships You.
You are the LORD God, who chose Abram, brought him forth from Ur of the Chaldeans, and named him Abraham.

You found his heart faithful before You and covenanted with him to give the land of the Canaanite, the Hittite, the Amorite, the Perizzite, the Jebusite, and the Girgashite—to give it to his descendants—and You have fulfilled Your words, for You are righteous.
"You saw the affliction of our fathers in Egypt and heard their cry beside the Red Sea.

You performed signs and wonders against Pharaoh, against all his servants, and against all the people of his land, for You knew that they had acted arrogantly against our fathers; and You made a name for Yourself, as it is this day.
You divided the sea before them, so that they passed through the midst of the sea on dry ground, and You hurled their pursuers into the depths like a stone into mighty waters.
You led them by a pillar of cloud by day and by a pillar of fire by night, to illuminate for them the way in which they were to go.
"You descended upon Mount Sinai and spoke with them from heaven; You gave them just ordinances, true laws, and good statutes and commandments.
You made known to them Your holy Sabbath and commanded them commandments, statutes, and law through Moses, Your servant.

You gave them bread from heaven for their hunger and brought forth water from the rock for their thirst; and You said to them that they should go in and possess the land which You had sworn to give them.
"But they and our fathers acted presumptuously; they stiffened their necks and did not listen to Your commandments.

They refused to listen and did not remember Your wonders that You had performed among them; they stiffened their necks and appointed a leader to return to their slavery in their rebellion. Yet You are a God of forgiveness, gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, and You did not forsake them.
Even when they fashioned a molten calf and said, 'This is your god who brought you up from Egypt,' and committed great blasphemies,

"yet You, in Your great mercy, did not forsake them in the wilderness: the pillar of cloud did not depart from above them by day, to guide them on their way, nor the pillar of fire by night, to light for them the way in which they were to go.
You gave Your good Spirit to instruct them; You did not withhold manna from their mouths; and You gave them water for their thirst.
For forty years You sustained them in the wilderness, so that they lacked nothing: their clothes did not wear out, and their feet did not swell.
"You gave them kingdoms and peoples and allotted them to every quarter, and they took possession of the land of Sihon, the land of the king of Heshbon, and the land of Og, king of Bashan.
You multiplied their children like the stars of heaven and brought them into the land that You had told their fathers to enter and possess.

So the children entered and possessed the land; You subdued before them the Canaanites who inhabited the land and gave them into their hand, together with their kings and the peoples of the land, that they might do with them as they pleased.

They captured fortified cities and a rich land, and took possession of houses filled with every good thing, hewn cisterns, vineyards, olive orchards, and fruit trees in abundance; and they ate, were filled, grew fat, and luxuriated in Your great goodness.

"But they were disobedient and rebelled against You; they cast Your law behind their backs and killed Your prophets, who had warned them in order to turn them back to You, and they committed great blasphemies.

Therefore You delivered them into the hand of their enemies, who oppressed them; and in the time of their distress they cried to You, and You heard from heaven, and according to Your great mercies You gave them saviors, who saved them from the hand of their enemies.

But when they had rest, they returned to doing evil before You; so You abandoned them to the hand of their enemies, who ruled over them. Yet when they cried to You, You heard from heaven and delivered them many times, according to Your mercies.

"You warned them, in order to turn them back to Your law, yet they acted presumptuously and did not listen to Your commandments; they sinned against Your ordinances, by which a person shall live if he does them; they turned a stubborn shoulder, stiffened their necks, and would not listen.
For many years You bore with them and warned them by Your Spirit through Your prophets, yet they did not give ear; therefore You gave them into the hand of the peoples of the lands.
Nevertheless, in Your great mercy You did not make an end of them or forsake them, for You are a gracious and compassionate God.

"Now therefore, O our God, the great, the mighty, and the awesome God, who keeps covenant and steadfast love, let not all the hardship that has come upon us—upon our kings, our princes, our priests, our prophets, our fathers, and all Your people—from the days of the kings of Assyria to this day, seem insignificant before You.
You are righteous in all that has come upon us, for You have dealt faithfully while we have acted wickedly.
Our kings, our princes, our priests, and our fathers have not kept Your law or listened to Your commandments and Your testimonies with which You testified against them.
Even in their kingdom, and amid the great goodness that You gave them, and in the broad and rich land that You set before them, they did not serve You or turn from their wicked deeds.
"Behold, we are slaves this day; and the land that You gave to our fathers, to eat its fruit and its goodness—behold, we are slaves upon it.
Its abundant produce is for the kings whom You have set over us because of our sins; they rule over our bodies and over our livestock as they please, and we are in great distress.
Because of all this, we are making a firm covenant and writing it down; and upon the sealed document are our princes, our Levites, and our priests."
Among those who set their seal were Nehemiah the governor, son of Hachaliah, and Zedekiah:
Maaziah, Bilgai, and Shemaiah—these were the priests.
And the Levites: Jeshua son of Azaniah, Binnui of the sons of Henadad, Kadmiel;
and their brothers Shebaniah, Hodiah, Kelita, Pelaiah, Hanan;
The chiefs of the people: Parosh, Pahath-moab, Elam, Zattu, Bani;

The rest of the people—the priests, the Levites, the gatekeepers, the singers, the temple servants, and all who had separated themselves from the peoples of the lands to the Law of God—together with their wives and all their sons and daughters capable of discernment,

joined their brothers, the nobles, and bound themselves by oath and curse to walk in the Law of God given by the hand of Moses, the servant of God, and to do and to keep all the commandments, judgments, and statutes of the LORD our God.
We will not give our daughters in marriage to the peoples of the land, nor take their daughters for our sons.
When the peoples of the land bring merchandise or any grain to sell on the Sabbath day, we will not buy from them on the Sabbath or on a holy day; and in the seventh year we will forgo every debt.
We have also obligated ourselves to contribute one-third of a shekel each year for the service of the house of our God:

for the showbread, the continual grain offering and the continual burnt offering, the Sabbath offerings, the new moons, the appointed feasts, the holy offerings, the sin offerings to make atonement for Israel, and all the work of the house of our God.

We have cast lots among the priests, the Levites, and the people concerning the wood offering, so that the households of our fathers may bring it at designated times, year after year, to be burned upon the altar of the LORD our God, as it is written in the Law.
We will also bring, year after year, the firstfruits of our soil and the firstfruits of all the fruit of every tree to the house of the LORD.

And we will bring the firstborn of our sons and of our livestock—as it is written in the Law—together with the firstborn of our herds and flocks, to the house of our God, to the priests who minister there.

Moreover, we will bring to the priests, to the chambers of the house of our God, the first of our dough, our contributions, the fruit of every tree, the new wine and the oil; and the tithe of our ground to the Levites, for they, the Levites, are the ones who collect the tithes in all the towns where we labor.
A priest, a son of Aaron, shall accompany the Levites when they receive the tithe, and the Levites shall bring up a tenth of the tithe to the house of our God, to the chambers of the treasury.

For the Israelites and the Levites are to bring the contributions of grain, new wine, and oil to the chambers where the vessels of the sanctuary are stored and where the ministering priests, the gatekeepers, and the singers reside; and we will not neglect the house of our God.

The leaders of the people settled in Jerusalem, while the remainder of the populace cast lots to bring one of every ten inhabitants into the holy city of Jerusalem, leaving the other nine shares to the towns.
The people blessed all the men who volunteered to reside in Jerusalem.

These are the provincial leaders who dwelt in Jerusalem; yet in the towns of Judah each man occupied his own hereditary holding—the Israelites, the priests, the Levites, the temple servants, and the descendants of Solomon’s servants.

Among the descendants of Judah and Benjamin who settled in Jerusalem, the Judahite line comprised Ataiah son of Uzziah, son of Zechariah, son of Amariah, son of Shephatiah, son of Mahalalel, of the descendants of Perez.
Maaseiah son of Baruch, son of Col-hozeh, son of Hazaiah, son of Adaiah, son of Joiarib, son of Zechariah, the Shilonite.
All the descendants of Perez who dwelt in Jerusalem numbered four hundred sixty-eight valiant men.
These are the Benjaminites: Sallu son of Meshullam, son of Joed, son of Pedaiah, son of Kolaiah, son of Maaseiah, son of Ithiel, son of Jeshaiah.
After him came Gabbai and Sallai, and their company numbered nine hundred twenty-eight.
Joel son of Zichri served as overseer over them, while Judah son of Hassenuah served as second in charge of the city.
Of the priests: Jedaiah son of Joiarib and Jachin.
Seraiah son of Hilkiah, son of Meshullam, son of Zadok, son of Meraioth, son of Ahitub, was leader over the house of God.
Their kinsmen who performed the temple service numbered eight hundred twenty-two; and Adaiah son of Jeroham, son of Pelaliah, son of Amzi, son of Zechariah, son of Pashhur, son of Malchijah.
His kinsmen, heads of fathers’ houses, numbered two hundred forty-two; and Amashsai son of Azarel, son of Ahasai, son of Meshillemoth, son of Immer.
Their kinsmen, mighty men of valor, numbered one hundred twenty-eight; and their overseer was Zabdiel son of Haggedolim.
Of the Levites: Shemaiah son of Hashub, son of Azrikam, son of Hashabiah, son of Bunni.
Shabbethai and Jozabad, among the chief Levites, had oversight of the exterior work of the house of God.
Mattaniah son of Micha, son of Zabdi, son of Asaph, was chief in beginning the thanksgiving in prayer; Bakbukiah was second among his kinsmen; and Abda son of Shammua, son of Galal, son of Jeduthun.
All the Levites in the holy city numbered two hundred eighty-four.
The gatekeepers—Akkub, Talmon, and their kinsmen who guarded the gates—numbered one hundred seventy-two.
The rest of Israel, the priests, and the Levites were distributed throughout all the towns of Judah, each in his inheritance.
The temple servants dwelt in Ophel, and Ziha and Gishpa were over the temple servants.
The overseer of the Levites in Jerusalem was Uzzi son of Bani, son of Hashabiah, son of Mattaniah, son of Micha; of the sons of Asaph, the singers were in charge of the work of the house of God.
For the king’s commandment governed them, providing a daily allotment for the singers.
Pethahiah son of Meshezabel, of the descendants of Zerah son of Judah, stood at the king’s hand in all matters concerning the people.
As for the villages in their fields, some of the descendants of Judah dwelt in Kiriath-arba and its daughter settlements, in Dibon and its daughter settlements, and in Jekabzeel and its villages.
They also dwelt in Jeshua, Moladah, and Beth-pelet,
in Hazar-shual and Beersheba with its daughter settlements,
in Ziklag and Meconah with its daughter settlements,
in Zanoah, Adullam and its villages, Lachish and its fields, and Azekah with its daughter settlements; and they encamped from Beersheba as far as the Valley of Hinnom.
The Benjaminites dwelt in Geba, Michmash, Aija, and Bethel with its daughter settlements,
and in Lod, Ono, and the Valley of Craftsmen.
Certain divisions of the Levites in Judah were assigned to Benjamin.

These are the priests and Levites who ascended with Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and with Jeshua: Seraiah, Jeremiah, Ezra, Amariah, Malluch, Hattush, Shecaniah, Rehum, Meremoth, Iddo, Ginnethoi, Abijah, Mijamin, Maadiah, Bilgah, Shemaiah, Joiarib, Jedaiah, Sallu, Amok, Hilkiah, and Jedaiah. These were the heads of the priests, together with their associates, in the days of Jeshua.
Sallu, Amok, Hilkiah, Jedaiah. These were the heads of the priests and their brethren in the days of Jeshua.
The Levites were Jeshua, Binnui, Kadmiel, Sherebiah, Judah, and Mattaniah, who, with his brothers, directed the thanksgiving;
and Bakbukiah and Unni, their brothers, stood opposite them in their appointed watches.
Jeshua begot Joiakim; Joiakim begot Eliashib; and Eliashib begot Joiada.
Joiada begot Jonathan, and Jonathan begot Jaddua.
In the days of Joiakim, the heads of the ancestral houses among the priests were as follows: for Seraiah, Meraiah; for Jeremiah, Hananiah;
for Ezra, Meshullam; for Amariah, Jehohanan;
for Malluchi, Jonathan; for Shebaniah, Joseph;
for Harim, Adna; for Meraioth, Helkai;
for Iddo, Zechariah; for Ginnethon, Meshullam;
for Abijah, Zichri; for Miniamin and Moadiah, Piltai;
for Bilgah, Shammua; for Shemaiah, Jehonathan;
for Joiarib, Mattenai; for Jedaiah, Uzzi;
for Sallai, Kallai; for Amok, Eber;
for Hilkiah, Hashabiah; and for Jedaiah, Nethanel.
In the days of Eliashib, Joiada, Johanan, and Jaddua, the Levites were recorded as heads of ancestral houses, as were the priests, under the reign of Darius the Persian.
The sons of Levi, the heads of ancestral houses, were written in the Book of the Chronicles down to the days of Johanan son of Eliashib.

The chiefs of the Levites were Hashabiah, Sherebiah, Jeshua son of Kadmiel, and their brothers, who stood opposite them to praise and give thanks, watch corresponding to watch, by the command of David, the man of God.
Mattaniah, Bakbukiah, Obadiah, Meshullam, Talmon, and Akkub, gatekeepers, kept watch at the storehouses of the gates.
These served in the days of Joiakim son of Jeshua son of Jozadak, and in the days of Nehemiah the governor and Ezra the priest and scribe.

At the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem, they sought out the Levites from all their places to bring them to Jerusalem, in order to celebrate the dedication with gladness, thanksgivings, song, cymbals, harps, and lyres.
The sons of the singers gathered from the district around Jerusalem, from the villages of the Netophathites,
from Beth-gilgal, and from the fields of Geba and Azmaveth, for the singers had built villages for themselves around Jerusalem.
The priests and the Levites purified themselves, and they purified the people, the gates, and the wall.
Then I brought the leaders of Judah up onto the wall and stationed two great choirs of thanksgiving, together with their processions, upon the wall, one proceeding to the right toward the Dung Gate.
Hoshaiah and half of the leaders of Judah followed them,
and certain of the priests' sons with trumpets—Zechariah son of Jonathan son of Shemaiah son of Mattaniah son of Micaiah son of Zaccur son of Asaph—
and his brothers Shemaiah, Azarel, Milalai, Gilalai, Maai, Nethanel, Judah, and Hanani, with the musical instruments of David, the man of God; and Ezra the scribe went before them.
At the Fountain Gate, directly opposite them, they ascended by the stairs of the City of David, at the ascent to the wall, above the house of David, as far as the Water Gate on the east.
The other choir of thanksgiving went in the opposite direction, and I followed it, with half of the people on the wall, above the Tower of the Ovens, as far as the Broad Wall,
and above the Gate of Ephraim, over the Old Gate, over the Fish Gate, and the Tower of Hananel and the Tower of the Hundred, to the Sheep Gate; and they halted at the Gate of the Guard.
Then the two choirs of thanksgiving stood in the house of God, and I and half of the officials stood with me,
together with the priests Eliakim, Maaseiah, Miniamin, Micaiah, Elioenai, Zechariah, and Hananiah with trumpets,
and Maaseiah, Shemaiah, Eleazar, Uzzi, Jehohanan, Malchijah, Elam, and Ezer, while the singers made themselves heard under Jezrahiah their overseer.
They offered great sacrifices that day and rejoiced, because God had made them rejoice with great joy; the women and the children rejoiced as well, so that the joy of Jerusalem was heard from afar.

On that day men were appointed over the chambers for the stores, the contributions, the firstfruits, and the tithes, to gather into them from the fields of the cities the portions required by the Law for the priests and the Levites; for Judah rejoiced over the priests and Levites who stood in their service.
They kept the charge of their God and the charge of purification, as did the singers and the gatekeepers, according to the command of David and of Solomon his son.
For in the days of David and Asaph of old there were chiefs of the singers, and songs of praise and thanksgiving to God.

In the days of Zerubbabel and Nehemiah, all Israel gave the daily portions to the singers and the gatekeepers, and they set apart a portion for the Levites, while the Levites set apart a portion for the sons of Aaron.
On that day, the Book of Moses was publicly read in the hearing of the people, wherein it was discovered written that no Ammonite or Moabite should ever be admitted into the assembly of God,
because they had not met the children of Israel with bread and water, but had hired Balaam to curse them—though our God transformed the curse into a blessing.
When they heard the law, they separated from Israel all who were of mixed descent.
Now before this, Eliashib the priest, who had been entrusted with the chambers of the house of our God and was closely allied with Tobiah,

had prepared for him a capacious chamber in which there had formerly been stored the grain offering, the frankincense, the vessels, the tithe of grain, new wine, and oil—the portions ordained for the Levites, the singers, and the gatekeepers—together with the contribution for the priests.
But during all this I was not in Jerusalem, for in the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes, king of Babylon, I had gone to the king, and after some time I requested leave from him.
When I returned to Jerusalem, I discerned the evil that Eliashib had done for Tobiah by making him a chamber in the courts of the house of God.
It grieved me profoundly, so I cast all of Tobiah's household goods out of the chamber.
I issued orders, and they cleansed the chambers; then I restored to that place the vessels of the house of God, together with the grain offering and the frankincense.
I also perceived that the Levites had not been given their portions, so the Levites and singers who performed the work had fled, each to his own field.
I contended with the officials and said, "Why has the house of God been forsaken?" Then I gathered them together and restored them to their posts.
All Judah then brought the tithe of grain, wine, and oil into the storehouses.

I appointed over the storehouses Shelemiah the priest, Zadok the scribe, and Pedaiah of the Levites, with Hanan son of Zaccur, son of Mattaniah, beside them, because they were reckoned faithful, and their duty was to distribute to their brethren.
Remember me, O my God, concerning this, and do not blot out the good deeds I have done for the house of my God and for its services.

In those days I saw in Judah men treading winepresses on the Sabbath, bringing in heaps of grain and loading them on donkeys, along with wine, grapes, figs, and every kind of burden, which they brought into Jerusalem on the Sabbath day; and I warned them against selling provisions on that day.
Men of Tyre also dwelt there, bringing in fish and all kinds of merchandise, and selling them on the Sabbath to the children of Judah, and in Jerusalem.
I contended with the nobles of Judah and said to them, "What is this evil thing that you are doing, profaning the Sabbath day?
Did not your fathers do the same, and did not our God bring all this disaster upon us and upon this city? Yet you are adding more wrath upon Israel by profaning the Sabbath."

And as the gates of Jerusalem grew dark before the Sabbath, I commanded that the doors be shut, and I ordered that they not be opened until after the Sabbath; I stationed some of my servants at the gates, so that no burden might be brought in on the Sabbath day.
So the merchants and sellers of all kinds of wares spent the night outside Jerusalem on one or two occasions.
I testified against them and said to them, "Why do you camp outside the wall? If you do so again, I will lay hands on you." From that time on they came no more on the Sabbath.

I commanded the Levites to purify themselves and to come and guard the gates, in order to keep the Sabbath day holy. Remember me, O my God, concerning this also, and spare me according to the greatness of Your mercy.
In those days I also saw Jews who had married women of Ashdod, Ammon, and Moab.
Half of their children spoke the language of Ashdod, and they could not speak the language of Judah, but spoke according to the tongue of each people.

I contended with them, cursed them, struck some of them, pulled out their hair, and made them swear by God, saying, "You shall not give your daughters to their sons, nor take their daughters for your sons or for yourselves."

"Did not Solomon king of Israel sin on account of these things? Yet among many nations there was no king like him; he was beloved of his God, and God made him king over all Israel—nevertheless, foreign women led him into sin.
Shall we then heed you, to do all this great evil, to act treacherously against our God by marrying foreign women?"
One of the sons of Joiada, son of Eliashib the high priest, was son-in-law to Sanballat the Horonite; therefore I drove him away from me.
Remember them, O my God, because they have defiled the priesthood, the covenant of the priesthood, and the Levites.
Thus I purified them from all that is foreign, and I assigned the priests and Levites to their duties, each to his task.
I also made provision for the wood offering at the appointed times, and for the firstfruits. Remember me, O my God, for good.
Now in the days of Ahasuerus—that is, the Ahasuerus who reigned over one hundred twenty-seven provinces stretching from India to Cush—
in those days, when King Ahasuerus sat upon his royal throne in the citadel of Susa,

in the third year of his reign, he convened a feast for all his officials and servants, while the military commanders of Persia and Media, together with the nobles and provincial governors, stood before him.
For one hundred eighty days in all, he displayed the resplendent wealth of his kingdom and the magnificent splendor of his majesty.

When those days had run their course, the king furnished a seven-day banquet in the garden courtyard of the royal palace for all the people, from the most humble to the most exalted, who were present in the citadel of Susa.

White and violet linen hangings were fastened with cords of fine linen and purple to silver rings on marble pillars; gold and silver couches rested upon a pavement of porphyry, marble, mother-of-pearl, and other precious stones.
Wine was served in golden vessels, and the royal wine flowed abundantly, in keeping with the king’s munificence.
The drinking proceeded according to ordinance: no one was compelled, for the king had instructed every steward of his household to allow each guest to drink according to his own inclination.
Queen Vashti likewise hosted a banquet for the women in the royal palace of King Ahasuerus.
On the seventh day, when the king’s heart was gladdened by wine, he commanded the seven eunuchs who attended him—Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha, Abagtha, Zethar, and Carkas—
to bring Queen Vashti before the king, crowned with the royal diadem, so that he might exhibit her beauty to the peoples and officials, for she was of surpassing beauty.
But Queen Vashti refused to appear at the king’s behest, conveyed through the eunuchs, whereupon the king was incensed, and his fury burned within him.
Then the king consulted the wise men who understood the times—for it was the king’s custom to seek counsel from all who knew law and justice—
namely, Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan, the seven princes of Persia and Media who enjoyed access to the king and occupied the foremost rank in the kingdom.
“What,” he asked, “does the law require concerning Queen Vashti, since she has not obeyed the command of King Ahasuerus conveyed by the eunuchs?”
Memucan replied before the king and the princes, “Queen Vashti has not merely wronged the king, but also all the officials and all the peoples throughout the provinces of King Ahasuerus.

For the queen’s behavior will become known to every woman, and it will move them to treat their husbands with contempt, saying, ‘King Ahasuerus commanded that Queen Vashti be brought before him, yet she did not come.’
This very day the noblewomen of Persia and Media who have heard of the queen’s conduct will repeat it to all the king’s officials, and there will be no end of contempt and indignation

“If it please the king, let a royal decree issue from him and be inscribed among the laws of Persia and Media, so that it may not be revoked: Vashti shall never again enter the presence of King Ahasuerus, and the king shall bestow her royal dignity upon another who is more worthy than she.
When this decree, issued throughout so vast a kingdom, is proclaimed, all women, from the most humble to the most exalted, will render honor to their husbands.”
The king and his princes approved of this counsel, and the king acted in accordance with Memucan’s advice.

He dispatched letters to every province of the kingdom, to each province in its own script and to each people in its own language, decreeing that every man should be sovereign in his own household and should speak according to the tongue of his own people.
After these events, once King Ahasuerus's fury had subsided, he recollected Vashti—both her conduct and the decree that had been imposed upon her.
Then the king's attendants who ministered to him said, "Let them seek out for the king young women—virgins of exceptional beauty.

And let the king appoint commissioners throughout every province of his realm, that they may gather all the beautiful young virgins into the women's quarters at the citadel of Susa, placing them under the custody of Hegai, the king's eunuch and guardian of the women, and let their cosmetics be provided for them.
Then let the young woman who finds favor in the king's eyes reign in Vashti's stead." This pleased the king, and he acted accordingly.
Now there was a Jew in the citadel of Susa named Mordecai son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish, a Benjaminite,
who had been exiled from Jerusalem with the captives deported along with Jeconiah king of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had carried into exile.

He had reared Hadassah—that is, Esther—his uncle's daughter, for she had lost both father and mother. The young woman was of comely form and fair to behold; and upon the death of her parents, Mordecai had taken her as his own daughter.

So, when the king's command and decree became known, and when many young women were assembled at the citadel of Susa under Hegai's custody, Esther too was taken into the royal palace and entrusted to Hegai, keeper of the women.

The young woman pleased him and obtained his favor; he hastened to furnish her with cosmetics, her allotted provisions, and seven select maidens from the royal household, and he transferred her and her attendants to the most desirable quarters of the women's house.
Esther did not disclose her people or her lineage, for Mordecai had enjoined her not to disclose it.
And day by day Mordecai would walk before the court of the women's house, to ascertain Esther's welfare and what was being done concerning her.

Now when each young woman's turn arrived to go in to King Ahasuerus—after twelve months had been completed for the women according to their ordinance, for such was the full period of their beautification: six months with oil of myrrh, and six months with spices and women's cosmetics—
when the young woman went in to the king, whatever she requested was given her to take with her from the women's house to the king's palace.

In the evening she would enter, and in the morning she would return to the second women's house, under the custody of Shaashgaz, the king's eunuch, guardian of the concubines. She would not return to the king unless the king delighted in her and she was summoned by name.

When Esther's turn came—she being the daughter of Abihail, Mordecai's uncle, whom he had adopted as his daughter—she requested nothing beyond what Hegai, the king's eunuch and guardian of the women, advised; and Esther found favor in the eyes of all who beheld her.
So Esther was taken to King Ahasuerus, into his royal residence, in the tenth month—that is, the month of Tebeth—in the seventh year of his reign.
The king loved Esther above all the women, and she obtained grace and favor before him beyond all the virgins, so that he placed the royal diadem upon her head and made her queen in Vashti's place.
Then the king held a great banquet—Esther's banquet—for all his officials and servants; he granted a tax remission throughout the provinces and dispensed gifts with royal liberality.
When the virgins were gathered a second time, Mordecai was sitting at the king's gate.
Esther had not yet disclosed her kindred or her people, just as Mordecai had commanded her; for Esther continued to obey Mordecai's instruction as she had during her upbringing.
In those days, while Mordecai sat at the king's gate, Bigthan and Teresh—two of the king's eunuchs, doorkeepers of the threshold—grew wroth and conspired to assassinate King Ahasuerus.
The matter became known to Mordecai, who reported it to Queen Esther; Esther then informed the king in Mordecai's name.
When the affair was investigated and confirmed, the two men were hanged on a gallows, and the incident was recorded in the book of the chronicles before the king.
After these events, King Ahasuerus exalted Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite, promoting him and setting his throne above all the officials who were with him.
All the king’s servants who were at the king’s gate bowed down and paid homage to Haman, for the king had so commanded concerning him; yet Mordecai neither bowed down nor paid homage.
Then the king’s servants who were at the king’s gate said to Mordecai, “Why do you transgress the king’s command?”
When they spoke to him day after day and he would not listen, they reported the matter to Haman, to see whether Mordecai’s refusal would be tolerated, for he had disclosed to them that he was a Jew.
When Haman saw that Mordecai neither bowed down nor paid homage to him, he was filled with rage.

But Haman disdained to lay hands on Mordecai alone, for they had made known to him Mordecai’s people; instead, Haman sought to destroy all the Jews throughout the kingdom of Ahasuerus, the people of Mordecai.
In the first month, that is Nisan, in the twelfth year of King Ahasuerus, Pur—that is, the lot—was cast before Haman, day by day and month by month, until the twelfth month, that is Adar.

Haman said to King Ahasuerus, “There is a certain people scattered and dispersed among the peoples in all the provinces of your kingdom; their laws differ from those of every people, and they do not observe the king’s laws, so it is not in the king’s interest to tolerate them.
If it pleases the king, let it be decreed that they be destroyed, and I will remit ten thousand talents of silver into the royal treasuries, entrusting it to those charged with the king’s affairs.”
So the king removed his signet ring from his hand and gave it to Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the enemy of the Jews.
The king said to Haman, “The silver is given to you, and the people as well; do with them as it seems good to you.”

Then on the thirteenth day of the first month the king’s scribes were summoned, and it was written according to all that Haman commanded to the satraps, the governors of each province, and the officials of each people, to each province in its own script and to each people in its own language; it was written in the name of King Ahasuerus and sealed with the king’s signet ring.

Letters were sent by couriers to all the king’s provinces, to destroy, to kill, and to annihilate all the Jews, young and old, women and children, in a single day—the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, that is Adar—and to plunder their possessions.
A copy of the document was to be issued as law in every province, published to all peoples, so that they might be ready for that day.
The couriers went out, hastened by the king’s command, and the decree was promulgated in Susa the citadel; the king and Haman sat down to drink, but the city of Susa was thrown into confusion.
When Mordecai learned of all that had been done, he tore his garments, clothed himself in sackcloth and ashes, and went out into the midst of the city, crying out with a great and bitter lamentation.
He advanced only as far as the king's gate, for no one arrayed in sackcloth was permitted to enter the king's gate.

And in every province, wherever the king's decree and edict reached, there was great mourning among the Jews, accompanied by fasting, weeping, and lamentation; multitudes reclined upon sackcloth and ashes.

When Esther's maids and eunuchs came and reported these things to the queen, she was exceedingly distressed; she sent garments to clothe Mordecai and to remove his sackcloth from him, but he would not receive them.
Then Esther summoned Hathach, one of the eunuchs whom the king had appointed to attend her, and commanded him concerning Mordecai, to ascertain what this was and why it was.
So Hathach went out to Mordecai in the city square before the king's gate.
Mordecai disclosed to him all that had befallen him, together with the precise sum of money that Haman had promised to weigh out into the king's treasuries for the annihilation of the Jews.

He also gave him a copy of the written decree that had been issued in Susa for their destruction, in order that he might show it to Esther and explain it to her, and he charged him to command her to enter the king's presence, to entreat his favor and to petition before him on behalf of her people.
Hathach returned and reported Mordecai's words to Esther.
Then Esther commanded him to answer Mordecai, saying,

"All the king's servants and the people of the king's provinces know that for every man or woman who comes to the king in the inner court without being summoned there is one law—to be put to death—except for the one to whom the king extends the golden scepter, that he may live; and I have not been summoned to come to the king these thirty days."
When Esther's words were reported to Mordecai,
he sent back this reply: "Do not imagine that you will escape in the king's house, alone among all the Jews.

For if you keep silent at this time, relief and deliverance will arise for the Jews from another place, but you and your father's house will perish; and who knows whether you have not attained to the kingdom for such a time as this?"
Then Esther sent this reply to Mordecai:

"Go, gather all the Jews who are found in Susa, and fast on my behalf; do not eat and do not drink for three days, night and day. I and my maidens will likewise fast; and thus I will go to the king, though it is not according to the law; and if I perish, I perish."
So Mordecai departed and did according to all that Esther had commanded him.

On the third day, Esther arrayed herself in royal raiment and took her station in the inner court of the palace, directly opposite the king’s apartments; meanwhile, the king was seated upon his royal throne within the royal audience chamber, facing the palace entrance.
When the king beheld Queen Esther standing in the court, she won his approval; he extended toward her the golden scepter he held, and Esther drew near and touched the summit of the scepter.
The king inquired of her, “What is your request, Queen Esther? What petition do you bring? Even to half my kingdom, it shall be granted to you.”
Esther replied, “If it pleases the king, let the king and Haman come this day to the banquet I have prepared for him.”
The king commanded, “Dispatch Haman at once, that Esther’s bidding may be executed.” So the king and Haman repaired to the banquet Esther had prepared.
At the wine banquet, the king said to Esther, “What is your petition? It shall be granted to you. And what is your request? Even to half the kingdom, it shall be fulfilled.”
Esther answered, “My petition and my request are these:

If I have won the king’s approval, and if it pleases the king to grant my petition and fulfill my request, let the king and Haman come tomorrow to the banquet I shall prepare for them; then I will act in accordance with the king’s word.”

Haman departed that day rejoicing and in buoyant spirits; yet when he saw Mordecai in the king’s gate, and Mordecai neither rose nor trembled before him, Haman was consumed with wrath against Mordecai.
Nevertheless, Haman mastered his indignation and went to his house; then he sent for and convened his friends together with his wife Zeresh.
Haman rehearsed to them the splendor of his wealth, the multitude of his sons, every distinction the king had conferred upon him, and his elevation above the princes and courtiers of the king.
Haman added, “Moreover, Queen Esther invited no one besides me to accompany the king to the banquet she prepared; and tomorrow, too, I am summoned by her along with the king.
Yet all this is of no avail to me so long as I behold Mordecai the Jew seated at the king’s gate.”

His wife Zeresh and all his friends counseled him, “Have a gallows erected, fifty cubits high, and in the morning entreat the king that Mordecai be hanged upon it; then you may go joyfully with the king to the banquet.” The proposal delighted Haman, and he had the gallows constructed.
That night sleep eluded the monarch, so he commanded that the book of records—the chronicles of the days—be brought and read before him.
There was found written that Mordecai had disclosed the conspiracy of Bigthana and Teresh, two eunuchs among the king’s doorkeepers, who had sought to assassinate King Ahasuerus.
The king asked, “What honor and advancement have been conferred upon Mordecai for this?” His attendants replied, “Nothing whatsoever has been done for him.”
The king inquired, “Who is in the court?” Now Haman had just entered the outer court of the royal palace to petition the king to hang Mordecai upon the gallows he had prepared.
The king’s servants answered, “Behold, Haman stands in the court.” The king said, “Let him enter.”

When Haman came in, the king asked him, “What should be done for the man whom the king delights to honor?” Haman reasoned within himself that the king could scarcely wish to honor anyone more than him.
So Haman said to the king, “For the man whom the king delights to honor,
let royal apparel be brought—the very robe the king has worn—and a horse upon which the king has ridden, with a royal diadem placed upon his head.

Let the apparel and the horse be entrusted to one of the king’s most noble officials, and let them array the man whom the king delights to honor, set him upon the horse, and lead him through the city square, proclaiming before him, ‘Thus it shall be done for the man whom the king delights to honor.’”

The king said to Haman, “Make haste; take the robe and the horse, exactly as you have spoken, and do so for Mordecai the Jew who sits at the king’s gate. Omit not a single word of all that you have said.”
So Haman took the robe and the horse, arrayed Mordecai, and led him through the city square, proclaiming before him, “Thus it shall be done for the man whom the king delights to honor.”
Then Mordecai returned to the king’s gate, while Haman hurried to his house, mourning, his head veiled.

Haman recounted to Zeresh his wife and all his friends everything that had befallen him. His wise men and Zeresh his wife said to him, “If Mordecai, before whom your downfall has begun, is of Jewish descent, you will not prevail against him; rather, you will surely fall before him.”
While they were still speaking with him, the king’s eunuchs arrived and hurriedly brought Haman to the banquet that Esther had prepared.
So the king and Haman came to drink with Queen Esther.

On the second day, while they were drinking wine, the king said again to Queen Esther, "What is your petition, Queen Esther? It shall be granted to you. What is your request? Even to half the kingdom, it shall be done."
Then Queen Esther answered, "If I have found favor in your sight, O king, and if it pleases the king, let my life be granted me at my petition, and my people at my request.

For I and my people have been sold to be destroyed, to be killed, and to be annihilated. Had we been sold merely into servitude, both men and women, I should have held my peace, for the calamity would not have been worth troubling the king."
Then King Ahasuerus said to Queen Esther, "Who is he, and where is he—the one whose heart has emboldened him to do this?"
Esther said, "The adversary and enemy is this wicked Haman!" Then Haman was terrified before the king and the queen.
The king arose in his wrath from the wine banquet and went into the palace garden, while Haman stood to beg Queen Esther for his life, perceiving that the king had resolved to bring ruin upon him.

When the king returned from the palace garden to the banquet hall, Haman was falling upon the couch where Esther reclined. The king exclaimed, "Will he even violate the queen with me in the house?" As soon as the word left the king's mouth, they covered Haman's face.

Then Harbona, one of the eunuchs before the king, said, "Behold, the gallows fifty cubits high stands by Haman's house; he erected it for Mordecai, who spoke in defense of the king." The king said, "Hang him on it!"
So they hanged Haman on the gallows he had prepared for Mordecai, and the king's wrath subsided.

On that very day King Ahasuerus bestowed upon Queen Esther the estate of Haman, the adversary of the Jews; and Mordecai presented himself before the king, because Esther had disclosed to him how Mordecai was related to her.
The king, moreover, removed the signet ring he had reclaimed from Haman and conferred it upon Mordecai, while Esther installed Mordecai over Haman's household.

Esther spoke once more before the king; she prostrated herself at his feet, wept, and implored him to avert the calamity devised by Haman the Agagite and to nullify the machination he had contrived against the Jews.
The king extended the golden scepter toward Esther, whereupon she rose and stood before the king.

Esther said, “If it seems good to the king, and if I have found favor before him, and if the matter appears proper before the king, and if I am pleasing in his eyes, let it be written to rescind the dispatches devised by Haman son of Hammedatha, the Agagite, which he wrote to annihilate the Jews throughout all the king's provinces.
For how could I endure to witness the disaster befalling my people, or how could I endure to witness the extermination of my kindred?”

King Ahasuerus said to Queen Esther and to Mordecai the Jew, “Behold, I have given Esther the house of Haman, and they have hanged him on the gallows because he stretched out his hand against the Jews.

Now you yourselves write in the king's name concerning the Jews whatever seems good in your eyes, and seal it with the king's ring; for a document written in the king's name and sealed with the king's ring is irrevocable.”

So the king's scribes were summoned at that time, in the third month, that is, the month of Sivan, on the twenty-third day; and in accordance with all that Mordecai commanded, it was written to the Jews, to the satraps, to the governors, and to the officials of the one hundred twenty-seven provinces from India to Cush—province by province, people by people, in their own script and language, and to the Jews in their script and language.
He wrote in the name of King Ahasuerus, sealed the letters with the king's ring, and dispatched them by mounted couriers riding swift horses bred from the royal stock.

The king granted the Jews in every city permission to assemble and to stand for their lives—to destroy, to kill, and to annihilate every armed force of any people or province that assailed them, together with their little ones and their women, and to plunder their possessions.
This was to occur on one day in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus, namely the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, the month of Adar.
A copy of the writing was to be issued as law in every province and published to all peoples, so that the Jews might be prepared for that day to take vengeance upon their enemies.
The couriers, mounted on royal steeds, rode out in haste, urged on by the king's command; and the decree was promulgated in the citadel of Susa.
Mordecai departed from the king's presence in royal raiment of blue and white, with a great crown of gold and a robe of purple fine linen; and the city of Susa shouted and rejoiced.
For the Jews there was light and gladness, joy and honor.

In every province and every city, wherever the king's command and decree arrived, there was for the Jews gladness and joy, feasting and a holiday; and many among the peoples of the land became Jews, for the fear of the Jews had fallen upon them.

On the thirteenth day of the twelfth month—that is, Adar—the royal decree and edict were to be executed; and on that very day, when the enemies of the Jews had anticipated subjugating them, the design was inverted, so that the Jews themselves exercised dominion over their adversaries.

Throughout every province of King Ahasuerus, the Jews assembled in their cities to assail those who sought their ruin; no one could withstand them, for a pervasive dread of them had descended upon all peoples.
Moreover, all the provincial officials, the satraps, the governors, and the king’s administrators sustained the Jews, because the fear of Mordecai had fallen upon them.
For Mordecai had become preeminent within the royal household, his renown traversing every province, and the man Mordecai continued to wax ever more illustrious.
Thus the Jews smote all their foes with the sword, with slaughter and devastation, and they dealt with their adversaries according to their own sovereign pleasure.
In the citadel of Susa, the Jews slew and destroyed five hundred men,
the ten sons of Haman son of Hammedatha, the adversary of the Jews; yet they did not stretch forth their hand against the spoil.
On that day the tally of those slain in the citadel of Susa was reported to the king.

The king said to Queen Esther, “In the citadel of Susa the Jews have slain and destroyed five hundred men, along with the ten sons of Haman. What, then, must they have accomplished in the remaining provinces of the king! What is your request? It shall be granted to you. And what further petition do you proffer? It shall be fulfilled.”
Esther replied, “If it please the king, let the Jews in Susa be permitted to act tomorrow also in accordance with today’s decree, and let the ten sons of Haman be hanged upon the gallows.”
So the king commanded that it be done; a decree was promulgated in Susa, and the ten sons of Haman were hanged.
The Jews in Susa assembled on the fourteenth day of Adar and slew three hundred men in Susa, but they did not lay their hand upon the spoil.

The rest of the Jews who were in the king’s provinces assembled and defended their lives, obtaining respite from their enemies; they slew seventy-five thousand of their haters, but they did not lay their hands upon the spoil.
This occurred on the thirteenth day of Adar, and on the fourteenth they rested and made it a day of feasting and gladness.
But the Jews in Susa had assembled on the thirteenth and the fourteenth, and rested on the fifteenth, making it a day of feasting and gladness.

Therefore the rural Jews, those dwelling in unwalled towns, observe the fourteenth day of Adar as a day of gladness and feasting, a propitious day, and as a day for exchanging portions with one another.
Mordecai recorded these events and dispatched letters to all the Jews in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus, both near and far,
enjoining them to keep, year after year, the fourteenth and fifteenth days of Adar,

as the days on which the Jews had obtained rest from their enemies, and as the month that had been transmuted for them from grief into joy, and from mourning into a propitious day; they were to make them days of feasting and gladness, of exchanging portions with one another, and of gifts to the poor.
The Jews undertook what they had begun and what Mordecai had written to them.
For Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the enemy of all the Jews, had devised a plot against the Jews to destroy them, and had cast Pur—that is, the lot—to confound and annihilate them.

But when Esther came before the king, he commanded by letters that the wicked scheme Haman had devised against the Jews should recoil upon his own head, and that he and his sons should be hanged on the gallows.
Therefore these days were called Purim, after the name Pur. For this reason, because of all the words of this letter, and because of what they had seen and what had befallen them,

the Jews established and accepted for themselves, for their descendants, and for all who joined themselves to them, that it should not fail that they keep these two days according to their writing and their appointed time in every year.

These days are to be remembered and kept in every generation, in every family, province, and city; the days of Purim shall not pass away from among the Jews, nor shall the remembrance of them perish from their descendants.
Then Queen Esther daughter of Abihail, together with Mordecai the Jew, wrote with all authority to confirm this second letter concerning Purim.
He sent letters to all the Jews, to the one hundred and twenty-seven provinces of the kingdom of Ahasuerus, words of peace and truth,

to establish the days of Purim at their appointed times, as Mordecai the Jew and Queen Esther had enjoined them, and as they had established for themselves and for their descendants, in the matters of their fasts and their lamentation.
The command of Esther confirmed these words of Purim, and it was written in the book.
King Ahasuerus imposed a tribute upon the mainland and upon the isles of the sea.

As for the complete catalogue of his puissance and might, together with the narrative of Mordecai's preeminence—whereby the king elevated him—are not these matters inscribed in the chronicles of the kings of Media and Persia?

For Mordecai the Jew was second in rank to King Ahasuerus; he was illustrious among the Jews, held in favor by the great multitude of his brethren, one who sought the prosperity of his people and spoke peace to all his posterity.
There was a man in the land of Uz whose name was Job; that man was blameless and upright, one who feared God and turned away from evil.
Seven sons and three daughters were born to him.

His livestock amounted to seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred yoke of oxen, and five hundred female donkeys, together with a very great household of servants, so that this man was the greatest of all the sons of the East.
His sons used to go and hold a feast in the house of each one on his day, and they would send and invite their three sisters to eat and drink with them.

When the days of feasting had run their course, Job would send and consecrate them; rising early in the morning, he would offer burnt offerings according to the number of them all, for Job said, "Perhaps my sons have sinned and cursed God in their hearts." Thus Job did continually, all his days.
Now there came a day when the sons of God presented themselves before the LORD, and the Adversary also came among them.
The LORD said to the Adversary, "From where have you come?" The Adversary answered the LORD and said, "From roaming over the earth and walking about in it."
