Do this now, my son, and deliver yourself, for you have come into the hand of your neighbor; go, humble yourself, and importune your neighbor.
Give no sleep to your eyes, nor slumber to your eyelids.
Extricate yourself as a gazelle from the hunter’s grasp, as a bird from the fowler’s hand.
Go to the ant, O sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise.
She has no chief, overseer, or ruler;
she prepares her bread in summer and gathers her food in harvest.
How long will you lie there, O sluggard? When will you arise from your sleep?
A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest—and
your poverty will come upon you like a robber, and your want like an armed man.
A scoundrel, a man of iniquity, walks with a perverse mouth;
he winks with his eyes, shuffles with his feet, and gestures with his fingers;
with perversity in his heart he devises evil continually, sowing discord;
therefore his calamity will come upon him suddenly, and in a moment he will be shattered beyond recovery.
There are six things the LORD hates, seven that are abominations to His soul:
haughty eyes, a lying tongue, hands that shed innocent blood,
a heart devising wicked schemes, feet hastening to run to evil,
a false witness who utters lies, and one who sows discord among brothers.
My son, keep your father’s commandment, and do not forsake your mother’s teaching.
Bind them continually upon your heart; fasten them about your neck.
When you walk, they will guide you; when you lie down, they will watch over you; and when you awake, they will converse with you.
For the commandment is a lamp, and the teaching is a light, and the reproofs of discipline are the way of life.
They will preserve you from the evil woman, from the smooth tongue of the adulteress.
Do not covet her beauty in your heart, nor let her eyelids captivate you.
For a prostitute can be purchased for no more than a loaf of bread, but an adulteress stalks a man’s precious life.
Can a man carry fire in his bosom and his clothes not be burned?
Or can a man walk upon hot coals and his feet not be scorched?
So is he who goes in to his neighbor’s wife; no one who touches her will go unpunished.
Men do not despise a thief if he steals to satisfy his hunger;
yet if he is caught, he must repay sevenfold and surrender all the wealth of his house.
He who commits adultery lacks understanding; he who does so ruins his own life.
He will incur wounds and dishonor, and his reproach will not be blotted out.
For jealousy enrages a husband, and he will show no mercy in the day of vengeance.
He will accept no ransom; he will not be appeased, though you multiply bribes.
My son, keep my words and treasure my commandments within you;
keep my commandments that you may live, and guard my teaching as the most precious object of your regard.
Bind them upon your fingers; inscribe them upon the tablet of your heart.
Say to wisdom, "You are my sister," and call understanding your intimate friend,
that they may shield you from the adulteress, from the foreign woman who flatters with her words.
For at the window of my house I looked out through my lattice,
and I beheld among the naive, discerning among the youths, a young man devoid of understanding,
traversing the street beside her corner and setting his course toward her dwelling,
in the twilight, in the evening, in the blackness of night and in darkness.
And behold, a woman comes to meet him, dressed as a harlot and wily of heart.
She is clamorous and defiant; her feet never settle in her own house.
Now in the street, now in the squares, she lurks by every corner.
So she seized him and kissed him, and with an impudent face she said to him:
"I am bound to offer peace offerings; today I have paid my vows.
Therefore I have come out to meet you, to seek you out earnestly, and I have found you.
I have spread my couch with coverings, with colored linens of Egypt.
I have perfumed my bed with myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon.
"Come, let us sate ourselves with love until morning; let us revel in caresses.
For my husband is not at home; he has gone far away.
He has taken a bag of silver with him; he will return only at the full moon."
With her many persuasions she seduces him; with her flattering lips she leads him astray.
Suddenly he follows her, as an ox goes to the slaughter, or as one fettered for the chastisement of a fool,
until an arrow pierces his liver; like a bird rushing into a snare, he does not know that it will cost him his life.
And now, my sons, listen to me, and attend to the words of my mouth.
Do not let your heart turn aside to her ways; do not stray into her paths.
For many are the victims she has cast down, and countless are all her slain.
Her house is the way to Sheol, descending to the chambers of death.
Does not wisdom cry aloud, and understanding raise her voice?
At the summit of the heights beside the way, at the crossroads she stands.
Beside the gates, at the city’s mouth, at the entrances of the portals she cries out. “
To you, O men, I call, and my voice is to the sons of men.
O simple ones, acquire shrewdness; O fools, gain understanding.
Listen, for I speak noble things, and from the opening of my lips comes what is right. “
For my mouth utters truth, and wickedness is an abomination to my lips.
All the words of my mouth are righteous; there is nothing crooked or perverse in them.
They are all straightforward to the discerning, and upright to those who attain knowledge. “
Receive my instruction rather than silver, and knowledge rather than choice gold.
For wisdom is better than rubies, and nothing one might desire can be set beside her.” “
I, wisdom, make my dwelling with shrewdness, and I attain knowledge of sound designs.
The fear of the LORD is to hate evil; pride and arrogance, the evil way and the perverse mouth, I hate.
Counsel and sound wisdom are mine; I am understanding, and strength is mine. “
By me kings reign, and rulers enact what is just.
By me princes govern, and nobles—all who judge in righteousness.
I love those who love me, and those who seek me diligently find me. “
With me are riches and honor, enduring wealth and righteousness.
My fruit is better than gold, yes, than fine gold, and my yield than choice silver.
I walk in the way of righteousness, in the midst of the paths of justice.
To bestow an inheritance upon those who love me and to fill their treasuries.” “
The LORD possessed me at the beginning of His way, before His works of old.
I was established from eternity, from the beginning, before the earth existed.
When there were no depths, I was brought forth; when there were no springs heavy with water. “
Before the mountains were set in place, before the hills, I was brought forth.
Before He had made the earth or its fields, or the first dust of the world.
When He prepared the heavens, I was there; when He drew a circle upon the face of the deep. “
When He made firm the skies above, when He strengthened the fountains of the deep.
When He gave the sea its bound, so that the waters should not transgress His command, when He marked out the foundations of the earth. “
Then I was beside Him, as a master craftsman, and I was His daily delight, rejoicing before Him always.
Rejoicing in His inhabited world, and delighting in the sons of men.” “
Now therefore, O children, listen to me, for blessed are those who keep my ways.
Hear instruction and be wise; do not turn away from it.
Blessed is the man who listens to me, watching daily at my gates, waiting beside my doorposts. “
For whoever finds me finds life and obtains favor from the LORD.
But he who sins against me injures his own soul; all who hate me love death.”
Wisdom has built her house and hewn out her seven pillars.
She has slaughtered her beasts, mixed her wine, and set her table in order.
She has dispatched her maidens; from the loftiest places of the city she proclaims her invitation.
“Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!” she says to him who lacks understanding.
“Come, partake of my bread and drink of the wine I have mingled.”
“Forsake your simple ways and live, and walk in the way of understanding.”
He who disciplines a scoffer procures disgrace for himself, and he who reproves the wicked incurs a stain.
Do not reprove a scoffer, lest he hate you; reprove a wise man, and he will love you.
Impart instruction to a wise man, and he will become wiser still; make known to a righteous man, and he will augment his learning.
The fear of the LORD constitutes the beginning of wisdom, and knowledge of the Holy One is understanding.
For by me your days will be multiplied, and years of life will be added to you.
If you are wise, you are wise for yourself; but if you scoff, you alone will bear it.
The woman Folly is clamorous; she is ingenuous and devoid of knowledge.
She sits at the door of her house, on a seat in the highest places of the city,
calling to those who pass by, who go straight on their way:
“Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!” And to him who lacks sense she says,
“Stolen water is sweet, and bread eaten in secret is pleasant.”
But he does not know that the dead are there, that her guests are in the depths of Sheol.
The proverbs of Solomon: a prudent son gladdens his father, whereas a foolish son brings sorrow to his mother.
Treasures amassed through wickedness yield no enduring benefit, but righteousness rescues from death.
The LORD will not allow the righteous to hunger, yet He frustrates the craving of the wicked.
A slack hand begets poverty, while the diligent hand acquires wealth.
A son who gathers during summer acts prudently, but a son who slumbers through harvest brings disgrace.
Blessings rest upon the head of the righteous, whereas the mouth of the wicked conceals violence.
The remembrance of the righteous is a blessing, but the name of the wicked decays.
A wise-hearted person accepts commandments, but a prating fool is overthrown.
Whoever walks in integrity proceeds securely, but whoever twists his ways will be exposed.
One who winks with the eye brings grief, and a prating fool will be overthrown.
The mouth of the righteous is a fountain of life, but the mouth of the wicked conceals violence.
Hatred incites contention, but love overlooks all offenses.
Wisdom is found upon the lips of the discerning, but a rod is reserved for the back of one devoid of understanding.
The wise store up knowledge, but the mouth of a fool hastens ruin.
A rich man's wealth is his stronghold, but the poverty of the poor is their ruin.
The work of the righteous leads to life, whereas the gain of the wicked leads to sin.
Whoever keeps instruction walks in the way of life, but whoever forsakes correction wanders into error.
Whoever conceals hatred speaks with deceitful lips, and whoever broadcasts slander is a fool.
Where words abound, transgression is scarcely absent; but whoever restrains his lips acts prudently.
The tongue of the righteous is as choice silver, but the heart of the wicked is worth little.
The lips of the righteous sustain many, but fools perish for want of discernment.
The blessing of the LORD makes rich, and He adds no grief to it.
To a fool, doing wrong is like sport, but wisdom delights a person of understanding.
What the wicked dread will befall them, but the desire of the righteous will be granted.
When the tempest sweeps by, the wicked vanish, but the righteous stand as an everlasting foundation.
As vinegar sets the teeth on edge and smoke irritates the eyes, so is the sluggard to those who dispatch him.
Reverence for the LORD lengthens days, but the years of the wicked are truncated.
The hope of the righteous is joy, but the expectation of the wicked will perish.
The LORD's way is a refuge for the upright, but destruction for those who practice iniquity.
The righteous will never be shaken, but the wicked shall not inhabit the land.
The mouth of the righteous yields wisdom, but the perverse tongue will be cut off.
The lips of the righteous know what is acceptable, but the mouth of the wicked speaks perversity.
Dishonest scales are an abomination to the LORD, whereas an honest weight is His delight.
When pride arrives, disgrace follows; yet wisdom resides with the humble.
The integrity of the upright guides them, but the perversity of the treacherous destroys them.
Wealth proves utterly inefficacious in the day of wrath, but righteousness delivers from death.
The righteousness of the blameless keeps his way straight, but the wicked falls by his own wickedness.
The righteousness of the upright delivers them, whereas the treacherous are ensnared by their own desires.
When a wicked man dies, his hope perishes, and the expectation vested in his strength vanishes.
The righteous is delivered from trouble, and the wicked takes his place.
By his mouth the godless destroys his neighbor, but through knowledge the righteous are delivered.
When righteousness prospers, the city rejoices; when the wicked perish, jubilation ensues.
By the blessing of the upright a city is exalted, but by the mouth of the wicked it is destroyed.
Whoever belittles his neighbor lacks sense, but a man of understanding holds his peace.
A talebearer reveals secrets, but he who is trustworthy in spirit conceals a matter.
In the absence of guidance, a people falls, but in an abundance of counselors there is safety.
He who puts up security for a stranger will surely suffer, but he who hates pledging himself as surety remains secure.
A gracious woman obtains honor, and ruthless men obtain riches.
A kind man benefits himself, but a cruel man harms himself.
The wicked earns deceptive wages, but he who sows righteousness reaps a true reward.
He who is steadfast in righteousness attains life, but he who pursues evil meets death.
The LORD abhors those of crooked heart, but those whose way is blameless are His delight.
Be assured that the wicked will not go unpunished, but the descendants of the righteous will be delivered.
Like a gold ring in a pig's snout is a beautiful woman without discretion.
The desire of the righteous results only in good, but the expectation of the wicked brings wrath.
One gives freely, yet grows all the richer; another withholds unduly, but comes to poverty.
A generous person will be enriched, and one who waters others will himself be watered.
The people curse the hoarder of grain, but a blessing rests upon the head of the seller.
He who diligently seeks good finds favor, but evil comes to him who searches for it.
He who trusts in his riches will fall, but the righteous will flourish like a green leaf.
He who troubles his own household will reap only emptiness, and the fool will be servant to the wise in heart.
The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life, and he who wins people over is wise.
If the righteous are recompensed on earth, how much more the wicked and the sinner!
He who embraces discipline embraces knowledge, while he who spurns correction betrays a brutish deficiency of understanding.
A good man draws favor from the LORD, but He condemns the man whose designs are wicked.
No human being is rendered secure by wickedness, whereas the righteous remain immovable.
A wife of valor is her husband’s diadem, whereas she who brings disgrace is like putrefaction in his bones.
The designs of the righteous are equitable, but the counsels of the wicked are duplicitous.
The words of the wicked lie in wait for blood, whereas the mouth of the upright rescues them.
The wicked are overturned and are no more, but the house of the righteous endures.
A man is commended according to his prudence, but a perverted heart is held in contempt.
Better to be of humble station and possess a servant than to be vainglorious and destitute of bread.
The righteous has regard for the life of his beast, but the tender mercies of the wicked are cruel.
He who tills his soil shall be satisfied with bread, but he who pursues vain illusions lacks discernment.
The wicked covet the spoils of malefactors, but the root of the righteous flourishes.
An evil man is snared by the transgression of his lips, but the righteous comes forth from distress.
From the fruit of his mouth a man is satisfied with good, and the recompense of his hands returns to him.
The way of a fool seems right in his own eyes, but a wise man heeds counsel.
A fool’s vexation is disclosed at once, but a shrewd man conceals disgrace.
He who utters truth proclaims what is just, whereas a false witness speaks deceit.
There is one whose rash words are like the thrusts of a sword, but the tongue of the wise is a remedy.
A lip of truth stands forever, but a tongue of falsehood endures but an instant.
Deceit resides in the heart of those who plot evil, but counselors of peace have joy.
No calamity shall befall the righteous, but the wicked are glutted with evil.
Lying lips are an abomination to the LORD, but doers of faithfulness are His delight.
A shrewd man conceals knowledge, but the heart of fools proclaims folly.
The hand of the industrious shall bear rule, but indolence becomes servile labor.
Anxiety in a man’s heart weighs it down, but a good word makes it glad.
A righteous man is cautious in friendship, but the way of the wicked leads them astray.
A slothful man does not roast his prey, but the wealth of a diligent man is precious.
In the path of righteousness there is life, and in its pathway there is no death.
A sagacious son heeds the discipline of his father, while the scoffer remains obdurate to rebuke.
By the fruit of his own speech a man nourishes himself well, whereas the very appetite of the treacherous is inflamed with violence.
The one who guards his mouth preserves his life, while he who gives free rein to his lips courts his own destruction.
The sluggard's soul craves and receives nothing, but the soul of the diligent is abundantly sated.
The righteous abhor falsehood, while the wicked comport themselves basely and heap disgrace upon themselves.
Righteousness stands sentinel over the way of the blameless, but wickedness subverts the path of the sinner.
One man amasses apparent riches yet possesses nothing, while another affects poverty yet commands great wealth.
A man's riches may serve as the ransom of his life, whereas the poor man remains unrebuked.
The light of the righteous shines with gladness, while the lamp of the wicked is extinguished.
Arrogance begets nothing but strife, yet wisdom resides with those who accept counsel.
Wealth amassed in haste dwindles away, but he who gathers little by little amplifies his store.
Hope deferred sickens the heart, whereas desire fulfilled is a tree of life.
He who contemns the word brings ruin upon himself, while he who reveres the commandment shall be recompensed.
The instruction of the wise is a fountain of life, diverting one from the snares of death.
Sound discernment wins favor, whereas the path of the treacherous is arduous.
Every prudent man acts with discernment, while the fool disseminates his folly.
A wicked envoy stumbles into adversity, while a faithful messenger brings healing.
Poverty and disgrace befall him who disregards discipline, but he who heeds reproof is honored.
A desire fulfilled is sweet to the soul, yet fools abhor turning away from evil.
He who consorts with the wise grows wise, while the companion of fools suffers harm.
Calamity pursues sinners, whereas prosperity rewards the righteous.
A good man bequeaths an inheritance to his children's children, but the wealth of the sinner is laid up for the righteous.
The fallow ground of the poor yields abundant food, yet without justice it is swept away.
He who spares the rod hates his son, but he who loves him disciplines him with diligence.
The righteous eat to the satisfaction of the soul, while the belly of the wicked goes hungry.
A woman's wisdom constructs her house, whereas folly demolishes it with her own hands.
He who walks in uprightness fears the LORD, but he who is devious in his ways despises Him.
Pride issues from the fool's mouth, yet the lips of the wise safeguard them.
In the absence of oxen, the feeding trough remains clean, but an abundant harvest arises from the ox's strength.
A faithful witness does not lie, but a false witness breathes out lies.
A scoffer seeks wisdom and finds none, but knowledge comes easily to the discerning.
Withdraw from the fool, for you will discover no discernment upon his lips.
The wisdom of the prudent is to understand his way, but the folly of fools is deceit.
Fools scoff at guilt, yet goodwill dwells among the upright.
The heart alone knows its own bitterness, and no outsider partakes of its joy.
The house of the wicked will be destroyed, but the tent of the upright will flourish.
There is a path that appears upright to a person, yet its terminus is the way of death.
Even in laughter the heart may ache, and the end of joy may be grief.
The backslider in heart is sated with his own conduct, whereas a good person finds satisfaction from within himself.
The simple believes everything, but the prudent gives thought to his steps.
A wise person fears evil and withdraws from it, but a fool rages and remains self-assured.
One who is quick to anger acts foolishly, and a person who schemes maliciously is hated.
The simple inherit folly, but the prudent are crowned with knowledge.
The wicked bow before the good, and the malevolent prostrate themselves at the gates of the righteous.
A poor person is hated even by his neighbor, but the rich have many friends.
Whoever scorns his neighbor sins, but blessed is the one who shows mercy to the poor.
Do not those who contrive evil stray from the path? Yet mercy and truth belong to those who plan good.
Every form of labor yields profit, but mere talk conduces only to poverty.
The wise person's crown is wealth, yet the folly of fools remains mere folly.
A truthful witness delivers lives, but a deceitful witness utters lies.
In the fear of the LORD there is strong confidence, and His children will have a refuge.
The fear of the LORD is a fountain of life, turning a person from the snares of death.
A king's glory lies in a multitude of people, but a prince is ruined without a populace.
Whoever is slow to anger has great understanding, but he who has a hasty temper exalts folly.
A tranquil heart is life to the flesh, but envy is rottenness to the bones.
Whoever oppresses the poor insults his Maker, but whoever is generous to the needy honors Him.
The wicked is driven away in his wickedness, but the righteous finds refuge even in death.
Wisdom rests in the heart of the discerning, but among fools it becomes conspicuous.
Righteousness exalts a nation, but sin is a reproach to any people.
A king's favor is toward a wise servant, but his wrath is against the one who causes shame.
A gentle rejoinder pacifies wrath, whereas a harsh utterance provokes anger.
The tongue of the wise commends knowledge, but the mouth of fools overflows with folly.
The eyes of the LORD pervade every place, scrutinizing the wicked and the good alike.
A healing tongue is a tree of life, yet perversity lodged therein shatters the spirit.
A fool despises his father’s discipline, but whoever heeds reproof acquires prudence.
The house of the righteous contains great treasure, whereas the income of the wicked is fraught with trouble.
The lips of the wise disseminate knowledge; the hearts of fools do not.
The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination to the LORD, but the prayer of the upright is His delight.
The LORD abhors the way of the wicked, yet He loves those who pursue righteousness.
Grievous discipline befalls him who forsakes the way, and he who hates reproof shall perish.
Sheol and Abaddon lie open before the LORD; how much more the hearts of human beings!
A scoffer does not love to be reproved; he will not go to the wise.
A glad heart brightens the face, but sorrow of heart crushes the spirit.
The discerning heart seeks knowledge, while the mouth of fools feeds on folly.
All the days of the afflicted are wretched, but a cheerful heart is a continual feast.
Better is a little with the fear of the LORD than great treasure accompanied by turmoil.
Better a dish of vegetables where love is than a fattened ox with hatred.
A wrathful man stirs up strife, but one slow to anger pacifies contention.
The sluggard’s way is like a hedge of thorns, but the path of the upright is a highway.
A wise son gladdens his father, but a foolish man despises his mother.
Folly is joy to one lacking sense, but a man of understanding walks a straight path.
Plans fail for lack of counsel, but with many advisers they succeed.
A man rejoices in an apt reply, and a timely word is exceedingly good.
The path of life leads upward for the wise, that he may turn away from Sheol below.
The LORD uproots the house of the proud, but He establishes the widow’s boundary.
The LORD abominates the thoughts of the wicked, but the words of the pure are pleasing.
He who is greedy for gain troubles his household, but he who hates bribes shall live.
The heart of the righteous ponders an answer, but the mouth of the wicked pours forth evil.
The LORD is far from the wicked, but He hears the prayer of the righteous.
The light of the eyes gladdens the heart, and good news nourishes the bones.
Whoever heeds life-giving reproof will dwell among the wise.
He who rejects discipline despises himself, but whoever heeds reproof acquires understanding.
The fear of the LORD is the instruction of wisdom, and humility comes before honor.
The designs of the human heart are a mortal prerogative, yet the utterance of the tongue is granted by the LORD.
Every course a person elects appears immaculate in his own estimation, but the LORD weighs the motives.
Entrust your undertakings to the LORD, and your designs shall be firmly established.
The LORD has fashioned all things for His own end; even the wicked are reserved for the day of calamity.
Every proud-hearted individual is an abomination to the LORD; rest assured, such a one shall not evade retribution.
Through steadfast love and fidelity, iniquity is expiated; and through reverence for the LORD, one turns away from evil.
When a person's conduct pleases the LORD, He reconciles even that person's enemies to him.
Better a modest portion conjoined with righteousness than abundant revenue procured through injustice.
A mortal may chart his course in his heart, yet the LORD determines his steps.
A divine verdict rests upon a king's lips; in judgment, his mouth must not prove treacherous.
Just balances and scales belong to the LORD; all the weights in the pouch are His concern.
Wicked conduct is an abomination to kings, for a throne is secured through righteousness.
Righteous speech is a king's delight, and the one who speaks with integrity is beloved.
A king's wrath is a harbinger of death, yet a wise person will propitiate it.
In the radiance of a king's countenance there is life; His favor is like a cloud bringing the late spring rain.
How far superior it is to acquire wisdom rather than gold, and to choose discernment rather than silver!
The highway of the upright veers away from evil; whoever guards his course preserves his life.
Pride precedes ruin, and an arrogant spirit precedes a downfall.
Better to be humble in spirit among the oppressed than to divide spoil with the arrogant.
Whoever gives heed to instruction prospers, and blessed is the one who trusts in the LORD.
The wise of heart are deemed discerning, and gracious speech augments learning.
Discernment is a wellspring of life to its possessor, but the chastisement of fools is mere folly.
The heart of the wise renders his speech judicious, and his lips further instruction.
Gracious words are a honeycomb: sweet to the soul and medicinal to the bones.
There is a path that appears upright to a mortal, yet its terminus is the way of death.
A laborer's appetite works on his behalf, because his hunger impels him onward.
A scoundrel excavates evil, and his speech is as a scorching fire.
A perverse person sows strife, and a whisperer alienates intimate friends.
A violent person seduces his neighbor and conducts him along a path that is not good.
He who winks his eye contrives perversities; he who purses his lips brings evil to pass.
Gray hair is a crown of glory; it is found along the path of righteousness.
Better is the patient than the warrior, and he who rules his spirit surpasses one who captures a city.
The lot may be cast into the lap, yet its every determination proceeds from the LORD.
A parched morsel accompanied by tranquility surpasses a house replete with sacrificial feasts embroiled in contention.
A discerning servant shall govern a shameful son and apportion the inheritance among the brethren.
As the crucible refines silver and the furnace gold, so the LORD assays the hearts of men.
A wicked man gives heed to iniquitous lips, and a deceitful tongue hearkens to a destructive tongue.
He who derides the indigent reproaches his Maker; he who exults in disaster shall not be held guiltless.
Grandchildren constitute the crown of the aged, and the splendor of children is their fathers.
Eloquent discourse ill befits a fool; how much less do mendacious lips befit a noble.
A bribe operates as a talisman in the eyes of its purveyor; whithersoever he turns, he prospers.
He who veils a transgression seeks love, but he who rehearses a matter alienates an intimate.
A single reproof penetrates a discerning man more than a hundred blows penetrate a fool.
A wicked man seeks only rebellion, and a merciless messenger shall be dispatched against him.
Better to encounter a bereaved she-bear than a fool in his folly.
He who requites evil for good shall find that evil never departs from his household.
The inception of strife resembles the bursting of a dam; therefore abandon contention before it erupts.
To justify the wicked and to condemn the righteous—both alike are an abomination to the LORD.
Wherefore should a fool possess the price of wisdom in his hand, when he is devoid of understanding?
A friend loves at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.
A man devoid of understanding strikes hands in pledge and becomes surety for his neighbor.
He who loves transgression loves contention; he who exalts his threshold seeks ruin.
A perverse heart finds no good, and a deceitful tongue precipitates ruin.
He who begets a fool does so to his grief; the father of a fool shall have no joy.
A joyful heart is a salutary remedy, but a downcast spirit desiccates the bones.
The wicked man takes a bribe from the bosom to pervert the paths of justice.
Wisdom abides before the face of the discerning, but the eyes of a fool wander to the ends of the earth.
A foolish son is a vexation to his father and bitterness to her who bore him.
It is likewise unseemly to punish the righteous and to scourge the noble on account of uprightness.
A man of knowledge restrains his utterances; a man of understanding is cool of spirit.
Even a fool, when he holds his peace, is reputed wise; he who seals his lips is deemed discerning.
A man who sequesters himself in isolation pursues nothing but his own craving, and in so doing sets himself in defiance of every manifestation of sound wisdom.
The fool evinces no delight in understanding; rather, his sole ambition is to parade the unexamined contents of his own heart.
When wickedness makes its appearance, contempt follows in its train, and disgrace arrives attended by reproach.
The utterances that issue from a man's mouth are like deep waters, whereas the wellspring of wisdom resembles a gushing torrent.
It is scarcely salutary to show partiality toward the wicked, or to wrest justice from the righteous in the adjudication of causes.
The lips of a fool precipitate contention, and his mouth all but cries out for blows.
A fool's mouth proves his own undoing, while his lips become a snare for his very life.
The whisperings of a slanderer are like delectable morsels, and they descend into the innermost recesses of a man's being.
He who slackens in his labor is brother to the one who perpetrates destruction.
The name of the the LORD constitutes a fortified tower; the righteous hasten into it and are rendered secure.
The wealthy man's riches serve as his fortified city, and in his own conceit they stand as a lofty rampart.
Before ruin, a man's heart exalts itself; yet humility precedes honor.
To render a reply before one has heard is folly and disgrace to the speaker.
A man's spirit can sustain him through infirmity, but a crushed spirit—who could possibly endure it?
The discerning heart acquires knowledge, and the ear of the wise actively pursues it.
A gift clears a path for a man and ushers him into the presence of the great.
The one who first presents his case appears just, until his neighbor arrives and subjects it to rigorous scrutiny.
The casting of lots puts an end to contention and adjudicates between the mighty.
A brother who has been offended is more formidable than a fortified city, and quarrels are like the bars of a citadel.
From the fruit of a man's mouth his belly is filled, and by the yield of his lips he is satiated.
Death and life lie within the power of the tongue, and those who cherish it shall eat of its fruit.
He who discovers a wife discovers a good thing and secures favor from the the LORD.
The impoverished man speaks in entreaties, whereas the rich man responds with harshness.
A man of numerous companions may be brought to ruin, yet there exists a friend who cleaves more closely than a brother.
An impoverished man who walks in his integrity is better than a fool whose lips are perverse.
Moreover, a soul bereft of knowledge is no blessing, and he who hastens with his feet sins.
A man's folly perverts his path, yet his heart chafes against the LORD.
Wealth multiplies companions, whereas the impoverished man is estranged from his neighbor.
A false witness shall not go unpunished, and he who breathes forth lies shall not escape.
Many solicit the favor of a prince, and all are friends to a benefactor.
All the kin of the impoverished despise him; how much more do his companions withdraw! He pursues them with entreaties, yet they have vanished.
He who acquires wisdom loves his own soul, and he who keeps discernment will find good.
A false witness shall not go unpunished, and he who breathes forth lies shall perish.
Luxury is unbecoming to a fool, and still less is it seemly for a servant to rule over princes.
A man's prudence makes him slow to anger, and his glory lies in overlooking a transgression.
The king's wrath is as the roaring of a lion, but his favor is as dew upon the grass.
A foolish son is the ruin of his father, and a contentious wife is as a continual dripping.
Houses and riches are an inheritance from fathers, but a prudent wife comes from the LORD.
Sloth casts one into a deep sleep, and an idle soul shall suffer hunger.
He who keeps the commandment preserves his soul, but he who is careless in his ways shall die.
He who is gracious to the poor lends to the LORD, and He will repay him for his good deed.
Discipline your son while there is hope, and do not be complicit in his death.
A man of great wrath shall bear the penalty; if you rescue him, you will have to do it again.
Hear counsel and receive instruction, that you may be wise in your latter days.
Many are the plans in a man's heart, but the counsel of the LORD shall stand.
What a man desires is his kindness, and a poor man is better than a liar.
The fear of the LORD tends toward life, so that one may rest satisfied and remain untouched by trouble.
The sluggard buries his hand in the dish, yet he will not so much as bring it back to his mouth.
Strike a scoffer, and the simple will become wise; reprove a discerning man, and he will gain knowledge.
He who plunders his father and chases away his mother is a son who causes shame and reproach.
Cease, my son, to listen to instruction, and you will wander from the words of knowledge.
A worthless witness scoffs at justice, and the mouth of the wicked devours iniquity.
Judgments are prepared for scoffers, and stripes for the backs of fools.
Wine is a mocker, strong drink a brawler, and whoever is led astray by it is not wise.
A king’s terror is like the roaring of a lion; whoever provokes him sins against his own life.
It is an honor for a man to withdraw from strife, but every fool rushes into contention.
The sluggard will not plow in winter; at harvest he will seek and find nothing.
Counsel in the heart of a man is deep water, but a man of understanding draws it out.
Many a man proclaims his own steadfast love, yet who can find a faithful man?
The righteous man who walks in his integrity—blessed are his children after him.
A king who sits on the throne of judgment winnows all evil with his eyes.
Who can say, “I have purified my heart; I am clean from my sin”?
Differing weights and differing measures are both an abomination to the LORD.
Even a child is known by his deeds, whether his conduct is pure and upright.
The hearing ear and the seeing eye—the LORD has made them both.
Do not love sleep, lest you come to poverty; open your eyes, and you will be satisfied with bread.
“Bad, bad!” says the buyer, but when he goes away, he boasts.
There is gold and an abundance of pearls, but the lips of knowledge are a precious jewel.
Take his garment, for he has stood surety for a stranger; and hold it in pledge for foreigners.
Bread gained by deceit is sweet to a man, but afterward his mouth is filled with gravel.
Plans are established by counsel, and by wise guidance one wages war.
Whoever goes about as a talebearer reveals a secret; therefore do not associate with a babbler.
Whoever curses his father or his mother—his lamp will be extinguished in utter darkness.
An inheritance gained hastily at the beginning will not be blessed in the end.
Do not say, “I will repay evil”; wait for the LORD, and He will save you.
Differing weights are an abomination to the LORD, and false scales are not good.
A man’s steps are from the LORD; how then can a man understand his way?
It is a snare for a man to say, “It is holy,” and only afterward to examine his vows.
A wise king winnows the wicked and drives the threshing wheel over them.
The spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD, searching all his inmost parts.
Steadfast love and faithfulness preserve the king, and by steadfast love his throne is upheld.
The glory of young men is their strength, but the splendor of old men is their gray hair.
Blows that wound cleanse away evil, and strokes make clean the innermost parts.
The heart of a sovereign is like a watercourse in the hand of the LORD, and He inclines it toward whatever He delights in.
Every man's course appears upright in his own eyes, yet the LORD examines the motives of hearts.
To execute righteousness and justice is more acceptable to the LORD than sacrifice.
Arrogant eyes and an expansive heart—the very lamp of the wicked—are sin.
The deliberations of the industrious redound to surplus, whereas every precipitate impulse issues in penury.
Treasures amassed by a mendacious tongue are a dissipating vapor and a deadly snare;
the violence of the wicked sweeps them away, because they refuse to execute justice.
The path of the perverse is devious, but the conduct of the pure is upright.
It is preferable to inhabit a corner of the rooftop than to share a dwelling with a contentious wife.
The wicked soul covets evil, and his neighbor finds no favor in his eyes.
When a scoffer is chastised, the naive acquires prudence; and when a wise man is admonished, he apprehends knowledge.
The Righteous One considers the household of the wicked and subverts the wicked unto calamity.
Whoever seals his ears against the outcry of the indigent shall himself cry out and receive no answer.
A clandestine gift appeases wrath, and a bribe concealed in the bosom pacifies fierce indignation.
To administer justice is joy to the righteous and dismay to workers of iniquity.
A man who strays from the path of discernment shall abide among the congregation of the shades.
He who delights in merriment shall become impoverished; whoever loves wine and oil shall not grow wealthy.
The wicked serves as a ransom for the righteous, and the faithless for the upright.
It is better to dwell in a wilderness than with a contentious and vexatious wife.
Desirable treasure and oil reside in the abode of the wise, but a foolish man squanders them.
Whoever pursues righteousness and steadfast love discovers life, righteousness, and honor.
A wise man ascends the city of the mighty and overthrows the stronghold in which they confide.
Whoever guards his mouth and his tongue preserves his soul from calamities.
Proud, haughty, mocker—such is the designation of him who acts in arrogant wrath.
The desire of the sluggard slays him, for his hands decline to labor.
All the day he covets greedily, yet the righteous gives and does not withhold.
The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination; how much more when he offers it with wicked design!
A mendacious witness shall perish, but the attentive man speaks in perpetuity.
A wicked man hardens his countenance, but the upright considers his conduct.
There is no wisdom, nor understanding, nor counsel that can avail against the LORD.
The horse is made ready for the day of battle, but deliverance belongs to the LORD.
A distinguished reputation is preferable to vast wealth; gracious esteem surpasses both silver and gold.
The affluent and the indigent encounter one another, yet the LORD is the Maker of them all.
The shrewd perceive calamity and conceal themselves, whereas the naive press forward and incur penalty.
The recompense of humility and reverence for the LORD comprises riches, honor, and life.
Thorns and snares beset the way of the perverse; whoever preserves his soul remains at a distance from them.
Instruct a youth according to his proper path, and even in senescence he will not deviate from it.
The affluent exercise dominion over the impoverished, and the debtor becomes servant to the creditor.
Whoever sows iniquity shall harvest calamity, and the rod of his wrath shall be consumed.
The generous shall be blessed, since he dispenses his bread to the needy.
Expel the mocker, and quarreling will subside; indeed, litigation and ignominy will abate.
Whoever cherishes purity of heart and possesses gracious speech shall find the king as his companion.
The LORD's eyes safeguard knowledge, yet He subverts the utterances of the treacherous.
The sluggard protests, “A lion lurks without; I shall be murdered in the thoroughfares!”
The mouth of a forbidden woman is a bottomless pit; one under the LORD's wrath will plunge therein.
Folly is tethered to a child's heart, yet the rod of correction banishes it from him.
Whoever extorts the indigent to aggrandize himself, or tenders gifts to the affluent, shall surely be reduced to penury.
Incline your ear and hearken to the sages' words; devote your heart to my understanding.
For it is delightful when you treasure them inwardly; let them be ever upon your lips.
That your confidence may repose in the LORD, I acquaint you this day—even you.
Have I not committed to writing for you thirty counsels and insights?
to impart to you the verity of words, that you may return truthful answers to those who sent you.
Do not plunder the indigent because he is poor, nor oppress the afflicted at the gate.
For the LORD shall champion their cause and despoil those who despoil them.
Do not fraternize with a choleric man, nor consort with one of furious temper,
lest you assimilate his conduct and ensnare your own soul.
Do not join those who pledge themselves as sureties for debts.
If you lack means to discharge the debt, why should your bed be seized from beneath you?
Do not displace an ancient landmark that your ancestors established.
Do you perceive a man diligent in his craft? He shall attend kings, not remain among the obscure.
When you sit at the table of a sovereign, scrutinize with meticulous circumspection the provisions arrayed before you;
and, should you be a person of ravenous appetite, impose upon yourself the most stringent restraint.
Do not covet his delicacies, for that fare is fundamentally deceptive.
Do not exhaust yourself in the pursuit of riches; be sufficiently discerning to desist.
When your gaze alights upon wealth, it is already vanishing, for it sprouts wings for itself and takes flight like an eagle toward the heavens.
Do not partake of the bread of a man with a grudging eye, nor covet his delicacies;
for as he reckons within himself, so he truly is. Though he says, “Eat and drink,” his heart is not with you.
You will vomit up the morsel you have consumed and squander your gracious words.
Do not speak in a fool’s hearing, for he will despise the sagacity of your words.
Do not displace an ancient boundary marker, and do not encroach upon the fields of orphans,
for their Redeemer is mighty; He will plead their cause against you.
Apply your heart to discipline and your ears to words of knowledge.
Do not withhold correction from a child; though you strike him with a rod, he will not die.
You shall strike him with a rod and deliver his soul from Sheol.
My son, if your heart is wise, my heart will rejoice—indeed, I too.
My inmost being will exult when your lips speak what is right.
Let not your heart envy sinners, but abide in the fear of the LORD all day long,
for surely there is a future, and your hope will not be severed.
Hear, my son, and be wise, and direct your heart in the way.
Do not associate with winebibbers, nor with gluttonous devourers of flesh;
for the drunkard and the glutton will be impoverished, and drowsiness will clothe them in rags.
Heed your father, who begot you, and do not despise your mother when she is old.
Acquire truth and do not sell it; acquire wisdom, instruction, and understanding.
The father of a righteous man will greatly rejoice, and he who begets a wise son will delight in him.
Let your father and mother be glad, and let her who bore you rejoice.
My son, give me your heart, and let your eyes delight in my ways.
For a prostitute is a deep pit, and an adulteress is a narrow well.
She lies in wait like a robber and multiplies the faithless among men.
Who has woe? Who has sorrow? Who has strife? Who has complaints? Who has needless bruises? Who has bloodshot eyes?
Those who linger over wine, those who go to sample mixed drinks.
Do not gaze upon wine when it is red, when it sparkles in the cup and descends smoothly.
In the end it bites like a serpent and stings like a viper.
Your eyes will see strange things, and your heart will utter perversities.
You will be like one lying in the heart of the sea, or like one lying atop a mast.
“They struck me, yet I was not sick; they beat me, yet I did not know. When will I awake, that I may seek another drink?”
Do not envy malefactors, nor covet fellowship with them;
for their hearts brood upon violence, and their lips give utterance to mischief.
By wisdom a house is erected, and by discernment it is made firm;
by knowledge its chambers are filled with every precious and delectable possession.
A sagacious man is mighty, and a man of understanding augments his power;
for by prudent counsel you shall wage your war, and in a multitude of counselors there is victory.
Exalted wisdom lies beyond a fool's grasp, so he does not open his mouth at the city gate;
one who plots evil will be called a master of schemes;
the conception of folly is sin, and the scorner is an abomination to humankind.
If you faint in the day of adversity, your strength is meager;
rescue those being led away to death, and restrain those staggering toward slaughter;
if you say, "Behold, we did not know this," does not He who weighs hearts perceive it? Does not He who guards your soul know? And will He not requite each person according to his deeds?
Consume honey, my son, for it is wholesome, and the honeycomb is sweet upon your palate;
know that wisdom is such for your soul: if you find it, there shall be a future, and your hope shall not be severed.
Do not lie in ambush, O wicked man, against the abode of the righteous, nor ravage his resting place;
for though the righteous man falls seven times, he rises again, whereas the wicked are brought down by adversity.
Do not rejoice when your enemy falls, and let not your heart exult when he stumbles;
lest the the LORD see and it displease Him, and He turn His wrath away from him.
Do not be vexed by evildoers, nor envy the wicked;
for the evil man shall have no future, and the lamp of the wicked shall be extinguished.
My son, revere the the LORD and the king, and do not consort with the seditious;
for their ruin shall arise suddenly, and who can know the downfall of them both?
These too are the sayings of the wise: it is not good to show partiality in judgment;
he who says to the wicked, "You are righteous," the peoples will curse him, and the nations will abhor him;
but those who rebuke the wicked shall find delight, and a good blessing shall come upon them;
he who returns a straightforward answer kisses the lips.
Prepare your work outdoors, and make ready for yourself in the field; and afterwards build your house;
do not bear witness against your neighbor without cause, nor deceive with your lips;
do not say, "I will do to him as he has done to me; I will repay the man according to his work."
I passed by the field of a sluggard and by the vineyard of a man devoid of understanding;
and lo, it was all overgrown with thorns, nettles had covered its surface, and its stone wall lay in ruins;
I observed and took it to heart; I saw and received instruction:
"A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest—
and your poverty shall come like a robber, and your need like an armed man."
These are likewise the proverbs of Solomon, transcribed by the men of Hezekiah, king of Judah.
To conceal a matter is the glory of God, but to search it out is the glory of kings.
As the heavens are immeasurably high and the earth profoundly deep, so the heart of a king is unsearchable.
Remove the dross from silver, and a vessel emerges for the refiner.
Remove the wicked from before the king, and his throne shall be established in righteousness.
Do not aggrandize yourself before the king, nor stand in the place of the great.
For it is better that one say to you, "Ascend hither," than that you be abased before a noble whose presence your eyes have beheld.
Do not precipitously rush into contention, lest, when your neighbor has shamed you, you be left without recourse at the last.
Argue your cause with your neighbor, yet do not disclose another's confidence.
Lest the hearer shame you, and your disgrace prove irrevocable.
A word aptly spoken is like golden apples set in silver filigree.
Like a golden ring or an ornament of pure gold is a wise rebuke to an ear that hearkens.
Like the coolness of snow in harvest season, a trustworthy envoy refreshes the soul of those who sent him; for he refreshes the soul of his masters.
As clouds and wind without rain, so is the man who boasts of a gift he never gives.
Through patient forbearance a ruler may be persuaded, and a gentle tongue can shatter the hardest resolve.
If you have found honey, consume only your sufficiency, lest you glut yourself and vomit it forth.
Withdraw your foot from your neighbor's house, lest he grow weary of you and come to hate you.
A false witness against his neighbor is as a maul, a sword, and a sharp arrow.
Trusting an unfaithful man in a day of distress is like a broken tooth and a slipping foot.
As removing a garment in cold weather, or pouring vinegar upon natron, so is singing songs to a heavy heart.
If your enemy hungers, give him bread to eat, and if he thirsts, give him water to drink.
For you will heap burning shame upon his head, and the LORD will reward you.
As the north wind brings rain, so a slanderous tongue brings an angry countenance.
Better to dwell in a corner of the roof than with a contentious woman in a spacious house.
Like cold water to a weary soul, so is good news from a distant land.
As a muddied spring and a polluted well, so is a righteous man who falters before the wicked.
It is not good to eat too much honey, nor is it glorious to seek one's own glory.
Like a city broken down and without walls is a man who lacks self-control.
Honor is as incongruous for a fool as snow in midsummer or rain during harvest.
Just as the sparrow flits and the swallow darts through the air, so an undeserved curse finds no place to alight.
A whip for the horse, a bridle for the donkey, and a rod for the back of fools.
Do not answer a fool according to his folly, lest you become like him.
Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he regard himself as wise.
Entrusting a message to a fool is like severing one's own feet and drinking violence.
A proverb in a fool's mouth is as useless as the dangling legs of the lame.
Bestowing honor upon a fool is as senseless as binding a stone into a sling.
A proverb on a fool's lips is like a thorn lodged in a drunkard's hand.
Hiring a fool—or any random passerby—is like an archer who wounds indiscriminately.
As a dog returns to its vomit, so a fool reiterates his folly.
Do you see a person wise in his own conceit? There is more hope for a fool than for him.
The sluggard says, "There is a lion in the road—a lion in the streets!"
As a door turns on its hinges, so the sluggard turns upon his bed.
The sluggard buries his hand in the dish, yet is too weary to return it to his mouth.
The sluggard is wiser in his own eyes than seven men who answer with discernment.
He who seizes a dog by the ears is like one who passes by and meddles in a quarrel not his own.
Like a madman shooting firebrands, arrows, and death,
so is the person who deceives his neighbor and says, "Was I not joking?"
Without wood the fire dies; without a whisperer, strife subsides.
As charcoal is to burning coals and wood to fire, so is a contentious person to kindle strife.
The words of a whisperer are like dainty morsels that descend into the innermost parts.
Fervent lips with a wicked heart are like a silver glaze over an earthen vessel.
The hater disguises himself with his lips, while he stores up deceit within.
Though his speech be gracious, do not believe him, for seven abominations reside in his heart.
His malice may be concealed by deception, but his wickedness will be exposed in the assembly.
Whoever digs a pit will fall into it, and whoever rolls a stone will find it rolling back upon him.
A lying tongue hates those it crushes, and a flattering mouth brings ruin.
Do not vaunt yourself concerning the morrow, for you cannot foretell what the day itself may engender.
Let a stranger extol you, and not your own mouth; let a foreigner commend you, and not your own lips.
A stone is heavy, and sand is weighty, yet the provocation of a fool outweighs them both.
Wrath is cruel, and anger is a torrent, but who can stand before jealousy?
Candid reproof surpasses affection kept secret.
The wounds inflicted by a friend are trustworthy, whereas an enemy's kisses are treacherous.
A glutted appetite spurns honey, yet to the famished even bitterness is sweet.
As a bird that strays from its nest, so is a man who strays from his dwelling.
Oil and incense gladden the heart, and a friend's counsel is sweet to the soul.
Do not forsake your friend or your father's friend, and do not repair to your brother's house in the day of your calamity; a neighbor nearby is better than a brother far away.
Be wise, my son, and gladden my heart, that I may answer the one who reproaches me.
The shrewd man discerns calamity and conceals himself, whereas the naive proceed and incur punishment.
Take his garment, since he has pledged himself for a stranger, and obtain security from him because of a foreign woman.
He who loudly blesses his neighbor at daybreak will have it counted as a curse.
A persistent drip on a rainy day and a contentious wife are comparable.
To restrain her is to restrain the wind, or to grasp oil with one's right hand.
Iron sharpens iron, and one man whets another.
He who tends a fig tree will eat its fruit, and he who guards his master will be honored.
As water reflects face to face, so the heart of man reflects the man.
Sheol and Abaddon are never satisfied, and the eyes of man are never satisfied.
The crucible refines silver, the furnace gold, and a man is assayed by the praise he receives.
Though you grind a fool in a mortar with a pestle along with crushed grain, yet his folly will not depart from him.
Know diligently the condition of your flocks, and give attention to your herds;
for wealth is not perpetual, nor does a diadem endure through every generation.
When the grass disappears, the tender grass appears, and the herbs of the mountains are gathered,
the lambs will provide your clothing, and the goats the price of a field;
and there will be enough goats' milk for your food, for the food of your household, and for the sustenance of your maidens.
The wicked flee though no pursuer is at their heels, whereas the righteous possess a leonine intrepidity.
When a realm transgresses, it proliferates rulers; yet a person endowed with understanding and knowledge perpetuates its order.
An impoverished oppressor of the poor resembles a torrential rain that devastates the harvest and leaves no sustenance.
Those who abandon the law extol the wicked, whereas those who keep the law contend against them.
Men of evil do not comprehend justice, but those who seek the LORD apprehend it in its totality.
A poor man who walks in integrity surpasses a wealthy man whose conduct is crooked.
A son of discernment keeps the law, but one who consorts with gluttons brings shame upon his father.
Whoever augments his wealth through usury and interest ultimately accumulates it for one who will be gracious to the poor.
Whoever refuses to heed the law renders even his prayer an abomination.
Whoever seduces the upright into an evil course plummets into his own pit, while the blameless inherit prosperity.
A wealthy man is wise in his own estimation, but a discerning poor man penetrates his pretensions.
When the righteous flourish, great glory abounds; but when the wicked ascend, people conceal themselves.
Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but whoever confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy.
Blessed is the one who continually reveres the LORD, but whoever is obdurately unyielding falls into calamity.
A wicked ruler over a destitute people is like a roaring lion or a charging bear.
A ruler devoid of discernment is a grievous oppressor, but one who abhors illicit gain prolongs his days.
A man laden with bloodguilt will flee until death; let no one sustain him.
Whoever walks in integrity will be delivered, but whoever is crooked in his ways will fall suddenly.
Whoever cultivates his land will have abundant food, but whoever pursues vain fantasies will be sated with poverty.
A faithful man will abound in blessings, but one who hastens to be rich will not be held guiltless.
To show partiality is not good, yet for a trivial inducement a man will transgress.
A stingy man hastens after wealth and remains oblivious to the poverty that will overtake him.
Whoever rebukes a man will afterward find greater favor than one who flatters with his tongue.
Whoever robs his father or mother and declares, “It is no transgression,” is a companion to a destroyer.
A greedy man stirs up strife, but whoever trusts in the LORD will flourish.
Whoever trusts in his own heart is a fool, but whoever walks in wisdom will be delivered.
Whoever gives to the poor will lack nothing, but whoever willfully ignores them will be laden with curses.
When the wicked rise, people hide themselves; but when they perish, the righteous increase.
A stiff-necked man, after repeated reproofs, is suddenly shattered, and no remedy avails.
When the righteous increase, the people rejoice; but when the wicked rule, the people groan.
He who loves wisdom gladdens his father, whereas one who consorts with prostitutes squanders his substance.
Through justice a king establishes the land, but a man given to exactions brings it to ruin.
He who flatters his neighbor spreads a snare beneath his steps.
An evil man is caught in his own transgression, while the righteous exults and rejoices.
The righteous discerns the cause of the poor, but the wicked is devoid of such understanding.
Scoffers set a city ablaze, but the wise allay wrath.
When a wise man contends with a fool, the fool only rages and scoffs, and there is no respite.
Bloodthirsty men hate the blameless, but the upright concern themselves with his life.
A fool gives vent to all his spirit, but a wise man restrains it.
If a ruler hearkens to falsehood, all his servants become wicked.
The poor and the oppressor meet together: The LORD gives light to the eyes of both.
A king who judges the poor with truth will have his throne established forever.
The rod and reproof impart wisdom, but a child left to himself shames his mother.
When the wicked multiply, transgression increases, but the righteous will witness their downfall.
Discipline your son, and he will give you rest; he will bring delights to your soul.
Where there is no vision, the people cast off restraint, but blessed is he who keeps the law.
A servant is not disciplined by words alone; though he understands, he will not answer.
Do you see a man hasty in his words? There is more hope for a fool than for him.
A servant pampered from youth will, in the end, prove a grief.
An angry man stirs up strife, and a hot-tempered man abounds in transgression.
A man's pride brings him low, but a humble spirit upholds honor.
He who shares with a thief hates his own soul; though he hears the curse, he does not tell.
The fear of man lays a snare, but he who trusts in the LORD is set securely on high.
Many seek the favor of a ruler, but a man's justice comes from the LORD.
An unjust man is an abomination to the righteous, and he whose way is upright is an abomination to the wicked.
The words of Agur son of Jakeh constitute the oracle; the man declares unto Ithiel, unto Ithiel and Ucal.
I am indeed more brutish than any man, and I lack the discernment proper to humankind.
I have not learned wisdom, nor do I possess knowledge of the Holy One.

Who has ascended to heaven and descended? Who has gathered the wind in His fists? Who has bound the waters in a garment? Who has established all the ends of the earth? What is His name, and what is the name of His son? Surely you know!
Every utterance of God is flawless; He is a shield to those who take refuge in Him.
Do not append anything to His words, lest He reprove you and you be exposed as a liar.
Two things I ask of You; do not refuse me before I die:
keep falsehood and deceitful words far from me; grant me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the bread of my allotted portion.
Lest I become sated and deny You, saying, “Who is the LORD?” or lest I become impoverished and steal, thereby profaning the name of my God.
Do not slander a servant to his master, lest he curse you, and you be found guilty.
There exists a generation that curses its father and withholds blessing from its mother.
There is a generation pure in its own eyes, yet unwashed of its filth.
There is a generation—how haughty are its eyes, and how pretentious its glances!
There is a generation whose teeth are swords and whose molars are knives, to devour the afflicted from the earth and the destitute from among humankind.
The leech has two daughters—“Give, give!” There are three things never satisfied, four that never say, “Enough!”
Sheol, the barren womb, land that is never satisfied with water, and fire that never says, “Enough!”
The eye that mocks a father and scorns obedience to a mother will be pecked out by the ravens of the valley and consumed by the vultures.
There are three things too wonderful for me, four that I cannot comprehend:
the way of an eagle through the sky, the way of a serpent upon a rock, the way of a ship upon the heart of the sea, and the way of a man with a maiden.
Such is the way of an adulteress: she eats, wipes her mouth, and says, “I have done no wrong.”
Under three things the earth trembles, under four it cannot bear up:
a servant who becomes king, a fool glutted with food,
an unloved woman when she marries, and a maidservant who supplants her mistress.
Four things on earth are small, yet they are exceedingly wise:
the ants are a people without strength, yet they store up their food in the summer;
the rock badgers are a people without power, yet they make their home in the cliffs;
the locusts have no king, yet they all advance in formation;
the lizard can be caught in the hand, yet it is found in kings’ palaces.
There are three things majestic in their stride, four that are majestic in their walk:
the lion, mightiest of beasts, who does not retreat before anything;
the strutting rooster; the he-goat; and a king secure against insurrection.
If you have foolishly exalted yourself, or if you have plotted evil, put your hand over your mouth.
For as the churning of milk yields butter, and the twisting of the nose draws blood, so the stirring of anger brings forth strife.
The words of King Lemuel—an oracle his mother inculcated in him.
What, my son? What, the child I bore? What, the son I consecrated by vows?
Do not give your strength to women, nor your ways to those who destroy kings.
It is not for kings, O Lemuel—it is not for kings to drink wine, or for rulers to drink strong drink,
lest they drink and forget the law, and pervert the justice of all the afflicted.
Give strong drink to the perishing, and wine to those in bitter distress.
Let them drink and forget their poverty, and remember their misery no more.
Open your mouth for the mute, for the rights of all who are dispossessed.
Open your mouth, judge righteously, and defend the rights of the poor and needy.
An excellent wife—who can find her? She is far more precious than jewels.
The heart of her husband trusts in her, and he will lack no gain.
She does him good, and not harm, all the days of her life.
She seeks wool and flax, and works with willing hands.
She is like the ships of the merchant; she brings her food from afar.
She rises while it is still night and provides food for her household, and portions for her maidens.
She considers a field and buys it; with the fruit of her hands she plants a vineyard.
She girds herself with strength and strengthens her arms.
She perceives that her merchandise is profitable; her lamp is not extinguished at night.
She puts her hands to the distaff, and her hands hold the spindle.
She opens her hand to the poor and reaches out her hands to the needy.
She is not afraid of snow for her household, for all her household are clothed in scarlet.
She makes bed coverings for herself; her clothing is fine linen and purple.
Her husband is known in the gates, when he sits among the elders of the land.
She makes linen garments and sells them; she delivers sashes to the merchant.
Strength and dignity are her clothing, and she laughs at the days to come.
She opens her mouth with wisdom, and the teaching of kindness is on her tongue.
She looks well to the ways of her household, and does not eat the bread of idleness.
Her children rise up and call her blessed; her husband also praises her.
Many women have done excellently, but you surpass them all.
Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain, but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised.
Give her the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her in the gates.
These are the words of the Teacher, son of David, king in Jerusalem.
“Supreme futility,” says the Teacher, “supreme futility! All is futile.”
What gain does a person derive from all his labor, the toil with which he toils in this earthly life?
A generation departs and a generation arrives, but the earth endures forever.
The sun rises and the sun sets; then, hastening back to the place from which it rises, it rises there again.
The wind proceeds southward and veers northward; circling round and round, it returns upon its circuits.
All rivers run to the sea, yet the sea is not full; to the place where the rivers flow, thither they return to flow again.
All things are wearisome—more wearisome than one can utter. The eye is never satiated with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing.
What has been is what will be, and what has been done is what will be done; there is nothing new in this world.
If there exists anything concerning which one may say, “Behold, this is new,” it has already existed in the ages before us.
There is no remembrance of former things, and even the things that are yet to come will not be remembered by those who follow.
I, the Teacher, was king over Israel in Jerusalem.
I devoted my heart to seek and to search out by wisdom all that is done on earth. It is a grievous business that God has imposed upon the children of Adam, that they may be busied with it.
I have observed all the deeds done on earth, and indeed, all is futility and a fruitless pursuit.
What is crooked cannot be straightened, and what is lacking cannot be reckoned.
I said to myself, “Behold, I have grown great and increased in wisdom beyond all who were before me in Jerusalem, and my mind has observed much wisdom and knowledge.”
I devoted my mind to knowing wisdom, and to knowing madness and folly; I perceived that this too is a fruitless pursuit.
For in much wisdom is much vexation, and he who increases knowledge increases sorrow.
I said in my heart, “Come now, I will test you with mirth, and see what constitutes the good.”
I said of laughter, “It is madness!” and of mirth, “What does it accomplish?”

I searched my heart, purposing to draw my flesh with wine while my heart still guided me with wisdom, and to lay hold on folly, until I might discern what is good for the children of humanity to do in this world during the count of the days of their lives.
I enlarged my works: I built houses for myself, and I planted vineyards for myself.
I made gardens and orchards for myself, and in them I planted every species of fruit tree.
I made pools of water for myself, to irrigate from them a forest of growing trees.
I acquired male and female servants, and I had servants born in my house; I also possessed great herds of cattle and flocks, more than all who had been before me in Jerusalem.
I also amassed silver and gold, together with the treasure of kings and provinces; I procured male and female singers, and the delights of the sons of men—concubines in abundance.
Thus I became greater and increased beyond all who were before me in Jerusalem, and my wisdom also remained with me.
Whatever my eyes desired I did not deny them; I did not withhold my heart from any joy, for my heart rejoiced in all my labor, and this was my portion from all my labor.
Then I turned to consider all the works my hands had accomplished and the toil I had expended to accomplish them, and behold, all was vanity and an exercise in futility; there was no profit on earth.
Then I turned to examine wisdom, madness, and folly; for what can the man who succeeds the king accomplish, save what has already been accomplished?
I perceived that wisdom has an advantage over folly, as light has an advantage over darkness.
The wise man has his eyes in his head, but the fool walks in darkness; yet I also knew that one fate befalls them all.
Then I said in my heart, “As the fate of the fool befalls me also, why then have I been so surpassingly wise?” And I spoke in my heart that this too is vanity.
For there is no enduring remembrance of the wise any more than of the fool, since in the days to come all will have been forgotten. How then does the wise man die?—along with the fool.
So I hated life, because the work done on earth was grievous to me; for all is vanity and an exercise in futility.
I hated all my toil in which I had toiled on earth, because I must leave it to the man who comes after me.
And who knows whether he will be wise or a fool? Yet he will have dominion over all my toil in which I toiled and in which I was wise on earth. This too is vanity.
Therefore I turned to cause my heart to despair of all the toil in which I had toiled on earth.
For there is a man whose toil is in wisdom, knowledge, and skill, yet he must give his portion to a man who has not toiled in it. This too is vanity and a great evil.
For what has a man from all his toil and from the striving of his heart with which he toils on earth?
For all his days are pains, and his occupation is vexation; even at night his heart does not rest. This too is vanity.
There is nothing better for a man than to eat and drink and to let his soul take pleasure in his toil. I also perceived that this is from the hand of God.
For who can eat and who can enjoy apart from Him?

For to the man who is good in His sight He gives wisdom, knowledge, and joy; but to the sinner He gives the task of gathering and collecting, to give to the one who is good in the sight of God. This too is vanity and an exercise in futility.
For everything there exists a designated season, and beneath the heavens an appointed hour attends every purpose.
There is a time to be born and a time to die, a time to plant and a time to uproot what has been planted;
a time to kill and a time to heal, a time to tear down and a time to build;
a time to weep and a time to laugh, a time to mourn and a time to dance;
a time to cast stones away and a time to gather stones, a time to embrace and a time to refrain from embracing;
a time to seek and a time to forfeit, a time to retain and a time to relinquish;
a time to tear and a time to mend, a time to keep silence and a time to speak;
a time to love and a time to hate, a time for war and a time for peace.
What substantive benefit, then, accrues to the laborer from his incessant toil?
I have discerned the grievous occupation that God has imposed upon humanity, whereby they might be preoccupied with toil.

He has rendered every undertaking fitting in its appointed moment; moreover, He has implanted an intimation of eternity within their consciousness, although no human being can fully apprehend the totality of God’s work from inception to consummation.
I have concluded that there is no superior good for them than to rejoice and to perform virtuous deeds throughout the span of their lives.
Furthermore, that every person should eat and drink, and discern felicity in the fruit of all his labor, constitutes a divine endowment.

I am persuaded that whatever God accomplishes possesses eternal permanence; nothing may be augmented thereto, nor anything excised therefrom; and God ordains it thus in order that humanity might revere Him.
That which is has already been, and that which is to be has already occurred; and God retrieves what has gone by.
Furthermore, I observed beneath the sun that in the very seat of justice, iniquity presided, and in the locus of righteousness, wickedness likewise held sway.
I reasoned within my heart that God will adjudicate between the righteous and the wicked, because an appointed season exists for every purpose and for every deed.
I further reflected in my heart regarding the lot of humanity, namely that God puts them to the test so that they might recognize themselves to be, in their mortal condition, akin to beasts.

For the destiny that befalls humanity and the destiny that befalls the beasts is identical: as the one perishes, so perishes the other, and both share one breath; consequently, humanity possesses no enduring preeminence over the beasts, for all is vanity.
All proceed to a single destination; all derive from dust, and all revert to dust.
Who can ascertain whether the spirit of man ascends on high while the spirit of the beast descends into the earth?

Therefore, I perceived that there is nothing superior to a person’s rejoicing in his own labor, for that constitutes his allotted portion; for who shall enable him to behold what shall transpire after him?

I turned again and beheld all the oppression wrought on earth: I saw the tears of the oppressed, and they had no comforter; power resided with their oppressors, and for them likewise there was no comforter.
Then I extolled the dead, who had already died, above the living, who yet remain alive;
and I judged that better than both is the one who has not yet come into being, who has not witnessed the evil deed accomplished on earth.
I also observed all toil and every skillful achievement, and perceived that it arises from one person's envy of another. This too is meaningless and futile.
The fool, folding his hands in idleness, devours his own substance.
Yet better is a single handful accompanied by tranquility than two full hands of toil and futility.
Again I turned and beheld meaninglessness on earth:

there is one who is alone, having neither companion nor brother; there is no end to all his toil, and his eyes are not sated with riches. "For whom, then," he asks, "do I toil, while depriving myself of good?" This too is meaningless, and it is an evil business.
Two are better than one, because they receive a good reward for their toil.
For if one falls, his companion will raise him up; but woe to the solitary one who falls and has no second to lift him up.
Likewise, if two lie together, they are warmed; but how can one be warmed alone?
And though one may be overpowered, two can stand against him; a threefold cord is not quickly severed.
Better is a poor yet wise youth than an old and foolish king who no longer knows how to receive admonition.
For the youth came forth from prison to reign, though he was born poor in his own kingdom.
I saw all the living who walk on earth, together with the second youth who is to stand in his place.
There is no end to all the people, to all who preceded them; yet those who come after will not rejoice in him. This too is meaningless and futile.
Exercise circumspection in your gait when repairing to the house of God; draw near to hearken rather than to tender the sacrifice of fools, for they know not that they are perpetrating evil.
Do not precipitate your utterance, and let not your heart hasten to bring forth a word before God, for God is in heaven while you are upon the earth; therefore let your words be few.
For dreams arise from abundant preoccupations, and the voice of a fool from a multitude of words.
When you vow a vow to God, do not defer its fulfillment, for He takes no delight in fools; render what you have vowed.
It is better not to vow at all than to vow and then fail to discharge it.
Do not let your mouth cause your flesh to sin, and do not say before the messenger that it was an error; why should God be incensed by your voice and ruin the work of your hands?
For amid many dreams and much futility there are many words; rather, fear God.

If you behold oppression of the poor and the perversion of justice and righteousness in a province, do not be astonished at the matter, for a high official is watched by a higher one, and still higher ones are over them.
Moreover, the profit of the land is for all; even the king is served by the field.
One who loves silver is never satiated with silver, and whoever loves wealth is never satisfied with its income; this too is futility.
As goods multiply, their consumers multiply; and what advantage has their owner but the sight of them with his eyes?
The sleep of a laborer is sweet, whether he eats little or much; but the satiety of the rich denies him sleep.
I have observed a grievous evil in this world: wealth hoarded by its owner to his own detriment.
That wealth is lost in a disastrous enterprise, and he begets a son, yet nothing remains in his hand.
Just as he emerged naked from his mother's womb, so he returns; he takes nothing from his toil that he can carry away in his hand.
This too is a grievous evil: just as he came, so he departs; and what does he gain from laboring to no avail?
