But, brothers, choose from among yourselves seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and wisdom, whom we may appoint to this duty.
But we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word.”

The proposal found favor with the whole assembly, and they selected Stephen, a man full of faith and the Holy Spirit, together with Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolaus, a proselyte from Antioch.
These men were presented to the apostles, who, after praying, laid their hands upon them.
And the word of God continued to increase, and the number of disciples in Jerusalem multiplied greatly; indeed, a large number of priests became obedient to the faith.
Stephen, full of grace and power, performed great wonders and signs among the people.
Then certain men from the synagogue known as that of the Freedmen, along with Cyrenians, Alexandrians, and others from Cilicia and Asia, rose up and disputed with Stephen.
Yet they were unable to withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he spoke.
Then they secretly instigated men to say, “We have heard him utter blasphemous words against Moses and God.”
And they stirred up the people, the elders, and the scribes; coming upon him, they seized him and brought him before the Sanhedrin.
Moreover, they set up false witnesses, who said, “This man never ceases to speak words against this holy place and the law;
for we have heard him say that this Jesus the Nazarene will destroy this place and change the customs that Moses handed down to us.”
All those seated in the Sanhedrin, fixing their gaze upon him, saw his face as the face of an angel.
The high priest asked, "Are these things so?"

The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham while he was still in Mesopotamia, before he settled in Haran, and He said to him, 'Depart from your country and your kindred, and come to the land that I will show you.'
So he departed from the land of the Chaldeans and dwelt in Haran; and after his father died, God removed him from there into this land in which you now dwell.
Yet He gave him no inheritance in it, not even a foot's breadth; but He promised to give it to him as a possession, and to his offspring after him, although at that time he had no child.
And God spoke thus: that his offspring would be sojourners in a foreign land, and that they would be enslaved and afflicted for four hundred years.
'But I will judge the nation that they serve,' God said, 'and afterward they shall come forth and worship Me in this place.'
And He gave him the covenant of circumcision; and so Abraham begot Isaac and circumcised him on the eighth day; and Isaac begot Jacob, and Jacob the twelve patriarchs."
"The patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt; but God was with him
and rescued him from all his afflictions, and gave him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh, king of Egypt, who appointed him ruler over Egypt and over his whole household.
Then a famine and a great distress came upon all Egypt and Canaan, and our fathers could find no sustenance.
But when Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent our fathers there first.
On their second visit Joseph made himself known to his brothers, and Pharaoh learned of Joseph's family.
Then Joseph sent and summoned his father Jacob and all his relatives, seventy-five persons in all.
So Jacob went down into Egypt; and he and our fathers died there,
and they were carried over to Shechem and laid in the tomb that Abraham had bought from the sons of Hamor in Shechem for a price in silver."
"But as the time of the promise that God had sworn to Abraham drew near, the people increased and multiplied in Egypt,
until there arose over Egypt another king who did not know Joseph.
He dealt shrewdly with our race and oppressed our fathers, forcing them to expose their infants so that they would not survive.
At that time Moses was born, and he was beautiful in God's sight. For three months he was nurtured in his father's house.
But when he was exposed, Pharaoh's daughter took him up and reared him as her own son.
So Moses was educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and he was mighty in words and deeds.
When he was forty years old, it came into his heart to visit his brothers, the sons of Israel.
And seeing one of them being wronged, he defended him and avenged him by striking the Egyptian.
He supposed that his brothers would understand that God was granting them deliverance by his hand, but they did not understand.
And on the following day he appeared to them as they were quarreling, and he urged them to be at peace, saying, 'Men, you are brothers; why do you wrong one another?'
But the one who was wronging his neighbor pushed him away, saying, 'Who made you a ruler and judge over us?
Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?'
At this word Moses fled and became an exile in the land of Midian, where he fathered two sons.
Now when forty years had passed, an angel appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in a flame of fire in a bush.
When Moses saw it, he marveled at the sight; and as he drew near to inspect it, the voice of the Lord came to him:
'I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham and of Isaac and of Jacob.' And Moses trembled and did not dare to look.
Then the Lord said to him, 'Remove the sandals from your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground.
I have surely seen the affliction of My people in Egypt, and I have heard their groaning, and I have come down to deliver them. And now come, I will send you to Egypt.'
This Moses, whom they rejected, saying, 'Who made you a ruler and judge?'—this is the one whom God sent as both ruler and redeemer, by the hand of the angel who appeared to him in the bush.
This man led them out, performing wonders and signs in the land of Egypt, and in the Red Sea, and in the wilderness for forty years.
This is the Moses who said to the sons of Israel, 'God will raise up for you a Prophet like me from among your brothers.'
This is the one who was in the congregation in the wilderness with the angel who spoke to him on Mount Sinai, and with our fathers, who received living oracles to give to us.
Our fathers were unwilling to be obedient to him; instead, they thrust him aside, and in their hearts they turned back to Egypt,
saying to Aaron, 'Make for us gods who will go before us; as for this Moses who led us out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him.'
And in those days they made a calf and offered a sacrifice to the idol and rejoiced in the works of their hands.

But God turned away and gave them over to serve the host of heaven, as it is written in the book of the prophets: 'Did you offer to Me slain victims and sacrifices for forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel?
You took up the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Rephan, the images that you made to worship; and I will remove you beyond Babylon.'"
"Our fathers had the tent of testimony in the wilderness, just as He who spoke to Moses directed him to make it according to the pattern that he had seen.
Our fathers in turn brought it in with Joshua when they took possession of the nations that God drove out before our fathers, until the days of David,
who found favor with God and asked to find a dwelling place for the God of Jacob.
But Solomon built a house for Him.
Yet the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands, as the prophet says:
'Heaven is My throne, and the earth is My footstool. What kind of house will you build for Me? says the Lord. Or what is the place of My rest?
Did not My hand make all these things?'"
"You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit; as your fathers did, so do you.
Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? They killed those who announced beforehand the coming of the Righteous One, and now you have become His betrayers and murderers,
you who received the law as delivered by angels and did not keep it."
When they heard these things, they were enraged in their hearts and gnashed their teeth at him.
But he, being full of the Holy Spirit, gazed into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God.
And he said, "Behold, I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God."
But they cried out with a loud voice and stopped their ears and rushed together at him.
Then they cast him out of the city and stoned him; and the witnesses laid down their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul.
And as they were stoning Stephen, he called out, "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit."
And falling to his knees, he cried out with a loud voice, "Lord, do not hold this sin against them." And when he had said this, he fell asleep.

Now Saul was consenting to Stephen’s execution, and on that very day a severe persecution erupted against the church in Jerusalem; consequently, everyone except the apostles was dispersed throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria.
Devout men, however, carried Stephen to his burial and made an elaborate lamentation over him.
Saul, for his part, was ravaging the church: he would enter houses, drag away both men and women, and consign them to prison.
Those who had been scattered, therefore, went from place to place proclaiming the word.
Philip descended to the city of Samaria and began proclaiming the Christ to them.
The crowds, with one accord, gave heed to what Philip was saying, for they heard him and witnessed the signs he performed.
For unclean spirits, crying out with a loud voice, came out of many who were possessed; and many who were paralyzed or lame were healed.
So there was great joy in that city.
Now there was a man named Simon who had previously been practicing magic in the city and astonishing the nation of Samaria, claiming himself to be someone great.
Everyone, from the least to the greatest, paid attention to him, saying, “This man is the Power of God that is called the Great.”
They paid heed to him because for a long time he had astounded them with his magical arts.
But when they believed Philip as he proclaimed the good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, both men and women were baptized.
Simon himself also believed, and after being baptized he was continually attending upon Philip; and as he beheld the great signs and mighty works being performed, he was utterly astounded.
When the apostles in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them.
These, having come down, prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit,
for as yet He had not fallen upon any of them; they had merely been baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus.
Then they laid their hands upon them, and they received the Holy Spirit.
Now when Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, he offered them money,
saying, “Give me this authority as well, so that on whomever I lay my hands he may receive the Holy Spirit.”
But Peter said to him, “May your silver perish along with you, because you thought you could acquire the gift of God with money!
You have neither part nor lot in this matter, for your heart is not right before God.
Repent, therefore, of this wickedness of yours, and pray to the Lord, if perhaps the intent of your heart may be forgiven you.
For I see that you are steeped in bitter gall and bound fast by iniquity.”
Simon answered and said, “You pray to the Lord for me, so that none of the things you have spoken may come upon me.”
So, after testifying and speaking the word of the Lord, they returned to Jerusalem, proclaiming the gospel to many villages of the Samaritans.
Now an angel of the Lord spoke to Philip, saying, “Arise and go southward along the road that descends from Jerusalem to Gaza; it is a desert road.”
So he arose and went, and there was an Ethiopian eunuch, a court official of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was in charge of all her treasure, and he had come to Jerusalem to worship.
He was returning, and sitting in his chariot he was reading the prophet Isaiah.
Then the Spirit said to Philip, “Approach this chariot and join yourself to it.”
Philip ran up and heard him reading the prophet Isaiah, and said, “Do you understand what you are reading?”
He replied, “How could I, unless someone guides me?” And he invited Philip to come up and sit with him.
The passage of Scripture he was reading was this: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he does not open his mouth.
In his humiliation his justice was taken away; who will declare his generation? For his life is taken away from the earth.”
The eunuch answered Philip and said, “I implore you, of whom does the prophet speak this—of himself or of someone else?”
Then Philip opened his mouth, and beginning from this Scripture he proclaimed Jesus to him.
As they were traveling along the road, they came to some water, and the eunuch said, “Look—water! What prevents me from being baptized?”
And he commanded the chariot to stop, and both Philip and the eunuch went down into the water, and he baptized him.
When they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord snatched Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no longer, for he went on his way rejoicing.
But Philip found himself at Azotus, and as he passed through he proclaimed the gospel to all the cities until he came to Caesarea.
Meanwhile, Saul, still exhaling murderous threats against the Lord’s disciples, went to the high priest
and solicited from him letters to the synagogues in Damascus, so that, should he discover any adherents of the Way—whether men or women—he might convey them, bound, to Jerusalem.
As he neared Damascus on his journey, a light from heaven suddenly flashed around him;
and, having fallen to the ground, he heard a voice saying to him, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me?”
“Who are You, Lord?” Saul queried. “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.
Nevertheless, arise and enter the city, and you shall be apprised of what you must do.”
The men traveling with him stood speechless, hearing the voice yet seeing no one.
Saul rose from the ground, but though his eyes were open, he saw nothing; so they led him by the hand into Damascus.
For three days he was blind, and neither ate nor drank.
In Damascus there was a disciple named Ananias, and the Lord said to him in a vision, “Ananias!” “Here I am, Lord,” he answered.
The Lord said to him, “Rise and go to the house of Judas on Straight Street, and inquire for a man of Tarsus named Saul; for behold, he is praying.
In a vision he has seen a man named Ananias entering and laying hands on him so that he might regain his sight.”
Ananias answered, “Lord, I have heard from many concerning this man, how much evil he has wrought upon Your saints in Jerusalem.
And here he possesses authority from the chief priests to bind all who call upon Your name.”
But the Lord said to him, “Go, for this man is a chosen vessel of Mine to bear My name before the Gentiles, their kings, and the sons of Israel.
For I will show him how great things he must suffer for My name’s sake.”

So Ananias departed and entered the house; and, laying his hands on him, he said, “Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus, who appeared to you on the road by which you came, has sent me that you may regain your sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit.”
And immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he regained his sight; and, rising, he was baptized.
Then, having taken food, he was strengthened. For some days he was with the disciples in Damascus.
He immediately proclaimed Jesus in the synagogues, declaring that He is the Son of God.
All who heard were amazed and said, “Is not this the man who made havoc in Jerusalem of those who call upon this name, and has he not come here to bring them bound before the chief priests?”
But Saul increased in strength and confounded the Jews dwelling in Damascus, demonstrating that this Jesus is the Christ.
After many days, the Jews conspired to kill him;
but their plot became known to Saul. They watched the gates day and night to kill him;
but his disciples took him by night and let him down through the wall in a basket.
When he had come to Jerusalem, he attempted to join the disciples, but they all feared him, not believing that he was a disciple.
But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles, and recounted how he had seen the Lord on the road and that He had spoken to him, and how he had spoken boldly at Damascus in the name of Jesus.
So he was with them, coming in and going out at Jerusalem, speaking boldly in the name of the Lord.
He spoke and disputed against the Hellenists, but they were seeking to kill him.
When the brothers learned of it, they brought him down to Caesarea and sent him away to Tarsus.
So the church throughout all Judea, Galilee, and Samaria had peace and was edified; and, walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit, it was multiplied.
Now it came to pass that Peter, passing through all parts, descended also to the saints dwelling at Lydda.
There he found a certain man named Aeneas, who had been bedridden for eight years, being paralyzed.
Peter said to him, “Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you; arise and roll up your mat.” And immediately he arose.
All who dwelt at Lydda and Sharon saw him, and they turned to the Lord.
Now in Joppa there was a certain disciple named Tabitha, which, being interpreted, is Dorcas; she was full of good works and acts of charity.
In those days she became sick and died; and, having washed her, they laid her in an upper room.
Since Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men to him, entreating him, “Do not delay to come to us.”

Then Peter arose and went with them; and when he had come, they brought him into the upper room. All the widows stood by him, weeping and showing the tunics and garments which Dorcas made while she was with them.
Peter put them all outside, and, kneeling down, he prayed; and, turning to the body, he said, “Tabitha, arise.” And she opened her eyes, and seeing Peter she sat up.
He gave her his hand and raised her up; and, calling the saints and widows, he presented her alive.
It became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord.
He stayed many days in Joppa with Simon, a tanner.
In Caesarea there dwelt a certain man named Cornelius, a centurion of the cohort styled Italian,
together with his entire household: a devout and God-fearing man, who wrought many alms among the people and petitioned God continually.
About the ninth hour of the day he beheld plainly, in a vision, an angel of God entering unto him and saying, “Cornelius.”
And he, having fixed his gaze upon him and being seized with fear, said, “What is it, Lord?” And he said to him, “Your prayers and your alms have ascended as a memorial before God.
And now send men to Joppa and summon a certain Simon who is called Peter.
This man is lodging with a certain Simon, a tanner, whose house is by the sea.”
And when the angel who had been speaking to him had departed, he called two of his servants and a devout soldier from among those who attended him,
and, having rehearsed all these things to them, dispatched them to Joppa.
The next day, as they were drawing near to the city while on their journey, Peter went up onto the housetop about the sixth hour to pray.
And he became hungry and desired to eat; but while they were preparing it, a trance fell upon him.
And he beholds heaven opened and a certain vessel descending, like a great sheet let down to the earth by four corners.
In it were all kinds of four-footed beasts, creeping things of the earth, and birds of heaven.
And a voice came to him: “Rise, Peter; kill and eat.”
But Peter said, “By no means, Lord; for I have never eaten anything common or unclean.”
And a voice came to him again a second time: “What God has cleansed, you must not treat as common.”
And this occurred thrice; and straightway the vessel was taken up into heaven.
Now while Peter was inwardly perplexed as to what the vision he had seen might signify, behold, the men sent by Cornelius, having inquired for Simon’s house, stood at the gate.
And, calling out, they asked whether Simon who is called Peter was lodging there.
And while Peter was musing upon the vision, the Spirit said to him, “Behold, three men seek you.
But arise, go down, and journey with them, doubting nothing, for I have sent them.”
And Peter, having gone down to the men, said, “Behold, I am the one you seek. What is the cause for which you are here?”

And they said, “Cornelius, a centurion—a righteous and God-fearing man, well testified to by the whole nation of the Jews—was divinely instructed by a holy angel to summon you to his house and to hear words from you.”
So, having invited them in, he lodged them. And on the morrow Peter arose and went forth with them, and certain of the brethren from Joppa accompanied him.
And on the following day he entered Caesarea. Now Cornelius was expecting them, having called together his kinsmen and intimate friends.
And as Peter was about to enter, Cornelius met him and fell at his feet and worshiped.
But Peter raised him, saying, “Rise; I myself also am a man.”
And conversing with him, he entered and found many assembled.
And he said to them, “You know how unlawful it is for a Jewish man to associate with or approach one of another nation; yet God has shown me that I should call no man common or unclean.
Wherefore, having been summoned, I came without gainsaying. I ask, therefore, for what reason you summoned me.”
And Cornelius said, “Four days ago, up to this very hour, I was in my house praying at the ninth hour, and, behold, a man stood before me in dazzling raiment, and said,
“‘Cornelius, your prayer has been heard and your alms remembered before God.
Send therefore to Joppa and summon Simon who is called Peter; this man lodges in the house of Simon the tanner by the sea.’
“So I sent to you at once, and you did well to come. Now, therefore, we are all present before God to hear all things that have been commanded you by the Lord.”
And Peter, opening his mouth, said, “In truth I now perceive that God shows no partiality.
But in every nation he who fears Him and works righteousness is acceptable to Him.
He sent the word to the sons of Israel, preaching peace through Jesus Christ—He is Lord of all.
“You know the word that went forth throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee after the baptism that John proclaimed,
how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power, who went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with Him.
And we are witnesses of all that He did both in the country of the Jews and in Jerusalem, whom they killed by hanging Him on a cross.
God raised Him up on the third day and granted that He should be made manifest,
“not to all the people, but to witnesses chosen beforehand by God—to us, who ate and drank with Him after He rose from the dead.
And He commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that He is the One ordained by God to be Judge of the living and the dead.
To Him all the prophets bear witness, that every one who believes in Him receives forgiveness of sins through His name.”
While Peter was yet speaking these words, the Holy Spirit fell upon all those who heard the word.
And the believers of the circumcision who had come with Peter were amazed, because the gift of the Holy Spirit had been poured out even upon the Gentiles.
For they heard them speaking in tongues and magnifying God. Then Peter answered,
“Can any man forbid water, that these should not be baptized, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have?”
And he commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to tarry certain days.
Now the apostles and the brothers dispersed throughout Judea heard that the Gentiles, too, had received the word of God.
When Peter ascended to Jerusalem, those of the circumcision contended with him,
saying, "You went in to men possessing uncircumcision and ate with them."
But Peter commenced and expounded the matter to them in orderly sequence, saying,

"I was in the city of Joppa, engaged in prayer, when, in an ecstasy, I beheld a vision: a certain vessel, resembling a great sheet, descending as though let down from heaven by four corners, and it came even to me.
Fixing my gaze upon it, I observed and discerned the four-footed creatures of the earth, the wild beasts, the creeping things, and the birds of the sky.
Then I heard a voice saying to me, 'Rise, Peter; slaughter and eat.'"
"But I replied, 'By no means, Lord; for nothing common or unclean has ever entered my mouth.'
Yet the voice answered from heaven a second time, 'What God has cleansed, you must not deem common.'
This occurred thrice, and then all was drawn back up into heaven."
"And behold, at that very moment, three men who had been dispatched to me from Caesarea stood at the house where we lodged.
The Spirit instructed me to accompany them without discrimination; moreover, these six brothers went with me, and we entered the man's house."
"He recounted to us how he had seen an angel standing in his house and saying, 'Send to Joppa and summon Simon, who is called Peter,
who will speak words to you by which you and all your household will be saved.'"
"And as I began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell upon them, even as it had upon us at the beginning.
Then I remembered the word of the Lord, how He said, 'John indeed baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.'"
"If, then, God bestowed upon them the identical gift that He also bestowed upon us who believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I to be able to hinder God?"
When they heard these things, they fell silent and glorified God, saying, "Then to the Gentiles also God has granted repentance unto life."
Now those who had been scattered by the tribulation that arose over Stephen passed through as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch, speaking the word to no one except Jews alone.
But some of them, men of Cyprus and Cyrene, upon coming to Antioch, spoke to the Hellenists, proclaiming the Lord Jesus.
And the hand of the Lord was with them, so that a great number believed and turned to the Lord.
The report concerning them reached the ears of the church in Jerusalem, and they dispatched Barnabas as far as Antioch.
When he arrived and perceived the grace of God, he rejoiced and exhorted them all to remain with the Lord with resolute purpose of heart.
For he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and faith, and a considerable crowd was added to the Lord.
He then departed for Tarsus to seek Saul,

and having found him, he brought him to Antioch. It came to pass that for a whole year they assembled with the church and instructed a substantial multitude; and it was in Antioch that the disciples were first called Christians.
In those days prophets descended from Jerusalem to Antioch.
One of them, named Agabus, stood up and signified through the Spirit that a great famine was about to come upon the whole inhabited world—which indeed came to pass in the days of Claudius.
So the disciples determined, each according to his means, to send relief to the brothers dwelling in Judea.
This they also did, sending it to the elders by the hand of Barnabas and Saul.
About that time, King Herod laid violent hands upon certain members of the church, meaning to afflict them;
and he put James, the brother of John, to the sword.
Perceiving that this gratified the Jews, he proceeded likewise to seize Peter—this during the days of Unleavened Bread.
Having arrested him, he consigned him to prison, committing him to four squads of soldiers for safekeeping, intending to bring him before the people after Passover.
Thus Peter was kept in custody, while the church unceasingly and earnestly interceded with God on his behalf.
On that very night, when Herod was about to produce him, Peter slept between two soldiers, bound with two chains, while sentinels guarded the prison before the door.
And behold, an angel of the Lord stood by, and a light illumined the cell; striking Peter’s side, he roused him, saying, “Arise quickly!” and the chains fell from his hands.
The angel said to him, “Gird yourself and bind on your sandals.” Peter did so. Then he said to him, “Wrap your cloak about you and follow me.”
Peter followed and went out, not knowing that what was being accomplished through the angel was real; he supposed he was beholding a vision.

Passing the first and second guard, they came to the iron gate leading into the city, which opened to them of its own accord; and going out, they advanced one street, whereupon the angel immediately departed from him.
When Peter recovered himself, he said, “Now I know truly that the Lord has sent His angel and rescued me from the hand of Herod and from all that the Jewish people expected.”
Having considered the matter, he went to the house of Mary, the mother of John who was called Mark, where many were gathered and praying.
When he knocked at the door of the gateway, a servant girl named Rhoda came to answer.
Recognizing Peter’s voice, she, in her joy, did not open the gate, but ran in and announced that Peter was standing before the gateway.
They said to her, “You are out of your mind.” But she vehemently affirmed that it was so, and they said, “It is his angel.”
Meanwhile Peter persisted in knocking; and when they opened, they saw him and were astounded.

Motioning to them with his hand to be silent, he related how the Lord had led him out of prison, and said, “Report these things to James and to the brothers.” Then, having spoken thus, he departed and went to another place.
When day came, there was no small commotion among the soldiers concerning what had become of Peter.
Herod, having sought him in vain and examined the guards, ordered them put to death; then he went down from Judea to Caesarea and took up residence there.

Now he was in a state of bitter hostility with the Tyrians and Sidonians; so they came to him with one accord, and having won over Blastus, the king’s chamberlain, they sought peace, because their country drew its sustenance from the royal provisions.
On an appointed day, Herod, arrayed in royal apparel and seated upon the judgment seat, delivered a public address to them.
The people shouted, “The voice of a god, and not of a man!”
Immediately, because he did not give glory to God, an angel of the Lord struck him down, and he was eaten by worms and breathed his last.
But the word of God increased and multiplied.
As for Barnabas and Saul, having fulfilled their ministry in Jerusalem, they returned, taking with them John, who was called Mark.
Now in the church at Antioch there were prophets and teachers: Barnabas, Simeon called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen, who had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch, and Saul.
While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, "Set apart for Me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them."
Then, after fasting and praying and laying their hands on them, they sent them off.
So, being sent out by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Seleucia, and from there they sailed to Cyprus.
When they arrived at Salamis, they proclaimed the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews, and they had John as their assistant.
Having traversed the whole island as far as Paphos, they found a certain man, a Jew who was a sorcerer and false prophet, whose name was Bar-Jesus.
He was with the proconsul, Sergius Paulus, an intelligent man, who summoned Barnabas and Saul and sought to hear the word of God.
But Elymas the sorcerer—for that is the meaning of his name when translated—opposed them, endeavoring to turn the proconsul away from the faith.
But Saul, who was also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, fixed his gaze upon him
and said, "O son of the devil, enemy of all righteousness, full of all deceit and villainy, will you not cease perverting the straight paths of the Lord?

And now, behold, the hand of the Lord is upon you, and you shall be blind and unable to see the sun for a time." Immediately mist and darkness fell upon him, and he went about seeking someone to lead him by the hand.
Then the proconsul, seeing what had happened, believed, being astonished at the teaching of the Lord.
Now Paul and his companions set sail from Paphos and came to Perga in Pamphylia; and John departed from them and returned to Jerusalem.
But they went on from Perga and arrived at Pisidian Antioch, and on the Sabbath day they entered the synagogue and sat down.
After the reading of the Law and the Prophets, the rulers of the synagogue sent to them, saying, "Brothers, if you have any word of exhortation for the people, speak."
So Paul stood up, and motioning with his hand, he said, "Men of Israel and you who fear God, listen. "
The God of this people Israel chose our fathers and exalted the people during their sojourn in the land of Egypt, and with a mighty arm He led them out of it.
For about forty years He bore with them in the wilderness.
And after destroying seven nations in the land of Canaan, He gave them their land as an inheritance.
All this took about four hundred and fifty years. And after that He gave them judges until Samuel the prophet.
Then they asked for a king, and God gave them Saul the son of Kish, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years.
And when He had removed him, He raised up David to be their king, concerning whom He testified, 'I have found in David the son of Jesse a man after My heart, who will do all My will.'
From this man's offspring God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, according to promise,
before His coming, John having proclaimed a baptism of repentance to all the people of Israel.
And as John was finishing his course, he said, 'What do you suppose that I am? I am not He. But behold, after me One is coming, the sandals of whose feet I am not worthy to untie.' "
Brothers, sons of Abraham, and those among you who fear God, to us the word of this salvation has been sent.
For those who dwell in Jerusalem and their rulers, because they did not recognize Him nor understand the utterances of the prophets, which are read every Sabbath, fulfilled them by condemning Him.
And though they found no guilt worthy of death, they asked Pilate to have Him executed.
And when they had carried out all that was written of Him, they took Him down from the tree and laid Him in a tomb.
But God raised Him from the dead,
and for many days He appeared to those who had come up with Him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who are now His witnesses to the people.
And we bring you the good news that what God promised to the fathers,
He has fulfilled to us their children by raising Jesus, as also it is written in the second Psalm, 'You are My Son, today I have begotten You.'
And as for the fact that He raised Him from the dead, no more to return to corruption, He has spoken in this way, 'I will give you the holy and sure blessings of David.'
Therefore He says also in another psalm, 'You will not let Your Holy One see corruption.'
For David, after he had served the purpose of God in his own generation, fell asleep and was laid with his fathers and saw corruption,
but He whom God raised up did not see corruption. "
Let it be known to you therefore, brothers, that through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you,
and by Him everyone who believes is justified from all things from which you could not be justified by the law of Moses.
Beware, therefore, lest what is said in the Prophets should come about:
'Look, you scoffers, be astounded and perish; for I am doing a work in your days, a work that you will not believe, even if one tells it to you.'"
As they went out, the people begged that these things might be told them the next Sabbath.
And after the meeting of the synagogue broke up, many Jews and devout converts to Judaism followed Paul and Barnabas, who, speaking with them, urged them to continue in the grace of God.
The next Sabbath almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord.
But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy and began to contradict what was spoken by Paul, reviling him.

And Paul and Barnabas spoke out boldly and said, "It was necessary that the word of God be spoken first to you. Since you thrust it aside and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we are turning to the Gentiles.
For so the Lord has commanded us, saying, 'I have made you a light for the Gentiles, that you may bring salvation to the ends of the earth.'"
And when the Gentiles heard this, they began rejoicing and glorifying the word of the Lord, and as many as were appointed to eternal life believed.
And the word of the Lord was spreading throughout the whole region.
But the Jews incited the devout women of high standing and the leading men of the city, stirred up persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and drove them out of their district.
But they shook off the dust from their feet against them and went to Iconium.
And the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.
In Iconium, they entered the synagogue of the Jews together and spoke so persuasively that a great multitude of both Jews and Greeks believed.
The Jews who refused to believe, however, stirred up the Gentiles and embittered their minds against the brethren.

So they remained there for a considerable time, speaking boldly in reliance upon the Lord, who bore witness to the word of His grace by granting that signs and wonders be performed through their hands.
The populace of the city was divided: some aligned themselves with the Jews, while others sided with the apostles.
When both the Gentiles and the Jews, together with their rulers, made a concerted attempt to mistreat them and stone them,
they perceived the danger and fled to the Lycaonian cities of Lystra and Derbe, together with the surrounding countryside,
and there they continued to proclaim the good news.
In Lystra sat a man powerless in his feet, lame from his mother's womb, who had never walked.
He listened to Paul as he spoke; and Paul, fixing his gaze upon him and perceiving that he possessed faith to be healed,
cried out in a loud voice, "Stand upright on your feet!" And he sprang up and began to walk.
When the crowds saw what Paul had done, they raised their voices in the Lycaonian language, crying out, "The gods have descended to us in human form."
They designated Barnabas as Zeus and Paul as Hermes, because he was the principal spokesman.
The priest of Zeus, whose shrine stood before the city, brought oxen and garlands to the gates and intended to offer sacrifice together with the crowds.

Upon hearing this, the apostles Barnabas and Paul tore their garments and rushed into the crowd, crying aloud, "Men, why are you doing these things? We too are men of like nature with you, bringing you good news so that you may turn from these futile things to the living God, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and all that is in them.
In past generations He allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways;
yet He did not leave Himself without witness, for He did good, giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling your hearts with food and gladness."
Even with these words, they scarcely restrained the crowds from offering sacrifice to them.
Then Jews arrived from Antioch and Iconium; after persuading the crowds, they stoned Paul and dragged him outside the city, presuming him to be dead.
Yet while the disciples stood around him, he rose and re-entered the city; and on the following day he departed with Barnabas for Derbe.
After proclaiming the good news in that city and making many disciples, they returned to Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch,
strengthening the souls of the disciples, encouraging them to remain steadfast in the faith, and declaring that it is through many afflictions that we must enter the kingdom of God.
Having appointed elders for them in every church, and having prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord in whom they had believed.
Passing through Pisidia, they came to Pamphylia.
After speaking the word in Perga, they descended to Attalia.
From there they sailed to Antioch, the place from which they had been commended to the grace of God for the work they had now completed.
Upon their arrival, they assembled the church and reported all that God had accomplished through them, and how He had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles.
And they remained there for a considerable time with the disciples.
Certain men who had descended from Judea were instructing the brothers that, unless you are circumcised according to the Mosaic rite, you cannot be saved.

When a considerable dissension and disputation arose between Paul and Barnabas and these men, the community appointed Paul and Barnabas, along with several others from their number, to ascend to Jerusalem to consult the apostles and elders concerning this question.
Having been commended by the church, they traversed Phoenicia and Samaria, recounting the conversion of the Gentiles and bringing great joy to all the brothers.
Upon their arrival in Jerusalem, they were received by the church, the apostles, and the elders, and they reported all that God had accomplished through them.
Yet certain believers from the Pharisaic party arose, insisting that it is incumbent upon the Gentiles to be circumcised and to be charged with observing the law of Moses.
The apostles and elders therefore convened to deliberate upon this matter.
After extensive debate, Peter rose and addressed them: "Brothers, you know that from ancient days God selected among you that the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel from my lips and believe.
And God, the Knower of hearts, bore witness by giving the Holy Spirit to them just as He did to us.
He made no discrimination between us and them, having purified their hearts by faith.
Now then, why do you test God by imposing upon the disciples' necks a yoke that neither we nor our fathers were able to bear?
Rather, we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, in precisely the same manner as they are."
The entire assembly then fell silent and attended to Barnabas and Paul as they narrated the signs and wonders that God had wrought among the Gentiles through them.
When they had concluded, James responded: "Brothers, attend to me.
Simon has explained how God first concerned Himself to take from the Gentiles a people for His name.
And the words of the prophets concur with this, as it is written: '
After these things I will return and rebuild the fallen tent of David; I will restore its ruins and erect it again,
so that the remnant of humanity may seek the Lord, together with all the Gentiles upon whom My name has been invoked, says the Lord, who accomplishes these things.'
Known to God from eternity are all His works.
Therefore I judge that we ought not to harass the Gentiles who are turning to God,
but rather to write to them, directing them to abstain from pollutions associated with idols, from sexual immorality, from what is strangled, and from blood.
For Moses has had, from ancient generations, those who proclaim him in every city, since he is read in the synagogues every Sabbath."

Then it seemed good to the apostles and elders, together with the whole church, to select men from among themselves and send them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas—namely Judas called Barsabbas, and Silas, men of prominence among the brothers.
They dispatched the following epistle: "The apostles and elders, your brothers, to the Gentile believers in Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia: Greetings.
Since we have heard that certain persons who went out from us, though we gave them no mandate, have disturbed you and unsettled your minds with their words,
it has seemed good to us, having reached unanimity, to select men and send them to you together with our beloved Barnabas and Paul—
men who have hazarded their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.
We have therefore sent Judas and Silas, who will also communicate the same things by word of mouth.
For it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to impose upon you no further burden beyond these essentials:
that you abstain from things offered to idols, from blood, from strangled meat, and from sexual immorality. You will do well to keep yourselves from these. Farewell."
Thus the men were dismissed and went down to Antioch; and having assembled the congregation, they delivered the letter.
When the people had read it, they rejoiced over the encouragement.
Judas and Silas, being prophets themselves, exhorted the brothers at length and strengthened them.
After spending some time there, they were sent away in peace by the brothers to return to those who had commissioned them.
But Paul and Barnabas remained in Antioch, teaching and proclaiming the word of the Lord together with many others.
After some days Paul said to Barnabas, "Let us return and visit the brothers in every city where we proclaimed the word of the Lord, to see how they are faring."
Barnabas desired to take with them John called Mark;
but Paul judged it inexpedient to take along the one who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia and had not accompanied them in the work.
A sharp provocation arose, so that they separated from one another; Barnabas took Mark and sailed to Cyprus,
whereas Paul selected Silas and departed, having been commended by the brothers to the grace of the Lord.
He passed through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches.
Paul likewise reached Derbe and then Lystra, where there was found a disciple named Timothy, the son of a believing Jewish woman, though his father was a Greek.
He was well attested by the brothers in Lystra and Iconium.
Paul desired that Timothy should accompany him; accordingly, he took him and circumcised him on account of the Jews dwelling in those regions, for all knew that his father was a Greek.
As they journeyed through the cities, they delivered the decrees that the apostles and elders in Jerusalem had adjudicated, enjoining the churches to observe them.
Thus the churches were fortified in the faith and increased daily in number.
Having been forbidden by the Holy Spirit to proclaim the word in Asia, they traversed the region of Phrygia and Galatia;
and, upon reaching the vicinity of Mysia, they attempted to enter Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not permit them.
Passing by Mysia, they descended to Troas.
During the night a vision appeared to Paul: a Macedonian man stood before him, imploring him and saying, “Cross over into Macedonia and help us.”
When Paul had seen the vision, we immediately sought to set out for Macedonia, concluding that God had summoned us to preach the gospel to them.
Setting sail from Troas, we sailed a straight course to Samothrace, and on the following day to Neapolis;
from there we proceeded to Philippi, a leading city of the Macedonian district and a colony, where we remained for several days.
On the Sabbath we went outside the gate beside a river, where we supposed there was a place of prayer; and, having sat down, we spoke to the women who had gathered.
A certain woman named Lydia—a dealer in purple cloth from Thyatira and a worshiper of God—was listening, and the Lord opened her heart to heed the things spoken by Paul.
When she and her household had been baptized, she urged us, saying, “If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come into my house and remain.” And she prevailed upon us.
Now as we were going to the place of prayer, a certain slave girl possessed by a spirit of divination met us, bringing considerable profit to her masters through soothsaying.
She followed Paul and us, crying out, “These men are servants of the Most High God, who proclaim to you the way of salvation.”
She persisted in this for many days, until Paul, greatly vexed, turned and said to the spirit, “I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her.” And it departed from her that very hour.
When her masters perceived that their hope of profit had vanished, they seized Paul and Silas and dragged them into the marketplace before the magistrates.
Bringing them before the magistrates, they declared, “These men, though Jews, are disturbing our city,
and they advocate customs that it is not lawful for us Romans to adopt or practice.”
The crowd then rose up in concert against them; and the magistrates, having stripped their garments from them, ordered them to be beaten with rods.
After inflicting many blows, they cast them into prison, charging the jailer to guard them securely.
He, having received such an order, thrust them into the inner prison and secured their feet in the stocks.
About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, while the prisoners listened to them;
and suddenly a great earthquake shook the foundations of the prison. Immediately all the doors flew open, and everyone's chains were unfastened.
The jailer, awakened from sleep and seeing the prison doors open, drew his sword and was about to kill himself, supposing that the prisoners had escaped.
But Paul cried out in a loud voice, “Do no harm to yourself, for we are all here.”
Calling for lights, he rushed in and, trembling, fell down before Paul and Silas;
and, having brought them out, he asked, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?”
They replied, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved—you and your household.”
Then they spoke the word of the Lord to him and to all who were in his house.
At that hour of the night he took them and washed their wounds; and immediately he and his entire household were baptized.
He brought them up into his house, set a table before them, and rejoiced greatly with his whole household, having believed in God.
When daybreak came, the magistrates sent the lictors, saying, “Release those men.”
The jailer reported these words to Paul: “The magistrates have sent to release you; therefore go forth now in peace.”

But Paul said to them, “They beat us publicly, though we were uncondemned Roman citizens, and cast us into prison; and now would they send us away secretly? No indeed! Let them come themselves and escort us out.”
The lictors reported these words to the magistrates, who were seized with fear when they heard that they were Romans.
So they came and apologized to them; and, after leading them out, they requested that they depart from the city.
After leaving the prison, they went to Lydia's house; and, having seen the brothers, they encouraged them and departed.
Having traversed Amphipolis and Apollonia, they arrived at Thessalonica, where a Jewish synagogue was situated.
In accordance with his established practice, Paul entered their assembly and, over the course of three Sabbaths, discoursed with them from the Scriptures,
explicating and adducing that the Christ was obliged to suffer and to be raised from the dead, and declaring, “This Jesus whom I proclaim to you is the Christ.”
A number of them were persuaded and attached themselves to Paul and Silas, together with a considerable multitude of devout Greeks and no small number of women of prominence.

The Jews, however, moved by jealousy, conscripted certain worthless men from the marketplace, raised a tumult, and threw the city into confusion; then, assailing Jason’s house, they sought to drag Paul and Silas before the populace.
Failing to locate them, they dragged Jason and certain brothers before the city magistrates, crying, “These men who have subverted the inhabited world have now arrived here as well,
and Jason has given them lodging; moreover, all of them contravene the decrees of Caesar, alleging that there is another king—Jesus.”
Upon hearing this, both the crowd and the magistrates were thrown into agitation.
After exacting adequate security from Jason and the others, they released them.
The brothers at once dispatched Paul and Silas by night to Berea; upon reaching that city, they repaired to the Jewish synagogue.

These Bereans proved more noble-minded than their Thessalonian counterparts, for they welcomed the message with exemplary eagerness, scrutinizing the Scriptures daily to ascertain whether these assertions held true.
Consequently, many of them believed, together with a considerable number of reputable Greek women and men.
When, however, the Jews of Thessalonica learned that the word of God had been proclaimed by Paul at Berea as well, they came thither, inciting and unsettling the multitudes.
The brothers therefore sent Paul off at once toward the sea, while Silas and Timothy remained behind.
Paul’s escorts conveyed him to Athens and then departed, bearing instructions for Silas and Timothy to join him with all dispatch.
While Paul awaited them in Athens, his spirit was provoked within him as he observed the city given over to idolatry.
Accordingly, he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and the devout, and in the marketplace each day with whomever he encountered.

Certain Epicurean and Stoic philosophers entered into disputation with him. Some derided him as a prattling seed-picker, while others remarked that he appeared to be a herald of foreign deities—this because he was proclaiming Jesus and the resurrection.
Seizing him, they led him to the Areopagus, saying, “May we ascertain what this novel teaching is that you are presenting?
For you are introducing strange notions into our ears, and we wish to know what these things signify.”
All the Athenians, together with the sojourning foreigners, devoted themselves to nothing so much as to narrating or hearing some novelty.
Paul then stood in the midst of the Areopagus and said, “Men of Athens, I perceive that in all things you are exceedingly religious.
For as I traversed the city and contemplated your devotions, I discovered an altar bearing the inscription, ‘To an Unknown God.’ What therefore you worship without knowing, that I proclaim to you. “
The God who made the world and all things therein is Lord of heaven and earth and does not dwell in temples fashioned by human hands.
Nor is He ministered to by human hands, as though He lacked anything, since He Himself bestows upon all life, breath, and every good.
From one man He constituted every nation of humanity to inhabit the entire face of the earth, having fixed their appointed seasons and the limits of their habitation,
that they might seek God, if haply they might feel after Him and find Him, though in truth He is not far from any one of us.
For in Him we live, move, and have our being, as even some of your own poets have declared, ‘For we too are His offspring.’ “
Being therefore God’s offspring, we ought not to imagine the Divine Nature as resembling gold, silver, or stone—an artifact fashioned by human artifice and meditation.
God, having overlooked the epochs of ignorance, now commands all people everywhere to repent.
For He has appointed a day on which He will judge the inhabited world in righteousness by the man He has designated, having furnished assurance to all by raising Him from the dead.”
Upon hearing of the resurrection of the dead, some scoffed; yet others said, “We shall hear you again regarding this matter.”
So Paul departed from their midst.
Nevertheless, certain individuals attached themselves to him and believed; among these were Dionysius the Areopagite, a woman named Damaris, and others besides.
After these events, having departed from Athens, Paul arrived in Corinth.

There he encountered a certain Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, who had recently arrived from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had commanded all the Jews to withdraw from Rome; and he attached himself to them.
Because they were of the same trade, he remained with them and labored, for they were tentmakers by profession.
On every Sabbath he reasoned in the synagogue, seeking to persuade both Jews and Greeks.
When Silas and Timothy descended from Macedonia, Paul was constrained by the word, testifying to the Jews that Jesus is the Christ.

But when they opposed him and reviled him, he shook out his garments as a symbolic repudiation of them and said to them, "The responsibility for your own destruction rests upon your own heads; I am innocent; from this moment forward I shall go to the Gentiles."
Departing from there, he entered the house of a certain man named Titus Justus, whose house adjoined the synagogue and who worshiped God.
Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord together with his entire household; and many of the Corinthians, upon hearing, believed and were baptized.
During the night the Lord said to Paul in a vision, "Do not fear, but speak and do not be silent,
for I am with you, and no one will assault you to injure you, for I have many people in this city."
And he settled there for a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them.
While Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews rose up unanimously against Paul and brought him before the judgment seat,
saying, "This man persuades people to worship God contrary to the law."
But as Paul was about to open his mouth, Gallio said to the Jews, "If indeed there were some injustice or wicked villainy, O Jews, I would reasonably bear with you;
but if these are disputes about doctrine and nomenclature and your own law, see to them yourselves; I do not wish to be judge of such matters."
And he drove them from the judgment seat.
Then all seized Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, and beat him before the judgment seat; and none of these things concerned Gallio.

Paul, having remained for a considerable span of additional days, took leave of the brothers, and, having shaved his head at Cenchreae because he was under a vow, sailed for Syria, accompanied by Priscilla and Aquila.
They reached Ephesus, where he left them; and he himself entered the synagogue and reasoned with the Jews.
When they urged him to remain for a longer time, he did not consent,
but took leave, saying, "I will return to you again, if God wills," and set sail from Ephesus.
Landing at Caesarea, he went up and greeted the church, then went down to Antioch.
After spending some time there, he departed, journeying successively through the Galatian country and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples.
A certain Jew named Apollos, an Alexandrian by birth, came to Ephesus; he was an eloquent man, mighty in the Scriptures.
He had been instructed in the way of the Lord, and, being fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John.
He began to speak boldly in the synagogue; but when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and expounded to him the way of God more accurately.
When he desired to cross into Achaia, the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to receive him; and upon arriving, he greatly assisted those who had believed through grace.
For he vigorously refuted the Jews in public, demonstrating through the Scriptures that Jesus is the Christ.
While Apollos remained in Corinth, Paul traversed the interior highlands and arrived at Ephesus, where he encountered certain disciples.
Paul asked them, "Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you came to believe?" "No, we have not so much as heard that there is a Holy Spirit."
So Paul asked, "Into what baptism, then, were you baptized?" "Into John's baptism," they answered.
Paul said, "John baptized with a baptism of repentance, enjoining the people to believe in the One who would come after him—that is, in Jesus."
Upon hearing this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus.
And when Paul laid his hands upon them, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they began to speak in tongues and to prophesy.
There were in all about twelve men.
Paul entered the synagogue and spoke boldly for three months, reasoning persuasively concerning the kingdom of God.

But when some hardened themselves and refused to believe, maligning the Way before the assembly, he withdrew from them, taking the disciples with him, and conducted daily discussions in the lecture hall of Tyrannus.
This persisted for two years, so that all the inhabitants of Asia, both Jews and Greeks, heard the word of the Lord.
God wrought extraordinary miracles through Paul's hands,
so that even handkerchiefs or aprons that had touched his skin were carried to the sick, and diseases departed from them, and evil spirits were expelled.
Some itinerant Jewish exorcists also attempted to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over those possessed by evil spirits, saying, "I adjure you by the Jesus whom Paul proclaims."
Seven sons of Sceva, a Jewish chief priest, were engaged in this practice.
But the evil spirit answered them, "Jesus I acknowledge, and Paul I know, but who are you?"
Then the man in whom the evil spirit dwelt sprang upon them, overpowered them, and prevailed so completely that they fled from that house naked and wounded.
This became known to all the Jews and Greeks dwelling in Ephesus, and fear fell upon them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was magnified.
Many of those who had believed came forward, confessing and divulging their practices.

And a considerable number of those who had practiced magic arts brought their books together and burned them before everyone; and when they reckoned their value, it amounted to fifty thousand pieces of silver.
Thus the word of the Lord increased and prevailed mightily.
After these events had run their course, Paul resolved in the Spirit to pass through Macedonia and Achaia and then go to Jerusalem, saying, "After I have been there, I must also see Rome."
Sending two of his assistants, Timothy and Erastus, into Macedonia, he himself lingered in Asia for a while.
About that time there arose no small disturbance concerning the Way.
For a certain silversmith named Demetrius, who fashioned silver shrines of Artemis, provided no small livelihood to the craftsmen.
He assembled them, together with workers in related trades, and said, "Men, you know that our prosperity depends upon this business.
And you see and hear that not only in Ephesus but throughout almost all of Asia this Paul has persuaded and turned away a great multitude, declaring that gods made by human hands are no gods at all.

"Moreover, there is danger not only that our trade may fall into disrepute but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis may be counted as nothing, and that her magnificence—she whom all Asia and the world worship—may be deposed."
When they heard this, they were filled with rage and cried out, "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!"
The city was filled with confusion, and they rushed with one accord into the theater, dragging along Gaius and Aristarchus, Paul's Macedonian companions.
Paul wished to go in to the people, but the disciples would not let him.
Even some of the Asiarchs, who were his friends, sent to him and urged him not to venture into the theater.
Now the assembly was in confusion: some cried one thing and some another, and the majority did not know why they had convened.
Some of the crowd brought Alexander forward, the Jews having pushed him ahead; and Alexander, motioning with his hand, wished to make a defense to the people.
But when they recognized that he was a Jew, they all with one voice cried out for about two hours, "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!"

The city clerk quieted the crowd and said, "Men of Ephesus, what person is there who does not know that the city of the Ephesians is guardian of the temple of the great Artemis and of the image that fell from heaven?
Since these things are undeniable, you ought to be quiet and do nothing rash.
"For you have brought these men here who are neither temple robbers nor blasphemers of our goddess.
If, then, Demetrius and the craftsmen with him have a grievance against anyone, the courts are open and proconsuls are available; let them accuse one another.
"But if you are seeking anything further, it shall be settled in the lawful assembly.
For we are in danger of being charged with rioting today, there being no cause for which we can account concerning this commotion."
And having said these things, he dismissed the assembly.
Once the tumult had subsided, Paul summoned the disciples, exhorted them, took his leave with an embrace, and departed for Macedonia.
Having traversed those regions and encouraged the believers with copious discourse, he entered Greece.
Having spent three months there, and because the Jews had conspired against him as he was about to sail for Syria, he resolved to return through Macedonia.
Sopater son of Pyrrhus, from Berea, accompanied him, together with Aristarchus and Secundus of Thessalonica, Gaius of Derbe, Timothy, and the Asians Tychicus and Trophimus.
These men had gone on ahead and were awaiting us in Troas.
After the days of Unleavened Bread, we sailed from Philippi and, within five days, reached them in Troas, where we sojourned seven days.
On the first day of the week, when we had assembled to break bread, Paul, intending to depart the next day, discoursed with them and prolonged his address until midnight.
There were numerous lamps in the upper chamber where we were gathered.

A young man named Eutychus, seated at the window, was overpowered by profound slumber while Paul continued speaking at length; succumbing to sleep, he fell from the third story and was borne away dead.
Paul descended, fell upon him, embraced him, and said, “Do not be alarmed, for his life is in him.”
Having returned upstairs, broken bread, and partaken, and having conversed with them at considerable length until dawn, he departed.
They brought the boy away alive and were exceedingly comforted.
We went on ahead to the ship and sailed for Assos, intending to take Paul aboard there, for he had arranged matters thus, intending to travel on foot himself.
When he met us at Assos, we took him aboard and came to Mitylene.
Sailing thence, we arrived the next day opposite Chios; the following day we touched at Samos; and the day after that we reached Miletus.
For Paul had determined to sail past Ephesus, lest he be detained in Asia, since he was hastening to reach Jerusalem, if possible, by the day of Pentecost.
From Miletus he sent to Ephesus and summoned the elders of the church.
When they had come to him, he said to them, “

You know how I conducted myself among you during the entire time from the first day I set foot in Asia: I served the Lord with all humility, with tears, and amid the trials that befell me through the plots of the Jews.
I did not shrink from declaring to you anything profitable, nor from teaching you publicly and from house to house.
I testified to both Jews and Greeks that they must turn to God in repentance and have faith in our Lord Jesus Christ.”
“And now, behold, bound by the Spirit, I am going to Jerusalem, not knowing what will befall me there.
Except that the Holy Spirit testifies to me in every city that chains and afflictions await me.
But I do not count my life as precious to myself, if only I may finish my course and the ministry I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify to the gospel of the grace of God.”
“And now, behold, I know that none of you among whom I went about proclaiming the kingdom will see my face again.
Therefore I testify to you this day that I am innocent of the blood of all.
For I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God.”
“Pay careful attention to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has appointed you overseers, to shepherd the church of God, which He purchased with His own blood.
I know that after my departure savage wolves will come in among you, not sparing the flock.
And from among your own number men will arise, speaking distorted things, to draw the disciples away after themselves.
Therefore be watchful, remembering that for three years I did not cease to admonish each one of you, night and day, with tears.”
“And now I commend you to God and to the word of His grace, which is able to build you up and to give you the inheritance among all those who have been sanctified.
I coveted no one’s silver or gold or clothing.
You yourselves know that these hands ministered to my needs and to those who were with me.
In all things I showed you that by laboring thus we must help the weak, and remember the words of the Lord Jesus, for He Himself said, ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’”
When he had said these things, he knelt down with them all and prayed.
There was much weeping among them all; they fell upon Paul’s neck and kissed him.
Sorrowing most of all because of the word he had spoken, that they should see his face no more, they accompanied him to the ship.
When we had torn ourselves away from them, we set sail and ran a straight course to Cos; on the following day we reached Rhodes, and from there we proceeded to Patara.
Finding a ship crossing to Phoenicia, we went aboard and set sail.
When we sighted Cyprus and left it to the left, we sailed on to Syria and landed at Tyre, for there the ship was to unload its cargo.
Having found the disciples there, we stayed seven days; and through the Spirit they kept urging Paul not to go up to Jerusalem.
When our days there were ended, we departed and went on our way, while all of them, together with their wives and children, escorted us outside the city. Kneeling on the beach, we prayed,
and said farewell to one another. Then we went aboard the ship, while they returned home.
When we had finished the voyage from Tyre, we arrived at Ptolemais, greeted the brothers, and stayed with them one day.
Leaving the next day, we came to Caesarea and entered the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven, and stayed with him.
He had four unmarried daughters who prophesied.
While we were staying there many days, a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea.

Coming to us, he took Paul's belt, bound his own feet and hands, and said, “Thus says the Holy Spirit: ‘In this way the Jews at Jerusalem will bind the man who owns this belt and deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles.’”
When we heard this, both we and the local people begged him not to go up to Jerusalem.
Then Paul answered, “What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be bound but even to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.”
And since he would not be persuaded, we ceased, saying, “The Lord's will be done.”
After these days we got ready and went up to Jerusalem.
Some of the disciples from Caesarea also went with us, bringing us to the house of Mnason of Cyprus, an early disciple, with whom we were to lodge.
When we arrived at Jerusalem, the brothers received us gladly.
The next day Paul went in with us to James, and all the elders were present.
After greeting them, he related one by one the things God had done among the Gentiles through his ministry.
And when they heard it, they glorified God. Then they said to him, “You see, brother, how many tens of thousands among the Jews have believed, and they are all zealous for the law.
They have been informed concerning you that you teach all the Jews among the Gentiles to forsake Moses, telling them not to circumcise their children nor to walk according to the customs.
What then is to be done? They will certainly hear that you have come.
“Do therefore what we tell you. We have four men who are under a vow.

Take these men and purify yourself with them, and pay their expenses so that they may shave their heads; then everyone will know that there is nothing in what they have been told about you, but that you yourself also walk orderly, keeping the law.

But as for the Gentiles who have believed, we have written, giving judgment that they should abstain from what has been sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from what is strangled, and from sexual immorality.”

The next day Paul took the men, and having purified himself with them, went into the temple, giving notice of the completion of the days of purification, until the offering was presented for each one of them.
When the seven days were almost completed, the Jews from Asia, upon seeing him in the temple, stirred up the whole crowd and laid hands on him,

crying out, “Men of Israel, help! This is the man who teaches everyone everywhere against the people and the law and this place. Moreover, he even brought Greeks into the temple and has defiled this holy place.”
For they had previously seen Trophimus the Ephesian with him in the city, and they supposed that Paul had brought him into the temple.
The whole city was stirred up, and the people ran together; they seized Paul and dragged him out of the temple, and immediately the doors were shut.
While they were seeking to kill him, word came up to the commander of the cohort that all Jerusalem was in confusion.
He at once took soldiers and centurions and ran down to them. When they saw the commander and the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul.
Then the commander came up and arrested him and ordered him to be bound with two chains. He inquired who he was and what he had done.
Some in the crowd shouted one thing, some another; and as he could not learn the facts because of the uproar, he ordered him to be brought into the barracks.
When he reached the steps, it happened that he was carried by the soldiers because of the violence of the crowd,
for the multitude of the people followed, crying out, “Away with him!”
As Paul was about to be brought into the barracks, he said to the commander, “May I say something to you?” He replied, “Do you know Greek?”
“Are you not the Egyptian who recently stirred up a revolt and led the four thousand men of the Assassins out into the wilderness?”
Paul said, “I am a Jew, from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no obscure city. I beg you to permit me to speak to the people.”
And when he had given him permission, Paul, standing on the steps, motioned to the people with his hand; and when there was a great silence, he addressed them in the Hebrew language, saying,
“Men, brothers and fathers, hear, I pray you, the defense I now offer before you.”
And when they heard that he was addressing them in the Hebrew dialect, they were seized by an even more profound silence; and he said:

“I am a Jew, born in Tarsus of Cilicia, yet nurtured in this city, educated at the feet of Gamaliel in punctilious adherence to the law of our fathers, and being a zealot for God, as are all of you this day.
I persecuted this Way even unto death, binding men and women alike and delivering them into custody,

as the high priest and the whole council of elders can attest; for, having received letters from them to the brothers, I was journeying to Damascus, that I might bring in bonds those who were there and convey them to Jerusalem for punishment.”
“As I was journeying and drawing near to Damascus, about midday, a great light from heaven suddenly blazed about me.
I fell to the earth and heard a voice saying to me, ‘Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me?’
I answered, ‘Who are You, Lord?’ And He said to me, ‘I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting.’
Those who were with me indeed saw the light, yet they did not comprehend the voice of Him who spoke to me.
I said, ‘What shall I do, Lord?’ And the Lord said to me, ‘Arise and go into Damascus, and there it shall be told you all things that are appointed for you to do.’
And because I could not see for the glory of that light, I was led by the hand by my companions and came into Damascus.”
“And a certain Ananias, a devout man according to the law, well attested by all the Jews dwelling there,
came to me; and standing by, he said to me, ‘Brother Saul, receive your sight.’ And in that same hour I received my sight and beheld him.
And he said, ‘The God of our fathers has appointed you to know His will, and to see the Righteous One, and to hear a voice from His mouth.
For you shall be His witness unto all men of the things you have seen and heard.
And now why do you delay? Arise and be baptized, and wash away your sins, calling upon His name.
“And when I had returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple, I fell into a trance,
and saw Him saying to me, ‘Hasten and depart from Jerusalem quickly, because they will not receive your testimony concerning Me.’
I said, ‘Lord, they themselves know that in one synagogue after another I imprisoned and beat those who believed in You.’
And when the blood of Stephen Your witness was being poured out, I also was standing by and consenting, and guarding the garments of those who slew him.
And He said to me, ‘Go, for I will send you far away unto the Gentiles.’”
They listened to him up to this word; then they lifted up their voices and said, “Away with such a fellow from the earth! For it is not fitting that he should live.”
And while they were crying out, and casting off their garments, and throwing dust into the air,
the tribune commanded that he be conducted into the barracks, directing that he be examined by scourging, so that he might ascertain the cause for which they were shouting against him in this manner.
But as they stretched him out with the thongs, Paul said to the centurion standing by, “Is it lawful for you to scourge a man who is a Roman and uncondemned?”
And when the centurion heard it, he went to the tribune and reported, saying, “What are you about to do? For this man is a Roman.”
So the tribune came and said to him, “Tell me, are you a Roman?” And he said, “Yes.”
The tribune answered, “I acquired this citizenship for a great sum.” But Paul said, “I, however, have been born a citizen.”
Immediately those who were about to examine him withdrew from him; and the tribune also was afraid, having learned that he was a Roman and that he had bound him.

But on the next day, wishing to know with certainty the charge on which he was accused by the Jews, he loosed him, and commanded the chief priests and all the council to assemble; and he brought Paul down and set him before them.
Paul, fixing his gaze intently upon the Sanhedrin, declared, "Brothers, I have conducted myself before God with an entirely good conscience up to this very day."
But Ananias the high priest ordered those standing beside him to strike him on the mouth.
Then Paul said to him, "God will strike you, you whitewashed wall! Do you sit there judging me according to the law, while you yourself transgress the law by commanding that I be struck?"
Those standing nearby said, "Do you revile the high priest of God?"
And Paul said, "I did not know, brothers, that he was high priest; for it is written, 'You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people.'"

But Paul, perceiving that one faction consisted of Sadducees and the other of Pharisees, cried out in the Sanhedrin, "Brothers, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees. It is concerning the hope and the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial."
When he had spoken this, a dissension arose between the Pharisees and the Sadducees, and the assembly was divided.
For the Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit, but the Pharisees acknowledge both.

Then a great clamor arose, and some of the scribes belonging to the Pharisees' party stood up and contended, saying, "We find nothing wrong in this man. What if a spirit or an angel has spoken to him?"
And when the dissension became great, the commander, fearing that Paul would be torn apart by them, ordered the troops to go down and seize him from their midst and bring him into the barracks.
The following night the Lord stood by him and said, "Take courage, for as you have testified to the things concerning Me in Jerusalem, so you must also testify in Rome."
