When day came, the Jews formed a conspiracy and bound themselves under a curse, saying that they would neither eat nor drink until they had killed Paul.
There were more than forty men who had made this plot.
They came to the chief priests and elders and said, "We have bound ourselves under a great curse to taste nothing until we have killed Paul.

Now therefore, you, together with the council, inform the commander to bring him down to you, as though you were going to investigate his case more accurately; and we are ready to kill him before he comes near."
But when Paul's sister's son heard of the ambush, he came and entered the barracks and reported it to Paul.
Paul called one of the centurions and said, "Take this young man to the commander, for he has something to report to him."
So he took him and brought him to the commander and said, "Paul the prisoner called me and asked me to bring this young man to you, because he has something to say to you."
The commander took him by the hand, withdrew privately, and asked, "What is it that you have to report to me?"
And he said, "The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the council tomorrow, as though they were going to inquire more accurately concerning him.

Do not be persuaded by them, for more than forty of their men lie in wait for him, having bound themselves under a curse neither to eat nor to drink until they have killed him; and now they are ready, waiting for your promise."
So the commander dismissed the young man, charging him, "Tell no one that you have disclosed these things to me."
Calling two of the centurions, he said, "Prepare two hundred soldiers, seventy horsemen, and two hundred spearmen to march as far as Caesarea at the third hour of the night,
and provide mounts so that they may set Paul on them and bring him safely to Governor Felix."
He wrote a letter in this form:
"Claudius Lysias, to the most excellent Governor Felix: Greetings.
This man was seized by the Jews and was about to be killed by them when I came upon them with the troops and rescued him, having learned that he is a Roman citizen.
Desiring to know the charge for which they were accusing him, I brought him down to their council.
I found that he was being accused about questions of their law, but had no charge against him deserving death or imprisonment.
When it was disclosed to me that a plot would be made against the man, I sent him to you at once, commanding his accusers also to state before you what they have against him."
So the soldiers, according to their orders, took Paul and brought him by night to Antipatris.
On the next day they returned to the barracks, leaving the horsemen to go on with him.
When they entered Caesarea and delivered the letter to the governor, they also presented Paul to him.
Having read it, he asked what province he was from; and when he learned that he was from Cilicia,
he said, "I will give you a hearing when your accusers arrive." And he commanded that he be kept under guard in Herod's praetorium.
After an interval of five days, the high priest Ananias descended to Caesarea with certain elders and an advocate named Tertullus, who laid charges against Paul before the governor.
When Paul was summoned, Tertullus commenced his accusation, declaring, “Through you we have attained much peace, and through your foresight salutary reforms are being effected for this nation.
In every respect and in every place, most excellent Felix, we receive these benefits with all gratitude.
Yet, lest I detain you overlong, I entreat you, in your clemency, to hear us with brevity.
For we have discovered this man to be a pestilence, inciting seditions among all the Jews throughout the world, and a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes.
He even attempted to profane the temple, and we apprehended him.
By examining him yourself, you may ascertain all these matters concerning which we accuse him.”
The Jews likewise assented, affirming that these allegations were accurate.
When the governor motioned to him to speak, Paul answered, “Since I know that for many years you have been a judge over this nation, I make my defense concerning myself with good cheer.
You can verify that no more than twelve days have elapsed since I ascended to Jerusalem to worship.
Neither in the temple, nor in the synagogues, nor throughout the city did they find me disputing with anyone or fomenting a riot among the crowd.
Nor can they substantiate before you the charges they now bring against me.
But this much I confess to you: according to the Way, which they designate a sect, I worship the God of our fathers, believing all things written in the Law and in the Prophets.
I cherish a hope toward God—which these men themselves also anticipate—that there shall be a resurrection of both the righteous and the unrighteous.
In this I also strive always to maintain a conscience void of offense toward God and toward men.
After many years, I came to bring alms to my nation and to present offerings.
In the course of these things they found me purified in the temple, neither with a crowd nor with tumult. But certain Jews from Asia—
they ought to have been present before you and to accuse me, if they had anything against me—
or else let these men themselves declare what crime they discovered when I stood before the council,
except for this one utterance that I cried out while standing among them: ‘Concerning the resurrection of the dead I am being judged before you this day.’”
Felix, being more accurately acquainted with the Way, deferred them, saying, “When Lysias the tribune comes down, I will determine your case.”
He then gave orders to the centurion that Paul be kept in custody, yet afforded some liberty, and that none of his own people be hindered from ministering to him.
After some days Felix arrived with his wife Drusilla, who was Jewish, and he sent for Paul and heard him concerning the faith in Christ Jesus.
As Paul discoursed about righteousness, self-control, and the judgment to come, Felix became terrified and answered, “Depart for the present; when I obtain a convenient season, I will summon you.”
At the same time he hoped that money would be given him by Paul, so he sent for him more frequently and conversed with him.
When two years had been completed, Felix received Porcius Festus as his successor; and, wishing to confer a favor upon the Jews, Felix left Paul bound.
Three days after Festus had entered the province, he ascended from Caesarea to Jerusalem.
There the high priests and the leading men of the Jews laid before him their case against Paul and importuned him,
requesting as a favor that he send for Paul in Jerusalem, since they were contriving an ambush to kill him along the road.
Festus, however, replied that Paul was being kept in Caesarea and that he himself was about to depart there shortly.
“Therefore,” he said, “let those among you who are influential go down with me and accuse him, if there is anything amiss in the man.”
After remaining among them no more than eight or ten days, he descended to Caesarea; and on the following day, having taken his seat on the judgment seat, he ordered Paul to be brought in.
When Paul had arrived, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him, bringing many and grave accusations that they could not substantiate.
Paul offered his defense, declaring that he had sinned neither against the law of the Jews, nor against the temple, nor against Caesar.
Festus, wishing to ingratiate himself with the Jews, answered Paul, “Do you wish to go up to Jerusalem and be judged there before me concerning these matters?”
But Paul said, “I am standing before Caesar’s judgment seat, where I ought to be judged; I have wronged the Jews in nothing, as you yourself know far better.

If, then, I am a wrongdoer and have done anything deserving of death, I do not refuse to die; but if none of the charges that these men bring against me is true, no one can hand me over to them. I appeal to Caesar.”
Then Festus, after conferring with his council, replied, “You have appealed to Caesar; to Caesar you shall go.”
Now after some days had elapsed, King Agrippa and Bernice arrived at Caesarea to pay their respects to Festus.
While they were staying there for many days, Festus laid Paul’s case before the king, saying, “There is a certain man left as a prisoner by Felix;
and when I was in Jerusalem, the high priests and elders of the Jews informed me about him, asking for a condemnation against him.
I answered them that it is not the custom of Romans to surrender any man before the accused has had an opportunity to face his accusers and to make his defense concerning the charge.”
“So,” he continued, “when they had assembled here, I made no delay, but on the next day, having taken my seat on the judgment seat, I ordered the man to be brought in.
When his accusers stood up, they brought no charge of the wicked things I had suspected.
Instead, they had certain disputes with him about their own religious observances and about a certain Jesus who had died, whom Paul asserted to be alive.
Being at a loss as to how to investigate such matters, I asked whether he would be willing to go to Jerusalem and be tried there concerning them.
But when Paul appealed to be kept for the decision of the Emperor, I ordered him to be kept until I could send him to Caesar.”
Agrippa said to Festus, “I should like to hear the man myself.” “Tomorrow,” he replied, “you shall hear him.”

So on the next day Agrippa and Bernice came with great pomp and entered the auditorium, together with the military tribunes and the principal men of the city; and at Festus’s command Paul was brought in.

And Festus said, “King Agrippa and all the men present with us, you behold this man concerning whom the whole multitude of the Jews petitioned me, both here and in Jerusalem, crying out that he ought no longer to live.
“I, however, have found that he has done nothing deserving of death; and since he himself appealed to the Emperor, I have decided to send him.

Yet I have nothing certain to write to our sovereign concerning him. Therefore I have brought him before all of you, and especially before you, King Agrippa, so that, after this examination, I may have something to write.
For it seems to me unreasonable to send a prisoner without also indicating the charges against him.”
Agrippa said to Paul, “You are permitted to speak on your own behalf.” Then Paul stretched out his hand and began his defense.
“King Agrippa, I deem myself fortunate to be making my defense before you today concerning all the charges the Jews bring against me,
especially because you are thoroughly acquainted with every Jewish custom and controversy. I therefore entreat you to hear me patiently.
All the Jews know the manner of life I have led from my youth, a life spent from the beginning among my own people and in Jerusalem.
They have known me from the outset, and if they were willing to testify, they would confirm that I lived as a Pharisee according to the strictest sect of our religion.
And now I stand on trial because of my hope in the promise God made to our ancestors,
the promise to which our twelve tribes hope to attain as they worship night and day. It is for this hope, O King, that I am accused by the Jews.
Why should it be thought incredible by you that God raises the dead?
“I myself was convinced that I ought to do many things in opposition to the name of Jesus of Nazareth.
This is what I did in Jerusalem: having received authority from the chief priests, I imprisoned many of the saints, and when they were put to death I cast my vote against them.
I punished them repeatedly in every synagogue and tried to compel them to blaspheme; and in my raging fury against them I pursued them even to foreign cities.
On one such journey I was traveling to Damascus with authority and commission from the chief priests,
when at midday, O King, I saw a light from heaven, brighter than the sun, shining around me and my companions along the road.
We all fell to the ground, and I heard a voice saying to me in the Hebrew language, ‘Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me? It is futile for you to resist.’
I asked, ‘Who are You, Lord?’ And the Lord replied, ‘I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.
But rise and stand on your feet, for I have appeared to you in order to appoint you as a servant and witness to the things you have seen and to those in which I will appear to you.
I will rescue you from your people and from the Gentiles, to whom I am sending you,

to open their eyes so that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins and an inheritance among those sanctified by faith in Me.’
“Therefore, King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision.
Rather, I first preached to those in Damascus and Jerusalem, throughout all the region of Judea, and to the Gentiles, that they should repent and turn to God, performing deeds worthy of repentance.
For this reason the Jews seized me in the temple and tried to kill me.
But having received help from God, I have stood firm to this day, testifying to both small and great, saying nothing beyond what the prophets and Moses said would happen:
that the Christ must suffer and that, as the first to rise from the dead, He would proclaim light to both our people and the Gentiles.”
While Paul was saying these things in his defense, Festus cried out in a loud voice, “You are out of your mind, Paul! Your great learning is driving you to madness.”
But Paul said, “I am not out of my mind, most excellent Festus, but I am speaking words of truth and sober judgment.
For the king knows about these things, and to him I speak boldly, for I am persuaded that none of this has escaped his notice, since this has not been done in secret.
King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you do believe.”
Agrippa said to Paul, “In a short time you would persuade me to become a Christian.”
Paul replied, “I would pray to God that, whether in a short time or a long one, not only you but all who hear me today might become such as I am, except for these chains.”
Then the king rose, and the governor, and Bernice, and those seated with them.
When they had withdrawn, they spoke with one another, saying, “This man has done nothing deserving of death or imprisonment.”
Agrippa said to Festus, “This man could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar.”
When it was decided that we should sail to Italy, Paul and some other prisoners were delivered to a centurion named Julius, of the Augustan cohort.
We boarded an Adramyttian vessel that was about to sail to the ports along the coast of Asia, and we set sail with Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica.
The next day we made landfall at Sidon; and Julius, treating Paul with humane consideration, permitted him to go to his friends and receive care.
Putting out from there, we sailed under the lee of Cyprus because the winds were contrary.
Having traversed the open sea off Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came down to Myra in Lycia.
There the centurion found an Alexandrian ship bound for Italy and put us aboard.
For many days we made slow headway and with difficulty came off Cnidus; since the wind did not allow us to hold our course, we sailed under the lee of Crete off Salmone.
Coasting along it with difficulty, we reached a place called Fair Havens, near the city of Lasea.
Since much time had elapsed and the voyage was now dangerous, because the Fast had already passed, Paul advised them,
saying, "Men, I perceive that this voyage will be attended by hardship and great loss, not only of the cargo and the ship, but also of our lives."
But the centurion paid more heed to the pilot and the owner of the ship than to Paul's words.

Because the harbor was unsuitable for wintering, the majority resolved to sail on from there, in the hope that, if possible, they might reach Phoenix—a harbor of Crete facing southwest and northwest—and winter there.
When a south wind blew gently, thinking they had attained their purpose, they weighed anchor and skirted Crete.
But before long a tempestuous wind, called the Northeaster, swept down upon us.
When the ship was caught and could not face the wind, we yielded and were driven along.
Running under the lee of a small island called Cauda, we managed with difficulty to secure the ship's boat.
After hoisting it up, they used supports to undergird the ship; and, fearing that they would be driven onto the Syrtis, they lowered the sea anchor and so were driven.
We were being violently battered by the storm, so the next day they began to jettison the cargo.
On the third day they threw the ship's tackle overboard with their own hands.
When neither sun nor stars appeared for many days, and while a severe storm continued to assail us, all hope that we should be saved was at last abandoned.
When there had been a long period of fasting, Paul stood up among them and said, "Men, you should have listened to me and not have set sail from Crete, and so avoided this hardship and loss.
And now I urge you to take courage, for there will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship.
For this very night an angel of God, to whom I belong and whom I serve, stood beside me
"and said, 'Do not be afraid, Paul; you must stand before Caesar; and behold, God has graciously given you all who sail with you.'
"Therefore take courage, men, for I trust God that it will be exactly as it has been told to me.
Nevertheless, we must run aground on some island."
When the fourteenth night had come, as we were being driven across the Adriatic, about midnight the sailors suspected that they were nearing land.
They took soundings and found twenty fathoms; and after a short distance they took soundings again and found fifteen fathoms.
Fearing that we might run aground on the rocks, they let down four anchors from the stern and prayed for day to come.
But as the sailors were seeking to escape from the ship and had lowered the boat into the sea under the pretext of laying out anchors from the bow,
Paul said to the centurion and the soldiers, "Unless these men remain in the ship, you cannot be saved."
Then the soldiers cut away the ropes of the boat and let it drift away.
As day was about to break, Paul urged them all to take some food, saying, "Today is the fourteenth day that you have continued in suspense and gone without food, having taken nothing.
Therefore I urge you to take some food, for this is for your preservation; for not a hair from the head of any of you will perish."
Having said this, he took bread and gave thanks to God in the presence of all, and breaking it he began to eat.
Then they all were encouraged and took food themselves.
We were in all two hundred seventy-six souls on the ship.
When they had eaten their fill, they lightened the ship by throwing the wheat into the sea.
When day came, they did not recognize the land, but they noticed a bay with a beach, and they resolved to run the ship aground there if they could.
So they cast off the anchors and left them in the sea, at the same time loosening the ropes that secured the rudders; then, hoisting the foresail to the wind, they made for the beach.
But striking a shoal where two seas met, they ran the ship aground; and the bow stuck fast and remained immovable, while the stern was being broken up by the force of the waves.
The soldiers' plan was to kill the prisoners, lest any should swim away and escape.
But the centurion, wishing to save Paul, kept them from their purpose, and commanded that those who could swim should jump overboard first and get to land,
and the rest on planks and on pieces of the ship. And so it happened that all were brought safely to land.
After we had been brought safely through, we recognized that the island was called Malta.
The native inhabitants showed us extraordinary kindness, for they kindled a fire and received all of us because of the rain that had set in and because of the cold.
Now Paul had gathered a quantity of brushwood and laid it on the fire, when a viper came out because of the heat and fastened itself on his hand.
When the natives saw the creature hanging from his hand, they said to one another, "Surely this man is a murderer, for though he has been saved from the sea, Justice has not allowed him to live."
He, however, shook the creature off into the fire and suffered no harm.
They were expecting him to swell up or suddenly fall down dead, but when they had waited a long time and saw nothing amiss happen to him, they changed their minds and said that he was a god.
In the vicinity of that place were lands belonging to Publius, the chief man of the island, who received us and entertained us hospitably for three days.
It happened that the father of Publius was lying sick with fever and dysentery; Paul went in to him, and after praying and laying his hands on him, he healed him.
After this took place, the rest of those on the island who had diseases came and were cured.
They also honored us in many ways and, when we were about to sail, put on board the supplies we needed.
After three months we set sail in an Alexandrian ship that had wintered in the island, bearing the Dioscuri—Castor and Pollux—as its figurehead.
Putting in at Syracuse, we stayed there three days.
From there we coasted along and arrived at Rhegium; and after one day a south wind sprang up, and on the second day we came to Puteoli.
There we found brothers and were urged to stay with them seven days; and so we came to Rome.
The brothers there, having heard about us, came as far as the Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns to meet us. When Paul saw them, he took courage and thanked God.
When we entered Rome, Paul was permitted to live by himself, with the soldier who guarded him.

After three days he called together the leading men of the Jews. When they had gathered, he said to them, "Brothers, though I have done nothing against our people or the customs of our fathers, I was delivered as a prisoner from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans.
They, after examining me, wanted to release me, because there was no cause for death in me.
But when the Jews objected, I was compelled to appeal to Caesar—not that I had any charge to bring against my nation.
For this reason, therefore, I have asked to see you and speak with you, since it is because of the hope of Israel that I am bound with this chain."
And they said to him, "We have neither received letters from Judea concerning you, nor has any of the brothers come and reported or spoken anything evil about you.
But we desire to hear from you what you think, for as for this sect, it is known to us that everywhere it is spoken against."

When they had appointed a day for him, more came to him at his lodging. From morning until evening he explained to them, testifying to the kingdom of God and trying to convince them about Jesus both from the Law of Moses and from the Prophets.
Some were persuaded by what was said, but others disbelieved.
And because they could not agree among themselves, they departed after Paul had said one thing: "The Holy Spirit spoke truly through Isaiah the prophet to your fathers,
saying, 'Go to this people and say, "You will indeed hear but never understand, and you will indeed see but never perceive."

For the heart of this people has grown dull, and with their ears they can barely hear, and their eyes they have closed, lest they should see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn, and I would heal them.'
Let it be known to you therefore that this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles; they will listen."
He remained there two whole years at his own expense, and welcomed all who came to him,
proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance.
Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus, called to be an apostle and set apart for the gospel of God—
the gospel which He promised beforehand through His prophets in the holy Scriptures—
concerning His Son, who was born of the seed of David according to the flesh,
and was declared with power to be the Son of God according to the Spirit of holiness by His resurrection from the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord.
Through Him we have received grace and apostleship to bring about obedience that springs from faith among all the nations for the sake of His name,
among whom you too are called to belong to Jesus Christ.
To all who are in Rome, beloved of God and called to be saints: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
First, I thank my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, because your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world.
For God, whom I serve in my spirit in the gospel of His Son, is my witness that I make unceasing mention of you;
I always entreat in my prayers that, by the will of God, I may at last be prospered in coming to you.
For I long to see you, that I may impart to you some spiritual gift for your strengthening;
that is, that we may be mutually encouraged among you through one another’s faith—both yours and mine.

I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that I have often intended to come to you—and have been hindered until now—in order that I might reap some harvest among you, as I have among the rest of the Gentiles.
I am a debtor both to Greeks and to barbarians, both to the wise and to the foolish;
hence my eagerness to preach the gospel also to you who are in Rome.
For I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes—to the Jew first and also to the Greek.
For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith to faith, as it is written, “The righteous shall live by faith.”
For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who by their unrighteousness suppress the truth.
For what may be known of God is plain to them, because God has shown it to them.

For His invisible attributes, namely, His eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly perceived, ever since the creation of the world, in the things that have been made, so that they are without excuse.
For although they knew God, they did not honor Him as God or give thanks to Him, but they became futile in their thinking, and their foolish hearts were darkened.
Claiming to be wise, they became fools,
and exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images resembling mortal man and birds and animals and creeping things.
Therefore God gave them up to the lusts of their hearts, unto impurity, to the dishonoring of their bodies among themselves,
because they exchanged the truth about God for a lie and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever. Amen.
For this reason God gave them up to dishonorable passions; for even their women exchanged the natural function for that which is contrary to nature,

and the men likewise gave up natural relations with women and were consumed with passion for one another, men committing shameless acts with men and receiving in themselves the due penalty for their error.
And since they did not see fit to acknowledge God, God gave them up to a debased mind to do what ought not to be done.
They were filled with all manner of unrighteousness, wickedness, covetousness, and depravity; they are full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, and malice;
they are gossips, slanderers, haters of God, insolent, haughty, boastful, inventors of evil, disobedient to parents;
they are foolish, faithless, heartless, and ruthless.
Though they know God’s righteous decree that those who practice such things are worthy of death, they not only do them but approve of those who practice them.
Consequently, you are without defense, O man—every one who judges—for in the very act by which you condemn another, you condemn yourself; for you, the judge, perpetrate the same offenses.
We know, moreover, that God’s judgment against those who practice such things is rendered in accordance with truth.
Do you suppose, O man—you who judge those who perpetrate such deeds while committing them yourself—that you will elude the judgment of God?
Or do you disdain the wealth of His kindness, forbearance, and patience, failing to recognize that God’s kindness is intended to lead you to repentance?
Yet, in accordance with your obduracy and unrepentant heart, you are accumulating wrath for yourself against the day of wrath and the revelation of God’s righteous judgment.
He will render to each according to his works:
to those who, by steadfast endurance in good works, seek glory, honor, and immortality—eternal life;
but to those driven by self-seeking ambition, who disobey the truth while yielding to unrighteousness—wrath and fury.
There will be affliction and distress upon every human soul that perpetrates evil—to the Jew first, and also to the Greek;
but glory, honor, and peace to everyone who practices good—to the Jew first, and likewise to the Greek.
For all who have sinned apart from the law will likewise perish apart from the law, and all who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law.
For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law who will be justified.
For whenever Gentiles, who lack the law, perform by nature what the law requires, they—though lacking the law—are a law unto themselves.
They demonstrate that the work of the law is inscribed upon their hearts, while their conscience bears witness and their thoughts alternately accuse or exonerate them,
on the day when God judges the hidden things of humanity through Jesus Christ, in accordance with my gospel.
But if you are called a Jew, repose upon the law, and make your boast in God,
and know His will, and discern what is excellent, having been instructed from the law,
and are persuaded that you yourself are a guide to the blind, a light for those in darkness,
an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of infants, possessing in the law the embodiment of knowledge and truth—
you, therefore, who instruct another, do you not instruct yourself? You who proclaim that one must not steal—do you steal?
You who say, ‘Do not commit adultery’—do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols—do you rob temples?
You who boast in the law—do you dishonor God by transgressing the law?
For, as it is written, ‘The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you.’
For circumcision is advantageous if you observe the law; but if you are a transgressor of the law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision.
If, then, the uncircumcised observe the ordinances of the law, will not his uncircumcision be reckoned as circumcision?
And will not the naturally uncircumcised, who fulfills the law, judge you—you who transgress the law despite possessing the letter and circumcision?
For a person is not a Jew who is one merely outwardly, nor is circumcision that which is external in the flesh.
Rather, the true Jew is one inwardly, and circumcision is of the heart—by the Spirit, not by the letter—whose commendation comes not from human beings but from God.
What, then, is the distinctive advantage of the Jew, or what utility does circumcision confer?
Much in every way. For first and foremost, they were entrusted with the oracles of God.
What if some were unfaithful? Does their unfaithfulness nullify the faithfulness of God?
By no means! Let God be true, and every human being a liar, as it is written: “So that You may be justified in Your words and prevail when You are judged.”
But if our unrighteousness commends God’s righteousness, what shall we say? Is God unjust in inflicting wrath? I speak in merely human terms.
By no means! For how then could God judge the world?
But if the truth of God has abounded to His glory through my lie, why am I still judged as a sinner?
And why not say—as some slanderously charge us with saying—“Let us do evil that good may come.” Their condemnation is just.
What then? Are we any better off? Not at all! For we have already charged that both Jews and Greeks are all under sin.
As it is written: “There is no one righteous, not even one;
there is no one who understands; there is no one who seeks God.
All have turned aside; together they have become worthless; there is no one who does good, not even one. “
Their throats are open graves; with their tongues they practice deceit. The venom of asps is under their lips.
Their mouths are full of cursing and bitterness. “
Their feet are swift to shed blood;
ruin and misery mark their ways;
and the way of peace they have not known.
There is no fear of God before their eyes.”
Now we know that whatever the law says, it speaks to those under the law, so that every mouth may be silenced and the whole world held accountable to God.
Therefore no one will be justified in His sight by works of the law, for through the law comes knowledge of sin.
But now, apart from the law, the righteousness of God has been manifested, being attested by the Law and the Prophets,
even the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe. For there is no distinction,
for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God,
and are justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus,
whom God presented as an atoning sacrifice through faith in His blood, to demonstrate His righteousness, because in His forbearance He had passed over the sins committed beforehand,
to demonstrate His righteousness at the present time, so that He might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus.
Where, then, is boasting? It is excluded. By what law? By that of works? No, but by the law of faith.
For we maintain that a man is justified by faith apart from works of the law.
Is God the God of Jews only? Is He not the God of Gentiles too? Yes, of Gentiles too,
since there is one God, who will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through that same faith.
Do we then nullify the law by faith? Not at all! Rather, we uphold the law.
What, then, shall we say that Abraham, our forefather according to the flesh, discovered?
For if Abraham was justified by works, he has a basis for boasting—but not before God.
For what does the Scripture say? “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.”
Now to the one who works, the wage is not reckoned as a matter of grace, but as a matter of debt;
whereas to the one who does not work, yet believes in Him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned as righteousness.
Just as David likewise speaks of the blessedness of the man to whom God reckons righteousness apart from works:
“Blessed are those whose lawless deeds have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered;
blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not reckon sin.”
Does this blessedness, then, pertain to the circumcision, or to the uncircumcision as well? For we say that faith was reckoned to Abraham as righteousness.
How, then, was it reckoned—when he was in circumcision, or in uncircumcision? Not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision.

And he received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness of the faith that he had while yet uncircumcised, in order that he might be the father of all who believe, even though they be uncircumcised, so that righteousness might be reckoned to them;
and the father of the circumcised who are not merely circumcised, but who also walk in the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham possessed while uncircumcised.
For the promise to Abraham and to his offspring that he should be heir of the world was not given through the law, but through the righteousness of faith.
For if those who are of the law are heirs, faith is emptied of its content and the promise is nullified.
For the law works wrath; but where no law exists, there is no transgression.

Therefore it is by faith, in order that the promise might be according to grace and be made secure for all the offspring—not only for that which is of the law, but also for that which is of the faith of Abraham, who is the father of us all—
As it is written, “I have made you the father of many nations”—in the presence of God, whom he believed, who gives life to the dead and calls into being what does not exist.
Beyond hope, he believed upon hope, that he might become the father of many nations, according to what had been spoken: “So shall your offspring be.”
And without weakening in faith, he took account of his own body, already as good as dead—he being about a hundred years old—and of the deadness of Sarah’s womb.
Yet he did not waver in unbelief with respect to the promise of God, but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God,
and being fully persuaded that what God had promised, He was able also to perform.
Therefore it was also reckoned to him as righteousness.
Now it was not written for his sake alone that it was reckoned to him,
but also for our sake, to whom it is to be reckoned, to those who believe in Him who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead—
who was delivered up for our trespasses and was raised for our justification.
Consequently, having been declared righteous through faith, we possess peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ,
through whom we have also gained entry, by faith, into this grace in which we now stand, and we exult in the hope of God's glory.
Moreover, we even boast in our afflictions, recognizing that affliction begets endurance;
endurance, in turn, produces proven character, and proven character produces hope.
Nor does such hope disappoint, for God's love has been lavished upon our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been bestowed upon us.
Indeed, while we were yet powerless, Christ died for the ungodly at the appointed time.
For scarcely will anyone lay down his life for a righteous man, though perchance someone might summon the courage to die for a truly good man.
Yet God demonstrates His own love toward us in this: while we were still sinners, Christ died on our behalf.
How much more, then, having now been justified by His blood, shall we be delivered from wrath through Him.
For if, while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of His Son, how much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved by His life.
Moreover, we even exult in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now obtained reconciliation.
Hence, just as sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin, so death spread to all humanity, inasmuch as all sinned.
For sin was indeed present in the world before the law; yet sin is not reckoned where no law exists.
Nevertheless, death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who had not sinned after the pattern of Adam's transgression—Adam being a figure of the One who was to come.

Yet the free gift is not commensurate with the trespass. For if, by the trespass of the one, the many died, how much more did God's grace—and the gift bestowed in grace through the one man, Jesus Christ—abound to the many.
Nor is the gift like the consequence of the single sinner's act: one trespass brought judgment unto condemnation, whereas the gift, arising amid many trespasses, brings justification.

For if, through one man's trespass, death reigned by means of that one, how much more will those who receive the superabundance of grace and the gift of righteousness reign in life through the one man, Jesus Christ.
Consequently, just as one trespass brought condemnation to all humanity, so one righteous act brings justification unto life to all humanity.
For as, through the disobedience of the one man, the many were constituted sinners, so, through the obedience of the One, the many will be constituted righteous.
Furthermore, the law was introduced so that the trespass might multiply; yet where sin multiplied, grace superabounded.
Thus, just as sin reigned in death, grace too might reign through righteousness unto eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.
What, then, shall we say? Shall we persist in sin so that grace may abound?
By no means! How can we who died to sin still live in it?
Or are you unaware that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into His death?
We were therefore buried with Him through baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life.
For if we have been united with Him in the likeness of His death, we shall certainly be united with Him in the resurrection as well.
We know that our old self was crucified with Him, so that the body of sin might be rendered powerless and we should no longer be enslaved to sin.
For anyone who has died has been freed from sin.
Now if we died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with Him.
For we know that Christ, having been raised from the dead, dies no more; death no longer holds dominion over Him.
The death He died, He died to sin once for all; but the life He lives, He lives to God.
So you too must reckon yourselves dead to sin but alive to God in Christ Jesus.
Therefore do not let sin reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its desires.

Do not present the parts of your body to sin as instruments of wickedness, but present yourselves to God as those brought from death to life, and present the parts of your body to Him as instruments of righteousness.
For sin will not be your master, because you are not under law but under grace.
What then? Shall we sin because we are not under law but under grace? By no means!
Do you not know that when you offer yourselves to someone as obedient slaves, you are slaves to the one you obey—whether to sin, which issues in death, or to obedience, which issues in righteousness?
But thanks be to God that, though you used to be slaves to sin, you have become obedient from the heart to the form of teaching to which you were entrusted.
Having been set free from sin, you have become slaves to righteousness.

I am speaking in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh. For just as you once presented the parts of your body as slaves to impurity and to ever-increasing wickedness, so now present them as slaves to righteousness leading to sanctification.
For when you were slaves to sin, you were free with regard to righteousness.
What fruit did you have then in the things of which you are now ashamed? The end of those things is death.
But now, having been set free from sin and enslaved to God, you have your fruit leading to sanctification, and the end is eternal life.
For the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.
Or are you unaware, brothers—for I am addressing those conversant with the law—that the law exercises dominion over a human being solely for the duration of his life?
For a married woman is legally bound to her husband during his lifetime; yet should her husband die, she is emancipated from the law appertaining to her husband.

Hence, if she becomes the wife of another man while her husband yet lives, she shall be denominated an adulteress; but if her husband dies, she is free from that law, so that she is not an adulteress upon becoming the wife of another man.

Accordingly, my brothers, you also have been put to death with respect to the law through the body of Christ, in order that you might belong to another—to Him who was raised from the dead—so that we might bear fruit for God.
For when we were in the flesh, the passions of sins, which were activated by the law, were operative in our members, producing fruit for death.
But now, having died to that which held us in bondage, we have been released from the law, so that we serve in the newness of the Spirit and not in the antiquity of the letter.

What then shall we say? Is the law sin? By no means! Rather, I would not have recognized sin except through the law; for I would not have known covetous desire unless the law had declared, “You shall not covet.”
But sin, having seized an occasion through the commandment, produced in me every species of covetous desire; for apart from the law, sin is dead.
Once I lived apart from the law; but when the commandment arrived, sin revived, and I died.
And this commandment, which was ordained for life, was found by me to be unto death.
For sin, having seized an occasion through the commandment, deceived me and through it put me to death.
So then, the law is holy, and the commandment is holy, righteous, and good.

Did that which is good, then, become death to me? By no means! Rather, in order that sin might be manifested as sin, it wrought death in me through what is good, so that through the commandment sin might become exceedingly sinful.
For we know that the law is spiritual; but I am carnal, sold under sin.
For I do not comprehend what I am doing; for what I wish to do, I do not practice, but what I hate, that I do.
But if I do what I do not wish, I assent that the law is good.
So now it is no longer I who accomplish it, but sin dwelling in me.
For I know that good does not dwell in me—that is, in my flesh—for the willing is present with me, but the performing of the good is not.
For I do not do the good that I wish, but the evil that I do not wish, this I practice.
But if I do what I do not wish, it is no longer I who accomplish it, but sin dwelling in me.
I find then this law: that when I wish to do the good, evil is present with me.
For I delight in the law of God according to the inner man.
But I perceive another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive to the law of sin that is in my members.
Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?
Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord! So then, I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh the law of sin.
There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has liberated you from the law of sin and death.

For what the law, enfeebled as it was by the flesh, could not accomplish, God accomplished by sending His own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and as a sin offering, thereby condemning sin in the flesh.
He did so in order that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who do not conduct ourselves according to the flesh but according to the Spirit.
For those who live according to the flesh orient their minds toward the things of the flesh, whereas those who live according to the Spirit orient their minds toward the things of the Spirit.
For the mind set upon the flesh is death, but the mind set upon the Spirit is life and peace.
Because the mind set upon the flesh is inimical to God: it does not submit to God's law, nor indeed can it.
Those who are in the flesh are incapable of pleasing God.
But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God resides in you. And if anyone does not possess the Spirit of Christ, that person is not His.
But if Christ is in you, although the body is dead because of sin, the Spirit is life because of righteousness.
And if the Spirit of Him who raised Jesus from the dead resides in you, He who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also impart life to your mortal frames through His Spirit who resides in you.
So then, brothers, we are debtors—not to the flesh, so as to live according to the flesh.
For if you live according to the flesh, you will die; but if by the Spirit you mortify the deeds of the body, you will live.
For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God.
For you did not receive a spirit of servitude leading again to fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, "Abba, Father."
The Spirit Himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God.
And if children, then heirs—heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ—if indeed we suffer with Him, so that we may also be glorified with Him.
For I consider that the afflictions of the present epoch are not worthy to be compared with the glory that is to be revealed to us.
For the creation waits with eager longing for the revealing of the sons of God.
For the creation was subjected to futility, not willingly, but because of Him who subjected it, in hope
that the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to decay into the glorious liberty of the children of God.
For we know that the whole creation groans and travails in birth pangs together until now.
And not only that, but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for adoption as sons, the redemption of our body.
For in hope we were saved; but hope that is seen is not hope, for who hopes for what he sees?
But if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with patient endurance.
Likewise the Spirit also comes to the aid of our weakness; for we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit Himself intercedes with inarticulate groanings.
And He who searches the hearts knows what the mind of the Spirit is, because He intercedes for the saints in accordance with God's will.
And we know that all things cooperate for good for those who love God, for those who are called according to His purpose.
For those whom He foreknew, He also predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son, so that He might be the firstborn among many brothers.
And those whom He predestined, He also called; and those whom He called, He also justified; and those whom He justified, He also glorified.
What, then, are we to say to these things? If God is for us, who can be against us?
He who did not spare His own Son, but handed Him over for us all, how will He not also, together with Him, graciously bestow upon us all things?
Who will lodge an accusation against God's elect? God is the One who justifies.
Who is the one who condemns? Christ Jesus is the One who died, and, more than that, was raised; He is at the right hand of God, and He also intercedes for us.
Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?
As it is written, "For Your sake we are being put to death all day long; we were considered as sheep for the slaughter."
But in all these things we are more than conquerors through Him who loved us.
For I am persuaded that neither death nor life, nor angels nor principalities, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers,
nor height nor depth, nor any other created thing, will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord.
I speak the truth in Christ—I do not prevaricate—while my conscience corroborates my testimony in the Holy Spirit,
that I am afflicted by profound sorrow and incessant anguish of heart.
For I could wish myself anathematized and severed from Christ on behalf of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh—
Israelites, to whom pertain adoption, glory, covenants, legislation, liturgy, and promises;
whose are the patriarchs, and from whom, according to the flesh, comes the Christ, who is God over all, eternally blessed. Amen.
Yet it is not as though the word of God has miscarried. For not all who descend from Israel constitute Israel,
nor are all Abraham's seed automatically his children; rather, “In Isaac shall your seed be called.”
That is, the children of the flesh are not ipso facto children of God; rather, the children of the promise are reckoned as offspring.
For this is the word of promise: “At this appointed time I will come, and Sarah shall have a son.”
Moreover, Rebekah conceived by one man, our father Isaac,
before the twins had been born or had perpetrated any good or evil, so that God's elective purpose might remain inviolable,
not on the basis of works but on the basis of Him who calls—she was told, “The elder shall serve the younger.”
As it is written, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.”
What then shall we conclude? Is there unrighteousness with God? By no means!
For He says to Moses, “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion.”
Consequently, it depends not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy.
For Scripture says to Pharaoh, “For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I might exhibit My power in you, and that My name might be proclaimed throughout all the earth.”
Thus He has mercy on whomever He wills, and He hardens whomever He wills.
You will say to me, then, “Why does He still impute fault? For who has withstood His will?”
But who are you, O man, to retort against God? Will what is molded say to its molder, “Why have you made me thus?”
Does not the potter possess authority over the clay, to fashion from the same lump one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?
What if God, though willing to manifest His wrath and make known His power, has endured with abundant longsuffering vessels of wrath fitted for destruction,
in order to disclose the riches of His glory upon vessels of mercy, which He prepared beforehand for glory—
even us, whom He has called, not from the Jews only but also from the Gentiles?
As He also says in Hosea, “I will call those who were not My people, ‘My people,’ and her who was not beloved, ‘Beloved.’”
“And in the very place where it was said to them, ‘You are not My people,’ there they shall be called ‘sons of the living God.’”
And Isaiah cries out concerning Israel: “Though the number of the sons of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved;
for the Lord will execute His word upon the earth, bringing it to consummation and cutting it short.”
And as Isaiah predicted, “If the Lord of Hosts had not left us offspring, we would have become like Sodom and been made like Gomorrah.”
What shall we say, then? That Gentiles who did not pursue righteousness have attained righteousness—even the righteousness that is by faith—
but Israel, pursuing a law of righteousness, did not attain to that law.
Why? Because they pursued it not by faith but as though by works; they stumbled against the stone of stumbling,
as it is written, “Behold, I am laying in Zion a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense; and whoever believes in Him will not be put to shame.”
Brothers, the earnest longing of my heart and my supplication to God on behalf of my fellow Israelites is that they might attain salvation.
For I bear them witness that they possess a zeal for God, albeit one not informed by true knowledge.
For, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish a righteousness of their own, they have not submitted themselves to the righteousness of God.
For Christ is the culmination of the law, so that righteousness may be granted to everyone who believes.
For Moses writes concerning the righteousness that derives from the law: “The one who does these things shall live by them.”
But the righteousness that comes by faith declares, “Do not say in your heart, ‘Who will ascend into heaven?’” (that is, to bring Christ down)
“or, ‘Who will descend into the abyss?’” (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead).
But what does it say? “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart” (that is, the word of faith that we proclaim).
For if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised Him from the dead, you will be saved.
For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth one confesses unto salvation.
For the Scripture says, “Everyone who believes in Him will not be put to shame.”
For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek, since the same Lord is Lord of all, abounding in riches to all who call upon Him.
For “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.”
How then will they call on Him in whom they have not believed? And how are they to believe in Him of whom they have never heard? And how are they to hear without someone preaching?
And how are they to preach unless they are sent? As it is written, “How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the good news!”
But not all have obeyed the gospel. For Isaiah says, “Lord, who has believed our report?”
So faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ.
But I ask, have they not heard? Indeed they have, for “Their voice has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the inhabited world.”
But I ask, did Israel not understand? First Moses says, “I will make you jealous of those who are not a nation; with a foolish nation I will provoke you to anger.”
Then Isaiah is so bold as to say, “I was found by those who did not seek Me; I revealed Myself to those who did not ask for Me.”
And concerning Israel he says, “All day long I have held out My hands to a disobedient and obstinate people.”
I inquire, then, whether God has repudiated His people? Far from it! For I myself am an Israelite, of Abraham's seed and of Benjamin's tribe.
God has not repudiated His people, whom He foreknew. Or do you not know what the Scripture says in the passage concerning Elijah—how he pleads with God against Israel?
"Lord, they have killed Your prophets and torn down Your altars, and I alone have been left, and they seek my life."
But what does the divine response say to him? "I have left for Myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal."
So too, in the present epoch, a remnant has emerged according to the election of grace.
But if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works; otherwise grace would cease to be grace.
What, then, is the conclusion? Israel did not attain what it sought, but the elect attained it, while the remainder were hardened.
As it is written: "God gave them a spirit of stupor—eyes that do not see and ears that do not hear—unto this very day."
And David declares: "Let their table become a snare and a trap, a stumbling block and a retribution to them;
let their eyes be darkened so that they do not see, and bend their backs forever."
I ask, then, did they stumble so as to fall irrevocably? Far from it! Rather, through their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles, so as to provoke them to jealousy.
Now if their trespass constitutes riches for the world, and their diminution riches for the Gentiles, how much more will their fullness be!
For I am addressing you Gentiles. Inasmuch as I am an apostle to the Gentiles, I glorify my ministry,
if perchance I may provoke to jealousy those of my own flesh and save some among them.
For if their rejection brings about the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance be but life from the dead?
If the firstfruits are holy, the whole lump is holy as well; and if the root is holy, the branches are likewise.
But if some branches were broken off, and you, a wild olive, were grafted in among them and became a fellow partaker of the root's richness in the olive tree,
do not vaunt yourself against the branches. But if you do vaunt yourself, you do not bear the root, but the root bears you.
You will say, then, "Branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in."
Granted: they were broken off through unbelief, but you stand by faith. Do not be haughty, but fear.
For if God did not spare the natural branches, neither will He spare you.
Behold, therefore, the goodness and the severity of God: severity toward those who have fallen, but the goodness of God toward you, if you abide in His goodness; otherwise you too will be severed.
And they, if they do not persist in unbelief, will be grafted in again, for God is able to graft them in.

For if you were hewn out of the olive tree that is wild by nature and were grafted, contrary to nature, into a cultivated olive, how much more will these natural branches be grafted into their own olive!
For I do not wish you, brothers, to be uninformed of this mystery, lest you be wise in your own conceits: a partial hardening has befallen Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles has entered.
And so all Israel will be saved, as it is written: "The Deliverer will come out of Zion; He will turn away ungodliness from Jacob.
And this is My covenant with them, when I remove their sins."
As to the gospel, they are enemies for your sake; but as to election, they are beloved for the fathers' sake.
For the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable.
For just as you once were disobedient to God but now have been shown mercy through their disobedience,
so too they have now become disobedient, in order that, through the mercy extended to you, they also may be shown mercy.
For God has shut up all in disobedience, so that He might show mercy to all.
O, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are His judgments and how inscrutable His ways!
"For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been His counselor?"
"Or who has first given to Him, that he should be recompensed?"
For from Him and through Him and to Him are all things. To Him be glory forever. Amen.

Therefore, brethren, I exhort you, by the compassions of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice—holy and acceptable to God—which constitutes your rational worship. Moreover, do not let yourselves be conformed to this age; rather, be transformed by the renewal of your mind, so that you may discern the good, acceptable, and perfect will of God.

For, by the grace conferred upon me, I declare to everyone among you not to think more highly of himself than is warranted, but to think with sober judgment, each according to the measure of faith that God has apportioned.
For just as we have many members in one body, yet not all members perform the same function,
so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members one of another.
Having gifts that differ according to the grace given to us, let us exercise them: whether prophecy, in proportion to faith;
whether ministry, in the execution of that ministry; whether teaching, in the act of teaching;
whether exhortation, in exhorting; the one who contributes, with liberality; the one who presides, with diligence; the one who shows mercy, with cheerfulness.
Let love be without hypocrisy: abhor what is evil, and cling to what is good.
Be devoted to one another in brotherly affection, and outdo one another in honoring.
Do not be slothful in diligence; be fervent in spirit; serve the Lord.
Rejoice in hope; endure in tribulation; persevere in prayer.
Share in the needs of the saints, and pursue hospitality.
Bless those who persecute you; bless, and do not curse.
Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep.
Be of the same mind toward one another; do not be haughty, but associate with the lowly; do not be wise in your own estimation.
Render to no one evil for evil; rather, take thought to do what is honorable in the sight of all.
If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all.
Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave room for the wrath of God, for it is written, "Vengeance is Mine; I will repay," says the Lord.
Rather, "if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink; for by so doing you will heap burning coals upon his head."
Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.
Every soul must submit to the governing authorities, for no authority exists save that which derives from God, and those authorities that do exist stand ordained by God.
Consequently, whoever arrays himself against authority opposes the divine ordinance, and those who set themselves in opposition shall bring judgment upon themselves.
For rulers are not a terror to good conduct but to evil. Do you desire to be free from fear of authority? Practice the good, and you shall garner praise from it.

For he is God’s minister unto your good; yet if you perpetrate evil, fear, for he does not wield the sword without cause, since he is God’s minister, an avenger inflicting wrath upon the one who practices evil.
Hence necessity compels submission, not merely on account of wrath but also because of conscience.
For this reason you likewise render taxes, for they are God’s ministers, devoting themselves assiduously to this very office.
Render to all their due: taxes to whom taxes are due, revenue to whom revenue, respect to whom respect, honor to whom honor.
Let no debt remain outstanding to anyone, save the debt of mutual love; for the one who loves another has fulfilled the law.

For the commandments, “You shall not commit adultery, You shall not murder, You shall not steal, You shall not covet,” together with any other commandment, are summed up in this saying: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”
Love does no wrong to a neighbor; therefore love is the fulfilling of the law.
Moreover, you know the season, that it is already the hour for you to rouse yourselves from slumber; for now our salvation stands nearer than when we first embraced the faith.
The night has advanced, and the day draws nigh. Let us therefore discard the deeds of darkness and array ourselves in the armor of light.
Let us comport ourselves honorably, as in the day: not in carousals and intoxication, not in sexual immorality and sensuality, not in strife and jealousy.
Rather, clothe yourselves in the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no forethought for the flesh to gratify its lusts.
Receive the person whose faith is infirm, yet not for the sake of adjudicating contentious opinions.
One individual is convinced that he may consume all things, whereas the feeble one subsists upon vegetables.
The one who eats must not disdain the one who abstains, and the one who abstains must not condemn the one who eats, for God has welcomed him.
Who are you to render judgment upon another's servant? Before his own master he stands or falls; and he will stand, for the Lord is able to establish him.
One person esteems one day above another, while another esteems all days alike; let each be fully persuaded in his own mind.
The one who regards the day regards it for the Lord; the one who eats eats for the Lord, for he gives thanks to God; and the one who abstains abstains for the Lord and gives thanks to God.
For none of us lives for himself, and none dies for himself;
for if we live, we live for the Lord, and if we die, we die for the Lord. Hence, whether we live or die, we are the Lord's.
For to this end Christ died and returned to life, that He might be Lord both of the dead and of the living.
But why do you judge your brother? Or why do you regard your brother with contempt? For we shall all stand before the judgment seat of God.
“As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to Me, and every tongue shall confess to God.”
So then each of us will render an account of himself to God.
Therefore let us no longer judge one another, but rather render this judgment: not to place a stumbling block or snare in a brother's way.
I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself; yet for the one who regards anything as unclean, to him it is unclean.
For if your brother is grieved on account of food, you are no longer walking in love. Do not, by your food, destroy the one for whom Christ died.
Do not let your good be maligned.
For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking, but of righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit.
For the one who serves Christ in this way is pleasing to God and approved by men.
So then let us pursue what conduces to peace and to mutual edification.
Do not destroy the work of God for the sake of food. All things are indeed clean, but it is evil for the person who eats and thereby gives offense.
It is honorable not to eat meat, nor to drink wine, nor to do anything by which your brother stumbles.
The faith that you have, hold as your own conviction before God. Blessed is the one who does not condemn himself in what he approves.
But the one who doubts is condemned if he eats, because his eating is not from faith; and whatever is not from faith is sin.
Now we who are strong are obliged to shoulder the infirmities of those who lack strength, rather than gratifying our own inclinations.
Let each of us seek to please our neighbor for what is good, toward edification.
For even Christ did not gratify Himself, but, as it is written, “The reproaches of those who reproached You have fallen upon Me.”
For whatever was written in former times was written for our instruction, so that through endurance and through the consolation of the Scriptures we might possess hope.
Now may the God of endurance and consolation grant you to be of one mind with one another according to Christ Jesus,
so that, with one accord and with one mouth, you may glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.
Therefore receive one another, just as Christ also received you, unto the glory of God.
For I declare that Christ became a servant of the circumcision on behalf of God’s truth, in order to confirm the promises given to the fathers;
and that the Gentiles might glorify God for His mercy, as it is written, “Therefore I will confess You among the Gentiles, and I will sing to Your name.”
And again He says, “Rejoice, O Gentiles, with His people.”
And again, “Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles, and let all the peoples extol Him.”
And again Isaiah says, “The Root of Jesse will come, even He who arises to rule over the Gentiles; in Him will the Gentiles hope.”
Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that you may abound in hope by the power of the Holy Spirit.
And I myself am convinced concerning you, my brothers, that you yourselves are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge, and able to admonish one another.
But I have written to you more boldly, in part, as reminding you, because of the grace given to me by God,
that I might be a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles, ministering the gospel of God, so that the offering of the Gentiles might become acceptable, sanctified by the Holy Spirit.
Therefore I have my boasting in Christ Jesus in matters pertaining to God.
For I will not presume to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through me for the obedience of the Gentiles, in word and deed,
in the power of signs and wonders, in the power of the Spirit of God, so that from Jerusalem and round about as far as Illyricum I have fully proclaimed the gospel of Christ.
And thus I make it my ambition to preach the gospel, not where Christ has already been named, so that I might not build upon another’s foundation,
but as it is written, “Those to whom it has not been announced concerning Him will see, and those who have not heard will understand.”
For this reason I was also hindered many times from coming to you.
But now, having no further place in these regions, and having for many years desired to come to you,
I hope to see you as I pass through on my way to Spain, and to be sent on my way there by you, after I have first enjoyed your company for a while.
But now I am going to Jerusalem, serving the saints.
For Macedonia and Achaia were pleased to make a certain contribution for the poor among the saints who are in Jerusalem.
For they were pleased to do so, and indeed they are debtors to them; for if the Gentiles have partaken of their spiritual blessings, they are bound to minister to them in material things.
Therefore, when I have finished this and have sealed this fruit for them, I will set out for Spain by way of you.
And I know that when I come to you, I will come in the fullness of the blessing of Christ.
Now I urge you, brothers, through our Lord Jesus Christ and through the love of the Spirit, to strive together with me in prayers to God on my behalf,
that I may be delivered from those who are disobedient in Judea, and that my ministry for Jerusalem may be acceptable to the saints,
so that, by the will of God, I may come to you with joy and be refreshed together with you.
Now the God of peace be with you all. Amen.
I commend to you our sister Phoebe, a deacon of the church at Cenchreae,

so that you may receive her in the Lord in a manner worthy of the saints, and may assist her in whatever affair she may require of you; for she herself has been a patroness to many, and to myself as well.
Greet Prisca and Aquila, my coworkers in Christ Jesus,
who imperiled their own lives on my behalf—men to whom not only I give thanks, but also all the churches of the Gentiles.
Greet also the church that meets in their house. Greet my beloved Epaenetus, the first convert in Asia to Christ.
Greet Mary, who toiled exceedingly on your behalf.
Greet Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen and fellow prisoners, who are illustrious among the apostles and who were in Christ before me.
Greet Ampliatus, my beloved in the Lord.
Greet Urbanus, our fellow worker in Christ, and Stachys, my beloved.
Greet Apelles, the approved in Christ. Greet those of the household of Aristobulus.
Greet Herodion, my kinsman. Greet those of the household of Narcissus who are in the Lord.
Greet Tryphaena and Tryphosa, who labor in the Lord. Greet the beloved Persis, who has labored much in the Lord.
Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and his mother, who is a mother to me as well.
Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and the brothers with them.
Greet Philologus and Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympas, and all the saints with them.
Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the churches of Christ greet you.
Now I exhort you, brothers, to keep watch over those who engender dissensions and stumbling blocks contrary to the teaching you have learned, and to turn away from them.
For such persons do not serve our Lord Christ, but their own appetites, and by smooth speech and flattery they deceive the hearts of the guileless.
For your obedience has become known to all; therefore I rejoice over you, yet I desire you to be wise in what is good and innocent in what is evil.
The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.
Timothy, my coworker, greets you, as do Lucius, Jason, and Sosipater, my kinsmen.
I, Tertius, who penned this letter, greet you in the Lord.
Gaius, my host and host to the whole church, greets you. Erastus, the city treasurer, greets you, and Quartus the brother.
Now to Him who is able to establish you according to my gospel and the proclamation of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery kept secret for eternal ages,
but now manifested and made known through the prophetic writings, according to the commandment of the eternal God, for the obedience of faith among all the nations—
to the only wise God, through Jesus Christ, be glory forever and ever. Amen.
Paul, called to be an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God, and Sosthenes our brother,
to the church of God that is in Corinth, to those sanctified in Christ Jesus, called saints, together with all who in every place invoke the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, both their Lord and ours.
Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
I give thanks to my God always concerning you for the grace of God that has been given to you in Christ Jesus,
because in Him you have been enriched in every way—in all speech and in all knowledge—
just as the testimony about Christ has been confirmed among you,
so that you are not lacking in any gift while you await the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ,
who will also confirm you blameless to the end on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.
God is faithful, through whom you were called into fellowship with His Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.

I appeal to you, brothers, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that all of you speak the same thing and that there be no divisions among you, but that you be made complete in the same mind and in the same judgment.
For it has been reported to me concerning you, my brothers, by members of Chloe's household, that there are quarrels among you.
What I mean is this: each of you says, “I am of Paul,” or “I am of Apollos,” or “I am of Cephas,” or “I am of Christ.”
Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized into the name of Paul?
I thank God that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius,
so that no one may say that you were baptized into my name.
I did baptize also the household of Stephanas; beyond that, I do not know whether I baptized anyone else.
For Christ did not send me to baptize but to proclaim the gospel—not with eloquent wisdom, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power.
For the word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God.
For it is written, “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the discernment of the discerning I will thwart.”
Where is the wise? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world?
For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, God was pleased, through the folly of what we preach, to save those who believe.
For Jews demand signs and Greeks seek wisdom,
but we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles,
but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.
For the foolishness of God is wiser than human beings, and the weakness of God is stronger than human beings.
Consider your calling, brothers: not many of you were wise according to the flesh, not many were powerful, not many were of noble birth.
But God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise; God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong;
God chose what is lowly and despised in the world, things that are not, to bring to nothing things that are,
so that no flesh might boast before God.
And it is from Him that you are in Christ Jesus, who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption,
so that, as it is written, “Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.”
When I came to you, brothers, I did not come proclaiming to you the testimony of God with any rhetorical superiority or wisdom,
for I had resolved to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and Him crucified.
I was present with you in weakness, in fear, and in much trembling,
and my discourse and my proclamation were not in persuasive words of wisdom, but in a demonstration of the Spirit and of power,
so that your faith might not rest upon human wisdom but upon the power of God.
Yet among the mature we do speak wisdom—not the wisdom of this age, nor that of the rulers of this age, who are being brought to nothing—
but we speak, in a mystery, the hidden wisdom of God, which God foreordained before the ages for our glory.
None of the rulers of this age has known it; for had they known it, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.
But, as it is written, “What no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man—what God has prepared for those who love Him.”
For to us God has revealed them through the Spirit, for the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God.
For who among men knows the things of a man except the spirit of that man which is in him? Even so no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God.
Now we have received, not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit that is from God, that we might know the things freely given to us by God.
And the things we speak we do not utter in words taught by human wisdom, but in words taught by the Spirit, comparing spiritual realities with spiritual discernment.
But the natural man does not accept the things of the Spirit of God, for to him they are folly; neither can he know them, because they are spiritually appraised.
But the spiritual person appraises all things, while he himself is appraised by no one.
For “Who has known the mind of the Lord, that he should instruct Him?” But we have the mind of Christ.
Brothers, I could not address you as spiritual people, but as fleshly, as infants in Christ.
