I gave you milk to drink, not solid food, for you were not yet able to receive it; indeed, even now you remain unable,
for you are still fleshly. Where jealousy and strife persist among you, are you not fleshly, walking according to merely human standards?
For when one declares, “I belong to Paul,” and another, “I belong to Apollos,” are you not simply acting as ordinary men?
What, then, is Apollos? And what is Paul? They are servants through whom you believed, even as the Lord assigned to each.
I planted, Apollos watered, but God caused the growth.
So neither the one who plants nor the one who waters amounts to anything, but God, who gives the growth.
The one who plants and the one who waters are one, yet each will receive his own reward according to his own labor.
For we are God’s fellow workers; you are God’s field, God’s building.
According to the grace of God given to me, I laid a foundation as a wise master builder, and another builds upon it; but let each one take care how he builds upon it.
For no one can lay a foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ.
Now if anyone builds on the foundation with gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, or straw,
each one’s work will be revealed, for the Day will disclose it, because it is revealed by fire, and the fire will test what sort each one’s work is.
If the work that anyone built upon it remains, he will receive a reward.
If anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss; yet he himself will be saved, but only as one escaping through fire.
Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?
If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him; for God’s temple is holy, and you are that temple.
Let no one deceive himself. If anyone among you thinks himself wise in this age, let him become foolish, that he may become wise.
For the wisdom of this world is foolishness before God. For it is written, “He catches the wise in their craftiness,”
and again, “The Lord knows that the thoughts of the wise are futile.”
So let no one boast in men. For all things are yours,
whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas or the world or life or death or things present or things to come—all are yours;
and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s.
Let every person, therefore, regard us as servants of Christ and as stewards of the mysteries of God.
Moreover, it is required of stewards that one be found faithful.
But to me it is a matter of the least consequence that I should be examined by you or by any human tribunal; indeed, I do not even examine myself.
For I am conscious of nothing against myself, yet on that account I am not justified; rather, the Lord is the One who examines me.

Therefore judge nothing before the appointed time, until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the things hidden in darkness and disclose the purposes of the hearts; and then each person will receive praise from God.

Now these things, brothers, I have applied to myself and to Apollos for your sake, that in us you may learn the lesson, “Do not go beyond what is written,” so that none of you may be inflated with pride on behalf of one against another.
For who makes you superior? What do you have that you did not receive? And if you did receive it, why do you boast as though you had not?
Already you are sated; already you have grown wealthy; apart from us you have already begun to reign—and would that you truly did reign, so that we also might reign with you.
For it seems to me that God has exhibited us apostles last of all, as men condemned to death, because we have become a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to human beings.
We are fools for Christ’s sake, but you are prudent in Christ; we are weak, but you are strong; you are held in honor, but we are dishonored.
To the present hour we both hunger and thirst, we are poorly clothed, we are buffeted, and we have no settled home.
We toil, working with our own hands; when reviled, we bless; when persecuted, we endure.
When slandered, we entreat; we have become, and remain, as the refuse of the world—the scum of all things.
I do not write these things to shame you, but to admonish you as my beloved children.
For though you may have ten thousand guardians in Christ, you do not have many fathers; for in Christ Jesus I became your father through the gospel.
I urge you, therefore, to be imitators of me.
For this reason I have sent Timothy to you, who is my beloved and faithful child in the Lord; he will remind you of my ways in Christ Jesus, just as I teach everywhere in every church.
Now some have become puffed up, as though I were not coming to you.
But I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills, and I will ascertain not the speech of those who are puffed up but their power.
For the kingdom of God does not consist in speech but in power.
What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love and a spirit of gentleness?
It is reported, indeed, that sexual immorality obtains among you, and of a kind not even named among the Gentiles—namely, that someone is cohabiting with his father's wife.
And you are inflated with pride, rather than having mourned, so that the one who perpetrated this deed might be expelled from your midst.
For I, though absent in body, am present in spirit, and have already rendered judgment, as though present, upon the one who has so wrought this;
when you are assembled in the name of our Lord Jesus, my spirit being present with the power of our Lord Jesus,
to deliver such a one to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord.
Your vaunting is not seemly. Do you not know that a little leaven leavens the entire lump?
Purge out the old leaven, that you may become a new unleavened batch, even as you are unleavened; for Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed.
Therefore let us keep the feast, not with old leaven, nor with leaven of malice and wickedness, but with unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

I wrote to you in my epistle not to associate with the sexually immoral—not at all meaning the immoral persons of this world, or the covetous and extortioners, or idolaters, for then you would have to depart from the world.

But now I write to you not to associate with anyone who is called a brother if he is sexually immoral, or covetous, or an idolater, or a reviler, or a drunkard, or an extortioner; with such a one do not even eat.
For what have I to do with judging those outside? Do you not judge those within?
Expel the wicked man from among you.
If any among you, having a dispute with another, dares to seek adjudication before the unrighteous rather than before the saints,
or do you not know that the saints will judge the world? And if the world is to be judged by you, are you unworthy to preside over the most trivial tribunals?
Do you not know that we are to judge angels—how much more, then, the mundane affairs of this life?
Therefore, if you have disputes concerning ordinary life, appoint as judges those who are held in least esteem within the church.
I say this to your shame: is there truly no one among you wise enough to arbitrate between brothers?
Instead, one brother brings suit against another, and that before unbelievers.
The very fact that you have lawsuits among you already constitutes a defeat. Why not rather suffer wrong? Why not rather be defrauded?
On the contrary, you yourselves perpetrate fraud and injustice, and even against your own brothers.

Or do you not know that the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived: neither the sexually immoral, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor those who practice homosexuality,
nor thieves, nor the avaricious, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor swindlers will inherit the kingdom of God.
And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.
“All things are permissible for me,” but not all things are expedient; “all things are permissible for me,” but I will not be brought under the power of any.
Food is for the stomach and the stomach for food, but God will bring both to nothing; and the body is not for sexual immorality, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body.
And God raised the Lord, and He will also raise us by His power.
Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? Never!
Or do you not know that he who is joined to a prostitute becomes one body with her? For it says, “The two will become one flesh.”
But he who is joined to the Lord is one spirit with Him.
Flee sexual immorality. Every other sin that a person commits is outside the body, but the one who is sexually immoral sins against his own body.
Or do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God, and that you are not your own?
For you were bought at a price; therefore glorify God in your body.
Now concerning the matters about which you wrote, it is good for a man not to have sexual relations with a woman.
But because of sexual immorality, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband.
The husband should render to his wife her conjugal due, and likewise the wife to her husband.
For the wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does; and likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does.

Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by mutual consent for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer; then come together again, so that Satan may not tempt you because of your lack of self-control.
Now I say this as a concession, not as a command.
I wish that all people were as I myself am; but each has his own gift from God, one in this way and another in that.
To the unmarried and to the widows I say that it is good for them to remain as I am.
But if they do not have self-control, let them marry; for it is better to marry than to burn with passion.
To the married I give this command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife must not be separated from her husband.
But if she does separate, let her remain unmarried, or else be reconciled to her husband; and a husband must not divorce his wife.
To the rest I say—I, not the Lord—that if any brother has an unbelieving wife, and she consents to live with him, he must not divorce her.
And if a woman has an unbelieving husband, and he consents to live with her, she must not divorce her husband.
For the unbelieving husband is sanctified through his wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified through her believing husband; otherwise your children would be unclean, but as it is they are holy.
But if the unbeliever departs, let him depart. The brother or sister is not enslaved in such cases; but God has called you to peace.
For how do you know, O wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, O husband, whether you will save your wife?
Nevertheless, let each person live as the Lord has allotted to him, and as God has called him. This is my rule in all the churches.
Was anyone called while circumcised? Let him not become uncircumcised. Was anyone called while uncircumcised? Let him not be circumcised.
Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but keeping the commandments of God is what matters.
Let each one remain in the condition in which he was called.
Were you called as a slave? Do not let it concern you; but if you are able to become free, make use of the opportunity.
For the one who was called in the Lord while a slave is the Lord’s freedman; likewise, the one who was called while free is Christ’s slave.
You were bought at a price; do not become slaves of men.
Brothers, let each one remain with God in the condition in which he was called.
Now concerning virgins, I have no command from the Lord, but I give my judgment as one who by the Lord’s mercy is trustworthy.
I think, then, that because of the present distress, it is good for a person to remain as he is.
Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek to be released. Are you free from a wife? Do not seek a wife.
But if you do marry, you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, she has not sinned. Yet those who marry will have tribulation in the flesh, and I am sparing you.
But this I say, brothers: the time is short. From now on, let those who have wives be as though they had none,
and those who weep as though they did not weep, and those who rejoice as though they did not rejoice, and those who buy as though they did not possess,
and those who make use of the world as though they did not make full use of it; for the present form of this world is passing away.
I want you to be free from anxieties. The unmarried man is anxious about the things of the Lord, how to please the Lord.
But the married man is anxious about worldly things, how to please his wife.

And there is a difference: the unmarried woman and the virgin are concerned about the things of the Lord, that she may be holy both in body and in spirit; but the married woman is concerned about worldly things, how to please her husband.
I say this for your own benefit, not to put a restraint upon you, but to promote what is seemly and undistracted devotion to the Lord.
But if anyone thinks that he is behaving improperly toward his virgin, if she is past her prime, and if it must be so, let him do what he wishes; he does not sin; let them marry.
But whoever is firmly established in his heart, having no necessity, but having authority over his own will, and has determined in his heart to keep his virgin, does well.
So then, he who gives his virgin in marriage does well, and he who does not give her in marriage does better.
A wife is bound to her husband as long as he lives; but if her husband dies, she is free to be married to whomever she wishes, only in the Lord.
But in my judgment she is happier if she remains as she is; and I think that I too have the Spirit of God.
Now concerning food offered to idols, we know that all of us possess knowledge; yet knowledge inflates with pride, whereas love builds up.
If anyone presumes that he has attained knowledge, he has not yet apprehended it in the manner that one ought to apprehend it.
But if anyone loves God, that person is known by Him.
Therefore, concerning the consumption of food offered to idols, we know that an idol is nothing in the world and that there is no God except one.
For even if there are those denominated gods, whether in heaven or on earth—as indeed there are many gods and many lords—
yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom all things proceed and toward whom we exist, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things proceed and through whom we exist.
Yet not all possess this knowledge; rather, some, habituated to the idol until now, eat food as though it were offered to an idol, and their conscience, being infirm, is defiled.
Food does not commend us to God: we are neither diminished if we abstain from eating nor augmented if we partake.
Take heed, however, lest your liberty become a stumbling block to the weak.
For if anyone sees you, who possess knowledge, reclining at table in an idol’s temple, will not his feeble conscience be emboldened to eat what is offered to idols?
So the weak brother, for whom Christ died, is ruined by your knowledge.
Thus, by sinning against your brothers and wounding their infirm conscience, you sin against Christ.
Therefore, if food causes my brother to stumble, I will never again eat meat, lest I cause my brother to stumble.
Am I not at liberty? Am I not an apostle? Have I not beheld Jesus our Lord? Are you not my work in the Lord?
If to others I am no apostle, yet to you I assuredly am; for you constitute the seal of my apostolic commission in the Lord.
This is my defense to those who scrutinize me.
Do we not possess the prerogative to eat and drink?
Do we not possess the prerogative to be accompanied by a believing wife, as the remaining apostles do, and the brothers of the Lord, and Cephas?
Or is it solely Barnabas and I who lack the authority to refrain from labor?
Who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? Or who tends a flock and does not drink of the flock's milk?
Do I articulate these matters merely from a human standpoint? Does not the Law itself declare the same?
For it is written in the Law of Moses, “You shall not muzzle an ox while it is threshing.” Is it for oxen that God is concerned?
Or does He not speak altogether for our sake? Assuredly, for our sake it was written, that the plowman should plow in hope and the thresher should thresh in hope of sharing in the harvest.
If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it excessive that we should reap your material things?

If others share in this right with respect to you, should not we do so all the more? Yet we have not made use of this right; instead, we endure everything, so that we may not hinder the gospel of Christ.
Do you not know that those who labor in the temple eat of the temple's provisions, and those who attend the altar share in the altar's offerings?
In like manner, the Lord has ordained that those who proclaim the gospel should derive their living from the gospel.
But I have availed myself of none of these things, nor do I write these things so that they should be done for me; for it would be better for me to die than for anyone to deprive me of my boast.
For if I preach the gospel, I have no ground for boasting, since necessity is laid upon me; woe to me, indeed, if I do not preach the gospel!
For if I do this of my own accord, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, I have been entrusted with a stewardship.
What, then, is my reward? That, in proclaiming the gospel, I may present it without charge, so as not to make full use of my prerogative in the gospel.
For though I am free from all, I have enslaved myself to all, that I might gain the greater number.
To the Jews I became as a Jew, that I might win the Jews; to those under the law I became as one under the law—though I myself am not under the law—that I might win those under the law.
To those without the law I became as one without the law—not being without the law of God but under the law of Christ—that I might win those without the law.
To the weak I became weak, that I might win the weak. I have become all things to all people, that by all means I might save some.
And I do all things for the sake of the gospel, that I may become a co-partaker of it.
Do you not know that in a race all the runners run, but only one receives the prize? Run in such a way that you may obtain it.
Every competitor who enters the contest exercises self-control in all things; they do it to receive a perishable crown, but we an imperishable one.
Therefore I do not run as one running aimlessly; I do not box as one beating the air.
Rather, I discipline my body and bring it into subjection, lest, after having preached to others, I myself should be disqualified.
For I am unwilling that you should remain unaware, brothers, that all our ancestors were beneath the cloud and all traversed the sea,
and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea,
and all partook of the same spiritual nourishment,
and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ.
Nevertheless, God took no pleasure in most of them, for they were laid low in the wilderness.
Now these things transpired as examples for us, that we might not crave evil, as they craved it.
Do not be idolaters, as some of them were; as it is written, "The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to make merry."
We must not engage in sexual immorality, as some of them did, and twenty-three thousand fell in a single day.
We must not put Christ to the test, as some of them did and were destroyed by serpents,
nor grumble, as some of them did and were destroyed by the Destroyer.
Now these things happened to them as an example, but they were written for our instruction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come.
Therefore, let anyone who supposes himself to stand take heed, lest he fall.

No temptation has overtaken you except what is common to humanity. God is faithful, and He will not permit you to be tempted beyond your ability; but with the temptation He will also furnish the way of escape, so that you may be able to endure it.
Therefore, my beloved, flee from idolatry.
I address you as discerning people; judge for yourselves what I say.
The cup of blessing that we bless—is it not a participation in the blood of Christ? The bread that we break—is it not a participation in the body of Christ?
Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread.
Consider Israel according to the flesh: are not those who eat the sacrifices participants in the altar?
What then do I mean? That food offered to idols is anything, or that an idol is anything?
No, but I do say that what the Gentiles sacrifice they sacrifice to demons and not to God; and I do not want you to become participants with demons.
You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons; You cannot partake of the table of the Lord and the table of demons.
Do we provoke the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than He?
"Everything is permissible," but not everything is beneficial. "Everything is permissible," but not everything is edifying.
Let no one seek his own interest, but that of his neighbor.
Eat whatever is sold in the meat market, making no inquiry on the ground of conscience.
For "the earth is the Lord's, and the fullness thereof."
If an unbeliever invites you to dinner and you are disposed to go, eat whatever is set before you, making no inquiry on the ground of conscience.
But if someone says to you, "This has been offered in sacrifice," then do not eat it, for the sake of the one who informed you, and for conscience' sake.
I do not mean his own conscience, but the other's. For why should my liberty be judged by another's conscience?
If I partake with thankfulness, why am I slandered concerning that for which I give thanks?
So whether you eat or you drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.
Give no offense to Jews or to Greeks or to the church of God,
just as I seek to please all people in all things, not seeking my own advantage, but that of the many, that they may be saved.
Be imitators of me, just as I also am of Christ.
Now I commend you because you remember me in everything and retain the traditions exactly as I delivered them to you.
But I want you to know that the head of every man is Christ, and the head of woman is man, and the head of Christ is God.
Every man who prays or prophesies with his head covered dishonors his head.
But every woman who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered dishonors her head, for it is one and the same as if her head were shaved.
For if a woman does not cover her head, let her also have her hair cut off; but if it is disgraceful for a woman to have her hair cut off or shaved, let her cover her head.
For a man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God; but woman is the glory of man.
For man did not come from woman, but woman from man.
Neither was man created for woman, but woman for man.
Therefore the woman ought to have a symbol of authority on her head, because of the angels.
Nevertheless, in the Lord woman is not independent of man, nor man of woman.
For as woman came from man, so also man is born of woman; but all things are from God.
Judge for yourselves: Is it proper for a woman to pray to God with her head uncovered?
Does not nature itself teach you that if a man has long hair, it is a disgrace to him,
but that if a woman has long hair, it is her glory? For her hair is given to her as a covering.
If anyone is inclined to be contentious, we have no such practice, nor do the churches of God.
In the following directives I have no praise for you, for your meetings do more harm than good.
For first of all, when you come together as a church, I hear that divisions exist among you, and in part I believe it.
Indeed, there must be factions among you, so that those who are approved may become evident among you.
Therefore, when you come together, it is not the Lord’s Supper you eat.
For in eating, each one goes ahead with his own supper. One remains hungry, another gets drunk.

What! Do you not have houses to eat and drink in? Or do you despise the church of God and humiliate those who have nothing? What shall I say to you? Shall I praise you? In this matter I do not praise you.
For I received from the Lord what I also passed on to you: The Lord Jesus, on the night He was betrayed, took bread,
and when He had given thanks, He broke it and said, “This is My body, which is for you; do this in remembrance of Me.”
In the same way, after supper He took the cup, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in My blood; do this, whenever you drink it, in remembrance of Me.”
For whenever you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until He comes.
Therefore, whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty of sinning against the body and blood of the Lord.
But a man ought to examine himself before he eats of the bread and drinks of the cup.
For anyone who eats and drinks without recognizing the body eats and drinks judgment on himself.
That is why many among you are weak and sick, and a number of you have fallen asleep.
But if we judged ourselves, we would not come under judgment.
When we are judged by the Lord, we are being disciplined so that we will not be condemned with the world.
So then, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another.
If anyone is hungry, he should eat at home, so that your coming together will not be for judgment. And when I come, I will set in order the remaining matters.
Now, concerning spiritual gifts, brothers, I would not have you remain in ignorance.
You know that when you were pagans, you were led astray unto mute idols, in whatever manner you were led.
Therefore I make known to you that no one speaking by the Spirit of God declares, "Jesus is accursed," and no one is able to declare, "Jesus is Lord," except by the Holy Spirit.
Now there are varieties of gifts, yet the same Spirit;
and there are varieties of ministries, yet the same Lord;
and there are varieties of operations, yet the same God, who works all things in all.
But to each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good.
For to one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, and to another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit;
to another faith by the same Spirit, and to another gifts of healing by the one Spirit;
and to another the working of miracles, and to another prophecy, and to another the discerning of spirits, to another various kinds of tongues, and to another the interpretation of tongues.
But all these are worked by the one and the same Spirit, distributing to each severally even as He wills.
For as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so also is Christ.
For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, whether slaves or free, and we were all given to drink of one Spirit.
For the body is not one member, but many.
If the foot should say, "Because I am not a hand, I am not of the body," it is not on that account any less a part of the body.
And if the ear should say, "Because I am not an eye, I am not of the body," it is not on that account any less a part of the body.
If the whole body were an eye, where would the hearing be? If the whole were hearing, where would the sense of smell be?
But now God has set the members, each one of them, in the body, as it pleased Him.
If they were all one member, where would the body be?
But now there are many members, yet one body.
And the eye cannot say to the hand, "I have no need of you"; nor again the head to the feet, "I have no need of you."
Nay, much rather, those members of the body which seem to be weaker are indispensable;
and those members of the body which we deem less honorable, upon these we bestow more abundant honor, and our less presentable members attain far greater presentability;
whereas our more presentable members have no such need. But God has tempered the body together, giving more abundant honor to that part which lacked it,
so that there should be no schism in the body, but that the members should cherish the same care for one another.
And whether one member suffers, all the members suffer with it; or one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it.
Now you are the body of Christ, and members in particular.
And God has set some in the church: first apostles, secondarily prophets, thirdly teachers, after that miracles, then gifts of healings, helps, governments, diversities of tongues.
Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Are all workers of miracles?
Do all have gifts of healings? Do all speak with tongues? Do all interpret?
But earnestly desire the greater gifts. Moreover, I will show you a way that is far more excellent.
If I should discourse in the tongues of human beings and of angels, yet be bereft of love, I have become a sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal.
And if I possess prophetic utterance, and apprehend all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I hold all faith sufficient to remove mountains, yet lack love, I am nothing.
And if I give away all my possessions to feed the poor, and if I surrender my body in order to boast, yet am devoid of love, I derive no benefit whatsoever.
Love is long-suffering; love is kindly disposed; love is not envious; love does not vaunt itself; it is not inflated with pride.
It does not act indecorously; it does not pursue its own interests; it is not readily exasperated; it does not tally wrongs.
It takes no pleasure in injustice, but exults in concert with the truth.
It shelters all things, credits all things, anticipates all things, and perseveres through all things.
Love is never brought to ruin. Whether there be prophecies, they shall be rendered void; whether there be tongues, they shall fall silent; whether there be knowledge, it shall be superseded.
For our knowledge is partial, and our prophesying is partial.
Yet when the consummate arrives, the partial shall be superseded.
When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I apprehended as a child, I reasoned as a child; upon becoming a man, I relinquished the ways of childhood.
For at present we perceive through a mirror, obscurely; but then, face to face. At present I know partially; but then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known.
So now abide faith, hope, and love—these three; but the greatest among them is love.
Pursue love with unremitting diligence, yet be fervently zealous for spiritual gifts, and especially that you may prophesy.
For the one who speaks in a tongue speaks not to human beings but to God, since no one comprehends him, though in the Spirit he utters mysteries.
But the one who prophesies speaks to human beings for edification, exhortation, and consolation.
The tongue-speaker edifies himself, whereas the prophet edifies the church.

I would that all of you spoke in tongues, but I would far rather that you prophesied; for greater is the prophet than the tongue-speaker, unless the latter interprets, so that the church may receive edification.
Now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues, what benefit shall I confer upon you unless I speak to you in revelation, or knowledge, or prophecy, or teaching?
Even inanimate objects that emit sound, whether flute or harp, unless they articulate distinct notes, how shall one discern what is being played or strummed?
For if a trumpet gives an indistinct blast, who will prepare for battle?
So also you: unless you utter an intelligible word through the tongue, how shall what is spoken be known? For you will be speaking into the air.
There are, perhaps, so many kinds of utterances in the world, and none is devoid of meaning.
If, then, I do not comprehend the force of a given voice, I shall be a barbarian to the speaker, and the speaker a barbarian to me.
So also you, since you are zealous for spiritual things, seek that you may abound in the edification of the church.
Therefore, let the one speaking in a tongue pray that he may interpret.
For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays, but my mind is unfruitful.
What, then, is the conclusion? I will pray with the Spirit, and I will pray with the mind also; I will sing with the Spirit, and I will sing with the mind also.
Otherwise, if you bless in the Spirit, how shall the one occupying the place of the uninitiated say "Amen" to your thanksgiving, since he does not know what you are saying?
For you indeed give thanks well, but the other is not edified.
I thank God that I speak in tongues more than all of you.
Yet in the church I would rather speak five words with my mind, so as to instruct others also, than ten thousand words in a tongue.
Brothers, do not be children in understanding; in malice be infants, but in understanding be mature.
In the Law it is written: "By people of strange tongues and by the lips of strangers I will speak to this people, and even then they will not listen to Me," says the Lord.
Thus tongues are a sign not to believers but to unbelievers, whereas prophecy is not for unbelievers but for believers.
Therefore, if the whole church assembles in one place and all speak in tongues, and uninitiated persons or unbelievers enter, will they not say that you are mad?
But if all prophesy, and an unbeliever or uninitiated person enters, he is convicted by all and judged by all;
the hidden things of his heart are made manifest, and so, falling upon his face, he will worship God, declaring, "God is truly among you."
What, then, brothers? Whenever you assemble, each one has a psalm, has a teaching, has a revelation, has a tongue, has an interpretation. Let all things be done for edification.
If anyone speaks in a tongue, let it be by two or at most three, and in turn, and let one interpret.
But if there is no interpreter, let him be silent in the church, and let him speak to himself and to God.
Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others discern.
But if a revelation is made to another who is seated, let the first be silent.
For you can all prophesy one by one, so that all may learn and all may be exhorted.
And the spirits of prophets are subject to prophets,
for God is not a God of confusion but of peace, as in all the churches of the saints.
Let the women keep silent in the churches, for it is not permitted to them to speak; but let them be in subjection, as the Law also says.
And if they desire to learn anything, let them ask their own husbands at home; for it is shameful for a woman to speak in church.
Or did the word of God go forth from you? Or did it reach you alone?
If anyone thinks himself to be a prophet or spiritual, let him recognize that what I write to you is the Lord's command.
But if anyone is ignorant, let him be ignorant.
Therefore, my brothers, be zealous to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues.
But let all things be done decently and in order.
I make known to you, brothers, the gospel I proclaimed to you, which you received and in which you stand firm,
through which you are being saved, provided that you retain the message I preached to you—unless, indeed, you believed in vain.
For I transmitted to you, as of primary importance, what I myself received: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures,
that He was entombed, and that He was raised on the third day, again in fulfillment of the Scriptures,
and that He appeared to Cephas, and subsequently to the Twelve.
Thereafter He appeared to more than five hundred brothers at one time, the majority of whom remain alive to this day, though some have died.
Then He appeared to James, and thereafter to all the apostles.
Last of all, as to one untimely born, He appeared to me as well.
For I am the least of the apostles, unworthy even to bear the apostolic name, inasmuch as I persecuted the church of God.

Yet by the grace of God I am what I am, and His grace toward me has not proven futile; rather, I toiled more abundantly than all of them—though it was not I, but the grace of God operative alongside me.
Whether, then, it be I or they, this is our proclamation, and this is the faith in which you have believed.
Now if it is proclaimed that Christ has been raised from the dead, how is it that some among you maintain that there is no resurrection of the dead?
For if the dead are not raised, then Christ Himself has not been raised either;
and if Christ is not raised, our proclamation is vacuous, and your faith is equally vacuous.
Moreover, we are discovered to be false witnesses concerning God, for we have testified that God raised Christ—whom He did not raise, if indeed the dead are not raised.
For if the dead remain unraised, Christ has not been raised.
And if Christ has not been raised, your faith is nugatory, and you remain entangled in your sins.
Then those who have died in Christ have perished as well.
If our hope in Christ is confined to this life alone, we are, of all human beings, the most pitiable.
But as it is, Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have died.
For since death came through a human being, the resurrection of the dead likewise comes through a human being.
For as in Adam all die, so in Christ all shall be made alive.
Yet each in his proper order: Christ as firstfruits; then those who belong to Christ at His advent,
then the consummation, when He delivers the kingdom to God the Father, having nullified every rule, authority, and power.
For He must reign until He has placed all enemies beneath His feet.
The final enemy to be annihilated is death.

For, as it is written, “He has subjected all things beneath His feet.” But when the Scripture says, “All things are subjected,” it is manifest that the One who subjected all things to Him is excepted.
When all things have been subjected to Him, then the Son Himself will also be subjected to the One who subjected all things to Him, so that God may be all in all.
Otherwise, what purpose is served by those who are baptized on behalf of the dead? If the dead are not raised at all, why are they baptized on their behalf?
And why do we ourselves imperil ourselves every hour?
I protest, brothers, by the pride I take in you in Christ Jesus our Lord: I face death daily.
If, from a merely human standpoint, I fought with beasts at Ephesus, what advantage accrues to me? If the dead are not raised, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.”
Do not be misled: “Bad company corrupts good morals.”
Awaken to righteousness, as is your obligation, and cease sinning; for some are devoid of the knowledge of God—I say this to your shame.
But someone will object, “How are the dead raised? And with what sort of body do they come?”
You foolish one: what you sow does not come to life unless it dies.
And what you sow is not the body that shall be, but a naked kernel—perhaps of wheat, or of some other grain.
But God bestows upon it a body as He pleases, and to each seed its own distinctive body.
Not all flesh is identical; rather, there is one flesh of human beings, another of beasts, another of birds, and another of fish.
There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies; yet the splendor of the heavenly differs from that of the earthly.
The sun possesses one glory, the moon another, and the stars another; for one star differs from another in glory.
Thus it is with the resurrection of the dead: what is sown in corruption is raised in incorruption;
what is sown in dishonor is raised in glory; what is sown in weakness is raised in power;
what is sown a natural body is raised a spiritual body. If there is a natural body, there is also a spiritual body.
So too it is written, “The first man Adam became a living being”; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit.
Yet the spiritual is not first, but the natural; afterward comes the spiritual.
The first man is from the earth, earthy; the second man is from heaven.
As is the earthy, so are those who are earthy; and as is the heavenly, so are those who are heavenly.
And just as we have borne the image of the earthy, we shall also bear the image of the heavenly.
Now this I declare, brothers: mortal human nature cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable.
Behold, I disclose to you a mystery: we shall not all die, but we shall all be transformed,
in an instant, in a flash, at the last trumpet; for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised imperishable, and we shall be transformed.
For this perishable must be clothed with imperishability, and this mortal must be clothed with immortality.

But when this perishable has been clothed with imperishability, and this mortal has been clothed with immortality, then shall be fulfilled the saying that is written: “Death is swallowed up in victory.”
“O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?”
The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law;
but thanks be to God, who grants us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.
Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast and immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that your labor is not futile in the Lord.
Now concerning the collection for the saints, I would have you follow the same arrangement I prescribed for the churches of Galatia.
On the first day of every week, let each of you set aside and store up whatever prosperity permits, so that no collections may be necessitated by my arrival.
When I come, I shall send, with letters of approval, those whom you approve to convey your gift to Jerusalem.
If it should prove expedient that I too make the journey, they shall accompany me.
I shall come to you after traversing Macedonia, for my route lies through Macedonia.
Perhaps I shall abide with you, or even winter there, that you may speed me on my way whithersoever I proceed.
For I am unwilling to see you now merely in transit; rather, I hope to remain with you for some interval, if the Lord permits.
Nevertheless, I shall remain in Ephesus until Pentecost,
for a wide and efficacious door has opened to me, though many adversaries oppose me.
When Timothy arrives, see that he may be among you without apprehension, for he labors in the work of the Lord, even as I do.
Let no one, therefore, treat him with contempt; instead, send him forth in peace, that he may return to me, for I await him with the brothers.
Now concerning our brother Apollos, I entreated him repeatedly to visit you with the brothers, yet it was not his inclination to come at present; he will come when opportunity affords.
Be vigilant, stand fast in the faith, acquit yourselves with manly courage, and be strong.
Let all that you do be done in love.
You know that the household of Stephanas were the first converts in Achaia and devoted themselves to the service of the saints.
I exhort you, brothers, to submit to such people and to every collaborator and laborer.
I rejoice in the advent of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus, for they have supplied what was lacking on your part;
for they refreshed my spirit and yours. Acknowledge such men.
The churches of Asia greet you. Aquila and Prisca, together with the church in their house, greet you warmly in the Lord.
All the brothers greet you. Greet one another with a holy kiss.
I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand.
If anyone does not love the Lord, let him be anathema. Our Lord, come!
The grace of the Lord Jesus be with you.
My love be with all of you in Christ Jesus. Amen.
Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy our brother, to the church of God that is in Corinth, together with all the saints throughout Achaia:
Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and the God of all comfort,
who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction with the comfort by which we ourselves are comforted by God.
For just as the sufferings of Christ overflow to us, so also, through Christ, our comfort overflows.
If we are afflicted, it is for your comfort and salvation; if we are comforted, it is for your comfort, which proves effective as you patiently endure the same sufferings that we also suffer.
And our hope for you is unshaken, because we know that as you share in our sufferings, so you will also share in our comfort.
For we do not want you, brothers, to be ignorant of the affliction that befell us in Asia, that we were burdened beyond measure, beyond our strength, so that we despaired even of life itself.
Indeed, we felt within ourselves the sentence of death, so that we might not place our confidence in ourselves but in God, who raises the dead.
He delivered us from so great a death, and He will deliver us; in Him we have set our hope that He will deliver us still.
You also must help us by your prayers, so that many may give thanks on our behalf for the gracious gift bestowed upon us through the prayers of many.

For our boast is this: the testimony of our conscience that we conducted ourselves in the world, and more abundantly toward you, in holiness and sincerity from God, not by fleshly wisdom but by the grace of God.
For we write to you nothing other than what you read and understand; and I hope that you will understand fully, even to the end,
just as you have understood us in part, that we are your boast, just as you are ours, in the day of our Lord Jesus.
In this confidence I intended to come to you first, so that you might receive a double benefit,
and to pass through you into Macedonia, and again to come to you from Macedonia, and to be sent on by you to Judea.
So when I planned this, did I act with frivolity? Or do I make my plans according to the flesh, so that with me there is Yes, yes, and No, no?
But God is faithful, and our word to you is not Yes and No.
For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, whom we proclaimed among you—through me, Silvanus, and Timothy—was not Yes and No, but in Him it has always been Yes.
For every promise of God finds its Yes in Him; and through Him we say Amen to the glory of God.
Now God, who establishes us with you in Christ and who anointed us,
has also sealed us and given us the Spirit in our hearts as a pledge.
But I call God as witness against my own soul that it was to spare you that I did not come again to Corinth.
Not that we lord it over your faith, but we are fellow workers with you for your joy, for you stand firm by faith.
For I resolved within myself that I would not return to you in grief.
For if I grieve you, who is there to gladden me save the one whom I have grieved?

And I wrote this very thing so that, upon my arrival, I might not be distressed by those who ought to have made me rejoice, since I had confidence in all of you that my joy would be the joy of you all.
For I wrote to you out of great tribulation and anguish of heart, and with many tears—not to grieve you, but to make known to you the surpassing love that I bear toward you.
If anyone has caused grief, he has not grieved me alone, but, in some measure—not to overstate the case—all of you.
The rebuke inflicted by the majority is sufficient for such a person.
So, on the contrary, you ought rather to forgive and comfort him, lest he be swallowed up by excessive sorrow.
Therefore I urge you to reaffirm your love for him.
For to this end I also wrote, that I might test you and ascertain whether you are obedient in all things.
If you forgive anyone, I also forgive; and what I have forgiven—if indeed there was anything to forgive—I have forgiven in the presence of Christ for your sake.
So that we may not be outwitted by Satan—for we are not ignorant of his designs.
When I came to Troas to proclaim the gospel of Christ, and a door was opened to me in the Lord,
I had no rest in my spirit, because I did not find my brother Titus; so, taking leave of them, I departed for Macedonia.
But thanks be to God, who in Christ always leads us in triumphal procession and, through us, spreads the fragrance of the knowledge of Him in every place.
For we are the aroma of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing,
to the one a fragrance from death to death, and to the other a fragrance from life to life. And who is sufficient for these things?
For we are not, like so many, peddlers of the word of God; but, as men of sincerity, as commissioned by God, we speak in Christ in the sight of God.
Are we commencing anew to commend ourselves, or do we require—as certain persons do—letters of commendation addressed to you or emanating from you?
You constitute our epistle, engraved within our hearts, recognized and perused by all humanity,
being manifested that you are an epistle of Christ, ministered through us, inscribed not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not upon tablets of stone but upon tablets of fleshly hearts.
Such confidence we possess toward God through Christ.
Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to reckon anything as deriving from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God,
who has also rendered us sufficient ministers of a new covenant—not of the letter but of the Spirit—for the letter kills, whereas the Spirit vivifies.

For if the ministry of death, engraved in letters upon stones, arrived in glory, so that the sons of Israel could not fix their gaze upon the face of Moses because of the glory of his countenance—a glory being brought to naught—
how shall not rather the ministry of the Spirit be in glory?
For if the ministry of condemnation possesses glory, how much more does the ministry of righteousness abound in glory.
For even that which was glorified has not been glorified in this respect, on account of the superabundant glory.
For if that which is being brought to naught was through glory, how much more is that which remains in glory.
Therefore, possessing such hope, we employ great boldness,
and not as Moses placed a veil over his face, so that the sons of Israel might not gaze upon the consummation of that which is being abolished.
But their minds were hardened; for until this very day the same veil remains upon the reading of the old covenant, not being unveiled, because in Christ it is abolished.
But until today, whenever Moses is read, a veil lies over their heart.
But whenever one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed.
Now the Lord is the Spirit; and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty.
And we all, with unveiled face, beholding as in a mirror the glory of the Lord, are being transfigured into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord Spirit.
Consequently, having been entrusted with this ministry in accordance with the mercy we have received, we do not succumb to discouragement.

On the contrary, we have renounced the clandestine practices born of shame; we do not conduct ourselves with cunning, nor do we distort the word of God, but, through the open proclamation of truth, we commend ourselves to the conscience of every person before God.
And if our gospel remains veiled, it is veiled only to those who are perishing.
In their case, the god of this age has blinded the minds of the unbelieving, lest the radiance of the gospel of the glory of Christ—who is the very image of God—should illumine them.
For we do not proclaim ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord, and ourselves as your servants for the sake of Jesus.
For God, who said, "Light shall shine out of darkness," has Himself shone in our hearts to bring to light the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Christ.
Yet we possess this treasure in fragile clay jars, so that the transcendent power may be seen to belong to God and not to originate in us.
We are hard-pressed on every side, yet not crushed; bewildered, yet not driven to despair;
persecuted, yet not forsaken; struck down, yet not destroyed.
We always carry in our bodies the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be revealed in our bodies.
For we who are alive are perpetually being handed over to death for the sake of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may be manifested in our mortal flesh.
Thus death is at work in us, but life in you.
Yet, possessing the same spirit of faith, in accordance with what is written, "I believed, and therefore I spoke," we too believe, and therefore we speak.
We know that He who raised the Lord Jesus will also raise us with Jesus and present us together with you.
For everything is for your sake, so that, as grace reaches more and more people, thanksgiving may overflow to the glory of God.
Therefore we do not lose heart; though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day.
For our light and momentary affliction is producing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure,
as we fix our gaze not on what is seen, but on what is unseen; for what is seen is transient, whereas what is unseen is eternal.
For we know that should the earthly tabernacle of our sojourn be dismantled, we possess an edifice from God—an eternal house in the heavens, not fashioned by human hands.
Indeed, within this tent we groan, yearning to be invested with our heavenly habitation,
provided that, once clothed, we shall not be found naked.
For those of us dwelling in this tent groan under our burden, inasmuch as we do not desire to be stripped bare, but to be further clothed, so that what is mortal may be engulfed by life.
Moreover, He who has fashioned us for this very end is God, who has granted us the Spirit as an earnest.
Hence we are ever confident, knowing that while we are at home in the body, we are away from the Lord;
for we walk by faith, not by sight.
We are well pleased, indeed, to be absent from the body and present with the Lord.
Therefore, whether at home or away, we make it our ambition to be well-pleasing to Him.
For we must all be manifested before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive the recompense for the things done through the body, whether good or evil.
Knowing, therefore, the fear of the Lord, we persuade men; yet we are manifest to God, and I trust that we are manifest also in your consciences.

We are not again commending ourselves to you, but we are furnishing you with an occasion for boasting concerning us, so that you may have something to say to those who boast in outward show and not in the heart.
For if we are out of our minds, it is unto God; if we are sober-minded, it is for your sake.
For the love of Christ constrains us, because we have concluded that One died for all, and therefore all died.
And He died for all, so that those who live should no longer live for themselves, but for Him who died and was raised on their behalf.
Consequently, from now on we know no one according to the flesh; even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know Him no longer in that manner.
Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation: the old things have passed away; behold, new things have come.
Now all things are from God, who reconciled us to Himself through Christ and gave to us the ministry of reconciliation.
Namely, God was in Christ reconciling the world to Himself, not reckoning their transgressions to them, and having committed to us the word of reconciliation.
We are therefore ambassadors for Christ, as though God were entreating through us; we implore you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God.
For He made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that we might become the righteousness of God in Him.
As fellow laborers with God, we entreat you not to receive the grace of God to no purpose.
For He says, “In a propitious hour I hearkened to you, and on the day of salvation I came to your aid. Behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation.”
We afford no occasion for stumbling in anything, so that the ministry may not be reproached.
But, as servants of God, we commend ourselves in everything—in great endurance, in tribulations, in necessities, in straits—
in beatings, in imprisonments, in tumults, in toils, in wakeful nights, in fastings;
in purity, in knowledge, in long-suffering, in kindness, in the Holy Spirit, in sincere love;
in the word of truth, in the power of God; through the weapons of righteousness, whether in the right hand or in the left;
through glory and dishonor, through ill report and good report; as deceivers, yet truthful;
as unknown, yet recognized; as dying, and behold, we live; as chastened, yet not put to death;
as sorrowful, yet ever rejoicing; as impoverished, yet enriching many; as having nothing, yet holding fast all things.
Our mouth stands open to you, O Corinthians; our heart has been enlarged.
You are not constrained in us, but you are constrained in your own affections.
Now, in like recompense—I speak as to children—do you also widen your hearts.
Do not become yoked together with unbelievers; for what partnership has righteousness with lawlessness? or what communion has light with darkness?
And what concord has Christ with Belial? or what share has a believer with an unbeliever?

And what agreement has the temple of God with idols? For we are the temple of the living God, as God said, “I will dwell in them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be My people.”
Therefore, “Come out from the midst of them and be separate,” says the Lord, “and touch no unclean thing; and I will receive you.”
“And I will be a Father to you, and you shall be sons and daughters to Me,” says the Lord Almighty.
Therefore, beloved, since you hold these promises, let us purify ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God.
Open your hearts to us: we have wronged no one, corrupted no one, and exploited no one.
I do not utter this to condemn you; for I have already declared that you dwell so deeply in our hearts that we are bound to live and die with you.
Great is my confidence in you; great is my boasting on your behalf. I am filled with consolation, and amid all our affliction I overflow with joy.
For even when we came into Macedonia, our bodies had no respite; rather, we were pressed on every side—conflicts without, fears within.
Yet God, who consoles the downcast, consoled us through the arrival of Titus,
not only by his coming but also by the consolation he had received from you, as he reported to us your longing, your lamentation, and your zeal on my behalf, so that I rejoiced all the more.
For even if I grieved you by that letter, I do not regret it; though I did for a moment regret it, I perceive that the letter grieved you, yet only for a season.
Now I rejoice—not because you were grieved, but because your grief issued in repentance; for you were grieved in accordance with God, so that you suffered no loss from us.
For godly grief produces a repentance unto salvation, a repentance not to be regretted; but the grief of the world produces death.

Observe what this godly grief has wrought in you: what earnestness, what defense, what indignation, what fear, what longing, what zeal, what vindication! In every respect you have demonstrated yourselves to be pure in this matter.

Therefore, although I wrote to you, it was not for the sake of the wrongdoer, nor for the sake of the one wronged, but in order that your earnest concern for us might be made manifest to you before God.
For this reason we have been consoled; and beyond our own consolation, we rejoiced exceedingly over the joy of Titus, because his spirit has been refreshed by all of you.
For if I boasted to him about you, I was not put to shame; but as everything we spoke to you was true, so also our boasting to Titus proved true.
And his affections toward you are all the more abundant as he recalls that all of you were obedient, and that you received him with fear and trembling.
I rejoice that in everything I may be confident in you.
Now, brothers, we are desirous of apprising you of the grace that God has lavished upon the Macedonian congregations,
for amid a most rigorous ordeal, their superabundant joy, conjoined with their extreme indigence, has overflowed into the opulence of their liberality.
I bear witness that they contributed in accordance with their capacity, and indeed beyond it, of their own spontaneous volition;
they besought us with great urgency for the favor of participating in this ministry to the saints.
Nor did they act merely as we had anticipated; rather, they first consecrated themselves to the Lord and thereafter to us, in conformity with the will of God.
Consequently, we exhorted Titus that, just as he had previously initiated this endeavor, he should also bring to fruition among you this grace as well.
But as you abound in every respect—in faith, in discourse, in knowledge, in all diligence, and in the love we have awakened within you—see to it that you abound in this grace also.
I am not issuing a command; rather, I seek to assay the genuineness of your love by the standard of others’ earnestness.
For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: though He was affluent, yet for your sake He became indigent, so that through His penury you might become affluent.
In this matter I proffer my counsel, for it is expedient for you—not merely to have commenced the work last year, but to have desired it.
Now, therefore, bring the execution to completion, so that your readiness of will may be consummated by a corresponding completion commensurate with your resources.
For if the willingness is present, the offering is acceptable in proportion to what one possesses, not in proportion to what one lacks.
For our purpose is not that others should find relief while you are distressed, but that equity should prevail.
At the present juncture, your abundance should alleviate their want, so that their abundance may in turn alleviate your want, and thereby equity be established.
As it is written, “He who gathered abundantly had no surplus, and he who gathered sparingly suffered no deficit.”
Thanks be to God, who has implanted in the heart of Titus the same solicitous concern for you.
For he not only acceded to our exhortation, but, being already most earnest, he set out for you of his own spontaneous accord.
Moreover, we are dispatching with him the brother whose commendation in the gospel is celebrated throughout all the churches.
And not only so, but he has been designated by the churches as our traveling companion in administering this grace, to the glory of the Lord Himself and as a manifestation of our readiness.
We are taking this precaution lest anyone should impugn us in connection with this munificent contribution that we administer.
For we are solicitous to conduct ourselves honorably, not only before the Lord, but also before men.
And we are sending with them our brother, whom we have repeatedly tested and found diligent in many undertakings, and who is now all the more diligent by reason of his great confidence in you.
As for Titus, he is my associate and collaborator on your behalf; as for our brothers, they are envoys of the churches, a glory to Christ.
Therefore, in the presence of the churches, exhibit to them the evidence of your love and of our boasting concerning you.
For, concerning the ministry to the saints, it is altogether superfluous for me to write to you.
For I know your readiness, the very thing of which I boast to the Macedonians, namely that Achaia has been ready since last year, and your zeal has stirred up the majority.
Yet I have sent the brothers, lest our boast concerning you in this respect be emptied, and so that you may be prepared, just as I have been saying.
Lest, should any Macedonians accompany me and discover you unprepared, we—not to say you—should be put to shame in this confidence.

Therefore I deemed it necessary to urge the brothers to go ahead to you and to prepare in advance the blessing you had promised, so that it might be ready as a genuine blessing and not as an exaction.
Now this I say: he who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and he who sows bountifully will also reap bountifully.
Each one must give as he has resolved in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.
And God is able to make all grace abound toward you, so that, having all sufficiency in all things at all times, you may abound in every good work.
As it is written, “He has scattered abroad; He has given to the poor; His righteousness endures forever.”
Now He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your seed for sowing and increase the harvest of your righteousness.
Being enriched in every way for all generosity, which through us produces thanksgiving to God.
For the ministry of this service is not only supplying the needs of the saints, but is also overflowing through many thanksgivings to God.
By the evidence of this ministry, they glorify God for your obedience to your confession of the gospel of Christ and for the generosity of your fellowship with them and with all.
And in their prayers for you, they long for you because of the surpassing grace of God resting upon you.
Thanks be to God for His indescribable gift!
Now I, Paul, entreat you by the meekness and gentleness of Christ—I who am lowly in your presence, yet bold toward you when absent.
I beseech you that, when I am present, I may not be compelled to exercise the boldness with which I intend to confront those who suppose that we walk according to the flesh.
For although we live in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh.
The weapons of our warfare are not carnal; rather, they are divinely powerful for the demolition of strongholds.
We cast down arguments and every lofty pretension raised against the knowledge of God, and we take every thought captive to the obedience of Christ.
We stand ready to punish every disobedience once your obedience is complete.
Consider what lies plainly before your eyes. If anyone is confident that he belongs to Christ, let him reconsider in himself that, just as he is Christ’s, so are we.
For even if I boast somewhat more abundantly concerning the authority that the Lord gave us for your edification and not for your destruction, I shall not be put to shame.
I do not wish to seem as though I were terrifying you by my letters.
For they say, “His letters are weighty and forceful, but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech is contemptible.”
Let such a person reckon that what we are in word by letters when absent, we shall be in deed when present.

For we do not dare to number ourselves or compare ourselves with some of those who commend themselves; but they, measuring themselves by themselves and comparing themselves with themselves, are without understanding.
We, however, will not boast beyond measure, but according to the measure of the rule that God apportioned to us—a measure that reaches even to you.
For we are not overextending ourselves, as though we had not reached you; indeed, we were the first to come even to you with the gospel of Christ.
We do not boast beyond measure in the labors of others; rather, we have hope that, as your faith increases, our sphere among you may be greatly enlarged,
so that we may proclaim the gospel in the regions beyond you, and not boast in work already prepared in another’s sphere.
But let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.
For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends.
I would that you might indulge me in a modicum of folly; indeed, do bear with me.
For I am jealous over you with the jealousy of God, since I espoused you to one husband, that I might present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.
But I fear lest, even as the serpent beguiled Eve through his craftiness, your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity and purity that are toward Christ.

For if one who comes proclaims another Jesus whom we did not proclaim, or you receive a different spirit which you did not receive, or a different gospel which you did not accept, you bear with him admirably.
For I reckon that I am in no wise inferior to these preeminent apostles.
Even if I am unpolished in speech, I am not so in knowledge; nay, in every respect we have been made manifest among you in all things.
Or did I commit a sin in abasing myself that you might be exalted, in that I preached the gospel of God to you free of charge?
I despoiled other churches, receiving support for my ministry to you.

And when I was present with you and in want, I was not burdensome to anyone; for the brethren who came from Macedonia replenished my deficiency; and in all things I kept myself from being burdensome to you, and so I shall keep.
As the truth of Christ is in me, this boasting of mine shall not be stopped in the regions of Achaia.
And why? Because I do not love you? God knows that I do.
But what I do I will also continue to do, in order to cut off occasion from those who desire occasion, that in the very matter in which they boast they may be found on equal footing with us.
For such are false apostles, deceitful workers, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ.
And no marvel, for Satan himself disguises himself as an angel of light.
It is no great thing, therefore, if his ministers also disguise themselves as ministers of righteousness, whose end shall be according to their works.
I say again, let no one think me foolish; but if otherwise, receive me even as a fool, that I too may boast a little.
What I speak, I speak not according to the Lord, but as in folly, in this confidence of boasting.
Since many boast according to the flesh, I will boast also.
For you gladly bear with the foolish, being wise yourselves.
For you bear with it if anyone enslaves you, if anyone devours, if anyone exploits you, if anyone exalts himself, if anyone strikes you on the face.
I speak in terms of dishonor, as though we had been weak; but in whatsoever any other dares—I speak as a fool—I dare also.
Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they the seed of Abraham? So am I.
Are they ministers of Christ? I speak as one beside himself—I am more so: in labors more abundant, in stripes beyond measure, in imprisonments more frequent, in deaths oft.
Five times I received from the Jews forty stripes save one.
Thrice was I beaten with rods, once was I stoned, thrice I suffered shipwreck, a night and a day have I been in the deep.

In journeyings often, in perils of rivers, in perils of robbers, in perils from my own countrymen, in perils from the Gentiles, in perils in the city, in perils in the wilderness, in perils in the sea, in perils among false brethren;
in toil and travail, in watchings often, in hunger and thirst, in fastings often, in cold and nakedness.
Apart from the things that are without, there is that which presseth upon me daily, the care of all the churches.
Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn with indignation?
If I must needs boast, I will boast of the things that concern my weakness.
The God and Father of the Lord Jesus, He who is blessed forever, knows that I do not lie.
In Damascus the governor under Aretas the king guarded the city of the Damascenes, desiring to apprehend me;
and through a window in a basket was I let down by the wall, and escaped his hands.
It is incumbent upon me to boast, though such boasting is unprofitable; nevertheless, I will proceed to visions and revelations of the Lord.
I know a man in Christ who, fourteen years ago—whether in the body I do not know, or whether out of the body I do not know; God knows—was caught up to the third heaven.
And I know such a man—whether in the body or apart from the body I do not know; God knows—
that he was caught up into Paradise and heard inexpressible words, which it is not lawful for a man to utter.
On behalf of such a one I will boast, but on my own behalf I will not boast, except in my weaknesses.
For if I should wish to boast, I would not be foolish, for I would be speaking the truth; yet I refrain, lest anyone credit me with more than he sees in me or hears from me.

And lest I should be exalted beyond measure by the surpassing greatness of the revelations, a thorn in the flesh was given to me—a messenger of Satan to buffet me—lest I should be exalted beyond measure.
Three times I pleaded with the Lord concerning this, that it might depart from me.
And He said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness.” Therefore I will boast all the more gladly in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest upon me.
Therefore I am well content, for Christ’s sake, with weaknesses, with insults, with necessities, with persecutions, and with distresses; for when I am weak, then I am strong.
I have become a fool; you compelled me. For I ought to have been commended by you, for I was in no way inferior to the super-apostles, even though I am nothing.
The signs of a true apostle were performed among you with all perseverance, by signs and wonders and mighty works.
For in what respect were you treated as inferior to the other churches, except that I myself did not burden you? Forgive me this wrong.

Behold, I am ready to come to you a third time, and I will not be burdensome to you; for I do not seek what is yours but you yourselves. For children ought not to treasure up for their parents, but parents for their children.
And I will most gladly spend and be spent for your souls; if I love you more abundantly, am I loved the less?
But be it so, I did not burden you; nevertheless, being crafty, I took you by guile.
Did I take advantage of you by any of those whom I sent to you?
I urged Titus to go, and sent the brother with him. Did Titus take advantage of you? Did we not walk in the same Spirit and in the same footsteps?
Do you suppose that all this time we have been defending ourselves to you? We speak before God in Christ; and all things, beloved, are for your edification.

For I fear that, when I come, I may not find you such as I wish, and that I may be found by you such as you do not wish—lest there be strife, jealousy, outbursts of anger, rivalries, slanders, whisperings, conceits, and disorders.

Lest, when I come again, my God should humble me before you, and I should mourn over many who sinned previously and have not repented of the impurity, fornication, and licentiousness which they practiced.
This marks the third occasion on which I am coming to you: every matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses.
I forewarned you before, and I do so a second time, as though present though now absent, that if I return, I shall show no leniency to those who sinned previously, nor to any of the rest.
Since you seek proof that Christ is speaking through me—He who is not weak toward you, but powerful among you—
for He was indeed crucified in weakness, yet He lives by the power of God. For we too are weak in Him, yet we shall live with Him by the power of God for your benefit.
Examine yourselves, to determine whether you are in the faith; test yourselves. Or do you not recognize that Jesus Christ is in you?—unless, of course, you are disqualified.
Yet I trust that you will come to recognize that we are not disqualified.
Now we pray to God that you may do no evil—not so that we may appear approved, but so that you may do what is good, even if we should seem disqualified.
For we can do nothing against the truth, but only for the truth.
For we rejoice whenever we are weak while you are strong; indeed, this is what we pray for—your complete restoration.
This is why I write these things while absent, so that when I am present I need not act with severity in accordance with the authority the Lord has given me for edification, and not for destruction.
Finally, brothers, rejoice; be restored; be encouraged; be of one mind; live in peace—and the God of love and peace will be with you.
Greet one another with a holy kiss.
All the saints send you their greetings.
The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with all of you.
Paul, an apostle—not derived from human beings, nor mediated through any mortal intermediary, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised Him from the dead—
together with all the brothers who accompany me, to the churches of Galatia:
Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ,
who surrendered Himself on behalf of our transgressions, so that He might rescue us from this present malign epoch, in accordance with the volition of our God and Father,
to whom be glory unto the ages of ages. Amen.
I marvel that you are transferring yourselves so precipitously from Him who summoned you in the grace of Christ unto a different gospel—
which is not, in truth, another, except that certain individuals are agitating you and desiring to pervert the gospel of Christ.
Yet even if we, or an angel descending from heaven, should proclaim to you a gospel divergent from that which we proclaimed to you, let him be anathema.
As we have previously declared, so I now reiterate: if anyone proclaims to you a gospel divergent from that which you received, let him be anathema.

For am I now seeking the approbation of human beings, or of God? Or am I striving to ingratiate myself with mortals? If I were still endeavoring to please human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ.
For I would have you know, brothers, that the gospel proclaimed by me is not of human derivation;
for neither did I receive it from a human being, nor was I instructed in it, but through an apocalypse of Jesus Christ.
For you have heard of my former manner of life in Judaism: that beyond measure I persecuted the church of God and ravaged it.
And I was advancing in Judaism beyond many contemporaries of my own generation, being exceedingly zealous for the patrimonial traditions.
But when God—who had segregated me from my mother’s womb and called me through His grace—was pleased
to reveal His Son in me, so that I might proclaim Him among the Gentiles, I did not immediately confer with human counsel,
nor did I ascend to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me; rather, I departed into Arabia, and then returned again to Damascus.
Then, after three years, I ascended to Jerusalem to become acquainted with Cephas, and I remained with him fifteen days.
But I saw none of the other apostles, except James, the brother of the Lord.
Now in what I write to you, before God, I do not fabricate falsehoods.
Thereafter I came into the regions of Syria and Cilicia.
Yet I remained personally unknown to the churches of Judea that are in Christ;
they had only been hearing, “The one who formerly persecuted us is now proclaiming the faith he once sought to demolish,”
and they glorified God on account of me.
After fourteen years had elapsed, I went up again to Jerusalem, accompanied by Barnabas and taking Titus with me.

I ascended in accordance with a revelation and laid before them the gospel that I proclaim among the Gentiles; yet I did so privately to those who seemed to be of consequence, lest somehow I should be running, or have run, in vain.
But not even Titus, who was with me and is a Greek, was compelled to be circumcised.
This was owing to certain false brothers who had insinuated themselves, slipping in by stealth to spy upon the liberty we possess in Christ Jesus, with the intent of reducing us to bondage.
